Three Days on a Desert Island Without Snuff

A friend and colleague of my father’s, a legendary Dnevnik photojournalist, when asked in the 1970s what it had been like in the Partisans, replied that it had been very hard. For wine there was only refosco, and for salami only Hungarian. It was gallows humor, at once a defense mechanism against painful memories of a traumatic war experience and a sotto voce criticism of the ideological instrumentalization of that experience under the previous system. Because war is always shit. And it is nothing unusual for people to respond to their experience of it in different ways—sometimes in ways that are hard for us to understand. That is why, when I watched the footage of a young evacuee who, on his return to Brnik airport, complained that he hadn’t been given a hot meal on the flight from the war zone, my first thought was that he was joking. Gallows humor. Because war is shit. Even if you experience it only briefly, as a tourist who happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time. It is easy to comment from armchairs and make fun of people who found themselves in this situation. In which, overnight, rockets and drones started exploding around their hotels. And who suddenly didn’t know how to get themselves out of this mess and back home to safety. It is true that it was mainly military targets in the Gulf states that were attacked, and the number of civilian casualties—with the exception of Iran, Lebanon and Israel—has been, at least so far, relatively limited. But when you are crouching in a hotel room with bombs falling around you, such rationalizing is harder than from a safe distance. So it is entirely understandable that people in such a situation react emotionally and fearfully. That they are not in a state to recite, in answer to a journalist’s question, a PR-perfect statement that would please us all. But with the young man who made the unfortunate statement at Brnik, it was not gallows humor. Nor did I detect in his statement any response to the danger of the situation he had managed to escape thanks to transport that the Slovenian government had organized very quickly. He did not seem traumatized by the war that is still raging where he came back from. He was traumatized by sandwiches. For wine only refosco, for salami only Hungarian. In essence, he came across like someone who had been stranded at an airport by force majeure, missed his plane, and then cursed the agency or airline that took his money for the trip and then left him in the lurch. A typical situation that regularly happens to anyone who travels often. Sometimes because of a volcano in Iceland or an unannounced strike, sometimes because they sell too many tickets and the cabin door is shut in your face. People are angry in these situations and say all sorts of things. But this young man was not overbooked; he was evacuated. From a war zone. Relatively quickly and, unlike many tourists from other parts of the world, at the state’s expense. OK, he was tired and sleep-deprived. Probably frightened too, although he didn’t talk about it. Still, one might have expected from him more contextual intelligence, which would have prevented him from coming across to the entire Slovenian public as an arrogant, spoiled brat. Me, me, me. Most people who went through a similar experience had no problem with it. After his statement provoked a storm of reactions and no small amount of mockery, voices have also been heard defending him. I too think he could slowly be left in peace. He has probably realized himself that he blew it. His statement was certainly inappropriate and probably thoughtless, but on the other hand it is not only about him. Arrogance, selfishness and problems with empathy are characteristics of the state of mind in today’s society. Moreover, the statement, through no fault of his own, resonated even more than it otherwise would have. On the one hand, it came at a moment of pre-election fever, and the story of the evacuation of Slovenian citizens from a war zone was immediately recognized as gratifying material for pre-election squabbling between political parties. For all their fervent invocations of overcoming differences and national unity, our political leaders, at moments when they really could and should stand together, always and every time fail the test. The media bear their share of responsibility too. The clickbait struggle for survival forces them into “reporting” that is more or less limited to chasing one statement or another. First from the people who found themselves in this predicament and who naturally react emotionally and subjectively. “It seemed to me they were rescuing everyone else before us,” went one typical headline. Then politicians are asked for their opinions, and they react less emotionally, but no more objectively. Publishing opinions is of course perfectly OK, but quality and credible journalism also needs facts. If one person says it is raining and another says it isn’t, the journalist’s job is to look out of the window, as Hubert Mewhinney of the Texas Spectator said back in the 1940s. But evidently there is little interest in facts; anger sells much better. Amid all the media attention on the Slovenian evacuation, I came across few pieces that clearly and comprehensively presented the circumstances and difficulty of rescuing people from a war zone and compared the speed and efficiency of the Slovenian rescue with the experiences of other countries. If it turns out that the government did a bad job, it deserves criticism. If it turns out that, given the difficulty of the situation and the experience of others, it was successful, then it would be decent and fair to acknowledge this, regardless of the feelings anyone otherwise harbors toward it. This does not mean that those in power should not be criticized, disagreed with or asked for more. But it would be nice if, in doing so, we thought critically and relied on facts. Looked out of the window now and then. Then we can quarrel to our hearts’ content. About hot meals and other important things too. We do live in a democracy, after all.
The French Presidential Race After the Local Elections

Arcis-sur-Aube, a small rural town of fewer than three thousand inhabitants, a good two hours’ drive east of Paris, was until recently known mainly as the site of the battle in which, in March 1814, Austrian, Russian and Prussian forces under Karl Philipp Schwarzenberg soundly thrashed Napoleon Bonaparte’s army and paved his way to exile on the island of Elba. Exactly 212 years later, on March 22 this year, a new clash took place in Arcis, this time an electoral one, in which, according to the Serbian media, Hitler defeated Zelensky and became mayor. That reporting on the local elections in France was even spicier in the Cyrillic part of our former country than elsewhere in the world is, of course, thanks to Vuk Karadžić and his phonetic spelling. The election was won by Charles Hittler, while Antoine Renault-Zielinski came third. Unfortunately, facts are not always kind to columnists in search of symbolism: although both ran “without a label,” as independent candidates are called in France, the winner Hittler is close to the center-right Horizons party of former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, while Zielinski had the support of the sovereigntist party Les Patriotes. Opinions always differ on whether the results of local elections affect the national balance of power. Still, this was the last significant electoral contest before the presidential election in April next year. The incumbent, Macron, cannot run. Most opinion polls give the best chances to Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN), who stepped into Marine Le Pen’s shoes after she was excluded from the presidential race by a court ruling for corruption—at least for now, since she has appealed. The rest of the political spectrum is shattered into a mosaic that more closely resembles a stained tablecloth in a Paris bistro than any traditional distribution of political forces. In the center is an increasingly isolated Macron, who since his surprise dissolution of the National Assembly after the European elections in June 2024 has been kept upright more by the pomp and glitter of the presidential office than by any real influence over the mess he largely cooked up himself. Since those elections four prime ministers have come and gone, among them the current one, Sébastien Lecornu, who resigned after only 26 days, then let himself be persuaded to return, and will soon, at six months in office, set the best interim time. His “longevity” is probably more a consequence of the fatigue of politicians and the public and of waiting for the denouement the presidential election will bring. While Macron’s months are numbered, centrist candidates are positioning themselves around him: former Prime Minister Attal, the center-right former Interior Minister Darmanin and, above all, another former Prime Minister, the re-elected mayor of Le Havre, Édouard Philippe. With his victory in the local elections he strengthened his position, unlike yet another former Prime Minister, François Bayrou, whom voters, after two terms, swept from the mayor’s office in Pau in the Pyrenees, probably sealing his otherwise chronic presidential ambitions. On the traditional right, the Republicans are somehow staying alive, although the prognosis remains uncertain despite victories in some larger cities. We have already talked about the far right. While Marine Le Pen is out for now, Jordan Bardella is successfully replacing her and still leads in the race for the Élysée Palace. There are two more influential players on this side of the spectrum. Éric Ciotti, former president of the Republicans, who after being ousted in June 2024, in a typically French coup de théâtre, first barricaded himself in the former party’s Paris headquarters, then founded his own, backed the far right, and last Sunday won in Nice—which is no small thing. Zemmour’s Reconquête is chasing the far right from its right. The greatest confusion reigns, where else, on the left—from the center to its extreme edge, where the capo di banda is the longtime leader of La France Insoumise, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Before the elections he found himself in trouble not only because of statements that many describe as borderline antisemitic, but also because of the killing of a young far-right activist on the sidelines of a campaign rally in Lyon. Members of Mélenchon’s previously dissolved Jeune Garde have been charged in the death of 23-year-old Quentin Deranque. On the margins, the Greens are fighting for survival; six years ago they achieved incredible success in the local elections, but after one term they were shown the door in most cities. France wouldn’t be France without the communists—who, incidentally, are counted among the more moderate leftists—and the socialists, once the dominant force on the left, today far from the positions and influence they had in the Mitterrand era. Weakened and divided, they are arguing about cooperation with the far-left Mélenchon—a mirror image of the dilemmas on the right regarding the far right. And then came the local elections and the hope that afterward it would be clearer who has the wind in their sails and who is running out of breath. But no. At first glance, the balance does not seem to have changed much. Among the larger cities, the right has remained at twelve, the center has one more with six, the whole left together has twenty-two—two fewer than before—and the far right has doubled its previous result with two. Everyone claims to have done well. The devil, as usual, is in the details. La France Insoumise won in Roubaix in the north—a big surprise. But that was more or less it. Where it supported the traditional left in the second round, it did it more harm than good. The Greens lost almost everything. They held on in Lyon, where mayor Grégory Doucet beat former Olympique Lyonnais president Jean-Michel Aulas by fewer than three thousand votes, but all the other big cities slipped away. The Socialists kept power in Paris and Marseille. This gives them hope that the curve is turning upward—it also matters that the winners were candidates who renounced the support of the far left. In the center, so-so. Macron’s Renaissance won in Bordeaux and lost in Paris and in many other places. The big winner of the center-right is Édouard Philippe—the only one of the likely presidential candidates who ran in the local elections, and whose victory strengthened his starting position. The classic right is numerically where it was, but it ceded Nice to the far right, which surely hurts. And finally the far right, which, on the wings of favorable forecasts, certainly expected much more: the hoped-for breakthrough did not come. They increased the number of their representatives on municipal councils, but mostly in their traditional region in the south; there was no visible expansion elsewhere. Moreover, at least in the larger cities it became clear that the cordon sanitaire of the traditional parties, though weakened, is still alive. They failed both in Marseille and in Toulon, where they had led comfortably after the first round. When it comes to the far right, we must not forget Reconquête and Éric Zemmour. His private partner Sarah Knafo, born in 1994, achieved an incredible 10.4 percent in the first round in traditionally left-leaning Paris, exceeding all predictions. In the second round she withdrew in favor of Macron’s culture minister Rachida Dati—who nevertheless did not succeed. But it is a sign that the extreme far right will be able to stir the pot in future. Besides Arcis-sur-Aube, there was another incredible story this time. In Strasbourg the socialist Catherine Trautmann won—a former mayor who first won in 1989, the year the Berlin Wall fell. Eight years later she became culture minister in Lionel Jospin’s government, and in 2000 she was briefly mayor of Strasbourg once again. A quarter of a century later she has returned. And won. To win, she allied with the center-right, angering the Socialists. The day after the election her political godfather, one of the last of the great Mitterrandist socialists, Lionel Jospin, died. There is certainly a lot of symbolism in that too, which everyone interprets in their own way. After the battle of Arcis-sur-Aube, Napoleon Bonaparte stayed on Elba for less than a year; Catherine Trautmann was in political exile considerably longer. Napoleon, like her, returned victorious. But then came Waterloo. Whether cooperation with the center-right will pay off better for the new-old mayor, and perhaps find imitators at the national level, time will tell. Even after the local elections, everything is still open regarding France’s future path. We don’t know who the new president will be—the only thing that is clear is that it won’t be Emmanuel Macron.
The World Rests on the Young

In Spain’s Asturias, time runs more slowly. Even if you want to have a glass or two in company, you will need a few hours if you stick to local customs. In Asturias they drink cider. But not just any old way, from big bottles and glasses, to quench your thirst. It is a real ritual. A specially trained master pours the cider from the bottle or cask in a stream as long as his arm can stretch, filling a glass held at an angle up to a third, just enough to cover the bottom. Supposedly so that it has fewer bubbles, which cause digestive problems. That circular evidently never reached the Styrians, or they wouldn’t so enthusiastically add bubbles to every spritzer they pour down their throats. But be that as it may, the art of pouring is not the only reason for the time-consuming nature of drinking in Asturias. Everyone in the group drinks from one glass. If a lot of people gather, as they did a month ago after a conference organized by Rural Youth Europe in the small town of Piloña, you drink very little cider. But you have more time for conversation. With very interesting young people. I was reminded of the group that gathered in Piloña by the comments after the latest parliamentary elections in Slovenia and the dismay of some that young people are turning to the right. That is true, not only in Slovenia but elsewhere too. We are far from the times when young people voted almost unanimously for left-wing political options. But that in itself is not a problem. Democracy is a system that allows everyone to freely give their vote to the political option that convinces them most. And trends, including across different demographic groups, change over time and in different circumstances. Democracy is not only when “our side” wins. For me personally, meeting representatives of rural youth from all corners of Europe who had gathered in Asturias was very interesting, and also encouraging. Most of them could hardly be counted among supporters of the left. That is not surprising, since the countryside in most countries is more conservative and traditionally minded. Some of them had taken part in the protests against the Mercosur trade agreement held weeks earlier in Brussels and beneath my office window in Strasbourg. But they were united by something else, something very important. Despite their political convictions and their dissatisfaction with how politics, European and national, treats the countryside, they are all committed defenders of democratic principles. And that is it. The most important thing. Democracy is strong when both “theirs” and “ours” agree on its fundamental values. But despite the ray of hope from Piloña, this is of course not the whole picture, nor the prevailing one, of how ideological preferences are moving among young people in Europe, including in Slovenia. At a time when political battles no longer take place between different ideological programs within a framework of shared democratic values—within which it is of course perfectly legitimate to lean left, right or center—but are a bitter polarization for or against those values, this naturally has consequences for young people too. And that really should worry us. Recently we have had a whole slew of opinion surveys showing that young people are increasingly losing trust in the democratic social system and are increasingly susceptible to “alternative” discourses that pave their way to power with division, the stigmatization of certain social groups, nationalism and authoritarianism. What can be done to restore trust in democracy, since without it democracy is doomed? Let us start with what we must not do. Condemnation of and dismay at political choices are the fastest way to make the situation even worse. To a large extent, young people’s choices are a revolt stemming from their personal experience of democracy, and above all from uncertainty about the future. Let us not forget that the young people voting today were born during the financial crisis and have lived through the migration crisis, a pandemic and wars that follow one another and are becoming ever more senseless and destructive. This is the first postwar generation that will almost certainly not have a better life than their parents. Young people in Europe are dissatisfied, frightened and angry. If all we can do in this situation is call them ungrateful fools, then we had better keep quiet. Trying to persuade them that democracy is the best system, and that in their ideological turn young people don’t know the real facts, are media-illiterate, uninformed and misled by disinformation spreading on social media, also has a limited effect. All this is at least partly true and requires action, especially regarding the regulation of social media and the (ab)use of artificial intelligence, but that alone will not be enough either. Because it offers a rational answer to convictions largely driven by emotion, dissatisfaction, anger and fear. An effective answer will require serious investment in the competences young people need to understand democracy, take part in it and defend it—above all through the education system and the democratic participation of young people in society. There is no way around this. But literacy alone is not enough. The foundation of a democratic society is critical thinking and empathy—not as a school subject, but as a practice young people experience in their everyday lives, in the classroom, in the local community, in a society where their voice is actually heard and taken into account. Where this is absent, sooner or later their opposites will prevail. But all this will remain without effect if we don’t address the real causes of the hardship from which distrust springs. Democracy cannot survive as a rhetorical slogan. It can survive only if it proves that it can respond to the legitimate expectations of young people—regarding housing, employment, health care, security, the future. And if it is represented by politicians of integrity who don’t just talk about democratic values but put them into practice. Especially when that is uncomfortable or hard for them. All this takes time and a great deal of effort. But there is also an important first step that is relatively simple. While we waited our turn for cider, I talked with Mattias, one of the leaders of Rural Youth Europe, who confided that his peers in the village in Spain where he comes from are often very critical and mocking about his work and networking in Europe. “This stuff means nothing to us and brings us nothing,” they say. “What should I tell them, how can I convince them about democracy?” “Before you start trying to convince them,” I replied, “ask them why they feel the way they do.” When we start not only listening to young people but also hearing them, that will be an important first step toward restoring their trust in democracy.

If you have been wandering around our corners of the world’s social media lately, you have probably come across artificially intelligent graphic depictions of love for traditional values. At the top, a robed gentleman with a thick beard through which rays of heavenly light shine. Below him, a father, a mother and a whole bunch of fair-skinned, blue-eyed children. Beside them, three soldiers with the tricolor. And of course the caption: God, Family, Homeland. These pastel outpourings of patriotism triggered a few reactions in me. First, the realization that artificial intelligence has a sense of humor. It dressed the three soldiers with the flag, who symbolize love of the homeland, in Soviet uniforms. The second realization was that we Slovenians are capable of quarreling about anything. The posts of artificially intelligent patriotism provoked very heated reactions. “Extremists, fascists!” came the cry from one side. “What’s wrong with God, family and homeland, you communist gang?!” came the indignant reply from the other. The digital infantry and the generals, anonymous accounts and well-known political and public figures squabbled—basically a total mess. Before I add a thought or two on this burning topic myself, I would like to stress that when it comes to love of God, I don’t feel particularly competent. Unlike many who claim, and behave as though, they have God on speed dial, I keep a respectful distance from him. In our family we are at best agnostics—ever since my great-grandfather returned from the First World War to Styria with his intestines shot through. Then he slowly died before the eyes of my ten-year-old grandfather Franček, who could never accept the explanation that this was God’s will and that God knows what he is doing. But agnostic or not, I absolutely respect other people’s beliefs. And I take particular pleasure in respecting the beliefs of those who show similar respect for mine. Even though I am not a believer, I am aware of how strongly Christianity has influenced our cultural heritage and identity. Whether we go to Mass or not, we have to admit that Christianity and its earthly bureaucracy have left behind all sorts of very cool things—from architecture to books and so on. Some less cool things too, but OK—who hasn’t? It is also true, however, that over the course of history we Europeans have bequeathed ourselves many other things as well. The Enlightenment, for example. Or the principle of the separation of church and state. And human rights, which protect the dignity of all people—not only those of the right faith or skin color. And democracy, in which the legitimacy of power rests on the results of fair and free elections, not merely on old books and politically motivated interpretations of their contents. I have also noticed that many interpreters of our Christian and predominantly Catholic heritage are very irritated by what its highest earthly agent says about all this. Not only the previous pope, but the current one too seems to many far too “woke,” since he keeps going on about things they don’t see, seek or recognize in God. What’s all this about compassion, solidarity and dignity for all? What good is faith to an honest man if he can’t use it as a sledgehammer to bash the heads of those he doesn’t like? There are, of course, also believers who understand Jesus’s teachings somewhat differently. “Don’t tell me what you believe; show me how you treat your fellow human being, and I’ll tell you what you believe,” the Texas Democrat and Presbyterian pastor James Talarico said recently. But, as I said, what do I know about it. And then we come to family. Unlike faith and God, here I would play my joker. I think family is great. I have so many children that I could run on the NSi list. And because I think family is a very good thing, I would like everyone who wants one to have it. All children who are without one because of life circumstances—or social prejudice. And all those who want to climb into the yoke of marriage with partners they love. Regardless of religion, skin color or sexual orientation. Because it takes nothing from me and my family, and gives a great deal to many. I know many see red at the thought of granting same-sex couples the right to marry or adopt children. Because it is supposedly unnatural. Because it threatens our existence. My dears, I too worry about the fate of human civilization, but I can promise you one thing: if our world goes to the dogs—and for now it seems to be very well on its way—it will most certainly not be because people love each other and want to have a family. And then we come to homeland. It is lovely and important to love one’s homeland. Some love it by being critical of it, because they want it to be even better. Some are convinced that you can love your homeland only by hating people who come from elsewhere. Because they threaten the homeland, and a homeland that is not threatened is, for a true patriot, like soup without salt. That is why after the elections we are promised special forces who will hunt people in the streets for deportation. Like in the US. Because it’s so great there. And if, by chance, there aren’t enough illegal crossings, since their number has fallen considerably in recent years, then in their home-defense zeal they can rotate their border vigilance by 180 degrees. When patriotism turns into hatred, people no longer flee in, but out. Like in Russia and North Korea. Because it’s so great there. Be that as it may, I hope we can all agree that faith, family and homeland are important values, even though we evidently don’t all understand them the same way. But that in itself should not be a problem. After all, we fought precisely so that we could have different opinions. So why such an uproar when people say this out loud? Or post it on their profile? Or include it in their election program? Here, my dears, we come to context and motive. Work and freedom are important values too, yet I would still advise caution about claiming that “work sets you free.” As with Hindu folklore motifs, the meaning of certain phrases is determined not only by form and semantics without context, but also by history. So what is wrong with the slogan “God, Family, Homeland”? Ask Grok or ChatGPT, if you really have no idea and are merely innocent victims of your own ignorance. As I said at the beginning, I really wouldn’t lecture you about your relationship with God. If you sincerely believe in him, you can expect that sooner or later he will explain to you himself what he thinks of your doings. As for family and homeland, friends, you will have to accept the fact that you have no monopoly on interpreting their meaning—and still less on deciding arbitrarily who has a right to them and who does not. Instead, I suggest you try to love yourselves a little more. Perhaps then you will find it easier to love other people too. If you don’t know where to start, ask ChatGPT.
The Persecution of the Differently Differently Differently Minded

“The differently minded” was the label adopted years ago by the pioneers of the Slovenian fight against wokeness. The nom de guerre of brave souls who began to raise their voices against the tyranny and single-mindedness of the civilizational values on which the Western world, and above all Europe, built after the Second World War its system of defense against a repetition of one of the darkest episodes in world history. Respect for human dignity, solidarity and empathy with people in distress, equality, human rights and political freedoms. Leaving aside the fact that the Western world has not always been the most consistent in respecting these values, that was not what bothered the differently minded most. The problem was these values in themselves, not the way they were, or were not, applied. It was, of course, a very transparent alibi for legitimizing hate speech against particular social groups. Homophobia, misogyny, hatred of refugees. Every time such speech met with a response, a counterattack followed, labeling the criticism a violation of freedom of expression, a liberticide, so to speak. From today’s perspective it is clear that these were not spontaneous outbursts of intolerance, but a strategy that sought, by stigmatizing certain social groups, to weaken the social, and also the constitutional and legal, safeguards of their human rights and freedoms. Once this protection stops applying to some, sooner or later it stops applying to everyone. All this unfolded, and is still unfolding, alongside simultaneous attacks on the judiciary, the media and civil society, as the most important democratic safeguards protecting society against authoritarianism and the dictatorship of the executive. The response to the offensive of the differently minded was confused. On the one hand, many demanded at all costs the intervention of prosecutors and the criminal prosecution of hateful discourse, even in cases where it did not—and most often it did not—reach the high threshold that Slovenian and European legal standards set for banning and prosecuting speech. All this was only grist to the mill of the differently minded, who gladly seized the opportunity to present themselves as victims of the undemocratic persecution of people with different positions and views on social questions. Politics responded in different ways, but what stood out was the doctrine of the former President, who, in the name of overcoming differences and respecting different opinions, sought a compromise at the arithmetic midpoint between defending fundamental civilizational values and spreading intolerance, thereby of course doing a great service to those who were paving their way to power with hatred. Melania Trump reminds me of the Bosnian joke about Mujo sitting on a rock. “What’s up, Mujo, sitting and thinking?” “Nah, Haso, just sitting.” Throngs of amateur and professional Melaniologists have for years, ever since she first moved into the White House, been feverishly following and analyzing her every public appearance, every look, gesture, shoe, outfit and hat. With the recent premiere of the documentary about our American First Lady, we may at last have an answer to the question of what lies behind those chronically pouting lips and half-veiled eyes staring catatonically into the unknown. Nothing. Nada. Neč, as young Melania would have said in her local dialect before she set off from Sevnica into the wide world to seek happiness and love. That, at least, is what one might conclude from the opinion of most film critics, who were, to put it very, very, very mildly, not well disposed toward the documentary that earned Melania a fat 28 million dollars. I admit I can’t judge for myself, since I haven’t yet managed to see the documentary. It isn’t showing anywhere in Strasbourg yet. And so far no one in France seems to be complaining much about that. But, you’ll say, these are the elitist hacks in the mainstream media who don’t care about the little man anyway. And indeed the opening attendance exceeded the gloating predictions and comfortably outperformed any documentary in the history of cinema. Which is of course logical. Not only because so much money was spent on promotion that you could have reshot every documentary in the history of cinema with it, but because we are dealing with a cult. You go to the cinema to show your devotion to the great, wise husband. Ticket sales in local American cinemas match local political support for Trump. It is similar in Europe, at least where the film is already showing. Only far fewer tickets are sold. Because in Europe we not only don’t like Trump much, we like him less and less. Slovenia is a story of its own in this American–European contrast. Because Melania was once from Sevnica, and so many try hard to believe that Melania is still ours. Nah, Haso, just Melania. There is no evidence of her supposed and much-vaunted attachment to her home turf. She reportedly mentions Slovenia only once in the film. She paid us the most attention when, with the help of her then lawyer, she sued her former fellow townspeople from Sevnica because some had tried to earn a dollar or two from her fame and name. But OK. In our case, it isn’t so much the fact that we Slovenians have also squabbled over whether the film is worth seeing—after all, we are capable of quarreling about anything. What is unusual is that for some political parties Melania, and above all her husband, still represent a trump card in which they believe and on which they are building political support ahead of the upcoming elections. That they did so years ago one could still somehow understand. But today? After everything we know and are served daily? The vulgarity, the authoritarianism, the morbid narcissism, the clear signs of cognitive decline, the Epstein files, the dalliances with porn actresses while our Melania was giving birth to our Barron, the violence and shootings by his semi-private masked agents, the attacks and threats against other countries, the insults left and right, the pally relations with dictators, the plans for resorts in Gaza, the Mar-a-Lago alternative to the United Nations, the appeasement of Putin and his aggressive policies? Hello? In circumstances in which even Trump’s greatest admirers and imitators on the European far right feel compelled to distance themselves from their discredited hero, who has become repellent even to their own voters, many here still see Trump as a political trump card up their sleeve. Because Melania. The key to her husband’s favor and the highway to a future in which Slovenia, together with the US, will rampage across the world. Or something like that. But not everyone is like that, you’ll say; fortunately we still have politics here that stands firmly on fundamental civilizational principles and values. Eh. Just as the right in Slovenia has problems with Trump, on the other side many have problems with his ideological companion in the Kremlin. A whole string of politicians, public figures and intellectuals are selling us, in one form or another, talking points written for them by Russian bots and intelligence services. Whether they do so out of conviction or not isn’t even that important; the effect is ultimately the same. Far be it from me to lump everyone together. In the end everyone must take responsibility for their own positions and actions, and one set of misdeeds cannot be excused by another. In this story, the Slovenian fans of the American president even have one advantage. We cannot accuse them of hypocrisy. They are completely open in their admiration of Trump’s policies. What we see in the US today, they would like to bring here too. Masked regime militias hunting people in the streets. The collapse and subordination of all democratic institutions that protect society from abuse of power, hatred as state ideology, power as the right to plunder, a Christian nationalism that has as much to do with Christianity as the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea has to do with democracy. They think it’s cool. They don’t hide it. On the other side we have the attitude of part of the Slovenian public toward Russian imperialism and Putin’s rampage through Ukraine. Alternative facts and projections that adapt reality to ideological preferences. A quasi-pacifism that throws responsibility for the aggression onto the victim. That will not and cannot condemn the fascistoid regime Putin has built in a quarter of a century in power. Systemic racism, homophobia, sexual and verbal violence against women, murders of journalists and political opponents. Everything they (rightly) condemn with indignation everywhere else, except in the Kremlin. Nodding along to assorted Lipuščeks and populist Resnicas. Down with the rotten West. Down with NATO. You know who else doesn’t like NATO? Putin and Trump. The further apart the two sides are, the more alike they become. The most grotesque thing about this Slovenian polarization is that we quarrel and divide to the death over our attitude toward two authoritarian leaders who, in their ideological characteristics, imperialist worldviews and obsession with force and power, are so close that it will soon be impossible to tell them apart. In the end we may achieve our cherished national unity at the absolute moral bottom. Where the extremes go so far that the horseshoe becomes a circle. And perhaps that is precisely the important message of Melania’s documentary. We may not learn much about her, but it holds up a mirror to us. Through her moral emptiness and our attitude toward her, a picture emerges of a society that doesn’t think, but just sits—and follows.

The recent American intervention in Venezuela, in which the country’s president and his wife were captured, caught most of the world’s politicians on the wrong foot. Not that they hadn’t expected something to blow up sooner or later, but Trump’s move was so brazen that they simply didn’t know how to react without tripping over their own feet and biting their tongues. An honorable exception, in my opinion, is Karl Erjavec, the self-proclaimed, I-swear-on-my-mother’s-life Mick Jagger of Slovenian politics. I don’t know whether Karl has commented on the American attack on Venezuela yet, but some time ago he said that “throughout history the borders of states have never been drawn for all eternity,” and that talk of the inviolability of borders is an “EU illusion.” We can agree with Karl’s interpretation of history and today’s geostrategic challenges or not, but his doctrine manages to explain and cover most of the current crises we are witnessing in today’s world, including the excursion to Caracas, without his being open to accusations of double standards. Or any standards at all. You Can’t Always Get What You Want, silly EU. Borders are not inviolable. Tough luck, that’s just how it is. Another question is why Karl is so enthusiastic about this state of affairs. Perhaps he believes that in the brave new world milk and honey will flow for Slovenians. With the Russians, Americans and Chinese, there are 1,902 million of us. We’ve got this. The American president can of course be accused of double, triple or manifold standards, but I doubt it would bother him much, since he makes no secret that principle, logic, facts and reason are characteristics that mark weaklings. Every time he speaks, he offers a new explanation for the attack on Venezuela. Maduro was a dictator. Maduro was a drug trafficker. By nationalizing the assets of American oil companies, Venezuela stole American oil. Maduro imitated Trump’s dance moves. He wasn’t nice. Who knows what was really going through his head. An amateur linguist on X hinted at the etymological origin of the attacked country’s name. It is a compound of two words, venez and uela, which in the language of the local natives mean Epstein and distraction. Who knows. In short: a total mess. But that doesn’t bother Trump. He does things above all because he can. The mess is not a consequence but the purpose. To show who’s boss. Under My Thumb, my friends. For Europe’s moral tightrope walkers, at least those who still care about the remnants of their own credibility and principles, the matter is more complicated. How to stand up firmly to Trump without his noticing. Because he doesn’t like that. First they tried to wriggle out by saying that Maduro was a dictator who did not accept defeat at the elections. But tough luck, because Trump very quickly tired of the pro-democracy narrative, which is not surprising given his own attitude toward respecting election results and his fondness for most of the world’s other authoritarians. Not to mention that he cut a deal with Maduro’s vice president for a couple of million barrels of oil and brushed off the opposition leader because she had stolen his Nobel Peace Prize. Then there are the drug trafficking charges. Even though Trump recently pardoned a former president of Honduras who had been convicted of similar misdeeds by an American court and was already serving a prison sentence in the US. Finally, there is the oil story. This excuse is too much to swallow even for the most hardened Trumpversteher. Where will we end up if we accept that the big simply take what they believe belongs to them? Who will be next? Greenland? European politics has reached the point at which it should realize that there are no more options in which Trump is fed and our value and security goat stays whole. That this puts us all in a very tight spot is clear—especially since it seems that for now we cannot stop the war in Ukraine without the US. But that does not change the fact that European politics should have seen through this long ago, instead of constantly using kneeling as the only solution while hoping each time for a different result. The intervention in Venezuela has also deepened the crisis of credibility for a large part of Slovenian politics, although, judging by the fieriness of the reactions, they evidently aren’t aware of it. On the left they raised a ruckus; on the right they expressed understanding for the attack. Much as with the war in Ukraine, only mirrored. Far be it from me to lump the American intervention in Venezuela and the Russian “special military operation in Ukraine” simplistically together. Zelensky is not Maduro, the US is not (yet) Russia, and the Russian special forces got a bloody nose when they landed near Kyiv. But there are some basic parameters and facts that one would expect principled politics to respect regardless of ideological preferences and domestic political interests. Fat chance. On one side we heard that this is a gross violation of international law. Maduro is a head of state who can be replaced only by the citizens of Venezuela. Both are true—but the same applies to Ukraine, where instead of insisting on respect for international law and the right of Ukrainians to decide their own fate, we heard all sorts of things and accusations against everyone and anyone except those who actually violated that same national sovereignty and international law. What is more: relativizing Russian aggression (America’s proxy war, blah blah, Zelensky’s a Nazi, blah blah, NATO is to blame for everything, blah blah …) is certainly not a message that would lead anyone—least of all Trump—to conclude that the gross trampling of international law doesn’t pay. If you are prepared to grant Tom an exclusive sphere of interest over his neighbors, it is hard to deny it to Harry. Paradoxically, in Slovenia today many of the most fervent opponents of American imperialism, with their positions, are objectively holding the ladder for American policy, which, hand in hand with Putin, is reshaping and destabilizing the world in the crudest way. Things are no better on the other side. The Slovenian right firmly took the side of the suffering Venezuelan people and supported the American intervention which, in agreement with the Venezuelan dictatorial regime, decapitated the Venezuelan dictatorial regime and ensured the continuity of the Venezuelan dictatorial regime. On Ukraine, they are slowly wriggling out of the vise between their initial support for Kyiv and their ideological sympathy for Trump’s and Putin’s antiliberal reshaping of society and the world. We haven’t heard much about support for Ukraine from our railway pioneer in a long time. Sorry, Volodya, our train is now going in a different direction. It seems that each side, from its own end, is prepared to make a pact with the devil, or at least to indulge him, in order to satisfy its own ideological needs. And then each, from its own extreme edge, helps push the world in the same direction. Down with NATO. Down with the EU. Down with liberal democracy. Sympathy for the Devil, as Mick Jagger would say—the real one, not ours. But for what is happening to us, a more fitting soundtrack is a song he wrote a few years earlier: As Tears Go By. And we can only hope that tears are all we will shed.

Almost exactly ten years ago, on January 23, 2016, Donald Trump said at a campaign rally in Sioux Center, Iowa, that he could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue in New York and shoot somebody and he wouldn’t lose a single voter. Whether that is actually true we, thank God, do not yet know. Although, when it comes to criminal liability for acts committed literally in full view of everyone, he has several times come very close to a standard of automatic unpunishability. Incidentally, according to the Slovenian dictionary I have evidently invented this last word, but I am sticking with it. It is not only about impunity or immunity, but about a state in which you can do whatever comes into your head and not answer for it. And this does not apply only to Trump. What is permitted to Jupiter is evidently, in the brave new America, also permitted to his oxen. Jonathan Ross, the ICE immigration agent who weeks ago in Minneapolis shot Nicole Good, a mother of three, three times, swore at her body and calmly walked away as if nothing had happened, has so far had nothing happen to him. Nor is there an investigation—or rather there is, but it focuses only on the victim and those close to her. It is not impossible that Ross’s colleagues who went after 37-year-old Alex Pretti on Saturday were also counting on unpunishability. Because he was carrying a pistol for which he had a permit, they shot him ten times. So much for the Second Amendment to the US Constitution, by which American conservatives otherwise swear. Whether there will be a serious investigation this time is not yet clear, although the first reactions of the US administration, and of course Ross’s precedent, do not inspire much confidence. Both tragic events took place in Minneapolis, in the US state of Minnesota, where an intensive hunt for illegal immigrants has been under way for several weeks, with incidents occurring regularly. In recent days, two children aged five and two were arrested and sent to Texas. The astonishing brutality and violence in the operations of Trump’s immigration officers are no accident, nor is the fact that this is happening in a city with a Democratic mayor. Violence and intimidation are not a side effect of the policy but its purpose. Trump has never hidden that these are punitive expeditions against cities and states where the Democrats are in power. And here is the main message. Trump is completely open in his rampage and demolition of all norms, whether it is barging around America or around international relations. In his own words, he is limited only by his own mind and his own morality. God help us. And until now European politicians have responded mainly by sticking their heads in the sand and convincing themselves that everything is fine. The emperor isn’t naked, just extravagantly dressed. But even Andersen’s fairy tale about the emperor’s new clothes misses the essence of the grotesque we are witnessing. Andersen’s emperor believed he was dressed because the court flatterers convinced him he was. Trump, on the other hand, knows very well that he is naked—and he revels in it. Obscene as the Michelin mascot with an OnlyFans profile, he guffaws and humiliates the frightened flatterers who, out of fear and a sense of powerlessness, still convince themselves and behave as if he were wearing the presidential garb of his predecessors. Who, in the opinion of many, were not all that great either, but were far from deserving to be simplistically lumped in the same basket. As far as Trump’s rampaging around the world is concerned, it seems that among many European and Western leaders there has at last been a turnaround. After he attacked Venezuela and threatened Greenland because he didn’t get the Nobel Peace Prize, insulted the military dead among allies who fought alongside the US in Iraq and Afghanistan, founded a Mar-a-Lago alternative to the United Nations, gathered a colorful bunch of authoritarians in it and, on top of that, proclaimed himself its chief for life, it finally dawned on many that things cannot go on like this. We heard Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech in Davos and the statements of other politicians that followed. That’s enough now, they said. We’ll go our own way. Well, let’s see. Far be it from me to underestimate the importance of this break. But it is much too early to assess the sincerity, durability and determination of this newly emerged European and Western self-confidence. I hope our political leaders will keep the following facts in mind as things unfold. First: the emperor is still naked and still revels in it. He still believes he is limited only by his own mind and his own morality. Those who, after the Greenland shock, would seek a return to “the good old days” should remember this. Nostalgia is not a strategy, said Carney. Second: it is not enough to grumble and say “dammit, that’s enough now.” This must also be backed by investment in the material basis of this newly emerged self-confidence and determination: in economic, energy, technological and military emancipation from the rampaging big brother. Third: the strengthening of military self-sufficiency, which Europe urgently needs because of Ukraine and more broadly because of the danger from Russia, cannot and must not be achieved by diverting funds from a socially cohesive, economically successful and open society. A socially just democracy that gives citizens material proof that it is willing and able to recognize and take into account their legitimate expectations is a security imperative. Otherwise Russia will bring us down without drones, tanks and guns. Bots will be enough, and our own peddlers of Russian (and American) Truths. To preserve our ability to decide our own fate in Europe, beating our chests outwardly will not be enough; we will also—and above all—need the morality and the mind we are able to show inwardly. It will not be enough to stand up only to the Trump of Davos, but also to the Trump of Minneapolis. We must consistently reject the ideas and discourses of hatred and division that are the driving force of both Trump’s and Putin’s authoritarianism. Even when we itch to grab an extra scrap of attention with a populist tweet or statement before an election. We live in risky and unpredictable times. In the end, what may decide things is our determination and consistency in defending the paramount importance of our fundamental values.

I ask the copy editors and the editor-in-chief to make an exception for once and not translate the headline into Slovenian. It is a deliberate use of a foreign language, warning of the danger that in the near future we will all have to speak English. OK, that explanation didn’t come out very well, but still, leave the headline alone—at least the Styrians should understand what I’m talking about. The digital media conglomerate Politico recently named US President Donald Trump the most influential political figure in Europe. That is roughly as if Zlatko Zahovič were named the most influential football figure in Ljubljana. It may be true, but it hurts all the same. In any case, it is a choice that says more about Europe than about Donald Trump. If he really is the politician with the most influence on events in Europe, that is above all because European politics enables and allows him to be. The latest submissive act of self-harm that the European decision-making elite has allowed itself is its response, or rather non-response, to the recent publication of the new American national security strategy. In this astonishing official document of the US administration, Europe faces the danger of “civilizational erasure.” “The larger issues facing Europe include activities of the European Union and other transnational bodies that undermine political liberty and sovereignty, migration policies that are transforming the continent and creating strife, censorship of free speech and suppression of political opposition, cratering birthrates, and loss of national identities and self-confidence.” On the other hand, the document does find some reasons for optimism. It highlights “the growing influence of patriotic European parties,” and so the strategy calls for “cultivating resistance to Europe’s current trajectory within European nations.” “Europe is dying,” the American President summed up the document briefly and succinctly in an interview with Politico. When I read all this, despite my numbed expectations of a more spineful stance by European politics toward the US, I nevertheless expected a sharp response this time. Holy spinach, I said to myself, this time they’ve really gone too far. They surely can’t just watch calmly and swallow a traditional ally accusing the European Union of destroying Europe and openly announcing its support for those who want to smash from within the European peace and civilizational project, built as an answer to the Second World War. They surely can’t … But they did. With rare exceptions among the leading and most influential politicians—among them the President of the European Council, António Costa—the reactions were of the kind we more often hear in tragic cases of domestic violence: but when he’s sober, he still loves me very much. Paradoxically, one of the more principled statements came from the leader of the French Rassemblement National, Jordan Bardella, one of those patriotic leaders to whom the US is offering selfless help in tearing down liberal-democratic Europe. “I don’t need a big brother like that,” responded clearly a politician who evidently follows and understands more carefully what European voters think about all this. Soon after the strategy was published, the US authorities announced the possibility of screening travelers’ social media posts before arrival, in order to bar those who don’t like the US and speak badly of President Trump. Imagine what would happen if they found content on someone’s account describing the US the way the US talks about Europe. It is clear, of course, that we live in a complex and dangerous world in which political decision-makers must constantly weigh ethical principles against reality. Moral politics is cool, but it cannot and must not ignore vital security, economic, energy and other interests. The problem is that current European politics is bewildered and lost both in remaining faithful to its most fundamental principles and in asserting its most basic interests. Evidently they hope that this oppressive mess will one day end by itself if only we stay silent long enough and cover our ears. This strategy is doomed to failure—for at least three reasons. First, because it ignores the psychological profile of “the most influential political figure in Europe.” He loves flattery but despises flatterers. Any concessions someone manages to win through groveling, gilded gifts and medals can be very short-lived and revoked as soon as the gentleman decides he’s had enough. On the other hand, it has been proven that much more can be achieved with a more principled stance than with constant bowing to ever new whims and demands. It’s not for nothing that Trump is called TACO—Trump Always Chickens Out. It is a nickname Trump earned for backing down every time he came up against an opponent in trade wars who didn’t immediately drop his trousers. Second, because ahead of possibly decisive midterm elections to the US Congress next fall, there are signs that things in the US are changing after all. Trump’s iron grip on his own party, his support among voters and the sense that no one can stop him from tearing down democratic institutions are under growing pressure. Far be it from me to advocate interfering in American domestic politics the way the US interferes in ours. It is American citizens who must decide how they will live in the US. But when the image of his absolute power is crumbling from within, Europe perhaps doesn’t need to throw him a lifebelt by maintaining the perception that he is still the only and strongest boss on the international stage. Finally, European politicians must also be aware of how their weakness and their bowing to the humiliating US policy toward Europe—because the “foreign strategy” really cannot be described otherwise—affect their own voters. Europe faces the most difficult existential crisis it has ever known. Whether it manages to overcome it and preserve its civilizational model on the foundations of values that current American policy is openly tearing down depends also on its ability to convince and mobilize its citizens to defend those values. What it is doing now in response to Trump’s open attack on those values has, to put it mildly, the opposite effect. Invoking the hackneyed slogan about how the EU comes out of every crisis even stronger will not help it. What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger. Perhaps—but only until it kills you. What will happen in the US, we don’t know. It is quite possible that changes will come there. The question, however, is whether Europe will survive until then. We don’t need to fight our traditional ally. But when it behaves the way it does, we must stand up for ourselves. Find a backbone and courage. We may never be bigger and we may never be stronger, but at least we will be able to look ourselves in the mirror. And still decide our own fate. As for English, we can learn it in any case.

In Astrid Lindgren’s Pippi Longstocking, the circus ringmaster solemnly announces the greatest wonder of all time: Mighty Adolf, the strongest man in the world, whom no one has ever defeated. When it comes to imagination, it is hard to outdo Astrid Lindgren and her Pippi Longstocking. But that is exactly what Elon Musk’s artificially intelligent house pet named Grok recently managed, announcing on the X network that Elon Musk, ladies and gentlemen, is fitter than LeBron James and Mike Tyson, smarter than Leonardo da Vinci and funnier than Jerry Seinfeld. The mightiest Mighty Elon, if you please. You will no longer find Grok’s claims about Musk’s mightiest might on social media, since they were quietly deleted just a day or two after being posted. Musk, for his part, put on digital sackcloth and ashes and said that Grok had “unfortunately been manipulated by adversarial prompting into saying absurdly positive things about me.” If Musk wanted to defend the intellectual authority of his in-house intelligence, he certainly didn’t succeed. It makes no difference whether Grok was inherently dumb or badly programmed by Musk’s invisible algorithm curators, who make sure artificial intelligence is aligned with the unintelligent (and ill-timed) interests of platform owners, or whether it is simply so sloppily put together that a few clever prompts can provoke it into uttering absurd nonsense. LeBron may be troubled by sciatica, but, dear Elon, the claim—however provoked—that you are fitter than he is may be funnier than Jerry Seinfeld, but it is certainly not intelligent. It would of course be a mistake to judge the impact of the ever faster development of artificial intelligence on society only on the basis of Grok’s nonsense. AI is a transformative technology. It brings much good, but like any technology it also creates risks. It is not that artificial intelligence is by definition good or bad. Like most human inventions since time immemorial (with the obvious exceptions of nuclear weapons and pineapple pizza), it is in itself value-neutral—which cannot always be said of those who control it and use it to pursue their not always most noble interests. Elon Musk has been caught several times influencing Grok’s answers to fit his worldview. In July this year he said he was changing Grok’s algorithm to stop it “parroting legacy media” claims that there is more political violence on the right than on the left. Soon afterward Grok began praising Hitler and calling itself “MechaHitler.” The mightiest Adolf, ladies and gentlemen. If you please. Musk, of course, apologized again. Never again. Until next time. Artificial intelligence is far from being as mechanical and autonomous as it often seems to us. Although some like to present it as magical and completely independent software, in reality it sits at the top of an enormous human pyramid. Behind every model are people who clean and label data, test prompts, rate answers, look for errors, design interfaces, prepare and correct instructions for algorithms, write and translate texts, record voices, photographs and videos, run data centers, mine minerals for chips, and check results in low-paid and often obscure conditions. Why is this important to know? First, because AI must be used ethically—and that requires knowing the environmental and social costs we cause by using it. Even more important, however, is to understand that at almost every one of these invisible levels of human intervention, hidden behind the guise of the apparent automatism and neutrality of machine learning, the outcome can be influenced. This is not a theoretical possibility—it is happening. And not always in as obvious and dumb a way as Grok worshipping the psychophysical abilities of its master. Artificial intelligence must be used intelligently. Superficial use of AI does not make us smarter, rather the opposite. People on social media who try to prove they are right by invoking artificial intelligence remind me of Botox victims arguing over which of them has the nicer lips. Lest anyone think I am staging a Luddite revolt against artificial intelligence: we cannot, and should not try to, turn back the clock, even if it were possible. AI not only promises but already brings enormous positive progress in many fields—from medicine and environmental protection to everyday life. But to harness this enormous potential for the benefit of society and individuals and avoid all the traps of manipulation and abuse, we must first invest considerably more effort in the education needed for us to understand and manage the technology, rather than having someone manage us through it. Regulation is also needed. The current frantic attempts, under American pressure, to have Europe give up its right to regulate the use of AI properly and prevent its abuse could have extremely serious consequences for the future of Europe as a space of democracy, human rights and freedoms. After all, everyone, including the Americans, accepts regulation and strict conditions in most other fields. Not just anyone can split atomic nuclei like logs in their woodshed, even though we know we must reduce the use of fossil fuels. We rightly require the pharmaceutical industry to go through all the demanding procedures before it puts new medicines on the market. I don’t see why we should give up the right (and the duty) to introduce similar safeguards for what Grok and its pals (and above all their owners) squirt directly into our brains. To make successful use of all the positive sides of technological development—and protect ourselves from the dark sides of its (ab)use—artificial intelligence must be demystified. Even in its most advanced, not yet existing version, it will not be a relationship between humanity and technology, but relationships between people—through and with the use of technology. Here too, in the end, it is about power relations. Our answer will require more human intelligence, creativity and self-confidence. If you are increasingly gripped by anxiety at the thought of the imminent domination of technology, which will subject humanity to the tyranny of artificially intelligent bots and robots, read Pippi Longstocking again. This is how Grok’s colleague ChatGPT explained her visit to the circus: “The scene in which Pippi defeats Mighty Adolf is a textbook example of the subversion of power. Mighty Adolf embodies institutional, adult, spectacular power that demands blind admiration. Pippi steps onto the stage as his complete opposite: a child, a girl, free and playful, with no need to prove herself. When she defeats Adolf, she shatters the notion of who is allowed to be strong—and who is supposed to stay weak.” In the book, the ringmaster warns Pippi that this is no place for jokes and that she had better behave before Mighty Adolf hears her impudence. Pippi answers with a cheerful nonsense rhyme—after she has pinned the giant flat on his back. Astrid Lindgren understood power relations. There is no danger that robots will ever rule us. If anyone subjugates us, it will be the mightiest Adolfs of flesh and blood. But only if we let them.

If authoritarian populists are Supermen—and evidently they and their supporters are convinced they are—then empathy and critical thinking are their kryptonite. In the battle for democracy and humanism, which each of us must wage every day in our own surroundings with humanity, solidarity and a critical attitude toward the world, the Maribor high school students at the recent debating competition came away with a draw. Bravo for the empathy they showed. As for critical thinking, however, the students and their mentors still have, in my opinion, some room for improvement. I admit I hesitated to comment on this event, since the media reports contained few details about the circumstances in which the decision to walk out was made. And details matter in such sensitive matters, and I really would not want to do anyone an injustice. Be that as it may, at the competition in Zagreb the Maribor students showed a great deal of empathy—certainly more compassion for and solidarity with the suffering of the Palestinians than many of those who immediately attacked them in the media and even called them “Satanists.” That is surely the first message of this event. Our attitude toward Palestinian suffering in Gaza is the most important test of our individual and collective humanity in today’s world. On this score the Maribor students cannot be reproached at all, unlike those who support and even justify the conduct of the Israeli army and government. But—as I said—empathy is important, but so is critical thinking, which means not only being critical of the world and of others, but also, and above all, constantly checking one’s own positions and opinions critically, on the basis of facts and knowledge. And here the decision to walk out of the competition raises quite a few questions for me. First, I have trouble understanding what the actual motion was that the Maribor students were supposed to debate. According to information I found online with some difficulty, the debate was about “regretting the establishment of the State of Israel as a consequence of the Second World War,” and the draw assigned the students the task of arguing against the regret. If that was the case, then the first serious problem is the way the topic was later presented to the Slovenian public. The Maribor students’ mentor said that opposing “regret over the creation of the State of Israel” would have forced the students to “defend genocide against the Palestinians.” Again—the media reports were sparse, and it is possible they conveyed the details of individual statements inaccurately. If I have misunderstood, I apologize, and above all I sincerely hope it was a reporting error, since equating the establishment of the State of Israel (as a consequence of the Second World War) with genocide against the Palestinians is a serious logical and ethical slip. The justification and justice of the establishment of the State of Israel can of course be debated—after all, opinions on it were divided among Jews themselves, both before Israel was founded and today. But the fact that the motion referred to the establishment of Israel as a consequence of the Second World War should have led the students to the realization that its establishment (whether we agree with it or not) was not the result of a frivolous decision by annoying Jews who just decided to go back to the Middle East and start mistreating Palestinians, but a consequence of the Holocaust, in which six million people were murdered. That is not, and never can be, an excuse for Israeli violence against the Palestinians, but it is a key part of the mosaic for a critical understanding of this long, tragic and bloody story. Second, the reference to the Second World War (that is, the Holocaust) allowed the Maribor students to place the defense of the establishment of the State of Israel 77 years ago in the context of the violence from which it arose, and to make their defense of Israel’s establishment conditional on opposing similar violence against the Palestinians. Even if they had lost because of this, they could have left the competition with their heads held high, since their pride would not have been clouded by the questionable automatic linking of Israel’s existence with genocide against the Palestinians. Because the only logical conclusion of that thesis is that violence against the Palestinians can be ended only if Israel ceases to exist. I strongly doubt the Maribor students and their mentors wanted to say that one genocide can be resolved only by another, the third in a row. Let me also recall that the solution to the Middle East tragedy, on which the reasonable and humane part of world opinion still insists, requires the existence of two states—a Palestinian one, which admittedly does not yet exist because of Netanyahu’s policies, and Israel, whose creation the students did not want to have to not regret. Here more critical thinking before the final decision on participating would certainly have come in handy. Third, it is also questionable that they evidently decided on the boycott in advance—but only in case the draw gave them the role of the opposition. That’s not OK. If they thought the topic was ethically unacceptable, it would have been logical to withdraw from participating in advance, regardless of which position they would have had to defend. Finally, we can ask whether the organizers made a mistake in choosing for a high school competition such a sensitive topic, one on which most of world politics is failing the test of humanity. After (critical) reflection, my view is that the decision was risky but not inappropriate. I believe that both the Maribor students and their peers are capable of debating even such complex and painful topics. Where else should they learn about and discuss them, if not at school and in activities like this competition? But for that they need appropriate and competent guidance and help. Symptomatic is the statement of the head of the Maribor high school, who said the students had shown a great deal of humanity and common sense. On humanity we all agree; as for common sense, Einstein already said it is the collection of all the prejudices we acquire by the age of eighteen. Heads up, Maribor students. Be proud and hold on to your humanity—in this you are setting an example for many of your elders. And in the new year, I wish you, and not only you, plenty of critical thinking and as little common sense as possible. Happy New Year.

Democracy is fragile and delicate. The first one, the Athenian, was the hardiest: it lasted a good two hundred years, until it was brought down from within by oligarchs—with the help of the wicked Spartans from outside. A story not without lessons for our time. Then it was dark for a very long time. Until the Enlightenment, which did not bring democracy but paved the way to it—via the beginnings of modern constitutional order in England at the end of the 17th century, to the American Revolution, which brought the first modern republic, and the French, which a few years later added human rights and freedoms. In the second half of the 19th century, quite a few countries already had at least the outlines of some institutions of modern democracy, but the real breakthrough came after the end of the First World War, when constitutional republics sprang up like mushrooms after rain on the ruins of the collapsed empires across Europe. A good 2,300 years separated them from the end of Athenian democracy. Twenty years later most of them had gone down the drain, at least as far as constitutional republicanism is concerned. With rare exceptions, they all reached the Second World War in various forms of experimentation with more authoritarian models of government. The end of the Second World War brought a new era of modern democracy and a European model based on social security, respect for the paramountcy of human rights and political freedoms, the democratic rule of law, and free and fair elections. For some, the democratic flowering began after the end of the hot war; the other part of Europe had to wait until the cold war that followed had ended too. Today we are where we are. To those who believe that democracy represents a historically logical, inevitable, final and irreversible stage in the development of human society, I would point out that democracies in the modern era have not managed to survive, all told, even a hundred years. In the Seychelles you will find tortoises that live considerably longer. One of the most fascinating chapters in this story is the fate of liberal democracy in Central and Eastern Europe—in the part that had to wait for it the longest. After long decades of longing, enthusiasm for democracy quickly began to wane, until in many cases—as most recent elections show—it has almost completely fizzled out. More and more people swear by changes in which not only human rights but also the other safeguards that protect individuals and social groups from mistreatment and the arbitrariness of executive power will no longer be paramount. Changes that, after this brief excursion into a society with more freedom, will return us to the state from which we wanted to escape for so long. Why enthusiasm for democracy in this part of Europe was so short-lived is particularly hard to understand, since at least by material indicators it can be argued that living standards have improved substantially—perhaps not for absolutely everyone, but at least on average. There are several explanations. Here I will mention only some that I find particularly interesting and that, in my opinion, together with others make up the mosaic of reasons why, after waiting so long for it, we so quickly stopped caring about liberal democracy. One of them is the theory of relative deprivation, which says that people feel deprived not because they actually don’t have enough, but because they have less than others (especially those they think really don’t deserve it)—or less than they think they should have. In the context of the arrival of democracy in the former socialist countries, we can add disappointment at what they actually got compared with what they believed they would get when they watched Western advertisements across the Iron Curtain. Among the many who worked on the theory of relative deprivation was the American political scientist Ted Gurr, a member of the National Commission on the Causes and Prevention of Violence, established by President Lyndon B. Johnson after the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy. In 1970 Gurr published the book Why Men Rebel, in which he argued that relative deprivation causes frustration, which turns into anger, which can turn into physical violence. The cycle need not always run to a violent end; frustrations can also be expressed differently—at elections, for example. While Gurr places his theory within a given community, the Bulgarian political scientist Ivan Krastev, with his thesis on the impact of Nutella on attitudes toward Europe and the Western model of democracy, placed the theory of relative deprivation in an international context. When, years ago, the claim emerged in Eastern Europe that Nutella there was of lower quality than in the West, Krastev pointed out that the reaction went beyond a question of taste or recipe. The affair of the inferior Nutella is not a story about a hazelnut spread but about dignity. People saw in it a message that they were being treated as second-class—as proof that the promised equality between East and West had still not been fully delivered. But it was the British historian Mark Mazower who, in my opinion, came even closer to understanding the most elemental reasons for the rapid disillusionment with democracy in Central and Eastern Europe. In his book Dark Continent (1998), he writes about the mistaken belief that the fall of the Berlin Wall was followed by a flowering of democracy in this part of Europe. In reality, Mazower argues, after 1989 these countries were exposed to the crudest form of market economy, while democracy still had to be built. And because we mistakenly believed we already had it, we shaped our attitude toward democratic values as a reaction to a system that, with economic shock therapies, growing inequality and social disorientation, quickly undermined any serious prospects for democratic development. Mazower advances a thesis that makes it possible to explain at the same time the causes of the crisis of democracy we feel today both in Eastern and Central Europe and in Western countries with a longer democratic experience. The latter arrived at the zero point of today’s dissatisfaction with democracy from the opposite direction, after gradually dismantling the postwar model of the welfare state, which after 1945 stabilized democracy by reducing uncertainty. After 1989, the turn toward deregulation and cutting social protections led them into a situation similar to that of the newly minted Eastern democracies—with similar consequences for the social foundations liberal democracy needs in order to survive at all. The West lost these foundations after 1989; the East never really established them.
