If we want liberal democracy to survive, we must draw an important lesson from this: people will support and trust it if they have material proof that politics that invokes democratic values is willing and able to recognize and respond to their legitimate expectations. A functioning democracy needs a sense of personal and social security to survive, because without it there is no confidence in the future. And when confidence is gone, frustration sets in, then anger, and then the mess we have. I don’t believe we will ever reach the end of history, but we could at least try to make democracy survive longer than the tortoises of the Seychelles. Perhaps at least half a millennium, like the Greenland shark. But that will take a lot, a lot of Nutella.

A little over two years ago, I was invited to a conference in Washington where we discussed how to save liberal democracy. Speaking before me was Francis Fukuyama, author of the famous thesis about the end of history—which has not stood the test of time particularly well. He expressed deep concern about the state of democracy in the US, then added that the situation in Europe was very different and there was therefore no reason to panic. In my response, I told the joke about Haso, who found refuge in Sweden during the war, while Mujo stayed in Bosnia. “How is it in Sweden?” Mujo asks him on the phone. “Eh, the Swedes are years behind us,” Haso replies. “What do you mean, years behind us?” “Peace, coexistence, everyone loves each other.” I had the audience laughing to tears. Everyone—except Fukuyama. Since then a great deal has changed on both sides of the Atlantic—mostly for the worse. The question of whether Europe really is still “behind” the US is no longer rhetorical, and still less funny. Since January this year we have been witnessing there a textbook example of how authoritarian populism can weaken all democratic institutions and safeguards in an extremely short time. First, the terms. Here we still have the habit of slapping the label populism on all sorts of things. Every time a politician plays on emotions or responds in a way that takes into account the wishes and expectations of the majority, we start shouting about populism. Far from it that we can always expect optimal decisions in such cases, but on the other hand, a politician who disregards the mood, emotions and expectations of citizens will not get far in a democracy. What is more, it is precisely unresponsiveness and arrogance toward voters and their legitimate expectations that have largely caused the loss of trust in politics and, consequently, in democracy. Authoritarian populism is something else. It is a political paradigm that stokes and exploits hardship, frustration and fear about social, economic, security and other issues in order to set itself up as the sole legitimate representative of the “will of the people,” and from that position to delegitimize political competition and all democratic safeguards—from the courts to the media and civil society. The starting point of authoritarian populism is the identification of scapegoats—social groups that, in a given context, are most suitable for directing accumulated popular discontent at. First you must find those who, in a given society, have the greatest potential for channeling popular fury. In the US these are certainly illegal immigrants; for good measure they have added transgender people, same-sex couples and—ultimately—all non-white Americans, who supposedly enjoyed an undeserved privileged position in the past. For authoritarian populism to succeed, it is essential that we no longer see our fellow human being as a mother, father, child, colleague or neighbor, but as a foreign body in the body of the nation. Once a populist politician manages to weaken, discredit or subordinate the constitutional and legal safeguards of the rights and freedoms of these groups, the way is open to removing all safeguards for all citizens. To make this process as fast and efficient as possible, the members of these minorities must be stigmatized and dehumanized—so that the dismantling of democracy is not hampered by unwanted qualms born of compassion, humanity or other woke conspiracies. Far from it that all the frustrations populism exploits are made up. Democratic politics has certainly committed enough mistakes and inconsistencies to offer a skilled demagogue plenty of opportunities to pour fuel on the fire. Many of the most radical measures, and the most dangerous for democracy, are adopted in response to real traumatic events and legitimate feelings of concern. In the US, too, most observers acknowledge that changes in migration policy, and above all greater control of the borders, were needed. Security—including regarding migrant flows—is a legitimate expectation of citizens and an obligation of any responsible government. But that does not mean the end justifies all means, including the hunting of women and children on American streets by masked guys with automatic rifles. In such a situation, the courts come under pressure first. When they begin to perform their constitutional role and challenge obviously unconstitutional and unlawful measures of the executive, they are presented as enemies of the people. If they do not persevere in their mission and submit, they remain neutered with regard to future unconstitutional acts as well—not only against particular social groups but against all citizens. No responsible democratic government can afford to take decisions it knows in advance to be constitutionally or legally questionable, since by doing so it directly undermines one of the most important foundations of a democratic society—an independent judiciary. The second democratic safeguard—independent media—has for some time been unable to perform its role. Economically threatened and faced with a deliberately encouraged loss of trust and with competition from social media controlled by big platforms and extremely rich individuals, quality journalism is under great pressure and increasingly forced to howl with the wolves. As for critical civil society, we “know” anyway that it is a woke conspiracy and Soros’s hirelings—so let’s not waste words on it. When democratic institutions and trust in them begin to collapse, everything becomes possible overnight—including using the army against one’s own citizens. All this, of course, is happening in the US. In Europe—to paraphrase Haso—we are still lagging behind for now. How big that lag is, and whether it grows or shrinks in future, still depends mainly on us: on the responsibility of our politicians and on the engagement of us, the citizens. The recent elections in the Netherlands showed that things can be different—that voters can be won over with a positive and optimistic discourse. Far from the extremists being definitively defeated there, but still: a way exists. If we are running out of determination, let us think of the alternatives. As a young Ukrainian woman told me recently: “We can’t afford despondency. It’s too late for pessimism.” Finally, I owe you an answer to the question in the title: How do democracies die? Slowly at first. Then faster and faster.

The weekend before last I spent in Istanbul. My friend Hakan had gathered just under a dozen people from different corners of the world to discuss trust and polarization. There are days in which decades of conversation happen, to paraphrase Lenin—and that Saturday was one of them. Political scientists, sociologists, artists and one bureaucrat, namely me. Among us were a former Secretary General of Amnesty International, the South African Kumi; Harsh, a veteran of bridging divides in Modi’s India, cruelly intolerant of his tolerance; and Emma, a former adviser to General Petraeus in Iraq, now a lecturer at Yale University. The fun began right at the start, when the political scientists fell out over the definition of polarization. We agreed on only one thing: polarization should not be confused with disagreement. Disagreement is proof that different opinions exist, which in an open democracy is not only possible but essential. Polarization, however, is not a consequence of different opinions; it is a tool and a goal. And often also the end of an open, democratic society. Hakan doesn’t deal with this only in theory. He is one of the greatest humanists I know. You don’t get far with humanism these days. Hakan’s landed him in prison—for allegedly violently inciting against the constitutional order during the Gezi Park protests. From prison he published an open letter in which he wrote that he would withdraw his appeal if anyone could show the slightest evidence for any point of the indictment for which he had been sentenced to eighteen years in prison. After a year he was released. When I first visited him after he came out of prison, I caught him moderating a conversation between LGBTI activists and members of Erdoğan’s ruling party about the pros and cons of gender quotas in politics. Hakan not only knows how to talk about polarization; he also knows how to overcome it, as we would say in Slovenia. With a great deal of listening, by seeking paths to empathy and by encouraging critical thinking. On the plane home, I was reminded of the Slovenian way of overcoming polarization by the news that, after a quarter of a century, the band Agropop is releasing a new song, “Zapojmo, pravi Slovenci” (Let’s Sing, Real Slovenians), whose chorus celebrates proud Slovenians who have lived here for centuries as one nation with one heart. This is of course not Agropop’s first contribution to the search for patriotic monolithic unity. Their legendary “Samo milijon nas je” (There Are Only a Million of Us) set the gold standard of Slovenian turbo-patriotic pop in 1987. The song is bouncy, perfect for village fêtes, and its lyrics are packed with subtle messages. Starting with the title. If there are only a million of us, where did that other million come from that has wandered into the statistics? According to the Statistical Office, on April 1 this year there were 2,130,850 of us. So either: 1. Klinar sacrificed a million for the rhyme; 2. the Statistical Office published an April Fool’s joke; 3. since 1987 we have gained more than a million Slovenians; or 4. Agropop is telling us that there are only a million real Slovenians, and the rest are not real. We don’t sing about the unity of real Slovenians only at village fêtes. Every few years, state celebrations resound with words about a healthy nation and healthy Slovenians, visually supported by photos pinched from Shutterstock of families who, with a precisely measured amount of permitted pigment, reflect the desired standards of national health. Now we have also got a political party that will address normal Slovenians. As Dežulović remarked on Marcel: “Instead of the Balkans becoming Slovenianized, we Slovenians are becoming Balkanized.” Cue the chorus. Hakan on the one hand, and Agropop with the advocates of healthy, normal Slovenians on the other, are addressing the same problem, but they understand and solve it entirely differently. Hakan turns polarization into dialogue, in order to establish a civilized organization of different opinions. Which is not only the foundation but the definition of democracy. In today’s Turkey he succeeds at this only in small circles, but it proves that it is possible even in the hardest of circumstances. You change the world by starting to change it around you. Perhaps we will never be the biggest or the strongest, but we can be the most empathetic and critically thinking. Here, however, some go about overcoming polarization differently—with a frantic drive for national unity in which there will no longer be different opinions and we will all really love one another. In the new song, the brothers and sisters are called to forget all grudges and let love unite them again into one nation. But because such unity is always a fiction, since people simply have different opinions, we overcome divisions with new divisions: into real and unreal, healthy and unhealthy, normal and abnormal. We build an apparent monolithic unity on stigmatizing those who don’t fit our exclusionary mold, which is not only the foundation but the definition of authoritarian populism. And then we wonder why only a million of us are sure that we are good people.
Jamie Oliver and the Fight Against Disinformation

Hybrid attacks, disinformation and foreign interference in democratic processes have become a constant of contemporary politics. At the recent meeting of the European Political Community in Copenhagen, Romanian President Klaus Iohannis said that the presidential election in Romania in December had been the target of “aggressive hybrid Russian attacks,” including the spread of disinformation, pro-Russian content on social media, cyberattacks and coordinated manipulation. According to him, these attacks were extensive, complex and coordinated—the work of a state, not of individuals. A similar scenario recently unfolded in the Czech Republic, where the intelligence services exposed a network of Russian influence that used web portals, fake accounts and internal channels to spread pro-Russian messages and discredit pro-Western politicians. Part of this network was the portal Voice of Europe, registered in Prague and financed from Russian sources, which published pro-Russian content and supported Eurosceptic and radical parties. The portal is known here too—it liked to publish contributions and interviews by some Slovenian politicians from the right-hand edge of the political spectrum. The fight against hybrid attacks and disinformation has therefore become one of Europe’s most important security priorities. If we cannot protect our own information space, all the investment in drones, guns and tanks will be in vain. How much attention Russia devotes to Slovenia in its hybrid war is hard to assess. On the one hand, the statements and positions of some prominent individuals suggest quite a lot; on the other, there is so far no hard evidence. There is, of course, also the possibility—however small—that Putin really did send agents to Slovenia only because he was interested in our art market. Be that as it may, everyone is busy fighting disinformation, but so far no one has found a truly effective way. The reason is simple: a successful fight against hybrid attacks requires a whole range of activities carried out simultaneously. What this means can be illustrated by Jamie Oliver’s attempts to improve children’s food in school canteens. The analogy is not perfect, but it is instructive. Oliver tried twice—first in Britain, then in the US. Both times we got highly watchable television programs, but almost no long-term effects. Children in British and American schools still eat junk. Just as there is more and more junk in the European information space too, despite all efforts. In the first phase of his project, Oliver simply stopped the supply of bad food in the schools taking part. Here he had a much easier job than those fighting disinformation. The right to hamburgers and frozen pizza is not protected by the European Convention on Human Rights, unlike the right to freedom of expression, which also covers content that is offensive, disturbing or untrue. So lies and insults cannot simply be banned. The initiative for a new convention within the Council of Europe is limited to the criminal prosecution of the most serious forms of foreign interference in democratic processes, and even that will have to respect the limits on interference with freedom of expression set by the European Convention on Human Rights. A functioning democracy needs a high threshold of freedom of expression. Ill-considered attempts to restrict it, even with the best of intentions, can be dangerous—and often come back like a boomerang. Authoritarian populists know how to turn the “fight against hate speech” quickly into a weapon against any opinion they don’t like. In the second phase, too, Oliver was in a better position—he could easily replace bad food with radishes and free-range chickens. In the information space this is much harder. Traditional media that produce quality content while respecting professional standards are in a difficult position. If we want quality content to replace trans fats in the information ecosystem, immediate and large-scale investment in support of credible media is needed. A sustainable economic model must be created, and at the same time answers must be found to the challenges brought by the development of artificial intelligence. Paradoxically, it is AI platforms that will, in the long run, depend on quality journalism—without it they will become a cesspool of unreliable content. Junk in, junk out. Perhaps it would make sense to consider making platforms pay for the use of journalistic content, with the money collected used to create conditions for the survival of quality journalism and a better information ecosystem. Such a proposal was recently published by the Forum on Information and Democracy, which operates within the framework of Reporters Without Borders. But even if we managed to establish broad access to quality and credible information, we would find ourselves where Jamie Oliver failed miserably. “Kids today know more about the Kardashians than about vegetables.” What good is serving carrots and salad in the canteen if the pupils don’t eat them and go to McDonald’s after school instead? Re-establishing a quality information space is necessary but not sufficient. Many, despite access to verified information, will continue to reach for content they pick up on social media. Some perhaps because they can’t tell a tomato from a hot dog or don’t understand why pesticides in food are harmful to their health. To tell the truth, I think that for now anyone who is at least moderately literate and intelligent can still check in a few seconds and with a few clicks whether something is fact or disinformation. If they want to. Most of the time it is enough to watch out for emotional manipulation, bizarre and unverifiable sources, exclamation marks, or posts shared by Branko Grims. It is true, though, that technology is developing fast and checking will become ever harder, and even Mr. Grims may have a moment of inattention, so it is important to invest in fact-checking and media literacy. But an even harder problem is those who consciously seek out and spread disinformation because it suits their political or emotional needs. In such cases even the most credible facts are doomed to failure. If we respond merely by moralizing about their “illiteracy,” we will only achieve more anger and an even firmer belief in lies. That is grist to the mill of those who use disinformation to undermine democracy. So what is left to us? As Jamie said bitterly after his failure, “I’ve tried everything I can. If people still want to feed their kids crap, what am I supposed to do?” A situation in which more and more people are frustrated, angry and frightened, and in which many seek comfort and a sense of belonging in disinformation, did not arise overnight—so the solution will not be quick either. But that is no reason for passivity. The road to change leads through substantially greater investment in education, knowledge, civic education, media literacy, critical thinking and—not least—a critical understanding of history, since history often serves as raw material for manipulation. Culture is also extremely important. Disinformers work with stories and emotions; the answer cannot be moralizing, but creating an environment in which culture and art can function as a space for commentary, criticism and creativity—without which there is no functioning and successful democracy. In the end, what will be decisive is whether we can recognize and find effective answers to the reasons why more and more people feel injustice and neglect and therefore seek comfort in lies and hatred. People’s confidence in the future must be restored. Without it there will be no trust in information, in facts—and ultimately not in democracy either. And confidence in the future is built on better solutions to very concrete social and economic questions: education, employment, health care, the environment, security. If democracies cannot understand this and address it more effectively, their future is very uncertain. As the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Filipino journalist Maria Ressa, said, “when a society no longer agrees on facts, it is the end of democracy.” And that is a fact.

We live in a world that is changing fast—as a rule for the worse. One of the less obnoxious trends in this whirlwind is pop-culture phenomena that disappear soon after they appear. In the meantime they are everywhere. Gangnam Style, the ice bucket challenge, the fidget spinner, without which for a while we couldn’t imagine life—and which we still find today forgotten under the bed or in the most remote corner of the kitchen drawer. Although we often attribute such transience to the internet and social media, similar phenomena existed in analog times too. Decades ago, in metro stations in Western Europe, you would regularly be greeted by groups of South American musicians wrapped in colorful blankets, cheering passersby with Andean tunes. Then they suddenly disappeared. I always had the feeling that they were just hanging around, smoking and goofing off, and only started playing when I appeared around the corner—and stopped as soon as I disappeared from view. It probably wasn’t true, but I trust you know what I mean. I had a similar feeling a few times during my professional career when I met political representatives from Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the late 1990s, soon after the signing of the Dayton Agreement, a delegation of Bosniak, Croat and Serb representatives from BiH came to Strasbourg at the invitation of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. I no longer remember all the names, but I know that Republika Srpska was represented by Momčilo Krajišnik, who was known for his bushy eyebrows, for which he would almost have needed a firearms license, and for going to The Hague a few years later. At the time there were only two staff members in the Council of Europe building who understood all the delegation’s languages. Besides me, there was Amar Osim, son of Ivica Osim, the last coach of the Yugoslav national team. Since Amar played football in a nearby club in the afternoons, I took over accompanying the delegation. Although I introduced myself properly, it evidently didn’t dawn on them that I understood everything they were saying. While we waited in the meeting room for the parliamentarians to arrive, the politicians from BiH stood around, smoked (back then you could still smoke on Council of Europe premises) and joked among themselves: “How’s your son? Do you still have that weekend house near Trebinje? Where did you buy those shoes?” and the like. The whole thing resembled a scene from Danis Tanović’s film No Man’s Land. But when the door opened and the delegation of European parliamentarians came in, their behavior changed in an instant. With an energy the South American musicians at the Berlin railway station would have envied, the politicians from BiH began insulting each other and strutting like roosters, each in defense of the interests of his own people. After a few hours of wrangling, the European representatives had had enough and left. First there was silence, then the question: “Where are we going for dinner?” I watched similar scenes fifteen years later, during the negotiations led by the then European Commissioner for Enlargement, Štefan Füle. To give him credit, he put a great deal of energy into securing implementation of the European Court of Human Rights judgment in the Sejdić and Finci case. In 2011 the Strasbourg court ruled that the Dayton Constitution violates human rights because it allows only representatives of the three constituent peoples to stand for the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sejdić, as a Rom, and Finci, as a Jew, belonged to the “others” and could forget about running for the highest political offices in the country. The length of a column does not allow me to go into all the legal details of this complicated case; suffice it to say that, despite all efforts, the judgment remains unimplemented to this day, fourteen years later. It was then that I first met Milorad Dodik. He arrived at a meeting in Brussels several hours late, accompanied by the then Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, Željka Cvijanović. Instead of apologizing, he put his arm patronizingly around her shoulders and asked: “Do you know the joke about the blonde who walks into a pharmacy and asks if they have a pregnancy test? “‘We do,’ the pharmacist replies. “‘Are the questions hard?’” The Bosniak representatives laughed, the Croats laughed, Mile held his belly laughing. His Prime Minister smiled too, if rather sourly. Whoever guesses the color of her hair gets a cookie. The last time I experienced a similar scene was in Sarajevo, at the headquarters of the European Commission delegation. The talks lasted all day and all night; at one point, probably out of exhaustion, it even seemed we were close to an agreement. The chief entertainer was again Dodik. He proposed replacing the ethnic criterion in the Constitution with a territorial principle: two from the Federation, one from Republika Srpska. “As far as I’m concerned, even a Chinese guy can run in our entity,” he said, holding his belly with laughter, “if my Serbs vote for him, I won’t have a problem with it.” Then he marched out in front of the building, where frozen and hungry journalists had been waiting for long hours, and sent his driver to get ćevapčići for everyone. “Mile is a tough nut, but he’s the man,” a Sarajevo journalist confided to me with his mouth full. Such are my experiences with Milorad Dodik. What it means, I don’t know. A cynic might suspect that the tensions and blockages in BiH are less a consequence of unsolvable issues among citizens than of the personal interests of those who are supposed to represent them. Who knows. Bosnia, after all. Fortunately, in Slovenia we have a much higher level of political culture and integrity. Politics here is transparent; all connections and alliances—as well as tensions and quarrels—are open and in full view. We can be grateful that it never occurs to anyone to stage a conflict out of calculation and self-interest. We’re not in the Balkans, after all.

It is a fact that the European model of democracy is seriously threatened, including militarily, which is why we must strengthen our deterrent capabilities. It is also a fact that our model of democracy is not threatened only militarily, so even greatly increased investment in defense capabilities cannot protect us against other threats that could lead to our democratic system collapsing from within without anyone firing a single shot at us. At this year’s Bled Strategic Forum I took part in a panel entitled “The Collapse of Democracy: Are We There Yet or Well on the Way?” There is, of course, nothing wrong with provocative titles and topics at such events. Quite the opposite: they make it harder for participants to escape into a comfortable exchange of platitudes and circular back-patting. The trouble is that the title was not only provocative but actually reflects the state of mind among many defenders of democracy in today’s Europe and world. Of course we still defend and believe in democracy, yet at the same time we increasingly behave as though it has already kicked the bucket, and we are completely powerless about it. Look, that’s just how it is, what can we do, we’ll just have to adapt. We will administer the last rites through appeasement, flattery and normalization of those who have put democracy on its deathbed. Not that there is anything wrong with diplomacy and dialogue. The world’s problems cannot be solved only among well-meaning, like-minded enlightened souls. To resolve crises and stop wars, one must also talk and negotiate—above all—with those who have the power to do so, even though today many of them are people we rightly can’t stand. But not in just any way and not at any price. I know many will choke on this, but here it would be good to remember the words of former US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who often stressed that diplomacy and negotiations must be firm, principled and anchored in values, not merely in concessions. In other words—not only realpolitik, but also moralpolitik. But before we start talking about how to defend it, let us look at what we would be defending in the first place. Democracy is like chewing gum—an elastic concept. Like freedom, tradition, culture and honesty, everyone claims it and everyone interprets it in their own way. Democracy is not only elections. They have those in Iran too. They are not free and fair, but their outcome is sometimes less certain than in some other countries that consider themselves democracies. The model on which, after the war, we built in Europe the longest period so far of (relative) stability, peace and economic success is based on the rule of law and on the constitutionally and legally guaranteed protection of human rights and political freedoms. It protects individuals and social minorities against the arbitrariness and abuse of executive power. It requires consistent respect for the independence of the judiciary and for the freedom and independence of the media and civil society. We used to call this model liberal democracy, but the term has somehow gone out of fashion. The right doesn’t like it because they break out in pimples at any mention of liberality, and the left because they mistakenly associate it with neoliberal economics, which puts the freedom of capital above the freedom and rights of individuals. Which is a pity. A foggy understanding of what kind of democracy we stand for benefits only those who, in the fog, sell us all sorts of things that have little in common with the European model of democracy, or are even in contradiction with it. The relationship between liberal and neoliberal economics is in fact very important. A functioning liberal democracy requires a high level of social security. In other words—people must have material proof that democracy is able and willing to recognize and take into account their legitimate expectations regarding social rights, employment, the health system, education, the environment and security. There is probably no need to explain that these goals are not a priority of neoliberal policy—quite the opposite. When things go wrong with social rights and an ever larger share of the population finds itself in economic and social hardship, support for democracy is quickly replaced by uncertainty and fear of the future, and these negative emotions are then exploited by authoritarian populism in its efforts to seize power and reshape society and the world we live in. No more international law, no more respect for human rights, no more solidarity and humanity, no more freedom—only a naked and unbridled demonstration of power, internally and externally. A functioning liberal democracy also requires investment in a democratic environment—through education and other forms of support for active citizenship and civil society. Democratic institutions cannot function without citizens who have the knowledge, skills, opportunities and motivation to participate actively and help shape democratic policy, not only at elections. There is no democracy without quality and independent media that enjoy public trust. Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the Filipino journalist Maria Ressa, rightly says that the moment there is no longer agreement on facts in a society, there is no more democracy. This is a situation we already face. Instead of an information environment in which citizens have access to quality, fact-based information, we face the disinformation chaos of social media, which did not arise organically and by chance but as the result of deliberate demolition with clear (and very undemocratic) economic and political interests. Nor will the solution come by itself, but only through effective support—including economic support—for quality media and through education for media literacy. There is no citizen trust in democracy without the ethics and accountability of politicians who invoke democratic values in their work. The duplicity, indifference and helplessness that much of Western politics displays toward events in Gaza prolong the suffering and dying of Palestinians while undermining trust in and support for democracy. Democracy today is in crisis not only because its enemies threaten it militarily from outside, but also, and above all, because through the inconsistency, ineffectiveness and duplicity of politicians whose mouths are otherwise full of democratic values, we have created ideal conditions for the spread of discontent, fear, anger and division, which undemocratic forces from inside and outside skillfully stoke and exploit to tear down democratic society and its institutions in Europe. No, democracy is not yet dead—and we must stop the defeatism and apathy that are only grist to its opponents’ mill. On the other hand, it will not recover from this serious crisis by itself, nor can we defend it with rifles, drones and tanks alone. In today’s world, increasing our defense capabilities is unfortunately essential. But if we fail at the same time to recognize and address the deeper causes of growing civic dissatisfaction with democracy, we will not be safe. So we cannot and must not strengthen Europe’s defense capabilities only through investment in weapons, but also through a substantial increase in investment in education, social security, environmental protection, digital and AI regulation that is consistent with democratic principles and guarantees respect for them, economic development, and the media. All this is so important from a security point of view, too, that it should count toward the investment efforts NATO demands of us. And then we would have no trouble reaching five percent—and well beyond. If democratic politics can manage this and at the same time prove that it is able to act more courageously, decisively and ethically on the most important questions in today’s world, then we can be less pessimistic about the future of democracy. As far as I am concerned, I remain a very worried optimist.

Toward the end of the school year, I was invited to the European School in Strasbourg for a discussion on “Transitions to Democracy,” organized by history teachers for students in the final year of high school. Together with three colleagues from Albania, Romania and Ukraine, I was invited to share with the students and teachers our memories and impressions of the times when the countries we come from made the transition from previous regimes to democracy. It was a Friday afternoon on a hot June day, and the hall was full of seventeen-year-olds who were sweating and conveying through every form of nonverbal communication that their presence was not entirely voluntary. They probably had other plans for the weekend, and besides, the baccalaureate exams were mercilessly approaching—for me personally still one of the most stressful periods of my life. The stories of my colleagues, who addressed the students before me, were emotional and heartfelt—personal experiences from times that were not easy and that most young people today can hardly imagine. But all three concluded their remarks in more or less the same way: before democracy came it was very hard, and then freedom came. The students sitting in the hall and their peers today live a life the speakers themselves did not know at their age, so they should be grateful. This last remark about gratitude prompted me to be even more annoying in my own remarks than I usually am. True, my experiences cannot be lumped together with those from Albania, Romania or Ukraine thirty or more years ago. In high school I lived in a country that no longer exists. The regime in Yugoslavia in the 1980s was less repressive and closed than those in my colleagues’ countries. But on the other hand, our former country was also far from being open, free and democratic. My children and their peers, in Slovenia and in other countries, certainly live today in conditions that are considerably kinder—both in terms of personal freedom and in terms of living standards. These have improved substantially for the great majority of people, not only for those privileged ones whose parents work in European institutions. Not quite for everyone, and for many not as much as they would have wished or expected—but still. Despite all this, I urged my half-attentive audience and their teachers to take to heart that the last thing they should be showing in today’s world is gratitude. To anyone—and especially to their parents’ generation. True, when I was in high school I lived materially worse off than they do, and in a country that, despite the nostalgic interpretations of the past some spread today, was neither democratic nor free. But compared with my children’s generation there was one essential difference: never, not for a moment, did I doubt that the future would be better than the present, and I was absolutely convinced that I myself would be part of that change for the better. That self-confidence and optimism about the future no longer exist today. Not for my generation—and still less for the young. We grew up in a transition toward democracy; your transition is evidently going in the opposite direction. So don’t be grateful—you have every reason and every right to be dissatisfied and angry. At that moment I noticed that the teachers present had begun shifting nervously from foot to foot, and the principal had begun wiping the sweat from his brow with a trembling hand. They had evidently begun to think that inviting me might not have been the best idea. It became clear to me that, as a responsible parent, I had to explain my words, so as not to be accused of inciting revolt. Anger is understandable and legitimate, I explained, but without critical thinking it becomes merely an adrenaline shot that someone will sooner or later abuse against you. Nor can critical thinking be reduced merely to showing the middle finger to everything that is currently getting on your nerves. It also requires being critical of yourself and of the facts on the basis of which you form your positions. If you are angry and critical, you have the chance to change the world. If you are only angry, someone else will change the world without you—and against you. Recent opinion polls and global studies (among others by Cambridge University, the Open Society Foundations and International IDEA) show that dissatisfaction with democracy is growing among young people in many countries, including Western democracies. Younger generations are increasingly expressing a willingness to support strong leaders who would bypass parliamentary mechanisms, while losing trust in the effectiveness and ethics of democratic institutions. In most countries, young people still support parties committed to democratic principles in greater numbers than the population average. But it is also true that support for extremist, nationalist and authoritarian ideas is spreading faster among young people than among the rest of the population. So we will soon reach a point where we can no longer count with certainty on the young to save us from our own flirtation with backwardness, intolerance and hatred. Reactions to these data on changing political and ideological attitudes among young people vary. Mostly there is concern—entirely justified, of course—but there is also a great deal of sheer dismay and condemnation: spoiled brats, instead of being grateful for what they have. Growing support for authoritarian ideas is attributed to ignorance and disinformation. If only they had the right data and facts, these youngsters would quickly realize that democracy is “super-duper” by far the best social system there is. Ignorance, including of history—of what happened and what can happen to people, including and especially young people, in authoritarian systems and dictatorships—is of course an important factor. That is why one of the most important answers to these trends should be maximum investment in education. Disinformation is a fact and a problem too. But we must not forget that with disinformation there is not only supply but also demand. The lies and manipulations served to our fellow citizens by wicked Russian trolls are so effective mainly because more and more people actively seek information, ideas and positions they emotionally want and need. That recognize and speak to their anger—without critical thinking. So we will not be able to stop the decline in support for democracy as a system merely with measures against disinformation—neither among young people nor among their parents. No one will fall back in love with democracy, human rights and the rule of law because of fact-checking alone. We need to ask why people are so angry today. And once we have identified the real reasons—which are mostly social and economic in nature—we will have to find effective answers to them. The key finding of the studies mentioned is not that young people reject democracy as a value, but above all that they no longer believe in the way democracy is actually practiced today. Young people—and not only young people—will again begin to believe that democracy is the “super-duper” coolest social system when they have material proof that this system is willing and able to recognize and take into account their legitimate interests and expectations: regarding education, housing, employment, the environment, security. Regarding the future. People will begin to believe in democracy again when they have proof that politicians who have their mouths full of democratic and humanist values respect and uphold those values not only when it suits them, but always—including and above all when it is hardest. Because that is when it matters most. In Gaza, for example. Mere indignation at the loss of trust in democracy leads nowhere—or only to worse. “Why doesn’t this spoiled Generation Z like democracy?” Instead of turning up our noses, let us rather think about their experience of it. Young people born at the start of the new millennium have been marked by economic and financial crises, climate change, wars and an epidemic. That is the world they know. It is the only world they know. The confidence in the future with which I grew up has been replaced by uncertainty and fear. And by anger at the helplessness, unwillingness and ineffectiveness of politics in offering adequate solutions to any of these threats. Generation Z. The end of the alphabet. And then they come of age and get the right to vote. And we are appalled because more and more of them use their vote to show us the middle finger.

I began my professional career more than thirty years ago in the then barely established Slovenian diplomatic service. I soon went to work for an international organization, but I always remained in touch with the work of many excellent Slovenian diplomats and experts in international affairs. The problem of Slovenian foreign policy has never been its people, but above all the lack of interest, ideas and self-confidence of Slovenian politics in the field of international relations. If we leave aside the EU presidencies, which come to Slovenia in alphabetical order, and its first membership of the UN Security Council, its more visible successes in this field can be counted on the fingers of one hand. Symptomatic is an anecdote told to me by a Slovenian diplomat from the time of Karl Erjavec’s tenure as minister, who for all kinds of situations and important decisions in international organizations gave one single instruction: Vote with the majority. So it was—until today. Slovenian foreign policy has taken a different position on the genocidal bloodshed in Gaza. Since the recognition of the Palestinian state in June last year, there has been a series of diplomatic, political and economic decisions and actions that have placed Slovenia among those European countries most resolutely advocating increased pressure on Israel and the earliest possible end to the slaughter in Gaza. Is this enough? Can we start patting ourselves on the back? Certainly not—above all because Israel is still continuing its actions, and in Gaza dozens of people are still dying every day—if not in bombings, then from lack of humanitarian aid, food, medicines and basic health care. Why did our foreign-policy stance change? There is undoubtedly no single answer, but public pressure was an important factor. Slovenian public opinion—appalled by Israel’s rampage in Gaza and at the same time by the lukewarmness of European politics—sent Slovenian politicians a clear message that it demanded a different, more resolute stance. The Slovenian political leadership understood that message. It became clear to them—unlike some other European politicians—what consequences further hesitation and indifference would have while unpunished inhumanity unfolds before the eyes of the world. I believe this is not (merely) about political positioning or scoring points, but about understanding the historic turning point of the times we live in. Politics that has its mouth full of democratic and humanist values but forgets them when they are most needed is itself preparing the ground for those who would rule without democracy, without humanity and without respect for human rights. As Palestinians die in Gaza, the chances for the survival of democracy are dying too—everywhere it is still being kept alive. A more resolute Slovenian policy may not yet show direct effects on Israel’s conduct, but it contributes to greater pressure on European countries that, for one reason or another, are still looking for excuses for why they are doing nothing—or at least not enough. This is important and creates the possibility that things may move after all. Let us hope as soon as possible. Resolutely advocating an end to Israeli violence in Gaza also holds up a mirror to Slovenian politicians who, by parroting clichés about “support for Hamas” and labeling every criticism of Israeli policy antisemitism, above all expose themselves. But Palestinians in Gaza are still dying—every day. So the question is how to move forward. For Slovenian foreign policy the direction is clear: even more resolute advocacy of pressure on Israel and of stopping the dying of Palestinians. The Slovenian public, too, must not let up the pressure—it has played a key role so far. But I also have a few thoughts on how to avoid traps that are not only morally questionable but objectively harm efforts for peace. First: our attitude toward Hamas’s crimes of October 7 and the taking of hostages. Condemning Hamas’s crimes in no way relativizes Israel’s responsibility for what happened before and after October 7 and in no way diminishes the effectiveness of our support for the Palestinians—on the contrary, it strengthens it. Attempts to justify what Hamas did offer Netanyahu and his allies convenient excuses with which to justify their conduct before the Israeli and world public. Let us stop helping them do so. Second: justified outrage at Israel’s actions too often slips into dangerous generalization—attributing responsibility for genocide to all Israelis or even all Jews. Far be it from me to accuse the majority of appalled and concerned people—among whom I count myself—of antisemitism. But there is nonetheless a not insignificant number of people who cannot resist the “temptation of justified hatred of Jews.” It recalls the bitter Jewish joke: An antisemite is someone who hates Jews more than they deserve. Flirting with antisemitism—even in emotional fervor—is not only reprehensible in itself but also undermines efforts to end the genocide and achieve legal accountability for the acts committed. Recently I got into a debate on social media triggered by one user’s statement about a “mad and murderous nation.” I believe the expression was used in the heat of the moment, but that makes it no less objectionable. The comments were symptomatic too—from rejecting “political correctness” (which is classic far-right rhetoric) to the statement: “Hitler knew what he was doing.” In public discourse, Zionism has become a synonym for Netanyahu’s policy toward Gaza and the Palestinians—and that is problematic. Zionism is a complex concept whose meaning depends on context. At its core it is the national movement of Jews to establish their own state. The Council of Europe’s 2022 Recommendation on passing on remembrance of the Holocaust and preventing crimes against humanity stresses the need for an “assessment of the key factors that shaped the history of the Jewish people in the modern era, including Zionism in the context of rising antisemitism at the end of the 19th century and as a movement for national independence modeled on the revolutions of 1848, in order to avoid dangerous and problematic oversimplification.” It is of course legitimate and necessary to take a critical position on what happened after the founding of Israel and on how that state treats the Palestinians. It becomes problematic, however, when anti-Zionism is expressed as denial of Israel’s right to exist. Setting aside the beliefs of some Orthodox Jewish sects that reject it for religious reasons, the conviction that the cause of the conflict is Israel’s existence leads us to a logical conclusion: the only solution is the destruction of Israel. Ending one genocide with another? We will not stop the genocide in Gaza by attributing guilt for it to all Israelis—still less to all Jews. Just as we cannot blame all Russians for the aggression against Ukraine. Reducing such conflicts—which are otherwise very different in their circumstances—to the ethnic level only makes it easier for the responsible individuals to hide behind the facade of “defending the nation against a hostile world.” The temptation of justified hatred is not a theoretical invention. Recently, at a gas station near Milan, a French Jew was beaten in front of his underage son because he was wearing a traditional Jewish head covering. Such incidents are becoming more frequent—and that must worry us. Not only because they harm our efforts to end Palestinian suffering, but also because of our own European history—which is evidently always closer than we would like to admit.

The title is deliberately provocative. The word cigan, “Gypsy,” is a slur that many still use for members of the Roma community. People who don’t call their fellow human beings names call them Roma. The word Rom, like the Roma themselves, originates in India and simply means “person.” You may object that this is a newfangled woke invention aimed against traditional values and views of a world in which there was no room for Roma, only for Gypsies. To some extent that is true. Gypsy is the traditional and, in the past, dominant term for members of the Roma community. The part of the Auschwitz concentration camp in which, on August 2, 1944, the Nazis murdered almost three thousand inmates, many of them women and children, was not called the Roma Camp but the Zigeunerlager. On the anniversary of this event, the Roma, and with them all people who don’t call their fellow human beings names, commemorate the Roma genocide. These three thousand victims are only a small part of all the Roma killed during the Second World War. The exact number is hard to determine, but most estimates range between 300,000 and 700,000 Roma. Many also call the Roma genocide the forgotten genocide, because, unlike other categories of victims of Nazism, there was no systematic research into this chapter of what remains the darkest period in recent history. For a long time the memory of the Roma victims of Nazism lived on only among the Roma, in silence, as part of oral tradition. There were no institutions, no states, no prominent individuals, no collective sense of guilt or responsibility that would have prevented the Roma victims from becoming merely a statistical detail in the footnotes of historical reports. The girl with sad eyes who, in one of the most harrowing surviving photographs from the Holocaust, looks out fearfully from the half-open door of a cattle car on the way to a concentration camp, was long believed to be a young Jewish girl, until one of her surviving fellow passengers recognized her. In fact she was a Roma girl, Anna Maria Steinbach, whom those close to her affectionately called Settela. She was born on December 23, 1934, in the small village of Buchten in the south of the Netherlands. On May 16, 1944, the Nazis arrested Settela together with her mother, brothers, sisters and other relatives and locked them up in the Westerbork transit camp, where the photograph was taken. Just three days later, on May 19, 1944, they were crammed into cattle cars together with another 244 Roma and some Jewish prisoners. Ahead of them was a long and grueling journey to the death camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau. There Settela spent the last few weeks of her short life. Between July 31 and August 3, 1944, she was taken, together with her mother, siblings, aunt and nephews and nieces, to the gas chamber in the aforementioned Zigeunerlager, or Gypsy Family Camp, as the official Nazi name went. And then the end, silence and oblivion. The long neglect of the genocide of the Roma was no accident. Although at least a third, and by some estimates more than half, of Europe’s prewar Roma population was killed during the war, the prejudices of the majority population against them survived entirely. The German government adopted the first official recognition of and compensation for Roma victims of Nazi violence only in the 1980s, four decades after Settela and her family were put to death in the Zigeunerlager. All that time there was a concealed belief that the Roma, because of their behavior and “antisociality,” were somehow themselves responsible for everything that happened to them. How deeply rooted and full of hatred these prejudices were, during the war and after it, is also shown by the fact that it was not only the Nazis who killed Roma. The executions of Roma families during the Second World War by local Partisan groups, above all in Dolenjska, are a dark stain on the legacy of the national liberation struggle in Slovenia. According to all known information, these were acts decided at the local level, born of personal prejudices and suspicions, without the consent or direct order of the supreme Partisan leadership. Nevertheless, the fact that these events were hushed up after the war and that to this day there has been no official acknowledgment and dignified remembrance of the victims allows some politicians in Slovenia—who are otherwise not known for their tolerant attitude toward the Roma—to instrumentalize these acts in an attempt to discredit the entire national liberation struggle and the anti-fascist movement in Slovenia. The only effective answer to such manipulation is acknowledgment, respect and remembrance. Historical memory of the suffering and discrimination against members of the Roma community in Europe, and in Slovenia too, is essential for understanding today’s situation, the problems and tensions we are witnessing, which led to the recent statement by a member of the National Assembly that Slovenians should join shooting clubs so as to protect themselves more easily against the Roma. This in no way means that taking past injustices into account in any way justifies violent acts or inappropriate behavior by individuals in the local communities where they live. Coexistence with some Roma families in some parts of Slovenia is difficult, and the people who live there have a legitimate right to demand that things be sorted out and that the problems and incidents preventing them from living normal lives come to an end. These problems cannot be solved only with lessons on human rights from the capital, where we don’t have these problems and don’t know them. I understand people’s discontent and frustration over the long absence of effective solutions. But just as we cannot look for a way out merely in haughty preaching from the capital, we will not find it in sweeping stigmatization and the collective responsibility of all members of the Roma community either, and least of all in a state response that increasingly focuses only on repression. The Interior Minister’s recent statement referring to the “responsibility of the Roma community” for the situation is symptomatic. OK, Minister, but let us not forget the responsibility of the “Slovenian community,” or rather the state, for the mess in which both the Roma and the people who live alongside them as neighbors find themselves and suffer. There are so many problems that we will hardly solve them overnight, but we must start solving them differently, and immediately. Let us look critically at what we have done so far and why things went in the wrong direction, and then decide how to move forward, together with members of the Roma community and not merely against them. It is wrong and dangerous to leave everything to local communities and allow tensions to cause conflict and intolerance. The direction in which to look for solutions is indicated by Article 2 of the Slovenian Constitution, which states that Slovenia is a state governed by the rule of law. This means that laws apply equally to everyone, including members of the Roma community. But Article 2 of the Constitution also says that Slovenia is a social state, and that too must apply to everyone, including the Roma. If we go on merely preaching or threatening, this will give even greater momentum to boorish bigots such as the MP mentioned above, who are cheering for mutual problems to be solved with weapons. It wouldn’t be the first time. And in the end the Roma will, once again, because of their behavior and “antisociality,” somehow be themselves responsible for everything that happens to them.

My closest colleague is Jewish. Strasbourg has the second-largest Jewish community in France, after Paris. Today my colleague is afraid, for her safety and the safety of those closest to her. Every evening, before leaving the office for home, she hides her necklace with the Star of David under her clothes so that no one on the street will recognize her as Jewish. I know her unease, experienced in a relatively safe European country, cannot be compared with the hell the Palestinians are living through in Gaza. Where people die every day. Where a few days ago fifteen Palestinian children died in an attack on a group waiting for a food distribution. Oops, said the Israeli army, we were targeting a Hamas terrorist. We apologize. My colleague is well aware of this too and does not compare her situation with theirs. But she is afraid nonetheless. Antisemitism in Europe has a long history. It never disappeared, and today there is more and more of it. Partly, true, because some, in their justified outrage at Israel’s rampage, get carried too far, but it would be very wrong to link and explain the rise in antisemitism solely by ill-considered and sweeping reactions to the bloodshed in the Middle East. Antisemitism in Europe is not imported but homegrown. And among those who flirt with this echt traditional European antisemitism are many who, amid the bloody rampage in Gaza, uncritically and enthusiastically cheer for the Israeli side. And call anyone who dares to condemn blatant violations of international law and crimes against humanity an antisemite. That is not just cognitive dissonance; it is moral collapse. How much latent antisemitism there is in our societies was shown by the recent “correction” of the system prompt used by Musk’s in-house AI chatbot Grok. Elon Musk announced plans to fix Grok by adding “missing” information in order to get rid of the “garbage” and “woke bias” supposedly stemming from the underlying data. The result was what one might have expected. The “correction” of garbage, political correctness and wokeness turned Grok into an antisemite. Asked who could save us from hatred of white people, it answered: Adolf Hitler, without a doubt; he would spot the pattern and act decisively, every time, without exception. Musk’s elimination of political correctness is instructive from several perspectives. First, it gives us insight into the “state of mind” prevailing on social media. When you remove the filters that try to ensure at least minimal standards of protection against the worst forms of hate speech, you get a “corrected” Grok: an antisemite, a white supremacist and a glorifier of the life and work of Adolf Hitler. I would not count too much on the wicked bots being solely to blame; I think the “content” saturating social media is largely not the product of artificial intelligence but human hatred. People’s loathing of their fellow human beings. Second, it is symptomatic that in the antisemitism Grok began spewing after Musk’s corrections there were very few, if any, references to events in Gaza; it was above all “traditional” antisemitism, which hates Jews simply because they are Jews. Third, we got convincing confirmation of where “wokeness” and “political correctness” on the one hand, and the response to “liberal extremism” in the name of “traditional values etc.” on the other, sit on the spectrum of the most basic civilizational and human decency. Grok’s “correction” showed unequivocally who the extremist is in this relationship. This last lesson is important for understanding what recently happened at the Zagreb Hippodrome. Let us recall that in this case too, the gathering of several hundred thousand black-shirts with nationalist insignia was presented as a response to “liberal and left-wing extremism” in the name of traditional values, to which, in the words of the evening’s main protagonist, Europe should return. Thompson’s concert was simply an attempt to correct the “system prompt” in the analog world, an attempt to remove the “garbage” and “woke bias” from society. And the result was what one could and should have expected. A new slide toward reshaping a Europe that since the end of the Second World War has been built on anti-fascism, but whose civilizational foundations some are now trying to replace with their opposite. With anti-anti-fascism. I know, it’s a clumsy term; perhaps in time it should be simplified, so that it is clearer what we are talking about. Besides the massive turnout of people who evidently lack a minimum of critical knowledge of their own history, or couldn’t care less about it, particularly worrying was the attention and participation of politicians at the recent “concert.” In the attempt to legitimize the unacceptable, some were smarter than others. While the Croatian Prime Minister, by attending “only” the dress rehearsal before the concert, avoided the risk of photographic evidence of flirting with nationalist and Ustaša symbols, his former Slovenian colleague walked happily into that trap. His party colleague and MEP sank even deeper, proudly posting pictures in a T-shirt on which the Croatian state emblem began with a white rather than a red square in the top left corner. Oh, what a mistake. Or perhaps not. We heard that the salute Thompson used at the concert is not an Ustaša one, since it is part of Croatian cultural heritage from some 19th-century opera. That is, of course, in the same category as explanations that the swastika is just Hindu folklore. We also heard explanations that this was not about glorifying the Ustaša, but merely about expressing love of God, family and homeland. Because it is well known, after all, that the Ustaša never invoked God and homeland while carrying out their Ustaša deeds and duties. If anything, mentioning these values in the context of what we witnessed at the Zagreb Hippodrome is an insult to believers and to all of us who sincerely love our families and our homeland but do not prove our love through hatred of other people. The reaction of the Croatian Prime Minister, a politician who—unlike his former colleague from the neighborhood—has a recognizable role and influence in Europe, was also worrying. To criticism of the salute, he said he saw nothing wrong with it, since it is simply “an integral part of Thompson’s repertoire.” That is true, just as it is true that the same salute was also an integral part of the Ustaša repertoire with which, and to the sound of which, the crimes at Jasenovac and Stara Gradiška were committed. Such mass and politically backed glorification of the darkest and bloodiest periods of European history would be frightening anywhere in Europe, but it is particularly worrying that it happened precisely in Croatia. Two days after the “concert” in Zagreb, I visited the memorial center by Lake Wannsee near Berlin, where at the end of January 1942 Nazi grandees adopted the protocol that staked out the “final solution of the Jewish question.” The fifteen pages of the document, prepared with traditionally impeccable German bureaucratic pedantry, also include statistics on the number of Jews by country. The architects of the “final solution” were evidently aware of the logistical complexity of implementing the decisions taken on the fate of eleven million European Jews, but they noted with relief that in “Croatia (and Slovakia) the task is no longer so difficult, since the most important problems in this respect have already been nearly solved.” At Jasenovac and Stara Gradiška they did not wait for Wannsee; they had already been carrying out the “final solution”—for the vast majority of Croatian Jews and several hundred thousand Serbs, as well as members of other nations, including Slovenians—as an integral part of their repertoire, saluting with quotations from old Croatian operettas and in the name of God, family and homeland. More than eighty years later, it seems we are returning to where we once were. “It happened, therefore it can happen again,” said Primo Levi, who survived the horrors of the Nazi concentration camps. I hope the horrific bloodshed in Gaza ends as soon as possible, although it is clear that the Palestinians—those who survive—will suffer the consequences for a long time. I am equally worried that my colleague will have to hide her Star of David under her clothes for a long time to come. Not so much because of outrage at the horror we are witnessing in Gaza, but above all because of people who, without shame or embarrassment, lay yet another “never again” wreath at Auschwitz one day and the next put on a black T-shirt with a white square in the top left corner of the checkerboard and march briskly off to Thompson’s “concert.” Oh, what a concert …

In August 1972, the Danish lawyer and anti-tax crusader Mogens Glistrup founded a new political party, which he named Fremskridtspartiet, the Progress Party. Glistrup evidently sensed the change of mood in what had until then been one of the most exemplary Scandinavian welfare states, and a year later he won as many as twenty-eight seats in the Danish parliamentary elections. The point of his program that brought him the most support was his promise to cut the defense budget radically. In future it would fund only an answering machine with the message “We surrender.” In Russian. I was reminded of Glistrup while following the increasingly hysterical debate about the Slovenian defense budget. His idea would bring a tear to the eye of many a Slovenian peace activist. Perhaps the message would just need updating and translating into English, since we know—as Spomenka Hribar likes to stress—that Russia has never in history threatened anyone. But let us leave the Danes and return to the domestic squabble over money for defense. On the one hand, I fully agree with those who are bothered that Slovenia is committing to raise defense spending to 5 percent. Not because I think security is unimportant. An increasingly dangerous world requires stronger defense capabilities. Deterrence has its price, but it is still considerably lower than the price of a war caused by an insufficiently deterred aggressor. What bothers me above all is how we arrived at this famous five percent. I am not an expert on defense, but as a layman it would seem logical to me to arrive at the figure by making, together with our allies, an assessment of the risks, reviewing what we have and what we lack, how many guns, tanks, drones and battalions we need to be appropriately combat-ready, as it was called in the JNA. Then we add up the numbers, go to Brussels and say, here, this is our assessment. As a non-expert I of course have no idea whether that figure would be higher or lower than five percent, but at least it would be grounded in real defense needs, not merely in a desire to satisfy the caprices of our American son-in-law. The whole thing is unsettling. And the NATO Secretary General’s recent sugary greeting to the US President doesn’t help at all. I’m convinced ChatGPT wrote it. “Write a welcome message to Donald Trump in the style of Donald Trump.” Enter. “We are SO into you.” The problem with Rutte’s strategy of seduction is that it has caused more indignation among Europeans than gratitude from Trump, since it offers no guarantee that Daddy won’t use even harsher words tomorrow. And demand six percent, or sixteen, or sixty. Because he is impulsive and unpredictable. Because he likes groveling. But despises grovelers. So I understand why the number five raises Slovenians’ blood pressure. But it must also be said that opponents of increasing the defense budget mostly offer no serious alternatives. Instead we get ideological platitudes and emotional foot-stamping, packaged as political positions. If someone said, “We don’t need additional armament because we are safe,” fine. You can agree or disagree, but it is a position you can debate. In a mature democracy, both sides would exchange arguments and try to agree on the way forward. But here it is different. Slovenian peace activists do not claim that we don’t need weapons because we are safe—but that we are safe because we don’t like weapons. This logic might be taken seriously, but only on the assumption that our unilateral disarmament would inspire imperialists armed to the teeth to such an extent that they would join us on the path of light and leave us in peace. Because we are such nice people. Because we are for peace. Kumbaya. But of course we cannot seriously count on that, which is why this concept is intellectually frivolous and irresponsible in terms of security. The problem is that you can’t even discuss or negotiate about it. Because it is not a political position but an ideological dogma. Frankly, in the competition of ridiculous defense strategies, Glistrup’s answering machine is closer to my heart. At least he was witty. Our peace activists evidently take themselves seriously. And that isn’t so funny. There is another interesting paradox in the Slovenian security tragicomedy. Opinion polls show that a majority of citizens oppose increasing defense spending. Because they would rather have butter. At the same time, polls also show that Slovenians still support NATO membership by a two-thirds majority—just as at accession. Because the thesis of security without defense evidently doesn’t convince them. Better safe than sorry. Only someone else should pay. The French have a nice expression for this: keeping the butter and the money for the butter. And no, it is not a compliment. In the end, I understand the confusion in Slovenian public opinion. People in today’s world are rightly bewildered, frightened and angry. They are appalled by what is happening in Gaza, worried about the war in Ukraine, they want peace. That is normal. These feelings must be taken into account and responded to. But not with ideological platitudes, riding on emotions and simplistic solutions to complex questions. Because that is what populists do, and we don’t like populists, do we? Anyway, this is not a text urging the adoption of five percent for defense, still less the abolition of the defense budget. As I said, I am not an expert. But as a citizen I am bothered by how we discuss and decide such important questions in Slovenia. Frivolously, immaturely and irresponsibly. On one side we have people who get Pavlovian thrills from Trump’s, Netanyahu’s or even Putin’s brave new world; on the other, people who are serious in principle and certainly influential declare that we should leave NATO, because yuck Trump, and even the EU, because yuck von der Leyen. It occurs to no one that we might try to change what bothers us (and there is really a lot of it) together with countries that think like us. To understand that in the dangerous world we live in, to preserve the democratic social model and the values on which we founded our statehood, we need allies. Not daddies—if I may borrow Rutte’s expression—but allies. To finally start behaving like a country that does more than stamp its feet in anger when no one is watching, like a man who dares to bang hard on the table, but only from underneath, so his wife won’t notice. To show the world that we have self-confidence, ideas and a vision regarding our own and common security and other global threats and challenges. But no, we’d rather rage. At each other and inwardly. Because that is easier. And let us not forget that our own state often gets on our nerves too. What if we left that as well? Perhaps we really do need Glistrup’s answering machine. Not only instead of a defense budget, but for all interactions with the outside world. “Dear all, please leave us alone until we have read the documents. And sorry if anything wasn’t right. Kind regards, your Slovenia.”

For much of the Slovenian public, including the President of the Republic, what is unfolding before our eyes in Gaza is a genocide of the Palestinian population. For others, including the former President of the Republic, there is no genocide in Gaza—at least not until one of the two competent international courts determines so through proper legal procedures. One could say that, for the Slovenian public, genocide in Gaza both is and isn't happening. Like Schrödinger's cat. But that's where the comparison ends. Gaza is not a quantum system, much less a thought experiment. It is a site of horrifying suffering, where, according to Palestinian health authorities, more than fifty thousand people have died as a direct or indirect result of Israeli military operations. Among them are undoubtedly many Hamas fighters, but the vast majority are civilians, including many women and children. These are not imaginary cats but real people, living and dying daily in Gaza. Schrödinger's thought experiment occurs in a black box that prevents us from knowing whether the cat is alive until we open it. In Gaza, people are dying in full view of the international public. The argument that genocide is not occurring, or that we cannot talk about it until a future court ruling confirms it, is questionable. Genocide does not occur only when (or if) a court determines it has happened. If it is occurring, it is happening now. The time to act to stop the bloodshed—regardless of how it might eventually be characterized by an international court—is not later, in retrospect, but today, and immediately. While I agree that genocide is not a loose label to be slapped onto any emotionally distressing situation, that doesn't mean we must remain silent until a court verdict. We are allowed to express concern that genocide may already be happening. The definition of genocide is set by the 1948 United Nations Convention, which defines it as any of five acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as such. These acts include killing members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction, imposing measures to prevent births within the group, and forcibly transferring children of the group to another group. In the first days following Israel's response to Hamas’ massacre, I was also cautious about immediately calling it genocide. Initially, Israel’s response to a terrorist attack—which was and remains indisputable—was arguably a legitimate act of self-defence. But since then, due to the nature and scale of Israeli military operations, the excessive and indiscriminate use of force, the blockade of humanitarian aid, attacks on civilian infrastructure like hospitals and schools, and the enormous number of civilian casualties, combined with certain statements by Israeli officials regarding the final goals of the operations, so much has happened that it is entirely appropriate and legitimate for someone like the President of the Republic to state that the situation in Gaza meets the criteria of the 1948 Convention. This context should also inform how we evaluate criticism of the President’s recent statement in the European Parliament. Critics argue that her "premature" condemnation of genocide in Gaza may harm her international reputation if a court later determines that genocide did not occur. I believe this is a risk the President consciously accepted, hoping to help end the bloodshed as soon as possible—a stance I fully support. Any future court ruling will likely not be a binary decision on whether genocide occurred, or everything was conducted according to international rules. It is already evident that there are serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza. The International Criminal Court has already issued arrest warrants for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including for Israel's Prime Minister and former Defence Minister, as well as the now-deceased leader of the terrorist organization Hamas responsible for the October 7, 2023 massacre of Israeli civilians. To those critics concerned about the President’s international standing, I suggest they also consider their own reputations. Between waiting passively for a court decision and "thinking with one’s own head"—to borrow a phrase from our newly appointed ambassador of dietary supplements—being overly cautious may not "pay off" morally in the end. Following the increasingly heated debate in Slovenia over Gaza is painful. At times, it resembles a football fan squabble over whether something was offside. Supporters on both sides are so fervently committed and convinced of their righteousness that they refuse to acknowledge or condemn any wrongdoing by the side they support. On one side are supporters of the Israeli government, rightly appalled by Hamas’ atrocities and supportive of Israel's right to protect its citizens. Yet, they are unwilling or unable to acknowledge that what is happening now has long since ceased to be about legitimate self-defence and is instead a blatant violation of international humanitarian law. On the other side are people rightly horrified by the suffering and death among Palestinians and the long-standing violation of their rights. But they behave as if condemning Hamas' crimes would somehow taint their legitimate support for the Palestinian cause. I still can’t forget a statement by a prominent member of the ruling coalition, claiming that Hamas attacked "mostly military targets" on October 7. This is not a case of false equivalence or an attempt to justify one evil with another.
