Hamas is a terrorist organization; Israel presents itself as a civilized, democratic state and cannot justify its violations of international law by pointing to the horrors committed by terrorists. The discrepancy in civilian casualties is so stark that we cannot talk about any "balancing" of responsibility. Still, we must remain human in our approach to the victims—Palestinian and Israeli alike—and not lose sight of our shared humanity. In the end, this Slovenian debate over whether or not it is genocide is not particularly productive when it comes to ending the horrors in Gaza. If and when an international court rules, it will likely focus on specific aspects, especially the intent behind the operations, since their nature already appears to match most of the five acts listed in the UN Convention. The consequences for Palestinian civilians, whether later defined as genocide or "merely" crimes against humanity, are equally horrifying in either case. Arguing over legal definitions is a distraction from the core issue: what is happening in Gaza is inhumane and unacceptable bloodshed that must end immediately, regardless of what a court may decide someday. It is also painful to see how events in Gaza are fuelling antisemitism. On one hand, it is grotesque that many of Netanyahu's ardent supporters in Slovenia have themselves previously flirted with antisemitic rhetoric. We also see how accusations of antisemitism are weaponized to attack and silence any criticism of Israeli actions. It's worth recalling the definition of antisemitism by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), to which Slovenia is a member. IHRA lists as antisemitism the use of double standards by requiring of Israel a behaviour not expected or demanded of any other democratic nation. I believe there is no doubt that any other state treating Gaza’s population in the same way would face equally harsh international condemnation, meaning criticism of Israel’s actions cannot automatically be equated with antisemitism. On the other hand, IHRA also defines as antisemitism the denial of the Jewish people’s right to self-determination—for example, by claiming that the existence of the State of Israel is a racist endeavour. Sometimes, the rhetoric goes even further. Just days ago on social media platform X, I read a statement by a journalist from public radio saying it had become "very clear why nobody in history has ever liked the Israelis/Jews/Yids." Support for Palestinians and condemnation of the Israeli government's actions is entirely justified. But this—this is something else entirely. Something very dark.
On Experts in Enemies of Humanity

The transition to democracy is not an event but a process. The same is true of the transition away from democracy. Nevertheless, there are events and periods that are turning points in these processes. In the history of the struggle for democracy and respect for human rights in Slovenia, one such period was the year 1984. The beginnings of an organized and influential movement for democratization came from the peace movement, which rebelled against the omnipresent power and influence of the Yugoslav People’s Army, from youth movements that openly questioned the ideology of their mentors, and from the LGBT community. For homosexuals, life in communist society was hard. They were labeled deviant, and most took care not to reveal their identity—let alone live it publicly. And then one day homosexuals in Slovenia decided they would no longer hide. In 1984, the Student Cultural Center ŠKUC founded MAGNUS as a Cultural Organization for the Socialization of Homosexuality. This was a key milestone at the beginning of profound social and political changes. I was eighteen at the time. I remember the reactions to the founding of MAGNUS and to the congress organized in Ljubljana. If they were fairly restrained in Slovenia, many in other parts of the country went berserk. A torrent of poisonous hatred was poured on the “faggots and lesbians from Ljubljana.” I admired the calm and determination of the LGBT activists. I understood that they were fighting for their rights, freedom and dignity, but also for mine. Ever since, I have been a committed advocate of the rights and equality of individuals and social minorities. For their sake, but also for my own. Without respect for the rights, freedom and human dignity of all groups and people in society, sooner or later there is no freedom and humanity for anyone. What went on in those times four decades ago, when the foundations of a democratic and open society in Slovenia began to be laid, can be seen in Boris Petkovič’s excellent documentary LGBTSLO1984, which in my opinion should be shown in all Slovenian schools during civic education classes. If the democratization of social space begins (among other things) with attitudes toward the LGBT community, the same holds when the process goes in the opposite direction. Homophobic discourse is today a central weapon of authoritarian populists for undermining liberal democracy. This is no coincidence. Liberal democracy is a social system based not only on regular elections but also on the constitutional, legal and actual protection of the rights and freedoms of individuals against abuse and arbitrariness by those in power. Authoritarian populism, meanwhile, is a political paradigm that claims the exclusive right to represent the nation as a monolithic and homogeneous community. On the basis of this exclusivity, authoritarian populism claims the right to delegitimize (and persecute) political competition, places itself above the courts and attacks critical media and civil society. To undermine the constitutional, legal and other safeguards that constrain it, populist authoritarianism focuses on exploiting, stoking and instrumentalizing social frustrations and prejudices against certain social groups. Above all migrants and homosexuals. This is a scenario we can follow in Hungary, and also in Trump’s war on diversity, equity and inclusion. When safeguards against abuse of executive power and the prejudices of an enraged majority no longer apply to one social group, they soon no longer apply to anyone. The doctrine of instrumentalizing homophobia to tear down liberal democracy is popular today among politicians in many parts of the world, but they are mostly imitators. The author of the concept is Russian President Vladimir Putin. In 2013, the Russian Duma almost unanimously (the only one who voted against was Ilya Ponomarev, who is now in Ukraine) adopted the Law on the Protection of Children from Information Advocating the Denial of Traditional Family Values, or, in short, the anti-LGBT law. It was the first time Russia said openly and without reservation that it did not intend to respect obligations regarding the rights of LGBT persons arising from the European Convention on Human Rights, “because this is contrary to Russian values.” Homophobic discourse is a constant of Putin’s authoritarianism. This is how the Russian vozhd put his understanding of human rights into words in December 2022, addressing members of the Russian Council for Civil Society and Human Rights: “Human rights doctrines are being used to destroy the sovereignty of states and to justify the political, financial, economic and ideological dominance of the West.” The head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, was even more explicit. “The aggression against Ukraine was necessary,” the church grandee explained, “because there was a danger that a pride parade would be organized in Donbas.” In Putin’s Russia, members of the LGBT community are an internal enemy threatening the sanctity and purity of the Russian nation and a fifth column of the decadent West, which seeks to establish global hegemony by destroying traditional family values. Homosexuals are, so to speak, enemies of humanity. In November 2023, the Russian Supreme Court declared the “international LGBT movement” an extremist organization. Now homosexuals are being imprisoned as terrorists. In recent days they have gone after publishers of “LGBT propaganda.” They face up to twelve years in prison. Several hundred book titles, among them Žižek’s collection of jokes, have been ordered banned and destroyed. The method has not been specified, but we know from history how this matter is handled when traditional values collide with degenerate art. All of the above is a long introduction to explaining why I was surprised by a recent statement by a prominent representative of the party Levica, member of the National Assembly Dr. Tatjana Greif. She posted on the social network X the completely daft claim that the grandfather of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had been a senior official of Nazi Germany. What does this have to do with the homophobia of the Russian regime? Wait a moment. First, it is surprising that someone who holds high political office, and a doctorate on top of that, would write something so dumb. The honorable doctor could have checked that the claim is false with two or three clicks and by using more reliable sources than the one she cites. Namely Maria Zakharova, director of the Information and Press Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry and one of the main mouthpieces of Kremlin propaganda. Which, of course, also includes spreading homophobic messages. “What is happening in Western countries regarding the LGBT question is a classic dictatorship of liberalism,” she replied in 2021 to a journalist’s question about the European Court of Human Rights’ decision on violations of these rights in the Russian Federation. In February this year she applauded Trump’s decision to cut most USAID humanitarian programs, which supposedly served “to promote the LGBT agenda” and “to fund genital transplants on rodents.” Some may think the honorable MP supports all elements of Russian policy—you know, yuck Europe, yuck Ukraine—except its attitude toward the LGBT community. Perhaps, but that reminds me of the joke about the journalist who, as she left the theater, asked the freshly widowed American First Lady, “Other than that, Mrs. Lincoln, how did you like the play?” I think a response to its member’s outburst could also be expected from the leadership of her party. I would expect them to react to the fact that a prominent member is riding the waves of the most primitive anti-EU sentiment and trying to discredit the President of the European Commission with obvious lies served up by the Russian propaganda machine. Not to mention that this is open support for an ideology and people who are undisguisedly hostile to the fundamental values of a democratic society, including and starting with hatred of the LGBT community. Why the honorable MP and doctor of science did not think it necessary to check dumb lies from the mouth of the leading Kremlin propagandist, she explains herself: “Maria Zakharova knows history and the enemies of humanity well; she is a woman who has never spoken in vain.” On the last part of the sentence I have to agree with the honorable MP. The words of Maria Zakharova and her bosses are never and in no way “in vain.” They have consequences. Including for the people the Russian regime labels enemies of humanity. What can happen when certain groups of people are labeled and dehumanized in this way, we know from history.

If the reports are true that the Slovak Prime Minister had to circle around Europe on his way to the military parade in Moscow because the Poles and the Baltics didn’t let him pass through their airspace, he can at least take comfort in the fact that it was probably the longest flight in history without jet lag. During the long flight, he also had plenty of time to prepare for Putin’s military extravaganza. Roses are red, violets are blue, Russia is sweet and so are you. I personally met with the Russian president twice, back in the days when one didn’t need to travel around their ass to get to their pocket just to reach Moscow. The first time was twenty-five years ago, in mid-January 2000, just a little over two weeks after Yeltsin named Putin as his successor. I was part of the first foreign delegation he met with after arriving in the Kremlin. Along with a group of European parliamentarians, we were on our way to Chechnya. The Second Chechen War was underway, and many claimed it was Putin himself who orchestrated terrorist attacks on his own citizens to seize power. As would later become his habit, Putin was already an hour and a half late for his very first meeting with a foreign delegation. When he finally showed up, the head of our delegation, good old Russell Johnston, scolded him like a misbehaving brat. Putin blushed, stammered, and promised to stay with us until we had exhausted all our questions. That took quite a while, mostly because Putin responded to every criticism by saying we had the wrong information and that we would see with our own eyes that the Russian Federation was firmly on the path to peace, democracy, rule of law, and human rights. The next day, we headed for the Caucasus. Before departure, the Russian Interior Minister suggested we wear Russian uniforms for our own safety, as Chechnya was teeming with snipers allegedly waiting just for us. Russell wasn’t convinced. “With all due respect, Mr. Minister, I think they’ll be aiming at you, not me.” In the end, only an older Turkish MP accepted the offer. Being of smaller stature, he looked in the oversized Russian uniform like the tiniest dwarf from the Disney cartoon Snow White—you know, the one with big ears with sleeves dragging to his feet. On our way to Chechnya, we first stopped in Makhachkala, the capital of Dagestan, where the local garrison commander hosted us at the Primorskoje Hotel. No Caucasian hospitality would be complete without traditional toasts. Those of us who understood at least some Russian were horrified when the drunkest of the already very drunk Russian officers stood up and toasted to the death of all Chechens. The next morning, we finally flew to Chechnya in several MI-8 helicopters. The one I was in had engine trouble, but the pilot responded to it with a few well-placed hammer blows. During the flight, Chechen rebels responded to our presence in their airspace with bursts of automatic gunfire. The pilot responded to the bullets by flying in zigzags. We responded to the shooting and zigzagging by drinking vodka, generously shared by a Reuters journalist flying with us. In Chechnya, we spoke with local residents who, under the watchful eye of heavily armed Spetsnaz gorillas, expressed their appreciation for the attention shown by the Russian army. We also visited a school where the Interior Minister had delivered a truckload of new computers. After the obligatory speech, the principal’s thanks, and a photo op with confused students, the computers were loaded back onto the truck and taken away. “Of course,” the principal said in response to my raised eyebrow, “we don’t have electricity.” As Putin had promised, we were able to see for ourselves the strength of Russia’s commitment to peace, democracy, rule of law, and human rights. My second meeting with the Russian president took place nearly three years later, in late November 2002. This time the delegation was smaller: just four of us, including the new president of the Parliamentary Assembly, its Secretary General, and my colleague Petr from Prague, who had studied in Moscow and insisted—despite our late arrival—on showing me the highlights of Moscow's nightlife. I’ll spare you the details but suffice it to say that Petr and I arrived the next morning at Putin’s suburban dacha in Volynskoye in less-than-optimal condition. This time, Putin no longer bothered pretending to be committed to anything. He received us in the company of two snarling Dobermans. It was like Lassie, but for psychopaths. After the meeting, we were invited to a nearby dacha by Dmitry Rogozin, then the future—and now former—Deputy Foreign Minister and Russian Ambassador to NATO. During the visit, Rogozin proudly showed us a Serbian Republic army general’s cap gifted to him by his close friend Ratko Mladić. At that moment, I had to step outside for air—I felt sick. And not because of the hangover. Rogozin made headlines in December 2022 when, during his birthday party at a hotel in occupied Donetsk, a Ukrainian rocket shrapnel hit him in the ass. I couldn’t find out what he was wearing on his head at that moment but hope springs eternal. Since then, I haven't met Putin again and doubt I ever will. But in my professional capacity, I’ve continued to deal extensively with Russia and observe its steadfast “commitment” to peace, democracy, rule of law, and human rights. In that time, we’ve seen everything imaginable—and unimaginable. From constitutional changes that abolished regional autonomy and strengthened the “vertical axis of power,” to the invasion of Georgia, laws branding NGOs as “foreign agents” to crush civil society, persecution of LGBTI individuals, the annexation of Crimea, and three years ago, the attempt to conquer all of Ukraine. In between, Putin solidified his power with murders of journalists and political opponents, imprisoned anyone who dared criticize his wars, and tossed out windows plenty of people who got on his nerves. He even found time to have the Duma decriminalize domestic violence. Putin’s Russia is a paradise for real men who can beat their wives whenever they “deserve” it. You can accuse Putin of many things—but wokeness isn’t one of them. Over the years, I’ve met many Russian citizens, activists, artists, and human rights defenders whom I deeply respect for their courage and commitment to democratic values. Sadly, most were forced to leave Russia, though some still persist, despite the risks. A year ago, I met someone organizing support for LGBTI people in Grozny, the capital of Chechnya. In Chechnya. Where bands of Kadyrov’s thugs amuse themselves by lynching gay people. To the so-called “peaceniks” who love to brand critics of Russian policy as Russophobes, I would remind them that no one has brought more suffering to Russian citizens than their own president. A quarter of a century ago, at my first meeting with Putin, the Russian president still pretended to be committed to European democratic values. Today, many in Europe are increasingly open about their admiration—or at least tolerance—for Putin’s ideas and actions, which are fundamentally at odds with the values of peaceful coexistence, international law, humanity, democracy, freedom, and human rights. All this determines whether Europe will face more war—or whether peace and reason will prevail. We all want peace. Only some of us doubt that we’ll get there by sending roses and violets to a deranged brute, hoping he won’t unleash his Dobermans on us too.

There’s been a lot of talk about Greenland lately, so I can’t resist the temptation to say a few things myself. I have a special bond with Greenland. I’ve been there. On official business — more on that later. And before you jump in to say one visit doesn’t entitle me to a “special bond,” remember: Greenland isn’t like Vrhnika, or Celje, or Munich — places you often pass through even if you don’t intend to. Greenland is far, and beyond it, there’s nothing. Figuratively speaking — unless you’re a flat-earther. Before me, Greenland was visited by Erik the Red, who, over a thousand years ago, was drifting through the northern seas after legal trouble and ended up on a vast landmass covered in ice. Erik named the territory “Greenland” to attract as many settlers as possible. That trick is still used today by real estate agents worldwide. There’s no data on whether Erik’s marketing ploy fooled anyone — at least until another real estate agent with imperial ambitions, Donald the Orange, came along. Clearly, he can’t resist the allure of green spaces untouched by his golf courses. Such lands are rare. Imagine the disappointment when his son returned from a recent visit and said: “Dad, it’s actually not as green as we thought.” Anyway, between Erik the Red’s landing and my own visit to Greenland, another notable figure lived there — my father’s friend Tarzan Mikkelsen. Why he was called Tarzan, how he and my father became friends, and why he ended up teaching in Greenland is a story for another time. But Tarzan once offered one of the most precise explanations of Danish political mentality. When my dad asked him why Denmark never had a revolution, Tarzan replied: “We came close two or three times — but then it started raining.” I’m not mentioning Tarzan Mikkelsen just to emphasize my emotional connection to Greenland. He also provides a segue to another Tarzan — one who also didn’t wear leopard-print briefs. This story has nothing to do with Greenland, but it’s too good not to share. A few years ago, Montenegro had a Minister of Agriculture named Tarzan Milošević. Unlike his Danish namesake, this Tarzan was named by his parents, not friends at a bar. In a TV interview about Montenegro’s EU accession plans in agriculture, the journalist couldn’t resist asking if his name had ever caused him trouble. Tarzan raised his eyebrows and replied: “Why? I’m not one of those Miloševićs.” But let’s return to Greenland — or rather, to the office of the late Lord Russell-Johnston, then President of the Parliamentary Assembly. This was 25 years ago, in the early days of the new millennium and the end of his term, during which I served as his political advisor and speechwriter. Russell was a passionate supporter of liberal democracy, postcard writing, Bordeaux, Chinese food, and travel. Behind his desk hung a large map of Europe. Every country he visited got a colored pin. He was starting to run out of both. One day, as he stared at the map, his eyes lit up. He leaped from his chair and pointed at Greenland. “We haven’t been there. Is that Europe?” “Yes and no,” I replied with the diplomatic precision expected of seasoned political advisors. “It’s linked to Denmark but not part of the European Union.” Russell looked disappointed. I quickly added that Greenlanders still enjoy protection under the European Convention on Human Rights. Weeks later, we were on a flight from Copenhagen to Kangerlussuaq, then the only airport in Greenland capable of handling wide-body aircraft. Planning the trip wasn’t easy — not just logistically, but diplomatically. The Danish government viewed Russell’s idea to fly in and talk to locals about human rights with considerable suspicion. Why, who knows. Kangerlussuaq is a dot in the middle of a white void. Back then, its infrastructure was more modest than that of Portorož airport, just with a longer runway. At one end stood the terminal, at the other, some aluminum barracks left over from when the area was a U.S. military base. A local bus, Route 1, ran between the airport and the “town.” According to the schedule, we had a 90-minute layover before a connecting flight to the capital Nuuk. That stretched into a day and a half. “When you arrive in Greenland,” the airport clerk kindly advised, “you take off your watch and put on a calendar.” While waiting, I took a ride on the bus. The driver was an older man from Denmark. He had come to Greenland as a young man and nearly went mad from boredom — but once back in Denmark, he began to long for the return. They call it Greenland fever. He’s now been driving buses in Kangerlussuaq for decades. And he’s as happy as a penguin. Back at the airport, we were told the plane wouldn’t be flying that day. In such cases, part of the terminal serves as a small hotel. Russell was given the presidential suite; I was offered an igloo by the runway. “You mustn’t miss this opportunity,” Russell said, handing me the key to his luxurious quarters. “It’ll be a once-in-a-lifetime experience.” “If it’s so unique, I’ll let you enjoy it,” I replied with a touch of arrogance — not expected from a seasoned political advisor. Russell muttered something gruff in return — it might have been “obstinate” or “prostate.” Probably the latter, because an igloo isn’t ideal for people who can’t hold their pee till morning. The next morning, we finally flew to Nuuk. From the plane, you could see green social housing blocks, reminiscent of Copenhagen’s working-class suburbs — an architectural symbol of Danish policy toward the Inuit: uprooting them from traditional environments to bestow upon them the blessings of the welfare state, sometimes removing children and sending them to “civilized” Denmark. All with the best of intentions, of course. To be fair, Denmark’s approach has changed, but the consequences remain — alcoholism and domestic violence are still a problem. We heard about this during our visit to Greenland’s first prison, newly opened at the time. Until then, prisoners were sent to Denmark, which only deepened trauma and complicated reintegration. The new prison in Nuuk was modern and open. Male and female inmates shared living spaces. “It’s much more humane this way,” the warden explained. “We put great emphasis on mutual respect between the sexes. It’s key to rehabilitation. Unfortunately, capacity is already full — we had a waiting list even before opening.” “No wonder,” Russell quipped, as I discreetly elbowed him — as seasoned political advisors do. We also met with Greenland’s government and parliament — a chance to see a new Greenland: confident and determined to claim long-denied respect and rights. That Greenland is even stronger today, as we see in its response to Donald Trump’s imperial posturing. What will come of Trump’s territorial ambitions remains to be seen. But there’s no doubt about how Greenlanders feel about them. I doubt Greenland will go to America. But Trump could well go to Greenland — if, God forbid, he runs into legal trouble again and, like Erik the Red, needs to hide in the icy wilderness from the hand of justice. “But I’m not one of those Trumps.” And if they catch him, he’ll probably be better off in Greenlandic prison than back home — or in El Salvador. The rehabilitation program would suit him perfectly. Maybe he’ll catch Greenland fever. Instead of ranting in the White House, he could spend the rest of his life peacefully driving Bus No. 1 in Kangerlussuaq. And we’d all be as happy as penguins.

Realpolitik, according to ChatGPT, is a political approach that gives priority to pragmatism, power and the interests of the state over ideological or moral considerations in decision-making. The key characteristics of realpolitik are a focus on the national interest and power as the main criteria of political action, and pragmatic decisions bound not by values but by what is effective and achievable. Realpolitik often involves compromises, diplomatic maneuvers, even manipulation or military force, and disregards moral ideals if they hinder the achievement of political goals. Especially in this last characteristic—disregarding moral ideals—realpolitik comes close to a political doctrine known in Slovenia by the slogan “neither left nor right, but forward.” When you google who the main protagonists of realpolitik were in the past, the internet offers you a colorful picture of personalities, from Machiavelli to Bismarck and Henry Kissinger. Frequently cited examples of realpolitik in modern times include American (and not only American) policy toward Saudi Arabia, or Germany’s policy toward Putin’s Russia until recently. Ideological purists and moral preachers will surely cry shame at all this. On the other hand, it is also true that international politics, and domestic politics too, in tackling the greatest challenges and threats, often require dialogue and cooperation beyond one’s own ideological convictions and interests. Without pragmatism, some will surely argue, there would have been no end to the Cold War or nuclear disarmament (while that still existed as an active international process). I can’t resist the temptation to write that the right path lies somewhere in between. On the one hand, a purist insistence on consistent respect for moral principles often runs into the obstacle of reality and turns into impotent moaning and complaining, or even into adjusting reality and facts and creating parallel realities in which we can lie to ourselves that we remain faithful to our ideals. An instructive example of the latter is the discourse of Slovenian “peace activists” regarding Russia and its aggression against Ukraine. On the other hand, in the conflict between interests and ethics, the pragmatism of realpolitik can side so obviously and exclusively with (its own narrow political and economic) interests that it loses all moral integrity and credibility and turns society and the world into a jungle in which only the strongest and most ruthless prevail and decide. A good example of this is Western policy toward the bloody tragedy in the Middle East. But we cannot and must not look for a middle path between interests and values at the arithmetic midpoint, still less in subordinating ethics to narrow and short-term political and economic ambitions. When it comes to positioning themselves between interests and morality, authoritarians and democrats are not in the same position. The former need not concern themselves with morality; trampling on ethical and humanist principles is, so to speak, part of their job description. It is different with liberal democracies, that is, states that base their social and political orientation on the values of democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights. They have very little room for maneuver when it comes to ignoring ethics and morality in their own policies. They should be aware of this. But evidently they are not. And if we are looking for the reasons why liberal democracy as a political and social system is in such crisis today, this is certainly one of the most important. In today’s world, which increasingly resembles the jungle mentioned above, ruled by the most uncouth primates, attitude toward and respect for fundamental civilizational, humanist and democratic principles is for liberal democracies not a question of momentary interests but of survival. Without a turn from realpolitik to moral politics, democracy as a social and political system is doomed to long-term subordination, or even extinction. The conflicts and attacks on the most fundamental values of solidarity, humanism, non-discrimination, respect for human dignity and freedom that we are witnessing in today’s world are not a sideshow but the central clash between the concept of a democratic society based on the Enlightenment and the authoritarian, anti-woke, russkiy mir bullying pushed by Trump, Putin and their increasingly emboldened cronies scattered around the world and Europe. What the final outcome of this civilizational conflict will be is hard to predict for now. The bullies seem to have the advantage, because they are big, ruthless and loud. But in the end what will also count is how those respond who—at least declaratively—advocate and swear by the values of a civilized, free and humanist society. What the world will look like tomorrow, and whether there will still be room in it for democracy and international order, is being decided in Ukraine and in the Middle East, and also on every occasion, big or small, when politicians committed to democracy must decide where they stand between momentary interests (as they themselves interpret them) and ethical conduct. That democracies are not powerless in this situation was shown by the recent elections in Canada. The price of flattery and compromise, meanwhile, was paid a few days ago by the governing Labour Party in Britain’s local elections. Moral horse-trading with Trump across the pond is grist to the mill of the little Trumps at home. This is a lesson our domestic defenders of democracy and democratic values should not ignore. Their fiery moralizing for domestic consumption rings hollow and two-faced if they are prepared to shove their principles into a corner so quickly for every opportunistic photo with Slovenia’s son-in-law or his oligarchs, and then even post these snapshots on social media, with nebulous captions that sound not only tasteless but also utterly frivolous.
Stop Creating and Go Do Some Work!

“What are you thinking for, go do some work” is for me one of the most obnoxious and primitive Slovenian idioms. It brings back memories of bullies in primary school, teenage pimples and stale sweat. The insinuation—if I may use such a complicated word for something so dumb—that there is a conflict between thinking and working seemed primitive to me then, as it does today. Actually, especially today, because it is no longer just the quip of juvenile thugs, but a political and ideological discourse that creates and stokes revolt against thinking and creating “elites.” Today, “what are you thinking for, go do some work” is part of the standard repertoire of what many call common sense, about which Albert Einstein already said that it is nothing but the collection of prejudices acquired by age eighteen. It is no coincidence that the Trump administration proudly calls its rampage through American institutions a “common sense revolution.” My aversion has several layers. First, it gets on my nerves because these are, quite simply, bullies, and mistreating one’s fellow human beings is something I personally can’t stand. Second, because it is a construct. Not only because thinking (and creating) is work, but also because people who do (physical) work are not by default incapable of thinking and creating. In my life I have met quite a few fools with doctorates and even more people whose life circumstances may not have allowed them a longer education, but who inspired me with their ideas, thinking, creativity and values. My third reservation is political. Incitement has clearly defined goals. As a rule, those who stoke the revolt of the “people” against the “elites” themselves come from political and economic elites and merely exploit the often real hardship and discontent of workers and other socially, economically and politically marginalized groups to promote their own political and economic interests. Rotten, but it works. All this goes through my head as I follow debates on the role of culture, art and artists in today’s Slovenia. What is happening here is, of course, nothing exceptional. The fight against “elites,” whether artists, scientists, journalists, civil society, judges, doctors or political competitors, is the driving force of authoritarian populism everywhere. Culture has a particularly important place in the populist ideological paradigm. While the liberal part of the political spectrum often has trouble understanding the importance of culture and art for democracy, those on the illiberal fringe understand it much better. They have deformed—actually turned upside down—the concepts of culture, art, tradition and identity, and are now using them successfully in their campaign to undermine democratic and humanist principles. In the hands of populists, “culture” becomes a uniform by which, on the battlefield of the culture war, we tell “ours” from “theirs,” and a club with which we beat the nation’s dangerous misfits over the head. From this perspective, every artist who does not fit the populist mold of nationally conscious creation is disruptive and dangerous. Artists who create not just to be liked, but follow their calling, which is not always adapted to market or political expectations, become targets for whipping up the masses and scoring political points. Greedy leeches on the breast of a nation that doesn’t think but only works. Artists who are too lazy and not Riefenstahl enough. They become part of what, in times we believed would never return, was called degenerate art, and for which some today—with an evident lack of, or contempt for, historical memory of green valleys soaked in blood—use the same term. It is not a matter of dividing artistic creation into what people like and what suits only the “elites.” In both you will find all sorts, from creative excellence to trash. De gustibus non est disputandum, said the ancient Romans, but people who haughtily sneer at “popular culture” get up my nose too. Personally, I am moved both by “Tam kjer murke cveto” and by Maja Smrekar. OK, not in the same way, but still. And I’m perfectly cool if one or the other isn’t your thing. But the fact is that we cannot and must not restrict freedom of artistic expression on the basis of personal preferences, reservations, prejudices and least of all political interests. And it is not only a matter of taste and personal preference. It is about freedom and success, including in development and the economy. Years ago, we invited the longtime director of the Ars Electronica festival in Linz, Gerfried Stocker, as the keynote speaker at a conference of European education ministers. The theme was education for a digital society. The assembled ministers were surprised not only by Gerfried’s long hacker hair and crumpled T-shirt, but above all by his view that culture is one of the most important components of preparing for a digital future. The key to a humane and humanist future, in which technology and artificial intelligence will play an ever greater role, is human creativity that creates, comments, challenges and criticizes. Gerfried’s message is clear. Go think and create if you want to keep working. Most of today’s children will in future do jobs that don’t yet exist. If we want to work and be successful tomorrow too, we need not only digital skills but also critical thinking and creativity. That is why we need culture. Not only the pleasant kind, but the annoying kind too. Slovenia built its state and its democracy on the foundation of its culture, among other things. Throughout history, this culture was co-created by many artists who were not to everyone’s liking, still less to the liking of every regime, but who nevertheless, or precisely because of it, made an important contribution to who we are and what we have achieved as a nation, a society and a state. That is exactly what the quarrel about the importance of culture and about real and fake artists in today’s Slovenia is about. Whether we will be independent and successful in the future too. And above all, whether we will go on thinking, creating and working. Not as day laborers for artificially intelligent bullies, foreign bosses and populist fools—but freely and for ourselves.

Recently I came across a Facebook post by my former high school teacher who, in the context of debates on whether Slovenia too should increase defense spending, complained that people had not read Hemingway’s novel A Farewell to Arms, implying that if they had, they would not be arming themselves. This teacher has always been very dear to me, because in times when single-mindedness was in fashion he encouraged students to think critically. And because he succeeded in this, this time I cannot agree with him. If we must drag Hemingway into this tiresome debate of ours, let us do it the way he taught us. In the debate on whether Russian imperialism should be deterred or embraced, only the title of A Farewell to Arms is more or less relevant. On the question of which side Hemingway would take in this dilemma, the novel For Whom the Bell Tolls, set during the Spanish Civil War, tells us more. Hemingway observed that war as a reporter and writer, but he never hid which side he was on. He never, for example, suggested that the Republicans lay down their arms in the name of peace and surrender themselves to the mercy of the Francoist Falange. He was, if I may use a more modern term, a Francophobe and a warmonger. In For Whom the Bell Tolls he created the character of the peacemaker Pablo, leader of a rebel band who does not want to provoke the fascists because he fears their reprisals. To prevent an attack on the Francoists, he steals the detonators and throws them into the river. Because when did detonators ever bring peace? Pablo repents in the end, but it is already too late. His peace operation has tragic consequences. But fiction is fiction, and reality is another matter. Except for some. For Spomenka Hribar, for example, who recently wrote in an open letter that Russia has never attacked anyone. Get it? She was not talking only about the latest excursion into Ukraine, but about any time in history. Never. Nikogda. People like Spomenka Hribar enjoy standing and influence among the Slovenian public. That is why such a statement is particularly shocking. Not because I disagree with it—in a democratic society it is normal for us to hold different positions on important questions—but because democracy also requires that these positions be based on facts, not on obvious untruths. Why many Slovenian intellectuals and politicians use a discourse that often coincides with what we hear from the Kremlin, I don’t know. But the fact is that through their influence they significantly shape Slovenian public opinion on one of the most important questions in the history of the Slovenian state so far. Why panic and buy weapons if Russia has never in history attacked anyone? This text is being written in Ukraine. I was invited to take part in the opening ceremony of the European Youth Capital, for which Lviv was chosen this year. The courage, creativity and stubbornness of young Ukrainians, after three years of a war forced upon them, deserve every support and admiration. The motto of Lviv 2025 is “It’s not easy, but we keep going.” I didn’t have the heart to mention Spomenka Hribar’s theses about Russian peacefulness to them. Perhaps she will find the opportunity and the courage to explain them herself. To their faces. History these days is a self-service restaurant. You pick what suits you; if something isn’t on the menu, you add it yourself. With their selective historical memory, Slovenian peace activists populistically claim an exclusive moral right to advocate peace and in this way try to delegitimize the views of people who seek a path to peace on the basis of facts and in the real world. Anyone who doesn’t think as they do is a warmonger. A Russophobe. Some take positions on this (and other questions) the way English children play children’s games. Simon says support Ukraine. And then half of them follow Simon without thinking, and half are against without thinking. Except that we are not English. We are Janezes. In this circus there are, of course, trolls too, warriors of Resnica (Truth), who warn against the folly of arming to defend against aggression and the danger of injecting vaccines to defend against disease. And they like to toss LGBTI people, women and migrants into the minestrone as well. I do have suspicions about where some of them get their zeal and talking points, but without evidence I will claim nothing. Perhaps the KGB really did send its agents to Slovenia exclusively to deal in works of art. Then there are some of the media. On the show Marcel, guests in the studio compete every Monday over who can agree more with the host. We check public opinion with polls. Are you for or against buying weapons? Are you for war or peace? Click, click, click. The answers to questions put this way are known in advance, and their credibility regarding the challenges we face is questionable, evidently also in the opinion of the respondents themselves. In the latest Eurobarometer, we Slovenians were, of all, the most massively in favor of Europe taking better care of our security. Better safe than sorry. The government is not finding its way very well in this confusion, and sometimes it seems only to add to it. We will increase defense investment, or we won’t, or we will, but we don’t know by how much or by when; in any case, don’t worry, because we’ll pull a trick and promise one thing in Brussels and spend the money differently at home. With such behavior the government is doing itself a disservice both with our European partners and with Slovenian voters. With the former it reduces its credibility; with the latter it creates doubt about the justification for increasing the defense budget. In the end it will have less influence on joint decisions, and implementing them may cause it considerable political damage with voters. Once again we have managed to make a mess of such important questions. The problem is not that we disagree—we do live in a democracy, after all—the problem is that we are unable to talk like adults, responsibly and on the basis of facts. Instead of engaging with arguments, we pelt each other with labels and ideological slogans. It is high time we got our act together and organized a serious public debate in which there is no room for trolls and untruths, and made an effort to reach the broadest possible consensus on the way forward. It is important to secure influence in shaping common European positions. True, we are small, but that does not mean we have to make ourselves even smaller. If there are to be greater European investments in defense, it matters how we reach that goal and what the consequences will be for social, economic, development and environmental policies, on which European security depends at least as much as on drones and tanks. Slovenia has legitimate interests here, and its citizens legitimate expectations. It is important that these positions and expectations are taken into account in future European defense policy. To achieve this, our European partners must take us seriously. To achieve that, we must first take ourselves seriously. So far, we are not doing very well at it.

The war in Ukraine has brought a great deal of confusion into the Slovenian sport of quarreling between Partisans and Home Guards. Suddenly many Partisans have reservations about national liberation struggle, while people who regularly flip out every time people gather for the commemoration at Dražgoše loudly support the fight against a foreign occupier. But we quarrel all the same. About populism, for example. There is confusion here too, above all because some can’t make up their minds whether populists are cool or not. The latest episode of this verbal civil war began with a special issue (funny how ambiguous the Slovenian language can be: izdaja means both “issue” and “betrayal”) of the weekly Mladina devoted to populists. In it, the editors allowed themselves an impermissible move and included Josip Broz Tito among the populists. Fire rained down on the editors from the left and the left. How dare you call Tito a populist? How dare you put him in the same category as the other populist scoundrels? Many of the comments were, as befits squabbling on social media, crude and insulting. Things went so far that Mladina’s editor Grega Repovž, exceptionally in his own name, published an editorial in the next regular issue expressing his dismay at a new low in discourse on Slovenian social media. Hardly had the affair died down a little, as the stormtroopers of Slovenian keyboards had sniffed out another bone, when posts began appearing on my feed of a text published in the magazine Disenz under the title “The Delusions of Anti-Populism” by the sociologist Grega Hrib, in which the author, in short, lectured bourgeois liberals that they don’t get populism, through which “hordes of angry voters who don’t care about political civility, the rule of law and established rules are showing liberal democracy the middle finger and slowly but steadily sending it to the dustbin of history.” Let me say at the outset that I agree with this analysis in principle. What bothers me is the gloating with which the author, throughout the piece, announces what he considers the more than deserved end of “bourgeois” liberalism, with the fury of—forgive me for mixing metaphors for decency’s sake—an enraged man who saws off the branch he is sitting on with a blunt knife to take revenge on his unfaithful wife. I believe one of the reasons for the quarrel about populism and liberal democracy is a mistaken understanding of the terms we are talking about. This is, of course, one of the characteristics of the period we live in, in which “hordes of angry voters” consistently take refuge in “facts” that suit them emotionally and ideologically. I do not count the author of the Disenz piece among the latter. He is someone who certainly knows a great deal and has read a great deal. In his analysis of populism and anti-populism, he cites the post-Marxist theorists Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe. As, incidentally, do all the left-leaning enthusiasts for populism I have come across in recent years. Laclau and Mouffe are to left-wing pro-populists what Friedrich Hayek is to enthusiasts of neoliberalism. A theoretical ace up the sleeve, after which there is no more debate. So let me explain how I understand populism and liberalism. As for the first, populism is not people-pleasing, which is a pathological need to be liked. A good example of a people-pleaser is Borut Pahor, whom many, mistakenly in my view, consider a populist. That does not mean his conduct did not often, wittingly or unwittingly, support populism, of which there is no shortage in Slovenia. A populist, in principle, couldn’t care less whether people like him; what matters above all is that they hate his opponents. A populist claims the exclusive right to represent the people and, in the name of that exclusivity, places himself above all political competition, while delegitimizing or subordinating the other branches of power and democratic safeguards, from independent media to civil society. Donald Trump, for example. But not only him. If we apply the above definition to Josip Broz, then we must surely agree that, despite all his merits in the fight against fascism, he showed no particular understanding for political competition, an independent judiciary, the oversight function of a democratically elected parliament over the executive, independent media or a critical civil society. All in the name of the people and the working class. And so Mladina was entirely justified in including him on the list on its cover. The muddle about liberalism is even worse. Here people confuse liberals as a centrist political platform, liberal democracy as a political system, neoliberalism as an economic dogma, and the libertarian, who is the gentleman scattering inanities across Slovenian social media from an armchair in London with a teddy bear in his hand. Liberals as a centrist political formation exist, at least in theory. They are characterized by a commitment to free enterprise, combined with advocacy of individual rights and freedoms. The existence and credibility of liberals, in Slovenia too, are threatened by the fact that a whole bunch of chancers hitch a ride under this label, understanding the center geometrically rather than in terms of values and ideology, and selling personal interests under the guise of liberalism, which they try to disguise by loudly shouting “neither left nor right, but forward.” Liberal democracy is a political system. Its shortest definition is regular elections plus the European Convention on Human Rights. Respecting the provisions of the Convention not only ensures that elections are free and fair, but also protects the rights and freedoms of individuals and minorities in society, with constitutional and legal safeguards, against abuse by the ruling majority. To this definition must be added social rights, which give citizens the material basis for trust in liberal democracy. Problems arise because people confuse liberal democracy and neoliberalism. The latter is based on the denial of the public interest and solidarity, and builds a bright future on the lowest possible taxes, the absence of any regulation, and the invisible hand of the market, which regularly takes care of the prosperity of the few, and which, neoliberals assure us, is supposed to trickle down to everyone in time. That has never happened; instead there has been social pauperization and political marginalization of an ever larger share of the population, which has responded, how else, by showing the middle finger and supporting populists. They offer no solutions, but unlike many defenders of liberal democracy, they at least recognize the pain and anger of the pissed-off plebs. And exploit them mercilessly to pursue their own economic and political interests. Economic neoliberalism is the main reason liberal democracy is doing so badly, as it destroys the material basis for voters’ trust in the political system. It causes fear of the future, which is grist to the populist mill. Populism exploits fear and stokes anger. The greatest threat to Western civilization is empathy, says Elon Musk. The ideological foundation of Trump’s revolution is the fight against diversity, equity and inclusion. Populism builds its authoritarian march to power on the manipulation of hatred and, when that is no longer enough, on repression. Yet equating liberal democracy and neoliberalism is not entirely without basis. The fact is that many politicians who had their mouths full of human rights and the protection of social minorities at the same time calmly ignored social rights, without which liberal democracy cannot function and which in the end prepares the ground for the rise of illiberal and authoritarian populism, which exploits people’s hardship to push them even further into the muck. So populism does not bring freedom to the “hordes of angry voters,” but quite the opposite. It puts into their hands an ever blunter knife with which they saw off you-know-what themselves. Out of (justified) rage at liberal democrats who serve them personal freedom without social rights, they cheer for populists who in return offer them political authoritarianism and economic misery camouflaged by the adrenaline of hatred. All that is left to them is to rage at gays, feminists and migrants, who are supposedly to blame for everything. Perhaps one day we will realize that there is no freedom without social security. And vice versa. Until then, good night and good luck.

Recently, social media erupted with the claim that U.S. President Donald Trump had been recruited into the KGB in 1987 and given the operative codename “Krasnov.” The source of this shocking revelation was Alnur Musaev, a former head of Kazakhstan’s intelligence service, who in his younger years served in the KGB’s 6th Directorate in Moscow. That division was responsible for counterintelligence operations in the economic sphere, with one of its main goals being the recruitment of businessmen from capitalist countries. According to Musaev, Trump — then a 40-year-old New York real estate investor — was one such recruit. Musaev dropped this bombshell where else but on Facebook. Despite the supposed credibility of the source, I thought it wise to verify the claim before writing about it. In the spirit of our times, I turned to artificial intelligence and used Elon Musk’s Grok app. And lo and behold — Trump’s very own pet AI estimated the likelihood that he’s a Russian agent somewhere between 75% and 85%. At last, everything explained. Trump is compromised and blackmailed. Despite Musaev and Grok, I remain skeptical. I believe a conspiracy theory remains a conspiracy theory — even if it suits my emotional needs. There simply isn’t enough evidence to assert that Trump is a Russian agent. But that’s not the real question. The question we should ask is: If Trump were a Russian agent, would he behave any differently than he does now? And the answer, of course, is no. So if his cruelty toward the victim of aggression and sympathy for the aggressor are not the result of kompromat, then we must logically look for the motivation elsewhere. In my view, it lies in the ideological convergence between these two “best friends forever.” Trump feels close to Putin. He wants to be his friend and ally. This was made painfully clear in his emotional reaction to Zelensky’s words in the Oval Office, and in his follow-up statement the next day: “Zelensky is always speaking badly about Putin,” he complained indignantly — about the president of a nation that has been a victim of Russian aggression for over a decade. Trump wants to be Putin. Or Kim Jong Un. He doesn’t want to be a president — he wants to be a ruler. He expects blind loyalty and admiration. During his last meeting with Kim, he said he wished his subordinates treated him the same way North Koreans venerate their Supreme Leader. And now, he’s making that happen. First, he North-Koreanized the Republican Party — and now he’s doing the same with the entire U.S. state and public apparatus. Just look at the eruptions of idolatry from his aides after the meeting with Zelensky. Secretary of State Marco Rubio — supposedly one of the “moderates” in Trump’s cabinet — slouched on the couch during the meeting like someone who’d just been conditionally released from a re-education camp. Trump wants to be Putin because they share imperial ambitions. A Russian victory in Ukraine sets a precedent — paving the way for a possible Anschluss of Canada, control of the Panama Canal and Greenland, and a real estate project in Gaza. The tragicomic paradox is that in Slovenia, the most fervent anti-American and anti-imperialist voices are now the most ardent supporters of the American imperialist — at least as seen through their view of the Ukraine conflict. Trump wants to be Putin because they share the same worldview. This isn’t just some columnist’s inflated rhetoric. The Financial Times published an analysis showing that under Trump, the Republican Party’s value system is now aligned with Putin’s Russia — and even further to the right than many of Europe’s far-right parties. (Although perhaps the analysis didn’t include all of them.) Trump and Putin are allies in a global jihad against “cultural Marxism” — which is the Alpine equivalent of what Americans call “wokeness,” and the Russians label as the corrupt and decadent West threatening the purity and survival of the holy Russian people. Different labels, same content. It’s a war against everything that forms the foundation of a free, open, successful democratic society. The state, the nation, and the leader are supposedly threatened by: trans people (blah blah blah), journalists (blah blah blah), migrants (blah blah blah), LGBTQ+ communities (blah blah blah), environmentalists (blah blah blah), NGOs (blah blah blah), feminists (blah blah blah)... It’s an ideologically framed revenge campaign by frustrated white men. A sledgehammer to reshape the world into a transactional jungle, where brute force overrides international norms, borders, individual rights and freedoms, and human dignity. Trump wants to be Putin — and Putin wants Trump. This ideological bromance is putting much of Slovenia’s political spectrum in a bind. The right is embarrassed because Trump embodies all the values of their political platform — except that he’s turned against Ukraine, a country they supported (out of conviction or opportunism) three years ago. They’re doing their best to manage the contradiction. The most amusing — and telling — attempt came from a “libertarian influencer” temporarily based in London, who claimed on X that left-wing extremists had forced Trump into what he’s doing. As in, “he didn’t want to, but had no choice.” The comment is interesting because it hints at a potential 180-degree shift — essentially saying that in the global fight against cultural Marxism, sacrifices must be made. Like Ukraine. You can’t make a fascist omelet without breaking some liberal eggs. The left, for its part, deals with the contradiction mostly by ignoring it. They love Trump because he’s doing to Ukraine everything they’ve long wanted and demanded. Aurelio Juri would award him the Nobel Peace Prize. MPs from the ruling coalition are forming a parliamentary friendship group with Russia. They don’t concern themselves with the ideological subtext or the inherent imperialism behind Trump’s undermining of Ukraine’s national liberation struggle. Since Trump is doing what they want in Ukraine, they project their rage at the U.S. onto Europe instead. That damn witch von der Leyen is to blame for everything. They don’t form their positions based on the real world — but on the world they wish existed. Like a bunch of sleep-deprived, Red Bull-fueled students playing SimCity all night, tweaking the parameters of reality as they build their utopia. Russia poses no threat, NATO is to blame for everything, Ukrainians are Nazis, and we’re safe because we don’t like war or spending on defense. And if SimCity crashes — because even a video game has limits — no problem. Reset. Play again. With this kind of mindset, the Slovenian Prime Minister is, as I write this, heading to Brussels for talks on increasing defense spending in response to the Russian threat and the undermining of the European civilizational model built after WWII. Many in Slovenia oppose higher defense spending because “we don’t like war.” It’s an appealing argument — but logically weak. It’s like believing that leaving your front door unlocked will protect you from burglars. Yet in one crucial way, I agree with the skeptics. It would be suicidal to increase defense spending by cutting funding for environmental protection, education, international aid, science and research, and — most importantly — for a socially secure society where people have the material conditions to believe in a better future. It’s precisely the neglect of these foundations of democracy over recent decades that has led to the accumulation of dissatisfaction and anger toward democracy — anger now skillfully exploited by its enemies, especially in Moscow, against whom we seek to arm ourselves. But investments in drones, tanks, and cannons to protect European democracy from external danger will be useless if they deepen the hole eating away at democracy from within. We’re not living in a computer game. In today’s dangerous world, there is no reset button. If we crash, it’s game over for democracy in Europe.

Imagine a gang of robbers entering a bank, emptying the vault, and to start things off, shooting a few employees and customers while taking the rest hostage. The police chief arrives on the scene and, speaking through a megaphone, first scolds the hostages for provoking the bloodshed, then negotiates with the robbers to release the captives. In exchange, the robbers are allowed to keep the loot — and even take a selfie with the police chief. At the press conference, the chief claims full credit for the peaceful resolution of the crisis and then demands that the freed hostages and the families of those killed pay half their income to the police union as compensation for the rescue. He celebrates his success at the estate of the gang leader — on May 9th in Moscow. It’s becoming increasingly clear that the war in Ukraine, started by Russia’s aggression, will — after three, or rather ten years — sooner or later end in some kind of truce. After all the destruction and loss of life, the first instinctive reaction is, understandably, relief. War is evil. People die in war. War must end as soon as possible. This reaction is legitimate and human, regardless of the circumstances under which the truce is likely to occur. On the other hand, it is equally legitimate — and necessary — to talk about these circumstances, especially the consequences, not only for Ukraine but also for Europe, the world, and Slovenia, which, though often behaving as if we’re in a parallel universe, is part of this Europe and this world. First, we should be concerned that, by all accounts, the agreement will hand victory to the aggressor. This is not just a moral issue — it’s a security risk. The aggressor has made clear that their imperial ambitions do not stop at the current front line, nor even at the outer borders of the current victim, but go well beyond. Second, this will not be a truce Ukraine, as the victim of Russian aggression, wanted or deserved after three years of bloody war and resistance. Still, that fact does not give us the right to dispute the agreement if Ukraine accepts it — even under duress, after the U.S., under Trump’s orders, turned its back on them overnight. Those unhappy with the outcome, yet unwilling or unable to help Ukraine defend its freedom and territorial integrity, have no right to sit in armchairs cheering for continued bloodshed. Third, even if such an outcome is inevitable given the current balance of power, we should at least maintain enough dignity, rationality, and self-preservation to refrain from celebrating it as a great victory. Doing so increases the chances that the next act of aggression — possibly against us — will end with a similar “peace solution.” Fourth, let’s take a closer look at the main architects of this “peace solution.” On one side is the re-elected U.S. president Donald Trump, who is now “solving” the war in Ukraine, emboldened by his “success” in ending the bloodbath in Gaza. I put quotes around these words not because I don’t welcome the end (for now) of the year-long bloody tragedy in Gaza, which followed a horrific attack on Israeli civilians. But we must ask: how did Trump bring about peace in the Middle East? Many claim that unlike his elderly, worn-out predecessor, Trump managed to pressure Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu into negotiations. I think it was more a case of Netanyahu realizing he’d get far more favorable terms from Trump than from Biden. And he was right. Trump first lifted sanctions on violent Jewish settlers in the West Bank — who were hunting Palestinians like rabbits — and then proposed his “genius” idea of deporting Gaza’s residents and transforming the area into a seaside resort “for global citizens.” Netanyahu could hardly believe his ears. To those who are outraged by this and still insist every truce in Ukraine must be supported, I’d point out: Trump’s “solution” also brings “peace” to Gaza. If there are no more Palestinians there, there’ll be no more conflict — only squabbles among “global citizens” over sunbeds and umbrellas on blood-soaked beaches. As for what Trump has been doing to democracy in the U.S. since his inauguration — I won’t waste words. We’re all witnessing it in real-time. At breakneck speed, he is dismantling or subjugating every democratic, public, and state institution to enrich his billionaire backers and prevent Americans from being able to democratically remove him once they finally realize what they’ve elected. The ideological ammunition in this anti-democratic blitzkrieg is a reactionary agenda built on division and hatred. In the name of “freedom,” he viciously attacks political opponents, social groups, and critical voices. His foreign policy consists of listing countries and territories he plans to dominate. In all of this, Trump is perfectly aligned with his new best friend forever, Vladimir Putin. Their alliance may be historically shocking, but it is ideologically completely logical. The second architect of “peace” is Vladimir Putin — a dictator who rose to power through terrorist attacks on his own citizens, started several wars at home and abroad, ordered the aggression against Ukraine, and is responsible for Bucha, Mariupol, and the deaths of thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The Russian president has had at least thirteen journalists murdered — not to mention political opponents. Critical voices in Russia are gone. The lucky ones end up in prison. The others fall out of windows. So these two comrades have now found a path to peace. Trump even demands that the victim of aggression — Ukraine — pay $500 billion in war reparations. This sum is much higher than the actual U.S. aid given to Ukraine, which was lower than Europe’s, and neither of which approaches the fortune Elon Musk — Trump’s adjutant — has amassed since Trump’s election. Trump “forced” Putin into the agreement by preemptively accepting all his conditions. Putin probably can’t believe his luck. He gets to keep the loot — and encouragement for future heists. As for Europe — there's not much to say. Most leaders are still in the first stage of grief: denial. They’re clearly still hoping to wake up and find that this nightmare is over. Trump from one side, and Putin from the other, are pressing every button — undermining, both externally and internally, the last shreds of power and influence a weakened and divided Europe may still possess. And in Slovenia? We’re taking selfies with Trump and Musk, swooning over Melania’s hat, writing letters to the Nobel Peace Prize committee, and forming friendship groups with Russia. Trump is, in fact, the perfect ideological Frankenstein for “transcending ideological differences” in our deeply polarized public and political life. For some, his bromance with Putin is a plus — Putin still enjoys hero status among part of the ideologically and cognitively dissonant left. For others, Trump backs their cultural war against everything that civilized, democratic societies should stand for. No more war in Ukraine! Hooray! Peace has arrived! No one bothers to think about what awaits us in the brave new world that Donald and Vladimir are building. "What a cute little country you have here on the sunny side of the Alps. It’d be a real shame if anything happened to it." Maybe it’s time to reconsider reopening the uranium mine at Žirovski Vrh. Second grade coal from Velenje mine and Melania won’t be enough in the transactional future, where only the strong decide. It won’t be enough for freedom, security, and independence either — but maybe, just maybe, it’ll allow us to crawl on, in humble survival. Hooray.
From Slovenia to America, for a Better World

In November 2016, just days after Donald Trump’s first victory in the U.S. presidential election, I received a request through an acquaintance from a Wall Street Journal journalist, asking whether I’d be willing to describe the pride I felt as a fellow Slovenian entering the White House. I gladly accepted the invitation and sent the journalist a message — which The Wall Street Journal never published. I don’t know why. “I understand that Americans love good rags-to-riches stories, but I don’t understand why so many Slovenians are so excited and proud to play the role of the ragged in this story. Because of them, we come across as an amorphous, primitive bunch of Eastern European buffoons, unwilling, unable, or uninterested in taking an ethical — or any — stance on events shaping the world around us, simply because we’re so desperate for attention and hope that some random connection to the decline of liberal democracy and basic human decency in the world’s most powerful country might bring us a buck or two. Slovenia fought for its independence in the name of values that are in many ways the polar opposite of those that brought Melania’s husband to the White House. I have nothing against the poor woman, but there aren’t enough Tic Tac mints in the world to make me root for a man whose core values I fundamentally reject — just because I was born in the same country as his wife.” For those who may have forgotten, I mentioned the mints in reference to Trump’s statement that he always freshens his breath before groping women. Because even if he’s a sexual predator, he’s still a gentleman. I remembered that never-published reply eight years later, while following the media and political reactions to the return of Slovenia’s son-in-law to the White House. If the situation weren’t so serious and troubling, this media and political circus might even be amusing. It’s not every day you see a prime minister competing with Branko Grims over who loves Donald Trump — or Elon Musk — more. But it’s not funny, because the situation is serious and troubling. Of course, it’s clear to everyone that politics must adapt to the new reality and find ways to safeguard national interests amid these changed and unpredictable circumstances. Trump will be president of the United States for the next four years, and we can’t just ignore that because we disagree with him or find him repugnant. We need smart diplomacy to help us get through the upcoming period with as little damage as possible. But what we’ve been witnessing since the announcement of the November election results is neither smart nor diplomatic. It’s a breathtaking display of opportunistic servility and shameless fawning. One senses confusion, discomfort, and helplessness. Not just elsewhere — here, too. The widespread idea that in Trump’s brave new world we should seek business opportunities and promotion for our country through his third wife, or even hope that Melania might make him slightly less brutal toward us than toward others, is humiliating. There are already final court rulings on how considerate Trump is toward Melania. Hoping he’ll be kinder to us because of her is just dumb. Appeasement is the wrong strategy when dealing with psychological profiles like Trump’s. The man obviously enjoys groveling — but he despises the grovelers. That’s the whole point: the thrill of watching others humiliate themselves. Appeasement is also unnecessary. It’s a panicked reaction to the artificially constructed myth of Trump’s political invincibility and inevitability, both in the U.S. and globally. This myth is partly fueled by Trump himself through a constant barrage of increasingly insane, scandalous, and dangerous moves — from banning plastic straws to real estate plans in Gaza. But we help fuel the myth too — especially the media, who, out of fear, opportunism, clickbait greed, lack of journalistic ethics, or sheer stupidity, uncritically repeat the narratives dictated by the White House. “Trump broke the president of Colombia in 24 hours,” “Trump brought Mexico and Canada to their knees” — these are just two of the typical headlines we’ve been reading in Slovenian media since the election, alongside in-depth analyses of the subtle messages in Melania’s hat. Yet these three examples also show that you get much further with Trump if you find your spine and stand up to him. Contrary to the image promoted by most media, in each of those conflicts — with Colombia, Mexico, and Canada — Trump was the first to blink. Deportations of undocumented Colombians are proceeding just as they did under Biden — with scheduled flights and no shackles on wrists or ankles. Punitive tariffs on Mexican and Canadian goods were delayed in exchange for hokey concessions mainly aimed at massaging Trump’s ego. This doesn’t mean that a trade war won’t escalate or spread in the future — only that we’ll navigate this madness far better if we find our backbone. Far worse and more dangerous are the consequences of uncritically feeding the Trump myth when the Slovenian son-in-law isn’t just threatening tariffs, but also announcing conquests of foreign territories — from Canada to Greenland, through Panama, and now even Gaza, which he’d clear of Palestinians to build seaside resorts for “global citizens.” At this point, reasonable people — if any remain in politics — must ask themselves where opportunistic normalization and rationalization of such rhetoric leads, especially when those words may become actions tomorrow. Those who loudly applauded his “role” in solving the Middle East crisis need to look in the mirror and ask whether they’re ready to share moral responsibility for his blundering — in which he disregards not only Palestinians, but ultimately Israelis too, serving only his ego and self-image as a global boss. We can only fear what his next “brilliant” ideas will be for ending the war in Ukraine — a war he says he recently discussed with Putin, who supposedly told him he wants “people to stop dying.” As if Putin had nothing to do with how the dying started. American journalist Ezra Klein had a simple response to Trump: Don’t believe him. Trump is hollow on the inside, and there’s nothing around him. Stop enabling him and holding his hand. If we stop believing him, eventually he’ll run out of breath.

Last Wednesday, just two days after the inauguration of the newest U.S. president, employees at the local TV station WDJT-TV in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, received a brief notice stating that weather forecaster Sam Kuffel, 31, had "left" the station. The management gave no reason for the young meteorologist’s departure, but a day earlier, conservative radio host Dan O'Donnell harshly criticized Kuffel over two of her Instagram posts, accusing her of "spreading lies that Elon Musk performed a Nazi salute at the presidential inauguration." He, quite justifiably in my opinion, described her posts as "vulgar." Let’s not forget — this is Elon Musk, a man who, in the eyes of millions, represents hope that speech might finally be freed from the chains imposed by corrupt liberal authoritarians. After all, we Slovenians are directly affected as well. The first politician to propose Elon Musk for the Nobel Peace Prize — precisely for his contributions to liberating speech — hails from our own country. Even the Slovenian Prime Minister recently proudly posted a selfie standing with Musk beneath the caption: "From Slovenia to America, for a better world." Elon liberates. He liberates even us — those of us who mean well at heart. That’s why it's right and just that the Milwaukee station's management reacted as it did. One must ask: What will become of Musk’s valiant fight for free speech if any weather girl can spout off whatever her wicked woke brain concocts about him? Anyone who watched Musk’s appearance at the inauguration closely would immediately realize that it was not a Nazi salute at all, but merely a gesture of enthusiasm and love — one that just happened to strongly resemble a Nazi salute. Let’s set aside the fact that many neo-Nazis recognized and celebrated it as such. They’re people too, and people can be wrong. After all, what do neo-Nazis know about Nazi salutes? We must, at all costs, prevent the woke from continuing to mix apples and apples in the same basket with impunity. Where that can lead was clearly demonstrated by the unpleasant experience I had after a recent post on the platform of Musk’s fellow freedom-of-speech warrior, Mark Zuckerberg. In my post, I summarized an article by American historian Timothy W. Ryback, who, on the eve of the 92nd anniversary of Adolf Hitler’s inauguration, described in The Atlantic — dryly and impartially, as befits a historian — the early weeks of the then-new German chancellor’s rule. That Monday morning, January 30, 1933, Ryback writes, Hitler first swore to uphold the constitution, then crossed the street to the Kaiserhof Hotel for lunch, and afterward, at his first meeting, explained to his newly appointed Reich ministers what his initial steps would be. He promised to drain the parliamentary swamp and announced the removal of key government officials, whose positions would be filled by loyal party soldiers. He declared he would take revenge on his political opponents. “Heads will roll in the sand,” the new chancellor vividly illustrated what lay ahead. He also mentioned increased military spending and withdrawing from international treaties. Special attention was given to purging the state of foreigners, whom he claimed were “poisoning” the nation’s blood. A few weeks later, on February 20, Hitler met secretly in Berlin with leading German industrialists, including the owner of the Krupp company and four directors of I.G. Farben. He told them, “In a democracy, it is impossible to maintain private enterprises,” and promised to destroy the trade unions and communists.
