The industrialists were thrilled and immediately offered three million Reichsmarks [worth about $30 million today] “to strengthen and solidify the Nazi party in power.” Just a month later, on Tuesday, March 21, a decree was issued granting amnesty to National Socialists convicted of crimes, including murder, committed “in the fight for national renewal.” Men convicted of treason were declared national heroes. The first concentration camp was opened that afternoon in an old brewery near the town center of Oranienburg, north of Berlin. The next day, the first group of prisoners arrived at a second camp in an abandoned munitions factory near the Bavarian town of Dachau. No sooner had I posted these dry historical anecdotes on Facebook than outrage poured in from all sides. Pathetic emojis, shallow comments, and above all, completely baseless comparisons between what I’d described and what we’ve been witnessing in recent weeks and days in the United States. Even the fired weather forecaster from Milwaukee might blush at such malicious oversimplifications and distortions of facts. Anyone who thinks clearly will see that these are not identical events — merely similar ones. It’s obvious they didn’t occur in the same social, economic, or political context as today. They simply resemble today’s circumstances and therefore cannot possibly have the same consequences. At worst, only similar ones. Superficial readers ignored important differences. While Hitler hesitated and delayed pardoning his stormtroopers, Trump did it immediately after taking the oath. While the Führer secretly courted industrialists behind the public’s back, Musk, Zuckerberg, and Bezos stood openly and transparently behind their leader at the inauguration — as befits a true democracy. And above all: Hitler did all this because he was an evil Nazi. Meanwhile, Slovenia’s son-in-law and Musk act — in their deeds and gestures — purely out of enthusiasm and love. Ryback’s article concludes with an event that my Facebook “friends,” in all their blindness, (so far) haven’t dared to link to current events surrounding the new U.S. president. On Thursday, March 23, 1933, delegates of the last Weimar parliament gathered at the Kroll Opera House across from the charred ruins of the Reichstag. Under a massive Nazi eagle, dramatically lit with outstretched wings and a swastika in its talons, Hitler, dressed in a brown stormtrooper uniform, introduced the “Law to Remedy the Distress of the People and the Reich” — effectively granting himself absolute power. Only the Social Democrats voted against it. Joseph Goebbels later marveled that the National Socialists had managed to completely dismantle a federal constitutional republic in such a short time by legal means. “The greatest joke of democracy,” he remarked, “is that it gives its mortal enemies the tools for its own destruction.” A joke, perhaps — but the woke, both then and now, have shown that they have no sense of humor. P.S. Just hours after I sent this article to the editor, Facebook removed my post for violating its standards — for which I am sincerely grateful to Mark Zuckerberg. It gives me hope that we will manage to defend freedom of speech from those who do not deserve it.

Elliot Carver was born in Hong Kong, the illegitimate son of a German woman who died during childbirth and Lord Roverman, a press tycoon. Carver studied communication sciences in Hong Kong and began his career at a local newspaper. Later, he worked as a meteorologist for a Hong Kong television station and eventually became its anchor. In his mature years, Carver took over his father's media empire and became a billionaire. Elliot Carver was known for his ruthless abuse of media influence. “Great men have always manipulated the media to save the world. Look at William Randolph Hearst, who told his photographers: ‘You provide the pictures, I’ll provide the war.’ I just took it one step further.” Elliot Carver doesn't exist. He is the villain from the 1997 James Bond film Tomorrow Never Dies. But he could exist. Or rather—he does. The extent to which today’s world resembles a Hollywood fiction from three decades ago is a sign of how far we’ve fallen. How dumb we’ve become. “The internet has made the world 20% dumber than it was,” says Timothy Snyder. The only reason we don’t realize it is because we ourselves are 20% dumber. History repeats itself—first as fiction, then as farce. Elliot Carver was a psychopath and megalomaniac. “Caesar had his legions, Napoleon had his armies, I have my divisions: TV, news, magazines. And by midnight tonight, I will reach and influence more people than anyone in the history of this planet, save God Himself… And the best He ever managed was the Sermon on the Mount.” Carver used the media to gain power, and power to make money. “Mr. Jones, are we ready to launch our new software?” “Yes, sir. As requested, it’s full of bugs, which means people will be forced to upgrade for years.” Elliot liked rockets. “Mr. Gupta, is the missile ready for launch?” “Push the magic button and Beijing is gone.” Elliot also had great influence over the U.S. president. “Mr. Wallace, call the president. Tell him that if he doesn’t sign the cable TV price-cutting bill, we’ll release the video of him with the cheerleader in the Chicago motel room.” But there are important differences. If the Bond screenwriters had brought a story about Elon Musk to producer Albert Broccoli in 1997, he would’ve kicked them out of his office. Even imagination—at least in 1997—had its limits. Back then, the CIA helped Bond catch Elliot. Today, the CIA would help Elon catch Bond. Elliot Carver didn’t lie about events, because in 1997 no one would believe people could be so uncritical about obvious falsehoods. To be the first to report on wars and scandals, he had to create them himself. “Good morning, my golden retrievers. What devastation will the Carver Media Group wreak upon the world today?” “Flooding in Pakistan, riots in Paris, and a plane crash in California.” Elon doesn’t bother trying not to lie. He does it consciously and deliberately. The lie isn’t an obstacle—it’s liberating. Elliot had to hide his plans for world domination. Elon does it completely openly. “I promise to report the news boldly and without fear. I promise to be a force for good, to fight injustice at every step, to crush intolerance, battle inhumanity, and champion freedom. Yes, that is the mission of my media corporation and empire.” Elliot was lying. Elon believes this. Elliot was a villain—because he didn’t have an “X.” Elon is a hero to many—because he does. Elon believes liberal democracy threatens freedom. Therefore, in the name of freedom, liberal democracy must be abolished—even at the cost of freedom itself. Elon believes he’s saving Western civilization from collapse. To do this, he must liberate speech. He’s doing that with his online platform, which has freed the masses from the shackles of censorship and ideological indoctrination by traditional media and liberal elites. And now, he’s not alone. Overnight, Mark Zuckerberg—the owner of Facebook—and other tech magnates have bowed to the new boss in the White House. I have some reservations about this supposed salvation of Western civilization. Let’s start with freedom of speech and the end of censorship. As Zuckerberg explained on Facebook on the People’s Uprising Day, it’s necessary to “remove many restrictions on topics like migration and gender, which are out of touch with the thinking of ordinary people,” and to “work with President Trump to counter governments that persecute American companies and promote increased censorship.” At first glance, this sounds (almost) reasonable. Censorship has no place in freedom. But let’s take a closer look at what this actually means. Facebook’s publishing rules recently added a clause allowing “accusations of mental illness or abnormality based on gender or sexual orientation,” because such claims are part of the “political and religious discourse on transsexuality and homosexuality.” The new rules also “allow room for various forms of speech, including calls for exclusion or insults within discussions of political or religious topics—such as debates about the rights of transgender people, migration, or homosexuality.” On the other hand, Mark still doesn’t allow comparing people or groups to animals, pathogens, or subhuman lifeforms like cockroaches and locusts. But to avoid overly limiting freedom, Facebook will allow women to be compared to household objects or property, and people to be likened to feces, filth, bacteria, viruses, diseases, and savages. You know, ordinary people. Western civilization. Freedom to call your fellow human “shit.” I don’t know about you, but these meticulously defined rules—crafted by Zuckerberg’s lawyers to codify how and how much it’s permissible to insult and degrade others—leave a bad taste in my mouth. A taste of excrement, filth, bacteria, viruses, disease. A taste of savagery. This isn’t freedom of speech. It’s freedom to hate. Facebook is also ending fact-checking. Because facts threaten freedom, Western civilization, and American corporations. To be clear, my objections to these changes are more ethical than legal. After all, freedom of speech does include the right to lie and insult. Freedom of speech is not absolute—it ends where the law says it must, to protect society from the worst forms of hatred and violence—but in principle, we can’t counter problematic discourse only by limiting speech, no matter how good the intentions. It’s different when control over social networks is abused for political purposes. This isn’t about freedom of speech. It’s about monopolizing hate. It’s not just about insults and lies, but about unregulated power—using algorithms to incite, spread, and exploit those lies and insults. It’s about incitement against individuals and groups that can lead to violence; about undermining democratic institutions and manipulating voters. A few years ago, the Cambridge Analytica scandal erupted because of secret election interference. Today, Musk is doing it openly, in full view. What’s most absurd is the enthusiasm of the bots—those blindly obedient foot soldiers of Musk’s quest for world domination—fulfilling commands just like some once followed instructions from the Central Committee. All while shouting about freedom. That’s where the joke ends. That’s where we must intervene—with regulation, with awareness, with determined defense of our democracies and our freedoms against the rampages of unhinged megalomaniacs. Musk may be crazy, but that doesn’t mean he won’t succeed. As Elliot Carver explained to Bond: “The distance between insanity and genius is measured only by success.”
The Year Democracy Ran Out of Breath

Democracy—the liberal kind, based on the protection of individual rights and freedoms, free and fair elections, and democratic rule of law—is in pitiful shape at the end of 2024. It's running out of breath. Not because its condition deteriorated overnight, but because it's been wheezing like a long-time chain smoker. The lungs are nearly gone. In this year's super-election cycle, over a billion people in more than eighty countries went to the polls. With few exceptions, the results all pointed in the same direction: the return of Donald Trump to power. But his victory wasn’t the final straw that pushed democracy into crisis. The return of Slovenia’s "son-in-law" to the White House isn’t the cause—it’s a symptom, a consequence of what so-called democrats have done to democracy over the years. The sorry state of liberal democracy is, above all, self-inflicted. After their electoral defeat, many blame Kamala Harris and the Democrats for becoming representatives of the social elite—"limousine liberals." It's an accusation often levied by anti-liberal populists who promise to drain the elitist swamps of power. Google the definition of populism, and anti-elitism will top the list of results. Defenders of liberal democracy often wave off these accusations, arguing, "What anti-elitism? These movements are led by the ultra-rich like Donald Trump." But it's not that simple, especially from the perspective of those who are clearly not elite—the economically, socially, and politically marginalized who feel, with good reason, that they’ve drawn the short straw. Their votes are rarely based on rational, critical analysis of their hardships' causes. More often, they are emotional. On one side, they see figures promising to understand their pain and anger. On the other, they see a politics preoccupied with whether Taylor Swift will show up at their campaign rally. I might be exaggerating—but not by much. Democracy has lost the support of the working class. Right-wing populist authoritarians are trying to build a dictatorship with the help of the proletariat. Poor Marx. Poor proletariat. Democratic forces—not just in the U.S.—are also losing support among minorities. Despite often being the targets of populist agitation themselves, some of these communities are turning away from liberal politics. In the recent election, Trump received significantly more support from Spanish-speaking Americans and even African Americans, especially young men. Similar trends are visible in the UK, among descendants of immigrants from the Indian subcontinent and among young Black Britons. For many of them today, the role model is no longer Nelson Mandela, but Andrew Tate. Authoritarian populists are not only gaining support from young men seeking refuge in toxic masculinity. In many recent elections, we've witnessed a marked shift to the far-right among younger voters. Democracy is losing the trust and support of the young because they feel it doesn't care about their future. Trump's win shocked many, though it was hardly a surprise. But perhaps even more damaging than his return to the White House was the response from the political and economic establishment, which had previously championed democratic values and denounced Trump's authoritarian populism. Overnight, they began currying favour with the new boss, some in Mar-a-Lago, others in Paris. We’re witnessing pathetic grovelling for attention and favours. Loyalty to democratic values becomes a mere obstacle to a new love affair. Appeasers, as Winston Churchill called them, are people who feed the crocodile, hoping it will eat them last. Democracy is losing dignity and credibility. Then we come to the bloody spectacle in Gaza. The horrifying civilian death toll, especially among children, climbs: ten thousand, twenty thousand, thirty thousand, forty thousand... We seem to have grown numb to the horror. Numbers in the thousands become statistics. Except for the people of Gaza. They can't get used to it. They can only try to survive. Many don’t. The world reacts with mechanical outrage and empty platitudes about compassion. The counter keeps ticking. Indifference, numbness, political impotence. Indifference, numbness, the impotence of democracies. What will happen in the coming year is anyone’s guess. I want to be optimistic, but it’s hard. I hope the dying will end. But the consequences will remain. For Palestinians, who are left with almost nothing but thousands of graves. For Israelis, whose "security operations" bring anything but lasting security. For Jews around the world, now facing rising antisemitism. While not every criticism of Israeli policy should be labelled antisemitism, many of the condemnations have crossed the line into outright hatred. We will all suffer the consequences. Accumulated suffering breeds accumulated hatred, which too often turns into violence—in the Middle East and beyond. The Western world's unwillingness or inability to decisively condemn Israel's actions and protect Palestinian civilians is causing immense, possibly irreparable harm to public trust in politics and democratic institutions. Liberal democracies have already lost the support of those drawn to authoritarian populism. Now they seem determined to lose the trust of everyone else, too. It seems history is repeating itself. First as tragedy, then as tragedy again. Only our indifference and hypocrisy are farcical. Democracy is losing its humanity. And without it, there is no democracy.

Columnists are often accused of acting like we know everything. That’s obviously not true. I, for one, openly admit I know everything—except economics. When it comes to that science, I prefer to turn to the experts. That’s what I did this time, trying to understand why some people are so enthusiastic about the economic policies of Argentine President Javier Milei. After a bit of online browsing, I came across a professional analysis that basically said: “Dude, what a boss, chainsawing everything, doesn’t give a fuck, total freedom, holy shit.” For those unfamiliar with economic jargon, let me clarify: this is expert approval of bold macroeconomic measures aimed at lowering inflation and boosting growth through radical public spending cuts, deregulation, and tax breaks for businesses. With a chainsaw. A similar approach is expected in the second term of the newly re-elected U.S. president. As far-right American commentator Ben Shapiro put it, “Milei is to Trump what Pinochet was to Reagan—a working experiment in economic reform that can transform rotting social bureaucracies into thriving capitalist societies.” Pinochet, man. Freedom, damn. Trump has delegated the task to wreck the shit out of (pardon the technical term) of the “rotting social bureaucracy” to Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy. Both businessmen will take on the task extracurricularly, while continuing their own business ventures—thereby supposedly eliminating any concerns about conflicts of interest. The newly re-elected American president plans to complement Milei’s doctrine with an aggressive trade policy and sharply increased import tariffs, aimed at screwing over anyone who gets on his nerves. Again, pardon the language—but it’s just the expert lingo. With such a positive response from experts to this bold economic policy, one might rightly ask: why hasn’t anyone tried this before? Because, dude, this is gold. But we’ve actually seen this movie before. Very similar methods underpinned the so-called Kansas Experiment in 2012, led by then-governor Sam Brownback. His tax reform—ironically dubbed the “march to zero”—slashed taxes for the wealthy, eliminated or severely reduced profit taxes for most businesses and self-employed professionals, cut social benefits, made health insurance harder to access for the poorest, closed a slew of schools, four public agencies, and laid off 2,000 public employees. The governor promised this would inject adrenaline into the economy, boost investment, and raise employment. Brownback proudly called his program the “march to zero.” But of course, it didn’t work out. After initial spending cuts, within a few years he had turned a budget surplus into a billion-dollar deficit. Investment and employment growth failed to materialize. Kansas’s economic growth lagged far behind other states—except those that, inspired by Kansas, also began marching to zero. Brownback and his allies tried to plug the budget hole however they could: they raided infrastructure funds, stopped highway repairs, and sharply increased sales tax, which disproportionately hurt the lowest-income residents—who ended up paying more tax than before the reform. After more than five years of chainsaw economics, even Brownback’s fellow Republicans had had enough. Despite holding the majority in the Kansas Senate, they repealed his reform laws. Chainsawing the economy is like fishing with dynamite: effective in the short term—but not without consequences. You might think the people of Kansas, after such a painful experience, came to their senses and punished the Republicans who backed the governor for five years. Not a chance. Even during the reforms, Kansas voters backed Donald Trump—one of Brownback’s biggest supporters—by large margins, and did so again four and eight years later. Today, MAGA Republicans still hold a majority in Kansas. As a reward for his efforts, Trump appointed Brownback as a special envoy for international religious freedom after his first election victory. The Kansas Experiment should be a cautionary tale for those hoping that the damage and suffering Javier Milei and Donald Trump will inevitably inflict—on everyone but the richest few—will eventually lead to a political turnaround and renewed support for more moderate economic and social policy. That’s wishful thinking that ignores the reality of post-rational voter behavior—not just in Argentina or the U.S., but in an increasing number of places around the world. When people are exhausted, frustrated, and angry, they don’t want Beyoncé. They want a guy with a chainsaw. And if that guy makes things even worse, they’ll just be more exhausted, frustrated, and angry. Which only plays into the hands of the chainsaw guys—not the smooth-talking celebrities who sing about democracy and human rights. Of course, post-rationality does have its limits. After enough repetition, even the most loyal fans of neoliberal populism might realize that their declining quality of life isn’t the fault of trans people, feminists, or migrants—but of the politics that exploited and deepened their suffering to gain power and profit. At that point, they might start to reconsider whether angry decisions are the best decisions—and whether they bet on the wrong horse. In a functioning democracy, they’d have the chance to vote for change. But the chainsaw foresters and their billionaire pals know this too. That’s why this new Kansas-on-steroids experiment is also being accompanied by a deliberate weakening of democratic institutions and safeguards. Just in case. They’re determined to dismantle democracy in order to protect freedom. Their own freedom, naturally—and only for themselves. If the original Kansas Experiment ended in farce, this time history could repeat as tragedy. This is exactly the kind of future envisioned by Tomaž Štih—known as Libertarec on Elon Musk’s social media platform—who is reportedly planning to launch a think tank to legitimize the liberation of freedom from democracy in Slovenia, too. “The U.S. will likely be less of a democracy and more of a classical liberal republic,” he writes, “since the individual will be somewhat strengthened and his surroundings won’t be able to outvote his decisions on all aspects of his life, including the contents of his workshop, his thoughts, and his speech.” His like-minded colleague Jože Biščak—editor at Demokracija weekly and Nova24 TV—adds that “U.S. citizens have never considered their system a democracy. The word 'democracy' is nowhere to be found in the Constitution. They talk about a republic. What matters to them isn’t (European-style) democracy, but freedom.” So now you know. Wham, bam, thank you ma’am, as the Americans say. They’re prepping us for freedom without democracy. Where a “somewhat strengthened” Individual will rule freely, unburdened by democracy, political freedoms, or human rights. If this reminds you of something, you’re absolutely right. We’ve seen this movie before—just in a different color—but the consequences will be the same. It doesn’t matter whether democracy is abolished in the name of the dictatorship of the proletariat or the exclusive freedom of slightly enhanced individuals. The paradise both types of liberators promise will never be seen—much less experienced—by the people. As experts in economics or social sciences might put it: we’re screwed. Sorry, man. Better luck next time.

Browsing social media is like scratching at barely healed wounds. You know it's unwise and that you'll regret it, but you can't resist the temptation. This is especially true for the queen of the people’s media, Musk's platform X, which has liberated the masses from the tyranny of reality and facts and finally allowed them to stop believing in what is, and instead believe in what they want or wish to be. Recently, I came across a post by someone named Matej, apparently traveling in Argentina. In the attached photo, he’s holding a plastic bottle of Coca-Cola in one hand (trembling with joyful excitement—OK, that bit is mine), and between his thumb and forefinger, the detached plastic cap. To all his followers and the unfortunate victims who stumbled upon the post—either by chance or thanks to Elon’s mischievous algorithm—Matej enthusiastically declared: “You know what freedom is? Being able to drink cold Coca-Cola without some bureaucrat telling you how to open it. And you don’t even spill it on yourself. I know you’re jealous. Long live freedom, fuck yeah!” Apologies for the vulgarity, but I didn’t think it right to censor Matej’s original work—and let’s admit, that final exclamation is the most charming part of his message. And the only part I can wholeheartedly agree with, vulgarity or not, even if Matej and I probably understand the concept of freedom quite differently. Still, long live freedom, fuck yeah! Matej’s post is not unique. Any foray into Musk’s platform will serve you a buffet of thoughts from village and urban eccentrics, hotheads, and self-proclaimed computer science professors, all passionately praising the wisdom of Elon Musk, Javier Milei, and of course, the greatest among them, Slovenia’s son-in-law, Donald Trump. Long live freedom, fuck yeah! So, on its own, Matej’s post wouldn't deserve much attention. Just another in a long line of nonsense awaiting anyone foolish enough to wander into Musk’s social network. On the other hand, it’s much more than that—a diagnosis of the state of Slovenian (and not only Slovenian) society. A sign of how far we’ve fallen in basic civilizational values like empathy, solidarity, responsibility—and rationality. Today, even the staunchest believers in the neoliberal interpretation of freedom probably understand that plastic bottle caps are attached not because bureaucrats gleefully enjoy every time Matej spills Coke on his shirt, but because these caps cause enormous environmental damage. True, we won’t save the world this way alone, but nothing stops you from doing much more to protect nature and, ultimately, humanity. But if, like Matej, you already resent attached caps, it makes sense you’ll feel the same about other painful but necessary environmental measures. I agree, many things are being handled poorly, and the lack of attention to environmental justice—placing the burden of action disproportionately on certain people—is a big issue. But plastic caps aren’t in that category. Matej, try holding the bottle with your thumb on one side and your middle, ring, and pinkie fingers on the other. You’ll still have your index finger free to press down that damn cap. Yes you can! Matej is, apparently, not only a social media sage but also a fellow columnist and entrepreneur. That’s fine and good. We need entrepreneurs. I’m not among the ideologues who bash anyone who earns a lot of money through hard work and talent. I don’t want to live in a society where people can’t become wealthy and enjoy their wealth. On the contrary, I believe fostering entrepreneurship not only brings but enables societal prosperity and progress. After all, we protected economic freedom in our constitution. But we also wrote in that Slovenia is a democratic and social state that guarantees and protects human rights and political freedoms. Upon independence, Slovenian citizens chose a social order based on balancing these freedoms. Yet increasingly, voices act as if the Constitution of the Republic of Slovenia contains only Article 74: Freedom of enterprise, fuck yeah! A large part of the media and political-economic elite bombards us ad nauseam with imported Muskisms, Mileisms, and Trumpisms. Apparently, we can't even come up with our own dumb and dangerous ideas—we import them, chewed up and fermented, like that alcoholic brew of manioc drunk by South American tribes. We pedestalize the lumpen-capitalist, who sees freedom in un-attached Coca-Cola caps. There’s not a day when the amorphous masses aren’t lectured about the leadership role of the economic elite. Ask Matej. He knows. Born and bred for the elite. Running a state is more of a managerial than a political job, says the president of the Slovenian Business Club. Disillusioned with the present, we blindly march toward a political system of capitalist self-management, where capital, unshackled from democracy and social responsibility, governs society and the state. Freedom, fuck yeah! Following Elon Musk’s glorious victory in the U.S. election, we can expect the idea of a managerial state takeover to gain further momentum. No more wasting money on social safety nets, healthcare, environmental protections, regulation, or taxation—all that junk that makes it harder for economic elites to carry out their enlightened societal mission. It’ll hurt a little at first, Elon promises the raging masses, like a giddy husband pressuring his wife into bedroom practices he picked up on Pornhub. The truth is—it already hurts. America is wealthy, but never in its history has wealth been distributed so unequally. That’s why so many Americans gave their vote to Trump. So things would finally be great for them too. But it won’t happen. In the future, it will hurt even more. But Musk doesn’t care. When people realize wealth never trickles down—but only up—he’ll cash in the profits of his investment in authoritarian populism. When people understand that their misery isn’t caused by migrants, gays, strong and independent women, or other scapegoats they’re currently taught to blame, it may be too late. By the time the barrel’s bottom falls out, democratic institutions and safeguards will be so weakened that they’ll have no place left for protest but up their own ears. The regime will respond to public discontent with authoritarianism and violence. All we’ll have left are Coca-Cola caps. And freedom will have gone where Matej sees it. Up your... well, you know where.
The Shallow Waters of Empty Political Broadness

For decades, Slovenians complained that we all had to think the same. Now we’ve been complaining for years because we don’t all think the same. In our collective relationship with democracy, it often seems like we don’t know what we want. Before independence, there was widespread support for political changes that would put an end to ideological uniformity. But now that we’ve finally—at least formally—established a system allowing for democratic competition of opinions, ideas, and ideologies, we suddenly feel fed up and yearn for politics devoid of ideological differences and division. At first glance, this may seem like a paradox. On closer inspection, less so. The key to understanding this fatigue with the democratic experience lies in dissatisfaction with the quality of democracy being served up by our political class. We wanted a system that would protect and encourage a diversity of views. Instead, we’re increasingly faced with political tribalism marked by rising emotion—mainly the worst kinds—and a dramatic lack of ideas. So it’s entirely logical that people are tired of it and are seeking alternatives to what is often—but in my view wrongly—labeled “ideological division.” In this situation, it’s both logical and legitimate for politics to recognize and respond to this frustration with new offerings and ideas that aim to restore trust in democracy and its institutions. But political marketing is like teleshopping on RTV Slovenia—just as not every of Madam Herta’s tonics will cleanse your liver, not every new platform will clean out the Augean stable of accumulated political sins, errors, and delusions. The risk of hastily and carelessly chasing the transcendence of differences is ending up in a society where differences no longer exist—or worse, must not exist. Where once again, united and undivided, we all think and are required to think alike. Back to the future. Forward into the past. One increasingly popular idea is that the country should be run by managers, since politicians supposedly just bicker and cause confusion. Last time, I compared this notion—voiced by the president of the Slovenian Business Club—to ideas from nearly a century ago. This time, I offer a fresher comparison. If anyone has taken the concept of a managerial takeover of the state to its logical conclusion, it’s Georgian billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili. His wealth equals a third of Georgia’s GDP, and he governs—like a feudal lord from his castle—out of a palace on the hills above Tbilisi. To be fair, Ivanishvili hasn’t entirely abandoned politicians—Georgia still nominally has a prime minister. But there's no doubt who the real boss is. As Politico reported, when current nominal PM Irakli Kobakhidze took office this February, he paused momentarily before Ivanishvili’s seat, as if asking permission to proceed to the podium. Though over three-quarters of Georgians want EU membership, the government is doing everything it can to derail that goal—clearly not in the interest of the supreme manager, who made his fortune largely in neighboring Russia. Business is business. Running a country is more of a managerial job than a political one, as the Slovenian Business Club president might say. Georgians held parliamentary elections on Saturday, and at the time of writing, it appears the results will be exactly what one would expect in a managerially run democracy. A second recent political offering in Slovenia doesn’t aim to abolish politics but proposes reconciliation and broadness as a cure for ideological division and infighting. At first glance, this seems nice. As my late grandmother Maca often said, “Kids, stop arguing.” The outlines of this new political option seem to address many of the unpleasant symptoms of the current state of democracy in Slovenia—personal attacks, exclusion, lack of dialogue, and the intolerance of political discourse. Great. I sign on. In principle. Because while that’s all very good, it’s not enough for a qualitative leap toward better democracy. To achieve that, we must go beyond addressing symptoms and start tackling the deeper causes of our current situation. The main problem with the proponents of political broadness is the superficiality with which they diagnose the reasons for Slovenia’s exhausted democracy. The issue, they claim, is that politicians don’t agree with one another. If we’d all just stop arguing, everything would be fine. As Grandma Maca would say. But—and forgive the repetition—we’ve already lived in a society where everyone had to agree. People have different interests and different worldviews. There’s nothing wrong with that. The point, the goal, and the foundation of democratic society is the civilized organization of disagreement. The idea of overcoming ideological differences is, at its core, deeply undemocratic. Instead of presenting clear political programs for voters to evaluate, parties offer content-free slogans about cooperation and third ways. These serve as alibis for doing whatever they please “in the national interest.” All of it rests on a fiction: that the people’s interests are homogeneous and can only be properly understood, interpreted, and implemented by an enlightened, “non-ideological” leader who thus rises above all political competition. This, dear readers, is literally the definition of populism. This doesn’t mean we can’t talk about common interests. Of course, we all want security, health, jobs, housing, high living standards, and economic development. But the doctrine of transcending ideological differences ignores the fact that we don’t all see or understand these shared goals in the same way—and that multiple paths can lead to each of them, not all of which end in the same place. And these paths are always ideological. A social democrat, a liberal, and a conservative may all agree we need a well-functioning healthcare system, but they will rarely agree on how it should be structured, operated, or funded. Democracy has a framework that defines and limits the legitimate ideological space for political action. That framework is the constitution. While not all Slovenians agree on every article, the constitution remains our best approximation and expression of common values, adopted by broad consensus under strict democratic procedures. It forms the basis for the civilized organization of disagreement, necessary for democratic governance—from election to election, through competition of ideas and programs, via democratically obtained mandates, whether independently or in coalitions, with accountability and oversight from democratic institutions. What concerns me about this political broadness platform is the lack of content—like buying a pig in a poke. To paraphrase Deng Xiaoping, they won’t say how they plan to catch the mice—they just promise that all cats will be the same color. Such an initiative might make sense if grounded in the constitutional framework. Slovenia’s constitution enshrines values like the welfare state and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms regardless of nationality, race, gender, language, religion, political or other beliefs, economic status, birth, education, social position, disability, or other personal circumstances. The proposed platform of broad cooperation doesn’t mention these values, much less make them a precondition for political cooperation. If it did, the possible alliances would look very different from what is currently being suggested. And that’s a serious problem. On the one hand, because the erosion of the welfare state—constitutionally protected—is the biggest generator of dissatisfaction and democratic distrust. On the other hand, because parts of the political scene are fueling this dissatisfaction to attack other foundational democratic values: human rights and the rule of law. This is where the real causes of our much-maligned polarization lie. It stems from a political paradigm that thrives on “us vs. them” divisions, fear, and intolerance; that denies facts; that rejects solidarity and empathy; that disrespects human dignity; that distorts history; that embraces homophobia; that questions women’s right to bodily autonomy; that champions nationalism and tribal chauvinism. In short, it undermines all the values we chose to enshrine in our constitution as the foundation of our shared state. Any expansion or alliance that doesn’t build on and respect core democratic values doesn’t resolve polarization—it deepens and legitimizes it by empowering its chief perpetrators. Whether that’s done knowingly or not ultimately doesn’t matter. The result is the same either way.

The infamous “Third Way” is surely one of the most popular yet slippery political strategies taken up by politicians and “politicians” of vastly different origins, stripes, and flavors. The quest for a new path, a different political model to rise above outdated forms and ideas of political action, has become something like a political Holy Grail—a miraculous source of lasting influence and power. Among the most recent to lose his bearings while searching for a third way—and briefly land on the front pages of (some) international newspapers—was a man named Andreas Münzhuber, one of the leaders of the German neo-Nazi party Der Dritte Weg (“The Third Way”). He met his end during a nostalgic hike near Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest in the Bavarian Alps, where he unwisely stepped on a wet root and fell to his death. At the opposite end of the political spectrum, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair made a much more visible and successful attempt at a Third Way years ago, with his own version of social democracy. In doing so, he confirmed the wisdom of Abraham Lincoln—that you can fool all the people some of the time, and some of the people all the time, but you can’t fool all the people all the time. Although Blair’s political legacy is now (rightly) scrutinized through the lens of his blind, boundless support for the U.S. intervention in Iraq, his broader political doctrine also deserves attention for its lasting consequences. Blair tried to “upgrade” classic social democracy with a Frankenstein-style ideological stew—economic neoliberalism combined with social liberalism. Margaret Thatcher with a human face. Anyone seriously examining the rise of populist authoritarianism will have to grapple with Blair’s legacy. Economic neoliberalism created a massive reservoir of disillusioned and angry members of the working class and lower-middle classes—people who had traditionally supported the left or the political center but now flock to nationalist and authoritarian peddlers of intolerance and hate. Blair’s focus on and support for minority rights ultimately did little to help those communities. On the contrary, when paired with the aggressive neoliberal impoverishment of the working class, it served populists an opportunity on a silver platter: to channel public frustration and rage toward the LGBTQ+ community, migrants, feminists, and other scapegoats blamed for everything wrong in today’s world. Given that some populist wannabe-authoritarians are drifting ever closer to outright fascism, a cynic might conclude that Blair’s and Münzhuber’s Third Ways ultimately lead to the same place—though, of course, Blair cannot be accused of intent, while Münzhuber, in his ideological zeal (and forgive the crassness given the tragic circumstances of his death), quite literally failed to watch his step. You could, in a way, count Russian President Vladimir Putin among Third Way seekers. His ideological formula—intended to guide Russia into a bright future—is brewed from seemingly contradictory ingredients: Soviet-style totalitarianism, religious nationalism, homophobia, and a fresh concoction of neo-fascism. Of course, not every politician trying to chart a new path out of the mess of public anger and political stagnation is comparable to Münzhuber or Putin. I do believe many are guided by good intentions in their Third Way pursuits. But we also know where good intentions often lead. Most of these attempts—from Macron’s “on the other hand” in France to our own “not left, not right, but forward”—have tended, in the end, to benefit the far right the most. The search for a Third Way isn’t limited to Europe. In feverishly polarized, pre-election America, two independent candidates are offering their own versions. Jill Stein—now a veteran of such political activism—is back at it. She’s known for dining with Vladimir Putin and for peeling off just enough votes from Hillary Clinton in key states in 2016 to help Donald Trump win. She’s offering American voters a Third Way again this year. Until recently, another such advocate was Robert F. Kennedy Jr., famous for his fervent anti-vaccine views, for burying animal carcasses in New York’s Central Park, and for his flexible interpretation of marital fidelity. He recently threw in the towel as an independent and endorsed Donald Trump. Apparently, to paraphrase the late Nejc Zaplotnik, it’s not the destination that matters—it’s the Third Way. At this point, some of you might expect me to comment on the recent announcement of a new Third Way initiative here in Slovenia. I must disappoint you. Yes, democracy is in trouble, and people are understandably disillusioned with politics as they know it. The search for new ideas and paths should therefore be encouraged in principle; we shouldn’t trip up anyone proposing something new a priori. But these things don’t happen in a vacuum. The current political and social state was shaped, in no small part, by some of the very people now presenting themselves as seekers of new ways. Historical memory and the consequences of their past actions—as well as experiences with other Third Way experiments—are why many people have legitimate questions and doubts. They’ll need to be persuaded with actions, not lofty slogans about broadness and openness. Trying to arithmetically solve growing political polarization—whether by “going through the center” or “widening the tent”—has so far yielded few democratic breakthroughs. Quite the opposite, in fact. Among the recent Slovenian reactions to a new Third Way initiative, I was struck by a comment from the president of the Slovenian Business Club. Asked whether this new political offering gave him hope for change, he replied he wasn’t too optimistic: “Running a country is more of a management job than a political one. Right now, we have too much politics and ideology, and not enough management.” My inner cynic, shaped by a casual interest in history, couldn’t help but recall the words of Reich Minister for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda Joseph Goebbels. In September 1933, at Geneva’s Hotel Carlton, he explained that “democracies only deliberate and never solve problems. The modern structure of the German state represents a higher form of democracy, where power, based on a popular mandate, is exercised authoritatively without any parliamentary interference that might dilute or obstruct the execution of the people’s will.” Now, to be clear: I’m not comparing the president of the Slovenian Business Club to Goebbels. Doing so would surely earn me a well-deserved lawsuit. I believe he is guided by the best of intentions—at least toward entrepreneurs and “all other citizens who live from their own labor.” But again, we know where good intentions often lead. Most past efforts at Third Ways haven’t yielded great results—but that shouldn’t stop us from trying to improve democracy and restore public trust in its institutions. Apathy only strengthens alternatives we know, from history, we’d do well to avoid. Still, doing something doesn’t mean doing whatever—especially if driven by nothing more than the desire for power. A better starting point would be asking why so many people are disappointed in democracy today. We should invest our efforts in expanding trust in politics and its institutions—not, heaven forbid, in expanding the room for future cronies to exploit public anger. The Third Way should lead to more, not less, freedom and democracy. I apologize if writing about previous Third Way experiments kept dragging me back to stories of populism and authoritarianism. Believe me, that wasn’t my intention. It just sort of happened—organically, inevitably. But maybe that, too, is telling.

"I am a black Nazi," declared a user named minisoldr ("little soldier") years ago on the pornographic website Naked Africa. Just days ago, CNN reported that this username belongs to none other than Mark Robinson, the current lieutenant governor of North Carolina, the Republican Party's candidate for governor in the upcoming November elections, and—at least until the CNN investigation—a favourite of presidential candidate Donald Trump, who once called Robinson "Martin Luther King on steroids." This is the same man who has stated he would like to see slavery reinstated. Probably due to an overdose of steroids. To be fair, the allegations about Robinson's behaviour on pornographic sites relate to a period before his political career began. That started relatively late, in April 2018, when Robinson passionately addressed a Greensboro city council meeting to oppose the cancellation of a gun show out of respect for the victims of the Parkland school shooting in Florida. Just a month earlier, 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz had killed 17 people and wounded another 17 with a semi-automatic rifle. From that point, Robinson's political career skyrocketed. He was promptly invited to a National Rifle Association convention—a lobbying organization whose main mission is to ensure that after each mass shooting, Americans respond with "thoughts and prayers" instead of considering gun control. Had Robinson limited his outbursts to Nazism, Holocaust denial, antisemitism, and similar themes, many—especially fervent Trump supporters—might have just shrugged it off. But little soldier, who CNN tracked down because he used the same username across other social networks where he identified himself by name, didn't keep his views to himself. On the contrary, upon entering politics, he became one of the loudest and most vulgar warriors in Trump's culture war against "wokeness." He's not just a climate change denier; he's also a fervent opponent of abortion rights. To Robinson, abortion is murder committed by women who irresponsibly hike up their skirts and men who can't resist dropping their pants. He wasn't embarrassed by the fact that he himself had once paid for an abortion for his then-girlfriend in the 1980s. In fact, he later married her, and—as he confided to fellow users on Naked Africa—extended his commitment to family values to include her sister, with whom the three of them enjoyed many happy hours. That, ultimately, may have been his undoing. Not the Nazism, but the fooling around with his sister-in-law. What Jupiter is allowed, the ox is not. Robinson's hypocrisy was also revealed in his statements about transgender people, frequent targets in his political speeches. Politician Robinson disdains them; soldier Robinson confessed he often enjoyed watching transgender porn. In his brief political career, Robinson has managed to deny the Holocaust, endorse theories about satanic Marxists and international Jewish conspiracies, and—above all—attack the LGBT community. This is no surprise. Intolerance and hatred toward LGBTQ+ individuals are a unifying theme among political extremists, authoritarian populists, and opportunistic hate-mongers across continents. Despite apparent ideological differences, homophobes—from Moscow to Miami, and from Ljubljana to Alabama—build their power paradigms on animosity toward minority groups. The Homophobic International. Homintern. From Russia with hate. People who think about homosexuals and other sexual minorities like Mark Robinson exist in Slovenia too. Don’t be fooled by their claims that they "have nothing against homosexuals" but just oppose the "LGBT ideology." This is an attempt to camouflage their hatred and intolerance as a fight against being openly criticized for their hatred. It’s cunning, vile, and effective. Around the same time CNN published its exposé on little soldier Robinson, a former Slovenian interior minister posted on social media in response to the nomination of EU Commission candidates: "Not just members of communist secret services and snitches—in the new European Commission, the homosexual lobby will also play a key role. The French commissioner candidate is a former partner of Prime Minister Attal. Did von der Leyen count him under the male or female quota?" For the uninitiated, the "homosexual lobby" trope is used to discredit any situation by claiming it involves, or is influenced by, at least one homosexual person. For example, if a gay man boards Bus 6 next to you at the main post office in Ljubljana, your ride to Črnuče isn’t just public transit—it’s part of the homosexual lobby. Ridiculous, vile, yet effective. Another similarity between the two stories is that both protagonists caused problems for their bosses. Robinson’s pornographic revelations came at a very inconvenient time for Republicans and Trump, further widening the polling gap behind the Democratic candidate in the North Carolina governor’s race and possibly threatening Trump’s chances in the state—jeopardizing his path back to the White House. Meanwhile, the Slovenian ex-minister’s homophobic outburst, which stirred quite a storm in Brussels, surely won't help Slovenia's commissioner nominee as she prepares for her hearing before the European Parliament. What both stories share is the lack of public rebuke from their respective party leaders. In the U.S., Republican politicians began scrubbing their online praise of Robinson, who was quietly removed from Trump’s North Carolina rally guest list. In Slovenia, I saw no distancing from the ex-minister’s homophobic comments by his political allies. On the contrary. The difference is that Robinson denied everything in true Trumpian fashion, calling it a false conspiracy by liberal media and corrupt Democrats. Our little soldier, on the other hand, bravely stood by his words: "What did I say that isn't true?" he asked in response to criticism. The homosexual lobby, right? Heh, heh, heh. The analogy between the two cases isn’t perfect. Robinson did things our former minister didn’t—and probably vice versa. But both examples are symptomatic of the depths to which political discourse has sunk in both the U.S. and Slovenia. Hatred and intolerance are framed as battles for freedom of speech, while tolerance, respect, and humanistic values are framed as threats to national survival and societal evil. The fact that Robinson’s scandal seriously endangered his political future while in Slovenia similar outbursts never carry any consequences suggests that, at least in this regard, we've sunk even deeper than the Americans. Apparently, it’s still riskier to be a black Nazi in America than to be the white Mark Robinson in Slovenia.

“Remember, democracy never lasts long. It soon wastes, exhausts, and murders itself. There never was a democracy yet that did not commit suicide.” These words by John Adams, one of the authors of the American Declaration of Independence, always struck me as overly pessimistic. I believed it was the gloom of a bygone era, when people weren’t as skilled with democracy as we are today. For a long time—especially after the fall of the Berlin Wall—most of us believed that democracy was doing just fine and would last forever. Then some began to worry that something might be wrong with it. And today, more and more believe that democracy itself is the problem. I think we can all agree that it's running out of breath. Maybe Adams did, after all, know what he was talking about. I don’t know exactly what made Adams so bleak, but I do have some thoughts on how and why democracy today—if not on the brink of suicide—is at least in such poor shape it may soon need to be hooked up to life support. Ironically, its decline began a few years before we in Eastern Europe discovered democracy and embraced it with boundless enthusiasm. Around the late 1970s, the Western world started adopting an economic and political doctrine based on the belief that society doesn't exist, the state is unnecessary, and social justice and solidarity are dangerous. The invisible hand of the market would supposedly bring prosperity to all—though admittedly, some sooner than others, as profits “trickled down.” This was the beginning of the end of the welfare state—a concept built after WWII primarily by European conservatives and Christian democrats. It was rooted in the pre-war European experience and in the conviction that social peace isn’t a cost, but an investment in a stable, prosperous, peaceful, and democratic future. Instead, today we have a growing reservoir of disillusioned and increasingly angry citizens who are, justifiably, more and more anxious about their own and their children’s futures. These people no longer believe in democracy and are increasingly willing to embrace populist authoritarian alternatives—alternatives that offer no real solutions but at least pretend to understand their anger and pain. Democracy has emptied itself out and gasped for air, just as Adams warned. If we just sigh and express concern, we will eventually see the rest of Adams’s prophecy fulfilled: the end of democracy. Which, believe me, would be deeply unpleasant. So perhaps it’s still worth trying to prove Adams wrong. There are no magical solutions, but there are some ideas about where to begin: 1. Restore hope and faith in the future. Democracy can’t function in a society where people fear for how they’ll live tomorrow—or for their children's future. Fear, anger, and hatred are the fuel of undemocratic and authoritarian alternatives. The worse off people are, the more frightened and furious they become, the more open they are to politics rooted in division and strongman leadership. But hope can’t be manufactured through hollow slogans. People need tangible, credible evidence that they will have jobs, their children quality education, proper healthcare, and that society won’t abandon them. Democracy needs hope in a better future—not just for a few, but for the whole of society. That hope can only be restored through strengthening the welfare state. In Slovenia, this isn’t just about safeguarding democracy’s future—it’s also required by Article 2 of our Constitution. 2. Restore trust in politics. In short, liberal democracy has largely been damaged by the very politicians who loudly proclaimed their devotion to democratic values—while often betraying them through opportunism, short-termism, inconsistency, lack of integrity, and plain incompetence. A suicide, as Adams described it—or at least a traumatic act of self-harm. Authoritarian populists have capitalized on opportunities gifted to them by these self-proclaimed democrats—especially those who refuse to see, or simply don’t understand, how their moral relativism about the obscene mass killing of civilians in Gaza undermines their credibility on any issue, especially when preaching about democracy, international law, humanity, or human rights. Or those in Slovenia who ignore the devastating effects of unresolved, consequence-free corruption scandals—like the TEŠ power plant case—on public trust in politics, and therefore in democracy itself. 3. Listen to, understand, and respect the people. It sounds simple and obvious, but politicians often struggle with this. They can’t resist lecturing people who worry about their economic and social circumstances on the virtues of democracy and human rights. People are fed up—with politics, with human rights, and with democracy. To save it, we must first address the social and economic pain that caused this loss of trust in the future, and therefore in democracy. This doesn’t mean we stop defending human rights or vulnerable groups—on the contrary. But we must recognize that effective, lasting protection of rights requires more than top-down rhetoric. It requires bottom-up tolerance, and material conditions that support it. Beyond addressing the root causes of the democratic crisis, we must also pay attention to its secondary manifestations—popular unrest, for instance. Just because populists exploit public anger and scapegoat minorities doesn’t mean all fears and frustrations are manufactured or undeserving of a response. Take migration. Yes, it’s fundamentally about solidarity, humanity, and international law, which obligates us to help people in distress. And yes, we need migration—our populations are aging and shrinking. But that doesn’t mean we can ignore the challenges migration can bring, especially when flows are large, rapid, and concentrated. Without investment in integration, we’re planting time bombs. If we want to stop authoritarians from exploiting these tensions and inciting hatred, we must respond effectively to real, short-term problems. It’s wrong to dismiss concerned citizens as bigots. But even worse—and sadly most common—is when mainstream politicians, in their weakness or incompetence, try to outdo populists in xenophobic rhetoric. Despite the evidence that this never works, some democrats still believe they’ll be the first in history to succeed at it. For those interested, Google: “Europe will be Christian, or it will be no more.” 4. Offer citizens opportunities to engage in democracy—and motivate them to do so. Some people, disillusioned with politics and democracy, turn to anti-democratic alternatives. Others simply tune out, believing they have no influence, especially within formal democratic institutions. But this doesn’t mean they’re indifferent to public affairs—many express their views on social media or at protests. Democracy must respond to this, and also adapt to how technology has changed people’s lives. There are plenty of good examples of deliberative and participatory democracy—especially at the local level. That’s important and promising. But there’s a caveat. First, we shouldn’t assume people are disillusioned with democracy just because they’re bored with its current forms or too lazy to vote unless they can use a smartphone app. Second, these alternative forms must have real impact. If they don’t, they’re just a trick—and deepen distrust. Take Macron’s citizen consultations in France, or the EU’s periodic “conferences on the future of Europe.” After the initial fanfare, we rarely hear about them again. Lastly, democracy also demands knowledge and skills. Of course, this applies primarily to politicians. A society that elevates mediocrities and amateurs to power is bad news for democracy. But citizens need democratic competence too—not as a prerequisite for participation, but as an investment in stronger, more resilient democracy. That’s why we need robust civic education in schools, where students gain the tools to participate meaningfully. But again—another caveat. Even the best programs won’t work if they’re taught in an environment where adults (including politicians) increasingly reject the very values we’re trying to pass on. Even if young people gain democratic skills, we’ll only be halfway to saving democracy if most adults still live inside bubbles of like-minded intolerance. And that won’t be enough. As John Adams said, in one of his less gloomy moments: “Liberty cannot be preserved without general knowledge among the people, who have a right to know and a desire to know.”
Under the Skin, We Are All Africans

Wandering through the American South is something I particularly recommend to nature lovers—especially fans of alligators, barbecued ribs, and seafood fried beyond recognition. And did I mention the alligators? Also, to church enthusiasts. In the Bible Belt states, there are truly a lot of churches. In the small town of Valliant, Oklahoma, which Wikipedia says has 754 residents, I came across the local newspaper, The Valliant Leader, in which no fewer than eleven churches advertised their services. This is partly due to the religious zeal of the local population—religion is an important part of their identity—but also because most belong to various Protestant sects, which are much less hierarchical and more autonomous than, say, the Catholic Church. In other words, if Mr. Žmauc and Mr. Žmauc’s neighbor, and the neighbor’s cousin’s friend lived in Oklahoma or Alabama instead of Ljubljana, they would more likely open a house of God (or three) than a pub. The South is also a vast open-air classroom for anyone who wants to know more about the history of the civil rights struggle of African Americans. From Paris, Texas, where they proudly display a several-meter-high replica of the Eiffel Tower adorned with a red cowboy hat—and where almost no one remembers Nastassja Kinski, let alone the times when public lynchings at the city fairgrounds were a favourite pastime. In 1893, the Paris townspeople tied sixteen-year-old Henry Smith, a Black teenager, to a stake and burned him alive. Smith’s death stands out because it was the first lynching to be photographed; pictures of his dying were made into postcards and souvenirs exchanged among the locals. In Little Rock, Arkansas, you can visit a museum presentation of the 1957 events when nine Black teenagers, relying on the 1954 U.S. Supreme Court decision banning segregation in public schools, attempted to enter Central High School. Violent protests followed. Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus sent the National Guard to support—the locals, not the teenagers. Things calmed only after President Eisenhower had had enough and sent in the legendary 101st Airborne Division to restore order and let the Little Rock Nine enter the school. From Little Rock, it's just a few hours' drive to Birmingham, Alabama, which Martin Luther King once called the most thoroughly segregated city in the U.S. In spring 1963, mass protests by Black youth were met by police chief Theophilus Eugene "Bull" Connor with dogs and water cannons. When that didn’t stop the peaceful demonstrations, members of the local KKK branch bombed the 16th Street Baptist Church, killing four Black girls aged eleven to fourteen. In New Orleans, Louisiana, the French Quarter is a must-see, but not far away is William Frantz Elementary School, where in 1960 first-grader Ruby Bridges, escorted by federal marshals, became the first Black child to attend the school. The resulting outrage led most white students to boycott classes for weeks. A famous black-and-white photo of Ruby walking up the school steps surrounded by plainclothes agents looks like something from a distant era. But that’s misleading. Ruby, who this March was inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame alongside Serena Williams, paved the way for others, including Kamala Harris, who entered school in California just a few years later. These events feel close—and ever closer—because time, at least regarding human rights and political freedoms, seems to be moving backward, not forward. In the U.S., and not just in the U.S. One of the most haunting photos in the Little Rock Museum shows a group of white women, girls, and children holding signs opposing school integration: “Integration is un-Christian,” one reads; another proclaims, “Integration is Communism.” This discourse from over sixty years ago painfully echoes language still heard today—in the U.S. and beyond. Remember the campaign slogan of a European Parliament candidate who fired up supporters with: “Europe will be Christian, or it will be no more.” As then, today any talk of social injustice or minority rights is swiftly branded as “leftist extremism,” “wokeness” (whatever that means), or, of course, “Communism.” The more things change, the more they stay the same, as the French say. It's disturbing how socially acceptable intolerance, including racism, has become. One of the more hyperactive ideological crusaders in the Slovenian online space, University of Ljubljana professor Žiga Turk, often weighs in on intergroup and cultural relations. A self-described “extreme realist,” he is highly sceptical of multiculturalism. Fair enough—everyone’s entitled to an opinion. But the attitude mirrors the doctrine of “separate but equal,” which allowed Black Americans legal equality, but only in segregated schools, buses, restrooms, and so on—until the Supreme Court overturned that in 1954, paving the way for those students in Little Rock and Ruby Bridges in New Orleans. Some in Slovenia, it seems, still haven’t reached that point—or worse, wish to return to a time before it. Because multiculturalism, apparently, just can’t work. Integration is un-Christian. Integration is Communism. Similar thinking can be found even among Constitutional Court judges. Recall the recent dissent from one judge who, disagreeing with a ruling that rejected a referendum on changes to the Family Code, complained that the majority opinion violated the "right to separation from others,” which he deemed the "second pillar of our tradition." Professor Turk sometimes goes even further. In other words, not just separate, but also unequal. Not long ago, he commented on a video of a looted store in South Africa by saying, "South Africa was once an orderly, fast-developing country. Then they introduced one man, one vote. And the majority voted for this." In doing so, the professor showed even more “conservatism” than Americans, who at least in principle granted voting rights to Black citizens after the Civil War—though they’ve continually tried to limit its scope ever since. As I mentioned, the man is a professor at the University of Ljubljana. At a roundtable on free speech hosted by a former president of the republic—which I attended—he sat next to the host as a sort of consigliere. We know how that turned out. The former president never missed a chance to miss a chance to use his moral authority against growing hatred in Slovenian society. So it’s no surprise when university professors wax nostalgic for apartheid-era South Africa, before those pesky Blacks got the right to vote. And it wasn't just a one-off slip. The professor recently claimed that when Europeans arrived in the Americas, the continent was "from the civilizational perspective, empty". "Racism," write Joseph L. Graves Jr. and Allan H. Goodman in their recent book published by Columbia University, "is systematic discrimination from a position of power, directed at individuals based on perceived membership in a socially defined racial group." How does this look in practice? Look at the professor’s posts on social media. Black South Africans don’t deserve voting rights. Indigenous Americans didn’t exist when Europeans arrived—from a “civilizational” standpoint. Racism is an excuse for hierarchical domination based on skin colour. Race is not a biological fact, according to Graves and Goodman, but a social construct created to justify colonization, looting, killing, and slavery. It underpinned the subjugation of Native Americans by white economic migrants from Europe, historical and modern genocides, the absolute rule of whites in apartheid South Africa, and the peaceful sleep of slave owners who bought and sold humans like livestock. Today, racism remains integral to the far-right populism attacking the democratic values of human rights, civil liberties, and dignity for all individuals and social groups. If race doesn’t exist biologically, that doesn’t mean we’re all the same. Diversity exists, but not because of race. It is shaped by environment and evolution, not genetics. DNA variations are within 0.1 percent. In other words, we humans are 99.9 percent identical. More than that: science has proven that we all originate from Africa. Genetically and beneath the skin, regardless of its colour, we are all still Africans. You, me, and you too, Professor Turk.
The Intellectual Guard and the New World Order

Gone are the days when we could make fun of backwoods Americans who set up people’s militias, dig bunkers, stockpile canned food and arm themselves to the teeth to defend themselves against a secret international cabal seeking to impose a New World Order. Now we have all that at home too. First we got the Styrian Guard, and now an open letter from Slovenian intellectuals demanding that the Slovenian government not vote for amendments to the pandemic agreement and the International Health Regulations at the World Health Organization, “in which large private economic interests have acquired impermissibly great influence through funding.” The New World Order is a conspiracy theory that warns of the danger of a secretly emerging totalitarian world government. It is supposedly being installed by a globalist power elite which, by orchestrating political, financial, migrant, health and other crises, seeks to rule the world through its outposts (the Trilateral Commission, the World Economic Forum in Davos, the World Health Organization, Jewish financial elites … insert as desired). In this latest case, which has attracted the attention and indignation of the eighty-two signatories of the open letter, the new world order is supposedly being established through the scheme of the Director-General of the World Health Organization to acquire new powers through changes to international regulations, thumb his nose at national sovereignty and, whenever the whim takes him, “declare an emergency in which laws do not apply and introduce measures at his own discretion.” What measures these might be, the signatories do not explain, but every self-respecting anti-vaxxer will know where the vaccine needle is buried. Such decisions, according to the signatories, “directly concern our national sovereignty and the basic vital interests of the population.” Which would be true in principle. If it were true. But it isn’t. At least not the part about the arbitrary introduction of emergencies and measures that thumb their nose at the domestic legal order of member states. If this were just a story from the backwaters of social media, probably no serious person would take it seriously. But because there are quite a few doctors of science and well-known personalities among the signatories, the State Secretary at the Ministry of Health had to deal with the matter, explaining with great patience and restraint why the open letter is, to put it mildly, misleading. That is the first lesson of this story. A doctorate does not guarantee you sense, but nonsense signed by people with doctorates gets more attention than it would otherwise deserve. The list of signatories is a colorful minestrone made up of individuals who have earned a reputation with the Slovenian public in one way or another. Some with their understanding attitude toward the reasons that forced Russia into aggression against its neighbor, or their concern about the fascism of the European Union; others with their skepticism toward vaccination; still others with organizing seminars on the extinction of the Slovenian nation due to feminism and the statement that Adolf Hitler had good intentions but unfortunately it didn’t work out for him in the end. But enough about the signatories. They don’t worry me as individuals, but as a symptom. First of all, as a symptom of frivolity and irresponsibility. The pandemic that struck the world in 2020 took an enormous number of human lives and caused enormous economic damage, with ongoing social, economic and political consequences. The possibility of new similar or even worse health threats in the future can by no means be ruled out. Preventing, and above all responding effectively to, such challenges is possible only through strengthened and effective international cooperation and solidarity. The World Health Organization is of key importance in this. Responsible people understand that after the Covid experience it will critically assess its performance and introduce changes that will ensure greater effectiveness in tackling possible future threats. Others write an open letter. In which they describe as a threat the efforts to address questions concerning “health and healthcare, the economy, education, the free functioning of society as a whole and human rights and civil liberties” with the help of international cooperation and solidarity as well. It is no secret that the negotiations on changes to the World Health Organization’s regulations are difficult and complicated. But there is nothing unusual about that, especially since they are taking place in circumstances marked by the post-Covid boom in disinformation and its abuse for political purposes. In this context, the open letter is not a warning about a threat but part of the problem that actually threatens “our freedom and well-being, health and life.” The letter is also a symptom of sovereigntism, or the fetishization of national sovereignty, which elsewhere is part of the political discourse of the far right, but here enthuses people from all corners of the political spectrum, which is also reflected in the list of signatories of this open letter. This ideological discourse, stoked on one side by far-right nationalism and on the other by obsessive anti-Westernism, rejects a model of European or international cooperation based on solidarity and common rules, aimed at finding solutions to challenges such as health crises, migration, the environment, peace and so on. Of course, no international institution is immune to problems and abuses. The WHO’s conduct during the pandemic can and must be the subject of critical examination and correction of any mistakes. But that is not done through conspiracy theories and weakening multilateral organizations. When, years ago, the Council of Europe was faced with corruption in its Parliamentary Assembly, it responded by establishing responsibility and imposing sanctions. Finally, I would point out that in recent weeks the spotlight has been on another international body, the International Criminal Court, which does indeed have important supranational powers. When prosecutor Karim Khan recently requested international arrest warrants for crimes in Gaza, Israel’s political leadership responded with indignant clamor about national sovereignty, which in the opinion of some gives you the right to do whatever you like with people and with international law. The existing world (dis)order, based on the United Nations Charter, is far from perfect, and far from being something we could not or should not be critical of. The long period of a unipolar world dominated by the United States after the end of the Cold War has led to a situation in which it often seems no longer to work. But instead of efforts to repair and strengthen it, more and more people see the solution in autarkic withdrawal within national borders and in a multipolar world in which US influence will be balanced by China and Russia. That authoritarians from those countries are enthusiastic about such a vision of the world isn’t nice, but it is at least to some extent logical. That people from countries like Slovenia cheer for it is harder to understand. In a new world order run by imperialist hegemons, we will be able to stick our sovereignty in our ear. Or somewhere lower down.

Weapons and military matters have never been close to my heart. I never liked playing with rifles and pistols, not even during my military service in the former JNA. There I did everything I could to get them to send me home, or at least leave me alone. I ended my active military engagement at my first weapons exercises at the end of my first year at university, when I literally threw my rifle into the cornfield. A few weeks later, an official on Mačkova Street cut my military booklet in half. Even more than military matters and weapons, I dislike war. Because in wars people die and towns and villages are destroyed. So I sincerely wish that wars, all wars, would end as soon as possible. And that peace would reign. My aversion to military matters does not mean I don’t respect people in the military profession, and even more those who are prepared to take up arms and risk their lives in the fight for freedom. Like the Slovenian Partisans once, or the Ukrainians today, in a national liberation struggle against a fascist occupier. I only wish they didn’t have to. Because they would live in a world ruled by peace and friendship among nations and freedom for all. But the world we live in is not (yet) like that. That is why I think about military matters not only emotionally but also rationally and critically. I don’t like armies and defense budgets and spending on armored vehicles and shells, but I understand that we need all this nonetheless. At least for now. I hope not for too long. It may take two to make a war, as the “peace activists” loudly try to convince us, but that doesn’t mean both are always equally responsible for it. Because often one of them is the aggressor and the other the victim. And a war that ends with the defeat of the victim does not bring peace but the victory of the aggressor and an incentive for new wars. Nor are all wars the same. The best are those that never begin. It would be loveliest if there were no wars, because all countries in the world were friendly and it never occurred to them to attack anyone. But, as I said, we are not there yet. In this non-ideal world, we can therefore prevent wars effectively above all by deterring potential aggressors in advance from their intentions to commit aggression against others.
