Because they know it won’t pay off. Because they risk getting a bloody nose. To be convincing in deterring potential aggressors, we must be ready to defend ourselves. That requires investment in weapons and the military, even if these things are otherwise not dear to our hearts. But we are prepared to accept them. Because we dislike war even more than we dislike weapons. And then we come to NATO. It was founded soon after the end of the Second World War to protect Western democracies from the military danger threatening them from the Soviet Union. And it did so quite effectively. The Cold War period is not something one looks back on with fond nostalgia, but the operative word in that phrase is “cold.” That states on both sides of the Iron Curtain did not come to blows for so many decades is no small thing. Especially since there was always the danger that they would use nuclear weapons in doing so. After the end of the Cold War came a thaw, which also brought closer relations between NATO and Russia. At that time I was working in Brussels and watched at NATO headquarters as a booth for interpretation into Russian was built into the hall where the North Atlantic Council meets. A world in which peace and friendship would reign never seemed closer than then. But after that everything went more or less downhill. Much of the credit for this goes to Vladimir Putin, who swung himself onto the Kremlin throne at the end of 1999. That does not exclude the fact that the West, including NATO, also has plenty to answer for. We can and must be critical of how some military interventions came about and how they were carried out and ended. It is true, though, that it mostly began its operations with a United Nations mandate. Not all of them, since international lawyers still argue above all about the mandate for military intervention against Milošević’s Yugoslavia after the mass violence against the Albanian population in Kosovo. The same goes for the decision of the European Court of Human Rights, which rejected a complaint against European member states over their participation in the bombing of the Serbian television building, in which 16 employees died. After the use against Serbian forces in Kosovo of ammunition containing depleted uranium, I wrote an article for my then boss Russell Johnston, President of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, which The New York Times published in January 2001 under the title “A Case of Depleted NATO Ethics in the Balkans.” That NATO has at times acted questionably in the past is a fact. That it is essential to ensure that it always and exclusively acts to provide defense against aggression and to protect international law is equally so. That is the task and responsibility of all member states, among them Slovenia. It is also true that there is an objective difficulty here, in that by far the greatest influence in the alliance belongs to the US, which you can always count on to protect above all its own interests, which are not always necessarily ours too. Just as it is true that we other NATO members voluntarily left them this role, by skimping for decades on investment in our own defense and freeloading on the US as the world’s only policeman. Paradoxically (for some), the way to limit America’s role in the world is not to cut spending on our own defense, but quite the opposite. Through Europe’s strategic sovereignty, as French President Macron said in a recent speech at the Sorbonne. Technologically, in energy and also militarily. Unless we accept that the Russians and Chinese will balance American influence instead of us. Or vice versa. There are sound rational arguments for NATO membership. The position that we don’t need membership because we are safe is legitimate, and we can agree with it or not. But the belief that we are safe because we don’t like NATO is naive, irresponsible and dangerous. The thesis that reducing our defense preparedness guarantees our security holds only on the assumption that aggressors, as a rule, attack only countries they know will be able to defend themselves. The “peace activists” resolve the illogic of their positions by basing their argument on a starting point that is dogmatic, ideological and emotional. NATO is the armed wing of the West, and the West is rotten and to blame for everything. Through the prism of this dogma, they see, understand and explain the world around them. NATO is to blame for the war in Ukraine because it expanded toward Russia. For example. If they get into a jam in their argument, as regularly happens, they return to the starting point. The West is rotten and to blame for everything. Anti-Westernism is very widespread in Slovenia, even though we are people who otherwise enjoy the advantages that life in a liberal democracy which (in principle) respects human rights and political freedoms brings us. It would be a paradox if we Slovenians had not built cognitive dissonance into our collective psyche. We are also convinced that EU membership has brought us benefits, while at the same time we couldn’t care less about it, as a recent Eurobarometer opinion survey showed. It is a paradox, though, that anti-Westernism, which in Slovenia is widespread above all among people who see themselves on the left of the political spectrum, is so much in harmony with the efforts of antiliberal far-right authoritarians. They see international alliances and norms as a conspiracy of progressive liberalism and an obstacle to establishing a “sovereigntist world order,” as Viktor Orbán put it a few days ago at a conference of American conservatives in Budapest. Putin deserves credit for bringing the positions of the far-left and far-right poles closer together, at least on matters that benefit him in carrying out his imperialist policy. In Slovenia, at least among some, this rapprochement no longer resembles a horseshoe but a closed circle. In this sad story, the “peace activists,” by assisting in the nationalist and authoritarian reshaping of the world, are helping to create a very dark future in which they too will not fare well. A foretaste of what may await them is offered by the fate of every Russian peace activist without quotation marks who dares to shout “nyet voyne” in the street. Because of its dogmatism and blind faith in the basic premises from which it derives its attitude to the world, sweeping contempt for the West resembles a conspiracy theory. “Not NATO, give us peace” and “not vaccines, give us health” reflect very similar patterns of thought. An emotional and ideological departure from logic, facts, responsibility and reason. If, God forbid, we are ever threatened by foreign aggression in the future, I would not be surprised if some smart alecks swore by ivermectin for air defense.

At first glance, one might say that Russian intelligence officers are wasting their effort and money here. In Slovenia, at least by their own account, no one supports Russia’s aggression against Ukraine or President Putin’s policies. Even one of the candidates in the European elections indignantly denied any sympathy for the Kremlin vozhd, delivering his indignant denial right after a touching farewell to a freshly expelled Russian spy. The choice of farewell gift went straight to my heart. To paraphrase the old Slovenian children’s rhyme: I’m just a little girl, I don’t know how to give wishes, so I give you a kiss and a little saber. Perhaps, as a reward for the effort invested in Slovenia, the expelled Russian snoop will get some Gauleiter post—or whatever the administrators of occupied territories are called in Russian occupier-speak—in Ukraine. There, with the gift from his Slovenian pals, he will be able to sabrer champagne from occupied Crimea, and the unruly local population too. His party colleague and leader denied any Russophilia even more indignantly, right after the publication of a video in which he summed up all the talking points from the Kremlin crib sheet on the causes of the special military operation. Resnica (Truth). Nomen nyet omen. Politicians who appeared on the recently exposed Russian propaganda outlet Voice of Europe also deny any harmony with the Russian president’s policies. Unlike the first group, they have some weighty arguments for their claims. They can in no way be accused of supporting Russian aggression. From the very beginning of this story, they have supported Ukraine. At first glance the whole affair is therefore illogical. Why would a Russian propaganda outlet invite someone who supports Ukraine? To get to the bottom of it, we probably need to put the question slightly differently. Why would a Russian propaganda outlet invite someone despite their supporting Ukraine? Some may think it was an attempt at balanced editorial policy and a presentation of different views. Who knows. The Kremlin has traditionally shown little sympathy for balance. Independent thinkers are quickly shown the door. Some only get as far as the window. To understand the cost-benefit analysis—as economists would call it—of what publishing these interviews brought the Russian propaganda machine, a broader view is needed. Was anything said in these interviews, besides support for Ukraine, that brings grist to the mill of Putin’s policies? Let us recall that from the very beginning Putin has explained and justified his platform of power, his attitude toward the world and also his aggression against a neighboring country by the need to defend the Russian nation and its traditional values from the destructive decadence threatening from the West. The populist wave that in recent years—with Russian help and under Russian influence—has swept over many Western democracies builds its march to power on talking points written in the Kremlin. On stoking fear and hatred of others and those who are different. Migrants, sexual minorities and women who think for themselves are to blame for everything. Sound familiar? Culture war played to a Russian score is the remote control with which Putin—so far very successfully—creates social polarization and steers us exactly where he wants us. Into the self-destruction of everything that distinguishes an open democratic society from nationalist authoritarianism and the prison in which the Russian vozhd has locked up his fellow citizens. The picture is similar on the other side of the political spectrum; there, too, no one supports the aggression and Putin’s policies. And they, too, have quite a few arguments for their claims. At least regarding the culture-war themes with which Putin snares their political opponents on the right. On the aggression against Ukraine, they support neither side. They are for peace. And they don’t like the Americans. On both counts, it is hard not to agree with them. Who isn’t for peace? And we all know the US has a great deal to answer for. There is probably no possible path to more peace and stability in the world that would not require criticism and correction of American policy toward most crisis hotspots, starting with its attitude toward Netanyahu’s killing of the Palestinian population in Gaza. But it is one thing to be critical, even condemnatory, on the basis of arguments (of which there is no shortage), and another to hold an a priori ideological dogma that in Pavlovian anti-Americanism has found a plug for every logical and ethical dead end into which the inevitable conflict between their noble-sounding slogans and reality leads them. At the extreme poles of the political spectrum, two mirror logics have been established that feed each other. For some, migrants, feminists and sexual minorities are to blame for everything; for others, the Americans, NATO and the West. Putin doesn’t care. Both suit him. Without the anti-American ace up their sleeve, the credibility of the “peace” theses collapses like a house of cards. They are for peace. To end the war, we must stop helping Ukraine. Because more weapons have never brought peace. I am convinced that they themselves understand that a peace achieved through Ukraine’s surrender would bring victory to Putin. Since this cannot logically be denied, such an outcome must be ethically justified, or at least relativized. The Americans were to blame for the war anyway. Their support for the Maidan revolution, Victoria Nuland, blah, blah, blah, NATO enlargement and so on. The complete repertoire of “arguments” explaining why Russia actually had no choice but to “protect its interests by armed means,” as President Putin explained a few days ago at the congress of “independent” Russian trade unions. The thesis of the responsibility of the victim, who prolongs the war by resisting the aggressor, is also, to put it mildly, questionable. This should be especially true in Slovenia, which, at least for now, is still for the most part proud of the courage and sacrifice we showed in the fight against fascism. The Slovenian nation did not fight the German occupier by holding hands and singing kumbaya. The moral predicament revealed by the analogy between the Slovenian and Ukrainian national liberation struggles cannot be dispelled by the fact that we Slovenians were fighting fascism. Because the Ukrainians are doing that too. How else to describe the imperialist, authoritarian, militarized and violent ideology of the Kremlin despot? I would particularly like to hear an explanation from people who otherwise never hesitate to stick similar labels on people who, by any serious criteria of fascistoid conduct, do not (at least for now) come up to Putin’s knees. With such discourses, of which there are many and ever more in the Slovenian public space, many will think that the stories about Russian intelligence rubles are not entirely made up. Who knows. So far I have seen no evidence that anyone here has been paid to take part in the Russian propaganda war. Besides, there are evidently enough candidates willing to play the role of useful idiots for free. We can think what we like about Putin and Russian intelligence, but they know us better than we know ourselves. With surgical precision they identify our frustrations, fixations and delusions and then simply push the buttons; we do all the rest ourselves. Why waste rubles when in the end the Slovenian mentality prevails? I don’t need a professional for this; I’ll fix it all myself.

On the very day I began writing this text, Eurobarometer published its latest data on the mood of voters in EU member states ahead of the June elections to the European Parliament. I can vividly imagine European public opinion researchers scratching their heads in confusion when the data from Slovenia reached them. We are well above the European average on the question of whether EU membership benefits us, yet near the bottom on expected turnout. Even more surprising is the figure on the reputation of the European Parliament. There Slovenia is right at the tail of all member states, with only the Czech Republic and France behind us. At the same time, we Slovenians are near the very top among those who think the European Parliament should get more powers and influence. We Slovenians are enthusiastic about the European Union, yet it doesn’t interest us. We are convinced that membership means we live better, yet we couldn’t care less. The logic reminds me of Woody Allen’s joke about two residents of a retirement home, in which the first complains that the food is terrible and the second agrees, adding that the portions are too small. These data put me in a quandary in writing an article about our attitude toward the European Union. If we were dissatisfied with it because we believed it had brought us nothing good and messed up everything that could be messed up, I would try to answer these reproaches and shed light on them from the other side. Because I believe that sweeping negativism and nihilism of the “nothing good about it” kind are very unwise and dangerous things. If Slovenians were uncritically enthusiastic about the EU, I would point out a series of its mistakes and weaknesses, because I believe that uncritical idolatry of any form of power is also a very unwise and dangerous thing. Perhaps, in thinking about Slovenians’ attitude toward the European Union, we should first think about ourselves and our attitude toward the outside world. The analogy with our attitude toward the former state is simplistic and, like most analogies, imperfect. But it is not entirely irrelevant, because the attitude we cultivate toward Brussels often very much resembles the one we once had toward Belgrade. Which is a paradox. After all, it was precisely European aspirations that guided and motivated us at the time of gaining independence and founding our own state. With the aim, of course, of becoming part of the European family as soon as possible. Now that we have achieved that, we are somehow confused. As the data from the latest Eurobarometer show. It reminds me of an old routine by the legendary comedians Cheech and Chong: I used to be totally messed up on drugs. Then I found Jesus. Now I’m totally messed up on Jesus. But joking aside. There is of course nothing wrong with supporting something while being critical of it. What is more, as I have already said, such criticism is a democratic necessity, especially when it comes to our attitude toward authority and power. But it is important that we are also critical of ourselves, remain rational and do not allow emotions to overcome reason, however justified our anger. We can be disappointed and furious with politics and politicians, but that should not be a reason to give up on democracy as a system. We can (and must) be critical of and angry about the social hardship brought by some people’s enthusiasm for neoliberal economics, as long as it doesn’t carry us into flirting with already tested (and barely survived) social utopias which in the past, in the name of a never-fulfilled promise of collective social justice and prosperity, denied us individual rights and freedom. We can dislike NATO and weapons, as long as we don’t start believing that this makes us safe and that no one will ever threaten us simply because we won’t be able to defend ourselves. We can be fed up with Fides and the non-stop ruckus at the oncology clinic, as long as this doesn’t seduce us into thinking we can abolish the health system and leave the care of our health to the homeopathic potions sold to us by quacks. We can and must be critical of the European Union, as long as we are aware of what Europe was like when there was no European Union and what it could become again if, by chance, it no longer exists in the future. A good ten years ago I was an adviser in the office of the then Secretary General of the Council of Europe, Thorbjørn Jagland, a former Norwegian foreign minister, Speaker of Parliament and Prime Minister. While serving in Strasbourg, he was a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, which he also chaired for a number of years. In 2012 the Peace Prize went to the European Union. On its behalf, it was received from Jagland’s hands at the ceremony in Oslo by the then President of the European Commission, José Manuel Barroso, and the President of the European Council, Herman Van Rompuy. The decision provoked stormy reactions in the media and among the public, many of them negative and mocking. Which was understandable in its way. Let us recall the historical context of the time. Europe had still not recovered from the consequences of the global financial crisis caused by the banking crash in the United States. The crisis caught the European Union unprepared. The monetary union created by the Maastricht Treaty was an unfinished project, lacking appropriate and effective safeguards and mechanisms for financial solidarity between member states in the event of crises like the one in 2008. The European banking system was on the brink of collapse. The consequences of the crisis—and of the way it was handled—were very painful, but not equally painful for all member states. Those in southern Europe not only went through a very deep recession but had to accept and implement extremely painful austerity measures in exchange for the financial assistance that saved them from bankruptcy. The social, economic, political and demographic consequences of these measures were extremely painful for the hardest-hit countries, above all Greece. Unemployment in Greece rose from less than 8 percent to 23 percent between 2008 and 2015. Almost 94 percent of households suffered a substantial drop in income. More than a third of the population found itself on the brink of poverty. The crisis also affected the health, and especially the mental health, of Greek citizens. The number of suicides rose. The demographic consequences, still felt today, included a marked fall in the birth rate and an increase in emigration, especially among the young. The fact that in some countries the crisis was so deep and painful also, and above all, because of the past financial irresponsibility of their political and economic leaders and elites did nothing to lessen the hardship citizens felt in the course of, and because of, the rescue. The crisis deepened the divide between Europe’s north and south. On one side, northerners accused southerners of irresponsible profligacy; on the other came reproaches that the richer member states did not care about their severe social hardship. But the citizens of both were united by common anger at the way European banks were bailed out. Perhaps somewhat simplified and generalized, but not entirely inaccurate, the prevailing belief was that profits always stay with the bankers, while losses, as a rule, are paid by taxpayers out of their own pockets. The global financial crisis did not mark the beginning of the social and political upheavals we are witnessing today, but it gave a great boost to the rise of populist politics and its increasingly successful march to power. Many Europeans, not only in the southern half of the continent, blamed the European Union and its measures to resolve the financial crisis for their problems and hardship. Whether all these effects were entirely justified and grounded in objective facts is of secondary importance. On a personal level, for many European citizens the culprits for all the misery were personified above all by two people, Angela Merkel in Berlin and José Manuel Barroso in Brussels. The image of the Oslo ceremony, at which the latter strutted about with a medal for services to world peace, made many people’s blood boil. I was puzzled by the decision myself. “OK, I get it, the EU is cool,” I said to Jagland, in the professional jargon we experts on European affairs use when talking among ourselves. “But why now of all times, when the EU is getting on everyone’s nerves?” “You don’t get it at all,” my boss replied, with the look bosses use when answering subordinates’ stupid questions. “They had to get the prize now, precisely because it’s getting on everyone’s nerves.” According to his explanation, the decision was considered and deliberately provocative. The aim was not to divert attention from the weaknesses and mistakes the European Union had committed in its responses to the financial crisis. As a social democrat, Jagland was of course sensitive to criticism that European leaders, in rescuing the financial system, had neglected the social effects it caused, and thereby endangered the political project to which he had been committed since the very beginning of his political career. In 1990 he published in Norway the book My European Dream, which, however, did not convince his fellow citizens to vote a few years later for joining the European Union. But that took away neither his courage nor his drive. Because he was worried that Europeans, in their anger, however justified, would forget that the project of European integration cannot be reduced merely to an opinion of the current leadership and a reaction to one of the otherwise frequent crises the European Union had gone through since its creation, he wanted to draw attention to its fundamental mission: ensuring peace and stability on the European continent. The Nobel Peace Prize was meant as a reminder that the project of European integration is, from its very beginning, first and foremost a peace project. And that in assessing the importance of its existence we must take into account not only legitimate aspirations (and the related criticism) about what an ideal Europe should be in our opinion, but also the memory of the Europe we had before it. He firmly rejected accusations that with this decision the Norwegian Nobel Committee was “rescuing” the EU leadership of the time from criticism and the political consequences of their controversial decisions. In his view, the warning about the existential importance of European integration for peace on the old continent was not addressed only to European citizens. It was also a reminder to the political leadership of the time in Brussels and other European capitals of where frivolity, arrogance, short-sightedness and political opportunism in responding to the legitimate expectations of their voters can lead. If voters do not have confidence and material proof that the European Union effectively protects their economic, social, political, democratic, security and other interests and rights, then not only the future of the EU institutions but stability and peace in Europe are at stake. To the question of how much my former boss and the other members of the Norwegian Committee contributed to securing the future of European integration, it is still hard to give a definitive answer, above all because that future is far from secure. Nor am I sure whether Barroso and his colleagues really understood the prize as a warning. On the other hand, in responding to the crises that followed, first migration and above all health, the European Union did show that it had learned something from its own mistakes. How much this was thanks to the Nobel Peace Prize is another question, but the fact is that the response to the global health crisis was considerably more Keynesian and based on solidarity, while the tiresome harping on about not being able to spend money you don’t have was, for now at least, put on the back burner for fear of the social and political consequences of another deep social crisis. That does not mean we can breathe a sigh of relief. Crises follow one another and compete with each other. Jean Monnet’s often-quoted observation in his memoirs, that Europe would be built through crises and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them, is, to put it mildly, facing ever harder tests. Blind faith in the thesis that the EU will emerge stronger from every crisis is colliding with harsh reality and with the traps set for European integration by illiberal populism and all sorts of prophets—right and left—of the wonderful future awaiting us on our return to the golden age of “free and sovereign” nation-states. That age, of course, never existed in history. But why let facts spoil effective populist lies? People today are disappointed with Europe, many are angry. This frustration often outweighs the benefits people actually enjoy because of their country’s membership of the European Union. As the Eurobarometer data show, Slovenia is a very good example of this apparent paradox. Apparent, because no politics can compensate for the loss of confidence in the future merely by invoking past successes. And the fact is that people today are afraid of the future. For a political, social, legal and economic project based on the principles of liberal democracy, this is a very bad omen, since it gives an opening to alternative ideological projects built on different value foundations. To stop the current trends, which are looking ever better for populist and nationalist authoritarians, the European Union—and those of its member states that still swear by the values on which the European project was founded from the start—must change a great deal in themselves. Merely pointing a finger at the scoundrels who don’t like democracy and human rights will not be enough. People expect a European Union that is successful, effective and consistent in recognizing their expectations and solving their problems. The European Union has gone through a whole string of crises in recent years, and one could say that life has turned Monnet’s maxim on its head. Today many see in it the sum of all the mistakes and weaknesses it has shown in dealing with them. Sometimes it seems that the EU and its bureaucracy do not take these frustrations seriously enough. They wake up a few months before the European elections, start clamoring about the threat posed by growing support for extremist, populist and anti-EU forces, and then, once they have again squeezed through an ever narrower eye of the needle, things go on more or less as before. What doesn’t kill us makes us stronger. Perhaps, at least until something kills us. The crisis in the Middle East and the killing of Palestinian civilians we are witnessing in Gaza is the latest of the crises further weakening the reputation of and support for the European Union. This is not changed by the fact that its powers to intervene directly are limited and that many project onto Brussels their frustration and anger at the positions, actions—and inaction—of their own governments. People are fed up, and Brussels is a handy target for directing anger. The extreme nationalist right cheers on Netanyahu’s conduct, because in him and in his ruthlessness toward the Palestinians and toward all international norms and obligations they see an ally in establishing unbridled sovereignty, in which power within and beyond its borders can finally do whatever it likes to consolidate its positions of power. As a bonus, they use their cheering for Netanyahu’s conduct as an alibi against accusations of their own latent antisemitism. On the other side, a large part of public opinion, appalled and outraged by the bloodshed, watches the confusion, indecision and double standards of most European governments. And into this situation barges Russia from the side, happily pouring fuel on a fire it largely helped to light. Equally dangerous is the marked retreat from the goals of the green transition and the measures to combat the consequences of environmental change, which followed the populist exploitation of the hardship and problems of European farmers. Instead of critically reviewing these measures and ensuring that they are economically sustainable and socially just—which, given the enormous funds the EU devotes to supporting agriculture, is not an insurmountable challenge—European leaders fell into the right’s demagogic trap and deepened divisions between people. Many, especially the young, feel that politics has opportunistically sacrificed their future in order to win a few points of support among people who will not have to live in that future. And in these circumstances we are now going to have elections to the European Parliament. So why, with all this, wouldn’t someone use these elections to show the European Union, and the part of politics that swears by it, the middle finger? Either by not voting at all, or by circling the names of those who sell stories—black, red or brown—about the happiness, security and abundance that await us once we finally free ourselves from Brussels’ shackles? For an answer, we need to go back into history. To think about why the European Union actually came into being. Where we were when it did not exist, and where we could return if it disappears. I cannot award Nobel Prizes in support of my views; I can only explain why I myself, in these circumstances and with all my criticism and well-founded reproaches, still—and increasingly—support the project of European integration and the European Union. The traditional cliché that the European project is an answer to the horrors we experienced in the Second World War convinces few people. Put crudely, people find it hard to imagine a direct link between the Brussels bureaucracy and the horror of the concentration camps. They react to such rhetoric much as they do to that hackneyed “never again,” which politicians utter once a year while laying this or that wreath and then forget, even though “here we go again” is pushing its way into every pore of social and political life. To understand this causal link better, we need to remember what Europe was like before the Second World War, and also what it was like immediately after it. Europe at the start of the Second World War was described in June 1940, after Nazi troops had marched into Paris, by the Newsweek correspondent in Bucharest, R. G. (Rosie) Waldeck. The fall of France, she wrote, crowned twenty years of democracy’s unfulfilled promises to master unemployment, inflation, deflation, labor unrest and party egoism; a Europe tired of itself and doubting the principles by which it lived felt almost relieved that everything had been settled, and considered Hitler an unpleasant but very clever man who had made his country strong—so why not try it that way? With minimal adjustments, this text could describe not only the mood in today’s Europe but also the key points of the election programs of ever more numerous and influential political parties. How it all ended, we know. You know, never again. The postwar European project was an answer to the Europe that Rosie Waldeck described. It was not (only) an attempt at economic cooperation that has only in recent years expanded into a political project, as some like to present it. Europe as an economic, legal, political and social project was conceived from the very beginning as a defense mechanism to protect Europeans from themselves. It laid the foundations for a different coexistence between European nations, which throughout history had as a rule settled open questions through wars and killing one another. Even the economic cooperation that represents the beginnings of what we today know as the European Union had political goals from the start. The reason for this was above all the conditions in war-ravaged postwar Europe. The first years after the defeat of Nazism have more or less been lost from our collective memory. They are usually squeezed into a shortcut between the German capitulation and the economic boom that lasted almost two decades in Western Europe, until the mid-1970s. But the first postwar years were different. Economic difficulties, the demographic consequences of the war, destroyed infrastructure and the debts states had run up during the years of fighting began to create a social climate that was becoming similar to the one a decade earlier. In France governments changed amid strikes, each weaker than the last; Labour in Britain was running out of breath; and in the opinion of some, the painful consequences of the war the Nazis had started were creating the conditions in Germany for their return. That was certainly the impression formed by George Marshall, the US Secretary of State, when in March 1947, on his way to Moscow, he visited a number of European capitals. The answer was the Marshall Plan, one of the most successful and effective economic aid programs in history. Without it, postwar Western Europe could easily have turned in a different direction. It matters for the project of European unification in at least two respects. First, it included a mechanism that made aid conditional on trade among the recipients. The first seeds of today’s single market were planted by the Americans. Second, with an injection that triggered the postwar economic boom, it enabled European politicians, above all Christian democrats, conservatives and people’s parties, to build a welfare state based on a high level of social protection and solidarity. Given the economic programs of most of the modern successors of these parties, this is almost hard to believe, but let us remember that these were politicians who had not only survived the war but had also experienced the prewar economic, social and political crisis that led to it. A text about the European Union that begins with today and ends deep in the past may strike many as upside down. I stress the importance of historical memory because I would like Slovenian voters not to send to the European institutions populist demagogues who sell us fairy tales about the wonders of unbridled sovereignty, nor oddballs who would like to shoot at chemtrails from Brussels and Strasbourg, spit on vaccines and peddle Russian propaganda. I would like people, in deciding whether to vote, and how and for whom, to be guided not only by legitimate questions, criticism and complaints about the conduct of the European Union and its member states today, but also by an understanding of its historical role and importance in preserving stability and peace on the European continent. This does not mean we should grant indulgences to today’s European political leaders—quite the opposite; it is a warning to them too. The European Union will be able to carry out its peace mission successfully only if it is based on the values on which it was built after the Second World War. And if it puts those values into practice. So that European citizens feel it and believe it. The formula for peace in Europe is, at least on paper, simple. A self-confident and strong European Union based on social justice and respect for human rights, respect for international law, humanism and solidarity, not just rhetorically but every time and consistently, including when it is hard and requires courage. When the European and all other elections come, support those political ideas and parties, whether left or right, that support such a European Union. If we let it collapse, no “never again” will save us. “Here we go again” is too close in today’s Europe for us to gamble recklessly with our fate.

On May 4, 2004, just a few days after Slovenia officially joined the European Union, a historic event we Slovenians had longed for for so long, the Slovenian flag was raised in front of the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. It was escorted to the flagpole by the then Speaker of the Slovenian Parliament, Borut Pahor, and carried by my eight-year-old daughter. She earned this honor by being, at the time, the only available child of Slovenian roots in the vicinity. The event stayed in her memory, not least because of the kindness of the gentleman who held her hand during the ceremony, his face lit up not by the state-building, statesmanlike frown he brought to maxillofacial perfection in later stages of his political career, but by a friendly smile. Two decades have passed since then, and in just over two months we Slovenian citizens will once again, for the fifth time, go to the polls to elect our representatives to the European Parliament. Again this time no records are expected for turnout, which from the very beginning has not exceeded one third of all eligible voters. It is true, though, that at the beginning we were, at least on the surface, much more enthusiastic about having finally become part of the European family and having fulfilled the so often repeated slogan Europe Now. Twenty years after joining, it seems that in Slovenia our attitude toward EU membership has gone from enthusiasm, through despondency, to increasingly widespread Euroscepticism. From Europe Now to Europe Yuck. To tell the truth, this is a trend not unique to Slovenia. It is also true that the European Union, its institutions, actions, decisions and non-decisions, can be reproached for many things. The problem is that most of those who point to mistakes and shortcomings, as a rule, have no ideas for how to fix them, or else offer the dismantling of European integration, a return to the “golden” age of nation-states, in which everyone was master of their own house and we didn’t have to bow to unelected bureaucratic bailiffs from Brussels. The fact that this golden age never existed doesn’t bother the sellers of sovereigntist fairy tales in the least. Nor do they care that European integration is in essence a peace process and an answer to centuries of nationalism and conflict between European nations, which culminated in a devastating world war. Advocates of the de-Europeanization of Europe, without alternative solutions, should realize that this is a path that leads Europeans back to where we have already been, to times when we settled our mutual relations mainly by killing each other. It seems that twenty years after our historic accession to the EU, we Slovenians are fed up with Europe. This is one of the rare points on which there is very broad consensus, both in public opinion and in politics. On the right, people complain not only about Europe but also about their existing political allies in it. At the recent EPP congress, which crowned the incumbent Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as its Spitzenkandidatin, among the few who voted against her were the entire delegation of the Slovenian SDS, as well as the SLS. More attentive observers of our recent history will certainly have been reminded, by MEP Romana Tomc’s recent statement that von der Leyen is not her president, of the wistful determination of Sonja Lokar as the Slovenian delegation walked out of the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. In her speech, the newly minted candidate to succeed herself warned of the danger of populism, and her opponents convincingly illustrated the reasons for her concern in their reactions at the congress. At the other end of the political spectrum, enthusiasm for Europe is lukewarm too. Levica (The Left) recently hosted the former leader of the British Labour Party, Jeremy Corbyn, in Ljubljana. Let us leave aside the irony that, at a time of internal dispute with the leader of the party’s most left-wing faction, you invite as a guest a man who in 2015, as leader of his party’s most left-wing faction, took the helm of British Labour and thereby helped anchor it firmly in opposition for another decade. In 2020 he was thrown out of the party, but before that, with his positions on the EU, he contributed to Brexit almost as much as Boris Johnson. Slovenian politics’ odd attitude toward the EU is also reflected in the profile of the people we send to represent us in Europe. To continue with Levica, it is worth recalling the former Spitzenkandidatin of the European Left in the previous European elections, Violeta Tomić. The center-left new faces also made some funny personnel decisions. In 2014 we sent Violeta Bulc to the Berlaymont palace in Brussels, where the European Commission sits. This trio fantastico is completed by the man who represented us for many years in an institution that is not part of the European Union but is nevertheless a very important part of the European institutional architecture. I am referring, of course, to Boštjan M. Zupančič, once the darling of the Slovenian liberal center, who, after the drudgery he had to endure in the service of protecting human rights at the Strasbourg court, found satisfaction and his true self in the most primitive misogyny and antisemitism. This time, too, the list of candidates for MEP will not be without its oddballs. The doyen of Slovenian foreign-affairs journalism, longtime correspondent Uroš Lipušček, recently announced his intention to take to the European dance floor. His program for Europe, based on a return to nation-states, imitates on this point the sovereigntist agenda advocated in most European countries by the far right, from the Lepenists in France to the AfD in Germany. Even more interesting is Lipušček’s view of current crises in Europe, above all the war in Ukraine. In his opinion, Ukraine, with its impudent resistance to the Russian occupier, is merely prolonging its own suffering and ours. Putin is not an imperialist “because Russia already has enough territory.” In Lipušček’s view, the size of Russia’s territory also justifies the fact that Putin is a dictator, “since in a country as big as Russia, Western-style democracy cannot work.” I leave judgment of candidate Lipušček’s professional qualifications to others. As for his ideological orientation, it is distinctly off the hoof. Who will represent us in Brussels and Strasbourg after the June elections has not yet been decided. According to the latest opinion polls ahead of the European elections, SDS is in the lead ahead of Svoboda, while Levica and the anti-vaxxer Resnica are battling for the last, ninth seat in the delegation. Personally, I wish the former more success, but it is ironic that it was precisely they who sent the first anti-vaxxer to Europe as a candidate for an even higher position. If we draw a line under it all, after twenty years we Slovenians have an attitude toward Brussels similar to the one we once had toward Belgrade. We curse and criticize, but even where the criticism is justified we very rarely offer real answers. We don’t go to European elections because we couldn’t care less. We are more or less uninterested in what the people we elected do in parliament; all that gets up our noses is how much they earn. With honorable exceptions, we send village eccentrics to the Brussels institutions and then wonder why we lack the influence and reputation we want and expect. We trash the EU for everything it does wrong and for many things it isn’t responsible for. We aren’t interested in the successes and positive changes membership brings. In our fury we would smash everything we have with a sledgehammer, without a thought for what could happen to us if we succeeded. This is far from saying that the EU does not deserve criticism and strict oversight. It has power, and any power you don’t keep a close eye on sooner or later goes bad. The democratic deficit is a real problem, and the solutions Brussels has offered so far, such as the much-vaunted Conference on the Future of Europe, have turned out to be more or less a token gesture and dust in our eyes. The European response to the 2009 financial crisis contributed in many ways to the situation that gives wings to far-right ideas. It can also be reproached for much regarding its attitude toward the tragedy in Gaza, although it is often criticized for things the member states deserve more. Among the politicians in Europe who most quickly and most decisively condemned the bloodshed caused by Israeli operations in Gaza was precisely the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs, Josep Borrell. So the problem is not that we are critical of the EU, but that there is no serious reflection, debate or smart idea about solutions. Actually, the only original idea came from Borut Pahor, who until recently enthusiastically advocated a European federation, but for most experts on European affairs this proposal was too original to be taken seriously. When, years ago, someone at the Foreign Ministry informally asked me for my opinion on a draft of a new foreign-policy strategy, I pointed out that there was nothing in it about what kind of EU we stand for. “Oh, who’s going to ask us for our opinion anyway,” came the reply. And to be completely honest, we can’t hold that against them.

Last Tuesday morning, angry farmers near the town of Pamiers in southwestern France—like others across the country—set up barricades. The protests were sparked by announced cuts to diesel fuel subsidies, burdensome bureaucracy, and low purchase prices for agricultural products. The farmers of Pamiers blocked National Road No. 20, heading toward the Andorran border. At 5:45 a.m., a blue BMW crashed at high speed into hay bales placed on the road. Behind the barricade, striking farmers were warming themselves with tea in a makeshift tent. Alexandra Sonac, a 35-year-old farmer and mother of two daughters, died instantly. Her 12-year-old daughter Camille died a few hours later. Alexandra’s husband was severely injured but is no longer in critical condition. The driver and two passengers in the BMW—all Armenian nationals who had been ordered deported after their asylum requests were denied—sustained minor injuries. The driver has been charged with involuntary manslaughter under aggravating circumstances. It is still unclear what the three Armenians were doing on the road that morning; one theory links them to cigarette smuggling, as tobacco in Andorra is three times cheaper than in France. The tragedy shocked the French public and further fueled the anger of farmers, who in the following days blocked most major cities and slowly began advancing toward Paris. The Pamiers tragedy reflects the complexity of the crisis unfolding in France—and more broadly, in Europe. The farmers' uprising is a response to the genuine hardship of rural France. Tractors now drive in convoys with coffins—memorials to Alexandra and Camille, and to the many French farmers who, in despair over their hopeless situations, have taken their own lives. Suicide rates among those working in agriculture are significantly above the national average. At first glance, French politicians hardly seem indifferent to farmers. Visiting the spring agricultural fair in Paris is an annual highlight of the French political season. No elected official dares miss the chance to sip wine, nibble on cheese, pat a cow or two, and proclaim unwavering support for French agriculture and the countryside. Farmers enjoy public sympathy far beyond their demographic share of the population. Yet political words never translate into effective action. And so once again, farmers have driven their tractors from the fields onto the roads. It’s also notable that in France—as in Germany and other European countries—the far right most loudly exploits the farmers' distress. This trend will significantly influence the outcome of the upcoming European elections. The fact that the Pamiers deaths were caused by a migrant whose asylum claim had been rejected is, for extremists, the perfect scenario—it fuses two key themes that fuel their path to power. France’s farmers' revolt is a striking example of the existential crisis of liberal democracy. It is driven by real problems, and to be honest, democrats bear a large part of the blame—simply because they’ve been the ones holding power in democratic systems for decades. Extremists have long been on the fringe. But now, the failures, greed, inconsistency, opportunism, hypocrisy, and incompetence of those who loudly proclaim democratic values are paving the way for extremists’ rise. To stop the far right, democratic forces must offer solutions. But painless fixes that won’t cause new dissatisfaction simply don’t exist anymore. Extremists have the easier job. They don’t have to solve problems; they just need to exploit the rage those problems provoke. The worse things get, the better it is for them. Let’s look more closely at what French farmers are protesting. First, incomes. Many earn less than the French minimum wage. There are many reasons. Environmental policy is one frequently cited cause. The increasingly hated green transition is also the reason for the proposed end to diesel subsidies. “Our tractors don’t run on electricity like the SUVs of the Paris elites,” the farmers shout. Just days before the Pamiers tragedy, President Macron spoke of the need to find solutions for those worried about making it to the end of the month, and those worried about the end of the world. On Friday, January 26, the Prime Minister announced a support package for farmers, including the continuation of diesel subsidies. That will help farmers through the end of the month—but it won’t stop the planet from burning. Not in France, nor anywhere else, have policymakers found ways to implement urgent environmental action in a socially just way—without disproportionately hurting already vulnerable populations. This fuels populist rage, though populists care little for social justice. Far-right leader Jordan Bardella speaks of “punitive environmentalism.” Let’s set aside the fact that these subsidy-fighting “warriors,” whether in France, Germany, or Slovenia, often get teary-eyed when talking about Argentine President Milei—hardly known for his fondness for state intervention or “socialist nonsense.” Why fix problems when you can exploit them for political gain? Poor folk are useful to populists—as long as they stay poor. Farmers’ incomes are also squeezed by low purchase prices imposed by big retail chains. “Let the state intervene and raise those prices!” is a common reaction. But that would raise prices at the grocery store. So would restrictions on agricultural imports—also high on the list of farmers’ demands. But it’s not that simple. Falling purchasing power is an issue that worries French voters even more than rural distress. Poor farmers, yes—but what about the rest of us? Another complaint is paperwork—required to access EU agricultural subsidies. “We work the fields from dawn to dusk and fill out forms all night,” farmers say. In truth, there’s probably more room here for fast relief than in other areas. The EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) allocates around €40 billion per year to farm support. That’s a huge sum. Many of the forms and checks farmers hate are there to prevent fraud—rare, but always high-profile when uncovered. Still, it’s clear procedures could be simplified, especially for small farms. Critics of CAP often argue it favors large landholders over family farms. Populists are quick to exploit farmers’ discontent with Brussels for their sovereignist, nationalist narratives. Down with the EU and its diktats! Never mind that farmers don’t actually want to give up EU money, which they’d lose if Europe were re-nationalized—they just want easier access to the aid they badly need. But who cares? Just poor folk. How this farmers’ revolt in France will end is still unclear. The measures announced by the Prime Minister last Friday have not yet calmed tensions. My GPS shows traffic around Strasbourg redder than the Ljubljana ring road. What’s clear is that this is part of a broader trend that will shape the political future of France and Europe. In this super election year, the main issues are climate change, migration, and war—both in Europe and beyond. So far, democratically minded politics has failed to deliver effective solutions for any of them that would convince voters. Anti-liberal authoritarians and nationalists are salivating. In fear for their positions, more and more European politicians try to imitate populist rhetoric to save their own skins. We’ve already seen how this ends. When choosing between a “sincere” populist and an opportunistic copy, voters always go for the original. To all our detriment. Populists care no more about making it to the end of the month than about making it to the end of the world. If we hand them the reins, those two timelines might align sooner than we think.

In recent days, we’ve learned that after a long flirtation between Real Madrid and Kylian Mbappé, France’s wonderkid will finally move to the Spanish capital at the end of the season. Although Mbappé already earns well over a million euros per week at PSG, he’s sure to earn even more in Madrid. Mbappé is an economic migrant, someone who has chosen to relocate abroad in search of a better life. Just before the winter transfer window opened for footballers, the member states of the European Union and the European Parliament reached an agreement on the terms for the transfers of migrants who don’t play football. If the EU Council formally confirms December’s political agreement on the Migration and Asylum Pact, Slovenia will, according to a so-called distribution key, take in 126 asylum seekers annually. For each, it will receive €10,000 from the EU budget. If Slovenia wishes to avoid this, it can block the transfer by paying €22,000 per person—a total of about €2.8 million annually. Or in football terms, what Mbappé earns in two weeks at PSG. To be clear, the comparison is not meant to trivialize the significance of the upcoming pact, which aims to better distribute the burden of caring for refugees among EU countries—a burden that currently falls primarily on the countries along the Union’s external borders. This is necessary and fair and could lead to a better, more humane treatment of people seeking refuge in Europe from fates they would likely suffer in their home countries. Still, the pact contains compromises designed to appease the increasingly dominant political and public stance on migration: that migration is a threat, and everything must be done to minimize it. Those who make it through ever-stricter filters will be redistributed—except where governments decide that even a few are too many and opt to pay to be rid of them. The fact is that, driven by short-sighted political interests and public opinion shaped by the populist far right—with more or less open support from other political factions—we are desperately trying to saw off the branch we’re sitting on. Shocking as it may sound, Europe’s biggest migration problem isn’t that there are too many migrants—but too few. According to EU Commissioner Ylva Johansson, Europe would need about a million additional legal migrants annually to offset its growing demographic deficit. Of course, this claim must be qualified. None of the issues caused by Europe’s rapidly aging population will be solved by throwing open the gates in a haphazard way. Sudden and massive influxes of migrants into just a few countries cause real problems—both for the host country and, even more so, for the migrants themselves. They solve no problems and create new ones. That’s why efforts to distribute migrants more evenly across EU member states are important and necessary. They create the foundation for a more humane and above all rational migration policy—one that doesn’t ignore the fact that Europe needs migrants almost as much as migrants need Europe. Reaching that point will be long and difficult. Most of the obstacles on this path are ones we’ve built ourselves. Overcoming them will require politics with courage, compassion, and reason. Politics that doesn’t just echo anti-migrant sentiment but has the courage and ability to implement the solutions necessary for managing migration flows effectively, humanely, and rationally. A policy that doesn’t “fight” migration, but manages it—by increasing legal pathways to enter Europe and investing in high-quality integration through education, employment policies, and social programs. We must do this for our own good. Our inability to understand this, let alone act in our own interest, starkly reveals how far we’ve fallen by surrendering to a chauvinistic politics that builds power on fear and hatred of the other. The sad reality is that in most European countries, migration policy is held hostage by increasingly inflammatory, irrational, and regressive discourses. These not only cause tremendous suffering and loss of life among those trying to reach Europe but also create consequences that, unless reason prevails, will bring social and economic damage to all of us in the not-too-distant future. None of this means that the arrival and integration of people with different cultural practices is easy. It can cause friction, tension, and even real threats that require action. The concerns of people affected by rapid changes in their environment cannot be simply ignored. But the fact remains: we are often the cause of those tensions. Incidents involving migrants are frequently exaggerated in the media and weaponized politically. People are afraid because we’ve made them afraid. We’ve backed ourselves into a situation where making decisions that support orderly, legal migration and integration is political suicide. Instead, politicians across the spectrum choose to mimic and flirt with anti-migrant rhetoric and policies—even though, as shown recently in the Netherlands, this strategy fails. Concessions to hatred only legitimize it and make it more socially acceptable. In such an environment, voters will always prefer the original to the copy. The current approach to migration has economic consequences. Most advanced economies face labor shortages in many sectors. These problems can’t be solved long-term by importing temporary workers from the Philippines or Thailand to pick potatoes or serve coffee. The current approach to migration is a moral issue. It’s marked by hypocrisy: the wealthiest countries are the loudest critics, even though only a tiny fraction of displaced people seek refuge in the West. The vast majority remain in their own countries or nearby—typically in less developed nations where the burden is significantly heavier. Often, the people fleeing are escaping situations that the West itself helped create. The current approach is a humanitarian crisis. People are dying. It’s a social issue. Hatred that overwhelms empathy and solidarity will sooner or later come back to harm us and our own. A society that hermetically seals itself in hatred of outsiders will eventually be poisoned by internal hatred as well. Solidarity, empathy, and respect for human dignity aren’t sausages to be sliced only for “our own.” It’s a threat to democracy. Short-sighted political opportunism that tries to compete with chauvinist anti-migrant narratives helps destroy the values and safeguards of democracy. For far-right populists, inciting fear of migrants is their main weapon—alongside other cultural battlefronts—in a liberticidal march to power. They stoke fear to justify “strong leaders,” not messy things like human rights and civil liberties that benefit migrants, homosexuals, and emancipated women—at the supposed expense of hard-working, white, native-born (especially male) citizens. Migrants are a resource—one that not just Europe, but most of the developed world needs as much as rare metals for semiconductors and EV batteries. And yet we do everything we can to avoid tapping into it. I don’t mean to take the comparison between people and raw materials too far, but just like semiconductors don’t grow on trees, turning migrants into citizens who contribute to society requires investment. And we simply won’t make it. As soon as anyone suggests investing in integration, someone yells, “All that money for migrants—what about our own people?” The result is that people still come, but they arrive in societies hostile to them, that don’t invest in their integration. This creates ghettos and social hardship—problems we could avoid, but don’t. For Slovenia, the upcoming Migration and Asylum Pact offers a chance to do things differently. Instead of deporting people who’ve already settled and found jobs here, we could use the €1 million from Brussels—plus the nearly €3 million we’d save by not paying to reject our quota—to successfully integrate our share of migrants, and perhaps even more. Not just because we want to be a humane, compassionate society—but because we need them. Not just a hundred-some—but maybe more. Who knows—among them or their children, along with drivers, caregivers, waiters, doctors, mechanics, and engineers, there might even be a future Mbappé.
A Handbook for Political Culture, or How to Help Democracy Survive 2024

The latest public opinion polls show that optimism is returning among Slovenians. That’s a lovely and important development—if perhaps a bit unexpected. Truth be told, the threshold for optimism in this poll was set quite low. To be counted as someone looking cheerfully toward the future, it was enough to believe that life wouldn’t get worse. This reminded me of the famous Balkan definition of optimism and pessimism: one person says, “Things are so bad they can’t get any worse,” and another replies, “Oh yes, they absolutely can.” I’ve never been entirely sure which one is the optimist and which the pessimist, but in today’s world, it hardly matters. We’re somewhere in that range. In my view, the year that just ended gave us few reasons for genuine optimism. We found no real solutions to any of the major global challenges—from climate change and the need for humane, rational migration management, to economic troubles, social injustice, and a digital transformation that sometimes feels on the verge of spinning out of control. One bloody war was joined by another. Despair over the mess we’re in is fueling the rise of dangerous political clowns, would-be authoritarians, and fear- and hate-mongering opportunists. If anyone can look forward to 2024 with optimism, it’s them. This year, several important elections await us—most notably the European elections in early June and the U.S. presidential election in November. Somewhere between the European and American elections, we’ll also mark a curious historical event: the 860th anniversary of the Erfurt latrine tragedy. On July 26, 1184, King Henry VI organized a peace conference in the German city of Erfurt. During the session, the floor collapsed under the weight of the assembled delegates. Unfortunately, they had gathered above a latrine, and sixty of them drowned in—you know what. I don’t mention this as a parallel to any current political event (and certainly not to wish any such fate on today’s politicians), but it’s a noteworthy exception to the common folk belief that politicians merely stir—you know what—without ever falling into it themselves. But back to the present, where, if nothing else, we are literally safe from falling into latrines. Figuratively, though, we’re constantly walking right above one. And every time we stomp our feet in rage instead of thinking clearly, we risk breaking another support beam. So what can we do? Are we really so powerless amid all this—you know what? People typically blame politicians for all crises and problems. And not without reason—they’re the ones holding the scissors and the cloth. But we often forget that in democracies, it is we who hand them those tools. As Thomas Jefferson put it, the government you elect is the government you deserve. Yes, people often vote in protest—angry and disillusioned by broken promises and the inability of those in power to solve problems. The frustration is understandable, and often justified. But it makes no sense to, in a fit of rage, vote for those even less prepared or capable of addressing the challenges we face. If you need an outlet for your anger, buy a punching bag. But in the voting booth, it’s better to use your brain. Of course, that’s easier said than done. Even though there are indicators, parameters, and methodologies that could help us make more rational choices and actions—in the interest of democracy and our future. Paradoxically, we started building democratic literacy for children first. Far be it from me to say kids don’t need democratic education, but it’s objectively difficult when we’re teaching children values and behaviors that are completely contradicted by the adults around them. Years ago, when a former president of Slovenia invited me—for the first and last time—to one of his consultations (on hate speech), he gave me 30 seconds at the end to present the Reference Framework of Competences for Democratic Culture. This is a simple and effective educational method developed by the Council of Europe, modeled after the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. (Yes, the one we all cite when lying about our language skills in job interviews—Spanish? C1! Olé!) I explained that the democratic culture framework is a methodology for teaching kids the values and behaviors we’d want to see in politicians. By the way, that former president and I never saw eye to eye on how to tackle hate speech. Maybe it was one of those “intentional mistakes” he later said he made to avoid appearing perfect. Those of you who read me regularly will recall I’ve often been critical of him, but I must admit—in this regard, he was very successful. The framework divides democratic competencies into four groups: Values – Respect for human dignity and human rights, appreciation of cultural diversity, respect for democracy, justice, equality, and the rule of law. Attitudes and Skills – Independent learning, analytical and critical thinking, listening and observing, empathy, adaptability, language skills, cooperation, and conflict resolution. Openness – Openness to different cultures, worldviews, beliefs, habits; respect and responsibility. Knowledge and Critical Understanding – From self-awareness and self-understanding to understanding the world around us. Each competency includes age-appropriate learning goals and assessment methods. There are handbooks for various age groups—but not, unfortunately, for the group that needs it most: politicians. Imagine a society governed by people—whether in power or in opposition—who possess empathy, respect for human dignity, justice, and cultural diversity. Politicians capable of critical thinking and self-awareness. Politicians who can not only speak but listen—and hear. Who take responsibility for their actions and mistakes, even those they make intentionally, just so no one thinks they’re perfect. Given the direction the world is spinning, that may seem like a fantasy. But it becomes painfully clear how far we are from it when you assess Donald Trump—or his countless copycats sprouting like mushrooms everywhere—by the standards above. Still, in democracies, we voters retain the power to create change. Don’t listen to those who claim “they’re all the same.” They’re not. Even if no one is perfect. Make your own handbook. Use it first to assess yourself—your values, your knowledge, your actions. Be demanding and critical of your own democratic competencies. Feeling empathy only for yourself and your own tribe doesn’t count. And if you reflexively take the opposite stance of everything you hear from scientists, doctors, or newspapers—without reflection—you’re not a critical thinker. You’re a fool. No offense. Then apply the same standards to the people you vote for. This has nothing to do with ideology. Vote left, right, or center—green, yellow, red, or purple. Just make sure the candidates possess at least as many democratic competencies as the average first-grader is expected to have. If that sounds like too much work, and you’d rather let loose your frustration at the next election—give the middle finger to the world and especially yourself—don’t complain when the consequences hit you. Because by ignoring the competencies and values democracy needs, you’re not just dragging yourself into the—you know what—but all of us. And with that, I wish you a Happy New Year. Olé.

The recent resignation of French Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne attracted a great deal of attention in many places, including Slovenia. First, probably, because such resignations mostly happen in the context of political crises, and second, because of the youth of the new Prime Minister, 34-year-old Gabriel Attal. Let us leave aside those who are surprised that Attal is gay, since such surprise, in my opinion, says more about them than about him. In France’s constitutional and political context, the change from Borne to Attal is far less surprising or unusual. First of all, because France is a presidential republic, and the Prime Minister, like the ministers, is appointed and dismissed by the head of state. Such changes at the Hôtel Matignon, the Prime Minister’s residence, are a constant in France. Attal is already the fourth Prime Minister since the start of President Macron’s first term. Changes can occur when the President judges that the Prime Minister is worn out, unpopular and not doing the job well enough. A change can also occur when the public judges that it is the President himself who is worn out, unpopular and unsuccessful. Sometimes French presidents, especially during a first term that they can still renew, decide to replace their prime ministers when these are too dynamic, successful and popular, since they steal the President’s luster and can become a troublesome rival at the next presidential election. In the opinion of some, this was the reason Macron’s first Prime Minister, Édouard Philippe, departed during Macron’s first term. This time, of course, that was not the scenario, not only because Borne never matched Philippe’s popularity, but above all because Macron cannot run for a third term. By being appointed head of government, with Macron’s blessing, Attal certainly becomes one of the possible contenders to succeed him, if not in three years, then in eight. Nor is it shocking, in the French political context, that the new Prime Minister is only 34. First, because he was chosen by someone who was only five years older when he was elected to the far more important office of President. The choice of a young, communicative politician seems all the more logical in the context of the upcoming European elections, which carry considerable domestic political weight in France, above all as regards the balance of power between the governing coalition and the far right. The far right narrowly won the last European elections; this time opinion polls point to a much larger lead, as much as 10 percentage points. The result of the European elections will set the starting positions for the next presidential election three years later. The National Rally’s campaign is being led very successfully by its president Jordan Bardella, who stands out for his dynamism, his communication skills—and his youth. He is 28.

“Hands off our children!” one of our political grandees recently exclaimed on social media, backing up his digital fist on the table with the accusation that someone was, with something, directly violating Article 54 of the Constitution of the Republic of Slovenia. The Constitution is an important thing, and violations of it are no laughing matter. For those of you who don’t know it by heart, Article 54 concerns the rights and duties of parents regarding the maintenance, education and upbringing of their children. Interfering with rights regarding the upbringing of children is a sensitive matter, whether it is the mother-in-law or the state looking over parents’ shoulders, let alone anyone else. Since this time the concern was expressed by someone who holds very pronounced views when it comes to children, I was of course curious to know who was threatening our children and how. There is no doubt that the gentleman knows a great deal about defending and protecting the people against social threats, since he was my former high school teacher of general people’s defense and social self-protection. And mentor of the defense club. This time he was enraged by a handbook entitled A Rainbow in Your Pocket, published almost four years ago, as part of a strategic partnership under the EU’s Erasmus+ program, by Legebitra, a civil society organization working in the fields of human rights, education, and mental, physical and sexual health, which campaigns for social and systemic changes based on respect for sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. Since I know that my former comrade teacher these days can hardly bear a rainbow in the sky, let alone a rainbow on a flag and evidently even less a rainbow in a pocket, the only surprising thing is that he waited so long for his outburst of indignation. The weekly Demokracija showed greater vigilance, warning parents soon after the handbook came out that their “children will be indoctrinated and turned into homosexuals.” Four years later, in a booster dose of vigilance, we now learn that behind the indoctrination turning our children into homosexuals lies LGBTQI+ ideology. This, as the message posted on social media warns, “with strong political support is increasingly present in Slovenian schools and kindergartens. LGBTQIA+ organizations are investing a lot of money and time in recruiting and training teachers in order to indoctrinate children in kindergartens and schools with LGBTQIA+ ideology.” So now you know. Thank God there are still people among us whose attention never flags on these matters. If you wanted to set up a club for the defense of children against LGBTQIA+ ideology, you would be hard pressed to find a better mentor. For the uninitiated, the doctrine of the existence of LGBTQIA+ ideology is based on the thesis that people who belong to sexual minorities do, in principle and in theory, have the right to equality and respect for their human dignity, but only until those rights begin to be publicly advocated, their respect demanded and put into practice. At that moment the rights of members of these social minorities are no longer rights but become an ideology and a conspiracy theory against which we may and must defend ourselves with everything that comes to hand and mind. We can learn from others here. I am writing this column on the way back from Vilnius in Lithuania, where I met human rights activists from Russia, Belarus and Ukraine. Among them were LGBTQI+ ideologues from the Russian Federation, who complained about a recent ruling of the Russian Supreme Court that effectively criminalized any activity by organizations defending the rights of sexual minorities in that country. Now they can no longer spread their theories even in theory without risking ending up in jail. In Putin’s Russia, not only children but adults too are safe from LGBTQI+ ideology. Even the best mentors have role models. In Slovenia we are still trailing behind Russia for now, but some are putting a lot of effort into catching up. Curiosity gave me no peace, so I sat down to read and find out how A Rainbow in Your Pocket threatens our children. It turned out to be a handbook intended to deepen school staff’s professional knowledge and skills in dealing with peer violence, bullying, name-calling, prejudice and stereotypes based on students’ personal circumstances. To the casual reader it may not be immediately clear how such activity could violate any article of the Constitution, including the rights and duties of parents. I admit that at first I was a little confused about this myself. Perhaps the critics believe that the incidence of such forms of peer violence does not reach the threshold that would justify interfering with parents’ right to bring up their children in the spirit of bullying, name-calling, prejudice and stereotypes based on students’ personal circumstances? A survey published in the handbook showed that in 2003 a mere 54 percent of respondents in Slovenia had been exposed to violence at school because of their same-sex orientation. By 2014 the share of those who answered that they had been discriminated against or harassed during their schooling had fallen to a negligible 30 percent. With such low numbers, it really wouldn’t do to make a rainbow elephant out of a fly. Hands off our children and their hands, with which they mistreat their classmates! I would add that for just under a fifth of them it was not peer violence at all; they were harassed and discriminated against by teachers. Hands off our teachers!
