Some may also wonder how such an interpretation of Article 54 of the Constitution can be reconciled with its Article 14, which states that in Slovenia “everyone shall be guaranteed equal human rights and fundamental freedoms irrespective of national origin, race, sex, language, religion, political or other conviction, material standing, birth, education, social status, disability or any other personal circumstance.” Readers more sensitive to traditional values will certainly recall the recent position of a constitutional judge who, in a dissenting opinion on the decision by which the Constitutional Court rejected the request for a referendum on amending the Family Code, warned of a violation of “the right to separate oneself from others.” The constitutional judge lamented that we do not allow “an empowered individual who thinks and acts independently of what the majority thinks” to have more rights than someone else. He stressed that the “right to separation” is “the second pillar of our tradition.” To a certain extent that is true. The legal order of Butale also knew a right to separation, at least as regards crime statistics. Let us recall the terrible robber Cefizelj, who smothered seven people and three women. A ruder and more superficial chronicler than I am might, at these reflections, recall the indignation of the Reich Minister for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, Joseph Goebbels, who in a speech in June 1935 sharply condemned all those “who shamelessly declare that Jews are people too.” When, a few days later, the main Jewish newspaper Jüdische Rundschau dared to object to the separation into people and Jews on which the German legal order of the time was based, the minister banned it without hesitation. I myself believe that such a comparison between the historical events described and today’s reflections on separation would be exaggerated and misleading. In the first case it was the persecution of certain social groups on the basis of their personal circumstances; in the second, merely protection against the personal circumstances of certain social groups. Even Cefizelj would get that these are two completely different things.

"\[...] marked the culmination of twenty years of democracy's unfulfilled promises to control unemployment, inflation, deflation, labour unrest, party egoism, and more. \[...] which was weary of itself and doubtful of the principles it lived by, almost breathed a sigh of relief when everything was sorted out... It believed that \[...] was a very smart man—unpleasant, but smart. He made his country strong. Why not try it that way?" If you insert “the fall of Paris” in the first blank, “Europe” in the second, and “Adolf Hitler” in the third, you get the original text of a report filed by Newsweek correspondent Rosie Waldeck in June 1940, from Bucharest, after the Nazi army marched into Paris. But if you don’t, you have a handy template for understanding many political events and disruptions we are witnessing today. Let’s not get our panties in a twist—as the Americans say—this is not about playing the Nazi card or calling every sprouting authoritarian "Hitler." But Rosie Waldeck’s article remains surgically precise in describing the social, economic, and political circumstances behind the meteoric rise of “unpleasant, but smart” politicians—then and now. “His ideas don’t scare me. People have a right to choose whoever they want. We’re tired of politics because they always lie to us,” said 26-year-old salesman Orlando Sanchez, explaining why he voted for Javier Milei. Mark Twain supposedly never actually said the famous quote, “History doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes,” as historian Niall Ferguson once corrected me in conversation. But Twain did say that history is like a kaleidoscope—the same, coloured glass pieces turning and mixing over time into different patterns. Occasionally, they settle into various shades of brown. People turn to “unpleasant, but smart” leaders when they feel democracy has let them down—when they feel they have nothing left to lose. When frustration, despair, and rage over “the unfulfilled promises of democracy—unemployment, inflation, deflation, labour unrest, party egoism, and more”—overwhelm reason, they become willing to support ideas and people who offer no real solutions—only the promise of radically changing a reality they can no longer endure. All it takes is for the “unpleasant, but smart” ones to point the finger at those allegedly responsible for all the pain. One reason we learn so little from history is that it's usually painful and unpleasant—we’d rather forget it. We’ve convinced ourselves that nothing bad can happen as long as we ignore the past thoroughly enough. Often, we do this by relying on the illusion of temporal distance. The events Rosie Waldeck described seem infinitely far away—another era, another world, one that’s gone and won’t return. This is dangerously misleading. Rosie sent her dispatch from Bucharest to editors in the U.S. less than a year after a 15-year-old Jewish refugee named Heinz Alfred Kissinger fled Bavaria with his parents. It’s entirely possible that while learning English, Kissinger read Waldeck’s articles describing the situation that had forced his family to flee Europe. Let’s not forget—Kissinger died just a few days ago. The Europe of the 1930s is separated from us by the span of a single human lifetime. Historical time is a funny thing—it doesn’t always flow in the direction we want. A few months ago, I sat on a panel with Francis Fukuyama, who admitted he had to revise his theory of the “end of history,” saying history in the U.S. is now unfolding—in the wrong direction. “Democracy in the U.S. is under threat,” Fukuyama warned, “but in Europe—with a few exceptions—you’re still doing fine.” In reply, I shared a joke about a Bosnian refugee during the war who had found safety in Sweden. He spoke with his brother back home by phone: “How’s life in Sweden?” “Eh, they’re twenty years behind us. Still living in peace and harmony.” We tend to believe that bad things only happen to other people, in other places. We’re the good guys. We’re safe. This, too, is why Rosie Waldeck’s article remains so instructive: it doesn’t just describe Germany—it describes Europe. When it was published, Hitler had already been in power for over seven years. What he had done during that time is chronicled by historian Saul Friedländer in The Years of Persecution: Nazi Germany and the Jews, 1933–1939. Today we like to think those events only happened "over there." But that’s not true. Historian Mark Mazower, in Dark Continent, shows that antisemitism, nationalism, obsession with demographics, survival, and national rebirth—through fetishizing childbirth, “family values,” and eugenics—as well as paranoia and hatred of others, were present in most European countries. After WWI, Europe saw a wave of new constitutional democracies. Two decades later, almost none remained. The trend across Europe was toward authoritarianism and nationalism. The tipping point came when Germany took things too far—not only inwardly, but outwardly, into global war and genocide, chronicled in Friedländer’s second volume The Years of Extermination: Nazi Germany and the Jews, 1939–1945. We also shouldn’t forget how many local collaborators, “good people,” joined that horrific endeavor. Of course, one can take the obsession with history too far. There’s a difference between learning from the past and being paralyzed by it—or convinced we can’t escape it. Fatalism and the belief in the inevitability of history repeating itself are even more dangerous than blind faith in an inevitably brighter future. The first leads to what Timothy Snyder calls the “politics of eternity”—the favorite tool of authoritarians like Putin, who promise no better future, just endless suffering and revenge for the pain supposedly caused by others. Historian Timothy Garton Ash calls it hyper amnesia—obsession with a warped, ideological version of history used to manipulate frustration and rage, without offering real solutions. As Oleksandra Romantsova, executive director of Kyiv’s Center for Civil Liberties and 2022 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, recently said in Strasbourg: “The problem with Russian history is that it’s unpredictable.” The politics of inevitability heads in the opposite direction. In this view, history isn’t unpredictable—it’s irrelevant and inconvenient. Dark periods are just temporary anomalies in a grand narrative that guarantees peace and progress by default, no matter what we do in the present. To reinforce this belief, we assign retrospective logic and inevitability to historical outcomes that could easily have gone differently: WWII had to end with Nazi defeat, the Soviet empire was always destined to collapse, the fall of the Berlin Wall could only mean the lasting unification of Europe under shared democratic values. We act as if things always sort themselves out—and for the better. And so we indulge in tantrums and destruction without considering the consequences. In the end, both the politics of eternity and the politics of inevitability send the same message: we have no real influence or responsibility over the future we’ll live in. But the truth likely lies somewhere in between. Garton Ash recommends “moderate memory”—knowing the facts and cultivating critical historical understanding, so we can learn from the past, but without pretending it locks in our future. The future is not set by the past—it depends on us. On how we address the same economic, social, and political issues Rosie Waldeck wrote about nearly a century ago, and which still confront us today. Fate will not bring us inevitable war, nor automatic peace and prosperity. The responsibility for the future lies with us—depends on what we do here and now. The fight for peace, freedom, and democracy is never over. And if we keep handing the kaleidoscope of history to the “unpleasant, but smart,” we may find ourselves once again staring at a familiar shade of brown. Dark brown. Today

The scenes coming from Gaza for weeks now are horrific. One of the most densely populated areas in the world is turning into an apocalyptic ruin — and a graveyard. According to available data, nearly half the victims are children. True, these figures come from health authorities under Hamas control and, in the view of many, should not be trusted. But what does that actually mean? That it wasn't five or four thousand children who died, but "only" three thousand? Two thousand five hundred? Numbers are not irrelevant — in fact, I sincerely hope Hamas is inflating them for propaganda purposes, because that would mean fewer actual victims — and every human life, especially that of a child, matters. Still, such discrepancies do not alter Israel's responsibility for the destruction and civilian casualties caused by retaliatory actions for the massacre carried out by Hamas on October 7. In the outrage over the devastation and human suffering — which I share — many are quick to label events as war crimes or even genocide. I remain more cautious with such judgments. Not only because these are legal definitions determined by international law, not by the intensity of emotions, no matter how justified, but also because I believe this kind of debate distracts from what truly matters: Israel must immediately change the way it conducts military operations in Gaza and take all measures to protect the civilian population and ensure access to all necessary forms of aid. This is an imperative rooted in basic humanity, and it is not contingent on whether future legal assessments will deem current operations to have been consistent or inconsistent with international humanitarian law. This does not mean Israel has no right to self-defence — it certainly does, including military action against Hamas murderers responsible for the crimes of October 7. But the imperative of defence and security also requires Israel to wage this war differently, with real and effective concern for civilian protection. What we've seen so far will leave scars and breed hatred. If anything, Israel should heed the bitter lesson of Bush's war on terror after 9/11: the only truly effective counterterrorist action is the one that stops more terrorists than it creates. The protests and expressions of solidarity with Palestinians, taking place around the world, including here, are for all these reasons expected and justified. They send a message to Israel that its actions are not only causing suffering to Palestinians but also harming its own standing and reputation. These protests apply pressure to Western governments, which, in the justified and understandable solidarity after the October 7 massacre, in their unwavering support, forgot that true friendship requires telling an ally hard truths — and protecting them from the consequences of actions born of pain and rage. They are a response to parts of that political class trying to use war and suffering to push their own agendas and stoke culture wars. And a red card to those who mask their latent (or not so latent) antisemitism with expressions of support for the current Israeli government. But then we see the defacing of the Jewish Cultural Center in Ljubljana, with the Star of David equated to the swastika. And other antisemitic incidents and outbursts of hatred, which have been rising sharply across Europe for years and have exploded in recent weeks. Strasbourg has the second-largest Jewish community in France. Today, they live in fear. Each evening, a colleague hides her Star of David pendant under her clothing before heading home, to avoid being recognized. The rise in antisemitism cannot and must not be arbitrarily attributed to those justifiably protesting Israeli policy or expressing solidarity with Palestinians. This is what former UK Home Secretary Suella Braverman attempted when she called the protests "hate marches." Many of the people responsible for antisemitic acts don't care about Palestinians at all — some even hate them almost as much as they hate Jews. Yet increasingly, we see people, in justified outrage over Gaza, who, unintentionally or in the heat of the moment, contribute to an atmosphere that trivializes or even normalizes antisemitism. As the controversial saying goes — which some claim is black Jewish humour born of centuries of persecution, and others see as pure hatred: "An antisemite is someone who hates Jews more than they deserve." This commentary refers to people who, in their outrage over Palestinian suffering, cannot or will not also express outrage over the brutal murder of more than 1,300 Jews by Hamas on October 7. Clear condemnation of that crime does not dilute sincere solidarity with Palestinians — it strengthens it. The same goes for those who, in their condemnations, fail to distinguish between the actions of the Israeli government and all Israeli citizens, or even all Jews — even as they rightly criticize Israel for failing to distinguish between Hamas and all Palestinians. Especially troubling is the invocation of the Holocaust in the context of Gaza. Simplistic comparisons between Israel's retaliatory actions and the Nazi genocide of six million Jews are grossly inappropriate and, by themselves, can reflect antisemitism. The IHRA definition of antisemitism — adopted by Slovenia — states that it's entirely legitimate to criticize Israel on the same terms as other countries. But equating Israel with the Nazi regime crosses the line and may constitute antisemitism. In other words, if civilizational standards applied to all states are not enough for your critique of Israel, and you must lean on the crutch of trivializing the greatest crime in human history, then perhaps it's worth thinking twice before you speak. Especially since that same message is echoed in the graffiti on the door of the Jewish Cultural Center, now being met with self-righteous handwringing. Also questionable is the increasingly broad-brush use of the term "Zionism," which for many has become a criminal ideology equated with other abominable "-isms." A 2022 Council of Europe recommendation on Holocaust remembrance and preventing crimes against humanity emphasized the need to treat Zionism in its historical context: as a response to rising antisemitism in the late 19th century and as a national independence movement akin to the revolutions of 1848. Simplistic interpretations of Zionism, now rampant, are labelled by the Council as "radical anti-Zionism" and a form of antisemitism. Yes, Zionism means many things to many people and is indeed used today to justify unacceptable policies and actions. But superficial critics of Zionism, deliberately or not, often question Israel's right to exist. They trace the roots of today's tragedy to the mere arrival of Jews in a land where Palestinians lived — and the founding of a Jewish state. Combining emotional fervour, ideological zeal, intellectual laziness, and historical shallowness, they cast the origin of Israel in the mold of colonialism and anti-colonial struggle, ignoring anything that doesn't fit that narrative. For example, that Jews already lived in the area before Israel's founding. Some came in the early 20th century as followers of Herzl's Zionist movement; many arrived in the 1930s fleeing Nazi persecution. When Hannah Arendt fled Germany in 1933, she joined a youth Zionist emigration group in Paris. After the war, Holocaust survivors — often literal skeletons — joined them in Palestine. And finally, hundreds of thousands of Jews expelled from other regional countries came as well. These frequently ignored facts do not justify actions against Palestinians or diminish their suffering under decades of occupation. But they do demand that we consider both the Nakba and the Holocaust when grappling with the complexities of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The Jewish state is a consequence of centuries of persecution, culminating in the crematoria of the Nazi death camps. That's why the late Palestinian intellectual Edward Said called Palestinians "victims of victims," refugees from refugees. Those who deny Jews the right to a state never offer an alternative: what should have happened to the Jews, in 1947 or today, if Israel didn't exist? That alone reveals how unhelpful the anti-colonial mindset is in solving this conflict. After decolonization in Africa, the Portuguese went to Portugal, the French to France, the Belgians to Belgium, the British to Britain. Where would you send the Jews? To Madagascar? And once again, although it may seem impossible in the current war, the only path to lasting peace remains the two-state solution. Both Palestinians and Israelis have the right to safety, peace, freedom, and a future built side-by-side as neighbours, not enemies. Achieving that requires many things. An immediate end to the suffering of innocent Palestinian civilians. A change in Israeli policy to create conditions for a two-state solution, instead of the current approach — especially the violent expansion of settlements — which deliberately undermines it. And finally, a determined fight against antisemitism, which never disappeared but is now growing and becoming disturbingly acceptable to many.

Homeland is not a legal term but a political and emotional reference. And because it is politics mixed with emotion, it is also one of the most inspiring, but also most abused, of concepts. Za domovino (For the Homeland) was the name of the newspaper of the Fifth Army District in the late SFRY, which covered more or less the entire territory of today’s Croatia. I did my military service in that district in the distant 1980s, the last six months in the editorial office of the publication mentioned above, which demanded loyalty to the (then) homeland in its very name. I got this privileged position in the editorial office, which had its premises in the military prison in the center of Zagreb, through connections. I am not in the least ashamed to admit that I did everything I could to make the grueling military service, which drove me to despair, easier. In exchange for a pass allowing unlimited free movement around Zagreb, I wrote some of my most lyrical texts during that period. My comrades at the typewriters and I competed to see who could take the mockery of the pathos glorifying the army and the ruling ideology furthest without the editors, or anyone else, noticing. For the homeland, middle finger first. Incidentally, when I met Josip, one of the two officer-editors, in Belgrade years later, he told me that it had been perfectly clear to him all along what we were up to. When war broke out in Croatia, Captain Josip, a Croat by nationality married to a Serb, remained loyal to the JNA and ended up in Belgrade, while his co-editor Captain Bojan, a Serb by nationality married to a Croat, joined the Croatian National Guard. It is one thing to love your homeland, and another when life forces you to choose between love and homeland. The British historian Timothy Garton Ash writes about a different concept of homeland in his book Homelands, subtitled A Personal History of Europe. For the author, homeland is not a unitary and exclusive concept based on blood and soil, but a community that also allows for multiple identities or homelands—hence the plural in the title—and is based on belonging to a common system of values. The American singer Marvin Gaye thought about it differently again in his song “Wherever I Lay My Hat (That’s My Home).” These are just three random associations that first came to mind as I followed the “scandal” that followed the Slovenian President’s words to Slovenian minority high school students in Trieste. “Your homeland is Italy,” said Nataša Pirc Musar, setting off a wave of indignation and condemnation, above all in Slovenia. I myself spent the first years of my life among the Slovenians across the border, and later too I regularly visited those parts, where my father’s family comes from. I went to kindergarten in the Trieste district of Roiano, to the nursery-school nuns, who didn’t talk much about the homeland. The nuns told us more about how children whose parents didn’t take them to Mass on Sundays would end up in hell. That worried me particularly, since on Sundays we really didn’t often go to church, but rather to my father’s friend Drago in Dolina near Trieste. Drago was a Partisan, wounded in the battle for Mrkonjić Grad. In Drago’s house only Nona prayed: in the postwar elections for the Italian Communist Party to win, and later often for the two unruly rascals, my brother and me, to get out of the house as soon as possible. “Off you go, off you go, with God and Mary,” she would wave to us with pursed lips as we left. Drago was attached to Yugoslavia, and he was not the only one among the Slovenians across the border who followed independence with considerable unease. It was not only about ideological positions; many in the minority worried about what would happen when there was no longer a strong neighboring state supporting them politically and financially, although it of course had its own calculations in doing so. A prominent representative of the Slovenian minority once explained to me some of the collateral consequences of this close connection of (part of) the Slovenian minority with the mother country. If you are always turned only toward Ljubljana, you turn your back on the state whose citizen you are. That is not good. We are Slovenians, part of the Slovenian nation and cultural space, and the bond with Slovenia and its support are extremely important, but if we want to be a successful and dynamic community, we must build our success and our development in the state in which we live, in it and with it. In essence, he said something very similar to what the President said the other day. It is true, however, that these words carry more weight coming from a member of the minority than when someone from this side of the border explains them to a member of the minority. Many reproached the President for speaking about the homeland when she should have spoken about the state. That is probably true, and perhaps it was just a slip of the tongue. Homeland is not a legal term but a political and emotional reference. And because it is politics mixed with emotion, it is one of the most inspiring, but also most abused, of concepts. Heroes sacrifice themselves for the homeland, receive monuments for it, and deserve our respect, gratitude and remembrance. On the other hand, patriotism is often—if I may use the hackneyed but nonetheless evergreen line of the British writer Samuel Johnson—abused as “the last refuge of a scoundrel.” Because homeland is an emotional category that everyone, from Josip to Bojan and Marvin Gaye, interprets and feels in their own way, invoking it, especially in a political context and when we link homeland to ethnic belonging, can quickly get us into trouble. Regardless, I believe the President can hardly be reproached, apart perhaps from imprecision. As for her critics in Slovenia, I am not entirely convinced whether they were really guided by sincere concern for the minority or simply could not resist the temptation to give the President a flick on the ear. Heh, heh, heh. The thesis that the Slovenians in Italy are Italian citizens whose homeland is Slovenia logically means that we have two categories of Italian citizens in Italy. Those whose homeland is Italy, and the others. Can we imagine how we would react if the Italian President came to Trieste and snapped at the minority that Italy is not their homeland? Especially since in the past it often behaved toward them in just that way. And what happens if we apply the doctrine of linking homeland to ethnic belonging to ourselves? Do we in Slovenia also have several categories of citizens? Staunch and not-so-staunch? Those who are Slovenian by blood and whose homeland is Slovenia, and those who have always lived here or who came to us, many of them generations ago, but whose homeland is, jus sanguinis ad perpetuam, exclusively and for ever and ever, elsewhere? It seems to me that in Slovenia we have not yet fully internalized the fact that we have our own state. In a democratic state, the fundamental status from which all rights and freedoms derive is citizenship, not ethnic belonging. This does not conflict with arrangements that grant minorities additional rights and protection, but it does not allow a system in which the majority nation has a privileged position over minorities by default. As is the case in Israel. Of course, this does not mean I do not respect love of one’s homeland. It is a powerful and, as a rule, noble, though often manipulated, feeling. But I suggest we allow people to have not just one, but, if that is how they feel, two or even more homelands. Like Timothy Garton Ash. The very expression “mother homeland,” which we use so often in connection with the Slovenian minorities and Slovenian emigrants, shows that the homeland is not necessarily just one; there can be at least two, the mother one and the non-mother one. The Slovenians across the border are indisputably part of the Slovenian nation and cultural space and need and deserve our attention and support. Ties with them are extremely important, for them and for us, but if we absolutely must talk about homeland, this is in no way in contradiction with the fact that, as the President said, their homeland is Italy—or, if the President will allow me, also Italy. How to put this into practice in today’s world and Europe was the task of the Group of Eminent Persons that, in 2011, under the leadership of Joschka Fischer, prepared the report “Living Together: Combining Diversity and Freedom in 21st-century Europe.” One of the “eminent persons” was the aforementioned Timothy Garton Ash. One of the group’s recommendations proposed a “hyphenated identity” as an answer to the traditional insistence on only one, exclusive and excluding identity, in which a growing number of Europeans do not find themselves and which causes many frictions and conflicts. A great deal has happened in the world in the last twelve years, above all many worrying things. The report has lost none of its relevance in that time. Rather the opposite. It can show us the way to a coexistence in which the Slovenians across the border are not merely Slovenians or merely Italian citizens, but part of both and a bridge between the two communities, cultures, nations and identities. To no one’s detriment and to everyone’s enrichment. It is true, though, that in light of a history in which the Italian state was often unkind to the Slovenian minority, it would have been more appropriate if the message to the minority that their homeland is also Italy had come in Trieste from the mouth of the Italian President, Mattarella. He and our President could have held hands while doing so, and then gone together to our side of the border, where our President could have addressed the members of the Italian national community in Slovenia with a similar message.

On Friday, October 13, in the northern French town of Arras, 20-year-old Mohamed M., born in the North Caucasian region of Ingushetia, stabbed and killed a 57-year-old French teacher, Dominique Bernard, in a school courtyard. The investigation confirmed that the attack was linked to events in southern Israel and Gaza. On Monday, October 16, all high schools in France started classes two hours later. First, meetings were held between teachers, school administrators, and French authorities, where they could discuss the shock and fear that have become part of their profession, as well as the measures needed to prevent such incidents in the future. At 2 p.m., memorial ceremonies were held in all schools, including a moment of silence and a discussion with students. These discussions focused on the terrorist attack in Arras but naturally also touched on the harrowing events unfolding in the Middle East. When my eleven-year-old daughter came home from school that day, she asked me at the door: "Are you for the Palestinians or for the Israelis?" The question was serious. She expected help and an answer that would help her understand a deeply troubling issue. Because she talks about it with her friends. Because she's getting all kinds of frightening information on social media. Because more and more people are dying in the Middle East. Because a teacher was killed in Arras. Because she's afraid. Whose side am I on? I stand in solidarity with the Palestinians. Because they have lived in exile or under occupation for seventy-five years. Because they have waited in vain all this time for the fulfilment of their right to existence and security, the right to their own state. Because they have endured many injustices. The routine of occupation and repression, as described by British historian Tony Judt, himself of Jewish descent: "Curfews, checkpoints, bulldozers, public humiliation, home demolitions, land confiscation, shootings, targeted assassinations." I stand with the Palestinians because their Arab neighbours, who attacked Israel in their name a few times to destroy it, left them more or less to fend for themselves after each defeat. I stand with the Palestinians who live in inhumane conditions brought about by both occupation and the incompetence, corruption, extremism, and factionalism of their leaders. I am horrified by the blood toll paid by innocent Palestinian civilians in Israel's response to the atrocities committed by Hamas in southern Israel. I respect and support calls to protect civilians and uphold international humanitarian law. I stand in solidarity with the Israelis. Because I firmly believe they have the right to security and their own state, created because of centuries of suffering by the Jewish people, culminating in the Holocaust, in which six million were murdered. I stand with the Israelis because, from the moment they declared their state based on a UN resolution, they have had to defend their survival with arms multiple times. "Our goal is clear," said PLO founder and first president Ahmed al-Shukeiri at the start of the Six-Day War in 1967, "we will destroy Israel and its people; for the survivors, if any, we have boats ready for deportation." I am horrified by the inhumanity of the massacre planned and carried out by Hamas terrorists against civilians in southern Israel. I respect and support Israel's right to take action against the perpetrators and ensure its security, in line with international humanitarian law. Solidarity with both is not an expression of moral equivalency or whataboutism that balances or excuses the injustices on one side with those of the other. It is simply an acknowledgment that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has long, complex, painful, and all too often bloody roots, which many treat as a historical smorgasbord, selectively picking what suits their emotional and ideological appetites. But it is also true that on the seventy-fifth anniversary of Israel's founding, the parties to the conflict are not in an equal position. Israel is a successful economy and regional military power, proud of its democracy—though increasingly under scrutiny by its Western allies. On the other hand, the state has not only found itself in but has largely created a situation that former Israeli Foreign Minister Abba Eban warned about as early as 1967: "A permanent rule over a foreign nation can only be justified by an ideology and rhetoric of self-glorification and exclusion, incompatible with the ethical heritage of prophetic Judaism and classical Zionism." Or as Prime Minister Levi Eshkol asked his adviser after the occupation of the West Bank: "Have you asked yourself how we will live with so many Arabs?" The answer came in decades of occupation that became a perpetual source of security risks for Israel and suffering for Palestinians. Even in this long, painful, and tragic history, the Hamas terrorist attack of October 7 marked a new threshold. It was a meticulously planned operation in which civilians—families, elderly people, young concertgoers, children—were deliberately chosen as targets. A surgically orchestrated massacre, deliberately echoing the cruelty and inhumanity once inflicted on Jews, culminating in the Holocaust. This cannot be justified by anything, and any attempt to relativize this crime is, at the very least, morally unacceptable. The same goes for denying Israel's right to defend itself and do everything within international law to destroy Hamas and ensure its security. In this context, we should be deeply concerned about some views that have emerged in the Slovenian public: that Hamas mainly attacked military targets, or a columnist expressing outrage that young Israelis found it "unproblematic to attend an electronic music festival five kilometers from the barbed-wire fence that separates Israeli prosperity from the economic and social devastation of Gaza, where 3.5 million people live under constant Israeli military oversight." What does this imply? That they got what they deserved? At the same time, it is also true that Hamas committed this crime with a specific intent: to provoke with unimaginable cruelty a wave of shock, pain, and rage that would override reason and push Israel into overreaction. U.S. President Biden warned of this during his visit to Israel: "I caution you—while you feel that rage, don't let it consume you. After 9/11, we in the U.S. were angry. And in seeking justice, we got justice—but we also made mistakes." Where such actions lead is highlighted by Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland: "The blockade of Gaza, which deprives more than two million Palestinians of food, water, and medicine... is not only immoral and contrary to international law, but also runs counter to Israel's own interests—because it weakens international support at the very moment it should be strongest—and undermines the goals Israel has set. If recent years have shown anything, it's that the more hellish life becomes in Gaza, the tighter Hamas's grip becomes." Saying Hamas knew exactly what it was doing is not relativizing its crimes. It's a warning not to play the role the criminal has assigned you. That Israel has the right to defend itself is beyond question and should not be debated. How it responds, however, is a valid topic for discussion. The international community must exert more pressure on Israel and remind it of the responsibility it bears—toward Palestinians, toward its own security, and toward the world. So it doesn’t walk blindly into Hamas’s trap. Likewise, it is essential to talk about a political solution to the conflict. And that solution must be based on acknowledging the complexity that Slavoj Žižek spoke about at the Frankfurt Book Fair—and for which he, unjustifiably in my view, received intense criticism and attacks, especially in Germany. The timing of Hamas’s attack was no coincidence. Along with its regional sponsors, Hamas wanted to sabotage new attempts at a lasting peace in the Middle East. Just as suicide bombings—with the help of Israeli extremists—undermined the Oslo peace process, they now aim to derail the normalization of relations between Israel and other regional states. If Israel is genuinely committed to destroying Hamas, not just militarily but also politically, then it must find adequate answers to the questions raised by Abba Eban and Levi Eshkol in 1967. Out of pain and rage must come a renewed resolve for a political solution—one that guarantees Israel’s right to exist and be secure. And one that also recognizes the same rights for Palestinians. "Whose side are you on?" my daughter asked me. "I’m on the side of the Palestinians and the Israelis," I answered. "And on the side of their right to live in peace, each in their own state." "But is that possible?" she asked. "It won’t be easy," I said. "But there’s no other way." I spared my eleven-year-old my fears about what might happen if we don’t find that way.

Recent events in the center of Ljubljana, where opponents and defenders of women’s right to decide freely about their own bodies came face to face, have raised a great deal of dust in the Slovenian public and politics, which has not yet settled—and doesn’t look as if it will any time soon. This is not the first time we have witnessed in Slovenia a very heated, at times even hysterical, debate on important questions of human rights protection. Unfortunately, it is also not the first time such a debate has been conducted on the basis of a very superficial knowledge of the issues, emotions, quick and often ill-considered reactions, and more or less concealed and often problematic political interests. Sometimes it helps to stop for a moment and think and talk, with less passion, about what is at stake and how to move forward. There was indeed a collision between different rights on Congress Square. But resolving such collisions is a complex matter that cannot be settled offhand, still less solely on the basis of, and in favor of, one’s own beliefs, however noble. Let us look first at the rights of those who organized the event on Congress Square “in memory of unborn children.” Much has been said about their right to freedom of expression, protected by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). I would add here that it was also about the right of peaceful assembly, protected by Article 11 of the ECHR. It is important to stress that the Convention not only obliges the contracting states, including Slovenia, to refrain from unjustified and impermissible interference with these rights, but also imposes on them a positive obligation to create the conditions for their unhindered enjoyment. In the case of the right of assembly, this also includes enabling and protecting peaceful gatherings—even if they were not announced and authorized in advance. This fact was systematically overlooked in the case of unannounced protests against the previous government, but it of course also applies during the term of the current one. On the other hand, both Article 10 and Article 11 also contain provisions that allow, and under certain conditions even oblige, the restriction of these rights. Among those conditions is the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. Here, of course, any such restrictive measure must be based on law and be “necessary in a democratic society.” The question of collision between different rights and freedoms is set out even more precisely in Article 17 of the Convention, which prohibits the abuse of rights and states that “nothing in this Convention may be interpreted as implying for any State, group or person any right to engage in any activity or perform any act aimed at the destruction of any of the rights and freedoms set forth herein or at their limitation to a greater extent than is provided for in the Convention.” What does all this mean for the events on Congress Square? For the organizers, certainly, that they planted their little flags on the basis of the right to freedom of expression and the right of peaceful assembly. The question, however, is whether, in exercising their rights, they interfered with the rights of others in a way the Convention does not permit. Many believe they did. Some claim it is impermissible to advocate publicly for changing a state of affairs established by the Constitution. That is, of course, not true. The Constitution can of course be changed, through procedures also laid down in the Constitution—and it is permissible to campaign publicly for changes. Imagine if we criminalized efforts to introduce regions or to change the way judges are appointed, a question that is currently already in parliamentary procedure. On the other hand, the question of free decision on the birth of children obviously cannot be equated with the introduction of regions, since the former is a human right protected by Article 5 of the Constitution and explicitly by Article 55. That article was not included in the Constitution because its authors wanted as many abortions as possible in an independent and democratic Slovenia, but because the view prevailed that the right to decide freely on the birth of one’s children is a necessary condition for establishing and preserving the democratic society we chose. Since I have referred to the ECHR several times, it is also worth mentioning how the European Court of Human Rights has dealt with this topic so far. Opponents of the right to abortion stress that in its case law to date the Strasbourg court has protected this right only to a limited extent, in cases where a ban on abortion could endanger women’s lives. That is true, mainly because the court’s decisions are also influenced by the positions of European states in which the right to abortion is restricted, with all the tragic consequences we are witnessing. However, the ECHR sets only minimum standards for the protection of human rights and in no way prevents member states from setting these standards higher in their domestic law, as Slovenia did with Article 55 of the Constitution, provided they do not thereby violate other rights protected by the Convention. And among those, let us recall, you will not find a right to restrict the rights of other people. The fact that in such an important respect of human rights protection as women’s right to decide autonomously about their bodies we are a step ahead of the minimum standards is a reason for pride, not embarrassment. That the organizers of the gathering on Congress Square advocated positions which, if implemented, would lead to the restriction of human rights is, in my opinion, beyond doubt. Whether they did so in a way that would require official interference in their right of peaceful assembly and freedom of expression is another question. Only a court could decide that competently, but I personally think not. Let us not forget that the Convention permits only restrictions that are necessary in a democratic society. That threshold must remain high. But even if their gathering was legal, that does not mean their campaign to restrict or even abolish constitutionally guaranteed human rights must be respected, still less that a respectful dialogue must be conducted about it. Respect for the right to freedom of expression does not include a right to automatic respect for what is expressed. A doctrine of taking all different opinions into account, which puts an equals sign between those who fight for human rights and those who demand their restriction, does not strengthen democracy but weakens it. The most appropriate and effective response in this case is an even more resolute protection of human rights by politics and civil society. Part of the latter did respond in this case. By using its right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. Everyone can have their own opinion on whether this was done in the most appropriate way. As for the response of politicians, each responded according to their own judgment. Some one way, others another. Everyone can have their own opinion about that too. And they certainly do.
On the Right Side of Survival

A few days ago, while distractedly flipping through television channels on a Saturday morning, a WWII song cheering the partisans to fight the occupiers suddenly rang out in the house. In a small village of Opatje Selo in Southwestern Slovenia, near the border with Italy, they were commemorating the anniversary of the return of the Slovenian Littoral to the homeland. I admit, it warmed my heart. At a time when many are attempting to revise history, questioning the national liberation struggle and demonizing anti-fascism, remembering those times when the Slovenian nation bravely resisted foreign occupation is important—for the past, the present, and the future. The celebration, as it should be, included standard-bearers, singers, and actors reciting the poetry of Karel Destovnik-Kajuh. There were, of course, also speeches, including one by the first president of a free, independent, and democratic Slovenia, Milan Kučan. In his address, he touched upon the ongoing year-and-a-half-long Russian aggression against Ukraine. "To be on the right side of history at this time means to be on the side of peace." His statement sparked many heated reactions in parts of the public. I don't understand why. In Ukraine, a bloody conflict is taking place, with thousands of young people dying on both sides. Ukrainian cities and villages are being destroyed. In ruthless Russian bombings, civilians, including children, are dying. Russian occupiers have committed a long list of war crimes in the occupied territories. Russian aggression against a neighbouring state is causing further destabilization of the international order and stability, which were already on shaky ground, to be honest. Who in their right mind wouldn’t want this carnage and human suffering to end as soon as possible? Whoever is not on the side of peace right now is certainly not on the right side of history. Not just history, but also of basic humanity. And ultimately, if anyone truly desires peace, it is first and foremost the Ukrainians, who were thrust into this senseless and destructive conflict by the Russian aggressor. Ukrainians, like the people of the Slovenian Littoral decades ago—and all Slovenians—want nothing more than to live in peace. And in freedom. That is the right of every nation. Then, and now. The first president of free, independent, and democratic Slovenia also spoke about the legacy of fascism, which brought so much suffering to the Slovenian nation. He pointed out that we still have not received a proper apology for the pain inflicted. That matters. Not only because of the past, but also the present, in which fascism, in various forms and places, is once again rearing its ugly head. Our future depends vitally on how we respond to the resurgence of such ideas and ideologies wherever they arise. Anyone who today is truly an anti-fascist and democrat in heart, words, and actions cannot close their eyes to the fact that the aggression against Ukraine is above all the result of an authoritarian policy that, for twenty years now and increasingly obviously, has built its power domestically by suppressing minorities and liquidating political opponents and critics, and externally through nationalist and imperialist aggression toward other countries. If that isn’t fascism, it’s damned close. This, of course, does not mean the world is black and white or that no one else bears any guilt. There are various views on how much blame each side carries, and disagreements on this point are normal and to be expected. The former president emphasized that different perspectives exist on the causes of the war. That, too, is normal, and we can and should talk and argue about it—as long as we don’t draw an equivalence between the victim and the aggressor. Because in that moment, we are no longer on the right side of history, but on the side of the aggressor. As I mentioned, the international order, stability, and peace were already in a dismal state before Russian aggression. There’s no doubt that Russia wasn’t the only one responsible. For years we lived in a unipolar world where the lone global power rarely missed an opportunity to fail in its dominance and cause harm. That this can no longer continue is clear. But it matters how we undertake the urgently needed overhaul of global stability and peace. In this dilemma, Putin is not and cannot be part of the solution; he and his policies are a big part of the problem. The former president noted that the Russian aggression against Ukraine is part of a geopolitical conflict between major powers. I agree. Russia attacked Ukraine as part of Putin’s plan to expand Russian territory to the borders of the former Russian empire and beyond. The United States and the European Union are helping Ukraine in part because the success of Putin’s lebensraum ambitions is not in their interest. But the fact that this war is also a conflict of great powers’ interests does not mean we can draw a false equivalence between them. One of these great powers is pursuing its interests through aggression, the others, through support for the victim of that aggression. Even more problematic is when this vague talk of geopolitical confrontation leads to conclusions about shared responsibility for ending the war. Yes, both sides in this great power conflict can contribute to ending the war, but not in the same way and not with the same consequences. Especially not for Ukraine. Russia can end the war in an instant by withdrawing its occupying forces. Ukraine’s supporters can only end the war by ceasing to help and abandoning it to the mercy of the aggressor. I am convinced that those who sincerely reject imperialism—any and all forms of it—cannot accept the notion that the war in Ukraine should or could be ended through backroom deals between great powers trading away someone else's territory, freedom, and survival. Half of Ukraine, and a handshake? That such "peace plans" are promoted by the likes of Trump is no surprise, as they benefit his ideological allies and cronies. But I also believe that those who are not ready to abandon the vision of a world based on international law, justice, freedom, and equality for all—regardless of their power or size—will not deny Ukrainians the right to a national liberation struggle against a foreign imperialist occupier who has never hidden his ambition to erase them from the map as a state and a people. I have great respect for the first president of free, independent, and democratic Slovenia. I have no doubt about his commitment to anti-fascist and democratic values. That’s why I don’t mind if we differ on some points. Because I know he sincerely wants peace. And because I believe he understands that those of us who view some issues differently also sincerely want peace in Ukraine. Because I believe he understands and respects that Ukraine and Ukrainians—like the people of the Slovenian Littoral and all Slovenians during the national liberation struggle against foreign occupation—do not merely want to remain on the right side of history, but also on the right side of survival. And for that, they need and deserve our support and help.

Recently, the Slovenian public was appalled to learn that one of the country’s formerly most influential and high-ranking judges, a former judge at the European Court of Human Rights, regularly posts antisemitic messages on social media. This realization only struck Slovenians after the UK’s The Jewish Chronicle, the oldest Jewish newspaper in the world, published an article about it. I don’t bring up this story to dwell on the individual in question. If anything, I feel pity toward him—amazed at the aggressiveness of his reputational self-destruction. What compels me to write again is the lack of serious response to this and other social pathologies in Slovenia’s public discourse. What happened following the Chronicle article is telling for several reasons. First, the outrage was fleeting. A few media pieces, a couple of reactions on social media—and then, oops, it happened, let’s move on. Second, even that feeble response came only after we were alerted from abroad. For years prior, this gentleman had been “entertaining” the Slovenian public sphere with his increasingly questionable pronouncements, gradually morphing from misogyny and conspiracy theories into full-blown antisemitism. And all that time—until someone tapped us on the shoulder from outside—this man continued to enjoy public attention, immunity from serious criticism, and was even regularly invited to speak in the media, including public television, as a supposed expert on human rights. Third, most commentary in Slovenian media focused primarily on how this was a major scandal and embarrassment for the European Court of Human Rights, where the individual served for years. But hardly anyone examined what this says about the country that nominated him—first electing him to its Constitutional Court, and later nearly appointing him to the UN Human Rights Committee, a move thwarted only by his own vile comments about the late Simone Veil, a former French minister and President of the European Parliament. Insisting on political and societal condemnation is essential. Without such a response, antisemitism—alongside other pathological discourses that have proliferated in Slovenia’s public life—creeps ever closer to full normalization and legitimacy. The message that society and politics send through silence to every individual or group harboring and stoking such hatred is: “If he can do it, so can I.” The antisemitism of “our top human rights and Jewish question expert” is not an isolated case. Former high-ranking government officials have denied the Holocaust, national security advisors have competed in racism and anti-migrant hatred, and prominent members of parliament have fearmongered about “the Great Replacement”—a white supremacist conspiracy theory. Not to mention babble about so-called “cultural Marxism,” a recycled version of the “cultural Bolshevism” Nazis raged against in the 1930s. The longer these outbursts go unanswered, the more banal and acceptable everyday hate becomes. We are frogs slowly boiling in the ever-hotter swamp of indigenous antisemitism and racism. A particularly telling example is the attacks on George Soros. The Jewish-Hungarian businessman and philanthropist has become a catch-all scapegoat—a dog whistle that unleashes the pack. And we’ve grown completely used to it, as if it’s entirely normal. It’s not. The demonization of Soros rests on thinly veiled traditional antisemitic tropes about a sinister global Jewish cabal pulling the strings of the world to the detriment of honest, ordinary, white, non-Jewish people. Or, as Elon Musk put it a few months ago: “Soros hates humanity. He wants to erode the very fabric of civilization.” After that tweet, Musk’s social network was flooded with antisemitic conspiracy theories. Putin and Trump attack Soros. So does the gentleman mentioned at the start of this piece, who, after receiving criticism from abroad, reportedly deleted his most blatant antisemitic posts—only to eagerly share a new one accusing Slovenia’s foreign minister of “destroying Slovenians and Slovenian identity on behalf of an international clique” because she met Soros’s son at a conference. Apparently, bashing Soros has become a kind of methadone therapy for suppressed antisemites who can’t hate openly. The second issue is that attacks on Soros are part of a broader effort to delegitimize and criminalize civil society—specifically the part that defends democratic values, fights racism and other forms of discrimination and hate, promotes equality and solidarity, and serves as a check on executive power. It’s no secret that through his Open Society Foundation, Soros has invested millions in support of such civil society—especially in Central and Eastern Europe. What’s shocking is that in the span of just over three decades, he went from being an ally of every government striving for democratic transition to, in the eyes of many, becoming the ultimate villain. He’s now targeted by those who are leveraging the very abuses and failures of that transition (many of which they themselves caused) to justify authoritarian power grabs. This dramatic reversal illustrates how much Europe—and the world—have changed since the fall of the Berlin Wall. Soros’s foundation funded essential democracy-building projects after the collapse of communism. It awarded thousands of scholarships to help new democracies cultivate experts in human rights and democratic governance. It supported programs for Roma integration—especially through education and culture. It founded a university that trained many of today’s top scholars and practitioners in democratic institutions. That university no longer operates in Budapest. It was driven to Vienna by a former Soros scholarship recipient—now Prime Minister—who cements his power by demonizing his former patron. Once, Soros was a hero for supporting democracy. Today, he’s a villain for supporting democracy. For years, we tiptoed in place, claiming to march toward a bright future grounded in shared democratic values. Now we’re marching confidently—in reverse. Some, even in jackboots. Today, being a “Sorosist” is a slur against anyone who advocates for and defends liberal democratic values and human rights. The same goes for the term “woke,” now a universal smear against efforts toward equality, solidarity, social justice, and environmental responsibility. “Cultural Marxism” is a made-up concept that ties it all together—a conspiracy theory with historical precedent. These labels are as vague as they are toxic. When American conservative commentator Bethany Mandel was asked in an interview to define the terrifying “woke indoctrination” she rails against in her book, she stammered, then fell silent. This is the heart of it: indiscriminate name-calling. Accusations without evidence. Verdicts without appeal. A badge to mark someone as an “enemy of the people.” It’s a discourse that serves as a decoy and cover for political ideas so extreme and dangerous that even those decrying “wokeness” and “cultural Marxism” (for now) dare not say them aloud. It’s camouflage—beneath which racism, antisemitism, misogyny, homophobia, chauvinism, and nationalism increasingly poke through. At its core: a hunger for unchecked power and greed. The main goal of all this shouting and finger-pointing is to dismantle decades of work toward a more open, compassionate, and democratic society. Populist demagogues from Moscow to Florida, from Budapest to the increasingly murky swamps of Slovenian social media and politics, build political capital by sowing division and hate. In the name of fighting these so-called “threats,” they ban books, attack democratic values, undermine democratic institutions, rehabilitate slavery and colonialism, and stigmatize minorities. They ruthlessly exploit the hardship and fear of those whom neoliberalism has humiliated and pushed to the margins. For the second time in less than a century, we are facing an explosive mix of social discontent, economic hardship, political distrust, fear of the future, and authoritarian ambitions of populist nationalists who build their path to power on division and hate. In the end, it’s all about one thing: power. No matter the cost. You know what? We’re not nearly woke enough. And when it’s too late, it won’t be enough to say “oops, let’s move on”—because there’ll be nowhere left to go. We’ll already be at the bottom. The very place we so often swore we’d never return to.

When, many, many, many years ago, I started work as a beardless trainee at the brand-new Slovenian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, an older colleague with long years of service taught me that you need only three things to succeed in public administration. “Always walk fast in the corridors, carry a thick bundle of documents—just change them now and then so they don’t turn yellow—and if there’s a queue at the photocopier, say out loud that you have something urgent for the minister.” At the time I found this enormously funny; I thought the old fox was joking. Today, after more than thirty years of working in bureaucracy, Slovenian and European, I am no longer quite sure it was just a joke. Officialdom is a world that often gets badly on the nerves of people who don’t belong to it but have to deal with it. Often with good reason. True, the public perception of bureaucrats is often a caricature, but it is also true that bureaucrats often behave like caricatures. On the other hand, no large system can be run without rules and structures and people who enforce those rules, put them into practice and provide the services expected of them. Lashing out indiscriminately at every official and at officialdom as such is therefore not only unfair but also harmful. The key to a bureaucracy as it should be is its efficiency, transparency, integrity and, above all, democratic oversight of it, including by a critical public. It was from this perspective that I read the criticism of the Brussels bureaucracy recently published in Večer by my fellow columnist Vesna Godina. I generally avoid polemics between columnists, because they too often degenerate into tiresome hair-splitting and a clash of wounded egos. But then again, what is wrong with a robust exchange of views? Let thoughts and ideas strike sparks. And from that perspective, with all due respect to my colleague, I must admit I was not overly enthusiastic about her text on the European Union. Not because it is critical, but because of how it is critical. An evident lack of knowledge about the subject you are writing about is hard to compensate for convincingly with ideological platitudes and far-fetched anecdotes. I very much agree that Brussels needs to be watched closely. It is a large (although this size, which is often bandied about, needs to be put in comparative context) bureaucratic apparatus with exceptional influence, and where there is great power there is also the possibility of great mistakes or abuses. It is even more important that the Brussels bureaucracy, as the holder of exceptional executive power, be subject to democratic oversight. And in this respect things are certainly not as they should be. The democratic deficit that has always plagued the EU remains a problem, despite the growing role and influence of the European Parliament in recent years and decades. That EU leaders are aware of this is clear; that they are not prepared to tackle the predicament effectively is clear too. The latest example is the Conference on the Future of Europe, launched with great fanfare in early 2020, which almost no one talks about anymore, nor about its results. But you won’t learn much about this predicament of the European Union from my colleague Godina’s text. Instead of critical reflection on the challenges and problems besetting the project of European integration today, the author preferred to focus on a collection of anecdotes and populist platitudes, in the style of the former Brussels correspondent of the British Daily Telegraph, Boris Johnson, who with stories about Brussels bureaucrats supposedly wanting to regulate the curvature of bananas and about European standards for condoms that Italian willies supposedly couldn’t meet, stoked Euroscepticism among the British public (the Italians probably weren’t thrilled either) and prepared the ground for Brexit, which brought him political gains and power. We also know what liberation from the Brussels colonial yoke has brought British citizens. What bothers people most is the astronomically paid bureaucracy, says Ms. Godina. True, Brussels bureaucrats (and Strasbourg ones too) cannot complain, and we cannot complain, about our salaries. Any whining about this would be a tasteless mockery of the many Europeans who don’t know how they’ll make it to the end of the month. But European salaries are not set by guesswork either. The main parameters are the incomes of comparable professional profiles in the member states, so that the European institutions remain an attractive employer for the most capable candidates. These parameters are, of course, pushed up by what people with comparable profiles can earn in the richer member states. If that were not the case, only people from poorer member states would work in the institutions. Alternatively, staff could be paid differently according to the country they come from. That would, of course, be unacceptable. And despite the author’s outrage at Brussels salaries, the latest data show that fewer and fewer candidates from some member states, especially the Scandinavian ones, are applying for competitions. The reason is that at home, with their education, they earn even more “astronomical” salaries than in Brussels. Members of the European Parliament get on people’s nerves, says my colleague. Now that one really doesn’t hold water. The European Parliament (which can also mess up, make no mistake) is the most important part of democratic oversight of a system that affects our lives in such important ways. Unreasoned and sweeping mockery of MEPs and the European Parliament, and the resulting low turnout in European elections, is shooting ourselves in the foot, as it weakens the body that we elect and that represents European citizens. Such a disparaging attitude toward a directly elected body further worsens the democratic deficit, but that of course is not important to the author; what gets up her nose, or rather the noses of the people in whose name she wields her pen, are the salaries of Brussels bureaucrats. Even more astonishing is the crowning proof of the EU’s baseness and harmfulness that the author draws from the sharp price increases that followed the introduction of the euro, most recently in Croatia. Dear colleague, you don’t have to be an expert in economics and monetary mumbo jumbo to understand that the blame for this swindle, neither in Croatia, nor in Slovenia, nor in the other countries that adopted the euro, lies not with Brussels but with those in Croatia, Slovenia and elsewhere who used the currency changeover to round prices in euros up generously. I lack the space, and even more the will, to comment on the remaining “arguments” about a wicked and colonialist capitalist Europe. The EU has made, and will probably continue to make, mistakes. Its response to “resolving” the financial crisis in 2009 under German influence was not only wrong and harmful but also objectively prepared the ground for the rise of nationalist populism, which today, paradoxically or perhaps not, attacks the European Union and its democratic values with arguments similar to those my fellow columnist uses in her text. Stories about international cabals pulling strings from behind the scenes, sucking the blood of honest people and running our lives, are older than the EU, but with it they have found a new target, popular at both extremes of the political spectrum. Yet despite populism, and precisely because of it, it is essential that we be critical of the EU. As citizens, we have the opportunity to vote responsibly and wisely in European elections and send people there who will know how to protect citizens’ interests effectively and oversee European executive power. As a country, we could be more self-confident and determined in Brussels (and elsewhere) about what we think is right and what is not. Calimero-style whining about the nasty, nasty Brussels colonialists is of course a possible alternative, but personally it doesn’t convince me. While we must not forget the mistakes, we must not overlook the achievements either, and above all the importance the European Union has for stability, security and prosperity in Europe. Its conduct during the Covid crisis and its response to the consequences of Russian aggression show that the EU has learned from its mistakes. A few days ago the European Digital Services Act came into force, which requires greater accountability and transparency from digital platforms, protects users and, above all, regulates such an extraordinary field with such far-reaching and potentially dangerous influence on society on the basis of democratic values. Without the EU, in the digital and consequently the analog world, we would be dancing to Chinese tunes and to Musk’s caprices and interests. This is just one example among many. Above all, we must never forget how and why the process of European cooperation and unification came about. As the antithesis of a bloody historical experience in which millions of people were murdered. Europe was, and remains, a peace project that protects Europeans from themselves. That is no excuse for sloppy work, for mistakes or abuses, but an obligation to get its house in order and behave responsibly toward the citizens it serves. If, in the heat of outrage over salary levels, the euro price of a shopping basket from Konzum or the shape of bananas, we forget how European states traditionally settled their mutual relations in the period before European integration, we certainly run the risk of history repeating itself, one way or another.

"Sir, do you perhaps speak English?" an older gentleman called out to me as he sat on a wooden bench in the village square. "Yes," I replied hesitantly. "Would you perhaps have five minutes to chat with me?" His name was Giuseppe. We met in the Calabrian village of Civita, perched high above the Pollino National Park—a stunning rocky landscape that rises from the Ionian Sea just a few kilometers away. If you stand on your toes, you can almost see two other seas—the Adriatic towards Bari and the Tyrrhenian—surrounding the heel, sole, and arch of the Italian boot. Giuseppe had spent ten years in America, in New York. When I asked what he did there, he simply showed me his hands. Now, he sits in the square every day waiting for tourists so he can practice his English. At the end of our chat, he asked me to write a message in a small notebook he pulled from his briefcase. It already contained half a dozen similar notebooks, filled with notes. He watched with delight as I wrote a few words. “Look at him, a real doctor,” he called out to indifferent passersby—following the Italian tradition of liberally bestowing the title of “doctor.” Giuseppe is a migrant—or more precisely, a former migrant. He is also a descendant of refugees. Civita lies in the heart of a region where the Albanian ethnic minority lives. His ancestors fled from Albania in the 15th century after the death of their national hero Skanderbeg, escaping the Ottomans. All signage is bilingual. At the village entrance, it says not only Civita but also Çifti. Many Arbëreshë, as they call themselves, still speak their Albanian dialect and preserve their cultural customs and traditions. The wooden bench where Giuseppe waited for English-speaking tourists sits in front of a small museum dedicated to the Albanian minority, where three of his friends were seated. Both Giuseppe's personal story and the history of Calabrian Albanians are not unique. They’re just fragments of a rich mosaic shaped by people who, since the beginning of civilization, have migrated—seeking survival, hoping for a better life, or fleeing danger to save their lives. Our world and our cultures, ways of life, traditions, and customs—with all their richness and complexity—are what they are because of those who left their birthplace and left a mark wherever they arrived. I admit, I’m not completely objective when it comes to people who left or were forced to leave their homeland. It’s also the story of my family. And I believe most of us would discover something similar if we thoroughly examined our ancestors’ past. My grandfather Vlado was born in Nabrežina near Trieste. Due to fascist violence, like many Slovenians from that region, he had to flee across the Rapallo border. He settled in the first village on the other side, in Unec, where my father was born. On my mother’s side, the story is similar—only my grandfather Franček and grandmother Anuncijata didn’t flee but were deported by the German occupiers from Sveta Ana in Slovenske Gorice to the Bosnian village of Boljanić near Doboj. They were forced to leave behind their newborn daughter because the meticulous Nazis didn’t have her name on their list. My aunt never lived to see her parents return from exile—she died a few months later. But my mother was born in Boljanić. And if it weren’t for the villagers who helped the young Slovenian family despite having little themselves, my mother wouldn’t have celebrated her 80th birthday recently—and you wouldn’t be reading this article. These examples aren’t empirical proof but glimpses that allow me to draw some conclusions. First: migration has always existed and always will. The idea that we can somehow stop it in this historically random era into which we were born is illusory and senseless. Second: migration does affect our culture and way of life. Newcomers bring their customs, leaving traces in their new environments. Today, we often automatically view this cultural influence as a threat. Yes, cultural clashes and conflicts do occur. But we too often ignore the progress and positive changes that migrants bring. Nationalists and chauvinists loudly proclaim that migrants threaten our culture and way of life—but rarely does anyone reflect on what our culture and tradition would be today without all the past influences they absorbed. The notion that any society’s cultural and civilizational development can or should be frozen at a politically convenient moment is arrogant, unrealistic, and dangerous. What nationalist extremists sell is a dystopia of monocultural bunkers defending and fighting each other across gun barrels. Third: the short-term effects of migration, especially in times of sudden surges, must not be underestimated. Not everyone comes with good intentions, and rapid population increases do create stress, cultural shock, economic and social strain, and political tension. But the fact that we’ll never completely stop migration doesn’t mean we can’t or shouldn’t influence and manage it. That requires measures on every level—from global (tackling root causes like war and climate change), to European and national (effective border controls), to local efforts (humane treatment and integration). This is about solidarity and empathy—but also pragmatism. Though it may sound provocative in today’s anti-migrant climate, Western societies—including ours—need migration. The reason is demographics. The economic and social time bomb of aging populations can’t be defused by creating government offices for birth rates. Again, this doesn’t mean opening borders and hoping for the best. But what’s worse—and more dangerous—is the current approach in most Western societies. The stigmatization and manipulation of fear surrounding migration, done for political gain, prevent the adoption of effective migration management policies—including security measures. Panic and scapegoating migrants as the cause of all our problems benefits only those who manipulate the issue politically. The rest of us pay the price—including the distraction from other serious problems. The UK offers a sobering example of where ideological obsession with migration can lead. There is growing political support for leaving the European Convention on Human Rights over a few thousand people arriving in small boats across the English Channel. That convention, drafted by British lawyers over seventy years ago, primarily protects British citizens—and is a key part of the Northern Ireland peace agreement. But no matter: for a few more votes, some politicians are ready to sacrifice it and join Belarus and Russia—the only European countries outside that human rights protection framework (aside from Kosovo, which includes the ECHR in its constitution). Stigmatizing people based on ethnicity, skin color, or religion also devastates social cohesion, which is essential for peace and progress—especially in countries where many people already have migrant backgrounds, often for generations. Instead of integration and its benefits, we see structural discrimination and growing demonization of citizens who’ve lived in their “new” countries for decades. This provokes radicalization and violence, as we’ve seen in many European countries—including France, where I’ve lived for thirty years. We hear a lot about migrants threatening “our culture.” Of course, not every external cultural influence should be accepted, especially those that clash with our values—equality, human rights, political freedoms, and opposition to discrimination and intolerance. These are protected by national and European law. A civilized society must insist that newcomers accept and respect these values. In my experience, the vast majority of immigrants in France have no problem with this. The paradox is that many of those who shout loudest about cultural threats share disturbing similarities with extremist newcomers. Ultimately, culture won’t just survive—it will thrive—if it's seen as positive and inclusive, even by those who arrive from elsewhere. Today’s anti-foreigner hostility, which dominates much of Europe, only fuels radical violence—on all sides. A central pillar of populist fearmongering about migration is the idea of religious incompatibility—specifically that Muslims threaten us. Years ago, I spoke with Dr. Ismail Serageldin, founding director of the Library of Alexandria—one of the Arab world’s most important cultural institutions. (Incidentally, Alexandria is also known in Slovenia as the destination of economic migrant women known as the “Aleksandrinke.”) Dr. Serageldin noted that while the Mediterranean has long been a site of war and conflict, it has also been a space of cultural and commercial exchange enriching both southern and northern shores. What we are witnessing today, he said, is not a clash of civilizations—but a conflict between grotesque caricatures of both sides that feed off one another. “But how can we change that?” I asked, still under the impact of terrorist attacks in France. “Look at what France and Germany did after World War II,” he said. “Anything is possible—if there is political will.” That will, sadly, is fading. Fear, intolerance, and hatred are rising. Compassion and solidarity are in retreat. In Athens, we’ve worked with schools on democratic citizenship programs.
