One student—a migrant—once wrote a line I’ll never forget: "Why does no one talk about the fact that we didn’t just arrive—we also left?" A child’s pain, caught between the sorrow of losing a home and rejection in a new one. As I spoke English with Giuseppe in Civita, tourists were sipping cocktails on nearby beaches. My phone buzzed with a BBC alert: a boat had capsized near Lampedusa, carrying 41 migrants. Another statistical entry in the sea of anonymous victims of our indifference—people who left, but never arrived.

Years ago, a dentist in the small Kansas town of Iola treated a girl brought in by her parents with a severe toothache. After briefly checking the parents’ health insurance, the dentist drilled the painful tooth a little, then filled it with Styrofoam. The Kansas dentist’s creative approach didn’t work. The girl later had to have her jaw amputated due to serious complications. Such tragic stories of people at the social bottom in one of the world’s richest countries are not uncommon, but this one is especially harrowing—not only because high insurance costs prevented the girl from receiving a standard ceramic or porcelain filling, but also because of Kansas Governor Sam Brownback’s economic experiment. In 2012, the Republican governor introduced a tax reform under the slogan “the march toward zero.” Brownback drastically cut taxes for the wealthy, significantly reduced or eliminated corporate and small business profit taxes, slashed social transfers, restricted access to health insurance for the lowest earners (hence the Styrofoam filling), closed numerous schools and public agencies, and laid off 2,000 public employees. The governor promised the reform would be an adrenaline shot for the economy, sparking investment and boosting employment. But it didn’t work out. In just a few years, Brownback turned a billion-dollar state budget surplus into a billion-dollar deficit. The expected growth in investment and jobs never materialized, and economic growth lagged significantly behind other U.S. states. To patch the budget hole, Brownback raided infrastructure funds, stopped highway repairs, and sharply raised sales taxes—hitting low-income people the hardest, who ended up paying more tax than before the reform. The Kansas experiment is one of the clearest examples of how destructive attempts to implement the neoliberal “trickle-down” dogma can be in practice—but it’s not the first such case. Three decades earlier, Britain’s “Iron Lady” Margaret Thatcher launched a neoliberal revolution as soon as she took office. She urged Britons to “find glory in inequality” and, in the name of this “value,” waged and won a war against powerful trade unions, privatized much of the state’s assets, and announced radical tax cuts. Paradoxically, Thatcherism still serves as a model for many—also in Slovenia—of how governments should manage the relationship between capital and society: everything for the former, because, after all, “there is no such thing as society.” Paradoxical because Thatcherism also failed—both for the people and by the goals it promised. Historian Mark Mazower, in his book Dark Continent, notes that before Thatcher took power, public spending accounted for 42.5% of the UK’s GDP. After ten years, it had dropped by just 0.7%. Spending levels barely changed—which marks a key difference from Brownback’s Kansas experiment, which went even further. Thatcherism used the money it “earned and saved” by privatizing state assets to fund welfare for the massive numbers of unemployed it created. According to Mazower, Thatcherism ultimately “failed” in part because even the Iron Lady didn’t dare significantly cut spending on health and education. The British were too attached to their public healthcare system and were unwilling to accept Styrofoam fillings. And it’s this “failure” of Thatcherism that explains why her neoliberal fiasco still enjoys a better reputation than it deserves. Because Thatcher didn’t go all the way, she caused less harm than she might have. But neoliberal experiments lost the support of key parts of Britain’s business sector. The financial markets’ reaction to yet another neoliberal revolution—this time by Thatcher’s very short-lived successor Liz Truss—made it clear that post-Brexit Britain was not willing to risk another ideological project of neoliberal experimentation. If anything, Margaret Thatcher fulfilled her promise to “celebrate inequality.” By the 1990s, the United Kingdom had become the most socially unequal society in Western Europe, with fourteen million citizens—nearly a third of them children—living in poverty. Her drastic cuts to housing investment caused an explosion in homelessness that continues to this day. Mazower notes that Britain’s neoliberal revolution found no imitators in the rest of Western Europe. Why? In his view, historical memory: even conservative politicians on the continent, like Helmut Kohl, still remembered the consequences of ideological battles and political violence from the 1930s—and were unwilling to risk a repeat. To be fair, Dark Continent was published in 1998, and later events showed that the rest of Western Europe’s historical memory wasn’t strong enough to prevent it from slowly following Britain’s path. The situation in Eastern Europe is even more complex. Mazower argues that the fall of the Berlin Wall marked not the triumph of democracy, but of capitalism. Democracy still had to be built, based on a new social contract—like the one the West forged after the bloodshed of WWII. But in Eastern Europe, the historical memory of the 1930s was replaced by a fresher, painful memory of authoritarian socialism. Understandable, perhaps, from a human perspective—but hardly ideal for building liberal democracy, which depends on social justice and solidarity. In other words, Eastern Europe jumped from socialist authoritarianism into the most ruthless neoliberal capitalism, without the legal and institutional safeguards to prevent abuse, theft, corruption, and other social pathologies. In rejecting their immediate past, neoliberalism was fetishized as the ultimate form of freedom. Any effort to establish social justice or solidarity was condemned as a return to authoritarianism. Under such conditions, building a functioning liberal democracy is not only difficult—it may be impossible. What emerges instead is a society increasingly defined by selfishness, dysfunction, polarization, and political manipulation through hate—echoing the darkest periods in modern history. The fact remains that neoliberalism not only doesn’t work—it causes harm. Thatcher, Brownback, and others have proven this. In the end, it’s ordinary people who suffer. This is why we now see a cultural war that, as in the 1930s, dominates social life—not just in the East, but in the West too, including in Slovenia. Neoliberalism needs and fuels a culture war—against feminism, migrants, the LGBTI community, and other scapegoats—because it distracts from the consequences of its own policies, while leveraging public discontent to strengthen the political power of those willing to serve it. These actors are ready to sacrifice civil liberties, human rights, social peace, and stability for their own interests. This is the reality represented in the U.S. by Trump, DeSantis, and their Republican allies, and in Europe by a far right that is becoming increasingly mainstream. Kansas showed how neoliberalism—even in its most visibly dysfunctional and destructive form—still empowers the far right through cultural war. Just two years after Brownback’s failed experiment ended, Kansas voted majority Republican for Trump in 2016. But the story can turn out differently: in the UK, conservatives are in serious trouble, and in Spain, the mainstream right’s flirtation with the far right didn’t pay off as many expected. Where Slovenia positions itself will depend on us. If we fall into the trap of blindly pledging allegiance to crude neoliberalism, shouting “communism!” at every policy aimed at achieving the social justice democracy requires, things won’t end well. Nor if we swing the other way, returning to discredited ideologies of our recent past. The framework for an independent and democratic Slovenia is laid out in our Constitution. It guarantees both private property and free enterprise, but also defines Slovenia as a social state that respects human rights and political freedoms. Within these constitutional bounds, we can pursue left-wing, right-wing, or centrist paths to a truly democratic, free, and successful society—based on democratic mandates earned through elections. Outside those bounds—whichever direction we stray—lies the risk of authoritarianism. Perhaps we could take inspiration, not just from the Constitution, but also from the vision of a society “in which few have too much and even fewer too little.” Before anyone accuses me of spreading communist ideas, let me clarify: this is a thought from Danish Protestant pastor Grundtvig in the second half of the 19th century. His legacy remains one of the foundations of Denmark’s welfare society—what’s left of it. But let that not discourage us. Perhaps we should stop trying to become a second Switzerland—and instead become even more Danish than the Danes.
The French Republic and Its Children

Responsibility for the recent violent outburst in France, after seventeen-year-old Nahel died from a police officer’s bullets in the town of Nanterre, was immediately attributed by some politicians around Europe, including in Slovenia, to illegal migrants. Which, on the one hand, is understandable. They are to blame for everything anyway. And once they are finally gone, milk and honey will flow and we will live in loving native harmony for ever and ever, amen. Just a little more intolerance and hatred and we’ll get there. If I understand correctly. A hallmark of far-right populism is that it ignores facts because it plays on emotions. It does not solve problems; it exploits them. What is true doesn’t matter; what matters is what people want to believe is true. The June events in France are no exception. The trigger was Nahel’s death, but there were many reasons, and illegal migrants were not among them. It is true that the frightening smashing, burning of schools and looting of shops we witnessed mostly involved teenagers from the suburbs, where many, like Nahel, have roots in former French colonies, but they are mostly the third, perhaps already the fourth, generation born in France. Their ancestors mostly came to the country entirely legally, because France invited them and needed them. They are French citizens, and the French Republic, as its institutions like to stress, is a mother who makes no distinction between her children. In principle, but more on that a little later. The June riots are the consequence of one, but by no means the only one, of the social, economic and political tensions and divisions that France faces and has been trying, not very successfully, to resolve for decades. Before the brief but very violent June riots, France experienced protests against pension reform this spring. The government’s measures were rejected by almost all sections of the population, and support for the protests at the beginning of the year even exceeded 70 percent. Anger at raising the retirement age to 64 often seems hard to understand from the point of view of many other countries where the bar is set even higher. That is partly why the British Guardian wrote that France is a paradise inhabited by people convinced they are in hell. The quip is witty, if perhaps not entirely accurate. Comparisons between pension systems in different countries are complicated, but there is nonetheless, in France, at least an apparent paradox between relatively moderate reforms on the one hand and popular fury on the other. The fact is that people were outraged not only by the content of the changes but also, and above all, by how they were adopted. Worried that the reform would not win majority support in parliament, Macron introduced it by decree, on the basis of the “notorious” third paragraph of Article 49 of the French Constitution. The French Republic is a mother with rules that often get on her children’s nerves. The so-called yellow vests were also fed up with Paris and the institutions of the French Republic a few years ago. It was a spontaneous revolt triggered in 2018 by the government’s decision to raise taxes on fuel in order to protect the environment. Such a measure of course affects people in the countryside differently from those who live in cities. The former are much more dependent on cars, or tractors, than the latter. There were very few French citizens from the suburbs among the yellow vests. Nor did the yellow vests concern themselves much with their problems. It was a revolt of the “native” middle and lower-middle class of the periphery against Paris, the capital of a state that could hardly be more centralized. The French Republic is a mother who is often kinder to the children she has right before her eyes. France clearly has problems. Some are similar to those faced by other European countries; others are homegrown messes with a distinctly French flavor. Despite the many differences between the three divisions in French society described above, all three have one thing in common: tensions in the relationship between the institutions of the French state and various groups of its citizens. Since 1958, France has had the so-called Fifth Republic, created by de Gaulle’s constitutional reforms. These were the general’s answer to the instability characteristic of the postwar period. France saw a succession of weak governments, incapable of reaching political consensus on any reforms. All this must have reminded de Gaulle of the period before the Second World War, when popular discontent with the ineffectiveness of politics during a deep economic crisis created the conditions for the rise of totalitarian ideas, not only in France but of course above all in Germany, and elsewhere in Europe. At the end of the 1950s, France was also marked by the war in Algeria, which was not only a conflict between France and its former colony but threatened to turn into civil war. During the Algerian crisis, the general returned to politics with the idea of a different, highly centralized political system that transferred much of executive power to the presidency. The new French Republic, in the general’s words, reflected “the spirit of the nation.” The project, which had its logic from the perspective of the time, is in my opinion today one of the causes of present-day problems. Again and again situations arise in which friction can be detected between the “spirit of the nation” and the will of the people. The discontent and anger this generates benefit above all political extremists. It seems that de Gaulle’s answer to the danger of totalitarianism half a century ago is today giving wind to precisely the politics and ideas the general tried to stop more than half a century ago. The perception of an arrogant and elitist centralized state power that enraged the yellow vests is in large part a reaction to the legacy of the Fifth Republic. The way the unpopular pension reform was adopted by decree is also part of this story. But it is reflected above all in the attitude toward the ethnic and religious minorities living in France, especially the descendants of immigrants who come mainly from former French colonies. These minorities officially do not exist in France. The Fifth Republic mandates complete equality of all citizens, regardless of their ethnic or religious origin. It is a noble idea in principle, but in practice it also has many negative consequences. The official non-recognition of minorities or “communities”—a term with a distinctly negative connotation in the context of the Fifth Republic—prevents the French state from identifying in time and addressing problems arising from pronounced actual social inequality between different segments of its population. Although it cannot be accused of not trying, it is often ineffective in its efforts. Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent on the recent US Supreme Court ruling that ended affirmative action in university admissions that “ignoring race will not equalize a society that is racially unequal.” And this largely applies to France too. Despite official oaths and collective emotion over the slogans of the French Revolution, French society has problems with equality and fraternity, and all this can also have consequences for liberty. How far things have gone was pointed out years ago, during the wave of terrorist attacks that shook France, by the then Prime Minister, the Socialist Manuel Valls. His statement about “ghettoization and apartheid in the French suburbs” shocked the French public but nevertheless led to a certain sobering up. Since then the French authorities have invested billions of euros in “problem zones,” but the effectiveness of these measures was again limited by constitutionally mandated “color blindness.” Without censuses and statistics giving an accurate picture of who lives where and how, measures, however well-intentioned, are less effective. According to the data that are available, France is a peculiar paradox when it comes to inequality. While by the GINI coefficient for income inequality it is among the more socially just countries in the Western world, according to statistics recently published by the Financial Times, income inequality between the majority and immigrant populations is far above that in the US, which is itself far from a society one would otherwise hold up as a model in this respect. The immediate cause of the latest riots, Nahel’s death from a police officer’s bullets, is also not unconnected to the peculiarities of the spirit of the Fifth Republic. As the British Guardian wrote, in France the concept of a police force that looks after citizens’ safety is often overshadowed by the police’s task of defending the security of the state against its citizens. And this often involves violence. Especially in the suburbs. In responses to the latest riots, many also pointed to the decision of the government under President Sarkozy to abolish the so-called neighborhood or community police. Officers permanently stationed in suburban neighborhoods, many of whom came from a similar social background, were replaced by police units that come there only occasionally, for checks and interventions. Instead of peacekeepers who knew the neighborhood and its people and often acted preventively, the suburbs got police officers armed to the teeth who keep order with batons and tear gas. The latest outbreak of violence, which can in no way be justified, arose, like the ones before it, from discontent that has been smoldering in France for a long time. Among many it strengthened the conviction that France must do more for the equality of all its citizens, since closing one’s eyes on the pretext of formal unity and equality evidently doesn’t work. On the other hand, the intolerant and racist extremists, among them former presidential candidate Zemmour, have again got wind in their sails. What France will look like tomorrow will depend on whether populist nativists prevail or whether politics and social consensus will recognize that France is not in trouble because many people of foreign origin live there, but because in the past it too often went about efforts to integrate them and secure their equality the wrong way. Perhaps the time has come for Mother Republic to open her eyes wide and take care of all her children.

On Sunday, November 11, 1945, the first “democratic” elections were held in postwar Yugoslavia. Under the agreement between Tito and Šubašić, the head of the Yugoslav government in exile, the elections were supposed to allow secret voting and the participation of different candidate lists, but Tito decided that so much democracy would not be to the people’s liking, so he made sure of circumstances in which the opposition saw no point in taking part, and it decided to boycott. At the polling stations, voters thus found themselves facing two boxes, one with the official list of the People’s Front, headed by Josip Broz, and the other, “black” one, with no list. Because of the high rate of illiteracy in Yugoslavia at the time, voting was done with small balls. Each voter pushed a fist first into one ballot box, then into the other, and at the end had to show the committee an empty palm. But, as if by chance, the boxes were not lined, so when a ball was dropped a “plink” could be heard, which helped the people’s rulers tell who was one of us and who wasn’t. Ježek mocked these peculiarities of people’s democracy in his legendary satirical song “Cinca marinca,” about the voter who is against us because he dropped his ball into the black box. The elections also brought an end to the short-lived Democratic Federal Yugoslavia, which was replaced a good two weeks later by the Federal People’s Republic of Yugoslavia. For a people’s government that thinks highly of itself, democracy is merely in the way. What would Ježek think What Ježek would have thought of the outburst of indignation in part of Slovenian politics and the public that followed, a week or two ago, the news that Magnifico would perform at the central celebration of Statehood Day, we do not know. But journalist Antiša Korljan recalled “Cinca marinca” in this context on the LGDG podcast, so I take this opportunity to commend him for his historical memory and reflexes. The analogy is certainly apt. “Plink, Magnifico at the state celebration? Plink, plink, didn’t he once say he voted against independence? Plink, plink, plink, he’s not one of us enough,” echoed, and still echoes, through the ever muddier swamp of Slovenian social media. “Plink,” the great leader of the only true opposition finally roared too. And announced that, by golly, he would not attend such a celebration. One really doesn’t know whether to laugh or cry. Magnifico supposedly once said somewhere that in the 1990 plebiscite on Slovenian independence he voted against independence. Maybe he did, maybe he didn’t. If he really did state publicly how he voted, he of course cannot complain if someone also publicly asks him why he decided that way. But that can in no way be a reason to treat him as a second-class citizen and object to one of Slovenia’s most successful and popular musicians performing at a state celebration. My dear friends, let us not judge too quickly Actually, I wish Magnifico would speak up and explain his decision at the time. Because it could help us confront critically some questions from that period. It is indisputable that almost thirty-four years ago the citizens of Slovenia overwhelmingly opted for an independent and democratic Slovenia, and we can be extremely proud of that. But that does not change the fact that at the time some people were worried about how an independent Slovenia would treat people who, in the opinion of part of politics and the public, were not Slovenian enough. That this fear was not entirely unfounded, independent Slovenia proved very quickly with the erasure, which was, and remains, the biggest stain on this so important and magnificent period of Slovenian history. So, my dear friends, let us not judge too quickly and point fingers at people who, in those uncertain times, decided as they did, perhaps also out of fear that for some they were not and never would be enough “ours.” So Magnifico is against us, because he supposedly dropped his vote into the black box. Plink, some of you may grumble, the comparison is not apt. In 1945 a ball in the black box was a vote against an authoritarian regime; in 1990 it was a vote against an independent Slovenia. Which is of course true, but in no way excuses the rampaging of those who are lashing out at Magnifico and his performance at this year’s state celebration. On the contrary, precisely this difference lays bare the full extent of the failure to understand basic democratic principles among those who, seventy-eight years later, are once again claiming the right to decide in the name of the people who is ours enough and who isn’t. In 1990 we also voted so that we would never again have to vote the way we did in 1945. Choosing democracy means choosing a social system in which people can think, speak and vote freely as they see fit. Only authoritarians advocate and use black boxes. In the name of the people, of course. Ronaldo on the substitutes’ bench How and for what Magnifico really voted, he himself can best explain. If he thinks it necessary and decides to do so. The fact is, however, that thirty-four years ago some residents of Slovenia had legitimate reasons to worry about what the future would bring them. So some voted as they voted, for one of the two options put to them in a democratic vote. But even more important than how these people thought about Slovenia thirty-three years ago is how they think about it today. And that is perhaps the most important message of Magnifico’s performance at the state celebration. That someone who decades ago may have had concerns about how the independent state would treat some of its citizens today performs with joy and pride at the celebration of its thirty-third anniversary is actually a very fine and sincere compliment to our country and to all of us, and proof that despite the initial slips—and despite the shouting and stamping of those who would still like to divide us into ours and not ours enough—we have made Slovenia a state of all its citizens, regardless of which box anyone dropped their vote into. Such a vision of society and the state is by no means a project of “woke” left-wing activists, but a matter of respecting and implementing constitutional principles and democratic values. These principles and values are today under attack from those who want to consolidate political power and authority by stoking intolerance and dividing people by political belief, gender, skin color, religion or sexual orientation. The President of the Republic also spoke about this at the state celebration, while her immediate predecessor grimaced and fidgeted in the front row like Cristiano Ronaldo on the substitutes’ bench. Perhaps in his thoughts he was already at the alternative celebration that advocates of conspiracy theories about “cultural Marxism” and “LGBT ideology,” packaged as alternative values, organized for him the next day. Or perhaps his shoes were just pinching. Who knows. Democratic, successful, inclusive!? The paradox of today’s Slovenia is that people who otherwise have their mouths full of condemnation of postwar authoritarianism and single-mindedness are, through their discourse and actions, trying to re-establish a very similar social system. Don’t be distracted by shades of color. The principle is the same; everything else is nuance. By performing at the state celebration, Magnifico showed what Slovenia means to him. The reactions to his performance, meanwhile, reveal to whom a democratic, inclusive and successful Slovenia is magnifico. And to whom it isn’t.

On June 8, France was shaken by news of a horrific attack in the town of Annecy, where a Syrian refugee, Abdelmasih H., stabbed six people with a knife—among them four children under the age of four. The attack on the children playing in a park by the lake evoked memories of October 14 last year, when a homeless man discovered the body of 12-year-old Lola in a courtyard of a building in Paris’s 19th arrondissement. Before her death, the girl had been tortured and raped. Surveillance footage quickly led to the suspect: 24-year-old Dahbia B., an Algerian national without legal status in France, who had already been issued a deportation order. Just two days after the Annecy attack, another child was murdered on the other side of France, in the Breton village of Saint-Herbot. Eleven-year-old Solaine, British by heritage but born in France, was shot dead by an enraged neighbor—an elderly pensioner from Antwerp, Belgium—who also seriously wounded her father. These tragic events are part of a very grim statistic. In France, up to 100 children under the age of 15 die violent deaths each year, most often due to domestic violence. Foreign nationals, such as those suspected in these three cases, represent a very small fraction of this morbid statistic. Yet, they attract significantly more attention—perhaps with the exception of the murder in Brittany. While the media extensively covered Solaine’s death, there were no mass demonstrations or political exploitation of the tragedy by far-right extremists. When the perpetrator is from Antwerp, nationality is treated as a coincidence. But if he’s from Syria or Algeria, it’s cited as evidence of an escalating threat—one that the notorious racist and former (and likely future) presidential candidate Éric Zemmour dubbed “Francocide.” According to Zemmour, migrants from the East kill the French simply for being French. Before continuing, let me be very clear: I have no intention of ranking or relativizing these unfathomable crimes. Each attack is a grave criminal act. The victims—those who lost their lives and the young children in Annecy who, thankfully, survived—as well as their loved ones, are owed justice. The perpetrators must be prosecuted and punished for their horrific acts. A thorough investigation of all circumstances surrounding the crimes is also necessary—not only to understand what happened, but to do everything possible to prevent such tragedies in the future. Within that context, the nationality of the suspects and victims is one factor to consider. If it proves relevant, it must inform both the legal classification of the crime (as an aggravating circumstance) and any future prevention measures. But if no such link is found, highlighting nationality becomes nothing more than indecent political exploitation of a tragedy—a cynical attempt to gain politically from the murder of children. Karine Bourdié, president of the French Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, called this shameful tactic “the instrumentalization of tragedy to light a fire at the entrance to a cemetery.” We have no shortage of similar hate-mongers here at home. When reality fails to supply enough scandal to fuel intolerance, they simply invent it. Remember the fabricated claim about 57 rapes supposedly committed by migrants in Ljubljana this year? Following Lola’s death, extremists in France began organizing public protests under a single banner: migrants are to blame, and so is President Macron for his supposedly lax immigration policy. Under pressure, even the president began pointing fingers at undocumented foreigners. In a television interview shortly after Lola’s murder, Macron initially denied any link between crime rates and migration, but then claimed that in Paris—“due to geographic and administrative reasons”—nearly half of all crimes are committed by migrants without legal status or still awaiting it. That statement drew criticism. First, Macron lumped together asylum seekers, undocumented foreigners, and legal residents like me and my family. He also confused arrest statistics with conviction data. Most importantly, experts pointed out that his insinuation of a link between rising migrant numbers and increasing crime was based on flimsy and misinterpreted data. A different picture emerged from a study by the CEPII research institute, which operates under the office of Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne. It found no such correlation. The only exception—statistically minor—was a slight uptick in petty thefts. But even that disappears, according to the study, when migrants have access to the labor market. In other words, people steal when they’re hungry—and stop when they can earn a living. Yet over half of the French public (and not only them) still associate their sense of insecurity with the supposed “threat” posed by migrants. The CEPII study attributes this to biased and sensationalist media coverage. Years ago, when the German regional paper Sächsische Zeitung began systematically reporting the nationality of crime suspects—including when they were German—fear of foreigners among readers dropped by 20%, and support for the far-right AfD declined by a similar margin. Lola’s death in France further confirmed this dynamic. The controversial television host Cyril Hanouna—repeatedly sanctioned for hate speech—declared on air that Lola’s suspected killer should be imprisoned for life without trial or psychiatric evaluation. In his view, migrants simply don’t deserve the protections of the rule of law. His show set viewership records. Hatred sells. The bigger problem with Macron’s statement was that he offered his poorly founded data in direct response to a question about the circumstances of Lola’s tragic death. In doing so—perhaps unintentionally—he lent credence to far-right conspiracies linking migration to the murder of a 12-year-old girl. Causal links are complex, sensitive, and often abused. So far, investigations and expert opinions suggest that the suspects' actions weren’t linked to the victims' nationalities, nor part of any broader organized pattern, as claimed by far-right conspiracy theorists. None of the three crimes are being investigated as terrorism. Psychiatric experts found Dahbia B. mentally competent but suffering from serious and complex personality disorders and a complete lack of empathy. Abdelmasih H., the Annecy attacker, has been placed in psychiatric care. The murderer in Brittany—who extremists conveniently ignore—acted out of a long-standing neighborhood dispute and was under the influence of drugs and alcohol. To me, the causal link lies elsewhere: in the deliberate stoking of hatred toward migrants for political gain on one side, and increasingly indifferent or even inhumane policies toward people fleeing to Europe on the other. Under the pressure of public opinion inflamed by extremists—enabled by weak and opportunistic politicians—society increasingly denies help to those in need. Organizations that save lives are harassed. Coast guards ignore distress calls—if they’re not doing worse. And it has consequences. After the latest tragic shipwreck off the Greek coast, hundreds are missing, including a hundred children. Their chances of survival are now virtually nil. “Who forced them onto that boat?” many will growl. But the real question—what and who paved their path to death—is legitimate. On one side: desperation, fear, and hope—often a result of crises in which the West has its share of responsibility. On the other: criminals who traffic in human lives. But also our own indifference and intolerance, which have helped turn the Mediterranean into a mass grave. Fortunately, many people still care—people who manage to preserve their humanity even in the most difficult moments. When far-right parades marched through French streets after Lola’s death, her parents were not among them. From their home in northern France, where they had retreated to grieve in peace, they issued a statement through their lawyer demanding that protesters and politicians stop exploiting their daughter for political purposes. “Allow us to preserve the memory of our little girl with respect and dignity.”
On Polarizations That Should Not Be “Overcome”

Quarreling really isn’t nice. And when someone quarrels as much as we Slovenians do, it’s no wonder many are fed up with us and calls are coming from all sides for us to stop arguing and dividing. Unity and dialogue are noble virtues that I support wholeheartedly. Almost always. But there are questions on which I would advise caution and reflection even to those most eager for harmony and dialogue. Some divisions should not simply be overcome, even with the best of intentions, and still less should coexistence and reconciliation be sought somewhere at the geometric midpoint. These are divisions and disputes over the fundamental democratic values we have protected in the Constitution. The European democratic and civilizational model rests on these values, and it was in their name that we won and built an independent state. Unfortunately, the most dominant polarization in Slovenia today is precisely over these fundamental principles. Whatever labels we use for ourselves and our political opponents, Slovenia has for a long time not been divided so much into left and right, social democrats, leftists, liberals, conservatives, Christian democrats or right-wingers. The main ideological battle is between those who believe in and defend the values of liberal democracy, whether left, right or center, and illiberal, authoritarian and populist politics with a cribbed handbook and discourse from foreign parts, from Florida to the Kremlin. DeSantis and Trump are trying their hardest, but in the end no one is more anti-woke than Putin and his cronies. I have also followed these changes in the Slovenian political space through my writing in recent years. From the very beginning I avoided commenting on day-to-day politics, and even more so taking a position on this or that party. When Večer’s editor-in-chief Matija Stepišnik offered me the chance to contribute, he suggested I write about European topics, democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Nothing controversial, then, since we were all for them, weren’t we? Not that I have no party preferences, but I express them through my vote at elections, not through columns. In my columns I advocate a political and social system that is democratic and pluralist and in which different democratic political options have equal opportunities. If anything, I would not want to live in a system in which everyone had to think the same as I do on every social question. Paradoxically, however, over the years my uncontroversial writing about generally accepted values has slowly come to resemble commentary on day-to-day politics more and more. Not because I changed the content of my columns, but because day-to-day politics began to split and divide over the values I write about. How far things have gone in the inability to distinguish between decency and pathology is also reflected in the reaction to my previous column, in which I condemned a blatantly antisemitic post by my former professor, constitutional judge and judge at the European Court of Human Rights. The gentleman couldn’t care less, as he wrote, because in my text I criticized him ad hominem rather than ad rem. In other words, he reproaches me for calling him an antisemite because of his antisemitic post, instead of debating with him whether antisemitism is justified or not. Because, you know, nothing is black and white and there are always two sides. Perhaps he expected that in the end we would overcome our differences and mutual polarization and, through dialogue, meet somewhere halfway. Agree that the Nazis were legitimately “addressing” a real threat, but got a little carried away in their response? Deeply worrying statements have been swarming lately. Among them, certainly, is the dangerous and extremely irresponsible saber-rattling about civil war, as well as the completely deranged calls to arms by a certain guy who sends dog whistles, as the Americans call them, to the homeland from his London armchair. And sells himself as a victim and dissident to boot. Whatever we think about the events and decisions that triggered these outbursts, from the hasty abolition of a hastily introduced holiday to the latest decision of the Constitutional Court, this cannot and must not be an excuse for such irresponsible playing with fire and inflaming passions that can lead to violence. The same goes for the drivel about “cultural Marxism,” a discourse of very questionable historical provenance that stokes and manipulates accumulated social discontent through attacks on social minorities. Or historical revisionism, which abuses the legitimate and noble idea of reconciliation and reverence for the dead to discredit anti-fascism, the foundation of Europe’s postwar order. It is particularly dangerous when such ideas are spread by people who listen only to themselves and have no one beside them who could and would dare demand that they rein in their horses before it is too late. Playing with fire at some point acquires its own dynamic, which in the end not even the one who first lit the torch can stop. When we founded our own state, we adopted a Constitution that clearly sets out the value framework of democratic pluralism in our society. It ranges from the provision that Slovenia is a social state that protects human rights and political freedoms to the articles protecting private property and free economic initiative. Within this framework we can and must think differently, and we can divide and quarrel to our hearts’ content. The competition of ideas and programs, with the mandate they receive from voters and under the oversight exercised by the institutions of the rule of law, an independent judiciary, the media and civil society, is the driving force that guarantees a democratic society peace, stability, security, justice, freedom and development. But when someone deliberately steps outside this framework and begins to undermine the constitutional foundations of Slovenian statehood and democracy—when they even begin to rattle sabers—the response simply cannot be mere whining about polarization and calls to overcome differences. If racism, authoritarianism, antisemitism, nationalism, hatred of social minorities and the denial of human dignity lie in wait on the other side of the divide, we need a firm and united response from the public and from all democratic political forces, regardless of their other political and ideological differences and squabbles. Not least so that in the future, too, we will live in a society in which we can go on thinking differently.
Our Expert on Human Rights and the Jewish Question

“Since 1850, when they obtained all political rights in the German Reich, the Jews managed to control about fifty percent of the media and seventy percent of all judges, so that they had a strong influence on films, theaters and literature. They were absolutely overrepresented, just as they are today in England, France and the USA.” This thought is the introduction to a short piece on the Jewish question entitled “What Did the Jews Do to Germany?”, posted on Twitter on Sunday, May 14, 2023, by the user @AlesValant, better known as Boštjan M. Zupančič, Harvard doctor, former judge of the European Court of Human Rights and of the Slovenian Constitutional Court, professor of law and international legal consultant, as the gentleman proudly presents himself on his profile. The thesis is certainly bold, but not entirely original. Let us look, for example, at what Dr. Joseph Goebbels, Reich Minister for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, declared in September 1933 at a press conference in the grand salon of the Hotel Carlton in Geneva: “The Jews have occupied leading positions in the German media, literature, theater, film, in the medical and legal professions and on the stock exchange. They have parliament and the political parties under their control.” You may feel that a comparison between the two doctors is inappropriate and exaggerated, since our doctor obviously cannot be held responsible for the crimes against Jews committed by the Nazi regime. True, but this argument cuts both ways. Dr. Goebbels reassured journalists who were worried by his words about the Jews having supposedly hijacked the state by assuring them “that the concentration camps are intended only for re-educating antisocial leaders into useful citizens.” “We will deal with this excessive Jewish influence in a humane way,” the Herr Reichsminister good-naturedly concluded his address to the assembled representatives of the fourth estate. And here is the difference. While Dr. Goebbels could theoretically still wriggle out by claiming that in 1933 he did not know what was in preparation, our doctor repeated—and updated—the words about the Jews and the hijacked state knowing full well what this “humane” rescue of the “hijacked” German state led to. But let us return to the post by our former constitutional judge. It continues as follows: “The Jews were responsible for numerous catastrophic bank crashes in Germany between 1870 and 1920. This is not Nazi or antisemitic or Arab propaganda, but is documented and even published in books written by Jewish Germans. Millions of German fathers lost their incomes, wealth and savings because of these Jewish banking gangsters and speculators.” In this part, the author of the post addresses the evergreen theme of blaming particular social groups, ethnic or religious minorities, for all the hardships experienced in times of economic crisis by honest, hard-working, white Christian men, or, in the above version, “millions of German fathers.” Even though the search for scapegoats in Europe has a long and bloody historical beard, it is losing none of its popularity among part of the political elite even today. Vigilance is certainly called for. Let us remember: according to the person our country sent to the European Court of Human Rights, “the Jews in England, France and the USA are today absolutely overrepresented.” That’s not all. As the man who was for many years a professor at the Ljubljana Faculty of Law warns us in his post, where there are Jews, there are also homosexuals, decadence and perversion. And vice versa. You know, birds of a feather. This is, of course, the phenomenon that Dr. Goebbels and his boss called “Kulturbolschewismus,” which many today translate as “cultural Marxism” and enthusiastically use as a sledgehammer in nationalist populism’s culture war against the values of liberal democracy. The concluding thought of the text posted by our legal giant goes like this: “The Jews brought moral decadence into German art and culture, theater and film. The first homosexual theater plays were staged in Berlin in the 1920s, and the first adulterous plays in the 1880s and 1890s by Jewish authors. Adultery, sexual perversions of all kinds, sadism, masochism, a great deal of homosexuality and decadent art, art that is completely ridiculous, so-called modern art, all this was pushed by Jewish intellectuals. And this caused great resistance among the German people. They also wrote mocking books and made fun of Jesus and Christianity.” Here we are, my dear fellow citizens. Deep down and sinking ever lower. Some may wave away my writing, saying we must not give such characters attention because it only encourages them. This is a doctrine based on the belief that intolerance and hatred disappear by themselves if we ignore them thoroughly enough. I am of a different opinion. Spreading antisemitic hatred like this would deserve not only sharp condemnation but probably also the attention of prosecutors, regardless of who was behind it. And Boštjan M. Zupančič is not just anyone. And this is not his first antisemitic rodeo. Our “top human rights expert” rampages on social media every day like an eighteen-year-old skinhead who can’t hold his drink. And nothing. From nowhere and from no one. Indifference and silence which, with every slip, normalize evil and hatred among us. In light of the tragic events we recently witnessed in Serbia, too, we should be worried about what can happen in a society that banalizes hatred and calls to violence. Today some here are urging people to arm themselves; supposedly we are threatened by civil war. Why no one looks at this man’s antisemitic fingers on the keyboard of hatred, let alone raps him on the knuckles, everyone will have to answer for themselves. Some probably because he is evidently still useful to them. When the Council for Combating Hate Speech was recently established, many opponents of the government’s decision enthusiastically quoted him as Slovenia’s greatest expert in the field of hate speech. Which in a certain sense he certainly is. As is evident from his posts. Others are probably embarrassed. Let us not forget that only a few years ago the guy was a hero of the Slovenian liberal center. A legal big shot and a provocative intellectual stallion kicking up dust behind him. This, for example, is what a journalist of the Ljubljana daily Dnevnik wrote on his departure from Strasbourg seven years ago: “Professor Boštjan M. Zupančič is often hard to understand, as he is inclined to go beyond conventional frameworks … Some object to this, others revere him. But no one has ever said he is a bad judge. He is one of the best Slovenian legal experts. Boštjan M. Zupančič leaves Strasbourg as a great legal authority.” Let us not forget that Miro Cerar’s government nominated this man as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. We avoided great embarrassment only because, before the procedure was concluded, he went off the rails and published on Facebook, and then in letters to the editor of The Guardian, a post in which, on the occasion of her death, he disgustingly attacked Simone Veil, former President of the European Parliament and the minister responsible for liberalizing abortion in France. Despite the affair, a few months later his professional colleagues chose him as one of the ten most influential lawyers in Slovenia. I do not, of course, think that the people who supported and revered this man share responsibility for his behavior in recent years, but their support in the past does now oblige them to react and condemn. This applies even more to Slovenian politics and the state. A man we sent to the highest office in the European human rights system is today behaving in a way that threatens Slovenia’s reputation. He did not march into the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Slovenia of his own accord; the National Assembly elected him there. At the time when he lashed out at Simone Veil, he was receiving a salary from the Ministry of Justice. The Slovenian state sent him to the European Court of Human Rights. It cannot now behave as if the antisemitic rampaging of a man who served as a judge on behalf of Slovenia during some very important cases before the Strasbourg court has nothing to do with it. We will not solve the predicament with silence and by pretending it does not exist. Our “great legal authority” is like Prince Andrew posting photos from Epstein’s parties every day. If we cannot and will not condemn such blatant antisemitism by someone to whom we only recently entrusted the highest judicial offices in Slovenia and in Europe, we become co-responsible both for the hatred and for its possible consequences. In the words of a former President of the Republic whose concern is otherwise very selective, this is behavior that takes us backward. By about ninety years, into the grand salon of the Hotel Carlton in Geneva.

A few weeks ago, I received an invitation that surprised me. The RAND Corporation, a well-known American nonpartisan and nonprofit research organization primarily recognized for its military research, invited me to a conference titled "Democracy in Crisis?" Funded by the U.S. Congress, RAND depends on support from both Democrats and Republicans. Their decision to address issues related to democracy—reportedly for the first time—was cynically commented on at the conference by Francis Fukuyama, famed for his "end of history" thesis. “If you're going to deal with democracy, you have to start with democracy in the U.S. And you can't do that critically and objectively without angering a large part of the Republican Party.” The RAND representatives didn’t respond to his remark, but I do give them credit for including a number of speakers likely to be critical of the state of democracy in the West, especially in the United States. That’s why I decided to accept the invitation. If we want to contribute to positive change, echo chambers of like-minded people patting each other on the back just aren’t enough. My remarks at the conference emphasized the necessity of social justice for democracy, and the idea that any credible effort to promote democracy globally requires consistent adherence to democratic values both at home and in foreign policy. The American participants—including quite a few Republicans—didn’t exactly give me a standing ovation, but they were willing to listen and discuss. Perhaps it helped that their most extreme colleagues were, at the same time, fraternizing in Budapest with their European comrades in the fight against “wokeness” and “cultural Marxism.” I admit I’m cheating a bit with this column, as it's essentially a transcript of my speech at the conference. Here’s what I said: “We live in times when everyone is a geopolitics and global security expert. I don’t know how RAND manages to stay in business under these conditions—but thank you for the invitation. We also live in times when our attention is consumed by geopolitical tensions and war. And of course, everyone now ‘knows’ the truth about what drove President Putin and the Russian Federation to launch an aggression against a neighboring country. The truth, however, is not universal, and everyone defends their version with passion and certainty. In this competitive market of alternative facts, I side with those who don’t believe that NATO threatened Russia into attacking. Nor do I buy the narrative that the invasion was necessary to protect the purity of the Russian people from the corrupting influence of the decadent West. If anything, the Kremlin would find plenty of like-minded allies in the West—especially in the U.S.—who agree with such views. Trust me, no one is more anti-woke than President Putin and his Kremlin comrades. In my opinion—and based on nearly three decades of working with both Ukraine and Russia, the latter being a member of the Council of Europe until it was expelled a little over a year ago—Putin was deeply alarmed by the prospect of Ukraine developing into a functioning liberal democracy. Even though the country faces numerous challenges—weak institutions, a lack of democratic experience, and endemic corruption—this was clearly the choice of the majority of Ukrainian citizens. They demonstrated this during the Maidan revolution, in subsequent elections, and in their resolute response to Russian aggression. A democratic Ukraine—economically, politically, institutionally, and socially functional and successful—posed a threat Putin couldn’t tolerate. Just imagine what could happen if his own citizens realized there was a viable alternative next door to nationalist autarky and authoritarian rule. Ukraine, therefore, is not only fighting for its survival. This is also a battle for liberal democracy—in Ukraine and around the world. But the threat to liberal democracy isn’t just external. There are internal dangers, too. First, we’re losing the support of many citizens who have lost trust in the institutions of liberal democracy and who are either indifferent to it or openly prefer authoritarian alternatives. This isn’t the first time in modern history we’ve seen this. Europe’s turbulent past offers lessons we should not ignore. To quote Newsweek’s correspondent from Bucharest, Rosie Waldeck, in June 1940, after Nazi troops marched into Paris: “The fall of France marked the climax of twenty years of democracy's unfulfilled promises to deal with unemployment, inflation, deflation, labor unrest, party selfishness, and more. Europe, weary of itself and its principles, almost sighed in relief when things were ‘put in order’… It thought Hitler was a smart man—unpleasant, but smart. He made his country strong. Why not try it that way?” And we know how that ended. As Mark Twain reportedly said: “History doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes.” The survival of liberal democracy depends on a contract with citizens—that their tomorrow will be better than their yesterday. When that contract is broken—or when people start believing it has been—when there is no social justice, democracy is in trouble. Second, we are losing the support of many young people. Yes, they are concerned. Yes, they are angry. And yes, they are more engaged than young people were a decade or two ago. But their activism is not always progressive or democratic. They feel, often rightly, that democracy has failed them. This happens when people fear the future. A 2020 survey found that a vast majority of young people in Western Europe are deeply worried about climate change. But over 50% said they trust authoritarian regimes more than democracies to deal with the crisis. A few years ago, only one in three young Dutch citizens said they considered living in a democracy important. Just three months ago, another survey showed that nearly a quarter of Dutch millennials and Gen Z believe the Holocaust never happened. I’m not picking on the Netherlands. But if that’s the state of democracy among youth in one of the world’s most stable liberal democracies, we should be seriously concerned about support elsewhere. Third, we must be alarmed by the fact that the model of liberal democracy is losing global support. The reasons are many, and not all of them lie at the feet of the West. But even in the context of Russia’s aggression, we must ask: why have so many countries and people outside the Western hemisphere chosen not to side with the West in condemning the invasion and supporting its clear victim? Could it be because of how the West itself respects its own sermons on democracy and international law? Have we always been consistent in our commitment to democratic principles? These are not “whataboutism” questions—those are just cynical tricks to justify one injustice with another. These are difficult but necessary questions we must answer critically if we want to restore trust in an international order based on democratic rule of law and respect for individual freedom and human dignity. For everyone. So, the answer to the question posed by the conference’s title is unfortunately a clear yes. Democracy is under threat. Reversing its decline and restoring trust and popular support—without which democracy cannot succeed or survive—won’t be easy. We’ll have to take a hard look in the mirror. We face a long-haul, intercontinental journey out of our comfort zones and deeply entrenched patterns of thought and behavior. We’ll need to rethink the link between prosperity and people’s trust in democracy. We’ll have to invest in education and give young people a real say in decisions about their future. We must offer them a perspective of the future they won’t fear. We’ll have to work hard to build a global alliance for democracy—one based on consistent respect for international law, mutual trust, solidarity, and dignity. As long as the most powerful say one thing and do another, things will only get worse. As I said: it won’t be easy. But in the end, ladies and gentlemen—do we really have a choice? Just look at the alternatives."

When The Road to Serfdom by Austrian-British economist Friedrich von Hayek was published by Routledge in March 1944, the initial print run was a modest 2,000 copies. Respectable, but nothing exceptional. Hayek wasn’t an unknown—he was a respected economist and professor at the prestigious London School of Economics. If you haven’t heard of him or his most infamous book, know that his name still brings a tear to the eye of every self-respecting neoliberal. On the website of the Ludwig von Mises Institute for Austrian Economics, based in Auburn, Alabama, Hayek—disciple of the Austrian school founder von Mises—is still celebrated. Here’s what they write with great excitement: “What F. A. Hayek saw—and all his contemporaries ignored—was the fact that every step away from the free market toward government planning is a threat to human freedom and a move toward dictatorship. Government planning leads to a society that is less livable, more brutal, and more despotic. Socialism, in all its forms, is incompatible with freedom.” They even quote Hayek: “Nazism, by its nature, is no different from communism. Capitalism is the only economic system compatible with human dignity, prosperity, and freedom. To deviate from this system is to empower the worst elements of society to manage what they do not understand.” So now you know. I don’t intend—nor do I have the economic expertise—to argue with Hayek’s entire body of work. After all, he won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1972, though the Swedish Royal Academy likely had a bit of fun with that decision, since they awarded it jointly to Hayek and his Swedish counterpart Gunnar Myrdal, a leading theorist of the welfare state and social policy. Hayek, reportedly, was none too pleased and grumbled, “They paired me with that damn ideologue.” The Road to Serfdom is not an economics text but an ideological pamphlet—one that hit Europe at the wrong time. The war experience, memories of the 1930s economic crisis and its consequences, and above all the post-war reconstruction led even conservative European politicians to realize it was better to read Keynes than Hayek. The result was the European welfare state model and the “glorious thirty years” of economic development and the entrenchment of a liberal democratic system based on human rights, rule of law, and pluralism. Hayek’s book found more attention in the U.S., particularly after an editor at Reader’s Digest condensed its 226 pages into a more digestible 20 for the average American reader. For those who found even that too much, General Motors released a comic-book version in 1950. In 18 panels, it illustrated how seemingly well-meaning intervention in the free market will inevitably lead to facing a firing squad. The comic’s main villains are “planners”—a euphemism for anyone supporting any form of state economic intervention in the name of public interest. The first two panels explain Europe’s alleged folly to a worried American observer: “To enable full economic mobilization during wartime, you voluntarily surrender many freedoms. You know regulation was forced upon you by your country’s enemy. But before the war ends, arguments arise that planning should continue in peacetime. Planners who want to stay in power support these ideas.” Europe largely ignored Hayek for over three decades—until the late 1980s, when the GM comic fell into the hands of newly minted British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. The timing was right. The Soviet Union, which had done its best to confirm Hayek’s warnings about planned economies leading to firing squads, was on the verge of collapse. The Iron Lady took the ideas seriously: she crushed the unions, deregulated everything, and sold off state assets. Budgets soared; the efficiency and profits of privatized companies—now free from labor costs and public accountability—grew rapidly. Neoliberalism had found its heroine, who brought Hayek’s comic to life. Rarely mentioned, however, is the paradox: under Thatcher, the supposedly parasitic British state cost taxpayers just as much as before. In 1978, just before she took office, public spending was 42.5% of GDP. A decade into her neoliberal rule, it had dropped to only 41.7%. Why? Because unemployment costs exploded—she managed to double them. Her famous line that “there is no such thing as society” wasn’t so much an ideological flourish as a description of the wreckage left by her total war on the public, the common, and the solidaristic. The consequences of her policies—for British society, politics, global standing, and even democracy—are still being chronicled in the daily papers. The profits Thatcher’s neoliberal reforms brought to British capital have since been wiped out by Brexit. Neoliberalism, like every ideological revolution worth its salt, eventually devours its own children. Over two decades after Thatcher, Republican Governor of Kansas Sam Brownback took things a step further. His 2012 “Kansas experiment” would likely have made even Hayek blush. Brownback’s “march to zero” tax reform drastically cut taxes for the wealthy, slashed or eliminated business taxes, reduced social support, closed schools for low-income children, shuttered four public agencies, and fired 2,000 public workers. Promising it would inject economic adrenaline, boost investment, and increase employment, the results were disastrous. Within a few years, Brownback turned a billion-dollar budget surplus into a billion-dollar deficit. The expected investment boom and job growth never came. Kansas lagged behind other states. To fill the hole, his administration raided infrastructure funds, halted road repairs, and hiked sales tax—hurting the poorest the most, who ended up paying more in taxes than before. Many no longer had enough even for “minimum food, shelter, and clothing sufficient to preserve health,” as Hayek had “benevolently” allowed for in The Road to Serfdom as acceptable state support that doesn’t threaten liberty. Logically, one would think voters would respond by kicking such experimenters—and their ideas—out of office. But experience shows otherwise. Hayek’s caricatured version of capitalism, generously aided by the auto industry, proved anything but the “only economic system compatible with human dignity, prosperity, and freedom,” as the Mises Institute in Alabama still claims. Quite the opposite. Neoliberalism, far from liberating, produced popular rage—which then fueled far-right populism that now actively and efficiently undermines the very values it claimed to uphold. The UK is not in good shape. The U.S. is worse. In Alabama, angry and disappointed voters overwhelmingly supported Trump in 2016, who later appointed Brownback as “Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom.” Today in the U.S., books are banned, curricula censored, and talk of structural racism and minority rights suppressed. Politically motivated and legally backed attacks on women’s reproductive rights are rampant. Sexual minorities are systematically stigmatized, incited against, and hated. Let’s go back to the comic. “Rising confusion in the country leads to protests. In a failed attempt to convince everyone they’re right, the planners create a massive propaganda machine—which will benefit the future dictator. The least educated—inspired by charismatic speakers—form a party. In desperation, the planners elect a new party leader, hoping he’ll impose a solution. They figure they’ll get rid of him later.” Panel 12 left a strong impression on me: “The first step of all dictators is to incite the majority against scapegoated minorities. In Germany, this was done with antisemitism.” But it doesn’t end there: “In the dictatorship unintentionally created by the planners, there is no room for differing opinions. Posters, radio, press—all spread the same lies!” The final two panels depict the ultimate consequences of interfering in the free market: “planned” morning calisthenics (eerily reminiscent of Yugoslav military drills) while a uniformed “planner” breaks golf clubs. The final panel shows citizens before a firing squad. It’s astonishing how precisely this ideological pamphlet describes the reality now playing out in societies that most fervently embraced Hayek’s ideas. In the name of fighting “socialism,” neoliberals are dismantling liberal democracy itself—a system based on “human dignity, prosperity, and freedom.” From the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Alabama, it’s not far to Florida, where Governor Ron DeSantis is “planning” his road to the White House by attacking minorities and progressive ideas. No firing squads—yet—but Americans are busily shooting each other. The analogy isn’t perfect: in Florida, they’re not breaking golf clubs. They’re banning books. Welcome to servitude. The shortcut version.

One must always seek compromise, even with the devil, said Budimir Lončar, the last Yugoslav foreign minister, in a recent interview with Delo about the war in Ukraine. Always? I can almost picture a young Lončar, twice-wounded partisan, quoting Jože P. Damijan by the campfire in a quiet forest: "Comrades, fighting against aggression is a fundamental right. But we must be pragmatic and ask ourselves whether we can win this war." I believe that Budimir Lončar, and many who think like him, genuinely want the war in Ukraine to end as soon as possible, and for the horrific destruction of Ukraine and the bloodshed on both sides to stop. I wholeheartedly support and share that desire. But I do not agree with his interpretation of the circumstances that led to the war, and even less with his suggestions for how to achieve peace. According to the logic of self-proclaimed exclusive defenders of peace, Ukraine will be forced to negotiate if we stop supporting it—yet they never explain how they intend to bring the other side, the one that started the war and could end it the fastest, to the negotiating table. Those advocating deals with the devil are aware of the shaky ethical ground they stand on. Hence the need to balance the moral equation: blame the Americans, claim the Russians were humiliated and threatened, portray NATO as the villain, say the Ukrainians brought it on themselves, that Russia cannot be defeated, etc. Ergo, let’s give them half of Ukraine and shake hands. Lončar’s interview offers a kind of "greatest hits" of superficial or outright false claims about the war being remote-controlled, about Russia being threatened by NATO, and about the West humiliating the Kremlin into a corner, leaving it no choice but to restore a just balance with weapons against the evil American bogeyman. To be clear, I agree with much of Mr. Lončar’s criticism of the United States. Through double standards, ruthless pursuit of its interests, and breaches of international law, the collective West has, in many ways, weakened the rule-based international order—something the Kremlin revisionists now exploit. When this bloody aggression ends, we must look in the mirror and ask why so much of the world is so critical of the West and its position on Ukraine. It’s easy to understand why, for example, Palestinians or Iraqis, among many others, might be ambivalent about Western foreign policy. The U.S. and the West have plenty to answer for, but the worst possible answer to their past sins is a new world order dictated by an autocrat in the Kremlin under Beijing’s command. Out of the frying pan, into the fire. As for the claim that Russia is threatened by NATO, it’s been refuted so thoroughly that it’s astounding anyone can repeat it without blushing. It’s like accusing someone of threatening an armed psychopath just by putting on a bulletproof vest—especially after the aggressor already drew their gun and opened fire. Before Putin, NATO-Russia relations were moving in a completely different direction. In the late 1990s, both parties signed an agreement of friendship and cooperation, explicitly stating NATO would continue expanding—a "historic process," as both NATO and Russia called it. Before Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014, there were no NATO troops or bases in NATO-member countries bordering Russia. NATO responded only after Russia seized Crimea—just as Finland and Sweden only sought NATO membership once it became clear that neutrality was no protection against a rampaging Russian bear. Without Putin, NATO wouldn't have been raising the Finnish flag in Brussels a few days ago. Even more absurd is the claim that Russia was "humiliated" by the West, supposedly justifying its aggression. Whatever one thinks of the chaos of the Yeltsin era, the fact is that Russia recovered significantly thanks to Europe’s (short-sighted) dependence on Russian energy. This fuelled not only the Kremlin’s economic comeback but also its geopolitical resurgence. The Russian economy—and especially the prosperity of its citizens—could have been even greater if profits from natural resources hadn’t been funnelled into the pockets of a few oligarchs, who now fund and support Putin's regime from their yachts and villas on the French Riviera, all while nodding along to his rhetoric about defending Russia's purity from Western decadence. Against this backdrop, it seems astonishing how many people don’t assign responsibility for aggression to the aggressor. On Easter Sunday, thousands marched in German cities carrying banners declaring, "The aggressor is not Russia, but NATO." Recent polls suggest nearly half of Slovenians now share this view. I suspect most don’t truly believe this nonsense, but rather express accumulated frustration, anger, and distrust toward the elites. Europe has seen this before. In the years before World War II, similar popular and political responses were evident. Then, as now, many European nations were gripped by public disillusionment and fury at the incompetence, hypocrisy, and detachment of democratically elected "liberal" elites. Back then, too, the economic crisis caused by the U.S. stock market crash led to high inflation, unemployment, even hunger—pushing people into the arms of aggressive, populist demagogues. At the time, many Europeans, including politicians, saw Fascist Italy and especially Hitler’s Germany as a rough but effective solution to economic and societal crises and a path toward a fairer world. Even in June 1940, after German troops marched into Paris, Jewish-American writer Rosie Waldeck, then Newsweek’s Bucharest correspondent, described the mood in Europe as follows: "The fall of France represents the culmination of twenty years of unfulfilled democratic promises to resolve unemployment, inflation, deflation, labor unrest, party selfishness, and more. A Europe disillusioned with itself, doubting its guiding principles, almost feels relieved. Hitler is a clever man, Europeans think—unpleasant, but clever. He succeeded in making his country strong. Why not try his way?" Denmark’s prime minister, Social Democrat Thorvald Stauning, said something similar: "I have the impression that Germany has certain plans to establish a lasting new order in Europe, with clear advantages over liberal egoism. It is in our interest to cooperate calmly and voluntarily and to adapt." And most importantly, many European politicians and citizens then, as now, viewed Hitler's increasing military preparations as a response to Germany’s humiliation at Versailles. Back then, just like today, many tried to convince themselves and others that to achieve peace, it was enough to turn a blind eye and strike a deal with the devil. Let him move a few borders—and things will settle down. Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov recently ended all speculation about why Russia invaded its neighbour: the goal is to establish a "new world order." If you want to know what life will be like under that order, look at how Russians live today and how Ukrainians suffer and die because of Russian aggression. I say this to those who wish to compromise with the aggressor. The devil isn’t just in the details. He reveals himself in every act of violence that brought and kept Putin in power. In every murdered or jailed journalist, activist, and political opponent. In the persecution of civil society and minorities. In weaponized homophobia. In Orwellian surveillance. In every breach of international law during Putin’s twenty-three-year rule. In the wars in Georgia, the devastation of Syria, the annexation of Crimea, the atrocities in Bucha and elsewhere under Russian occupation. In the abduction of Ukrainian children. In the psychopathic indifference with which Putin sends thousands of Russian soldiers to their deaths and the deliberate bombing of civilian targets and infrastructure aimed at breaking Ukraine’s resistance through terror. I respect Budimir Lončar's experience, and like him, I truly wish for a swift end to the war. I, too, am alarmed by the nuclear sabre-rattling. That is why Putin must be stopped. If he achieves his goals in Ukraine, he won’t stop—just like Hitler didn’t stop after taking Poland and Czechoslovakia. That is what history tells us about the consequences of "pragmatic" tolerance of "minor adjustments" for past injustices and humiliations. See you in the next war. So we must not abandon Ukraine. This war, too, will likely end at the negotiating table. I hope soon. But real negotiations will only begin when the Kremlin leader, charged with war crimes, realizes he has more to gain at the table than through force. As long as pragmatic peacemakers keep offering him a neatly wrapped victory disguised as compromise, there will be no peace. And that should scare the hell out of us.

In France we are living through another of those fairly frequent periods in which filling the gas tank takes much more effort than simply driving to the nearest gas station. When “social movements” happen, as mass protests and strikes are called here, the refineries are strategically blocked first, and as a result yellow covers saying “hors service” soon appear on the fuel nozzles. Out of order. Those of us who live in Strasbourg and other border towns are privileged: if fuel runs out on the French side, we drive across the border to Germany. Unless, of course, the bridges leading there are blocked. That has happened too. For people who don’t live near the border, who in a country as big as France are of course the vast majority, the blockade of refineries has much more far-reaching and unpleasant consequences. This is especially true for those who have to drive to work, school or the doctor. In France, people don’t protest with kid gloves. They strike in such a way that as many people as possible suffer the consequences as much as possible. Paris has been drowning in garbage for weeks. Using public transport, from the metro to trains and planes, is a lottery. In city centers, the smell of freshly baked croissants has been replaced by the stench of burning car tires. In schools there are classes one day and none the next. In many other countries, such tactics would quickly boomerang on the strikers and turn public opinion against them and their demands. In France it is exactly the opposite. Public opinion, by a considerable majority, in spite of everything and increasingly, understands and supports the strikers’ demands, in this case concerning the raising of the retirement age from 62 to 64. Protest is part of French culture and folklore. Alongside the bust of Marianne, who represents the French Republic and its values, an extended middle finger could also be used as a symbol of French society. When the French are fed up with those in power, they express their feelings in a very direct way. They have done so since 1789. Intergenerational solidarity It is also fascinating that, at least when it comes to protests, there is incredible intergenerational solidarity in France. Compared with our part of the world, where protests about pensions and pensioners struggle to attract anyone without thoroughly gray hair, in France students and high school pupils also protest against changes to pension legislation. Not yet as massively as on many occasions in the past, but if that changes, Macron will be in even greater trouble. In this respect, things have changed over the last fifty-five years. If in May 1968 the young rioted against the old, today they protest for them. Everyone takes part in the debate on pension legislation. People talk about it at work, pupils at school. Tara, my ten-year-old daughter, from whom you otherwise have to drag words out with pliers, asks at the front door as soon as she gets home from school whether this Macron really had no other option than to use 49.3.
