That is, of course, the article of the French Constitution that allows the government to pass laws by decree, which was used this time too, because the government feared it did not have enough votes in parliament. And yet. The situation France is going through today is not merely a consequence of the French passion for protest. The anger and discontent are real; this is not folklore. To someone watching events from abroad, it may seem that the French are overdoing it. After all, in most Western societies it is accepted that, because of demographic changes alone, the pension system must be adjusted, since the existing one will sooner or later break down. The change introduced in France, raising the retirement age to 64—especially considering that the new law provides for a whole range of exceptions for specific professions—is not excessively radical either. With the increase, the retirement threshold will move closer to the OECD average. Many other countries have also embarked on changes to their pension legislation, and although these are very sensitive issues everywhere, as a rule there has been no such unrest elsewhere. Permanent pension reform But what is sensitive elsewhere is sensitive squared in France. The French have been reforming their pension system more or less constantly since Mitterrand’s victory a good four decades ago. One of his first fulfilled campaign promises was lowering the retirement age from 65 to 60. If someone made a film about France’s pension reform shenanigans, it could be called Forward into the Past. Incidentally, Mitterrand did not change the retirement age through the normal legislative procedure either, but, like Macron now, by decree. The state of emergency and the blockade of normal life are very reminiscent of the time when I came to France almost thirty years ago. Then-President Jacques Chirac sent his Prime Minister Alain Juppé to pull the chestnuts out of the fire; Juppé proposed (merely) extending contributions for the special regimes but, after three weeks of protests involving millions of people who completely blocked the country, was forced to give in and withdraw the proposal. That happened on December 21, 1995, the day on which Emmanuel Macron, a pupil at the Lycée Henri-IV in Paris’s fifth arrondissement, celebrated his eighteenth birthday. If, while celebrating with his classmates, he had any attention left for what was going on around him, he could have drawn many a useful lesson from that time for use today. Not least the words of the old fox who then sat in the chair he occupies today. “Shit flies in squadrons,” Jacques Chirac liked to say. The “notorious” Article 49.3 of the French Constitution As I write, there are between one and three million people on the streets of France, depending on whether you believe the police or the organizers. Bordeaux city hall is on fire; flights are being canceled because kerosene is running out. Parisians are worried about rats. Public radio stations are playing classical music. The French are, yet again, very angry. One of the reasons for this is, in my opinion, specifically local. France has a system of government that irritates people. Since Macron came to power, it has irritated them squared. Despite swearing by equality, fraternity and liberty, France is a very centralized, bureaucratic and elitist state. That does not mean it is not democratic, but its characteristics—a presidential system that concentrates most political power in one person, a relatively narrow circle of people who dominate politics and business and who attended the same schools, and also peculiarities such as the “notorious” Article 49.3 of the French Constitution—give people the feeling that power is remote from them and that they have no influence over it. And so they take to the streets. In fact, similar constitutional arrangements, in which the government ties the adoption of a law to a vote of confidence, exist in many other systems and do not attract much criticism. The peculiarity of France is that the link between the decree and the confidence vote is not automatic and simultaneous, hence so much criticism of it being “undemocratic.” Macron’s style of governing, which many experience as arrogance, only adds fuel to the fire. Here, perhaps, lies an important lesson for some politicians closer to home. The troubles of “non-extreme politicians” In a television appearance this week, Macron (very slightly) put on sackcloth and ashes and said that his only regret was that he had not managed to convince people with his proposals. And he is absolutely right about that. He did not manage it. And it is not only he who has this problem, but most “non-extreme” politicians in European countries, whether left, right or center. Politics today has trouble pushing through even changes that are objectively in people’s interest. Thirty years of waiting for money to trickle down from the top, of forcing an economic doctrine that privatizes profits and socializes losses, have led a great many people to stop believing. Not only in the politicians in power; they have also lost faith in the political system those politicians represent. Ever since the end of the Second World War, liberal democracy’s contract with citizens has been based on the promise and expectation that tomorrow will be better than yesterday. Fewer and fewer people believe that today. The moment social solidarity and social justice become mere rhetorical platitudes or, worse, are treated by politics as an unnecessary cost and a threat to the economy, and the moment hope for a better future is replaced by fear, liberal democracy is on the brink of collapse. Populists offer no solutions, but they have the advantage because they respond to popular rage and thereby pour fuel on the fire. How this ended in Europe in the past we ought to know, but we have evidently forgotten. To tell the truth, among the crowd of politicians who flirt with neoliberalism, Macron may not even be the worst. Part of his problem is that he gives the impression that he is. Of everything people saw and heard in his interview, what irritated them most was that he came across as too smug. A president for the rich. France is up in arms today, but I believe life will soon return, at least on the surface, to its usual course. Beneath the gray facade of normality, however, it will keep smoldering. The traditional political parties, whether left, center or right, are running out of breath. The only ones with the wind in their sails, waiting for their chance, are the far-left populist Mélenchon and the far-right populist Le Pen. Macron will probably survive this crisis one way or another and remain until the end of his term. What will happen after that, no one dares predict for now. The horizon is darkening. The squadrons are approaching.

Recently, the Simon Wiesenthal European Center sent an open letter to the President of the Republic of Slovenia, Nataša Pirc Musar, expressing concern over "expressions of antisemitism, xenophobia, incitement to violence, conspiracy theories, fake news, glorification of dictatorships and terrorist organizations" in Slovenia. The Simon Wiesenthal Center is a serious organization, dedicated to monitoring and combating neo-Nazism, incitement to violence, Holocaust denial, and antisemitism in Europe. It also serves in a consultative role to the Council of Europe. As it appears, the letter was prompted by social media posts from a journalist at the Slovenian national broadcaster RTVSLO. The journalist came under fire for vocally criticizing Israel and its policies toward Palestinians. It is a known fact that criticism of Israeli policy often masks antisemitism. But it is equally true that some Israeli politicians often try to suppress legitimate criticism by labeling it as antisemitism. The line between justified critique and unacceptable antisemitic undertones is not always clear or easily understood. Israeli politics itself may have contributed to this confusion. As the late British historian Tony Judt—himself of Jewish origin—once described it: “The habit of branding any foreign criticism with the brush of antisemitism is deeply ingrained in Israeli political instinct. Ariel Sharon exaggerated it characteristically, but he was only the latest (this article was published in Haaretz in 2016, editor’s note) in a long line of Israeli leaders to do so. David Ben-Gurion and Golda Meir had similar habits. But Jews outside Israel pay a high price for this tactic. It not only deters them from criticizing Israel themselves—fearing they’ll be associated with bad company—but also encourages others to view Jews everywhere as de facto accomplices in Israel’s misconduct. When Israel violates international law in occupied territories, when it publicly humiliates people living on the lands it has seized, and then responds to criticism by crying ‘antisemitism,’ it creates the impression that these are not merely Israeli actions—but Jewish ones. That the occupation is not Israeli, but Jewish. And if you take issue with that, it must be because you don’t like Jews.” To help distinguish legitimate criticism from antisemitism, the intergovernmental organization IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance), of which Slovenia is a member, adopted a non-legally binding working definition of antisemitism in 2016. It states: “Antisemitism is a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews. Rhetorical and physical manifestations of antisemitism are directed toward Jewish or non-Jewish individuals and/or their property, toward Jewish community institutions and religious facilities.” Because the definition is quite broad, it is accompanied by examples meant to help identify antisemitism in various contexts. One of the first lines reads: “Manifestations might include the targeting of the state of Israel, conceived as a Jewish collectivity. However, criticism of Israel similar to that leveled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic.” This is an important distinction. If Israel is criticized by the same standards as any other country, it is not antisemitism. In this light, one must evaluate whether the accusations raised in the open letter to the Slovenian president were justified. The IHRA also sets limits for criticism of Israel. For instance, denying the Jewish people's right to self-determination—such as by claiming that the existence of the state of Israel is a racist endeavor—is considered antisemitism. IHRA also considers comparisons between Israeli policy and that of the Nazis as going beyond acceptable critique. The working definition has sparked reactions, including criticism. The Council of Europe’s Commission against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI) issued an opinion in December 2020, welcoming the definition as a tool for better understanding antisemitism, but also warning: “Any attempts to misuse the working definition and its examples to silence or stigmatize as antisemitic legitimate criticism of Israel and Israeli policy—especially toward the Palestinian people and in the context of Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories—would undermine the fight against antisemitism and should be rejected.” In any case, antisemitism is widespread and growing—in Europe and globally. Including in Slovenia. Therefore, the attention paid to us by the Simon Wiesenthal Center is certainly welcome. Perhaps, however, it could be broadened slightly, because alleged antisemitism in the context of criticism of Israeli policy is just one facet of the issue. There is also persistent, traditional hatred of Jews and Judaism—well-known in Europe for centuries and culminating in the Holocaust—which continues to exist, despite ritual invocations of “never again” by politicians once or twice a year during wreath-laying ceremonies for the six million Jews murdered by the Nazis. That’s why the Simon Wiesenthal Center is right to remain vigilant against neo-Nazism. In a future letter to Slovenian authorities, they might also address, for instance, the government granting “socially beneficial organization” status to an association whose members underscore their “traditional and patriotic” values with Hindu ornaments. But antisemitism in society doesn’t only manifest through explicit tattoos—it also surfaces through more subtle and complex discourses, conspiracy theories, and patterns of thought. The IHRA’s list of examples can help identify these. Antisemitism includes lies, dehumanization, demonization, or stereotypical accusations—about Jews or Jewish influence as a community—which manifest in myths about global Jewish conspiracies or Jews controlling the media, economy, government, or other social institutions. A real-world illustration: an interview with Laura Towler, a British antisemite and white supremacist, published in Slovenia’s Demokracija weekly in September 2020 and later shared by the SDS party website. Towler, deputy director of the group Patriotic Alternative, complained that “Jews dominate important positions in government and media, through which they advocate for open borders.” There are also frequent attacks on individuals of Jewish background, involving explicit or implicit antisemitic messages. Here’s one from Twitter, written by a former judge at the European Court of Human Rights—still highly regarded in some circles of Slovenian politics: “If we know that Josip Ribičič (Fisher) was a Jew from Trieste, then the cause of the psychopathic cruelty of the post-war massacres in Slovenia is obvious. If Kučan’s grandfather was a rabbi in Prekmurje, then the link with the psychopath Soros is clear.” Sometimes such statements, like the one above, mention Jews directly. Other times they rely on stereotypes, insinuations, and caricatures—like the infamous image of puppeteers with hooked noses—leaving little doubt as to the target. Either way, they trigger deep-seated prejudices and hostility in parts of the population. Such discourse is so common in Slovenia that we’ve grown used to it and barely react. Still, the demonization of George Soros—a staple of a certain Slovenian political folklore—has long been recognized as antisemitic in tone. The same goes for the popular conspiracy theory of “cultural Marxism,” which recently even appeared in a parliamentary interpellation. God forbid I suggest that everyone who eagerly spreads such problematic rhetoric is a die-hard antisemite. With a generous dose of goodwill, I can accept that many simply don’t realize what they’re saying or supporting. That’s why I believe it’s important to consistently and clearly call them out whenever they cross the line of what is decent and acceptable in a democratic society. Since we’re clearly not doing a great job of this ourselves—and have become so accustomed to such discourse that we barely notice it anymore—perhaps we really do need some external help. That’s why I welcome future letters from the Simon Wiesenthal Center. Hopefully with a broader view of how antisemitism manifests in Slovenia—to alert us, and help us confront ideologies that have already brought so much suffering to the world. Until we’re capable of doing it ourselves. Clearly, we still have a long way to go.

Among the signatories of the recent letter "Stop the War in Ukraine" are many people I know and deeply respect. Their voices rightly carry weight and credibility in public discourse. This time, however, I disagree with them. I believe their intentions are noble, and they sincerely want peace. But unfortunately, that is not enough. I worry that such letters, despite the best intentions, do not contribute to the prospects for a swift end to this bloody war. In the first paragraph, the authors express "unconditional support for Ukraine's undeniable right to defend itself" and clearly state that Ukraine is "the victim of Russian aggression, which cannot be justified." However, in light of everything that follows, this reads merely as a disclaimer. The rest of the letter is used to promote proposals and ideas that are clearly at odds with the noble principles stated in the introduction. Statesmen who support military aid to Ukraine are labelled as "sleepwalkers" who are "drifting towards a potential new world war." Effective military aid, which Ukraine urgently needs to defend itself against "unjustifiable aggression," is deemed unacceptable by the signatories because it "further increases the danger of direct confrontation between Russia and the West." This seems a very minimalist interpretation of "unconditional" support for Ukraine's "undeniable right to defence." Logically, one would expect the "power and responsibility" for ending the war to lie primarily with the side that started it and could thus end it most swiftly and easily. But the letter makes no such demand. Russia, apart from the introduction, is not portrayed as an aggressor, but merely as a partner in peace efforts and in constructing a new security architecture that must consider its interests, however defined. The sweeping claim near the end of the letter—"you have no mandate for war"—lumps everyone together with the aggressor. This is a relativization of responsibility for aggression. It is astonishing that the authors invite everyone except Ukraine to join the "alliance for a ceasefire, for halting further armament, and for launching negotiations." In a peace initiative intended to end "unjustifiable aggression," there is evidently room for the aggressor, but not for the victim. The idea that Russia needs a new "alliance" to end the war comes across as an attempt to frame the aggressor as a hapless actor who stumbled into a situation beyond its control and now needs help. This too is a relativization of responsibility for aggression. Perhaps unintentionally, the letter echoes some key points of Kremlin propaganda. In the third paragraph, Ukraine is no longer the victim of Russian aggression, but the site of a "proxy war between Russia and the U.S." A few days after the letter's publication, Vladimir Putin himself claimed that Russia is merely defending itself in Ukraine against an American attack. The call for arms reduction as a path to peace is wishful thinking when it excludes the Kremlin. If implemented, it would primarily weaken Ukraine. The authors appear to believe this would force Ukraine into negotiations, but they provide no reason why Putin would then be willing to negotiate. Because of our public letters and petitions? In reality, reducing aid to Ukraine would only distance us further from peace. Putin will only negotiate when he calculates that he can gain more at the table than on the battlefield. In other words, the less military aid Ukraine receives, the less unity there is within the EU, and the more infighting there is over support for the victim of aggression, the less willing Russia will be to negotiate, and the longer this bloody war will last. In the debate sparked by this public appeal, any critic risks being labelled a warmonger. I reject that label. No one has a monopoly on moral high ground or reason in the pursuit of peace and an end to bloodshed. While I disagree with the letter's content, I believe its authors and signatories acted in good faith and sincerely want the war to end. At the same time, I expect them to accept and respect that those of us who understand "unconditional support for the undeniable right to self-defence against aggression" differently also want peace and an end to the war. I do not fault the authors for their romantic nostalgia for the good old days, but I do not believe this can be a foundation for lasting security and stability in today's Europe or the world. The "this or that" Russia mentioned by the letter's authors is very different from the Soviet Union known to Willy Brandt. There will be no peace as long as we naively project traits onto Putin that he does not possess and in fact scorns, and as long as we look for the causes of war everywhere except in his fascistoid imperialism. Putin's political path has always been grounded in violence. To gain power, he organized terrorist attacks against his own citizens and launched a second war in Chechnya. To stay in power, he invaded Georgia, seized Crimea, and now has attacked all of Ukraine. Along the way, he has murdered journalists and political opponents, bombed hospitals and civilians in Syria with cluster munitions, and dispatched Wagner mercenaries to Africa. Let us not forget the Russian mercenaries who plotted a coup in Montenegro—and today are active in Moldova and Serbia. Pax Kremliana is war, violence, and chaos. That is Putin's "this or that" Russia and those are its interests, which we are told must be respected in a new security architecture. Putin has established a regime that continuously generates conflicts because it would collapse without them. In his political paradigm, war is a defence against the threat posed by peace. Any security architecture that does not account for this fact is not worth the paper it is written on. It is telling that the authors of the letter chose World War I as their historical reference point. Perhaps this is because comparisons with World War II would be more awkward and uncomfortable—not only due to the ideological and psychological similarities between the protagonists of both periods of bloody lebensraum imperialism, but also because there were, even then, European statesmen who refused to sleepwalk into war, instead resolutely championing peace—at least for themselves and their own people, even at the cost of others' freedom and survival. We know how that bargain ended. Churchill described such statesmen as men who feed the crocodile in the hope that it will eat them last. No offense, but that won't do. Because I agree with you: this is about the lives of our children and their descendants in a world without fear, a world that can sustain humanity. Ukraine is not only fighting for its own survival, but for us and our security too. It would be wise and just to help them as best we can, not to trip them up in their national liberation struggle against a foreign occupier—even if done with the best of intentions.

We've reached a point where the present is beginning to resemble a Soviet-era joke: "Radio Yerevan, is it possible to predict the future?" "In principle, no problem. It's the past that’s more difficult—it keeps changing." Slovenia’s independence is undoubtedly one of the most important turning points in the country’s history. Preserving the historical memory of all phases of our state-building should be a matter of national consensus. If anything, we should be worried about the possibility of a Museum of Contemporary History without a collection that professionally presents the period in which Slovenian citizens won not only an independent state, but also the right to decide their own future. We founded our country on the values of liberal democracy. That’s why it would be absurd—God forbid—if someone tried to use this pivotal chapter of our past to promote illiberal populism. But it’s not just Slovenes who struggle with history—this is a European problem. Some are doing everything they can to forget it. From a human perspective, that’s understandable. No one has accumulated as much horrific history in the past hundred years as Europeans have—not only in Europe but beyond. Historian Timothy Snyder calls this intentional collective amnesia the "politics of inevitability"—a stubborn belief that we can secure a brighter future only by forgetting all the conflicts, suffering, and darkness of the past. This belief is grounded in the naïve idea of the "end of history"—that the future will forever be just a better version of the present. History is reduced to ritual slogans like “Never again.” In Slovenia, a very popular slogan is that we must stop dividing ourselves into Home Guard collaborators and Partisans. Optimism, faith, and forward-looking perspectives are, of course, not inherently wrong. The problem arises when intentional forgetting leads us to ignore warnings that things are moving in the wrong direction. The late British historian Tony Judt also described this incredible faith in the absolute uniqueness of the present and the belief that we have nothing left to learn from the past. The problem with a social project based on progressive civilizational values but deliberately forgetful of its dark chapters is that people—lacking both lived experience and critical historical knowledge—are no longer able to fully grasp the importance of those values. They don’t know—or don’t want to know—what can happen (because it already has, as Primo Levi wrote) when there is no more democracy, no more human rights, no more respect for human dignity, and no more humanity. This isn’t just theoretical. A few years ago, a study by Yascha Mounk and Roberto Foa showed that only a third of young people in the Netherlands believed it was important to live in a democracy. And just recently, on Holocaust Remembrance Day, data was released showing that nearly a quarter of young Dutch people born after 1980 believe the Holocaust is a myth or that its death toll has been greatly exaggerated. Two years ago, Timothy Garton Ash and Antonia Zimmermann published a study showing that more than half of young Europeans place more trust in authoritarian regimes than in democracies when it comes to addressing the climate crisis. To paraphrase Tito: “With youth like this, the nation has every reason to fear for its future.” But let’s not only blame the young. The attitudes of older generations are often even worse—and unlike the young, they have no excuse. They know, and they remember. To a degree, the “politics of inevitability” in Slovenia could be embodied by former president Borut Pahor, whose complacency in facing historical atavisms often bordered on innocent naïveté. His concept of national reconciliation, wrapped in a white marble fog of forgetfulness, was like a Slovenian version of Vinterberg’s Festen, where family members, under the baton of a self-admiring patriarch, sing through gritted teeth: "We love each other. We really, really do." The politics of inevitability falters the moment this supposedly unprecedented present becomes a disappointment for those who feel neglected, forgotten, economically, socially, and politically marginalized. Then, the idea of an endless extension of the current status quo ceases to inspire optimism and instead breeds discomfort, anger, and fear of the future. That’s when—and that’s how—the “politics of eternity” gains traction. This is the populist strategy of framing the present as constantly under threat, trapped in a loop of return to some glorified (or invented) moment in the past. That moment—ritualized and manipulated—becomes the basis on which authoritarian populism builds its myth of martyrdom and heroism, claiming exclusive legitimacy for its ideological narrative and demand for dominance. Instead of offering hope or promises of a better future, populism offers a bitter and angry people only the stoking of hatred—blaming supposed scapegoats for their suffering. Instructive examples of the politics of eternity include Serbia’s obsession with the Battle of Kosovo and Orbán’s sabre-rattling over the Treaty of Trianon—both more political fiction than historical fact. The most current example, of course, is Russia’s Putinist interpretation of World War II—referred to there as the “Great Patriotic War.” While the Red Army’s crucial role in defeating Nazism and the massive sacrifices of the Soviet Union should never be downplayed, what stands out is the sanitized, ritualized narrative that ignores everything that happened before Germany’s invasion of the USSR—including the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact—and minimizes the Holocaust because it disrupts the narrative of uniquely Russian suffering. In Russia’s collective consciousness, WWII has been reduced to a duel between Russia and Nazism—one in which Russia, or the Soviet Union, was the lone victor. From this narrative springs the myth of Russia as the “chosen nation,” entitled to do whatever its leader deems necessary in defence of its “sacred historical mission.” The tragic consequence of this “politics of eternity” is the abuse of WWII memory to justify Russian aggression against Ukraine—under the pretence of “denazification” and the “liberation of suffering Ukrainian brothers,” leaving Putin, the self-proclaimed “anti-fascist,” with “no choice” but to attack and destroy a neighbouring state. "Just like back then, the entire West is once again siding with the Nazis," Russian political and media warmongers declared on the 80th anniversary of the Battle of Stalingrad. We in Slovenia also struggle with understanding history. We've even managed to argue over the organizational framework for professionally presenting the history of our independence in a museum. Don’t be distracted by the patriotic posturing or the ultimatums and motions of no confidence—at its core, that’s what this is really about. All the accusations of being “unpatriotic,” of denying or renouncing this chapter in our history, are both inaccurate and indecent. They're being weaponized in a culture war to polarize society into “us” and “them.” This is an attempt to transform historical truth and collective memory—something that belongs to all of us—into a political Groundhog Day, where we wake up every morning in a spun version of June 1991. But we don’t need that. Slovenian independence deserves a politics that respects historical facts—not one that rewrites them. At the time of writing, I don’t yet know what will come of the “action plan” announced at a recent press conference by some indignant independence-era leaders. To be honest, I’m not that interested. I don’t wish to diminish the significant roles they played in Slovenia’s independence. But that doesn’t mean all credit belongs solely to them—nor does it give them the exclusive right to interpret that history. That right belongs to historians. And no one can claim or alter the political legacy of independence. It is inscribed and protected in our constitution. Finally, to those who say they're doing nothing more than what the previous regime did for half a century: yes, precisely that—and one of the main reasons why Slovenians overwhelmingly supported and participated in independence was our determination to never again let anyone do that to us. People fight for historical truth and professional historical presentation of our independence not because they don’t care—but because they do. Because they love their country and are proud of it. And sometimes, precisely because of that love, they are also critical. That’s what separates genuine patriotism from nationalism.

These are hard times for us (and not just for us, to be clear)—the old farts who still believe in the values of liberal democracy and preach about them. Sometimes I feel like those American homeless people who roam around bus stations with shopping carts full of junk, harassing indifferent passersby with shouts about sin, doom, and salvation. From one (extreme) side, we're scorned as leftist sellouts privileging dubious minorities and individuals at the expense of honest citizens. From the other (extreme) side, we're accused of being naive and corrupt servants of Western devils and capital. And in between are those who often pay lip service to democratic values but couldn’t care less when it really matters. Human rights, the rule of law, democracy—blah, blah, blah. Once a year they say “never again” and move on. Neither left nor right, just forward. Democracy isn’t going well for us. We’re living in a time of widespread discontent, anger, and fear about the future. It’s not the first time in history. And historically, such periods haven’t brought much good. The question is whether we are capable of learning from history—or will we passively accept that the future will painfully resemble those past episodes any reasonable person would want to avoid, not just forget? A frequent and perfectly rational objection I often hear when defending liberal democracy is that this system has never truly worked—that in the end, it always benefitted a few and left the majority behind. And yet—though I risk confirming the suspicions of those who see me as a backward-looking old idealist—I would dare say there was a time when liberal democracy more or less worked. I’m not saying we should go back to the past, but we can learn from it, try to extract what worked under specific circumstances, and consider whether something similar can be adapted for today’s challenges. If ever, liberal democracy worked in Western Europe during the immediate post-WWII period. The reason was fairly simple: it may have been the only time in modern history when human rights and political freedoms were in harmony with social rights. Of course, it wasn’t an ideal society—not even close, especially when viewed from today’s perspective. But it was a positive trend. We must understand historical periods not as snapshots but as films. That time was marked by reconstruction, growth, and optimism about the future. After the bloodiest conflict and atrocity in human history, Europe was getting back on its feet. Critics will say it was due to unique historical circumstances that can’t be replicated today. But postwar reconstruction was not just historical determinism. History—and the future—is made by people. The defining feature of the postwar period was political consensus that reconstruction must be based on social justice and solidarity. That’s a lesson we still haven’t learned—or refuse to. And it’s a big reason things are going so wrong today. There was a shared belief that without social justice, there is no democracy, no security, no sustainable economic or social development. Since then, we’ve had systems offering “social justice” without freedom, and others offering freedom (of capital) without social justice. But we’ve consistently failed to combine freedom and solidarity. Postwar European politicians, mostly from conservative and Christian democratic parties, pursued policies that would make today’s self-styled heirs of those traditions’ hair stand on end—if they still had any. Public education, public healthcare, investment in infrastructure, housing, high employment, care for the unemployed and the socially vulnerable—these all had a cost. Across the Atlantic, during the Eisenhower administration (a Republican, remember), the top tax rate on corporate profits was over 90%. But there was consensus that it was a price worth paying. What drove these politicians wasn’t ideological altruism but memories of the Great Depression, inflation, social crisis, and the catastrophic consequences Europe (and others) had suffered. Yes, you’ll say, but that was due to the exceptional economic conditions of the postwar boom. True—but that boom didn’t just happen. In the early postwar years, many parts of Europe were heading toward another 1930s-style crisis. What changed that was the Marshall Plan. A reminder to those who fixate only on (often valid) critiques of the U.S.: the U.S. militarily intervened twice in one century to save Europe from itself—and then paid again to make sure Europe didn’t collapse a third time. Another important motivator for European social concern at the time was the Soviet Union. That may sound odd now, but back then few (if any) could predict the Soviet totalitarian experiment would collapse into a prison rather than a worker’s paradise. Western governments cared for their workers in part out of fear that they might otherwise be tempted by sovietization. That story ended in the 1970s and 80s. First came dramatic economic changes: the collapse of Bretton Woods, two oil crises, and the third industrial revolution. After Hungary in 1956 and especially Prague in 1968, hardly anyone in the West still believed in the workers’ paradise of the East. When The Gulag Archipelago was published in 1973, even the most hardened romantics lost their illusions. The West began to celebrate its ideological victory, which would be confirmed after the Soviet collapse (helped along by its disastrous invasion of Afghanistan). But the West had its own problems. And this time, in responding to economic crises and inflation—especially in traditional industries like steel, mining, and heavy industry—governments forgot the lessons of half a century earlier. Instead of addressing the social costs of necessary reforms, they imposed ruthless neoliberal policies: low taxes, reckless deregulation, sell-offs of unprofitable state industries, privatization of public services. The Iron Lady led the charge, the most ruthless but far from the only one who embraced a system where money was to flow upward and, eventually, trickle down. We’re still waiting for the trickle. The social consequences are worsening. Neoliberalism is still with us. And for some, inexplicably, still seen as the only salvation. Yes, of course, the shocks of the 1970s demanded new responses. Propping up outdated industries and artificial employment would have ended badly. Demographic change was also a major factor—Europe was aging, and still is. But neoliberal shock therapy brought only short-term gains—and even those were mostly superficial. Long-term, it’s been catastrophic. A society that systematically marginalizes large swaths of its population can never be democratic, secure, or successful. Privatization initially improved corporate balance sheets—owners could abandon unprofitable but socially vital activities and shed “excess” workers. State coffers filled from sales—but also drained rapidly due to rising unemployment and poverty. During Margaret Thatcher’s rule, public expenditure levels stayed about the same as before. What changed was the redistribution of wealth and a social tsunami that deepened as capital exploited globalization without economic or social safeguards, relocating production for higher profits. No one considered the political and social consequences of creating a massive pool of marginalized, forgotten, and increasingly angry citizens. It was only a matter of time before someone began exploiting that frustration and fear of the future. And that was just the beginning. Thatcher was followed by Tony Blair and his “Third Way.” Blair—recently a guest at the Bled Forum—is still a role model for many centrist politicians who preach "not left, not right, just forward." Yet his damage to democratic values may even surpass that of his political predecessor and rival. First, because he essentially continued Thatcher’s neoliberal policies, masking her social indifference with sanctimonious emphasis on human rights and civil liberties. His hypocrisy—especially in his fervent support for Bush’s invasion of Iraq and his one-sided stance on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict—did irreparable harm to the credibility of democratic values. To the marginalized masses, Blairism was proof that human rights were just tools for granting privileges to the undeserving at their expense. Then came the financial crisis, whose costs were dumped on taxpayers—thanks in part to the EU’s own missteps. To many who paid the highest price for rescuing banks, democracy has come to mean a system where profits are privatized and losses socialized. The way out of this mess won’t be easy. But we must find it—if we don’t want to live through one of those futures that’s already happened. Because we might not survive it next time. The path forward is a firm political and social consensus on justice and solidarity at every level, and integrating these values into solutions for all social and global challenges—from technology to economy to environment and politics. This is no revolution or left-right war. It’s about honoring the principles written into Slovenia’s constitution. It’s about the survival of liberal democracy—still the only model based on the idea that freedom and justice do not have to be traded for each other. Neoliberal slogans, still parroted by parts of Slovenian politics and business, waste our precious time and threaten our future, stability, sustainable development, freedom, and democracy. Our constitution declares that Slovenia is a social state. Let’s stop acting like that’s just empty rhetoric or a sneaky leftist conspiracy. It’s the foundation—the prerequisite—for fulfilling all other constitutional values, including the protection of private property and free enterprise. At least in a society where people– as the Slovenian anthem aspires - no more shall foes, but neighbors be.
A Dangerous Understanding of Human Rights

On December 7 last year, President Vladimir Putin addressed the members of the Council of the Russian Federation for Civil Society and Human Rights by video link. In his introduction, he first thanked the council members for their perfectly clear civic position on the special military operation and their support for the “right reasons and the need” for that operation. He then complained that something was seriously wrong with the understanding of human rights in today’s world. This is how he put his thoughts into words: “The existing approaches require comprehensive analysis, since they are used to achieve completely different goals, far from constructive ones. Thus we see that human rights doctrines are being used to destroy the sovereignty of states and to justify the political, financial, economic and ideological dominance of the West.” In his indignation at the danger of human rights, which restrict states in exercising their sovereign power and are abused as a means of ideological domination over honest citizens, Putin is by no means alone in the world. This view of the protection of human rights and political freedoms is also shared by many politicians in the West, who warn of the danger of cultural Marxists, woke socialists, gender theorists, homosexuals, Soros hirelings, liberals, feminists, commies and the like. Despite some local peculiarities and differences between the newly minted conservatives in different parts of the world, they have a lot in common. The first is the populist appeal to defending the interests of the “little man.” In most cases, the label “little people” conceals white men who feel cheated and threatened because their privileged position in society, at work and in the family is supposedly on the chopping block in today’s world. The fact is that ruthless economic neoliberalism and globalization dictated by capital, without any social, economic or other safeguards, have economically, socially and politically marginalized a large part of the middle and lower-middle classes in many countries, and an important part of that population is, of course, precisely these angry white men. In the populist paradigm, human rights are an instrument used to hand out undeserved privileges to disruptive, socially harmful and suspicious groups and individuals, at the expense and to the detriment of “ordinary” people. Through culture war, populism stokes and exploits popular anger to undermine democratic institutions and oversight mechanisms (courts, media, civil society). Tragically, in the end the victims of populism are both the stigmatized groups and the enraged masses who, following the populist’s score, hate everyone except the leader and rebel against everything except him. The latter are merely cannon fodder (in Putin’s case literally) for authoritarian ambitions of power and greed. When it no longer needs him, populism discards the “little man” like a used paper tissue. In the end, my dear little white men and all other ordinary people, it is not about us; it is only and exclusively about power. The second common point of populist neoconservatives from the Kremlin to Mar-a-Lago is directing popular anger and prejudice above all against three groups: women—especially those who dare to demand equality—same-sex persons and migrants. Different regional contexts add others to the list of scapegoats, from Black people to Roma or Ukrainians, but the patterns of stoking hatred and exploiting anger for political purposes are the same everywhere. In Slovenia, too, some are expressing concern that something is seriously wrong with the understanding of human rights in today’s world. A few days ago, a judge of the Constitutional Court lamented this. This is how he put his thoughts into words in a dissenting opinion on the decision by which the Constitutional Court rejected the request for a referendum on the amendment of the Family Code: “These are dangerous changes in the understanding of human rights, as a result of which they have become something entirely different and consequently are no longer capable of performing their basic task: detecting actual violations of human rights.” To be fair, the dissenting opinion cannot be disputed in its entirety. In the very first paragraph, the judge correctly noted that his vote against the decision was “problematic, since, had I acted lege artis, I should have supported it. The National Assembly could not have acted otherwise than it did.” What reason he had to carry on after this observation is probably known only to himself. Lege artis, lege schmartis, perhaps. In the rest of his dissenting opinion, the judge strung together a whole series of thoughts touching on every single topic on the all-star list of neoconservative grievances and frustrations, and the evergreen populist cliché about the “mass violation of the rights of ‘ordinary people’” was not missing either. Among the constitutional judge’s many penetrating observations, the one about the difference between a bus and marriage particularly caught my attention. He says: “The relationship between spouses represents the innermost core of the protection of privacy; it is hard to imagine a more intimate sphere of values. It would therefore be entirely mistaken here to object that advocating two separate marriages is some kind of continuation of the doctrine of Separate but equal on which segregation in the US was based. Riding public transport, where the magnificent revolt of Rosa Parks flared up, is the place where a person is least a private individual. The declaration of lifelong belonging between two persons through marriage lies at the completely opposite end of the right to the recognition of private values. And it is right that individuals should have the possibility of doing so within an institution they cherish intimately. And they no longer have that possibility. The uniformity of the institution has prevailed.” So now you know. In rejecting the referendum, the Constitutional Court overlooked the legal principle of quod licet on the trolleybus, non licet at the wedding. If you are racking your brains over how the intimate feelings of a heterosexual bride or groom could be hurt if a same-sex couple also declares lifelong belonging through a uniform institution, the constitutional judge has an answer ready. It is a violation of the “right to separate oneself from others.” Apparently this is even “the second pillar of our tradition.” I must admit that in three decades of working professionally on human rights, I had never heard of this. I can assure you, cross my heart, that there is no article in the European Convention on Human Rights that would allow “an empowered individual who thinks and acts independently of what the majority thinks,” in the name of “separating oneself from others,” to deny and restrict those others’ right to equality. If the honorable constitutional judge will allow me a piece of advice, were I plowing such bold new legal ground, I would make a considerably greater effort to explain what was going through my head, so that no one would by chance badly misunderstand me when I mentioned a “right to separation.” Finally, I would like to stress that, despite disagreeing with his reasoning, I am of course by no means lumping the honorable constitutional judge together with the Russian president. Although it is right that the judge should know with whom he shares his concern about the understanding of human rights in today’s world, these are very different things. Putin is a nationalist imperialist who has established a completely authoritarian regime at home and launched aggression against a neighboring country. The honorable judge has merely made a few howlers. As an individual he would be fully entitled to do so, but given his office he should not take it amiss if his reasoning raised many a legal eyebrow. When constitutional judges make howlers, “ordinary” people, and even more so “unordinary” ones, can end up bearing the consequences. I suspect the honorable judge realized this too in the end. He concluded his text with a lucid interval, saying that he does not wish to impose his “grumpy” opinion on anyone—and that, out of scientific rigor, he himself has some doubts about it. I give him credit for that. A dissenting opinion from one’s own dissenting opinion may seem a little confusing, but it does give hope that our empowered constitutional judge, “who thinks and acts independently of what the majority thinks,” will in future be prepared, even if through gritted teeth, to take the Constitution into account as well.
Don’t Praise the Day Before Večer

When my grandfather Franček turned one hundred, the mayor, a journalist and a photographer came to his little house below the Pohorje hills. The news of yet another Maribor resident who had reached such a venerable age was published, where else, in Večer. That is the mission of a local newspaper. One whose lens and focus are very close to people. My grandfather’s wife Darinka always said that she needed Večer to know whether her city bus stop had been moved and what the opening hours of the duty shops were. True, most people today look up such information on the internet, but that in no way diminishes the importance of local media. It is not only about content, but about closeness between the medium and the people. Večer is a local newspaper. But not only local Večer is Maribor’s local newspaper. But Večer is not only a local newspaper. It is an important part of the mosaic that makes Maribor a city. The Styrian metropolis, which is not only a regional economic, administrative, cultural, sporting and social center, but also an extremely important counterweight to Ljubljana and its structural centralism, which stems from its position as the capital of a small country. A medium that not only covers the city and the region but is made by journalists and other contributors who live, work and breathe with their city and their region is the oxygen that sustains and supports all other forms of social activity and life. Can you imagine Maribor’s cultural life covered only by journalists and critics from Ljubljana? A football club that lives with its city and the microcosm of its supporters and fans, but depends for its media ratings on the attention of people who have seen the world in green since birth? Can you imagine tackling all the pressing social, economic, political, transport, environmental and other challenges and problems, not only in Maribor but also in Koroška, Prekmurje and other parts of eastern Slovenia, if the people of Maribor, Styria, Koroška and Prekmurje obtained their information only from Ljubljana newsrooms? We usually talk about sovereignty in the context of states (and football), but it exists at other levels too. What good to Maribor is decentralization in the form of relocating one national agency or some obscure state office, or an airport that never took off, if at the same time it risks losing an important lever of its own influence, autonomy, authenticity and identity? They can send correspondents, you’ll say, but there are fewer and fewer of those too. And the few that remain, however excellently they do their work, cannot replace the loss of an independent source of information of its own for Slovenia’s second-largest city and the whole eastern part of the country. Information for itself and about itself. And their editors sit in Ljubljana anyway. Not that we Ljubljančani are local chauvinists by default (OK, perhaps with the exception of football); it is not a matter of bad intentions but of the (frog’s-eye) perspective from which we observe the world around us. But who still reads newspapers? Večer is the newspaper of Maribor and Styria. But it is also more than that. Večer is a national newspaper. It is an important part of the Slovenian media landscape. In a country where you can count the daily newspapers on the fingers of one hand, and for those not published in Ljubljana you’ll stop at the middle finger, losing one would do irreparable damage to its citizens’ access to information. Sure, sure, you’ll say, but who still reads newspapers? And that is true. There are fewer and fewer of us. That is also part of the problem, not only for Večer but for other print media, not only in Slovenia but all over the world, where we no longer form our opinions on the basis of information but choose our information according to our beliefs. The pluralism of opinions that is the driving force of a functioning democracy is slowly being replaced by a pluralism of facts that allows everyone to seek out the “truths” that confirm them in the positions, fears and prejudices they already hold. Technology, artificial intelligence and algorithms have accelerated this phenomenon and made it almost invisible. But technology doesn’t pull the strings by itself. Even with algorithms and artificial intelligence, it is ultimately about interaction between people. Including between those who manage and those who are managed. That in such a situation the danger of manipulation is not merely a theoretical threat is fairly obvious. A pillar of defense against authoritarian populism Many are critical of the media. Often rightly so. Many do not trust them, but this distrust is often a reflection of a wider revolt against everything that, in their eyes, represents an institution of the system that left them in the lurch. The causes of the dissatisfaction that led to such a reaction are also often legitimate and justified. We live in a world in which many really have been pushed to the economic and political margins. On the other hand, such uncritical criticism and such sweeping rejection of everything and everyone, including the media and the journalistic profession, can be dangerous. It creates ideal conditions for demagogic manipulation by those who exploit people’s distress in order to tear down democratic institutions and seize power. Independent and professional media, together with independent courts and an active civil society, are a pillar of defense against authoritarian populism, which is why they are also the first target of illiberal politics in subordinating and tearing down democratic institutions. Without journalists and media that work according to the professional principles of journalism, there is no access to reliable sources of information. And without that, there is no democracy. And like all important things in life, professional journalism needs something to be paid, invested and taken care of: society must provide the material and other conditions necessary for it to function. This does not apply only to public media. It is not about taxpayers covering the losses of private media owners, but about creating the right conditions for their normal functioning. Media ownership must be properly regulated, monopolies and abuses prevented, above all illegitimate interference in editorial autonomy. If advertising, especially by public institutions and companies, is non-transparent, unregulated and unsupervised, politics has a handy lever for putting pressure on the media. The same goes for the precariousness of the journalistic profession, which is why safeguards and material conditions for journalists’ normal work must urgently be established. Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects not only freedom of expression but also freedom of access to information. Every reduction, every shrinking, every abuse of the media space that comes about because of our couldn’t-care-less attitude to such a strategic good as information carries a risk to our fundamental human rights and political freedoms. It represents a risk to democracy and freedom. Let us not delude ourselves that we will be able to fill the void left by the decline of professional journalism with the “sources of information” offered to us by the market and the internet, with clickbait tabloid platforms and politically controlled mouthpieces that at best make money from our naivety and at worst manipulate us in order to limit our freedom to decide our own fate. Systemic problems that require systemic solutions What prompted me to write, of course, was news of the current difficulties facing Večer, which is also my newspaper. Ever since editor-in-chief Matija Stepišnik invited me to contribute almost five years ago, I have responded to his trust, if not with the consistent quality of my contributions, then at least with the regularity of my writing. In these five years I have not once missed a deadline or skipped a slot. If Večer doesn’t tire of me, which they would of course be fully entitled to, I would like to carry on. The difficulties Večer faces, which could lead to drastic cuts in the newsroom and thus in the paper’s ability to maintain the necessary level of quality and professionalism, are to some extent specific and, I hope at least, temporary. On the other hand, they are structural threats facing all professional news media, at home and around the world. And because these are systemic problems, they need systemic solutions. A start would be for us to realize how dependent our freedom is on the existence of media that operate according to the principles of the profession and journalistic ethics. And then, as citizens, to demand that politics act accordingly. That it stop trying to subordinate and control the media politically and instead create the conditions for their normal functioning. Part of the responsibility of course lies with journalists and their professional organizations. Above all, we must demand that they remain faithful to the principles of their profession and that, in hard times, they do not look for shortcuts and solutions that would further accelerate the deterioration of the position in which journalists, the media, and with them we ourselves, have found ourselves. But while waiting for politics to become more responsive and responsible, we readers can also do something. Times are hard and every euro counts, but the few we spend on buying a newspaper or subscribing to one medium or another are a smart investment in defending our own freedom of information and freedom to decide our fate. Finally, I would like to add my two cents and ask you for one thing. If you like reading me, subscribe to Večer and read me every other Tuesday. If I get on your nerves, subscribe to Večer and read it every day except every other Tuesday. And a happy New Year. To everyone at Večer and to all of you.

One of the most common arguments among those who place the blame for the war in Ukraine on all sides is the belief that Vladimir Putin launched the attack on the neighbouring country because he felt threatened. I share that opinion, but I do not agree with the claim that this sense of threat was caused by the West and the alleged alliance between NATO and Ukraine, which supposedly aimed to bring Ukraine into the North Atlantic Alliance and NATO to Russia's borders. Based on evidence, I am convinced that on February 24, Putin attacked Ukraine because he judged that even the possibility of a European, economically successful, corruption- and oligarch-free, and democratic future for Ukraine represented a serious threat to his regime. Far from being close to that ideal before February 24 of this year, it was nevertheless evident that the majority of citizens were determined that this was the future they wanted for themselves and their children. Ukrainian democracy, though weak and imperfect, gave them the opportunity to fight for such a future. Putin simply could not allow that. What if Russian citizens started looking across the border and comparing themselves to the "khokhols," as they pejoratively call their Ukrainian neighbours? And began to realize that even in this part of Europe, a different destiny was possible than the one the omnipotent Kremlin leader has been peddling for over two decades. The chatter about how the West betrayed and threatened Russia often centers on alleged promises about NATO's non-expansion eastward and disputes over who respected the Minsk agreements least. But understanding the full picture of complex relations between the West and the Russian Federation requires a broader view that includes the dynamics of those relations over the past thirty years. Indeed, there has been a trend of increasing tensions, especially in the last decade, but the primary responsibility for this lies in the Kremlin. In 1994, as a greenhorn diplomat, I found myself by duty in the room at NATO headquarters in Brussels where the North Atlantic Council meets. What struck me most was the workers installing a new interpreter booth—for the Russian language. The definitive end of the Cold War, I thought. Another optimistic sentiment from the post-Berlin Wall era that aged poorly after the turn of the millennium. Nevertheless, that memory from almost thirty years ago is relevant for understanding today's relations between Russia and the West. I was far from alone in believing that the decades of tension and cold conflict were finally behind us. Many politicians on both sides of the former Iron Curtain believed the same. In Brussels and other European capitals, as well as in Moscow, there was a prevailing belief that from then on, the West and Russia would no longer be adversaries, but partners. A year later, I began working at the Council of Europe, just under two months before the Russian Federation joined that European organization for the protection of democracy, the rule of law, and human rights. Upon joining, Russia's top officials, including President Yeltsin, signed a letter pledging that henceforth they would not threaten or harass anyone and that any internal or external conflicts would be resolved peacefully. This belief in mutual friendship and cooperation extended to the military sphere as well. In May 1997, then NATO Secretary General Javier Solana and Russian Prime Minister Yevgeny Primakov signed the "Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation, and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation." This happened at a time when the accession of the first Eastern European and Baltic states was already underway. The Russians didn’t like it, but it was more a matter of prestige and grievance—"why expand if we are friends and allies?" The Baltic states clearly didn’t want to take the neighbour at its word. Today, it's clear they were right. Things only went downhill after the millennium. On December 31, 1999, President Yeltsin stepped down and appointed Vladimir Putin as his successor. The romance with the West was irrevocably over. What followed was a bloody second war in Chechnya, and in the summer of 2008, Russia attacked Georgia. Nevertheless, until recently, there were no NATO military bases or troops under NATO command near Russia's European borders. That changed only after Russia occupied Crimea, when in 2016 NATO decided to deploy forces in the Baltic states and Poland. After this year’s Russian invasion of the rest of Ukraine, NATO decided to form additional multinational battle groups in Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, and Slovakia. Even Ukraine's possible NATO membership, which had no realistic prospect before this February, would not have marked a turning point in NATO expansion to Russia’s borders. Norway has been a founding NATO member, the Baltic states and Poland joined in 1999, and soon Finland will join as well. All these countries border Russia, but (at least for now), Russia has not launched any "special military operations" to protect its security there. Ukraine is clearly the exception. As I said, because the reasons lie elsewhere. This piece is neither a tribute to nor an apology for NATO, which has its own baggage. I do not deny the alliance’s past sins, but I maintain that threatening the Russian Federation is not one of them. There is ample historical evidence that the Russian bear is willing to tolerate much within its self-proclaimed sphere of influence—except democracy. Analogies with the past can be loose, but not in this case. Putin's view of Russia and its place in the world is quite simplistic. He sees the main reason for all crises and especially for the loss of Russian power and influence in the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The main goal of his policy is to restore the previous state, repeating only slightly adapted patterns of behaviour from former Soviet imperialists. The ideological foundation is no longer Kremlin-style communism or socialism, but Putin's newly fashioned nationalist, anti-liberal paradigm, which—in alliance with the top of the Russian Orthodox Church—peddles nonsense about the spiritual purity and superiority of the Russian people. Supposedly, that justified the attack on Ukraine as the only way to defend the Russian people from the paedophilic decadence of the rotten and corrupt West. British historian Tony Judt, in his monumental "Postwar: A History of Europe Since 1945," describes in detail the thinking of Soviet leaders in the days leading up to the Soviet army’s bloody suppression of the Hungarian uprising in the autumn of 1956. Until the very end, there was a willingness to grant some of Prime Minister Imre Nagy’s demands, including the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Hungary. On October 31, the Presidium of the CPSU Central Committee even expressed readiness for such negotiations. What tipped the scale was not Nagy’s declaration of Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and neutrality, but the announcement of a multi-party system. The Kremlin would not tolerate that, fearing that demands to end the Communist Party's monopoly could spread to the USSR and its satellites. The similarity to Putin's actions regarding Ukraine is obvious. What if Soviet citizens and their comrades on the eastern side of the Iron Curtain began looking at the Hungarians and realizing that a different fate was possible in that part of Europe too? Putin tried to replay the Hungarian pattern in the fall of 2013, when he pressured then-Ukrainian President Yanukovych to revoke, at the last minute, the signing of the EU Association Agreement in favour of closer ties with Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union. What followed was a citizen uprising and the Maidan revolution. Yanukovych eventually fled to Russia, and Putin took revenge by orchestrating conflict in eastern Ukraine and, weeks later, occupying and illegally annexing Crimea. No story, and certainly no revolution, is black and white—Maidan included. I recently spoke with Ukrainian historian Georgiy Kasianov from the University of Lublin, who was critical of the role nationalists played in those dramatic days but was unequivocal in stating that provocateurs were a minority and that the vast majority of protesters took to the streets to demand a democratic future for their country, based on human rights, political freedoms, and the rule of law. This balance of power was also clearly reflected in all subsequent Ukrainian elections, in which nationalist and far-right parties fared significantly worse than in many EU countries. I should note that Kasianov expressed strong disagreement with the claim that the Ukrainian revolution was a Western-organized and financed conspiracy. Without understanding the background and real reasons behind Russian aggression against Ukraine, we will not find a path to ending the war and stabilizing Europe. Concessions based on the "sense of threat" felt by paranoid populist authoritarianism and imperialism can only perpetuate conflict. Putin creates and inflames a sense of external threat because it is a key tool for maintaining power. In the name of "external danger," he enacts and justifies exceptional measures against political opposition, critical media, civil society, and anyone who dares question the wisdom and authority of the Great Leader. Putin's war is a war against democracy, both at home and in the neighbourhood. The real security guarantees Russia and its citizens need are those that protect them from the destructiveness of their current leadership. But no one can provide those guarantees from the outside. The changes Russia needs will have to come from within.

In the apartment to the left of the elevator on the ground floor of the tower block in Ljubljana’s Vodmat where I grew up lived a short gentleman who got very angry with us children when we played soccer in front of his balcony. If, despite his stamping and arm-waving, he didn’t exactly strike fear into us, it was different with the burly man in the green uniform of the Ljubljana city transport company who came to visit late in the evening and knocked very quietly on the door to the left of the elevator. We were afraid of him because he was big—I remember he had boots like tank treads—scowling, and always glancing around furtively. If he had nothing to hide, he wouldn’t be hiding from people like a thief, we thought. Whenever conversation among the neighbors turned to the unusual couple on the ground floor, there was always someone who lowered their voice, drew quotation marks in the air with their fingers and said, “You know, the two of them are …” One evening, as I was waiting alone for the elevator, I suddenly found myself face to face with the mysterious visitor. I think the encounter frightened him even more than it did me. His friend’s door stayed shut, the elevator just wouldn’t come, so for the first time I really looked at him up close. And I realized that the expression on his face, which we had always taken for scowling and anger, was in fact sadness and fear. People also had plenty to say about a neighbor on our floor who worked at the same place as my father. We weren’t afraid of him; he was polite and friendly. He often came over for coffee, and sometimes for lunch. Until one day he was found in his apartment. They say he had taken his own life. My grandmother Anuncijata, who lived in the center of town, had an acquaintance called Lorelei. He was a florist and often gave my grandmother beautiful bouquets. Simply because she always greeted him kindly and always found time to chat with him. Because she accepted him as a human being. Without belittling, without mockery, without contempt. Without quotation marks. Homosexuality was indeed decriminalized in Slovenia by the criminal code that came into force in 1977, but that did not do away overnight with deeply rooted prejudices. Society at the time did not accept homosexuals and did not want to have them before its eyes. I think we can hardly imagine the distress and pain in which thousands of people lived and eked out an existence, pushed to the margins by social intolerance. Many into depression, some into alcohol, some, like our neighbor, into death. I remembered these experiences with homosexuals from my youth a few days ago when I came across a news item in the French media about the wedding of two 72-year-old women in a retirement home in the town of Valenciennes near the Belgian border. Andrée and Liliane met at a children’s shelter when they were eleven. Both without family, they have been inseparable ever since. First friends, then a couple from the age of 25, for almost half a century now. In silence, because they were always afraid of how those around them would accept their love. They have now been in the retirement home for a decade, in the same room. Only their guardian and one of the nurses knew about their relationship, and both respected their wish for privacy, even though, as it turned out, it was born of fear. When the residents of the home went on an outing to a nearby beach this summer, the conversation over lunch turned to marriage for all, as same-sex couples’ right to marry is called in France. Andrée and Liliane could not believe their ears. Until that moment they had been convinced that same-sex partners could only marry in films and TV series. When they were finally persuaded that this was not so, Andrée proposed to Liliane on the spot. Preparations for the wedding began as soon as they returned to the home. The wedding dresses were ordered online, and since Amazon doesn’t offer many models for brides of such mature years, a nurse at the home altered them on her sewing machine. When the big day came, almost all the residents of the home set off for the town hall, with transport provided by a team from the municipal administration. The ceremony was conducted by the mayor with his sash across his chest and with all the republican pomp that only the French can manage. In the photos published by the media, the faces of Liliane and Andrée are glowing with happiness. And pride. Because after 47 years they no longer have to hide their love from others. Because they can love each other in full view of everyone. I am not telling the story of Andrée and Liliane out of a guest worker’s enthusiasm for everything abroad being better and more progressive than at home. For France, at least, that is far from true. Although the law that recognized the right of same-sex couples to marry has been in force for almost a decade and none of the parliamentary parties opposes it today, its adoption was preceded by stormy and massive protests, at which a good part of the center-right also chased political points, not to mention the far right. And as the Slovenian experience with the decriminalization of homosexuality has shown, not even the law changes deeply rooted prejudices overnight. A year ago I wrote about fourteen-year-old Dinah from the Alsatian town of Kingersheim near the Swiss border, whose mother found her hanged in her bedroom. According to her mother, Dinah saw no other way out because of the constant harassment, mockery and abuse from her peers, both at school and on social media. Dinah was a popular and sociable high school student, a good pupil and athlete, always surrounded by friends. She wanted to become President of the Republic, her mother said. At thirteen she decided to confide her sexual orientation to her peers, and her life turned into hell. I write about my childhood neighbors, about Lorelei, Andrée and Liliane, and about Dinah to remind us that we are talking about people. Because we evidently like to forget that. We are talking about people who are still often discriminated against, exposed to prejudice, pushed to the margins of society, stigmatized as perverts, pedophiles, a danger to children and society, exploited to stoke intolerance, abused to promote populist and authoritarian political ideas. Simply because they are different. We usually associate the persecution of certain social groups with authoritarian and backward regimes. In Putin’s Russia, homophobia is a political instrument for holding on to power. In the name of fighting LGBT+ ideology, which supposedly threatens the spiritual purity of the Russian nation from the decadent West, the Patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church blesses and supports the aggression against Ukraine. Unfortunately, we can see again and again that homophobia exists and flourishes in democracies too. Here as well. It is not only about extremists who collect political points with prejudice and hatred. Let us remember the shameful calculation and cowardice of the then governing “liberal” party, which seven years ago did not want to engage seriously in the referendum on the Family Code, saying it was a sensitive matter and the people should decide. Let us remember the claims of one of the candidates in the last presidential election that he had nothing against same-sex unions but was against “LGBT+ ideology.” As if stigmatizing certain social groups becomes legitimate and acceptable if you wrap it in a fraudulent package that presents a personal circumstance as a deliberate (and perverse) ideological choice. Homosexuality and transgender identity are not ideologies, unlike intolerance and hatred toward same-sex unions and transgender people. A few days ago, the American and global public were shocked by footage of the father of the shooter at a gay club in Colorado Springs, who, drunk with hatred toward same-sex partners, said how relieved he was to learn that his son was not gay but merely a mass murderer. Whatever we think of this guy (and the worst, in my opinion, is not bad enough), at least we cannot accuse him of hypocrisy. Which cannot be said of people who package their prejudices in cultural, religious and other excuses. Who grant certain social groups only half their rights and only half their human dignity, because they regard them as only half human. It doesn’t work. You can’t be just a little homophobic, just as you can’t be just a teeny bit racist or just a little antisemitic. In the days before the referendum on the Family Code seven years ago, I wrote that claiming same-sex couples have no right to marry because they can register their partnership is like telling Rosa Parks to stop making a fuss, since she can sit at the back of the bus. Everyone has the right to their religious and political beliefs, but that gives no one the right, in the name of their beliefs, to commit violence against their fellow human beings and push them into a subordinate social position. Attitudes toward homosexuality and transgender people are one of the important indicators of how civilized and open a society is. In recent days, an avalanche of attacks and the crudest insults has been unleashed on a transgender person who, with great courage and dignity, spoke publicly about her life. The trigger was an invitation to talk about transgender identity to high school students in Postojna. The well-known political hucksters of prejudice and intolerance spoke up, then the youth choir of a political party that sees itself as center-right, and after them the internet infantry, which translates sotto voce stigmatization into the crudest forms of verbal violence and hatred. It’s about the children, you say? I partly agree with you. It is also about children. I have four myself, and what worries me most is that they might grow up and live in a society subjected to the violence of your prejudices, frustrations and delusions. It is not the people to whom you deny equality and human dignity who belong in quotation marks, but your morality and humanity. Take a look in the mirror. If you can’t do it for the sake of the people you cause distress and injustice to, then at least do it for the children.

Dear President-elect of the Republic of Slovenia, first of all I would like to congratulate you wholeheartedly on your election. With your victory, Slovenia has reached an important milestone: the first woman in the highest office of the state. I hope that with your election we have taken an important step toward real equality between women and men in Slovenia. But a long road still lies ahead of us. I believe that a radical shift along that road will be one of your priorities. I welcome your victory because in the past, and during the election campaign, you clearly and firmly stood up for human rights, political freedoms, democracy and the democratic rule of law.
