You have shown that you understand this is not a matter of ideological or political alignment, but of championing and safeguarding the constitutional foundations of our democracy and its pluralism. These are civilizational values that all decent political parties in a functioning democracy should stand up for, whichever side of the political spectrum they come from. This is the constitutional framework within which lively political battles and political divisions are not a weakness but a reflection of political pluralism and political maturity. On condition, of course, of a considerably higher political culture. The times when we built the future on the compulsion that everyone think and feel the same are, I hope, behind us once and for all. If I may, I would suggest that you add social rights to the above set of political freedoms and human rights. Here, too, it is of course not a matter of left or right. Different political platforms will always have different emphases and different paths, but for all those who are genuinely committed to a functioning democracy it should be clear that it is not possible without social justice. A society based on the neoliberal structural economic, social and political marginalization of part of its citizens will never be truly democratic and will always be in danger of falling prey to the political hucksters of populist and authoritarian alternatives. You have promised to work to overcome differences and divisions among citizens. Good. But I hope you will go about it differently from your predecessor. I hope you will look for the point of unity in consistent respect for democratic values, not at the arithmetic midpoint between those who stand up for those values and those who can’t stand them. I am glad that in a month you will become President, because you have promised not to keep quiet. That you will use the authority that comes from winning the election clearly and firmly in cases where the democratic and civilizational values we wrote into the Constitution at independence are violated and threatened. These values are not violated in the abstract and therefore cannot be defended merely with abstract platitudes that evaporate on contact with concrete attacks on human rights and human dignity. Of which there have unfortunately been ever more in Slovenia in recent years. Partly because of the silence of those who should have spoken up but didn’t. In honoring your commitment to speak up, things will not always be easy and comfortable for you. It is a responsibility that requires wise judgment and a great deal of knowledge. I am convinced you lack neither, and for those areas in which, despite your rich career, you have less experience, I recommend a wise choice of advisers. On the domestic as well as the international stage, as you have already experienced, it is easy to slip. The fact is that silent politicians enjoy no small support among Slovenians. Given what some people allow themselves to say in the political arena, this is understandable in a way. If you take no position on anything, at least you won’t offend anyone. After all, your predecessor won two terms this way, and your direct rival also profited from playing the ostrich on pressing social problems. But that is not the right way. When democracy is in crisis, false even-handedness and silence are objectively the allies of its enemies. In the times we live in, we cannot defend and preserve democracy by sticking our heads in the sand, even if, supposedly, with the best of intentions. So as not to anger and divide people. If we followed your predecessor’s wisdom to the end, after your term we would no longer need to elect your successor but could simply draw lots. “Jože, the die is cast, until now it was Nataša, now it’s your turn. What am I supposed to do? Nothing, just post photos and keep quiet.” I hope you won’t hold my bad joke against me; you of course did not come to the highest office in the land by lot, but through the trust that a majority of voters placed in you because of your positions. With that you have gained moral authority, but also a moral obligation to all who gave you their vote. Being the president of all citizens is a noble ambition, but it cannot be an alibi for “overcoming differences” at the lowest common denominator of attitudes toward democratic values. Finally, allow me to respond to your statement that now is the time to forget the past and build the future. It is of course possible that you simply wanted to bury past grudges and start afresh, and that is fine. But if, in a rather widespread manner, you happen to be suggesting that we solve unresolved problems from the past by simply forgetting about them, I would nevertheless suggest that you think about it carefully once more. The recent history not only of Slovenia but of all of Europe was dramatic, hard and also bloody. Deliberate forgetting may be an understandable human reflex, but it carries the risk that the future we are supposed to build will be dangerously similar to the past we want to forget. Many are evidently convinced that still-smoldering traumas can be resolved by pushing them even deeper into the collective subconscious and placing a white marble slab over them. On which, in the name of a reconciliation that is not one, we ritually lay carnations and wreaths. A critical understanding of history is essential to understanding the present and to understanding the importance of democracy and democratic values. This is especially true for generations who have no direct memory of times when there was no democracy, no respect for human rights and human dignity. Who do not know what happened in those times to people like them, and what could happen to them too in the future. Out of reverence for the victims, but also for the sake of our own security and future, we must preserve the memory of the times in which Europe, first gradually and then ever faster, sank into a whirlpool of incomprehensible inhumanity that culminated in the gas chambers and crematoria of the concentration camps. Without memory and a critical understanding of Europe’s past, it is impossible to understand the challenges of today’s Europe and to recognize and respond in time to warnings that history may have begun to repeat itself. Dear Madam President. I know you are familiar with, and agree with, the words of Primo Levi: “It happened, therefore it can happen again.” To prevent that, it is not enough merely to repeat these words; they must also be put into practice in everyday life, every time humanist values are denied, every time there is stigmatization and dehumanization of certain social groups, intolerance and hatred. In your presidential campaign you promised that you would respond to such phenomena, of which, unfortunately, there are more and more here too. I do not doubt that you will keep your promises. You need not try too hard to acquire anyone else’s wisdom in this regard; follow your own, thanks to which you won the election convincingly. I wish you much courage and success in this. I hope you won’t take my letter amiss. I have neither the intention nor the right to lecture patronizingly someone who has received a mandate in democratic elections, but I believe that in today’s times no one who cares about a safe, free future that is kind to all people can afford to stay silent. In the end, the duty to speak up critically applies not only to politicians but also to engaged citizens, such as I would like to be myself.
We Cannot Rely on Prosecutors Alone

A few weeks ago, two people were murdered outside the gay bar Teplaren in Bratislava. The killer was a young man, the son of a far-right activist. Without insinuating anything about anyone, it cannot be ruled out that at home, over Sunday lunch, they chatted about the danger of LGBT ideology. A few days ago, an older man threw a firebomb at a processing center for irregular migrants in Dover in Britain and then took his own life. It is only by chance that he was the sole fatality of the attack. Perhaps he believed he was defending his homeland against a foreign invasion, as the new-old British Home Secretary Suella Braverman recently described the challenge of irregular migration. In Slovenia, too, hate speech against certain individuals and groups is on the rise. Violence is appearing as well. Luckily we have, for now, avoided the worst forms and the loss of human life. But that is not because of a lack of intolerance and hatred, and still less because we are so determined and successful in fighting such phenomena. Rather the opposite. If we leave things as they are, it is only a matter of time before we lay flowers and light candles for the first time, in solidarity and mourning for the victims of violence that we could and should have prevented. There is a lot of hatred in Slovenia. Just under two years ago, the weekly Demokracija published a text in which the author compared people of other races to pests and weeds that must be exterminated. The editors insisted it was merely satire. This is a typical example of hate speech, of the kind of “satire” that Der Stürmer editor Julius Streicher perfected in his career, which found its epilogue at the Nuremberg tribunal. The aim of dehumanizing future victims is gradually to lower society’s inhibitions about violence against them. The “satire” in Demokracija recently had its judicial epilogue, and rightly so. A similarly appropriate reaction came these days from the Agency for Communication Networks and Services. In its inspection of a June conversation between a host and a viewer who called for the use of weapons on the program Kdo vam laže (Who Is Lying to You) on Nova24TV, it found that it constituted incitement to violence and hatred against a group of people. That case is also still being examined by the prosecution. On the other hand, speech that reaches the necessarily very high threshold for legal sanction is relatively rare in Slovenia, at least compared with speech that does not reach that necessarily very high legal threshold for prosecutorial intervention in freedom of expression, but which nonetheless spreads intolerance and hatred and thereby indirectly creates conditions in which violence sooner or later occurs. That by no means implies there is no reason for alarm. One reason we are so ineffective in responding to rising intolerance and hatred is confusion about what hate speech actually is. Some use the term only for speech that reaches the legal threshold for intervention and prosecution, others for any statement that “offends, shocks or disturbs,” even though such speech—according to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights—cannot be prohibited or punished despite being offensive. The European Court does not even use the term “hate speech”; in each case it determines, according to the specific circumstances, whether a given speech enjoys protection under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights or not. To get beyond the muddle that can lead, on the one hand, to prosecutorial hyperactivity and overly hasty and overly deep interference in freedom of expression and, on the other, to unresponsiveness towards expressions of intolerance and hatred which, despite being protected under Article 10, increase the risk of violence in society, some experts use the term dangerous speech instead of hate speech. It is not defined by the threshold for prosecution and in every case requires at least a social response and a social sanction. If, after years of floundering in Slovenia over prosecutorial interpretations and the understanding of Article 297 of the Slovenian Criminal Code, things are, I hope, slowly being put in order, our biggest deficit lies precisely in the social response to and sanctioning of hatred and intolerance. We do not know how, and do not manage, to react to dangerous speech that we cannot and must not sanction legally. The concept of freedom of expression in a democratic society remains an unsolvable riddle for many in Slovenia. The fact that we cannot and must not ban or punish a particular statement out of respect for freedom of expression does not mean we cannot—or even must not—condemn it in the strongest terms. By socially condemning, denormalizing and debanalizing hatred and intolerance in society, we in no way violate freedom of expression; quite the opposite, we create the conditions for more effective protection of all human rights, political freedoms and democratic values in society. If we do not understand this and do not do it, we share responsibility for the situation we are in, in which violence is already occurring and will occur again. In this context, because of the influence that comes with the position and its associated responsibilities, particular attention must be paid to the role of the President of the Republic. Out of respect for the office the current head of state is leaving, I will understandably be restrained in my comments. The outgoing President certainly cannot be reproached for a lack of determination in standing up for tolerance, dialogue and mutual respect at the declaratory and abstract level, but that determination somehow never came to the fore when there were concrete outbursts of hatred, stigmatization and dehumanization of certain individuals and social groups, especially the most dangerous ones, expressed in the media or by holders of political power. Let us recall that throughout his term, amid ever more frequent concrete outbursts of verbal violence, including the one in Demokracija mentioned above, which in the end was sanctioned by the courts, the President remained deafeningly silent in the name of respect for different opinions and freedom of expression. This deficit in prevention cannot be compensated for by wringing one’s hands and lamenting post festum in response to situations in which the banalization of hatred actually leads to violence. To assess the seriousness of dangerous speech, and the related need for a legal or social reaction to it, the power relationship between the one who spreads hatred and intolerance through speech and the one who is its target and victim is also key. The most despicable and most dangerous hatred is that spread by someone in a position of political influence and power against individuals and social groups because of their personal circumstances, religion, nationality, sexual orientation, gender or skin color. Very dangerous, too, is speech that, through deliberate insults and lies, stokes and directs the fury of its ideological supporters with the aim of discrediting institutions that serve as democratic safeguards in society, or the individuals working in them. Here, too, we frequently witness attacks on the judiciary, the media and civil society. Such conduct not only violates the human rights of individuals and can lead to violence; it also represents a serious threat to democracy. One of the conditions for the credibility and effectiveness of efforts against the spread of intolerance is consistency. Far from everyone being the same, inappropriate discourse nevertheless does not occur only on one side of the political field. As an illustration I can cite the phrase “death to Janšism,” about which I have serious reservations. Although I fully agree with the prosecution’s assessment that it does not constitute a death threat and therefore cannot be prosecuted, I do not understand what it is that people want to convey with it that could not be expressed with words such as “down with Janšism.” Mentioning death in any context objectively does nothing for the level of political culture or the fight against intolerance in society. If anything, this and similar discourse hands easy volleys to all those who try to deflect attention and relativize their own conduct by pointing their finger at others. The latest court and prosecution proceedings, as well as the AKOS decision regarding Nova24TV and the Prime Minister’s firm response to the violence to which the spread of intolerance and hatred led, are a sign that in Slovenia we are at last slowly beginning to realize how deep we have sunk. But there is still a long way to go before current trends are reversed. On that path, we cannot and must not rely on prosecutors alone. Without freedom of expression there is no functioning democracy, so overly hasty and overly deep interventions must be avoided, even with the best of intentions. The self-regulation of professional media associations has an important role, and above all the moral authority and moral integrity of those who occupy the most influential political and other positions in society. In the long term, education for democratic citizenship is also key, through which we pass on to young people the knowledge, democratic values, solidarity, empathy and capacity for critical thinking that enable them to recognize and resist the stoking of prejudice and the spread of intolerance and hatred in society. But to succeed in passing democratic and civilizational values on to younger generations, we must begin immediately, decisively and effectively to fight the spread of intolerance and hatred among those—and above all by those—who are in positions of power here and now.
A Little Glossary of Coded Intolerance

While following this year’s presidential campaign and many rather tiresome pre-election debates, my attention was caught by a very well-mannered gentleman who assured us very zealously that he respects, by golly, the rights and equality of same-sex persons, and only opposes “LGBT ideology.” What the hell this is supposed to be, he did not explain in detail, but as far as one could understand, what irritates him is the doctrine according to which the abstract and theoretical equality of same-sex persons, which the likable gentleman accepts in principle in full, should also be confirmed in law and implemented in practice. Bad joke aside, “LGBT ideology” is a frequently used, but not the only, phrase with which individuals, especially in politics, try to disguise and at the same time justify and enforce their prejudices. To make reading between the lines easier, I have prepared a little glossary of coded intolerance. LGBT ideology When the Russian Duma adopted a law banning “homosexual propaganda” on June 11, 2013, only one Russian parliamentarian abstained, Ilya Ponomarev. Incidentally, when a year later he was the only member of the Duma to vote against the annexation of Crimea, he left for Ukraine, where he joined the Ukrainian territorial defense right at the start of the Russian aggression. The law banning homosexual propaganda was a workaround by which Putin’s regime tried to get around a formal prohibition of discrimination against LGBT persons, which would have contradicted the Russian Federation’s membership of the Council of Europe. It was also a milestone in Russia’s membership of the organization. Whereas until then Russian politicians had responded to all criticism of disrespect for human rights and democratic principles in a soothing manner, along the lines of “no problem, it’s a misunderstanding, we’ll fix everything, you don’t have enough information,” on the rights of same-sex persons they showed openly and without disguise for the first time that they did not share European democratic values. Since recriminalizing homosexuality would have too obviously violated the legal standards to which Russia had committed, the law “merely” banned any discourse that would present homosexuality to children as a normal human circumstance and a human right. From that moment, same-sex persons were treated as second-class citizens, as perverts threatening the purity of the Russian nation. The Russian approach of stigmatization and discrimination soon found imitators in other European countries. In the name of fighting “homosexual propaganda” and “LGBT ideology,” a law on the Russian model was adopted in Hungary, and quite a few towns in Poland declared themselves “gay-free” zones, in which there are no homosexuals, or they are so frightened that they don’t dare go out among people. According to the opponents of “LGBT ideology,” LGBT individuals are in principle equal citizens with all rights, but because of their unnatural perversion it is necessary to protect children from them and prevent LGBT persons from exercising their abstract equality in practice. To justify and disguise discrimination based on sexual orientation and identity, personal characteristics are presented as a deliberate choice of an unacceptable, perverse and socially harmful ideological orientation. The moment politics labels same-sex orientation an ideology harmful to children, this personal characteristic is classified as a deviant threat, and same-sex persons become, in the eyes of the public, predators endangering the safety of children and the moral purity of society. Gender ideology The Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence was opened for signature on April 7, 2011, in Istanbul, at the end of the Turkish chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. The first to proudly sign it was the then Turkish foreign minister. A decade later, Turkey left the convention by decree of President Erdoğan. The reason? The convention, and above all “gender ideology,” supposedly threatened traditional family values. Turkey was not alone in rejecting the Istanbul Convention. Quite a few countries have not signed it, and in many countries that have acceded to it, conservative and especially far-right forces are doing their utmost to convince the public that the Istanbul Convention is paving the way to the end of human civilization and humanity in general. What is it really about? Since violence against women is largely structural in nature, the problem cannot be solved without confronting the wider questions of gender inequality. This inequality is, of course, not a consequence of biological differences between the sexes but above all of social constructs, prejudices, traditions and stereotypes that put women in a subordinate position. Article 3 of the Istanbul Convention therefore provides that, in the convention, “gender” means the socially constructed roles, behaviors, activities and attributes that a given society considers appropriate for women or for men. And the first paragraph of Article 12 obliges the parties to take “the necessary measures to promote changes in the social and cultural patterns of behavior of women and men with a view to eradicating prejudices, customs, traditions and all other practices which are based on the idea of the inferiority of women or on stereotyped roles for women and men.” And this is what has most enraged the supporters of “traditional values,” among which many of them evidently also count the inferiority of women. Critical race theory In July this year, the Anti-Woke law, or the law against critical race theory, came into force in the US state of Florida. Unlike “LGBT ideology,” which is an entirely invented construct and conspiracy theory, critical race theory (like gender theory, but not “gender ideology”) is an established sociological discipline that studies how structural racism in the United States has influenced American legislation and still influences the lives of non-white citizens today. The credit for the law protecting young people from the danger of critical race theory goes to Florida’s far-right Republican governor Ron DeSantis, who is paving the way for his presidential ambitions with his crusade against “political correctness.” On signing the law, he declared that critical race theory causes discrimination and humiliates white pupils, who feel inferior and ashamed because of teaching about structural racism. He did not talk about whether systemic racism against non-white citizens exists in the US; he only stressed that mentioning such indecencies embarrasses and disadvantages members of the white majority. Slovenia’s son-in-law Donald Trump, whom DeSantis is breathing down the neck of, could of course not stay quiet and called teaching about racism and respect for diversity in society a “toxic danger.” Soros, Soros hirelings George Soros, the American businessman and philanthropist, is often used as a universal means of disqualifying anyone whom populism identifies as an obstacle to taking power. In far-right discourse, Soros hints at the existence of conspiratorial international networks that run the world from behind the scenes at the expense and to the detriment of honest citizens. It is (poorly) coded promotion of the conspiracies, stereotypes, caricatures, patterns and discourses of traditional European antisemitism. Invoking Soros is also a very popular means of disqualifying and stigmatizing civil society. The matter is not innocent. Antisemitism is very much present in Europe—as many as a quarter of Europeans believe that Jews have too much influence in the business and financial world. If it helps, this prejudice is also often expressed through caricatures of puppet masters controlling social and political events from behind the scenes. Cultural Marxism What this is all about was described better than I could by the former prime minister in an interview with the Hungarian weekly Mandiner in December 2020. Allow me to quote him. “The Communist Manifesto of the 19th century states that to create a new world, that is, communism, the nation, the family, private property, private education and religion must be dismantled. Paradoxically, despite enormous sacrifices and suffering, communism did not achieve this goal through violence and dictatorship. That is why the same goals are being pursued in a different way. Through the mass media, universities, the culture industry, multinational institutions, mass migration, imposed multiculturalism and the activities of some political parties. Something is happening that is quite cleverly hidden, but anyone who knows history and political concepts can see the direction in which it is all developing. That is why it must be resisted. And we are doing that. By protecting and supporting the family, valuing our own nation and other nations, protecting the right to private property and private initiative, and safeguarding freedom of religion. By knowing what we are and wanting to be that.” Anders Breivik also devoted a great deal of attention in his manifesto to the importance of the fight against cultural Marxism. That will do for now. The list above is, of course, not complete. Intolerance in our society is on the rise, and amid the lack of response, and also in the name of the doctrine of “respecting absolutely all different opinions” advocated by the departing standard-bearer from the presidential palace, it is becoming ever more everyday and normal. But so that no one gets their knickers in a twist, as the charming English idiom has it, I allow that some people use prejudice and hatred wrapped in platitudes and conspiracy theories out of ignorance, so this glossary is meant for them too. May it help them in the future to avoid the risk of expressing—all right, perhaps unintentionally—ideas through their discourse that they should be damned ashamed of.

Last Thursday, Vladimir Zelensky of course did not call on the West to launch a pre-emptive NUCLEAR strike on Russia. Regardless, his statement was a communications and political blunder. It handed Kremlin propagandists a chance to spin it misleadingly but effectively. It was a mistake, even if his comment—in the original, not the Kremlin "translation"—can be understood, at least from the perspective of the Ukrainian public. The West has responded to Russia’s increasingly loud nuclear sabre-rattling with threats that any use of nuclear weapons would prompt an immediate and decisive response using CONVENTIONAL weapons against Russian military targets. Zelensky's logic, from the Ukrainian point of view, is thus legitimate and coherent. If you're seriously worried about a Russian nuclear strike on Ukraine, then don't wait until it causes tens or hundreds of thousands of casualties—do everything to prevent it, including the pre-emptive use of CONVENTIONAL weapons. The logic is similar to earlier calls to close the airspace at the start of the aggression—appeals that, like this recent one, fell on deaf ears in the West. Zelensky misjudged how such a statement would resonate with the broader public, including among those who otherwise support Ukraine but are, justifiably, afraid of escalation—especially the increasingly serious threat of nuclear weapons use. The response to Russian aggression, and especially to Moscow’s nuclear blackmail, requires resolve but also a cool head. But if the West does not use conventional weapons pre-emptively, it doesn’t mean the nuclear threat is over. Unfortunately, the world finds itself in a situation where there are no longer comfortable or simple exits from the looming danger. We cannot just turn back the clock or magically reset the world to its previous state (well, maybe without Ukraine on the map, but Facebook philosophers say they brought it on themselves), pretending the crisis is over. With his aggression against a neighbouring state—and, above all, with the debacle of his supposedly mighty military, now laid bare—Putin has cornered himself with no visible exit. But an exit does exist, it lies on Ukraine's internationally recognized borders. Putin has unleashed a storm of external aggression and internal violence against his own population and believes he cannot stop if he wants to stay in power. Yielding to his aggression only reinforces his belief that he can succeed—not just this time, but in future episodes. He had no rational security reasons for attacking Ukraine. It was a logical step in escalating his imperialist policy of building a "Russian world," the foundation upon which he has built his authoritarian regime for over twenty years. Bargaining with Ukraine’s fate doesn’t eliminate the nuclear threat—it only delays and amplifies it. If Ukraine falls, new victims of Putin's imperialism and new nuclear threats will follow. The beginning of the end of this crisis will come the moment Putin realizes there is no way out of the mess he's created through increasingly desperate nuclear posturing. That is why unity, resolve, and clear-headedness are essential. Giving in to nuclear blackmail sends a dangerous message to others who share Putin’s worldview. North Korea's ballistic missiles, which Kim Jong-un is now enthusiastically launching over his neighbours, are also delivering that message. The problem with "peace-making" at the expense of Ukraine's survival isn't just that it's morally unacceptable—it’s dangerous and will take us even further from peace. A global security architecture that includes Russia? Absolutely—but only one that does not legitimize and encourage violent border changes by fascist-leaning dictators with nuclear weapons. I understand and share people’s fears about the growing threat of nuclear escalation. Honestly, I’m damn scared, too. Psychologically, I even understand the escapism that sees naive shortcuts as a way back to safety, peace, and cheaper gas. Horrified and frightened by the mounting consequences of the aggression, many seek a solution in appeasing the aggressor. Putin is mad and unpredictable and has nuclear weapons. Zelensky can be influenced, so let's cut Ukraine off from aid and force them to surrender. The moral dilemmas such an approach creates are often resolved by equating the bully with their victim. Of course, I’m not saying Zelensky, Ukraine, or the West are spotless. As I often read in comments on my writings, no situation is purely black-and-white. You know what? I agree. But the shades of grey are often so drastically different that we cannot and must not lump them together. Nothing—absolutely nothing—that we can criticize Ukraine or the West for justifies Russia’s aggression and crimes on the occupied territory of its neighbour. But not all advocates for "peace" at the cost of Ukraine's survival are the same. Many express genuine compassion and solidarity with Ukrainians and attempt to resolve the unavoidable moral conflict between their principles and the consequences those principles bring upon Ukrainians by insisting they act in Ukrainians' best interest. If they stop their national liberation struggle, the bloodshed will end. Sound familiar? Others blame everyone except the Kremlin for the war and the threat of nuclear catastrophe. Still others resolve the issue with apathy and cynicism. Last Friday, Newsweek’s senior commentator Josh Hammer put it this way: "Let’s be as clear as possible: the average American citizen doesn’t and shouldn’t care whether an ethnically divided, strategically insignificant, historically disputed Slavic backwater or two in eastern Ukraine ultimately takes orders from Kyiv or Moscow." Fuck you, stupid Slavic Untermenschen—why should we trouble ourselves over your lives? "A line must be drawn somewhere," declared Frederick Blair, Canada’s immigration director in June 1939, when nearly a thousand Jews fleeing Nazi Germany on the ship St. Louis were denied entry. The U.S. and Cuba had already turned them away, claiming too many among them were communists and spies. The trick of stigmatizing the victim and morally equating them with the perpetrator to wash one’s conscience and avoid helping people in distress wasn’t invented yesterday. We also know how those stories end. Damn, I’m scared. I want this senseless bloodshed to end as soon as possible. But let’s not forget who pushed us to the brink of nuclear catastrophe. The threats of nuclear war do not come from Kyiv, Brussels, or Washington. They come exclusively from Moscow. This must stop. Resolutely, but with a cool head. The road to peace requires a clear and convincing message: nuclear blackmail, let alone the use of nuclear weapons, cannot benefit Putin's regime. It is not a viable path to victory for his imperial ambitions—it can only accelerate the inevitable end of his terrorizing of neighbouring states, Russian citizens, and the world. Once again, we face a moment where we must decide whether and how to confront fascist evil. The future of Ukraine—and all of us—depends on where we draw the line.
Family Values from Tehran to Tallahassee

On Monday, September 19, just before the opening of this year’s United Nations General Assembly, a high-level summit titled Transforming Education was held at the UN headquarters. The goal was to reaffirm political attention and support for ambitious and concrete actions to address the global education crisis that denies hundreds of thousands of children—especially in developing countries—access to consistent and quality schooling. The effects of this crisis reach beyond the children themselves; they are a major obstacle to social development and the capacity to respond swiftly and effectively to economic, social, security, and environmental challenges. However, due to last-minute changes in the schedules of most heads of state and government—who were expected in New York on Monday but diverted to Queen Elizabeth’s funeral in London—the main speakers at the summit ended up being those who hadn’t been invited to the funeral. The discussion at the Economic and Social Council chamber, right next to the UN Security Council hall, was opened by Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi. In his address, Raisi stressed that education must be rooted in justice, patriotism, and family values, adding that he meant “normal families, not unnatural communities promoted by certain Western societies.” Outside the UN building, protesters erected a symbolic graveyard on the lawn with tombstones bearing the names of hundreds of victims of the Iranian regime. At the forefront stood a large photograph of 22-year-old Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being arrested by Iran’s morality police for not wearing a headscarf. Iranian authorities described her death as regrettable, but that didn’t stop massive protests, led largely by courageous Iranian women, who have been violently dispersed by security forces. So far, more than 40 protestors have been killed. At the official opening of the UN General Assembly the following day, Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro was the first to speak. He shared his interpretation of human rights, centered on "defending the family, protecting life from birth, self-defense, and rejecting gender theory." Roughly 1,500 kilometers to the south, in Tallahassee—the capital of Florida—state governor Ron DeSantis is busy pursuing his 2024 presidential ambitions. Determined to outflank Donald Trump from the right (a difficult but apparently not impossible feat), DeSantis enacted the “Don’t Say Gay” law in the spring, which bans any mention of sexual orientation or gender identity in Florida’s elementary schools. The law closely mirrors legislation introduced earlier in Hungary, and before that, in the Russian Federation. DeSantis has given sweeping powers to local school boards—now filled with his allies—to interfere with curriculum and cleanse textbooks of all “progressive filth,” not only references to homosexuality but also discussions of racial discrimination or critical race theory, which our Slovene in-law Donald (Trump) calls “toxic propaganda.” Critical race theory is an interdisciplinary field that studies systemic racism and how social concepts of race and ethnicity influence law, politics, and media. Recently, DeSantis—alongside Texas Governor Greg Abbott—made headlines by sending migrants legally awaiting asylum processing to Martha’s Vineyard, the “liberal” island off the coast of Massachusetts, and to the residence of U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris. We know all too well what Trump’s Republicans, especially the Supreme Court majority, think about women's right to bodily autonomy and reproductive choice. Their mantra “It’s about the children” applies only from conception to birth—after that, those children are largely left to fend for themselves, especially if they are born on the wrong end of a trickle-down economy. In this global club of “defenders of family values,” there are of course many politicians and parties across Europe, but one figure stands out—Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin has long built his politics on systemic homophobia in the name of Russian culture, spiritual purity, and protection from Western liberal decadence. In his recent address to the Russian people, justifying the need for “partial mobilization” after a series of defeats in Ukraine, he also cited the need to protect Russians from the threat of Western “pseudo-values.” His efforts are vigorously supported by the leadership of the Russian Orthodox Church. In March, Patriarch Kirill justified the attack on Ukraine by citing the need to protect Russia (and apparently its neighbors) from the “imposition” of pride parades. Some might wave this off—suggesting that such attitudes toward homosexuality, gender equality, and non-discrimination are just coincidences, akin to everyone supporting turning right on red. But of course, they’re not. Regardless of their relationships or views of each other, these politicians represent local variants of the same ideological pathology. Homophobia, misogyny, denying women the right to control their own bodies, and hostility toward migrants are carefully chosen levers to undermine and shield against liberal democracy. Western right-wing populism, Russian nationalist imperialism, and Iranian theocracy all exploit fear, frustration, and prejudice. By scapegoating certain social groups, they offer disillusioned citizens easy targets for their real or imagined grievances—while paving or fortifying their own paths to power. Homophobia and related ideologies built on intolerance and hatred are effective threads for unraveling the often sloppily stitched sweater of liberal democracy. Denying equality and human dignity to one group becomes a powerful tool for eroding solidarity, empathy, and social responsibility toward anyone. First they came for the gays... Humanistic values aren’t sausages you can slice to your liking and serve only to yourself and your kind. A society that denies equality and dignity to some will, sooner or later, deny them to all. The erosion of solidarity and empathy is precisely what makes right-wing populism so appealing to neoliberals. The so-called “natural laws” that declare homosexuality unnatural are also convenient justifications for a society in which the majority have little or nothing, while a tiny few hold almost everything. It is especially cynical and vile to see these ideas spread in the name of defending families and children. In the populist worldview, the family is defended by hatred toward others, and children's rights are determined by the sexual orientation of their parents—not by their need for love, protection, and care. The solution is not to surrender the defense of family values and children's rights to populism. Quite the opposite: it is precisely in the name of families and children that this ideology must be opposed. Families can only be truly protected through social, economic, housing, employment, and educational policies that give everyone, regardless of personal circumstance, a chance for a dignified life and the freedom to decide when and how to start a family. Children’s interests can only be protected by creating a society in which all children are safe, their rights respected, and they have access to quality education, as well as all forms of social and physical safety and well-being. The alternative is an ideology that “protects” families and children by pushing LGBTQ+ people into segregation, women back to the kitchen, and those in need into abandonment. If we allow these ideas to prevail, we will soon find ourselves in a society that is hostile to everyone—especially families and children.

In May 2014, directly after the Russian occupation of Ukraine's Crimea, an event called the Holy Alliance took place in the beautiful baroque Liechtenstein City Palace in Vienna. Among the attendees were Marion Maréchal-Le Pen, the even more extreme niece of far-right Marine Le Pen, prominent Le Penist party member Aymeric Chauprade, Spanish prince Sixtus Henry Bourbon-Parma, the then-leaders of Austria's Freedom Party Heinz-Christian Strache and Johann Gudenus (both later infamous for their Ibiza vacation scandal), the head of Bulgaria's far-right Ataka party Volen Siderov, and, according to media reports, several Croatian far-right extremists. The Holy Alliance gathering was funded by Russian oligarch Konstantin Malofeyev, known for his connections in the Kremlin and the upper echelons of the Russian Orthodox Church. The central theme was defending Europe from "liberal ideas and homosexuality in the name of patriotism and Christian family values." A few months later, a similar meeting with similar topics and attendees took place in Moscow and occupied Donetsk. The themes of these and similar meetings form the ideological thread connecting the culture wars of far-right politics in many European countries, the U.S., and elsewhere. Though the emphasis and national contexts differ, the culture war always centers around the same discourse: opposition to liberal values, homosexuality, and the perceived decadence of liberal elites. In the U.S., this narrative is led by Trump and his followers under the MAGA brand, used to ban schoolbooks and curricula, attack the Capitol and constitutional institutions, deny election results, and restrict the rights of women and social minorities. These are policies, ideas, and people whom President Joe Biden recently labelled as "semi-fascism." In Europe, much is heard about the danger of "cultural Marxism." Former Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša explained it in Hungary's Mandiner weekly in December 2020: "The Communist Manifesto from the 19th century states that to create a new world—communism—one must dismantle the nation, family, private property, private education, and religion. Paradoxically, communism failed to achieve this goal despite massive violence and suffering. Therefore, the same objectives are now pursued differently: through mass media, universities, cultural industries, multinational institutions, mass migration, imposed multiculturalism, and certain political parties. Something is happening, skilfully hidden, but anyone who knows history and political concepts can see the direction this is heading." Norwegian extremist Anders Breivik, who murdered 77 mostly young people in Oslo and on the island of Utøya, also focused extensively on the fight against cultural Marxism in his manifesto. The Vienna meeting of the Holy Alliance also featured strong representation from Russia, including philosopher, political scientist, and ideologue Alexander Dugin, who recently came to international attention following the assassination of his daughter and ally Darya Dugina. Alexander Dugin is certainly a controversial figure, though Western media often exaggerate his direct influence on Putin. Until recently, he was relatively unknown in Russia. Still, even if not a modern-day Rasputin whispering into Putin’s ear, his writings provide insight into the ideology dominating Russian political and intellectual circles and reflected in Putin's policies toward Russia, its "near abroad," and the world—especially the West, the U.S., the EU, and Ukraine. Dugin outlined his ideas of Eurasia and the Russian world in his 1997 treatise "Foundations of Geopolitics." This work is essential for understanding the backdrop of recent events, including the aggression against Ukraine, showing that the ideas behind Putin’s policies are deeply rooted in Russian political psychopathology and have been since at least the fall of the Soviet Union. The central thesis of Dugin’s "Foundations of Geopolitics" is the establishment of a Eurasian empire dominated by Russia. He claims ethnic Russians are "bearers of a unique civilization" and a "messianic people" with "universal significance for all humanity." According to Dugin, the Russian people can only serve as the core of a vast empire. "Abandoning the creation of an empire," he warns, "would mean the end of the Russian people as a historical reality and civilizational phenomenon. Such a refusal would be national suicide. Without an empire, Russians will disappear as a nation." If you can't quite place where these words sound familiar from, try translating them into German. They’d fit in Mein Kampf like a hand in a glove. In 1997, Dugin wrote this about Ukraine: "Ukraine as a state has no geopolitical, cultural, or universal significance, no geographic uniqueness, no ethnic exclusivity. Ukraine as an independent state with territorial ambitions presents a huge danger for all of Eurasia, and without solving the Ukrainian problem, it is generally meaningless to speak of Russian geostrategy." Sound familiar? Putin expanded Dugin's thesis in his pseudo-historical pamphlet "On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians." Despite its title, the claim of unity rests on the assertion that Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians are one people, and Ukraine is an artificial construct. Putin ends the article with the peaceful assurance that Russia never was and never will be anti-Ukrainian, and that the future of Ukraine should be decided by its citizens. Six months later, he launched the "special military operation." But the architects of the Eurasian empire did not confine their search for support to the far right. To make real inroads, they had to seek backing across the political spectrum, including the centre. This became especially effective after the attack on Ukraine, in a strategy reminiscent of another key element from Dugin's "Foundations of Geopolitics," which calls for "beheading the Atlanticist anaconda." Dugin wrote—again, in 1997—that Russian security services and their allies must "provoke all forms of instability and separatism within the borders of the U.S. It is especially important to stir up geopolitical disorder in American domestic politics, to encourage all kinds of separatism and ethnic, social, and racial conflicts, to actively support all dissident movements—extremist, racist, and sectarian groups—thus destabilizing internal political processes in the U.S. At the same time, it would make sense to support isolationist tendencies in American politics." Everything we've seen regarding attempts to influence U.S. elections and other recent votes, including Brexit, as well as the Holy Alliance meetings and financial support for far-right movements, suggests this plan did not remain a dead letter in Dugin's book. The attempt to establish a Eurasian empire with Russia at its helm is being carried out not only through direct intervention in American and European societies and politics but through the skilled exploitation of our own weaknesses and mistakes. Putin and his cohort have so far proven to be excellent psychologists. To dismantle Western democracies, they needn’t expose themselves much. Through their bots, they push buttons tied to accumulated frustration and anger, offering each person exactly what they want emotionally—for some, a fight against liberal democratic values, for others, resistance to American policies and influence. They subtly nudge us toward what we instinctively want, and then we continue on our own, some more slowly, others with gusto. Right-wing populism and Pavlovian anti-Americanism on the political left are both nourished by the mistakes, inconsistencies, injustices, and delusions of Western liberal democracies. These include selfishness, ruthless economic interests, double standards, breaches of international law, and unrestrained neoliberalism, which in recent decades has created countless humiliated, marginalized, and angry citizens in the West. Not only is this worth condemning, but it is largely to blame for why the Kremlin finds it so easy to undermine Western liberal democracies. We will not save the liberal democratic model without deep geopolitical, societal, and economic changes. But we must recognize the difference between a system that, while imperfect and inconsistent in upholding its own humanistic and democratic values, still contains mechanisms of self-correction—through elections, independent judiciary, media, and civil society—and an ideology and regime that responds to all criticism with violence, proudly promotes nationalism, authoritarianism, hatred of minorities, contempt for democratic values, and dominance over other nations as its mission. I doubt my writing will change the minds of those who admire Putin’s ruthless challenge to democratic values. But I have a message for those who see him as a solution to the wrongs and injustices perpetrated by the West. I understand, respect, and in many ways share their outrage. But Putin is not the answer. His success would drag us from the rain into the boots of vampiric nationalist imperialism that sustains its power through suppression of democratic rights, aggression, and hatred toward critics and minorities. These tensions and manipulations reached a boiling point with Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. I too dearly wish the bloodshed would end soon. I support peace initiatives. But we must not forget that Russia is the aggressor, and Ukraine is fighting for its survival—just as we Slovenians did more than seventy years ago. If anyone, in the name of peace, has trouble supporting a Russian defeat, let them at least support Russia's withdrawal from Ukrainian territory. Any other outcome would mean a victory for the aggressor. A compromise where the wolf is fed, and the goat is blamed will not bring peace. The outcome of this war will determine the Europe and world we live in tomorrow. It is naive and dangerous to believe that Putin is using energy supplies to pressure Europe merely because of sanctions, and that lifting those sanctions would return things to the way they were. Can anyone really believe that if sanctions were lifted, Putin would again supply energy reliably and at low prices, thereby helping Western countries avoid social instability and crisis—which only play into his hands—while giving them time and opportunity to find alternatives and thus neutralize his most powerful weapon, supported by the invisible hand of the market and catastrophic panic-mongering? No, my friends. Lifting sanctions would only bring political and moral discredit to the European Union, while allowing Russian policy to selectively support those countries and politicians willing to bow to its aggressive imperialism. The consequences for Europe's future, stability, and security are not hard to imagine. In this aggression against Ukraine, I stand firmly with the victim—as a democrat, a European, a humanist, and above all, a committed anti-fascist. And I urge those who see Putin's Russia as a solution to the world's accumulated problems and injustices to reconsider. I don’t think they are fascists—on the contrary, I’m convinced they are not. Precisely because of that, I urge those who see themselves as today’s digital Spanish Republicans to critically assess whether, in bashing the EU, sanctions, liberal democracy, military aid to victims of aggression, and in applauding protests organized by the far right and Russian bots in European capitals, they haven’t inadvertently ended up on the wrong side in this never-ending struggle against fascism.

Right next to the fence on the north side of the White House in the U.S. capital lies Lafayette Park, named after the French aristocrat and hero of the American Revolution, the Marquis de Lafayette. Incidentally, it was across this park that former President Donald Trump walked in June 2020 after ordering security forces to violently disperse peaceful protesters, just so he could pose with an upside-down Bible in front of St. John’s Church on the other side. In the park stands a grand statue of the seventh U.S. President, Andrew Jackson, on horseback, bearing the inscription: "Our Union must be preserved." It is unknown whether Trump had the time to read that inscription during his walk, but even if he did, it clearly did not leave much of an impression. Long before that June day, and especially after January 6, 2021—when his supporters violently stormed the U.S. Capitol to try to prevent the certification of Biden's victory—Trump had already begun to do exactly what Jackson warned against: dividing the country and its citizens with lies, hatred, and attacks on constitutional institutions in a ruthless attempt to return to the White House, whatever the cost. Jackson made his now-famous statement at a dinner in 1830 in response to demands from Southern states for the right to nullify federal laws they deemed unconstitutional. It was about, what else, taxes. Jackson won that round, then died a little over a decade later. If he had known what would later happen to the Union he so cherished, he might have fallen off his horse. Fifteen years after his death, a bloody Civil War began. This time it wasn’t just about taxes but about the secession of Southern states unwilling to accept restrictions on slavery introduced by President Abraham Lincoln. Perhaps a point worth pondering for those who believe the right to self-determination is always inherently just and noble. Then, 175 years later, Trump walked past his statue. Today, the issue isn’t slavery per se, though the effective realization of Trump’s agenda—which fuels and divides American public life—would inevitably lead to a highly segregated society where certain groups—women, the lower classes, ethnic and social minorities, immigrants—would be pushed into a position of utter subjugation and marginalization without basic human rights. In a word: slavery. The June ruling by a Supreme Court packed with Trump appointees, which struck down constitutional protection for abortion rights, is just the latest, though not the only, step in that direction. Trump is not alone. He is clearly supported by "his" Supreme Court. Beyond the issue of abortion, what I find horrifying is the court's stance on the death penalty. Although most Americans oppose state-sanctioned killing, recent appeals from death row inmates regarding the inhumanity and cruelty of lethal injection were flatly rejected. The prevailing opinion came from Trump nominee Brett Kavanaugh, who argued that the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits cruel punishment, "does not guarantee a painless execution." Such inhumane cynicism is now part of American constitutional law. Trump is backed by most Republicans, whom he has coerced into blind obedience and the repetition of his blatantly stupid lies about "stolen" elections. Only his vassals can survive politically in the party. Anyone who resists is excommunicated. One of the latest to experience the consequences of resisting Trump’s lies and attacks on American democracy is Liz Cheney, the influential and ultra-conservative soon-to-be former representative from Wyoming. She now hints she might run for president herself. On the other hand, another potential Republican candidate, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, bans books and school programs promoting equality and human dignity. He plans to prohibit pension funds from considering environmental impacts when making investment decisions. He is supported by influential conservative religious organizations. Religion—or rather, a reactionary, incendiary, and aggressive distortion of Christianity known as white Christian nationalism—is a key weapon in Trump’s renewed march on American politics. Trump and the trumps—whether in Latin or Cyrillic script—pay no heed to the consequences of their actions. Only power matters. They speak solely to their base: those who feel, for various reasons, betrayed and forgotten. People who are afraid and buy into the lie that hatred, nationalism, selfishness, and discrimination bring safety and stability. Democracy needs a variety of views and opinions, but it also needs a common rational and civilizational framework. Principles and values that everyone—regardless of political stance—accepts as the foundation of a democratic and civilized society. Trump and his ilk not only reject those values, but they have also made tearing them down the centrepiece of their political agenda. The means is the end, and the end is the means. I just returned from a trip across the Eastern United States. Americans are, as a rule, extremely polite and kind. But beneath that courteous surface, something is simmering. Tensions and polarization are visible at every turn—in political signs on lawns, in slogans on shirts and hats, in reactions to questions about where you're from and what you're doing, in offhand comments about what they think of their own country. In university-town, post-hippie Ithaca in upstate New York, every store and restaurant displays signs proclaiming that women's reproductive rights are human rights. Just three hours' drive west in Pennsylvania, a kind elderly lady in a roadside diner asked where we were headed. When I said Washington, she recoiled. "It's full of criminals," she snapped, and rushed to tell her friends about the Europeans going to the swamp Trump had promised to drain. This fall, Pennsylvania will elect a governor. Everywhere you go, there are signs supporting far-right Trump ally Doug Mastriano, accused of antisemitism and espousing the most extreme positions on abortion, minority rights, and immigration. All this, of course, is not a deep analysis but merely a collection of personal impressions and anecdotes. But impressions are what they are. Driving past quaint houses with perfectly manicured lawns in the lush hills of Pennsylvania, I couldn’t help but recall a scene from the film Cabaret: a sunny afternoon in an idyllic beer garden on the German countryside, where cheerful people chat and laugh until a young, blue-eyed blond boy begins to sing a fanatical song, soon joined by everyone else. "Tomorrow belongs to me," they all sing. They looked so friendly. Comparing these latest impressions to a trip years ago at the start of Trump’s presidency, it is paradoxical that I left the U.S. more worried this time. Despite Trump’s victory then, there was widespread engagement and resolve to resist unacceptable ideas and policies. Today, those ideas have become an entrenched part of reality, even with a new occupant in the White House. Among critics, one senses resignation; the initiative lies with those who claim the future for themselves alone. I cannot shake the feeling that, in a confrontation with authoritarianism, democracy is powerless and lost. Its purpose is to uphold democratic rules and values, while authoritarians exploit the deliberate subversion of those rules for political gain. And thus, they seem to control the game, even when (temporarily) out of power. Not just in the U.S. Like many, I love to travel and always return filled with experiences, impressions, and emotions. This time, one of those emotions was sadness. I don’t know what the future holds for travel—a passion that burdens both the wallet and the environment. I love traveling in the United States. Some may criticize me for that and see it as proof of my pro-American stance, but that’s not true. What makes traveling in the U.S. fascinating is the abundance of cultural references, scenes, places, customs, cities, music, people, and buildings we've absorbed all our lives through film, music, and literature. Traveling in America is like traveling through those references—like walking through a movie. And not all movies are happy or funny. Some are sad. Some are frightening. This last one was especially troubling in terms of the future of that country—and the world.

Journalists going into politics is not a phenomenon unique to Slovenia. Before embarking on their political careers, such well-known leaders as Winston Churchill and Al Gore worked in journalism, as did such notorious politicians as the French far-right Éric Zemmour and Sarah Palin, who worked as a sports journalist before presidential candidate John McCain pulled her out of anonymity. Most would probably agree that it would have been better if Sarah had stuck to her first love, as she would probably have done less damage there, with all due respect to the journalistic profession. The recently deceased President of the European Parliament, David Sassoli, also worked as a journalist for many years, and among politicians still living and active, Boris Johnson must of course be mentioned. BoJo was a Brussels correspondent and columnist for the British Daily Telegraph. He wrote his last column for the paper just before the Brexit referendum, which was his springboard to the top of British politics, from which he recently fell so ingloriously. Johnson was the same kind of journalist as he is a politician: rotten and mendacious. But in Johnson’s case the immorality was not a consequence of his move from journalism into politics, but of his personality. So neither his case nor the other transfers mentioned are an argument for sweepingly condemning anyone who decides to take this step. There is no reason why a good journalist cannot also become a good politician. Things get complicated when a politician wants to return to journalism after his career, and this is precisely what bothers many commentators about the latest moves in Slovenia. Incidentally, this is apparently what Boris Johnson is thinking about these days, perhaps out of love for the journalistic profession, or perhaps also because the Daily Telegraph paid him 270,000 pounds a year for his weekly columns. With that money you can afford a lot of active holidays in Jezersko. Comparisons with other countries are interesting, but neither Churchill nor Sarah Palin, and still less Boris Johnson, can give us a definitive answer as to whether such transitions are acceptable or harmful—for journalism, for politics and for democracy. They are certainly always complicated and sensitive, above all because independent media in a democracy are one of the pillars of the system of oversight of politics. Moves from one status to the other, and especially back again, therefore raise legitimate questions about the risks to the system of oversight and safeguards without which democracy cannot function. In Slovenia’s case we also have the specific problem that we are a very small pond in which many fish know each other. The effectiveness of oversight of democracy here is objectively limited even if no journalist goes into politics. An even bigger problem in Slovenia is that politics has such a bad reputation. For many, politics really is a whore, as my late grandmother Anuncijata liked to say, and anyone who goes from journalism into politics does not take a job but, at least in the eyes of many, sells out. Politics has an extremely bad reputation in Slovenia. Anyone who enters it risks being marked forever. This is a serious problem, as it encourages negative selection of those to whom we entrust the running of the state. The problem is that we will not solve the bad reputation of politics by condemning journalists who go into politics or take jobs in it, but only by improving people’s trust in it. We need better politics and better politicians. To achieve this, one of the necessary conditions is that as many people as possible with knowledge, integrity and standing enter politics. Journalists included. The argument related to their role in overseeing politics cannot be taken as absolute. If the anathema on political engagement applies to journalists, why not also to judges and civil society activists? Police officers, doctors? Will we really get to a better democracy by sweepingly blocking the way to it for many people who are qualified and have already proved it through their expertise and principled conduct in their own field? In my opinion, that is not the right way. The sensitivity of such transitions is a reality, so individuals who choose to make them take on personal responsibility and must accept that their conduct will be monitored even more closely and carefully by the public. We also urgently need a series of systemic and social changes. The greatest responsibility lies with politics, which alone can regain lost trust and reputation. If, for such a large part of the public, politics remains nothing but a rotten puddle, then let us not complain that there are so many shady characters, village eccentrics and mediocrities in politics. The journalistic guild also bears great responsibility, as it must insist uncompromisingly on respect for the professional rules and ethics of its profession. Both regarding those who are “only” journalists and especially regarding the “special returnees” who would like to come back from politics into journalism. That does not mean that journalists should not have their own opinions and beliefs. In Slovenia we are trapped in a binary polarization between the concept of “independent” journalists without values or ideology and the concept of a “balanced” media space in which journalists are merely socio-political workers and obedient foot soldiers of one political option or another. The first is fiction; the second is the antithesis of democracy. There is nothing unusual or undemocratic about a journalist having political beliefs. The same goes for media outlets. For most media in developed democracies, it is known whether they lean left, center or conservative. What matters, of course, is that they understand the basic rules of journalism, such as the difference between reporting and opinion, and consistently respect journalistic ethics. For more than a century, the British Guardian has carried the motto “Comment is free, but facts are sacred” in its masthead. The problem arises when an individual or an outlet subordinates journalistic professionalism to ideology and writes at the dictation of its political godfather and master. Another big problem, not only for Slovenian journalism but for democracy in Slovenia, is the precariousness of the journalistic profession. Journalists in Slovenia generally have less trouble paying for active holidays in Jezersko than paying their bills. This is, on the one hand, a major existential threat to journalists and, on the other, a danger to democracy. Precariousness creates vulnerability to pressure. And as for moves into politics, journalists should decide on them because they believe they can still achieve and prove something in that field, not because otherwise they cannot survive or escape pressure, smears and threats. We will not have a better democracy in Slovenia by denying journalists a priori the possibility of going into politics, but when we manage to raise substantially the level of political culture, professionalism and integrity. Above all among politicians, but also in the media. We ourselves can do a lot for this too. After all, we still have the opportunity and the right to choose for ourselves whom we read, listen to, watch and vote for.

In December 2010, 26-year-old street vendor Tarek al-Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in protest against local government corruption in the Tunisian city of Ben Arous. His death sparked the Arab Spring—waves of protests and uprisings that spread across much of the Arabic-speaking world. We know how it ended. In Tunisia—the only country where a transition to constitutional democracy occurred—President Kais Saied is now consolidating all power through constitutional reform. Elsewhere, the outcomes were even worse—and bloodier. Yet in its early days, the Arab Spring brought hope for freer, more just societies in that part of the world. Messages of support, solidarity, and aid poured in. One of the first to respond was the Council of Europe, not just because these events were happening in our neighborhood, but because the Arab Spring reflected a yearning for societal change rooted in values that the Council itself upholds. In May 2011, the Council of Europe was preparing for its annual ministerial conference in Istanbul. Incidentally, this was the same conference where the Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence Against Women and Domestic Violence (Istanbul Convention) was opened for signature. In response to the developments across the Mediterranean, member states called for a decision on how to support neighboring countries. Everything was happening at the last minute. As an advisor in the Secretary General’s cabinet, I was tasked over the weekend with drafting a political declaration. Since I was on vacation in Ljubljana at the time, the text—two and a half pages defining the Council’s policy toward neighboring countries—was written in my mother’s kitchen in the suburbs. The declaration defined the Council’s role as offering flexible, context-sensitive support based on the needs of those countries. I included a sentence stating that cooperation with the Council of Europe could not be value-neutral, but should aim to strengthen pluralistic democracy, human rights, and the rule of law. That’s where things got complicated. Some countries felt the wording was too vague and demanded that any neighboring country wishing to cooperate with the Council explicitly commit to “respecting European values.” Likely well-intentioned, they were nonetheless deaf to concerns about how such phrasing might be received—especially in countries with bitter colonial histories, where the phrase “European values” doesn’t carry the same connotations. Even more problematic is the fact that the widely used term “European values”—employed by EU institutions, the media, and the public alike—runs counter to the idea that these values are supposed to be universal. Recall that the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights two years before the Council of Europe adopted its own European Convention. Claiming ownership over the concept of human rights is counterproductive—it plays directly into the hands of those who depict democratic values as Western imperialist manipulation. This is compounded by the West’s own hypocrisy and inconsistency in upholding those values—both internally and abroad—over the decades. A tragic paradox of that period, now seen in hindsight, is that many of the same European countries demanding commitments to “European values” from their Mediterranean neighbors were themselves, through misguided responses to the financial crisis and the dismantling of the social welfare state (a precondition for democratic values), laying the groundwork for the rise of populism and domestic assaults on those same values. Then came the moral collapse during the refugee crisis—a collapse that is still unfolding. Today, the “values” defining Europe are less and less democracy, human rights, and the rule of law, and more and more nationalism, intolerance of minorities, and authoritarianism. Those who say that we cannot understand—let alone counter—nationalist populism, especially in its violent form as seen in Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, without critically examining Western policies, are absolutely right. Over recent history, Western actions have often undermined the very values it professes to champion. Evidence that we haven’t yet reached a turning point—or have moved further away from one—can be seen in some of the responses to the war in Ukraine. In order to stop one despot from using energy as a weapon, we turn to Saudi Arabia for help. Out of the frying pan and into the fire. The moral outrage over the murder of Anna Politkovskaya and other Russian journalists doesn’t quite square with handshakes exchanged with the butcher of Jamal Khashoggi—just one of many examples. Yet I cannot agree with those who fail to recognize (at least in part) the current global malaise as a consequence of Western leaders’ failures—and instead fall for the populist trick of blaming democratic values themselves for problems born of those leaders’ hypocrisy and neglect. Those who reject liberal democracy because of Trump should, for consistency’s sake, stop believing in socialism because of Stalin. The narrative that liberal democracy is merely a tool of American hegemony and that Putin’s authoritarian, nationalist regime will create a fairer world order is a recipe for disaster—and bloodier conflicts ahead. A Russian victory in Ukraine would not just be a win for Putin, but a triumph for Trump and Trump-like figures around the world—regardless of their local differences—who share a vision of a global order based on raw power, hate, neoliberal or oligarchic plunder, the destruction of the welfare state, the environment, and international peace. In Slovenia’s increasingly bitter and polarized debate on Ukraine, the question of fundamental civilizational values is mostly absent. Arguments are rooted less in facts and more in emotionally charged "truths" gathered online. We’re shifting from a fact-based community to what George W. Bush’s advisor Karl Rove once proudly called the “faith-based community.” First with vaccines, now with Ukraine. In this swirl of emotion-driven discourse, we see bizarre alliances and arguments that would be laughable in another context. Anti-imperialists quoting Kissinger to downplay Russia’s aggression. Conservatives citing Žižek to condemn Putin—despite their ideological proximity. People so anti-American that they excuse everything Putin does, even the very same abuses they denounce in the U.S. or at home. An increasing number now see Putin’s nationalist, regressive vision as a justified response to the West’s liberal “decadence.” We must start talking about values again—based on facts, not feelings or conspiracy theories. Instead of excusing or enabling the blatant trampling of universal values, we must focus on resisting those who most endanger them—whether that’s Putin and his ilk or Western leaders whose hypocrisy, greed, and opportunism sabotage their credibility. Maybe we should return to the United Nations Charter, which established these values as the foundation for global coexistence, stability, and peace. If we’ve failed to uphold them so far, it’s not because the values were wrong—but because our commitment to them was weak. The UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights were born from a world war. Surely, they can help prevent the next one—if we honor them consistently. By the way, Article 51 of the UN Charter affirms every member state’s right to self-defense in the event of armed attack. Perhaps the first step toward a better world would be to fully respect that legal right—for Ukraine—and support its exercise of that right as dictated by international law, collective security, dignity, justice, and reason.
Contributions to the Biography of Vladimir Vladimirovich

On Friday, July 8, sixty-year-old Aleksei Gorinov, a lawyer and municipal councillor from Moscow, was sentenced to seven years in prison for "spreading false information" about the Russian army. His "crime" was a public statement at an April meeting of the municipal council of Moscow's Krasnoselsky district, in which he condemned the decision to organize a dance competition "while a war is taking place in Ukraine, where children are dying." More than two months of detention and the threat of a harsh prison sentence did not break Gorinov's rebellious spirit. During the trial, he held a sign in the glass cage that read: "Do you still need this war?" Gorinov is the first individual to be convicted under the draconian law passed by the Russian parliament less than a month after the start of the aggression against Ukraine, imposing strict penalties on anyone who "spreads false news" about Putin's "special military operation." His conviction is only the tip of the iceberg and a new warning to anyone daring to publicly criticize the official narrative of "denazification" of the neighbouring country. Next in line is Ilya Yashin, one of the few opposition politicians still remaining in the country. Yashin faces up to ten years in prison for discussing the massacres in Bucha on social media. Before Gorinov and Yashin, thousands of Russian citizens had already been arrested, detained, and sentenced to short "administrative" prison terms for peacefully protesting against the aggression in the early weeks of the war. Repression did not start with the war. "You must know that Russians are trying. Quietly, they go to prison for 10, 15 years," said members of the Pussy Riot collective during a recent concert in Ljubljana, where they performed as part of the Lesbian Quarter festival. Civil society in Russia has been completely dismantled through a ruthless and systematic campaign by the authorities that began years before February 24 of this year. Many civil society activists were forced to seek refuge abroad or fell silent at home. All influential human rights organizations have been labelled "foreign agents" or "undesirable organizations" by the Kremlin regime, meaning that any Russian citizen who cooperates with them risks imprisonment. The same has happened with the media. Those few that survived Putin's years-long crackdown, including the murders of several prominent journalists, shut down after the war in Ukraine began. For all these reasons, claims—also echoed by official Ukraine—that all Russian citizens are to blame for the war because they supposedly support Putin should be taken with caution. While opinion polls indicate he enjoys majority support, in a country like today’s Russia, one likely thinks twice before responding to an "anonymous" survey. The real picture is likely different.
