To understand why many Russian citizens condemn Putin’s policies, we must recall what he has been doing for over two decades—not just to neighbouring countries, but to Russian society and its citizens. Let us remember how Putin came to power. Just a month after Boris Yeltsin appointed the until-then-unknown FSB officer as prime minister, explosions rocked apartment buildings in Moscow, Volgodonsk, and the Chechen city of Buynaksk in September 1999, killing 300 people. At the end of September, Putin blamed Chechen terrorists for the bombings, unfazed by the fact that just a day earlier, local police had caught and arrested three FSB agents planting explosives in another apartment building in Ryazan. The official investigation later "concluded" it had been a drill. Mere coincidence, supposedly. Putin used the explosions as a pretext to bomb Grozny and start the Second Chechen War. Just a few months later, this propelled him into power when, on New Year's Eve 1999, Yeltsin appointed him as his successor. In the spring 2000 elections, Putin, still riding the wave of war-fuelled popularity, won with 53% of the vote. It is a lesson he seems eager to repeat today with the war in Ukraine. Whether or not Putin orchestrated the bombings remains an open question. But Andrei Kovalyov, a Russian dissident, chair of the Human Rights Commission, and a Duma member who led the investigation, was convinced he did. Kovalyov, whom I had the opportunity to meet personally, strongly opposed Russian aggression in Georgia in 2008 and the annexation of Crimea in 2014. In March 2010, he authored the manifesto "Putin Must Go." He passed away in August 2021 at the age of 91. Unlike the apartment bombings, the Beslan school siege in September 2004 and the Moscow theater hostage crisis in Dubrovka two years earlier were undoubtedly carried out by Chechen terrorists. Yet two facts stand out in both cases. First, the reaction of Russian security forces, which in both instances resulted in massive casualties. In Beslan, over 330 people died, mostly children; in Moscow, 170 of the 850 hostages perished. That many died due to the way the rescues were conducted is beyond dispute. Many Moscow hostages suffocated from gas released into the theatre, though the official investigation never identified who released it. Both tragedies were also used by Putin to further consolidate his grip on power. After Beslan, he "reformed" the constitution, stripped power from Russia’s regions, and reinforced what he called a "vertical of power." Following the Dubrovka tragedy, Putin, annoyed by critical reporting from the last independent national TV network NTV, replaced its leadership and completely subordinated its editorial policy. Media control was not limited to reshuffling staff but also involved shutdowns and murders of journalists. The best-known case is the October 2006 murder of Anna Politkovskaya, but the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), a partner of the Council of Europe’s platform for journalist protection, has documented 82 journalist killings in Russia, most of them after Putin came to power. Other sources cite even higher numbers. Mysterious deaths also befell political opponents and other individuals deemed dangerous by the Kremlin. Boris Nemtsov in 2015, Boris Berezovsky in 2013, Stanislav Markelov and journalist Anastasia Baburova in 2009, Sergei Magnitsky in 2009, Sergei Yushenkov in 2003, and Alexander Litvinenko, poisoned with radioactive polonium in 2006 in a London hotel. Litvinenko likely died because he and Berezovsky prepared a report blaming Putin for the September 1999 bombings. Berezovsky was one of the Russian oligarchs who opposed Putin and paid for it with his life. Others, like Mikhail Khodorkovsky, were imprisoned or exiled. The rest are loyal cronies who, in exchange for their allegiance, became obscenely wealthy at the Russian people’s expense and are allowed to enjoy their riches as long as they remain silent and financially support Putin and his policies. Even a brief and incomplete contribution to Vladimir Vladimirovich’s biography cannot omit his stance toward homosexuals—not because they are the only minority targeted by his authoritarian paradigm, but because homophobia, in alliance with the Russian Orthodox Church, has from the start been politically instrumentalized to justify and reinforce his domestic authoritarianism and the narrative of conflict between the "pure Russian nation" and the "degenerate liberal West." All of this is, of course, just a snapshot and far from a complete political profile of Vladimir Putin. But it is enough to conclude that his invasion of Ukraine was no tragic accident or response to external threats, but the logical culmination of his vision for Russia and its role in the world. The road to aggression against neighbouring states was paved by years of systematically destroying freedoms and oppressing Russian citizens. Putin is a man who launched a war to rise to power, and he evidently believes that only through war and conflict can he maintain and strengthen that power. From Chechnya, through Georgia, Syria, the annexation of Crimea, and now the full invasion of Ukraine. Those who, even with the best intentions, view Putin as some kind of modern Brezhnev, a gruff Soviet or Russian leader who, despite all his barking and blustering, retains a minimum of rationality and readiness for reasonable negotiation, cannot and must not ignore this fact. Putin is not Brezhnev. Conflict and war are the foundation of his regime. That does not mean we should not negotiate with him. On the contrary, every effort should be supported to end this senseless bloodshed as soon as possible. But there will be no lasting peace if negotiations begin with concessions at others’ expense—concessions that reward and embolden aggression—and with naive appeals to reason and moderation, which Putin lacks and openly despises. Even more should this record of "accomplishments" give pause to those who, in their own countries, staunchly defend democracy, political freedoms, equality, human dignity, media freedom, civil society, social justice, and the fight against corrupt elites, yet in the context of Russian aggression against Ukraine, explicitly or implicitly seek to relativize or even justify the raging fury and imperialist ambitions of a repressive autocrat, a corrupt oligarch king, a bigot, nationalist, and homophobe. Because, well, what about... In doing so, they not only betray their own principles but also all Russian citizens who have lost their freedom in opposing Putin’s policies, and some even their lives. People who see in Putin a leader who will punish the corrupt West and establish a new, fairer world order should seriously reflect on whom they are backing. "In Russia, we have a new Hitler," said Masha Alyokhina of Pussy Riot to The Guardian recently. Reductio ad Hitlerum? I dearly hope that’s all it is.

The Russian Federation became a member of the Council of Europe on February 26, 1996. Its path to membership was paved by a letter addressed to the organization by then-Russian leaders: President Boris Yeltsin, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, and the speakers of both chambers of the Russian parliament. In the letter, they formally committed that the Russian Federation would faithfully uphold its obligations as a member of the Council of Europe, as well as the specific requirements set by the Parliamentary Assembly as a condition of membership. Yeltsin and his associates promised, among other things, that the Russian Federation would resolve domestic and international disputes peacefully and refrain from all forms of threats or force toward its neighbours. They also pledged to resolve existing international border disputes in accordance with the principles of international law and with respect for existing treaties. Finally, Russia, through its top officials, condemned the concept of dividing foreign countries into two categories, treating some as spheres of special influence known as the "near abroad." We know what happened to those formal promises. Less than three years after champagne corks popped at the Palace of Europe in Strasbourg, explosions rocked residential buildings in Moscow. Then-unknown FSB official Vladimir Putin replaced Yeltsin and ordered that the internal conflict in Chechnya be resolved by highly unpeaceful means. You might wave this off, saying that international promises and treaties are just dead letters, and that in the events leading up to the war in Ukraine, everyone was violating them. Perhaps. But the final sentence, about the "near abroad," is key to understanding why the invasion of Ukraine happened and what is needed to end the war and establish lasting peace and stability. You might wave this off again, saying that the near abroad doctrine doesn't threaten Slovenia, since it concerns former Soviet republics and perhaps ex-members of the Warsaw Pact. Don't celebrate too soon. To understand how elastically Putin interprets this doctrine, recall his recent musings on Peter the Great and Russia's right to take what it considers its own. It is abundantly clear that Russia is also eyeing the Balkans—right at our doorstep, if you will. Debates on the war in Ukraine and our stance toward it are exhausting, but necessary. Exhausting because they are full of generalizations, oversimplifications, and attempts to discredit interlocutors when arguments run out. The debate is often reduced to a binary polarization between pacifists and Russophobes, as stated by the newspaper Delo. This is inaccurate and undignified. I firmly support Ukraine as the victim of Russian aggression, but I reject being lumped together with just about everybody who currently think similarly. I reject opportunistic anti-Putinism on Ukraine that otherwise shamelessly plagiarizes Putin's own ideological authoritarian paradigm rooted in nationalism, cultural warfare, and hatred of the different. But because this debate is necessary, helping shape public opinion and positions on a crisis that directly threatens us, I will now focus on what I agree on with other participants in the discussion, rather than just what divides us. I fully agree that the war should end as soon as possible, along with the unnecessary bloodshed and destruction of Ukraine. For the sake of Ukrainians, the thousands of young people dying on both sides of the front, and the broader security, economic, political, and social consequences of the war in Europe and the world. But to achieve lasting peace, we must understand why the war happened. Many openly or implicitly look for the reasons in Ukraine. It's true—Ukraine has many flaws, from corruption to far-right extremism to missteps in dealing with Russian-speaking citizens. But the picture isn't complete without analysing how Ukraine's stance on these issues has evolved over time, or comparing it with the extremism, corruption, and treatment of minorities by the aggressor. The Maidan protests ousted Ukraine's most corrupt president, who fled to Russia. Ukrainians then clearly showed they wanted a different kind of country and future. Arguing that there are extremists (in far greater numbers) on the other side, and that the other side treats minorities even more ruthlessly, does not excuse Ukraine's problems—but it does make it grotesquely cynical to use them to justify aggression. If Ukrainians want EU membership, they'll need to clean house—but not under bombs or foreign invasion. The argument that Russia is protecting "its own" in Donetsk and Luhansk collapses under scrutiny. The "liberated" cities have been reduced to rubble, and it is mostly conscripted local residents who are dying during this "liberation," used by Putin—untrained and unequipped—as cannon fodder for his imperialist goals. Many blame the West, especially the U.S. and NATO. I agree they carry heavy responsibility. The cynicism, hypocrisy, short-sightedness, and inconsistency of Western leaders over decades paved the way for Putin and his ideological copy-cats to ruthlessly pursue their aims: from the "war on terror" to CIA black sites and Guantanamo, to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the neoliberal gutting of the economic and social base without which liberal democracy cannot function. There will be no lasting peace or global stability until the West looks in the mirror and does some serious housecleaning. The West's sins paved the way for Putin, but they are no justification for his rampage and aggression. The world won't be fairer or safer if we replace hypocrites with rabid authoritarians. We must criticize the West. I understand critiques of the U.S. and NATO. But please—let's stop projecting noble motives onto a fascistic autocrat as if he were a Cyrillic Che Guevara. Putin's aggression against a neighbouring country is the most brutal assertion yet of the near abroad doctrine. He attacked Ukraine because, according to this doctrine, it is his to do with as he pleases. A quarter-century ago, the international community demanded that Russia renounce and condemn this doctrine. Today, large parts of the public—even in Slovenia—accept it and treat it as a legitimate reason for Russia to treat its neighbours like dirt and deny them the right to freely choose their own future. Many who express solidarity with Ukraine point to the West's hypocritical indifference to other wars and injustices, from the Palestinian question to the long-forgotten carnage in Yemen, for which a Western ally, authoritarian Saudi Arabia, bears responsibility. This is also evident in refugee policy, where solidarity is doled out according to religion and skin colour. The West has not shied from brutally pursuing its interests. We must condemn this. I agree it's shameful and intolerable. These injustices must be corrected—not tomorrow, but today. But not at the expense of Ukrainian victims and suffering. Let's fix all injustices, not excuse some with others. Let's reject the inverted cynicism of British defence Minister Rifkind during the Bosnian war, who condescendingly told MPs that helping Bosnia wouldn't be fair to Angola and Cambodia, which the world had already abandoned. I strongly support those striving for a world without weapons. But I advise caution in naively applying this noble goal to a conflict between a weaker defender and a much stronger aggressor. The only one who can end this war immediately is Putin—but there's no sign he intends to. If we have no control over the arms and actions of the stronger side, then denying help to the weaker is indirect military support for Russia. That's not a moral judgment—it's a fact. The claim that military aid to Ukraine prolongs the conflict is true only on the most cynical level. Without help, the aggressor wins. Ukraine's resistance is a national liberation struggle for survival. Peace at any cost—a peace that acknowledges and legitimizes Putin's imperial ambitions—would not only be disgraceful but would fail to bring peace. On the contrary, it would give Putin a springboard for further aggression and destabilization of the world. Putin attacked Ukraine because it's crucial to achieving his imperial policy. For years, he has used energy as a weapon to destabilize the world and reshape it to his liking. For a peace on his terms. A Pax Kremliana. With Ukraine, he now adds food to his arsenal. To achieve his goals, Putin is willing not only to kill every Ukrainian he can get his hands on and sacrifice thousands of his own young citizens, but also to starve half the world. He doesn’t even try to hide it. At the end of April, Kremlin mouthpiece RIA Novosti published an article titled "Russia Has Much More Terrifying Weapons Than Missiles to Use Against the West," accompanied by a photo of wheat stalks. Hunger—already likely inevitable—will kill millions and force even more to flee westward. This is not a side effect of the war in Ukraine. It is, from the start, one of its primary aims. We can imagine the consequences if we multiply the recent refugee crisis—which was exploited to bring illiberal authoritarians to power across the West—by ten. Peace at any cost, which would freeze the status quo, is Putin’s victory. From that moment on, the world will depend on the mercy or cruelty of a Kremlin autocrat who can pull the trigger whenever he pleases. Regardless of the consequences — or precisely because of them. And as of February 24, it’s more than clear he’s prepared to do just that.
Feeding the Crocodile and Other Lessons from the War in Bosnia

"Between April 1992 and October 1995, a country in Europe was destroyed. Tens of thousands of its inhabitants were murdered. More than a million were expelled, deported, or forced to flee in fear for their lives," reads the opening sentence of the 2001 book The Worst of Times by Brendan Simms, a Dublin-born professor of the history of international relations at the University of Cambridge. If it weren’t for the dates mentioned, many would likely think this quote refers to Ukraine. And not without reason. Historical parallels are always risky. They are never perfect, often misplaced, and not infrequently abused. But that doesn’t mean we can ignore them. The moment we stop critically comparing the present with the past, we stop learning from history — and expose ourselves to the risk of repeating its mistakes, even the most dangerous and bloody ones. Of course, Russia is not Serbia, nor are the Bosnian Serbs, through whom Belgrade waged its aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the same. Russia is a nuclear superpower. This fact justifies a degree of caution regarding direct involvement in the conflict in Ukraine. I agree that it’s wise to think twice before getting into a fistfight with a rabid bear holding a nuclear bomb in its paws. But the solution cannot be to pretend the bear is just a sulking teddy that needs comforting. Ukraine itself doesn’t realistically expect foreign military intervention. What it needs is firm international support in defending itself against a foreign aggressor — and military aid and equipment so it can defend itself. That’s why, in deciding how we respond to this crisis, we must not forget the lessons of the war in Bosnia. Let’s look at how Brendan Simms summarized the thinking of some of the highest and most influential British figures regarding the Bosnian conflict three decades ago: The West Is to Blame "The decision (by the European Community, at Germany’s initiative) to recognize Slovenia and Croatia collapsed the concept of a peace conference — there was no longer any leverage over the parties involved." Lord Carrington, former British foreign minister, NATO secretary general, and EC negotiator during the Bosnian war "If the parties seek to adjust borders, prior recognition may hinder them." Douglas Hogg, UK Minister of State for Foreign Affairs De-Revoltization "The Yugoslav army has a constitutional role in maintaining public order in cases of mass civil unrest." Mark Lennox-Boyd, senior official at the British Foreign Office The Serbs Are the Good Guys "One of the biggest obstacles was the demonization of the Serbs. Izetbegović himself committed some crimes to drag the Americans into the war. He was a terrible little man." Lord Carrington No Security Architecture Without Serbia "The British were somewhat pro-Serbian due to historical ties and remained so out of pragmatism. Serbia was clearly the biggest and most important, so it had to be kept onside — there was no agreement possible without it." Lord Carrington Everyone’s the Same "It is unwise to assign blame to only one side where all parties have committed horrific crimes." Jeremy Hanley, UK Minister of State for the Armed Forces "This isn’t a simple fight between good guys and bad guys. It’s a conflict of such inhumanity that the civilized world cannot comprehend it — and it cannot be blamed solely on the Serbs." Sir Nicholas Bonsor, Undersecretary of State for Foreign Affairs "It’s impossible to say which side is responsible for the shelling of Sarajevo." Baroness Chalker, UK Minister for Overseas Development "They’re all equally awful and equally bad — but there are more Serbs than the others." Lord Carrington Military Aid Only Harms the Weaker "Such a move would not help those it’s intended for — the Bosnian Muslims. On the contrary, lifting the arms embargo would tempt the Serbs and Croats to redouble their efforts and ensure that by the time more weapons arrived, the government forces would already be neutralized." David Hannay, UK Ambassador to the UN "Allowing more weapons into the region would only lead to many more deaths — civilians and soldiers, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs alike." Ivor Roberts, UK Ambassador to Belgrade Peace Has a Price "The Muslims would do well to accept the partition of the country as proposed by international negotiators and stop trying to change the outcome on the battlefield." Patrick Bishop, journalist for the Sunday Telegraph, summarizing views from the Foreign Office "There will be no peace in Bosnia until the land is divided." Lord Carrington While the circumstances of the two Bosnian war and the aggression against Ukraine are not identical, the similarity between the logic and arguments used by the British government in the early 1990s and those used today by advocates of peace at any cost — even at the expense of territorial integrity, the right to self-defence (UN Charter Article 51), and the survival of the Ukrainian state — is striking. Recently, the newspaper Delo characterized the division of opinion in Slovenia over how to resolve the Ukrainian crisis as a dispute between "pacifists" and "Russophobes." I believe that’s overly loose in the first case and extremely unfair in the second. Supporting Ukraine is not the same as hating Russians. Even less acceptable is labelling opposition to Putin’s nationalist imperialism and domestic authoritarianism as "Russophobia." In fact, if the aggressor wins, it will take Russians themselves a very long time to free themselves from Putin’s yoke — not to mention what that would mean for global security. I don’t believe that most of those labelled as pacifists by Delo have bad intentions or the cynicism and imperial arrogance that oozed from the rhetoric of British politicians and diplomats three decades ago. I believe they sincerely desire peace. It is right that we talk about this. The crisis is deep and complex, and no one has 100% of the answers. But I do believe these people should be aware that their arguments about Ukraine often echo the discourse we already heard in Europe under similar circumstances. And it was not without consequences. The war in Bosnia lasted longer, caused more destruction, and took more lives because proper help didn’t come in time. Had it arrived sooner, the world might never have heard of Srebrenica. And all who sincerely strive for peace should reflect on the words of former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who, in his report on the Srebrenica massacre four years after the war, sharply condemned the false moral equivalence through which international mediators and others viewed the Bosnian conflict. "For too long," Annan wrote, "there was a widespread belief that all sides bore equal responsibility for the atrocities. The arms embargo on the internationally recognized government of Bosnia and Herzegovina served only to freeze the military balance of power in the former Yugoslavia." He described the various diplomatic efforts as “appeasement.” I use the English term not to provoke editors or readers of Večer, but simply because I have not yet found a good Slovenian equivalent. To better understand what the UN Secretary-General meant, let me quote Winston Churchill: "An appeaser is one who feeds a crocodile — hoping it will eat him last." This is a truth that those seeking peace in Ukraine must not ignore. We will not achieve peace by closing our eyes to who Putin is and what he wants. Simms’s book focuses mostly on British politics at the time and its attitude toward the war in Bosnia, but that doesn’t mean the British were the only ones who contributed to prolonging the conflict. He also mentions UN bureaucrats who bent over backward not to provoke the Serbs — the strongest force in the region. Some UN officials even claimed that Sarajevo wasn’t technically under siege, that Serb shelling was often provoked by the Muslims, and that the Bosnian government frequently bombed or sniped its own people — allegedly to provoke Western intervention. Recall French President François Mitterrand’s visit to Sarajevo in June 1992. Debates over the motives behind this unannounced visit continue to this day — especially given France’s long historical sympathy for the Serbs, which influenced its Yugoslavia policy. Today, Boris Johnson, who covered the Bosnian war as the Sunday Telegraph’s Brussels correspondent, is one of the fiercest Western supporters of Ukraine, something Ukrainians deeply appreciate. Still, it’s not out of the question that his current passion may also be partly linked to domestic political troubles. This also invites comparison with recent visits to Kyiv by other leaders. The credibility of Johnson’s outrage over Putin’s human rights violations and breaches of international law must be weighed against his own behaviour toward those very values — and not just his. Simms’s book title is a play on words that evokes "The Finest Hour" — how the British remember the start of WWII under Churchill’s leadership, when they did what they would later deny Sarajevo’s legitimate government. Slovenia won its own finest hours — once during the partisan resistance, and again in the war for independence. Principle and responsibility for peace and international law demand that we also recognize Ukraine’s right to defend itself — and that we help it in every way we can.

On May 24 this year, in the small Texas town of Uvalde, 18-year-old Salvador Ramos first shot his grandmother at home and then went to the school he had once attended and shot 19 children aged ten and eleven, and their teachers. The American public was once again, as so many times before, shocked, appalled and helpless. Many once again, as so many times before, took refuge in thoughts and prayers. And once again, as so many times before, warnings were heard that the tragedy must not be politicized. “Politicizing a tragedy” is an expression the American gun lobby and politicians use to prevent debate about why there have already been more than 230 mass shootings in the United States this year, and about why any 18-year-old can buy an assault rifle at the local store, without any check on whether he intends to shoot empty cans, grandmothers or ten-year-old children. And then, once again, as so many times before, Paul Gosar, a congressman from Arizona, chimed in, describing the killer as a “transsexual leftist illegal alien,” so the left-wing rabble should keep quiet, since he was one of theirs. Gosar simply made this up. Ramos, like most of his victims, was a Spanish-speaking American citizen. But the message is clear: why restrict real, white Americans’ access to guns if the “beaners” are shooting each other? Paul Gosar is not an unknown name in Slovenia. Three years ago, this gentleman received the Golden Order of the Republic of Slovenia for services in the international diplomatic field from President of the Republic Borut Pahor. In the President’s opinion, Paul Gosar deserved the highest state decoration for his “contribution and cooperation in strengthening relations between the Republic of Slovenia and the United States of America, for strengthening Slovenian-American friendship and further closer partnership between the two countries,” as the President’s office wrote on its website. Paul Gosar. Congressman and former dentist from Arizona. Gosar, who is “sincerely proud of his Slovenian roots,” but who did not even wait for the blood of 21 victims to dry before exploiting the tragedy for yet another hateful outburst against people of different roots, political beliefs and sexual orientation. Gosar, who “strives to preserve the memory of his Slovenian origin and mentions it in official appearances,” but whom even his own family has disowned because of his “racism, corruption, ignorance and hatred.” In the 2018 election, six of his nine siblings appeared in a campaign ad for Paul’s opponent, imploring voters for God’s sake not to vote for their extremist and racist brother. Incidentally, dear Mr. President, Paul’s siblings are also of Slovenian descent. If anyone in that family deserves the highest Slovenian state decoration, it is they, for their courage and determination in rejecting intolerance and standing up for values that, as you never fail to mention, you yourself swear by. Paul Gosar, who, in the President’s opinion, “participated with particular commitment in the establishment of the friendship group in the US House of Representatives,” took part with similar particular commitment, last year and this year, in white nationalist gatherings organized by Nick Fuentes, a veteran of the 2017 neo-Nazi rally in Charlottesville. Whether our compatriot from Arizona appeared before the assembled flower of American neo-Nazism, amid loud chanting in support of Hitler and Putin, decked out with the regalia of the Slovenian Golden Order for services on the international diplomatic stage, the American media did not report. We are lucky that they evidently aren’t much interested in either President Pahor or his Golden Order. Paul Gosar, our man in the US Congress, who is now being investigated by that same Congress over his alleged involvement in preparing the violent protests and the attack on the house of American democracy on January 6, 2021. Our pride from Arizona was in contact several times in the days before the attack with the extremists, to whom he openly promised a pardon on Twitter in advance. Paul Gosar, vice-chair of the Slovenia friendship group in the US House of Representatives, whom even the leadership of his own party disowned after his latest appearance at Fuentes’s neo-Nazi gathering. “There is no place in the Republican Party for white supremacists or antisemitism,” Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell snapped at our honoree. Being so extreme that you manage to derail the leadership of a Republican Party sunk in Trump’s cesspool is an achievement of a special kind. Paul Gosar, who offered to replace John McCain in the US Senate just hours after McCain announced that he had an incurable brain tumor. I don’t know what the foreign-policy strategy for the future development of Slovenia’s relations with the US is, but my advice would be not to rely too much on the friendship group in Congress. If the image of our country in the US Congress is shaped by what decent members of Congress think of Paul Gosar, we can be seriously worried. So what! our President might retort; most of the misdeeds mentioned above date from after April 19, 2019, when Gosar received the highest Slovenian state decoration. But, Mr. President, Paul Gosar was not born yesterday. Paul Gosar is a veteran of racism, extremism and hatred. Paul Gosar did not wake up one morning with the highest Slovenian decoration on his pajamas and say to himself, OK, I’ve got this now, from now on I can hate and behave like a pig to my heart’s content. Our President invited, hosted and honored a man whom no other politician with any self-respect would touch with a bargepole, let alone decorate. Perhaps he didn’t know who he was. Perhaps. But even if it was a slip and the President simply ran out of time to Google whom he was decorating, that does not explain why Paul Gosar, after all the racist, extremist, indecent and anti-democratic outbursts of the last three years, still wears the highest Slovenian decoration today. Thoughtlessly decorating a notorious racist might still be counted as a mistake; persisting in that decision raises the suspicion of a deliberate act. The first is embarrassing; the second is dangerous. Dangerous because it continues the process of normalizing and legitimizing the most extreme forms of right-wing culture war in Slovenian politics, which, under the pretext of respecting absolutely all opinions, including the most despicable, imports American alt-right ideology to us, sometimes translated from Hungarian, sometimes directly from Arizona or Palm Beach. The fight against all social minorities, homophobia, hatred of difference, hatred of migrants, manipulation and exploitation of fear and insecurity, trampling on democratic values and the rule of law, denial of the right to abortion, the fight against gender equality. That is the discourse of our compatriot Paul and his extremist cronies, including Slovenia’s son-in-law, who of course holds Gosar in high esteem. But Paul Gosar is not appreciated only by former President Trump and evidently still by President Pahor. He is also esteemed by part of Slovenian politics. His lie about the massacre in Texas, which Gosar later deleted out of fear of the appalled reactions of the American public, was immediately retweeted by one of the members of the National Assembly, otherwise a known fighter against the danger of “cultural Marxism,” which is of course a staple in the discourse of white supremacists, racists and neo-Nazis. For the uninitiated, “cultural Marxism” is a far-right conspiracy theory with antisemitic undertones, which the American far right began reviving a decade or two ago from the ashes of Nazi slogans about “cultural Bolshevism.” Elsewhere in the world, the fight against “cultural Marxism” is talked and written about by characters like Breivik and Tarrant, who used it to justify their mass murders; here, it is babbled about in parliament. Dear Mr. President, the joke wore thin long ago. Awarding a decoration to a blatant racist and bigot is, of course, not the only cause of the moral mess we have got ourselves into, partly by tolerating and justifying the undermining of basic civilizational and humanist values in Slovenian society, but it is certainly one of its symptoms. You have a few months left to correct this disgrace and strip the gentleman of the Golden Order for services. We know you promised not to be a moral authority, and you have kept that promise consistently, but you don’t even need moral authority in this case. A little elementary decency would be enough for a minimum of hygiene. It won’t solve all our problems overnight, but it can help the state, its citizens, and you too, dear Mr. President, to look at ourselves in the mirror in the morning with a little less embarrassment.

In the United States, differences between political ideologies are typically measured by levels of fiscal and social conservatism or liberalism. With some terminological adjustments—since many on the European left or right react strongly to the term liberalism, in any form or context—we can essentially define ideological currents in Europe similarly. The further right one moves, the stronger fiscal and social conservatism becomes; the further left, the more policies emphasize solidarity, inclusion, concern for all social groups, the public interest, and corresponding tax policy. Many therefore conclude that entrepreneurs fare better under right-wing governments, while people with lower incomes, students, pensioners, and the socially vulnerable do better under left-wing ones. That’s generally true. Generally, because right-wing populism is not averse to distributing public funds—but usually does so out of political self-interest rather than to strengthen the welfare state. Also because comparisons between left and right over time reveal, for example, that workers, pensioners, or students in Germany often fared better under the conservative Konrad Adenauer than decades later under the social democrat Gerhard Schröder. Similar conclusions could be drawn across much of Western Europe. The reason is simple. The post-war European social model—which also underpins European integration—was largely established by conservative leaders and Christian democrats. It was based on the welfare state: a society whose economic, fiscal, institutional, and political systems were rooted in solidarity and the social well-being of all citizens. This doesn’t mean that political consensus existed on all key societal issues. Far from it. Left-wing parties then, as now, emphasized greater solidarity and redistribution of wealth. But even right-wing leaders understood and supported the imperative that society must care for all citizens. The European welfare state was not just inclusive—it was founded on public healthcare, education, and support for the socially vulnerable. This approach was driven not only by moral convictions but also by rationality and pragmatism. European leaders of all stripes had firsthand experience with the consequences of economic crises, social inequality, polarization, and the build-up of public anger. They remembered 1930s Europe and faced the rise of the Soviet Union—whose inefficacy in creating a workers’ paradise they could not yet foresee. Today, some use this fact to argue that post-war conservatives built the welfare state only out of fear of communism. Even if that were true, it doesn’t invalidate the Western welfare state model. It simply shows that Soviet communism was a disastrous response to a genuine societal need for social justice and stability—needs without which progress and sustainable prosperity are impossible. Post-war European politicians also understood the deep connection between the welfare state and political order. After the trauma of Nazism and World War II, that order was founded on liberal democratic values—human rights, political freedoms, pluralism, and democratic rule of law. Democratic rule of law means not only that citizens must obey laws (a principle found in authoritarian regimes too), but also that the state must be held accountable and operate within clearly defined limits. Liberal democracy’s values should not be a matter of political polarization but a shared civilizational foundation for pluralistic democratic society. And they can only be realized within a socially just society. This understanding of the indivisibility of political freedoms and social rights is reflected in most democratic constitutions and international human rights instruments. The preamble of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (adopted in 1948 in Paris) affirms the commitment to "fundamental human rights, the dignity and worth of the human person, and the equal rights of men and women," as well as to “social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom.” This doctrine of indivisibility led to the expansion of the European Convention on Human Rights with the European Social Charter (1961, revised in 1996). The logic is simple: freedom of expression or religion means little to someone who is homeless or hungry. The Charter expanded international protection to include housing, health, education, workers' rights, employment, reduced working hours, equal pay, parental leave, social security, and protections against poverty, exclusion, and discrimination—including for migrants and people with disabilities. This wasn’t a leftist revolution, but a consensus among ideological opposites united by liberal democratic values. Of course, not all European countries embraced this indivisibility. While membership in the European Convention on Human Rights is mandatory for Council of Europe members, only 35 of 46 have ratified the 1961 Social Charter. Just 16 accept collective complaints, which give the Charter real enforcement power. Even fewer have ratified the 1996 revised version. Why? There are many reasons—but a key one is Margaret Thatcher. Along with Ronald Reagan, she seized the fall of the Soviet Union as a chance to break free from the “shackles” of social justice. In came neoliberalism: full freedom for capital, minimal taxation, minimal state, and minimal public sector. Her famous line—“There is no such thing as society, only individuals”—captured this mindset. And her influence extended beyond conservatives to centrists and center-left leaders like Schröder and Blair, and others who explored the “third way.” Since the 1980s, we’ve been waiting for wealth to “trickle down” from the few who hoard it in neoliberal economies. It hasn’t. What we’ve gotten instead are disillusioned masses, growing inequality, social tensions, and illiberal populism. So where does Slovenia stand in all this? Formally, we are among the countries committed to the indivisibility of political and social rights. We’ve ratified both European Social Charters. Article 2 of our Constitution declares that Slovenia is a social state. But our commitment is mostly formal. In practice, the social state has become a subject of political polarization. While in much of Europe—even among politicians—people are realizing that wealth doesn’t trickle down but only accumulates upward, and that neoliberalism threatens European democracy, many in Slovenia still cling to clichés about the invisible hand of the market and the delicate birds of capital. Any advocacy for social justice is immediately branded as extreme leftism or communism. A false conflict is fabricated between the social state and a successful market economy. Investors are sought who care only about executive pay—not infrastructure, schools, healthcare, environmental protection, or anything a serious long-term investor should value. The height of absurdity was an attempt to declare two left-leaning parties unconstitutional for advocating implementation of Article 2 of the Constitution. Not that there's anything wrong with caring about constitutionality—far from it. We certainly shouldn’t let political parties freely undermine citizens’ constitutionally guaranteed rights. Fortunately, we have a Constitutional Court that can distinguish legal substance from populist weeds. That said, proposals by the political left to strengthen the social state are not the only legitimate ones. It’s perfectly valid to disagree with them. Article 2 of the Constitution, like others, allows multiple paths—so long as none violate the Constitution or prevent its values from being realized. In other words, social justice does not justify abolishing property rights or free enterprise. But the reverse is also true: property and enterprise must not be pursued in ways that dismantle the social state. Balancing constitutional values requires legal literacy, political culture, and commitment to democratic principles. As long as we remain within constitutional bounds, we can and should debate freely—without insults, disqualifications, or hysterical appeals to the court. In a democracy, it’s the voters who decide how constitutional values should be pursued. Long live the social state, individual freedoms, and pluralistic democracy.

In the rich collection of media platitudes about this and that in politics, the one about elections being a celebration of democracy ranks quite high on my personal list of the most misguided. Not because elections are unimportant, but precisely because they are important. For democracy, elections are not a holiday but a working day. On election day, we neither celebrate nor commemorate democracy. In elections we put democracy into practice and lay its foundations. And speaking of foundations, anyone who has ever built a house, a garden shed or a skyscraper knows that you can’t afford carelessness and mistakes if you want the structure not to sag, crack or collapse in on itself at the first serious load. I have been to many elections in my life. First as an active citizen, old enough to remember the times when we could vote but could not choose, so I conscientiously exercise my constitutional right and civic duty every time. In the first part of my career, I also took part as an observer in many elections in various European countries. I did this at the first elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the signing of the Dayton Agreement, when we traveled there on American military aircraft because there were no regular flights yet. I observed several elections in Albania, including those after the great crisis in the country that followed the collapse of the pyramid savings schemes. At that time some political grandees underlined the points of their election programs with bursts from Kalashnikovs, but what has stayed most in my memory is a long night we spent in a hovel high in the Albanian mountains. There, the chairman and vice-chairman of the polling committee, from the Socialist Party and the Democratic Party, suspiciously examined every ballot paper and argued about whether it was valid or not. It took so long because they had only one pair of glasses between them. When, sometime around four in the morning, I yawned widely once again and hinted that it was time to return to the hotel, my boss, the British parliamentarian Russell, replied that it was out of the question. “Elections are a serious matter and every vote counts,” he told me sharply. Most of my observation experience was in countries with very short experience of democracy. Voting took place in exceptional circumstances, in countries suffering the consequences of war or major social crises. We observed and saw everything possible and impossible. From creative counting of ballots and the presence of armed men at polling stations to less serious but still dubious electoral practices such as family voting, in which, for example, the head of the family votes for his wife, children, parents, father-in-law, mother-in-law and sister. Given everything I saw and experienced, it is no wonder that by comparison my experiences of elections in Slovenia were downright boring. Nothing unusual ever happened there. And I was always very proud of that. This time, unfortunately, it is different. Given everything that has happened in recent weeks and days, I can’t help thinking now and then of experiences from countries that were only just learning democracy. And often had serious problems learning it. I posted the ballots that members of my family received from Slovenia at the last minute at the local French post office on Saturday, April 23. Now I can only keep my fingers crossed that, despite the holidays, they will make it back to Slovenia in time and be counted in the end rather than ending up in the bin. “Elections are a serious matter, every vote counts,” as Russell said. And not only does every vote count; everything must also be done to give every adult citizen the opportunity to exercise their constitutional right and vote. Whether this fundamental condition for free and fair elections was met in this year’s elections in Slovenia is still an open question. A lot happened in the weeks and days before the elections. We have had some problems for some time. Evidently, the legal deadlines and procedures are inadequate, as they cause systemic problems, which this time we aggravated with some ill-considered moves. These things will need to be regulated by law as soon as possible, certainly before the next elections. The question arises of whether the date chosen for the elections by the President of the Republic was appropriate, since even a glance at the calendar would have told him that it was a day squeezed between the Easter and May Day holidays, and that there was therefore a high risk of delays both in sending postal items abroad and in their return to Slovenia. We can also be critical of how we responded to holding elections during the pandemic. We are not the first country that has had to find answers on how to enable all citizens to vote in exceptional circumstances. What is striking is that in most cases we chose options that were detrimental to exercising the fundamental constitutional right to vote. In France, presidential elections are taking place in the same period. On Sunday, all French citizens could vote, including those who had tested positive for Covid-19, since appropriate sanitary protocols were in place at polling stations. In France there is a political consensus that, in the current circumstances, the risk to public health is smaller than the danger to democracy posed by a not insignificant share of voters being unable to vote. We decided otherwise, and what is striking is that we have more restrictions on exercising the right to vote than on the right to visit shopping centers without masks, Covid certificates or other protective measures. Then we created confusion over medical certificates that doctors refuse to issue. Then the mistakes of an employee of the National Electoral Commission. Then the shifting of responsibility from the Electoral Commission to the Slovenian Post Office—and back—over who is to blame for the ballots being sent abroad so late that many Slovenian citizens living abroad will not be able to vote this time, at least not in a way that would ensure their vote is counted in the final result. The communication of those responsible about all these complications was often arrogant and disrespectful towards voters and democracy. Even if, for most people, and I hope also for me and my family, it works out in the end by a hair’s breadth, it was still unnecessary and caused plenty of resentment, anger and distrust of institutions. And without trust in institutions, democracy cannot function. Incidentally, part of the commentariat on social networks reacted to these shenanigans by asking why people living abroad have the right to vote in Slovenian elections at all. My answer is that a great many Slovenian citizens live abroad, having left their homeland for various reasons, many related to the fact that Slovenia is not North Korea but is economically, politically and institutionally embedded in international networks and economic and other cooperation. Many have left in recent years for jobs related to EU membership. Abroad there are many top experts and also successful athletes we like so much to boast about. To them and other Slovenians living abroad, as to all Slovenian citizens, the Constitution guarantees our constitutional rights, including the right to vote. I am not a supporter of conspiracy theories, so without evidence I will not throw around accusations of deliberate manipulation and restriction of the possibility to vote. Most of the mistakes were probably not intentional, and I have no evidence that they were politically motivated. The main criterion for assessing slips in electoral procedures is, of course, whether they decisively affected the final result. In the hope that this will not be the case, it is already clear today that in preparing the elections we allowed ourselves so many mistakes and so much sloppiness, even if unintentional, that as a country with more than three decades of experience of democracy we should be thoroughly ashamed. Despite all the ups and downs, I believe that by the day you read this we will have a newly composed parliament with full legitimacy. That is very important, but not enough to breathe a sigh of relief. With all the shenanigans we allowed ourselves in conducting this election, we further disappointed and angered many citizens, and thereby deepened the already low trust in institutions, politics and, in the end, democracy. Many, not entirely unjustifiably, were left with a bitter aftertaste and the feeling that politics is merely a circus (to which some debates and the behavior of some politicians contributed greatly) and a kitchen they have no influence over. Without voters who trust political institutions, there is no functioning democracy. If we treat their constitutional rights the way we did this time, some will be even more receptive to alternatives to democracy that are based not on free and fair elections but solely on the authoritarian argument of power and might. If we are serious about wanting a functioning democracy in Slovenia, then we must speak critically about all the mistakes and weaknesses and start correcting them. The day after these elections, not the day before the next ones. More than celebration, democracy and its fundamental rules need competence, responsibility and respect.
Civil Society, Foreign Agents, and Other Enemies of the State

Without civil society, there is no democracy. That is why the right to association is protected by Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. This right can only be limited under very strict and narrowly defined conditions. The fact that civil society often annoys those in power is not among the exceptions that would justify measures against it. And yet, more and more rulers across Europe are having increasing trouble with this. The trendsetter was — who else — Russian President Vladimir Putin. On Valentine’s Day in 2013, Vladimir Vladimirovich addressed Russian intelligence officials to activate a law adopted a few months earlier on “foreign agents.” “Any direct or indirect interference in the internal affairs of the Russian Federation by foreign agents is unacceptable,” he told the gathered domestic agents on the holiday of love. Smert shpionam — as Ian Fleming would put it. From that day forward, all civil society organizations in Russia that were “funded from abroad” and engaged in “political activity” were required to register as ‘foreign agents’, submit to special financial oversight, and label every publication with a state-mandated self-denunciation. The law didn’t explicitly ban their activities, but the stigma, which carries extremely negative connotations in Russia, effectively crippled them. Domestic donors withdrew, state-controlled media attacked them relentlessly, and most critically, people became afraid to engage with them or collaborate. The law was designed to grant the regime maximum arbitrariness in defining both the “foreign” nature of funding and what qualifies as “political” activity. Russia’s Ministry of Justice, for example, labelled funds from the Council of Europe as foreign — even though Russia was still a full member at the time and had contributed to that very budget. The definition of “political activity” was even more arbitrary — essentially a label the state could slap on anyone it disliked. Some NGOs tried to comply with the law, often with little success; some disbanded themselves, others persevered — until later legislation on “undesirable organizations” gave the Kremlin the power not only to disable but to outright ban civil society groups and threaten prosecution for anyone working with them. A few NGOs moved their operations abroad. One of them was the Moscow School of Political Studies, renamed in 2012 — in a failed attempt to dodge the foreign agents law — to the Moscow School of Civic Education. Founded in 1993 in the kitchen of Lena Nemirovskaya and her husband Yuri Senokosov — she an esteemed art historian, he a PhD in philosophy — the school was born from the failed coup attempt against Mikhail Gorbachev in August 1991. In just a few years, their kitchen project became a respected institution. Its mission was simple: Democratic transition requires people who understand democratic values, the rule of law, and human rights. Over nearly two decades, more than 15,000 individuals from government, political parties, media, civil society, and business were trained in its seminars held in an old Soviet hotel in Golitsyno near Moscow. Under Boris Yeltsin, the school was even a partner of the state, a symbol to the outside world of Russia’s democratic commitment. It developed a vast network of prestigious partners at home and abroad and inspired similar initiatives in other post-Soviet and Eastern European countries. The model was always the same: education and dialogue on the values and skills needed in a democracy — in cooperation with the Council of Europe, and, at least initially, with state support. But then things began to change — first, as mentioned, in Russia. Yeltsin stepped down in 1999, replaced by Putin, who had a very different view of both democracy and civil society. Yesterday’s allies in democratization became first a nuisance, then a threat, and finally outlaws. What began in Russia soon spread elsewhere. The Council of Europe’s political schools have never changed what they do: they still support and educate for democracy. What has changed is how some European politicians now see democracy. Yesterday’s allies are now Enemy Number One. A few years ago, during a directors’ meeting of all schools in Ljubljana, we discussed changing the name — partly because of the Russian experience. “How about ‘Academy for Democracy’?” I suggested. “For God’s sake, don’t mention democracy,” came the reply. “It’ll just get us in more trouble.” Democracy — at least the kind based on the European Convention on Human Rights — is no longer a societal consensus in many parts of Europe. The pattern is the same everywhere; the only difference is intensity. Here’s how it usually goes: Phase One: Everyone is for democracy; democracy is for everyone. Civil society is a partner to political authorities, who at least publicly profess support for democratic principles and active citizenship. But since those in power often used these democratic slogans sloppily — one hand in the till, the other with fingers crossed — they paved the way for: Phase Two: Anti-liberal populism. This is where Putin’s distinction between “social” and “political” activity appears. In the populist worldview, civil society may care for the weak — but must not question the systemic causes of poverty or propose solutions. In this logic, liberal democracy is no longer seen as a shared civic value, but just one political ideology among many. Thus, advocating for democracy — though protected by the constitution — is now labelled “political activism” or even “partisan bias.” This opens the door to stigmatization, suppression, or outright bans. In this paradigm, it becomes imaginable to prosecute someone for reading the constitution in front of parliament, or for encouraging voter turnout. When this starts happening, democracy is in trouble. Phase Three: Full-blown authoritarianism. Civil society and NGOs no longer exist. Only foreign agents and enemies of the state remain. The circle is complete. No democracy. No freedom. Authoritarianism leads to repression, which can — ultimately — lead to aggression, both internal and external. Russia’s war in Ukraine did not happen by accident. It is a brutal but logical step in a long descent into Putin’s rabid, nationalist authoritarianism. We see where it leads. But we mustn’t forget how it started: with the dismantling of political freedoms, corruption and cronyism, the persecution of independent media, political opposition, and civil society. We mustn’t forget that on Valentine’s Day 2013, civil society in Russia became a “foreign agent” and Enemy Number One, simply for its “political activity.” The Moscow School can no longer operate in Russia. Its seminars are now held abroad — with partner institutions and universities from Berlin to Oxford. Until recently, hundreds of participants from across the Russian Federation still attended, despite the risks and costs. A few years ago, I spoke at one of their conferences at a hotel on the outskirts of Stockholm. At the end of the event, we found ourselves in a small room, passing around a bottle or two of vodka, wrapped in cigarette smoke — like old parties in Ljubljana’s student dorms. “Ah, Matjaž,” they told me, “it’s beautiful here, but Golitsyno was even better. You must come. When we return to Golitsyno…” That’s why I always accepted their invitation — the energy, inspiration, and deep admiration for people who, even in the most difficult circumstances, never gave up fighting for shared democratic and civilizational values, and never lost the courage or hope that decency, humanity, and reason would eventually prevail. Despite everything. Until February 24, 2022. Until Phase Three.

In February 1945, the Allied leaders — Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill — gathered in the seaside resort of Yalta in Crimea, just a missile’s throw from today’s devastated and martyrized Mariupol. The central item on the conference agenda was the demilitarization and denazification of Germany. Their goal — to eliminate Nazi parties, institutions, organizations, laws, and cultural influence from German public life — rested on the determination that top political and military leaders of the Third Reich should be held accountable before an international tribunal. Karma is a bitch. So is history, sometimes. Who would have thought that Putin’s bloody march toward the “demilitarization and denazification” of Ukraine, which began eight years ago with the occupation of Crimea, could end in a fashion prepared on that very same Crimea seventy-seven years ago by his infamous predecessor and increasingly apparent role model — Josif Vissarionovich Stalin. Just a few years ago, comparisons between Putin and Stalin might have seemed superficial — a kind of Cyrillic “reductio ad Hitlerum.” Not anymore. Vladimir Vladimirovich has done everything in his power to make such comparisons — not just in Cyrillic but also in Gothic script — entirely relevant. In a 2017 interview with his Hollywood admirer Oliver Stone, Putin warned that "excessive demonization of Stalin is an attack on the Soviet Union and Russia." Though he added, of course, that the horrors of Stalinism should not be forgotten. At the time, The Washington Post assessed that these statements revealed how Putin sees himself as a softer, Stalin-lite version of his authoritarian predecessor — inheriting all his virtues, but none of his sins. Patriotism and the cult of a strong leader — without the paranoia. Well, there’s little softness left now. Putin is catching up with his idol even in sins, and at full speed. The Russian public has followed suit. According to data from the independent Levada Center, the percentage of Russians who felt “respect” for Stalin rose from 29% in 2018 to 41% in 2019. Stalin's approval rating regarding his role in Russian history also grew, reaching 70%. In the same poll, 46% agreed that the "successes of the Soviet era justify the human losses of Stalinism." These figures from three years ago help explain today’s high public support for Putin’s “special military operation.” That support is not merely the result of censorship or a lack of information — it's also the result of years of propaganda, pressure, and disinformation. Yes, many Russians oppose the war — and they deserve recognition, especially for doing so under risk of great personal harm. But it’s also true that this is not just Putin’s war. A significant majority of the Russian public supports the aggression — not just because they’re unaware of what's truly happening (aside from Russian casualty numbers), but because they agree with the goals Putin outlined in his sinister speech the morning of the invasion: “Demilitarization and denazification” of Ukraine as euphemisms for punishing and annihilating a nation that, according to the fanatic in the Kremlin, has no right to exist — because “historically,” it never existed in the first place. Here lies another parallel between Putin and Stalin. What we’re witnessing in recent weeks (and really, years) is not the Kremlin’s first attempt to subjugate and punish Ukrainians. In the early 1930s, Stalin's “special agricultural operation” caused the death of millions, mostly Ukrainians. They died of hunger — just like survivors in Mariupol are dying of hunger today. Historians still debate whether Holodomor was a crime against humanity or a genocide. But one fact is clear: it was a deliberate act by Stalin’s regime to starve into submission those Ukrainians deemed not sufficiently loyal to the Soviet state. Putin’s psychopathological evolution from Stalin-lite to full-blooded Stalin was fully revealed in his March 16 speech, in which he declared that the “Russian people will always be able to distinguish true patriots from scum and traitors, and simply spit them out like a fly accidentally swallowed.” He expressed his conviction that “this natural and necessary self-cleansing of society will only strengthen our country, our solidarity, cohesion, and readiness to respond to any challenge.” End quote. End illusions. How fragile Russia’s moral authority to "denazify" anyone truly is, was neatly illustrated by a cartoon published recently by the Russian embassy in Paris. In classic antisemitic style, worthy of a Der Stürmer cover, the U.S. and the EU were depicted as two hooked-nosed men injecting the weakened corpse of Europe with Russophobia, neo-Nazism, sanctions, and — believe it or not — COVID-19. Then again, the Russian ambassador isn’t the only one in Europe who apparently missed the memo about what hooked-nose caricatures and similar antisemitic iconography represent. So it's time we returned to Yalta. When Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill proposed creating an international criminal court to demilitarize and denazify Hitler’s Germany, they faced a legal dilemma. International law at the time allowed for prosecution of crimes against peace and war crimes but had no clear framework for trying political and military leaders for crimes against civilians. Churchill supposedly suggested a pragmatic solution: line up Nazi leaders and shoot them. Stalin didn’t object but was open to other options. Roosevelt insisted on due process — which was absolutely right. Where extrajudicial measures were used, we still suffer the consequences. The legal basis for the Nuremberg Trials came from the London Charter of August 1945, which added a new category to international law: crimes against humanity. It introduced the criminal liability of political and military leaders for actions committed against civilians. Article 6 of the London Charter — the foundation for the Nuremberg Trials — included among crimes against humanity: “Murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, and other inhumane acts committed against any civilian population, before or during the war…” If anyone wants to understand how that grim legal language looks in practice, they should watch what the Russian army and its mercenaries are doing in Mariupol. If Putin and his military and political accomplices are not brought before an international tribunal to answer for the horrors committed in Ukraine, it will certainly not be for lack of evidence. But if they are held accountable, then perhaps — though not in the way Putin intended — his stated goal will be fulfilled. If not “denazification,” then at least: Destalinization. Of Russia.

Lenin once said there are decades when nothing happens — and days when decades happen. February 24, 2022, was certainly one of those days. The Russian aggression turned Ukraine into a hell overnight, where people's very survival is directly threatened. We all awoke to a new world — even more ominous and dangerous than the one that ended with the incursion of Russian tanks onto Ukrainian soil. A war in the heart of Europe is not something we Europeans can — as we’re accustomed to — ignore due to geographical distance. No more "out of sight, out of mind." The war isn't somewhere else this time — it has come to us. All serious political parties in Slovenia have clearly and firmly condemned the Russian aggression. To claim otherwise is simply false. But I believe all serious political parties should also take a clear stand against those who are justifying or relativizing Russia’s responsibility for the attack on Ukraine. And there’s no shortage of them in Slovenia. According to a survey by the Valicon public opinion agency, a striking percentage of people in Slovenia blame the war (also) on the U.S., NATO, or even Ukraine itself. Not all Kremlin propaganda ruminators are fringe Twitter trolls. One of Slovenia's major media outlets published an op-ed by a long-time columnist shortly after the Russian invasion, arguing that Russia’s position is “fundamentally rational, logical, fact-based, and legitimate.” From various commentators — now self-proclaimed experts and seekers of “alternative truths” — we’re hearing a barrage of arguments placing the blame anywhere but the Kremlin. Some evidently can’t resist Putin’s narrative about Ukraine needing "denazification." I’ve written before about Ukraine’s problems with extremists — but to get a fuller picture, I recommend examining the life and legacy of Ivan Ilyin, a bona fide Russian fascist who died in Switzerland in 1954 and whom Putin had ceremoniously reburied in Moscow in 2005. Or look into the ideas of Alexander Dugin, Putin’s court philosopher and sometime political actor. Putin quotes Ilyin in his speeches, interviews, and articles. The views of Ilyin and Dugin — their stance toward democracy and Russia’s role in its neighbourhood and the Western world — have left an indelible mark on Putin’s domestic and foreign policy. Today, their ideology is being violently implemented in Ukraine — with tanks and bombs. The fact that someone used to be a communist doesn’t mean they can’t be an ultra-nationalist today. We now hear voices claiming that civilians are partly responsible for their own deaths — because Ukrainians stubbornly resist and refuse to lay down arms before a superior occupying force. It’s almost like our battle of Dražgoše all over again, isn’t it? A common argument is that Russia is merely protecting its legitimate security interests, supposedly threatened by broken NATO promises. But some people seem to need constant reminding that NATO did not attack Russia — Russia attacked Ukraine. Let’s leave aside the fact that the historical context and circumstances of those alleged promises are far more complex than the Sunday-night security analysts would have us believe. What stands out is the deeply imperialist logic behind this “anti-imperialist” talking point: a world where great powers have exclusive rights to enforce their interests by negotiating over the heads — and at the expense — of smaller countries. In this worldview, Ukraine has no right to decide for itself whether to join NATO or the EU. No right to a democratic future. And in Putin’s most extreme version, no right to exist at all. If anyone doubts this, they should read his speech justifying the “special military operation.” The populist right, in Slovenia and worldwide, should especially look at its own doorstep. The problem is not just fringe figures, but their first team. Sure, most now forcefully condemn Putin’s aggression — and that’s the only correct stance — but it doesn’t change the fact that many of them were singing a different tune just days ago. From Trump, who called Putin a "genius" right before the invasion and now proposes a “brilliant” idea to bomb Russia with planes painted in Chinese colours; to Bolsonaro and Le Pen, the latter having, like mainstream figures such as Fillon and Schröder, accepted roubles for loyalty; and Salvini, who until recently was parading around Red Square in a Putin T-shirt — only to have one stuffed mockingly in his face by a Polish mayor during a “humanitarian” visit to the Ukrainian border last week. Salvini’s — and not only his — panicked distancing from Putin and sudden compassion for Ukrainian refugees is not only short-lived but also hypocritical. Of course, every real gesture of help to those fleeing Ukraine deserves full support. But not when it comes from people trying to score political points on the backs of the suffering — especially when their “compassion” is so selective. This contradiction was most clearly voiced on French radio last Wednesday by Robert Ménard, the mayor of Béziers and a long-time associate of the French far-right: "This is not moral. We cannot have different categories of victims. There are not Christian Europeans we must help, and Middle Eastern Muslims we can ignore. There is a double standard. Today in Béziers we welcome everyone seeking refuge. Three or four years ago, we did not — and that was wrong. Bombs don’t care if they fall on my friends in Kyiv or my friends in Aleppo." He actually apologized. Instead of doubling down in racist entrenchment like many of his ideological comrades, he held up a mirror to them. The hypocrisy of some of these newly minted Putin critics — like Salvini, Trump, and the rest — shows not only in their attitudes toward refugees, but in the fact that their entire political careers are built on ideas very similar to the ones Putin has used to dominate Russia for over two decades — and now seeks to impose on his neighbours. Using laws and “extra-legal” means to persecute political opponents, muzzle independent journalists, suppress freedoms, and fortify a “vertical of power” as an alternative to the “weak and corrupt” liberal democracy — one which Putin has despised and rejected from the very beginning. The global far-right and illiberal populists have long been fascinated by (and often funded by) Putin’s decisiveness in the culture wars — fighting against all forms of social liberalism: feminism, tolerance, diversity, and other “degenerate Western delusions.” They embraced his homophobia, baked into his obsession with a neo-Soviet, Eurasian empire; his nationalism, and his mythic vision of Russia as the last bastion of spiritual and moral purity in a battle against a “decadent, gay, drugged-up” West. In their newly discovered anti-Putin enthusiasm, they either fail to notice — or refuse to — that the Russian tanks and bombs killing Ukrainian civilians today are the brutal but logical consequence of exactly what they admired in Putin all along. As the Patriarch of All Russia, Kirill, put it in his sermon supporting the “special military operation”: Russia is merely defending itself against the “Western genocide of countries that refuse to hold pride parades.” The moral of the story? You can’t credibly criticize Putin in Ukraine if you’re inspired by Putinism at home. And vice versa. Some people should be deeply ashamed. But all is not lost. Let’s follow the example of the mayor of Béziers. Now is the time, despite our differences, to come together and do everything we can to stop the war and help those affected. Everyone. That’s something we should be able to agree on. There are plenty of other big, important topics left for us to argue about — at least as long as we remain a democracy, built on the freedom to decide our own future, and one that does not divide people into humans and lesser humans.

Over breakfast with my family on the morning after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, I read a report by Marta Shokalo, editor of the Ukrainian service at BBC. “I dressed my ten-year-old son. We had breakfast as far from the windows as possible, but he was so scared he vomited. We brought candles and some water to the basement. That will be our shelter if things get worse.” February 2022. In Europe. The war in Ukraine is not the first armed conflict on European soil since World War II — everyone from the former Yugoslavia knows this — but it is undoubtedly the most dangerous for peace and stability. Not only in Europe, but globally. As we watch the reports of fighting in disbelief and shock, we also have to deal with the "whataboutists" — those who ruminate and regurgitate talking points from Putin’s disinformation arsenal. Warriors for “alternative facts.” Yesterday they were amateur epidemiologists, today they’re Kremlinologists and geopolitical experts. Have the Americans done plenty of dirty deeds? True. Have Palestinians suffered grave injustices? I agree. Are there neo-Nazis in Ukraine? Yes, there are. But there are plenty in Russia too. And even in our own backyard we have party youth organizations that call on Breivik for help, and "patriotic" societies with public-interest status. None of that, in my view, is a valid reason for a foreign invasion. Was Western policy opportunistic, hypocritical, inconsistent, and short-sighted for years? Certainly. But none of that — absolutely none of it — can justify or legitimize the aggression against a neighbouring country or the blatant violation of international law. I’m not a Kremlinologist, but I happen to be among the first people who had the chance to meet Putin. In January 2000, I accompanied a group of European parliamentarians — the first Western delegation, as the British Guardian put it — to meet with the then-interim president of the Russian Federation, just two weeks after Boris Yeltsin’s dramatic resignation. The main purpose of the visit was to assess the situation in Chechnya, where fierce fighting was ongoing over control of the capital, Grozny. Before our trip to the southern Caucasus, Putin received us in the Kremlin. The meeting began with what would later become his trademark: a nearly two-hour delay. When our delegation leader, Lord Russell-Johnston, scolded him like a schoolboy for the delay, Putin flushed red — from rage, not embarrassment — and replied through clenched teeth and with an icy stare that the meeting would last “as long as necessary” to exhaust all our questions. What followed wasn’t a meeting so much as a three-hour string of Putin monologues. He ended with a lecture telling us not to draw conclusions until we had seen the situation in Chechnya with our own eyes. “Don’t be fooled by foreign propaganda,” he snapped. To be honest, during our 48 hours in Dagestan and Chechnya, what we mostly saw was propaganda. It started even before departure, in Moscow, when they tried to hand us Russian military uniforms. What better PR than a delegation of Western politicians in uniform, “witnessing the truth” of Russia’s “pacification” of Chechnya. “Why, exactly?” Russell asked the Ministry of Interior staff. “For safety reasons,” replied a Russian officer. “There are Chechen snipers in the area we’re visiting.” “Thank you very much,” Russell replied with typically British sarcasm, “but if they’re out there, they’ll probably be aiming at you — not me.” In Chechnya, we visited a primary school accompanied by Interior Minister Vladimir Rushailo, who handed out computers to bewildered children. The school hadn’t had electricity for months, and before we even left, the computers were being packed back into boxes and reloaded onto the truck they came in. This surreal experience helped me understand something about Putin’s political communication. It doesn’t rely on facts and doesn’t even attempt to be convincing. It isn’t so much an attempt to deceive — even they don’t believe such shoddy lies would convince anyone at home or abroad. Whether in the cynical talk of “pacification” in Chechnya twenty-two years ago or today’s ominous claims about the “demilitarization and denazification” of Ukraine, the aim is ritualized and ruthless displays of power. Inside Russia, citizens are expected to repeat and internalize these disinformation lines as proof of loyalty and blind obedience to the regime. Toward the outside world, the message is contempt: I don’t respect you enough to even lie convincingly. But there's a crucial difference between the year 2000 and today: social media. Maskirovka — the Russian term for intentional disinformation — is now on steroids. In 2000, we knew little about Chechnya due to lack of information. Today, the confusion stems from too much information — and misinformation. No one has weaponized social media more effectively than the Kremlin. Compared to 2000, today there are far more people outside of Russia who consume and parrot Kremlin disinformation. Some do so out of financial or political opportunism; others because these lies skilfully manipulate their emotional and ideological biases. Trolls whisper what the whataboutists want to hear — so they’ll do exactly what the trolls want.
