The champions of alternative facts cling to their Pavlovian anti-Americanism, even when they often defend the very values that Putin’s war seeks to destroy. I’m stunned by the naivety of those who believe that bartering away Ukraine’s right to determine its own future would stop this aggression. Churchill said appeasers are “people who feed the crocodile, hoping it will eat them last.” Russian missiles aren’t falling on Kyiv because Ukraine wanted to join NATO — although, given what's happening, that desire is hardly unreasonable. The real reason is that Ukraine is a liberal democracy. Weak, vulnerable, plagued with problems like corruption and clientelism — yes — but still a democracy, where governments are freely elected and replaced. That is something Putin cannot and will not tolerate on his borders, lest his own subjects get similar ideas. Russia joined the Council of Europe exactly twenty-six years ago — three months after I started working there as a young European civil servant. Upon joining, top Russian leaders, including Yeltsin, pledged to resolve conflicts peacefully and to renounce the doctrine of the “near abroad,” under which Russia had trampled across Europe — from Hungary in 1956 to Czechoslovakia twenty-two years later. But paper accepts anything. After Georgia, Crimea, and now Ukraine, those commitments mean nothing. As I write this, the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers is deciding on measures under Article 8 of the organization’s statute. Russia’s right to representation has been suspended for flagrant violations of its obligations and principles. I lost my illusions much earlier. It happened when Russia passed laws banning “homosexual propaganda,” and later when the government started crushing civil society, freedom of expression, media freedom, and the right to peaceful protest — by labelling activists “foreign agents” and through other repressive tactics. Until then, Russia’s response to every human right or civil liberties violation was that it was all a misunderstanding, or a result of “false” information. But from that point on, it became clear: they do not share or accept the core principles of an open, democratic society. And they stopped pretending otherwise. It was a painful realization. I love Russia. I love Russian culture. I have many Russian friends and acquaintances. Until that moment, I wanted to believe that the post-Berlin Wall reunification of Europe, based on shared democratic values, could remain a cornerstone of our future. But from that moment on, things only went downhill. And those values are now being trampled not only in Russia but across several European countries — some of which are currently condemning the invasion of Ukraine, albeit tactically. Still, that cannot justify the pathetic attempts to excuse the inexcusable or relativize the responsibility for this aggression. People who look for blame anywhere but the Kremlin for the Russian tanks rolling through Ukrainian streets should be ashamed — not only in front of the Ukrainians now caught in a war, but also in front of the many Russian citizens who do not support this war and who, despite pressure and threats, are protesting against it.

With a nod to the 1979 song Novo vrijeme by the band Buldožer, about new times that look very much like the old ones. “A former MP, who was even speaker of the National Assembly, might have known that we are no longer in the eighties, when insulting those in power was allowed.” This is how the editors of the Maribor outlet e-Maribor commented on the fine imposed on Dr. Pavel Gantar for upsetting the director general of the police. The stern lecture to Dr. Gantar that the times when you could mock the regime with impunity are long behind us is not only comic; it is also inaccurate. The former Yugoslav regime was never as tolerant, liberal and forbearing towards social criticism, dissidents and civil society as the editors of the Maribor digital outlet imagine. People who in those days had enough responsibility, commitment to their democratic principles and courage to resist the pressure of centralized ideological uniformity, and thus paved the way for democracy and independence, could tell them more about it. If the subject interests them, they can ask those directly involved, among them, as it happens, Dr. Gantar himself. That times were not as rosy as the worthy Maribor Yugo-apologists imagine is proved, after all, by the arrest and military trial of the Ljubljana Four. That everything turned out the way it did is thanks to civil society and the people who exposed themselves most in resisting the ideological repression of the army and Belgrade, among whom, well I never, Dr. Gantar again played a visible role. And of course the mass protests on Roška Street. Which, incidentally, were not registered. The criticism of Dr. Gantar for not understanding that times have changed helps us understand how some people in Slovenia understand the difference between the previous regime and democracy. It is not a comparison based on respect for democratic standards, freedom of expression, respect for human rights and political freedoms, but simply a measuring of the muscle and ruthlessness of past and present rulers towards criticism and disobedience. In the logic of mocking Dr. Gantar, the previous regime was not bad because it suppressed and persecuted social criticism, but quite the opposite: because, in their view, it did not do so firmly enough. Because it was weak and indecisive and allowed various Dr. Gantars and the like to badmouth the authorities. That, in their view, is no longer the case. These are different times now, Dr. Gantar; now it’s our democracy. Taken to its ultimate conclusion, this bizarre logic could even reproach the Yugoslav regime for giving in to the pressure of civil society and critics like Dr. Gantar and releasing the Four from prison. But let us leave the brilliance of the Maribor media eccentrics aside for a moment. The story of Dr. Gantar’s punishment—and he is not the only one to have met such a fate recently—sets a new milestone in the (mis)understanding of freedom of expression in our country. This question has received a great deal of attention, debate and argument in recent years, mainly because of the unstoppable spread of hate speech in the Slovenian public space. On one side were many who, worried by the slide into hateful discourse, called on prosecutors for help; on the other, those who experienced any reaction to inappropriate and intolerant statements as an assault on liberty and an attempt to silence “dissenters.” Let me say first that I too have for many years consistently and publicly advocated a sharper and more consistent response to hateful and dangerous speech, which in Slovenia really has spilled over all the limits of the decent and acceptable. But I have often wondered whether, in all the cases in which many demanded the intervention of the prosecution, the line had been crossed of what, under the law and the international legal standards governing freedom of expression, can be prohibited or punished. Years ago, when the Holocaust was presented in Slovenia as a “Jewish” conspiracy, I wrote that the response of society and the state to hate speech cannot and must not be reduced merely to the question of criminal prosecution. Repressive interference with freedom of expression must be limited to a narrow circle of the most serious cases involving direct incitement to violence. Without freedom of expression there is no democracy, so we must be extremely careful with restrictions, even when we are guided by the best intentions. Overly broad and arbitrary use of criminal sanctions also carries the danger of abuse and suppression of freedom of expression. It is simply too important for the normal functioning of democracy. It is one of the fundamental political freedoms which, through the right of individuals to express their opinions and through the free and independent functioning of the media and civil society, makes democratic oversight of the executive possible. That is why the European Court of Human Rights protects not only opinions that are agreeable and unproblematic but also statements that “offend, shock or disturb.” Then, as today, I was convinced that society’s response to hateful and dangerous speech cannot be based primarily on repressive interference with freedom of expression. Then, as today, I was convinced that the most effective defense of democracy and means of fighting hate speech is a clear and firm social response. Returning to the fine imposed on Dr. Gantar, the first question to ask is whether his tweet can even be characterized as language that offends, disturbs or shocks. And even if the answer is yes, there comes the even more important question of whether such a statement, even if someone in public office feels hurt by it, may be restricted at all, let alone prosecuted, on the basis of the case law of the European Court of Human Rights. Evidently a court will decide on this, so I do not intend to comment further. In any case, I stand by my position of principle on the most appropriate response—a social, not a repressive one—to a conditionally problematic use of freedom of expression. If any of the moral authorities in office recognizes in Dr. Gantar’s tweets inappropriate and offensive criticism of the police’s work, they can respond and condemn the statement. There is absolutely nothing wrong with that. The critical public will judge whether it agrees with such an interpretation and response. But before anyone starts lumping Dr. Gantar’s criticism of the police—whether justified or inappropriate—together with some of the statements that have prompted debates about hate speech in recent years, two things must be stressed. First, the case law of the European Court of Human Rights does not give people in public or political office more protection against public criticism than private individuals, but quite the opposite. The Kamnik District Court recently put this principle in a judgment as follows: “It is precisely criticism of the authorities of the day (politicians, public officials, parliamentary and other political parties, the government and the opposition, holders of power and public authority) that enjoys the highest level of legal protection and thus the greatest freedom.” It is also important to know that the power relationship between the one who expresses hatred and those who are hated is key to defining and recognizing hate speech. Intolerance towards social minorities is one thing; criticism of the authorities, however offensive, disturbing and shocking, is another. Understanding, taking into account and respecting these differences is key to respecting freedom of expression and to the normal functioning of pluralist democracy. In this lies the qualitative difference between the previous regime and the new times that we wanted and fought for in the 1980s, including through the struggle for an independent and democratic state. The Maribor media guardsmen and their sympathizers evidently do not understand this, or do not want to.

In the early days of the war for Slovenian independence, I found myself near the Lazaret border crossing, between Debeli Rtič in Slovenia and Muggia on the Italian side. The scene was surreal. On our side, a state of war prevailed. The border station was surrounded by Slovenian police, while inside was a group of conscripts being screamed at by furious officers of the former Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA). Just a few meters away, crowds of people from Trieste were gathering, watching the drama unfold across the border with interest. Some stood at a nearby bar, drinks in hand; others were unbothered, calmly sunbathing and swimming in the sea. On one side: Kalashnikovs. On the other: Aperol Spritz. That experience will stay with me forever. Just a few weeks earlier, I had been studying for final exams with peers from all over the world at the College of Europe in Bruges, Belgium, planning summer vacations—and then overnight, I found myself in the middle of a military conflict. At that moment, like every Slovene, I realized how fragile the boundary is between peace and war, between normal daily life and complete chaos. We are right to be proud of the victory in Slovenia’s independence war. It lasted ten days. Seventy-six people lost their lives, including nineteen on the Slovenian side. We owe them gratitude and respect. Compared to the other bloody conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, our war was relatively short and less bloody—but that in no way diminishes the significance of the victory or the sacrifice of those who gave their lives for an independent Slovenia. What’s striking, though, is how rarely anyone today considers how easily our war could have gone differently—lasting longer, causing far greater destruction and casualties. The idea that we may have narrowly escaped the tragic fate of some other Yugoslav nations is simply too frightening and uncomfortable. No one wants to think about what might have happened if the rabid nationalist generals in Belgrade had decided to throw everything at us—bombing all targets, civilian ones included—just as they did elsewhere in the region without hesitation later. I’m convinced that Slovenia would have ultimately prevailed regardless. The only question is: at what human and material cost? I wonder whether, in that case, anyone would have dared label resistance against a stronger occupier as cowardice or betrayal—simply because of civilian casualties. The belief that war is a temporary aberration and peace the automatic norm is a psychological defence mechanism—not unique to us. Europe has behaved similarly for decades, even though—historically speaking—we’re living in just a fleeting moment since the last war in which Europeans slaughtered millions of other Europeans. The memory of war is still alive, but more as ceremony and ritual than as a historical lesson with relevant messages for our time. Because something already happened, we believe it can’t happen again—not because it’s impossible, but because the thought is too disturbing. To maintain our peace of mind, we act as though the descent into inhumanity we witnessed in the 1930s was a one-off, never to be repeated. Periodically, politicians don solemn expressions, lay a wreath or two, and solemnly declare: “Never again.” In truth, no one really believes that “again” is possible. Our behaviour—and our responsibility—reflect this. Instead of empty ceremonial platitudes, I’d rather offer politicians and the public the words of Italian Jewish writer Primo Levi, who survived the horrors of the concentration camps: “It happened, so it can happen again.” A few years ago in Strasbourg, I participated in a roundtable organized by the European Movement. I ended up in an argument with a local economics professor who took issue with my claim that the European Union is, first and foremost, a peace project. “Oh, come on with that nonsense,” he said. “Who still cares about war in Europe? Let’s talk about the future, not the past.” First, I reminded him of my own experience with war in Slovenia. Then I politely suggested he share his theory with the son of my good friends—who was sitting in the audience, born during the siege of Sarajevo. “Explain to him that war in Europe is no longer relevant.” Today, I could add Ukrainians to that list—and others. I understand the psychological need to believe we’ll always live in peace. Who would want to wake up each day fearing they’ll end it in a shelter or on the run? But I’m also convinced that, in the decades after World War I, many ordinary Europeans—people like you and me—watched the slow slide into chaos with disbelief and disapproval, yet still believed war wouldn’t return. “Oh, come on. What war? Let’s talk about the future, not the past.” “Hold my beer,” said history. And repeated itself. We live in a time of rising tensions over critical resources—from water to food to energy. The world, battered by the effects of self-inflicted climate damage, is on the edge of a nervous breakdown. Let’s recall how empires—and especially their leaders—have historically behaved whenever they felt their interests or Lebensraum (as it was called in those supposedly unrepeatable times) were threatened. Hold my beer… Despite all our tragic experiences, we are once again being sold a vision of the world built on national egoism, transactional relationships, zero solidarity or cooperation—a world where you can only win or survive if someone else loses. We live in a time of pandemic, in which we have—individually and collectively—failed the test of solidarity and reason. Armies are building up on Europe’s borders. But come on—what war? Let’s focus on the future, not the past. We live in a time where difference frightens and threatens us. A time where we passively accept that children are drowning in our rivers. A time where people are once again compared to parasites, where hatred and even antisemitism are used shamelessly to discredit critics and political opponents. But let’s stop worrying about the past. Let’s look forward, not back. We live in a time when certain European politicians are deliberately undermining the only effective mechanism that, for nearly seventy years, has successfully protected us from ourselves—from our historical reflex to resolve conflicts through confrontation rather than cooperation. The European project was created precisely as a counterpoint to the darkest and bloodiest chapter in Europe’s long history of wars and conflicts. That’s why the European Union was—and remains—first and foremost a peace project. Yet today, some are once again selling us the idea that the solution lies in national self-sufficiency and the adrenaline rush of inflated nationalism and sovereignty. That we should once more tackle shared problems not together, but each on our own—and against each other. Hold my beer, says history. Democracy is far from a perfect system. Inconsistency, incompetence, narrow interests, social injustice, and a lack of political culture and integrity create dissatisfaction, hardship, and injustice. Many are rightfully fed up with politics and politicians. Many are understandably disappointed with democracy and are searching for alternatives—strong leaders, aggressive rhetoric, the emotional comfort of scapegoating others for their own discontent. Efficiency at the cost of freedom. Security at the cost of humanity. Nationalist swagger at the cost of our future. Déjà vu. Authoritarianism has never brought safety, stability, or peace. In the end, the suppression of freedom and humanity always leads, inevitably, to conflict and violence. But hey—you know how it goes: look forward, not back. If there's one thing that annoys me, it's sensationalist fearmongering for the sake of clickbait. Despite all the above warnings, I don’t believe this is a time for panic—still less for surrendering to fate. I’ve always described myself as a deeply concerned optimist. I believe that in the end, humanity and reason will prevail. But we’ll have to fight like hell to make it happen. In European history, peace has never been the default—it’s been the exception, a brief moment of clarity. This current stretch, despite a few tragic regional setbacks, has been the longest yet. If we want to keep it going, we need to be far more responsible, consistent, and decisive in confronting political ideas and actions that threaten stability, freedom, and peace. I don’t believe war is inevitable. But I do worry about people who blindly believe that peace is. It happened. So it can happen again.
There is no such thing as fascist-neutral

One of the most amusing comments I came across in this year's iteration of the perennial January debate about fascism and anti-fascism—ignited every year by the anniversary of the Battle of Dražgoše—was a tweet by a prominent self-styled advocate for “alternative thinkers,” claiming that fascists today are merely a subculture. Move along, nothing to see here, as the French might say. Apparently, fascism has reached its "Omicron phase" and turned into something we’ll never get rid of, but will simply have to learn to live with. Endemic fascism. On second thought, I revise that assessment: the comment wasn’t amusing. If there is anything more despicable than denying the existence and danger of fascism—with lines like “they’re not neo-Nazis, they’re patriots,” or “those aren’t Nazi symbols, it’s just Hindu folklore”—it is its trivialization. All of this raises the question: what is fascism, and how do we recognize it? There is no shortage of definitions. Even Wikipedia or a basic political science crash course will give you a similar description of a societal system based on total state control, nationalism, and zero tolerance for political opponents, critics, and minorities. But perhaps no one has described the features of fascism—or what Umberto Eco called ur-fascism, or eternal fascism—more clearly than Eco himself in an essay published over twenty-five years ago in The New York Review of Books. His words have chillingly stood the test of time and seem even more relevant today than when they were first written. To anyone who, during this most recent Dražgoše-triggered episode of Slovenian culture wars, cynically asked what fascism actually is, I recommend reading Eco’s essay. Multiple times. Eternal fascism cultivates a cult of tradition, rejects modernism, and fetishizes irrationality. The Enlightenment and its legacy are seen as degenerate. Culture and liberal intelligentsia are enemies because they betray traditional values. Dissent is betrayal. Eternal fascism thrives on fear of difference, on external enemies and foreign invaders. It exploits social and economic frustrations and appeals to people suffering from hardship and political humiliation. As comfort, it offers those without a clear social identity the most general privilege of all: being born in the same country. Eternal fascism is by definition nationalist and racist. It is macho, disrespectful to women, and intolerant toward sexual minorities. It is populist or selectively populist, as Eco describes it. The bearer of rights is not the individual, but the People—as a monolithic entity that expresses a collective will. But since no large group of individuals truly shares a unified will, it is the Leader who claims the right to interpret it. The People are merely a theatrical fiction. Because nothing can be above the People, eternal fascism rejects “rotten” parliamentary democracy. Under Mussolini, the legislature became a fictionalized executive power, subordinating the judiciary and media, and issuing laws itself. Eternal fascism uses Orwellian Newspeak, built on a reduced vocabulary and syntax, to limit the capacity for complex and critical thought. Though most often quoted for its list of fourteen traits, Eco’s essay is worth reading in full—especially the part about the Italian resistance movement. He writes: “In my country today, there are those who say the myth of the Resistance was a communist lie. It’s true that the communists exploited the Resistance as if it were their private property, since they played the main role in it; but I remember partisans with scarves of many colours… In my country today, some say the liberation war was a tragic period of division and that all we need now is national reconciliation. The memory of those terrible years should be repressed, refoulée, verdrängt. But Verdrängung breeds neurosis. If reconciliation means compassion and respect for all those who fought their war in good faith, then forgiveness does not mean forgetting.” While resistance to fascism was not solely the domain of the communist left, Eco also sees ideological plurality in totalitarianism. “If by totalitarianism we mean a regime that subordinates every individual action to the state and its ideology, then both Nazism and Stalinism were totalitarian regimes.” Indeed, a hallmark of fascism is the glorification and instrumentalization of violence—a level that not only Nazism, but also Stalin and the Khmer Rouge elevated far beyond anything Italian fascism ever reached. That’s not to say Mussolini wouldn’t have tried if given more time. What stands out in Eco’s essay is the recognition that most—if not all—of the characteristics of eternal fascism are also recognizable in extreme populism, albeit perhaps at a lower level of intensity. For some, this is enough reason to scream “fascism” at every mention of tradition, nationhood, or fear of outsiders. While I wouldn't claim that caution is unnecessary, trivializing such weighty terms can backfire—especially when they start to lose their meaning. First, because of the very social frustrations and injustices that Eco also writes about. The fact that these are emotions which populism (and fascism) exploit doesn’t mean they aren’t real—or even justified. We live in a time where many people have very real reasons to feel economically, socially, and politically marginalized. Labelling every such expression of dissatisfaction—however emotional, aggressive, or offensive—as fascism only plays into the hands of those who seek to exploit social tensions for their own gain. It fuels identity-based polarization in which opinions, ideas, and values lose meaning and are reduced to slogans—like uniforms on a battlefield in a cultural war, helping us distinguish “us” from “them.” When social conflict is reduced to a hollow culture war, populism (and eventually even fascism) is already halfway to victory. For similar reasons, in confronting disturbing social phenomena, we should avoid rhetoric of violence and death. Regardless of the context or intention, such language risks normalizing and trivializing violence—not only verbal—in both politics and society. In the end, those who benefit most are the ones with the least scruples—or even the greatest eagerness—for using violence. This is not to suggest that we must be tolerant or understanding of the intolerable. Eco says we must remain vigilant: “Ur-fascism is still around us, sometimes in plain clothes. It would be so much easier if someone appeared on the world stage and said, ‘I want to reopen Auschwitz, I want the Blackshirts to march again in the squares of Italy.’ Life is not that simple. Ur-fascism can come back under the most innocent of disguises. Our duty is to uncover it and point our finger at every one of its new forms—every day, in every part of the world.” At the same time, in resisting fascism, it does us no good to slap the “fascist” label too hastily or too broadly, branding anyone who disagrees with us. Nor should we ignore the questions, dilemmas, injustices, and fears that populism exploits and mercilessly manipulates. Anti-fascism is a core civilizational value, but it does not entitle anyone to always be right in everything—except, of course, when it comes to fascism. On that front, you can only be against it or for it. There is no such thing as fascist-neutral.

I often have the feeling that we disown the past, dislike it or are embarrassed by it. And so we often make up little stories about what was, because we believe it will make it easier to live with what is. Through an emotional, ideological or manipulative prism we create history à la carte. We choose, as we wish and need, tales and legends about our own past, historical fictions about times that never were, or were not the way we claim they were. Part of the left, for example, is very sensitive to right-wing descriptions of life in the former common state and under the previous regime. These accusations are not always the most accurate and often lapse into absurd descriptions of hardships that never existed. A shortage of fruit yogurt, for example. Fact check. We had fruit yogurt in Yugoslavia, and it was available to everyone. I know, because even then I didn’t like it. But all the fruit yogurt in the world cannot change the fact that the previous regime was not free. And all the yellowed photographs of working people and citizens winding en masse along the Adriatic coastal road towards proletarian holidays in Fiat 600s and 101s cannot change the fact that Yugoslavia was not paradise on earth. Remember, this was a country in which only one truth was tolerated in the media, with room on television only for glorifying the one and only authority. This was a country in which journalists were not allowed to ask the regime awkward questions. This was a country in which the judiciary and prosecution had to work as the executive dictated. In which civil society was branded and persecuted as a danger to the nation and the state. This was a country in the party’s grip of a personality cult, ideological uniformity, enforced unity, paranoia about external enemies and repression. This was a country in which criticism of the authorities was unpatriotic, treasonous and criminally prosecuted. True, we had yogurt. And Coca-Cola. Just like today. Comparisons with other Eastern countries that were in an even rougher embrace of socialist love are misleading. Just because some had it even worse and had even less freedom does not mean we had it good. And for all its relative liberalism, the previous regime was paranoid and relentless towards ideas and people it suspected of threatening it. Equally misleading are little stories about a proletarian paradise compared with the exploitation of the working class in the capitalist West. There was more socialism in Scandinavia than in our country. What we had above all were slogans. By attributing credit for social justice to a monolithic authoritarian regime, they do a disservice to those who strive for this civilizational value in a democracy. It is grist to the mill of neoliberals, since it makes it easier for them to dismiss demands for more social justice in society as an unconstitutional Bolshevik conspiracy. The biggest problem with yogurt-provoked sotto voce Yugo-nostalgia, however, is that it quite stupidly calls into question the reasons for establishing an independent state. If we had it so good before, why did we go our own way? If independence was not motivated by efforts for democracy, a socially just society and individual freedoms, then it was merely a nationalist project to establish a mono-ethnic state. In their furious reaction to lies about fruit yogurt, some walk straight into the trap of those who want to re-establish uniformity of thought in the name of a different ideology, but with the same authoritarian aftertaste. On the other side of the yogurt polarization we have politics and ideology that do not change history but invent it. The historical paradigm of right-wing populism is based on the fairy tale of a return to the good old days that never existed. It sells us a return to a state that never existed, the Carantanian panther, and fairy tales about national, sovereign states as the only forms of state organization that can ensure the nation’s prosperity and protect it from external enemies. There are quite a few problems with this story. The first is the claim that sovereign nation-states are the natural state of stability and security. Historically, this is a plain lie. With very rare, unstable and short-lived interruptions, most European nations throughout history struggled from war to war within empires. In a few cases at the head, mostly as a subordinate part of one of them. Timothy Snyder calls this the European myth of the wise nation. According to this narrative, European nation-states have a long and rich history. And yet the myth of the wise nation is invented. In Western and Central Europe there were practically no nation-states in history. In Eastern Europe there were a few, but they did not meet a glorious fate. The nation-states in the Balkans laid the foundations for the First World War, and after it six new nation-states emerged in Eastern Europe, all of which had been removed from the map by the middle of the Second World War. In the narrative of those who advocate a return to the warm and safe bosom of the wise and sovereign nation, European integration is not a civilizational step forward that for the first time in history created the conditions for European nations to coexist without conflicts and wars, but a departure from the ideal of the nation-state. The argument of those who advocated the “liberation” of the United Kingdom from the Brussels yoke, according to Snyder, “rests on the assumption that the British nation-state would re-emerge once the layers of European integration were removed and the previous state of ‘independence’ restored. But there never was such a thing. The historical process of the loss of empire coincided with the historical process of European integration, which created the Britain that exists today.” Populism loves to talk about sovereignty. It is a word that tickles many people in the tummy, or a hand’s breadth lower. “Nobody’s gonna screw with us, we do what we want” has become a doctrine that is making its way back from the vocabulary of frustrated misfits at the counter of the local bar into the discourse of high politics. Less and less Europe, more and more nation. Fewer and fewer European values, more and more Nazis. The problem with sovereignty is not that states should not have the right—and the duty—to freely and democratically adopt and enforce laws on their territory. To ensure the security and prosperity of their citizens and, if necessary, protect them from the dangers that threaten them. But the fact is that European states achieve these goals much more successfully as part of European integration than outside it, and especially than as illiberal banana republics, which some politicians sell as the alternative. Sovereignty has its precise legal meaning in international law. Sports commentators are also very fond of it when they rave about “summer” football and sovereign victories. In history, however, sovereignty was not so much the right of nations to decide their own fate as the exclusive privilege of the ruler to maintain his power at their expense by coercion. That is how the Nazi court jurist Carl Schmitt interpreted sovereignty. For him, the only sovereign state was one that allowed the government to introduce a state of exception and thus enabled it to rise above the laws and the constitution at its own discretion and without any oversight. That is precisely why we should be thoroughly worried when insistence on respect for the constitution and the laws begins to be presented as an unnecessary formality, or even as annoying and unpatriotic obstruction of those in power and harm to the nation. In a democracy, the rule of law can never be subject to the discretion of politics, even with the best intentions. The institutional, legal, political and economic antithesis of the “traditional” understanding of sovereignty was brought by European integration, first with the founding of the Council of Europe and the adoption of the European Convention on Human Rights, and then with the European Communities, from which the European Union emerged. It is based on the democratic rule of law, which means that the rights and freedoms of individuals are protected by laws and the constitution against the arbitrariness of the authorities, and on pluralist democracy, which allows citizens freely to choose their government. Both are the complete antithesis of sovereignty as Schmitt understood it. In the jargon of the political doctrine slowly spreading from modern Russia across the eastern part of Europe, this right of the ruler to do whatever he pleases is called “bespredel,” or unlimited power. The newfound enthusiasm of a growing number of Europeans for such a social order is reminiscent of Stockholm syndrome. One would not expect people to renounce of their own accord, and with such zeal, their right to influence society and hand it over to someone who, in the end, can do with them whatever comes into his head. Sovereigntists achieve this with a dystopian presentation of a world in which everyone threatens everyone, and everyone threatens us most of all. Relations, whether between nations or within them, are reduced to the belief that you can only win if someone else loses. In such a world, in which we are constantly under threat, there is of course no room for cooperation and integration, still less for pluralism, social criticism and individual freedoms. Fear, distrust and hatred are psychological ammunition, and with them the populist sovereigntist maintains power and justifies authoritarianism and repression. A return to the good, sovereign old days is a fairy tale, but not all fairy tales have a happy ending.

Looking back on three decades of Slovenia's experience with democracy, we must admit that much is not as we had hoped or wished. Citizens dislike politics and politicians, they don’t trust institutions, and increasingly, they dislike one another. Liberal democracy—based on respect for human rights and political freedoms, the democratic rule of law, and pluralism—has disappointed many. But we rarely ask ourselves whether democracy is failing because it is inherently flawed or because we misunderstand it and aren’t very good at practicing it. Of course, no social system is without faults. Winston Churchill once said that democracy is the worst form of government—except for all the others. But before we grab our pitchforks for yet another revolution, left or right, we should ask whether we ourselves are more to blame for the shortcomings of democracy than democracy itself. When we criticize politics, the blame usually—and rightly—falls on the supply side. I'm not saying all politicians are the same, but Slovenia’s political class certainly includes a critical mass of behavior and misconduct that justifies public dissatisfaction. Yet this doesn’t mean there aren’t problems on the demand side too. For many Slovenians, the ideal politician is someone who claims to be neither left nor right, but centrist—or even apolitical and above party lines—non-ideological, representing the “silent majority,” transcending past divisions, and, of course, working for the people. This might be a bit caricatured, but it's probably accurate enough. Before every election, we hope for a savior. If not a “new face,” then at least a face. This public attitude reflects deep disillusionment with politics and its institutions, which is understandable. The problem is that this image embodies the full repertoire of populist clichés. Such an understanding of political ideals doesn’t solve the problems of democracy—it deepens them. Some reasons for these problems are global, others are homegrown and carefully nurtured here. The first is the stubborn belief that democracy requires unity. That is partly true. There is unity around very broad societal values—such as prosperity, development, security, and so on. These are what we like to call “national interests,” because it sounds important. But political promises regarding such goals aren’t enough to make an informed voting decision. A party that promised poverty, economic decline, and danger at every turn wouldn’t stand much chance. Most national interests are subject to various ideological interpretations and political paths, which is perfectly fine. The right to implement such programs belongs to those who win a democratic mandate. But unity should primarily exist around core societal values—less abstract ones—which must not only be mentioned but respected and concretely upheld. These are the values enshrined in the Constitution: human rights, political freedoms, rule of law (including respect for international obligations), a social state, public education, public healthcare, free economic initiative, and more. These values were, at least during the establishment of Slovenian democracy, part of a social consensus. Maintaining that consensus is the kind of unity Slovenia should strive for. Yet we often fail—often under the presidential doctrine of uncritical equidistance toward all opinions. Instead of defending the Constitution in unison, we undermine it in the name of unity. As for differing views that remain within constitutional principles, the frantic push for national unity can become problematic. In the name of unity and national interests, critical media, dissatisfied citizens, civil society, and all opinions inconvenient to those in power are labeled as disruptive, unpatriotic, illegitimate, or even illegal. In such a climate, pluralist democracy can no longer function properly—and may even collapse. Pluralism doesn’t tolerate unity at all costs; it requires a civilized, rational competition of ideas based on shared constitutional values, with effective mechanisms of democratic oversight. It needs political culture—not political conformity. The second issue in Slovenia’s understanding of democracy is the belief that only “non-political” or “non-ideological” politics is good. As a result, we face an inflation of political initiatives that present themselves as apolitical or supra-political, all claiming to “work for the people.” The problem is that the slogan “we work for the people” is usually not a promise but an alibi. Decisions about what the people want are most often left to the free interpretation and current interests of political opportunists. The tragic paradox is that the ultimate winner of the battle against ideology is usually an ideology—sometimes left, more often right, always with authoritarian ambitions. Pluralist democracy can function only if citizens can choose among different programs and concrete commitments that take political and ideological stances on fundamental societal issues. You can't have a pluralist democracy if the political space is seen as ideologically neutral, where anyone can do whatever they want as long as they claim to work for the public good. The third strike in our conceptual misunderstanding of democracy is our attitude toward the past. It’s actually a sub-problem—a uniquely Slovenian offshoot of our obsession with being non-ideological. “Let’s stop dividing into partisans and collaborators! Let’s focus on the future, not the past!”—these are two evergreen slogans of the Slovenian approach to tackling difficult social issues. Noble, but naïve and risky. Without critical understanding of the past, we cannot solve present problems—much less build the future. The European model of liberal democracy emerged as a response to Europe's bloody experience with authoritarian, nationalist, and violent anti-liberalism. Given how similar today’s societal, political, and economic tensions are to those of the 1930s, learning from history would serve us well. It’s easy to preach that we should forget the past—but what do we do when today's and tomorrow’s problems start to look dangerously similar to yesterday’s? Democracy in Slovenia is in trouble. Dissatisfaction and anger with the current political class are often justified. Wanting new people in politics, fresh ideas, different approaches, more young people, and especially more women is wise and necessary. But new faces will bring real change only if they respect and promote the core values of pluralist democracy—not rise above them or behave as if those values don’t apply to them. At a minimum, we must demand that politicians clearly state what they stand for, what they will do, and with whom they will cooperate if elected to power. Not vague platitudes, but concrete political positions, programs, and commitments on all important societal issues. We will not achieve better democracy if we keep falling for new bags while buying the same—or very similar—cats. If we draw a line under 30 years of Slovenian democracy, we can blame politicians for many things. But not a single one appointed themselves to an elected position. Joseph de Maistre and George Bernard Shaw warned long ago: democracy is a system that gives people the government they deserve. So, happy holidays—and let’s hope for a wise new year.

Besides sovereignty, “the people” is perhaps the most inspiring—and also one of the most abused—concepts in political history and present-day politics. In Slovenia, it appears in the second paragraph of Article 3 of our Constitution, which declares that power in Slovenia belongs to the people. Abraham Lincoln concluded his historic Gettysburg Address by referencing the people three times. On the other hand, North Korea also calls itself a “people’s” republic. In the name of the people, Nazi Germany’s infamous Volksgerichtshof (People’s Court) sent thousands of political opponents to concentration camps and the gallows. It operated outside constitutional bounds, embodying a Nazi interpretation of sovereignty as articulated by Hitler’s court jurist Carl Schmitt—who claimed sovereignty meant the authority to rise above the constitution and laws in times of emergency. This doctrine of unchecked national sovereign power—and its bloody consequences—prompted the construction of a different legal and civilizational model after the war. Europe built this model on the principle of pooled sovereignty and the transfer of agreed national competencies to a common community. The British historian Niall Ferguson, who teaches at Harvard and Stanford, recently corrected me in a conversation, explaining that Mark Twain never actually said that “history repeats itself,” but rather that “it rhymes.” I was disappointed to lose such a handy quote, but Twain did say something else about history that vividly captures the flow and interweaving of past and present: “There is no such thing as a new idea. It is impossible. We simply take a lot of old ideas and put them into a sort of mental kaleidoscope. We give them a turn and they make new and curious combinations. But they are the same old pieces of colored glass that have been in use through all the ages.” “The people” and “power” are two such pieces of colored glass that have appeared in various combinations throughout modern political history. Though we typically associate them with democracy, in the twentieth century, their union often cast darker shades through the historical kaleidoscope. The problem isn’t that power shouldn’t belong to the people, but rather in operationalizing this noble principle into a functioning societal system. While the Constitution guarantees that citizens exercise their power directly, this is more of a rhetorical flourish. To put it simply, even in a small country like Slovenia, it's impossible to imagine two million people directly wielding legislative, executive, and judicial power. Power is exercised through institutions—and the forms and functioning of those institutions offer various social models, all claiming to represent the people, yet governing in vastly different ways. On one side is pluralist liberal democracy, where citizens exercise their authority through elections—as guaranteed by Article 3 of the Constitution—and occasionally through referendums. On the other side are illiberal and authoritarian regimes, which interpret the relationship between people and power quite differently. In its most extreme form, this was articulated by Reich Minister for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda Joseph Goebbels in his September 1933 speech at Geneva’s Hotel Carlton. “Democracies merely talk and never resolve problems,” he said, “unlike Germany, where the people and the government are one, and the will of the people is the same as the will of the government and vice versa. The modern structure of the German state represents a higher form of democracy, where power is exercised authoritatively based on the people’s mandate, without any possibility of parliamentary interference that would neutralize or paralyze the execution of the people’s will.” Rejection of parliamentary pluralist democracy was widespread in 1930s Germany—and not just there. It was fueled by (often justified) disappointment in the weakness, irresponsibility, selfishness, incompetence, and corruption of then-mainstream political parties. Riding a wave of similar frustrations, Benito Mussolini rose to power through his March on Rome. In the aftermath of World War I, amid a global pandemic and economic crisis, many people lost faith in liberal democracy and sought salvation in authoritarian alternatives—politics that, in the name of the people, were willing to place themselves above constitutions, laws, and basic norms of human decency. Sound familiar? We’ve spun the historical kaleidoscope several times since then, but we should not ignore the fact that today’s arrangement of colored pieces increasingly resembles patterns Europe has seen before. It’s not hard these days to find reasons for frustration and disappointment with liberal democracy. Many criticisms directed at democratic institutions a century ago—albeit in different forms—still resonate today. Political systems struggle to solve global and societal challenges—from economic crises and social issues to demographic shifts and environmental threats. The consequences of political failure are passed on to people, who understandably grow angry and disillusioned. Now, on top of all that, a global pandemic drags on with no clear end. Some of us, myself included, initially hoped that a crisis of this magnitude might awaken the best in individuals and communities: rationality and solidarity. That hope has largely gone unfulfilled. In this era, it's not only our health that's endangered, but also our democracy and freedoms. As Henry Kissinger recently said: “National cohesion and resilience depend on trust that institutions can foresee catastrophe, arrest its impact, and restore stability. When the COVID-19 pandemic is over, many will assess their institutions as having failed. Whether that assessment is objectively accurate is irrelevant.” In such circumstances, it is unsurprising that many—disillusioned with representative and pluralist democracy—are once again looking for alternatives. The perception that power is distant, unresponsive, and incompetent often rests on well-founded grievances. Citizens are losing trust in democratic political institutions—and democracy cannot function without that trust. Finding effective responses to these challenges is not just legitimate; it’s essential. It is understandable that many seek to “return power to the people.” There’s nothing wrong with that—in fact, it's commendable. The real question is how we do it. The danger is that “returning power” is once again hijacked by politicians who claim the exclusive right to define who the people are and what they want. Some advocate for the supremacy of direct democracy, replacing representative democracy with referendums. In Slovenia, the recent popular vote that overturned the water law has strengthened this argument. Although referendums are certainly a vital form of democratic expression, their use still requires safeguards—without which they can become instruments of majority tyranny that suppress minority rights, or tools for the pseudo-legitimization of authoritarian rule. Just think of some of the topics and ways referendums have been used—not only here, but in neighboring countries. One clear response is broader citizen participation in politics. Freedom of expression—including through protest—is essential for a functioning democracy. But we must ask whether such expressions are seen as a check and correction on representative democracy—or as its replacement. The most likes on social media do not equal a democratic mandate. Not every protest or mass mobilization is automatically progressive. A 2020 study led by Timothy Garton Ash found that in Europe, over half of young people concerned about the environmental crisis trust authoritarian leaders more than democratic ones to solve it. Of course, I am not claiming that the current democratic model is perfect or beyond improvement. But while we search for alternatives, we must first strengthen and reform the system we already have. The problems causing anger and distrust in democracy stem not from flawed democratic principles, but from inconsistent implementation. Democracy demands legitimacy, competence, integrity, transparency, and accountability in governance. We clearly cannot rely on the goodwill of politicians alone—effective oversight mechanisms are necessary to keep power in check. Civil society—so often targeted by populists—is crucial here, along with the judiciary and independent media. In Slovenia, the work of organizations like the Legal Network for the Protection of Democracy and the Voice of the People initiative is a powerful example of such civil society action. They apply democratic pressure on political authorities, demand accountability, and draw strength from democratic constitutional values—thereby reinforcing them. This is one of the things that gives me hope that we can preserve and strengthen democracy—and that the historical kaleidoscope won’t spin us back to authoritarian verses, even if we once believed we’d left those behind for good. And even if Mark Twain never actually said that history rhymes—it doesn’t mean it can’t.

The title may surprise some and lead them to think that I have finally broken my rule of not commenting on day-to-day and party politics in Slovenia, or even that, a few months before the elections, I have opportunistically decided to jump on this or that bandwagon. That is not the case. I have already expressed my disagreement with calls for “death to Janšism.” Not because it is a death threat, as the prosecutor’s office has also concluded, but because it is a crude form of political discourse, of which there is already far too much in Slovenia. Today I will go a step further and explain why calls of “down with Janšism” and other -isms do not appeal to me either. Ever since independence, Slovenia has held a very stubborn belief that most of our crosses and troubles are caused by Slovenian disunity. We experience division as a curse placed in our cradle by the wicked witch of fate because we didn’t invite her to the christening and party at the birth of the state on June 25, 1991. And since it is a curse, there is of course no shortage of princes convinced that with their magic kiss they can reawaken us into unity and lead us into a brighter future, for ever and ever, amen. First among them is the President of the Republic, who constantly tries to bring the nation together in a warm, but value-indifferent, uncritical, everything-is-equal embrace. And after all these years, he has evidently not been very successful. From the despair of the Slovenian obsession with division, a real industry of party-political platforms has been born, promising us heaven on earth in the name of overcoming differences and in the much-vaunted center, which here has been emptied of ideology. Many politicians and parties, with a few sincere exceptions, would like to be in the center and claim to be in the center, because there, in their view, you can be ideologically nowhere and anywhere at the same time. Because there you can promise everything and do nothing, or whatever suits you. They would all connect and unite us so that we would no longer wander left or right but just march smartly forward. My thesis is not that we are not divided, because we evidently are. Not only that: after almost two years of the pandemic, we as a society are not just divided but scattered, and we have serious trouble functioning as a civilized and rational community of people. But I am firmly convinced that it was not division that got us into this mess, but the fact that we divide over the wrong things and in the wrong way. The curse of Slovenian (and not only Slovenian) society and democracy is not that we are not united, but that we don’t know how to be disunited in a civilized and rational way. Remember the kind of regime we lived in in the former state. There was no room there for any division whatsoever. Anyone who had a disunited thought quickly got a rap on the knuckles or on the head. We lived, breathed and thought as one. At least in the official, public and permitted sphere. One nation (OK, a few nations), one regime, one ideology. Given that the end of political uniformity of thought was one of the main motives for independence, it is a tragic paradox that today we put a variation of that same uniformity on a national pedestal. The functioning pluralist democracy we fought for thirty years ago and protected in our Constitution requires, as the name says, pluralism. A space based on constitutional values for the exchange and contest of different programs, ideas and ideologies. It also requires a political culture that guides and binds politics to competence, integrity, transparency and accountability, and of course a system of safeguards that protect democracy when politics fails to respect these imperatives. Instead of such democratic pluralism, in Slovenia (and not only in Slovenia) we are sinking into the swamp of tribal cultural polarization, in which ideas, proposals and programs do not count or decide anything; only identity does. Who you are, who you are with, who you are against. In this paradigm, the aim of political action is not to obtain a democratic mandate to implement programs approved in elections, but complete and permanent dominance over the political opponent. By any means and at any price. This is the result of compromising with authoritarian populism, which we are witnessing in many parts of Europe and the world. Populism is not an ideology and does not need ideas. It requires warriors and enemies and does not tolerate critically thinking citizens and political competition. It operates with labels and slogans that serve as targets and instructions to the infantry on whom to sink their teeth into and whom to attack. Commies, Soros hirelings, feminists, faggots, multi-culti traitors. Those who respond to labels and insults from one side in the same way are walking into the trap that populism sets for them. The British Guardian recently published the findings of a survey conducted by the YouGov-Cambridge Globalism Project, which show that political conflicts, or the culture war as it is called in the West, in many democracies are based not so much on differences in people’s views and political opinions as on blind tribal loyalty to one’s own camp and hostility towards those who support the other side. If things have gone that far in countries with a much longer historical experience of democracy, then it is clear that where there is less such experience, and where the institutions and safeguards of pluralist democracy are consequently weaker, the situation is all the worse and more dangerous. And here I want to return to my disagreement with politics reduced to a fight against -isms of one kind or another. If we want to dig ourselves out of the mess and finally start building the civilizational social model because of which and in the name of which we became independent thirty years ago, we too must give up labels, generalizations and ad personam political warfare. The answer to the devalued, everything-is-equal pursuit of unity, which is an ally of populism and objectively paves the way to uniformity of thought, cannot be an uncritical and absolutist digging into our own trenches, our own labels and slogans, because that leads to accepting and legitimizing the culture war as the only form of political action. Whatever my political beliefs, I would never want to live in a society in which everyone thought, or even had to think, like me. That does not mean, of course, agreeing to everything and respecting everything—quite the opposite—but pluralist democracy needs a competition of ideas, not a war with people, however much we dislike them. In Slovenia, we should build unity on respect for the Constitution. In it we wrote down the fundamental values on which, three decades ago, we were determined to build our future. The rule of law requires respect for the Constitution and the laws, and an independent judiciary that is not and cannot be the tool of one side or the other. We wrote into the Constitution that Slovenia is a welfare state, which is no obstacle to different political options pursuing this goal in different ways, but they cannot ignore or nullify it. We wrote that we are a state that respects human rights and political freedoms. This is an imperative that cannot be subject to the goodwill of the current majority or to political horse-trading. We must fight for effective democratic oversight mechanisms, independent media and an engaged and critical civil society, without which there is and can be no functioning democracy. We must resist the argument of “first it was you, now it’s our turn,” because it leads to clientelism, corruption and the defeat of democracy. We must resist balancing one partial interest against another, one indecency against another, constitutionally protected democratic values against their authoritarian alternatives, knowledge against stupidity, culture against nationalist iconography, critical thinking against blind obedience, facts against emotionally selected “truths” collected on social networks, solidarity and responsibility against selfishness. Let us stop accepting the thesis that this is a choice between left and right. Perhaps we will manage to take a qualitative step towards democracy when we are able to distinguish between a personality disorder and a political idea and program.

On October 5 this year, in the Alsatian town of Klingersheim near the Swiss border, Amira walked into her 14-year-old daughter Dinah’s room and found her dead. According to her mother, Dinah committed suicide because she saw no other way out due to relentless bullying, ridicule, and insults from her peers—both at school and on social media. Dinah had once been a popular and sociable high school student, a good pupil and athlete, always surrounded by friends. “She wanted to become president of the republic,” her mother said. But when, at 13, she decided to confide in her peers about her sexual orientation, her life turned into hell. To continue their torment even during afternoons and weekends, some of her classmates and former friends created a WhatsApp group where they posted insults about the “dirty lesbian” and “dirty mixed-race girl.” Dinah’s mother Amira was born in La Réunion, a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean. Dinah had already attempted suicide in March of this year, but the new school year and her enrollment in a new high school gave her some hope that her suffering might end. It was in vain. When she begged her tormentors on social media to leave her alone, they responded: “We hope you succeed next time.” Dinah’s parents do not only blame her peers for her death but also the school administration, which, according to them, had been informed of the bullying but failed to act. Both the police and school authorities launched an investigation to determine whether there was a causal link between the hell Dinah endured and her decision to take her own life. The results of that investigation are not yet known. However, a study conducted nearly a decade ago at Mireil University in Toulouse showed that suicidal tendencies are significantly more common among young people attracted to the same sex or uncertain about their sexual identity—mainly due to the hostile, intolerant, and abusive reactions of their peers. This tragic reality is not only illustrated by Dinah’s story but also by the suicides of 19-year-old transgender psychology student Doona, who threw herself under a train at the Montpellier railway station in September last year, and 17-year-old Avril, who took her life in Lille last December. Dinah, Doona, and Avril all committed suicide in France—a country not usually seen as overtly homophobic, at least not at first glance. For several years now, the French Ministry of Education has issued guidelines to schools for preventing peer bullying and harassment, which include measures against homophobic verbal and physical violence. Recently, the French Parliament unanimously approved a draft law enabling criminal prosecution of so-called "conversion therapy" to “cure homosexuality.” If the victim of such “therapy” is a minor, the draft law provides for up to three years in prison. Yet Dinah’s tragic case and the political rhetoric of likely presidential candidate Éric Zemmour—whose crusade in defense of the “white, heterosexual, Catholic Frenchman” enjoys strong support in public opinion polls—demonstrate that homophobia remains deeply rooted in French society. Hatred based on sexual orientation is not just a fringe pathology even in the “more liberal” part of Western Europe. A reluctance—or at least a lack of determination—to ensure equal rights and respect for human dignity remains present even in parts of the political mainstream. This was evident in a recent secret vote in the Italian Senate, where a bill was blocked by a margin of 154 to 131 votes. The bill would have defined violence against LGBT persons, people with disabilities, and acts of misogyny as hate crimes. Members of far-right parties claimed the law would restrict free speech and promote homosexual propaganda in schools. Such arguments strongly resemble rhetoric found in parts of Eastern Europe, where political movements base their vision of a new Eastern conservatism on similar ideas. Homophobia is one of the bludgeons used by far-right populism to demolish the European democratic model, which is based on human rights, pluralistic democracy, and the rule of law. American historian Timothy Snyder interprets the populist obsession with homosexuality as an attempt to justify authoritarian rule under the guise of protecting the nation’s purity from the supposed threat of decadent liberal democracy from the West. The strategic advantage of polarizing society around sexual orientation is that—unlike arguments over social progress, economic performance, material well-being, or personal freedoms—it requires no facts. Stirring up prejudice and intolerance suffices. The extent of intolerance at the institutional level is starkly illustrated by the fact that nearly a hundred Polish municipalities and regions declared themselves “LGBT-free zones.” Some have since reversed these declarations—but only out of fear of losing European funding. Notably, the term “LGBT-free” strongly resembles “Judenfrei”, the Nazi designation for areas “cleansed of Jews.” I won’t go so far as to draw further conclusions or call anyone a Nazi, but the terminological similarity is too striking to ignore. The insidiousness of measures targeting the rights and dignity of LGBTI+ individuals in countries that officially remain committed to European human rights standards lies in their claimed justification: they do not attack homosexuals per se but the so-called “LGBT ideology.” According to this logic, LGBTI people are supposedly equal citizens with full rights—but the law prohibits anyone from explaining that this is the case, especially to children. Bizarre, but unfortunately effective. To justify and conceal discrimination based on sexual orientation and identity, personal characteristics are reframed as deliberate choices of an unacceptable, perverse, and socially harmful ideological orientation. Some don’t even bother to pretend anymore; they openly incite against the “ideology” of human rights and other core values of civilization. Dinah, according to her mother, committed suicide because she could no longer endure the abuse she suffered at school in a country where the fight against hatred and discrimination based on sexual orientation and identity is not only enshrined in law but, at least for now, enjoys broad political and societal consensus. It is almost impossible to imagine the personal anguish and suffering experienced by young LGBTI people in countries where intolerance is politically weaponized, and where “homosexual propaganda in schools” is legally banned. The logic of hatred and intolerance, if taken to its extreme, paints a chilling projection of a possible future in which Éric Zemmour wins the French presidential election and implements parts of his ideological platform. After Dinah’s death, hundreds gathered in the town of Mulhouse, including many children, to express outrage at the tragedy and demand protection of human rights and respect for the dignity of LGBTQ people. Under legislation already in place in some European countries, such an expression of opinion could be banned—and even criminally prosecuted.
The Vulgar Charm of the Bourgeoisie

At the end of September, leaders from Eastern Europe and the Western Balkans concerned about family values, with a few guests from elsewhere, gathered at a demographic summit in Budapest. Also present in Budapest was the notorious French columnist and wannabe president Éric Zemmour. His credentials regarding devotion to family values were revealed on the cover of the French weekly Paris Match just before the summit began, with a photograph of Éric in the sea embracing his “very close adviser” Sarah Knafo, who is neither Zemmour’s wife nor the mother of his three children. Personally, I believe consenting adults can do whatever they like with each other and with themselves, even climb drainpipes, but it is hypocritical to hand out moral lessons on family and Christian values while doing so and to advocate political ideas that have very little in common with those values. Éric Zemmour is no unknown in France. Even before revealing his presidential ambitions, not yet officially confirmed, he was first a journalist and then a columnist at the Paris daily Le Figaro, a political commentator on television; he has also written several books and earned two court convictions for racism and hatred of Muslims. His latest book, published this year under the title France Has Not Said Its Last Word, with which he launched his march on the Élysée Palace, sold more than a hundred thousand copies in four days. He was born in France in 1958 to Jewish parents who had immigrated from Algeria a few years earlier. Although he attended the local synagogue in his youth, after his father’s death he, as he puts it, assimilated. His very close associate from the cover of Paris Match, herself also of Jewish origin, cited precisely his distancing from Jewish identity and community as the reason for his appeal. What is more, the projection of France as a country of white Christians, or rather Catholics, is the foundation and ever-present thread of his political ideology. To Zemmour it is perfectly clear who threatens such a France most. Black people and Muslims. And the bogeyman of the “great replacement,” which also so excites the Slovenian far right. In 2016 he declared that all Muslims support jihad and that young people from immigrant families would have to choose between France and Islam. If they choose wrongly, they can pack their bags. Or have them packed for them. For this he earned his second conviction for racial hatred. He later added to this thought by declaring that France is in an ethno-religious war and faces a gangrene of savages determined to exterminate the white, heterosexual, Catholic man. Besides Arabs, Black people and homosexuals, Éric is also greatly irritated by the judiciary and the media. They are counterweights that are becoming stronger than the government and must therefore have their toes trodden on, he growled recently at a gathering of his ideological crony, the mayor of Béziers, Robert Ménard, who in 1985—oh, the irony—was among the founders of Reporters Without Borders. What this treading on toes might look like in practice, Zemmour illustrated last week at the Paris security equipment fair, where he grabbed an automatic rifle and pointed it at the journalists following him. Bang, bang, bang. Ha, ha, ha. Opinion polls today, six months before the first round of the presidential election, show that such ideas have considerable support in France. With around seventeen percent, Zemmour is breathing down Marine Le Pen’s neck and threatening her place in the second round. For now, he has more support than any representative of the traditional conservatives from the Republicans, who have not yet agreed on who will carry their colors. Above all, he is well ahead of all the candidates from the left of the political spectrum, which is even more thoroughly fragmented. At first sight, Zemmour’s arrival on the political scene benefits President Emmanuel Macron most, who will be seeking a second term. Whereas a month ago he was level with Marine Le Pen, today he stands alone at a relatively high twenty-five percent, roughly where he was at the same point before the last election, while his main rival so far has lost more than a third of her support. But Macron’s lead may also melt away. On the one hand, if we add up Zemmour, Le Pen and the Republicans, plus various radical sovereigntist village eccentrics, the right has almost half the potential votes, if not more. Any consolidation around the most successful candidate of the right, although of course it will be neither automatic nor complete, could endanger Macron’s victory in the second round. Moreover, Macron will probably have great difficulty collecting votes from the left in the second round, since his French version of the doctrine of “neither left nor right, but forward” has disappointed and infuriated many left-wing voters, so many predict that in a second round between Macron and a candidate of the right they simply won’t go to the polls. The effect of Zemmour’s arrival on the political scene is already being felt among the possible Republican candidates. Even Michel Barnier, until recently Brussels’ Brexit negotiator and an ardent supporter of the EU, recently declared that on migration he opposes the primacy of European law over national law. Very important above all will be how the duel between Zemmour and Le Pen plays out. The leader of the National Rally has for some time been working on a (relative) deradicalization of her party and on appealing to more centrist voters. It was precisely this that created the opportunity Zemmour is exploiting to the full. But there is another difference between them that may in the end tip the scales in favor of the more experienced Marine Le Pen. Although at first sight there seem to be few differences between their political programs, except that on every point Zemmour is a boat length more radical and intolerant, a more detailed analysis shows that they do not address exactly the same part of the electorate. The National Front, dressed up as the “more moderate” National Rally, has strengthened its position in recent decades mainly by taking the votes of a proletariat and lower middle class disappointed with the left. Zemmour, who comes across as a British Euroskeptic Nigel Farage who went to good schools, addresses above all the elite or, as he calls it, the patriotic bourgeoisie. The very conservative, Catholic and privileged part of the French white middle and upper class, which is traditionally sovereigntist, bristling at Europe and frightened of social and demographic changes in which it sees a threat to its privileged position. It mobilizes en masse on issues related to LGBT rights and the right to abortion. In the past, it was to some extent sympathetic to Sarkozy’s flirting with more extreme themes, and after his rather inglorious departure from the political scene some of it moved to Le Pen, although many probably resent being in the same sack as the plebs. No wonder they grabbed Zemmour like a dog grabs a sausage. A link between Zemmour and Sarkozy, still influential in his party, who publicly rejects Zemmour, is also Sarkozy’s former chief ideologue and the architect of his opening to the far right, Henri Guaino. The gentleman, who is in court these very days over the illegal financing of Sarkozy’s second presidential campaign, was also the first political mentor of Zemmour’s aforementioned very close adviser, who also runs his presidential campaign. Although Zemmour tries to appeal to the lower middle class too, an alliance between the bourgeoisie and the yellow vests is not going very well for him. This was seen most recently during the dizzying recent rise in energy prices, when Le Pen called for protection of the most vulnerable, while Zemmour made it clear that he did not intend to deal with such things, since his mission is to defend France (not the French). In his political paradigm there is not much room for “ordinary” citizens. Clearly this is the ground on which Le Pen will look for a counterattack. In his first televised debate with the leader of the left-wing France Unbowed, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Zemmour also showed that he quickly runs out of breadth and depth. Whether the subject is health, the weather or petrol prices, by the second sentence he will start talking about Islam and immigrants. What will come of all this is not yet entirely clear. Although the centrist Macron will most likely win a second term in the spring, ideas that were roundly defeated in the recent German elections have a better chance on the western bank of the Rhine of becoming part of the political mainstream.

Populism is a term frequently used in politics, most often to describe people, opinions, or actions we disagree with. This reckless name-calling of anything and everything stems from the fact that everyone interprets populism in their own way. Disagreement exists not only over who qualifies as a populist but also whether populism itself is inherently negative. The term populism first appeared in a very different context than today. The American Populist or People's Party emerged in the late 19th century as a left-leaning agrarian movement advocating for economic and political reforms in favor of farmers, particularly in the western United States. A more positive (and romantic) view of populism was developed by Argentine political theorist Ernesto Laclau and his partner Chantal Mouffe. They saw populism as a radical, emancipatory response to stagnant and unjust liberal democracy. Their perspective resonated with parts of the Slovenian left, which viewed left-wing populism as a counterforce to the rise of neoliberalism and the far right in Slovenia's political space. Perhaps the most common—and least precise—interpretation describes populism as a simplistic politics that aims to please everyone at all costs. According to that standard, there would be no doubt who the biggest populist in Slovenia is. I’m skeptical of this view. While I don’t deny that someone who treats politics as an ego trip can be a populist, I’d argue that trying desperately to please everyone is not populism per se—it’s more accurately described as popularism. Still, this pursuit of likability, built on deliberate ethical non-commitment and a “both-sides” approach to values, objectively benefits those who disdain the principles of liberal democracy. These are the very actors described as populists by German-American political scientist Jan-Werner Müller. He defines a populist as someone who arbitrarily claims the exclusive right to represent “the people.” Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde offers a similar explanation, arguing that populism, in all its forms, always involves invoking “the people” while stigmatizing “the elites.” This strategy can be deployed from either the left or the right. Mudde sees populism not as an ideology but as a political strategy used by powerful, charismatic leaders to seize and consolidate power.
