Johns Hopkins political scientist Yascha Mounk, in his book The People vs. Democracy, describes illiberal democracy—characteristic of populism in power—as “democracy without rights.” In such a system, elections are held regularly, but without effective safeguards to ensure they are also free and fair, to protect political freedoms, guarantee minority rights, or enable independent media and courts to carry out oversight. The power of the people becomes the tyranny of the majority, personified, interpreted, and executed by the “people’s leader”—or in other words, the populist. Populism, then, should not be recognized based on name-calling among political opponents, but rather by examining its relationship with checks and balances—the institutions that ensure democratic oversight. In liberal democracy, these institutions are vital for upholding pluralism, political freedoms, human rights, and the rule of law. In the populist view of power, they are seen as obstacles to executing “the will of the people”—which, let us repeat, is unilaterally defined and enforced by the populist himself. How does this manifest in practice? Let’s start with the judiciary. Courts are the most common and effective barrier to populists trying to implement the “people’s will” in unlawful or unconstitutional ways. Populism attacks this barrier in two ways: first, by seeking control over the judiciary through the appointment of judges who are willing to cooperate, cover for, and legitimize dubious populist decisions. Everyone knows how important judicial appointments were to former U.S. President Donald Trump. Over four years—and thanks to some maneuvering by the Republican majority in Congress—he managed to appoint three Supreme Court justices: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett. He also appointed over 250 judges to lower federal courts. While judicial appointments are routine and necessary, the fact that Trump appointed as many judges in one term as many of his predecessors did in two is striking. Populists often rush to take control of the judiciary. In countries with weaker democratic traditions and oversight mechanisms, we often see attempts to accelerate judicial takeovers through selective purges, orchestrated disciplinary actions, and similar tricks. Populists also fight independent judges and prosecutors they can’t control through smears. Terms like “traitors of the people” and “crooked judiciary” are common populist rhetoric when the courts are doing their job. The media face similar treatment. Since illiberal democracies are (still) not fully authoritarian, they are forced to coexist with media outlets critical of their policies. Populists try to gain control through financial takeovers of private media and, in public media, by reshuffling leadership and exerting pressure. A public media outlet that is independent—and thus capable of criticizing those in power—is, for the populist, an unacceptable anomaly. Populists often can’t or won’t distinguish between what is public and what is state-owned, and thus, in their view, theirs to control. Media that resist are attacked. Labels like "MSM" (mainstream media) and "fake news" are go-to insults—used not just by Trump. Populists also discredit facts and truth itself. The phrase “alternative facts,” coined by Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway to justify blatantly false claims about inauguration crowd sizes, encapsulates this mindset. In a world where everyone gets their own facts, truth no longer exists. Media are evaluated not by professionalism, independence, or adherence to journalistic ethics, but by their loyalty—or lack thereof—to the leader and his ideology. This logic also underpins the idea of “media balance,” where the goal is not fairness or objectivity, but an alignment with political power. The third pillar of democratic oversight that populists particularly despise is civil society. Trump’s expression after ordering police to violently disperse anti-racism protesters outside the White House—so he could walk to St. John’s Church and pose with a Bible held upside down—says it all. In Europe, civil society is protected by Articles 11 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Article 11 guarantees freedom of association; Article 12 protects the right to peaceful protest, without requiring prior approval or permits. In populist-run states, both rights are under serious threat. In a system where the “people’s will” is embodied solely by the populist, all other expressions of citizen will—especially critical ones—are by default suspicious and unacceptable. Some countries have even legally adopted terms like “foreign agent” to more easily restrict these European Convention–guaranteed freedoms. The fundamental problem for populists is that even successfully capturing all oversight mechanisms and societal subsystems doesn’t guarantee long-term immunity from public dissatisfaction—including from former supporters. The reason is simple. Populism exploits often legitimate grievances to delegitimize political competition and seize power—but it has neither the interest nor the ability to fix the problems it campaigned on. Without independent courts, free media, and active civil society, there’s no protection against government incompetence and corruption. Staffing institutions based on loyalty rather than expertise leaves a society ill-equipped to tackle economic, social, environmental, technological, developmental, or health challenges. Even scapegoating, fearmongering, culture wars, nationalism, and minority-bashing can’t provide lasting relief from public anger once people realize they’ve been conned. At that point, all populism has left is repression—and the already-blurred line between illiberal democracy and full-blown authoritarianism fades even further.

The tendency to experience every life event as unprecedented and unique may be human, but it can lead to improvisation and repetition of past mistakes—mistakes we could avoid if we were more willing to learn from history instead of eagerly trying to transcend it. History does not repeat itself, said Mark Twain, but it rhymes. It doesn’t replicate in identical forms, as similar events—such as epidemics of infectious diseases and their consequences—are shaped by changing social and other circumstances over time. Still, it’s fascinating how certain patterns of behaviour—both individual and collective—persist like a mutated virus, constantly finding new ways to overcome the immune system of our supposed Enlightenment progress. That is one of the messages in Doom, a book by British historian Niall Ferguson, professor at Stanford University, about the history of catastrophes, from those that helped bring down the Western Roman Empire to COVID-19. The book, written at the end of last year during the still-ongoing pandemic, shows the risks of trying to write history in real time. In his conclusion, Ferguson suggests that this pandemic will likely not rank among the top twenty largest epidemics in recorded history—those in which more than 0.05% of the global population died. By my quick calculation, we are already on that list. Ferguson’s optimism rests on his trust in containment measures and the then-impending availability of vaccines. But in doing so, he seems to forget his own lesson about the importance of learning from past experience. History teaches us—and his book provides vivid examples—that the existence of a rational solution does not guarantee a rational or effective response, either by governments or the public. Infectious diseases are a constant in human history. The toll has often been unimaginable by today’s standards. The plague wiped out more than a third of Europe’s population in the Middle Ages. Until the mid-19th century, responses to such threats were not based on science but on careful observation and conclusions about disease transmission. Many of the restrictive measures introduced worldwide in response to COVID-19 were already known in the Middle Ages, down to the smallest detail. Quarantine was first introduced in Ragusa (modern-day Dubrovnik) and got its name in Marseille, where it was extended from 14 to 40 days based on inspiration from the Bible. Medieval authorities closed borders and imposed social distancing. Even a form of what we now call the “vaccination-pass-test” system existed centuries before vaccines or testing. In Ferrara, Italy, movement was allowed only for those carrying a certificate of health (fedi di sanità). In Florence, authorities delivered food and medical care to those who were ill or unable to work due to the epidemic—comparable to modern pandemic measures like compensating those in quarantine so they wouldn’t go to work and infect others. Even the hardship faced by restaurateurs and cultural workers during an epidemic is not new. The 1665 outbreak of plague in London led to a ban on all “plays, bear dancing, games, ballad singing, martial sports, and other gatherings of people, as well as public feasts and rowdy drinking in taverns.” As with COVID-19, plague containment measures met with mixed responses. Some rejected them on religious grounds. One of the most notorious movements were the flagellants—groups of men who travelled from town to town, forming circles, whipping themselves with metal-tipped lashes, and collapsing to the ground. They believed that only through martyrdom could they stop divine punishment. During their pilgrimages, which lasted thirty-three and a half days, they didn’t bathe, shave, change clothes, or sleep in beds. Public bivouacking and strange group behaviour as a response to pandemics, therefore, are not new. Some flagellants also attacked Jewish communities, leading to brutal massacres in places like Frankfurt, Mainz, and Strasbourg—where I live. Antisemitism and conspiracy theories have long been part of the story of epidemics, and even today, antisemitic memes about supposed disease profiteers are widespread in anti-vaccine discourse on social media. Equating the “injustices” faced by anti-vaxxers with the crimes committed against Jewish Holocaust victims is offensive and completely unacceptable. I’m not saying all anti-vaxxers are extremists or antisemites, but they should be aware of the company they keep. Scientific progress, especially in understanding the causes of infectious diseases, has diminished religious explanations for epidemics but also created space for other irrational theories and behaviours—many of which persist today. Daniel Defoe, best known for Robinson Crusoe, recorded his impressions of a plague outbreak in early 18th-century London in a journal published in 1722. He wrote: “People’s fears increased strangely in those difficult times. They were more dependent on prophecies, astrology, charms, dreams, and old wives’ tales than ever before. Whether this unfortunate trait was initially promoted by those who profited from publishing prophecies, I cannot say, but such books truly terrified people.” Three hundred years ago—and it could have been written today. Of course, it wasn’t always ignorant masses at fault. Ever since medicine became a profession, there have been doctors whose vanity, incompetence, irresponsibility—or plain stupidity—caused harm. In the early 19th century, some American doctors recommended highly toxic mercury, electric shocks, or blowing tobacco smoke into the rectum to treat cholera. The president of the New York Medical Society swore by plugging the rectum with greasy cloth or beeswax to treat cholera-induced diarrhoea. Ivermectin is merely the latest chapter in a long tradition of bizarre and dangerous “cures.” One of Ferguson’s key conclusions is that we cannot strictly separate natural disasters from man-made ones, because their course and impact depend heavily on how societies and governments respond. The mortality caused by a pathogen also reflects the social and political system it strikes. Ferguson devotes an entire chapter to the psychology of political incompetence, inspired by British psychologist Norman Dixon’s work on military incompetence. Dixon identified the bad commander as someone who, despite poor decisions, refuses to change course, fails to learn from experience, clings to a failing strategy despite evidence to the contrary, bolsters himself with pompous self-aggrandizement, ignores contradicting information, and always blames others. Although Dixon studied military leaders, the same traits can appear in political leaders—especially those who treat politics like warfare. During a public health crisis, this can have dire consequences, not only in health but across society. As American foreign policy elder Henry Kissinger recently noted, national unity and success depend on people believing that institutions can foresee disasters, mitigate their effects, and restore stability. When the COVID-19 pandemic ends, many will judge their institutions as failures. Whether that judgment is objectively fair won’t matter. Although the pandemic is still ongoing, growing evidence suggests that Kissinger is right. After a year and a half, people in many places are increasingly desperate, frightened, and angry. These emotions—often justified—create perfect conditions for the spread of political populism. The danger of populism lies not in the questions it raises, but in the consistently poor answers it offers. The virus is not the only threat to societal stability, democratic institutions, and values. It is the inadequate response to the health crisis and the political exploitation of human suffering. If we lose our freedoms after the pandemic, we won’t be able to blame the bats and pangolins. We, the people, will be responsible. Nature merely cooperated.

Let me state at the outset that I sincerely support efforts to bring more decency into Slovenian public life, especially politics. Our public discourse has become so coarse, petty, offensive, inappropriate, degrading, dirty, rude, aggressive, uncultured, illiterate, exclusionary, insolent, sexist, and disrespectful that it simply cannot go on like this. Law can be part of the solution, but it cannot and must not become a bludgeon used to strike down everything someone dislikes. The mess we’re getting ourselves into in Slovenia in the name of promoting greater respect and decency in public discourse partly stems from our tendency to lump many different things together. Chief among these is the conflation of various categories of “problematic” speech—from rude to outright hateful. We also too often overlook that alongside the content and form of speech, who is speaking, about whom, and to whom also matters. In public space, various individuals and groups interact with vastly different social statuses and professional or personal circumstances. These differing contexts mean they don’t all bear the same obligations or possess the same rights in how they communicate publicly. This is not discrimination—it’s simply a fact that the appropriateness or illegality of a publicly spoken word cannot be judged in isolation from the social positions and power dynamics between speaker and subject. Freedom of expression is protected under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It is one of the fundamental freedoms essential for the functioning of a pluralist democracy. Without freedom of expression, there can be no free exchange of opinions, no democratic oversight of government, no pluralism, and no free and fair elections. At the same time, Article 10 and the rich case law of the European Court of Human Rights allow, under strict conditions, certain restrictions on free speech to protect the public interest and the rights, freedoms, and dignity of others. These limitations must not only be prescribed by law but must also be necessary, meaning the legitimate aim cannot be achieved in a less restrictive way. These are the standards we should keep in mind when considering how to respond to the crudeness and indecency now widespread in Slovenian public life. The question is whether we can or even should respond with laws and punishments—even if the intention is noble. The problem is that neither the Convention nor the Court's case law provides a precise legal definition of hate speech. You won’t find a simple and universally applicable measuring stick to quickly determine what’s allowed and what’s not. The Court’s guide to case law on Article 10 runs to 132 pages. The Court doesn’t usually refer to “hate speech” as such, but rather to permissible speech—speech that, despite being problematic, still enjoys protection under Article 10. Whether speech is permissible or not must be assessed case by case, depending on specific circumstances—not just the content but also the context and the personal and social standing of both speaker and subject. These factors critically influence the consequences of restricting (or not restricting) speech for both the individuals involved and for democracy more broadly. It’s one thing when politicians talk among themselves. The public has every right to expect respectful language and avoidance of crude or offensive speech in such exchanges. This standard applies not just to formal settings like parliament but to any public communication—including on social media. These platforms are no excuse for political misbehavior. Of course, this doesn’t mean political debate must be sterile. Passionate clashes of opinion are part of pluralist democracy. But as one of my former bosses with long experience in the British Parliament liked to say: play the ball, not the man. The traditional belief that politicians will eventually be punished at the polls for their rudeness and insults has been turned on its head by populism. Today, some politicians deliberately use inflammatory and offensive language toward their opponents and critics to stoke, direct, and exploit voter resentment, intolerance, and hatred. The way politicians treat institutions—especially those with democratic oversight roles like the judiciary and media—is just as important. Restraint doesn’t mean criticism should be stifled; criticism is not only allowed but essential. But it should be reasoned and respectful. The tone politicians use toward these institutions reflects their respect (or lack thereof) for their constitutional roles in safeguarding democracy and the rule of law. It is especially vital how politicians speak about social minorities. Their language shapes not only public discourse but also public attitudes toward these groups. It can profoundly affect their social standing, rights, dignity, and even physical safety. This is precisely where the danger of hate speech is greatest. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers defines hate speech as: “All forms of expression that spread, incite, promote or justify racial hatred, xenophobia, anti-Semitism or other forms of hatred based on intolerance, including aggressive nationalism and ethnocentrism, discrimination and hostility against minorities, migrants, and people of immigrant origin.” While this is a political definition, and not all statements within this category necessarily cross the legal threshold for restricting free speech, their possible legality does not mean they cannot or should not be condemned—especially when coming from politicians. On the contrary: the excuse of “respecting all opinions” has been precisely what has legitimized and normalized indecent, offensive, and even hateful rhetoric in Slovenia. Finally, there’s communication between politicians and citizens. Because of its crucial role in democracy, we must be especially cautious and restrained about restricting or punishing speech in this context. That doesn’t mean we give up on encouraging respectful discourse, but the European Court of Human Rights explicitly allows for speech that “offends, shocks or disturbs.” This certainly doesn’t extend to spitting on MPs or storming the national broadcaster’s offices, as we've seen in Slovenia. Those are not expressions of free speech—they are threats to safety and physical integrity, and they must be sanctioned, either administratively or criminally. It’s a different matter when citizens express themselves publicly, even if their words might subjectively "offend, shock, or disturb" politicians and officials. The Latin saying "Quod licet Iovi, non licet bovi"—"What is permitted to Jupiter is not permitted to the ox"—cannot apply here. In democracy, it’s the opposite: politicians enjoy less protection from criticism, no matter how unfair, harsh, or noisy it may seem to them, and they bear greater responsibility than ordinary citizens. The path to more dignity and fewer insults in Slovenian public life must begin with the Jupiters. Including, perhaps, by no longer comparing people to farm animals.

Many who are old enough will probably remember the joke about a communist bigwig (insert any name) who, during a stroll through the countryside, met a peasant with a nag in a sorry state. “What’s wrong with the horse, comrade peasant?” “I don’t know, comrade (insert any name), it won’t eat, it’s losing weight, and it looks at me so sadly.” “Play it revolutionary music. It lifts people’s spirits, so why not livestock?” A week passes and the bigwig goes for another stroll to check the effects of his advice. This time the peasant is seriously worried, as the horse’s knees are buckling from wasting away. “Rub it with garlic,” comrade (insert any name) tosses off cheerfully, smiling condescendingly. When he runs into the peasant again a few days later, the peasant is sitting glumly on a stump. “Where’s the horse?” the man from the Central Committee (insert any name) asks him. “It croaked, comrade,” the peasant replies grimly. “What a pity,” replies the party official, “I had so many more ideas.” Like most jokes from the socialist era, this one caricatures the painful reality of the time. It mocks the party’s approach to organizing agriculture. In reality, that approach had consequences that were not funny at all and often tragic. Millions of Ukrainians died in 1932 and 1933 from a famine to which political decisions from Moscow largely contributed. Even more murderous was China’s Great Leap Forward, which began in 1958 and in four years claimed tens of millions of human lives. All this happened in systems that, in their ideological iconography, held peasants in very high regard. Today in Slovenia there are no more communists, except in the heads and behavior patterns of some former communists. There are fewer and fewer farmers too, but they still represent, in democracy as well and at least for some, a very important part of their ideological paradigm. As in communism, the farmers themselves often benefit least from this attention. This is nicely illustrated by the ideologically charged fetishization of the phrase “healthy peasant common sense.” It is so often abused to justify and cover up all kinds of nonsense and prejudice that it has become almost insulting. Especially to farmers. A few days ago, I saw a news report about a young Slovenian farmer. The guy struck me as a bit of an enthusiast and as stubborn as a farmer has to be, but above all well-read and smart. Not peasant-smart or common-sense-smart, but simply intelligent. My first objection to the phrase “healthy peasant common sense” is that it suggests an absence of ability and interest in tackling the more complicated intellectual knots we associate with “ordinary,” unhealthy and non-peasant intelligence. Romanticizing “if it’s round it’s a shovel, if it’s pointed it’s a pickaxe” is condescending to farmers. I have enormous respect for this profession. It requires a great deal of knowledge, experience, understanding of nature and harmony with it, as well as sacrifice, very hard work and the ever-present risk of loss and defeat. On the other hand, there is also the satisfaction that comes from producing food. Something you have created yourself, from the soil and with nature. That pride, raised to the hundredth power, that we ordinary mortals feel at every cherry tomato or basil leaf we manage to grow on our balconies. The importance of agriculture for society is also exceptional. The level of self-sufficiency in food production is of strategic importance. Locally produced food has enormous environmental potential. Successful farming requires a lot of knowledge. A good farmer is an expert worthy of every respect. In his field. It is quite another matter, however, when the expertise associated with cultivating the land and raising livestock begins to be attributed a kind of magical status as the only original, pure and uncorrupted wisdom, holding the key to understanding and solving absolutely all the increasingly complicated and difficult social, economic and political challenges of the modern world. To solve the problems with vaccination, all we need is healthy peasant common sense, the health minister recently declared. Really? Why? Because their authenticity and connection to the land give farmers supernatural abilities to understand the predicaments of the epidemic? If it’s round it’s the virus, if it’s pointed it’s the spike? A health minister who relies on healthy peasant common sense to help solve the epidemic is like a peasant who relies on the advice of the comrade from the Central Committee to treat his sick horse. In the context of a health crisis and distrust of experts, this is pouring oil on the fire. If anywhere, “healthy peasant common sense”—in its ideological anti-establishment version, of course, not in the intelligence and knowledge needed for farming—is reflected in the thinking and arguments of anti-vaxxers. “Healthy peasant common sense tells you that to breathe you need air, not a muzzle,” an indignant anti-vaxxer snapped at me a few days ago in a comment on my post about the need to respect protective measures and vaccination. If anything, solving the problems in responding to the epidemic requires an understanding of the social damage caused by populism in league with social networks. Politics that paves its way to power with conspiracy theories, alternative facts and exploitation of distrust of the establishment risks having trouble persuading the public about the response to the pandemic, because with its ideological discourse it legitimizes and fuels anti-vaccine ideas and instincts. Remember what happened to Trump when, at a recent rally, he suggested his supporters get vaccinated. Just as communism did with the working class, for part of politics today the glorification of peasantness is full of ideological charge. As in the time of the Cultural Revolution, today, if somewhat more refined and less crude, peasantness is an instrument of the culture war, aimed at everything stigmatized as elitist, bourgeois, intellectual and corrupt. As in chess, pawns are used and sacrificed to achieve higher goals and victory over the opponent. The “purity” of the rural spirit and world, as opposed to the decadence of the bourgeois West, is the main message of the newly composed political conservatism that has spread to us via the East. Of course, in all societies there are differences in prevailing political beliefs between cities and the countryside. But these are differences that are legitimate and normal in every democratic community. Democracy needs a left, a center and a right; leftists, liberals and conservatives. There are more of some in the cities and more of others in the villages. But today it is often a polarization that spills far beyond the outer limits of the pluralist democratic space. Farmers, entirely innocent, are abused as a symbol of the defense against openness, tolerance and modernity. The ideological charge does not mean that peasantness has supporters only on the right. The mystification of the natural order and wisdom also excites the odd kumbaya alternative type in a stretched-out sweater, but that doesn’t make the mess any smarter, more progressive or more respectful of farmers. Even more than in peasantness, the ideological bias is evident in the emphasis on “healthy.” “Common sense,” said Albert Einstein, “is the collection of prejudices acquired by age eighteen.” And prejudices are the driving force of far-right political populism. A healthy nation against an unhealthy one, purity against impurity, us against them. Healthy peasant common sense tells you that homosexuality is unnatural—stallions don’t mate with each other, you know. Heh, heh, heh. The rebelliousness offered by the anti-establishment message of healthy peasant common sense is not critical; rather the opposite. It is often manipulation, disguised in the apparent authenticity and openness of social networks. The ideological interpretation of “healthy peasant common sense” is not aimed at every elite, but above all at political competitors. It revives another trait that has always been very dear to authoritarians of all colors. An attitude to authority based not on democratic legitimacy and trust but on obedience to the master. This is also reflected in the joke above. The poor peasant knew very well that following the comrade’s advice would not end well, but, as healthy peasant common sense says, authority is authority; if it demands it, you hand over your lard too. Intelligence without adjectives would have told the peasant to ignore the party directives and go to the vet for ivermectin. For the horse, not for himself.

Since we have had the internet and social networks, people mostly communicate in bubbles. If you are tired of mutual back-patting, I suggest you post a thought or two about vaccination, and your bubble will fizz and foam as if someone had thrown a handful of baking soda into your glass of Coca-Cola. Even if most people in your communication silo agree on most things, they certainly don’t agree on vaccination. Debates on this topic do not follow the patterns we see on other issues, and above all they do not match the division that in Slovenia—rather superficially and inaccurately, in my view—we call the split between left and right. Opinion polls in Slovenia show that people, regardless of their other political beliefs, are divided roughly in half on vaccination. This means that in your bubble, whether “left” or “right,” quite a large percentage of your otherwise like-minded friends will disagree with you. I experienced this recently when I dared to make fun of some of the arguments of vaccine opponents on Facebook. Many reacted very strongly and indignantly. They accused me of all sorts of things, from a lack of empathy for those who suffered consequences after vaccination or even lost their lives, to supporting the greatest violation of human rights in human history. The first accusation is out of place and offensive. I sympathize with everyone who has suffered consequences in the pandemic, including the most tragic ones. A few, unfortunately, because of vaccination; many, incomparably more, because of the virus. I also feel compassion and responsibility towards everyone whose lives the pandemic turned upside down, whose schools it closed, whom it condemned to unemployment and poverty, and in whom it caused serious and long-lasting health and psychological problems. The fact is that no medical intervention is without risk, and vaccination is no exception. But the undesirable consequences of vaccination must be compared with the undesirable consequences of not vaccinating, for the individual and for society. And here science, facts and reason offer only one answer. People who do not get vaccinated expose themselves to an incomparably greater health risk than the vaccinated. If we applied anti-vaccine logic to all medical procedures, all we would have left in the fight against disease would be cold-water cures. Perhaps not even that. According to the US Consumer Product Safety Commission, an average of 87 Americans drown in their own bathtubs every year. On the other hand, the debate about human rights is legitimate, but it is not as clear-cut as the fighters against vaccination want to present it. The social contract of a modern, civilized and democratic society—and the system of human rights and freedoms that enables and protects this contract—is based not only on rights but also on responsibility and solidarity. It is a constant search for balance between individual rights and the public interest, which sometimes, especially in exceptional circumstances, also dictates restrictions. These must, of course, be adopted and enforced in a manner provided for by law and democratically; moreover, any restriction of rights must be necessary, which means that the effect cannot be achieved in another, less restrictive way. It must also be proportionate, since the interference with rights cannot pose a greater threat than the cause that dictates the restriction. Given our experience so far with measures adopted by the authorities in response to the virus, or under the cover of responding to it, criticism and vigilance are certainly warranted, but that does not change the fact that individual rights and freedoms are not unlimited and unconditional, and above all they end where they begin to threaten the rights—and health—of others. The European Court of Human Rights recently ruled that compulsory vaccination of school-age children does not constitute a violation of the European Convention on Human Rights. It should worry us that anti-vaccine sentiment is driven by social, psychological and political triggers similar to those of populism. Both are fueled by discontent, anger, loss of trust and fear. Both may address some legitimate questions, but they offer the worst possible answer. For both, facts and science are a conspiracy of political and financial elites and the mainstream media. There is little difference between the “alternative facts” that Trump’s adviser Kellyanne Conway spoke of and all the gems collected from the internet that anti-vaxxers cite in support of their rejection of a response to the pandemic grounded in medical science. In today’s world, more and more people seek truth with their emotions, not their reason. The American historian Timothy Snyder says that freedom depends on citizens who are able to distinguish between the truth and what they want to hear. Authoritarianism arrives not because people say they want it, but because they lose the ability to distinguish between facts and desires. Of course, not all anti-vaxxers should be lumped together. On the one hand, we are dealing with conspiracy theorists, the cognitive cousins of village eccentrics who believe the Earth is flat. We have activists who, in the fight against the profits of pharmaceutical multinationals, are prepared to sacrifice their own and your health. New Age my-body-is-my-temple enthusiasts who will defeat the virus with whole grains and yoga. Amateur pharmacists and Sunday epidemiologists. Defiers who won’t get vaccinated because they don’t like the government. Those who quietly don’t get vaccinated because they don’t dare, or aren’t allowed, to defy the government. And besides them, many people who are afraid, which is human and understandable. They need to be persuaded and informed. But at a certain point, even the hesitant of the “I’m not an anti-vaxxer, but…” type need to be reminded of the importance of trusting facts and science. It is not true that we don’t know. There is enough scientifically supported information proving not only the usefulness but the necessity of vaccination if we want to prevent the collapse of the health system, protect the most vulnerable and live normally again. If some people still don’t know this, perhaps it is because they don’t want to know it. Anti-vaccine sentiment is also about a breakdown of solidarity. An individual decision to get vaccinated protects not only the vaccinated person but all of us. Without very high vaccination coverage, we will not be able to control the pandemic. The cry of me, me, me, rejecting any responsibility for others and for the common good, embodies the neoliberal attitude to society. Which, as Margaret Thatcher liked to say, does not exist; there are only individuals and their rights and interests. Let the invisible hand of the market take care of regulation. Or the invisible hand of the virus. After all, they say only the old and weak die. Some say that resistance to vaccination is a revolt of the humiliated and insulted, who have been deprived of everything, including their human dignity. Everything has been taken from them, so they fight for the last thing they have left, their body. I think there is some truth in this. But even justified frustrations are no excuse for rejecting rationality and solidarity, since in doing so we endanger not only our own and your health but also our freedom and our future. It is not only about Covid-19. We must ask ourselves how, without trust in science and without solidarity, we will tackle all the other social and global challenges. We are losing the fight against climate change because of the same patterns of behavior we see in anti-vaccine sentiment. It’s not true. I don’t care. In this light, I find it increasingly hard to bear calls to treat anti-vaxxers only with reverence and kid gloves. Because they don’t take criticism well. Because they feel like victims. Because if we are not kind and understanding enough, they will be offended and even more determined not to get vaccinated. People who are still hesitating must certainly be persuaded and informed, but for God’s sake, let us stop behaving as if conspiracy theories and alternative facts were a fundamental human right. People whose hair otherwise stands on end at Pahor-style platitudes are, on vaccination, lamenting a new division and lecturing on the need to respect absolutely all different opinions, without any critical assessment of their value or consideration of the consequences for individuals and society. My dears, we are not divided into those who want to get vaccinated and those who don’t. No one wants to get vaccinated, just as no one wants an appendectomy. We are all worried and we all want to live normally again; it is just that some seek the solution in trust in science and in solidarity, and others on Facebook.

Ljubljana at half past four in the morning. I drive slowly through the almost empty city. I am catching the first morning flight from Trieste’s Ronchi airport to Rome, where the Italian presidency of the G20, the forum of the world’s twenty largest economies, has organized the first meeting of culture ministers in the history of the group. What does culture have to do with the economy? Quite a lot, but more on that later. At Dolgi most I turn left onto the motorway heading west. How many times we drove this route with my parents, going back from Ljubljana to Trieste, where I spent the first years of my life. Except that back then there was no motorway, of course; we carried on along that narrow, winding asphalt track connecting Ljubljana with Trieste, and Istanbul with Paris. The Orient Express, in a Fiat 124. Now and then, traffic jams on the Primorska motorway allow me to relive those endless drives across Notranjska and the Karst to the sea. This time the motorway is more or less empty, thank God, as I don’t have much time before my flight. A good twenty minutes later I drive past Unec, which is of course a very important place. That is exactly where the Rapallo border ran, drawn after the First World War. And because it was the first place in the old Yugoslavia, it was there that my grandfather Vlado and his younger sister Ivanka fled from Nabrežina at the end of the 1920s. They were driven out by the fascists, who wanted to pour respect for the Italian state, culture and civilization into them with castor oil. Almost a hundred years later, his grandson is driving in the opposite direction to talk with Italians about culture and its role in society. A paradox? Not at all. The initiative of the Italian minister Dario Franceschini places culture and cultural heritage in a context diametrically opposed to the one used by the Duce and his blackshirts. In the middle of the large round table at which we sat during the opening session in Rome’s Colosseum was written: “Culture unites people.” For him, and for most of the other participants—I wouldn’t dare claim it categorically for all of them—culture is not an instrument for creating an exclusionary, nationalist identity, nor a uniform by which you recognize your own and your enemies in the populist culture war. Culture, art and cultural heritage are a creative, transformative force that not only generates economic growth and jobs but also brings to society innovation, reflection, an understanding of the past and present, and the search for the new. In Rome we talked about culture that does not separate people but opens them up to one another. At Unec, my grandfather managed to escape the fascists, at least for a while, and it was there that he met my grandmother, who came from one of the wealthiest families in the village. In Rakek they built a bourgeois villa, just a stone’s throw from the Church of the Sacred Heart, which Jože Plečnik renovated a few years later. Of all that wealth, nothing was left to us after the war. It is true, though, that, as far as I know, unlike many others, nothing of ours was nationalized. My grandfather had many excellent qualities; he knew everything about forests, knew every blade of grass, made the most beautiful little water mills and whistles out of bark, but he was no great shakes at business. When the political commissars came, there was precious little left to seize. He managed to pass his complete lack of business acumen on to my father, and I haven’t fallen far from his tree either. But money worries were of the least importance. A few years after arriving in Unec, at the end of May 1932, on the day of my father’s christening, Ivanka was shot by a jealous border guard, Djordje, because she had fallen in love with someone else. Her new beloved, Jože, after the tragic death of his sweetheart, took refuge in a wooden shed outside the village, where he was found dead the next day. He had taken his own life. So did the murderer, who succumbed to his wounds in the military hospital in Ljubljana. “Three deaths in a love tragedy near Rakek” was the headline of an article published in the Ljubljana daily Jutro on May 25. “A terrible tragedy at Rakek,” the newspaper Slovenec had written the day before, concluding that it was all the fault of “the disarray of today’s youth, who find no refuge or support anywhere. Parents, take care and watch where your children go and with whom they associate.” In my family we didn’t write tragedies and dramas; we staged them. From the old Rapallo border to today’s state border is a little under half an hour on the motorway. I cross it at Fernetiči. If I had more time, I would take the old road from here. Not the coastal costiera, but that narrow asphalt road winding through the Karst villages. Each of them holds a memory of moments spent with my father, who has been gone for 14 years now. From the motorway I still catch a brief glimpse of the houses of Nabrežina, high on the cliff above the sea. Below is Duino Castle, a symbol of power and luxury; above it the village where Slovenian stonemasons and fishermen lived, who watered every stone of the luxurious building with their sweat, the building in which Rainer Maria Rilke wrote his elegies. Until a few decades ago, you could still stop at the Bar Gruden in Nabrežina. My family really wasn’t cut out for business; hospitality was the only exception. My grandmother, the one from the wealthy family in Unec, was also manager of the Bežigrad café before she retired. Today they sell bicycles there. A few minutes later I am at Ronchi airport, or Ronchi dei Legionari, as the Italians call it. Trieste airport is one of the few that seem even smaller and more deserted than Ljubljana’s. The plane that took us to Rome was stylistically in keeping with the airport. The cabin smelled of cigarette smoke. I hope they maintain it better than they clean it, I thought, and closed my eyes. In a few months, Alitalia will be no more. It is supposedly being replaced by a new airline, ITA. I wish it the best of luck. The Italians have a phenomenal culture and cultural heritage, they make beautiful cars, but they evidently aren’t born for the airline business. Like us. At Fiumicino I was met by protocol staff and a car with a driver. The privilege of taking part in a ministerial meeting where I was standing in for the Secretary General of the Council of Europe. The next day and a half were full of incredible impressions and experiences. The conference itself, of course, with its opening in the Colosseum, an evening concert at the Quirinal, the president’s palace, a working session in the Palazzo Barberini, beneath a 400-square-meter Renaissance fresco by Pietro da Cortona, and finally the closing at the Villa Borghese and a tour of the collection and an exhibition in which, among the old masters Caravaggio and Bernini and the marble statues of strapping Romans with small willies, the kitschy sculptures of the British artist Damien Hirst lie in impostor-like, subversive ambush. Art in conversation with art, challenging and commenting on it. Very good. In a few hours of free time, I also managed to visit the exhibition of the notorious and socially engaged Banksy at the Chiostro del Bramante. One of the most harrowing works is a doormat on which the word “welcome” is embroidered. The yellow strip is made of life jackets that, along with many bodies of the unfortunate, washed up on European beaches during deadly refugee crossings of the Mediterranean. Art that comments, challenges and accuses. After the conference I am driven back to Rome’s main airport. On the right I see a mighty building of white marble. It is the most important structure of the new city district that Mussolini had built for the world exhibition planned for 1942. Because of the war, the exhibition never took place, but the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana, a monumental building with abstract arches and neoclassical statues, remained. On it is a restored inscription that the Duce himself had engraved there. It describes Italians as a people of poets, artists, heroes, saints, thinkers, navigators and transmigrants. What he meant by that last one is not entirely clear to me, but I am sure he was not thinking of people who, fleeing war and poverty, risk everything to secure a better life for themselves and their families. A paradox? Not to me. This too is part of history, of cultural heritage, which matters because it reflects what we were, sometimes at our best, sometimes at our worst. If we preserved only the legacy of beautiful stories, the world would be much poorer. Authoritarians love monuments. Ancient Rome, which left humanity such an extraordinary architectural heritage, was not known for its humanism either. In the end, culture and heritage are not determined solely by the ideology that built them, but by our understanding of them and our relationship to them. Today the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana houses the global headquarters of the fashion house Fendi. Instead of the leather boots of the Duce’s squadristi, its marble corridors echo with very expensive high heels. The journey back from Ronchi to Ljubljana takes me longer than the outward one. The Primorska motorway lives up to its reputation and serves me a monumental traffic jam. I leave it at Logatec and return by the old road. In those forests my grandfather and I used to pick mushrooms. For a snack, he always had in his pocket a piece of parmesan, hard as stone, wrapped in a handkerchief, which he cut with his pocketknife as if it were a truffle. Grandpa was a man of the Karst and a conscious Slovenian. But castor oil and fascists or not, Italian culture always was and remained an important part of his identity.

Writing has got me into trouble a few times in my life. All my troubles so far I brought on myself in my first twenty-five years, which is also logical, since until then I lived under an undemocratic, authoritarian regime. In my first years at grammar school, my father was summoned to the school because of my editorship of the school magazine. “They are always criticizing something and wanting to change it,” the headmistress complained. In my final year, an offended and furious teacher demanded not only educational measures but also punishment along political lines because of my critical writing. When I wrote for Tribuna and sold banned copies on the streets of Ljubljana, plainclothes police officers lurked around me. Over the next few decades I had less trouble with interventions of this kind, until recently, when a complaint about my writing and public appearances apparently made its way from Ljubljana to Strasbourg. I am not, of course, talking about criticism, which is always welcome. There is no democracy without a clash of different opinions, including between dissenters and those who dissent from the dissenters, but democracy cannot tolerate authoritarian dictate and censorship by the thoughtless. In all this, I stress the word apparently, since until I have something in black and white, I want to believe it is just a slip or a misunderstanding. If I am wrong, I will gladly apologize. For many years I have been writing and speaking in the Slovenian media about issues that are of key importance for Slovenia today. I am far from the only one in Slovenia who knows something about European integration and cooperation, democracy, human rights and the rule of law, but after almost three decades of working professionally on these issues—in an international environment—I am certainly among those who know something about these subjects. I cannot imagine that anyone could be such a crackpot as to want to shut me up simply because they disagree with my opinion. It is true, though, that we live in rather crackpot times. Misunderstanding or not, let me say straight away that I have no intention of stopping writing. My professional path grew out of my personal beliefs and values. I also write because I am a patriot and a convinced European, and I care what happens to my homeland and to Europe. If you are truly committed to democratic values, you cannot defend them only on weekdays from nine to five, as the Americans say. When I joined the Council of Europe almost twenty-six years ago, I took an oath that I would be guided in my work solely by professionalism and loyalty to the organization and its values. I gave that word, and I keep that word. The Council of Europe is not, of course, a debating club where anyone can say and do whatever comes into their head. We are an intergovernmental organization with important tasks and powers. There are rules and limits on who may speak on behalf of the organization and when. I often represent the organization and its positions, but exclusively in areas within my remit. Many Slovenian journalists who have in the past asked me for an official response on questions outside my competence can testify to that. Respecting these rules is required by the professionalism mentioned in the oath. Public communication in a personal capacity is different. Since the Council of Europe is a serious and respected institution, there are rules for such cases too. Publishing articles requires authorization, and I have it for my columns. The most important obligation for every staff member, however, whether speaking personally or representing the organization, is the second part of the oath, which commits us to loyalty to the values of European cooperation, democracy, human rights and the rule of law. These were also the subjects I was asked to write about for Večer years ago. Until recently, these issues were of little interest to most people. Human rights, blah, blah; democracy, blah, blah; rule of law, blah, blah. Yawn. Why write about it at all, since we’re all in favor? Well, today we evidently no longer are. That is probably why my writing has become disturbing to some. Since I have not changed my views since they got me into trouble in my youth, someone else evidently must have changed theirs. On shared European civilizational values, post-war politicians in the West—incidentally, almost exclusively from Christian Democratic and conservative parties—laid the foundations for post-war reconstruction and lasting peace in Europe. The victory of these values after the fall of the Berlin Wall ended, at least for a while, the ideological division of the European continent. On the values of European integration we won an independent and democratic Slovenia, and we wrote these values into our Constitution and protected them there. Today some want to convince us that they are unpatriotic. Only a few years ago it would have been hard to imagine any serious politician in Europe talking about “some kind of” or even “invented” European values. Ladies and gentlemen, if we have a problem, I am not the cause. Whereas until yesterday there was a broad political and social consensus on fundamental European values in most European countries, including Slovenia, among all political groupings except the extreme ones, today some want to politicize and relativize these values and present them as just one option among others. This is, of course, no accident. Democratic principles and the rule of law are not a set of loose ethical aspirations but an elaborate system of rules and procedures which, through laws and the constitution, protect society and individuals against abuse of power by the authorities and allow voters, at regular intervals, to decide freely who will lead them. In populist discourse, European values are therefore increasingly presented as a conspiracy of alienated Eurocratic elites seeking to use them to deprive the little man of the right to hate whomever his heart desires and tradition commands. Even funnier is the claim that European democratic values are a political program of the left, which uses them to maintain continuity with the communist past. This is, of course, completely daft. The thesis that people who advocate European democratic values, human rights and the rule of law are by default extreme leftists can only be the product of a pathological mentality for which everything slightly to the left of the far right is communism. We also increasingly hear reproaches that EU membership and the obligations that come with it threaten national sovereignty. Sovereignty is a word that tickles many people’s tummies, although it has very different meanings in different contexts. In sport, for example, commentators like to talk about sovereign victories. From international law textbooks we learned during our studies that sovereignty is the power of a state to exercise authority effectively on its territory. In this respect, the thesis that EU membership threatens national sovereignty in today’s world stands on rather shaky legs. In facing global economic, security, technological and other challenges, European states can, as a rule, exercise their sovereign authority and influence more effectively within the European Union than they could alone. This is especially true of states of our size and relative influence. Provided we approach membership smartly, responsibly, strategically and confidently, which we have not always done very well in the past. Without the support, security and influence made possible by integration with European partners, we would quickly be easy prey for bigger, stronger and more ruthless players. Co-decision allows far greater sovereignty than being unable to influence one’s own fate in practice. But sovereignty also has a third, more sinister interpretation, elaborated by Hitler’s court jurist Carl Schmitt. For him, sovereignty was the power of the ruler to decide on the state of exception and single-handedly suspend the validity of all legal norms. The sovereign is the one who has the power to place himself above the law and do as he pleases. In the name of the people, of course. We are not there yet, and I hope we never will be. Surely no one is such a crackpot as to want to separate us from Europe and its values thirty years after we won an independent state and established democracy. Although…

Ozren is a mountain in northern Bosnia, between Doboj and Zavidovići. At its foot, in the small village of Boljanić, my mother Julijana was born in August 1943. “In the first days, the newborn daughter had a somewhat misshapen, elongated little head. She was healthy and lively. We all came to love her,” my grandfather Franček wrote in his Memories from My Life. My mother also got a second name, Ozrenka, after the mountain beneath which she was born. The reason was not only the natural beauty of her birthplace but above all my grandparents’ gratitude to the people of the area, who, despite their own deprivation and the hardships of war, did everything to help a young family expelled by the Germans from Styria to Bosnia. On those, thank God, rare but intense occasions when media in the service of truth turn their attention to my biography, the blame for my perverse character and worldview is most often attributed to my late father. But even if my father was not without sin, a large part of the blame for what and who I am—not only me but also my brothers Andrej and Gregor—must surely be attributed to my mother, her life experiences, her personality and her values. In the service of truth, it would certainly be right for me to reveal the full extent of her influence and responsibility. When the Germans, with the help of local collaborators, came for my grandmother and grandfather, they gave them only a few hours to prepare for the journey. They were allowed to take only their eldest daughter, my aunt Breda. Their second child, newborn Marija, who had not yet been entered in the official registers of the pedantic occupying bureaucrats, they were forced to leave with neighbors. In the cattle wagon in which they traveled to Bosnia, my grandmother was still bleeding from the birth of a child who had been torn from her arms and whom she would never see again. Marija died only a month later, from one of the childhood illnesses, in the arms of a woman who was not her mother. Immediately after arriving in Bosnia, my grandmother and grandfather began supporting the Partisans, and so that the family would have something to eat, my grandfather also began distilling brandy. You can deport Grandpa from Styria, but you can’t deport Styria from Grandpa. Grandma sold Grandpa’s schnapps in nearby villages while also running errands for the committees of the National Liberation Struggle. During her pregnancy, on her way back from a meeting of the Women’s Antifascist Front in Tuzla, my grandmother was captured by Chetniks, who shoved a shovel into her hands and forced her to dig her own grave. She was saved from the bullet at the last moment by an officer who started shouting that they were not going to kill pregnant women. Soon after my mother was born, typhus broke out in Boljanić. Since there were no medicines, the neighbors advised my grandmother to bathe her in urine. Today, a similar therapy, and not only for external use, is recommended against the coronavirus and a whole host of other health problems by the Bollywood star Akshay Kumar. Whether there was a causal link between the stinking bath and my mother’s survival, I don’t know, but the fact is that the experience did not give her any particular affection for alternative medicine. So this year, as soon as it was possible, she got vaccinated against Covid, and in contact with anti-vaxxers her temperament usually prevails over her otherwise exemplary tolerance. I remembered all the horrors my grandparents, my mother and my aunt lived through during the war when, as a teenager, I brought a friend from Germany to visit my grandmother. When we were leaving, I apologized to Grandma for the pain this thoughtless invitation must have caused her. She looked at me as if I had lost my mind. “Matjaž, war is shit”—Grandma Anuncijata never minced her words—“but you can’t hate a whole nation. Every person decides for themselves whether to be good or bad.” Later she told me a story from one of the offensives against the Partisans, when a German soldier burst into the house. Grandma, with my mother in her arms, started shouting at him in shock, like a wife at a husband who stumbles home drunk in the morning. The man put down his rifle, sat down beside her and, in tears, began apologizing and showing her pictures of his six or seven children waiting for him at home. In the end he left them a month’s supply of powdered milk. Yes, war is shit. And everyone, not only in war, decides for themselves whether to be a good or a bad person. Of course my mother doesn’t remember most of these events, except from what she was told, but they had an important influence on her attitude to people and the world. She cannot stand intolerance, hatred or nationalism. She is a die-hard anti-fascist, but, as the child of parents who were taken into the unknown in a cattle wagon, also a person with deep compassion for all those who, anywhere and on any side, shared a similar fate and often met an even more tragic end. Compassion, solidarity and humanity are values we were brought up with from childhood. They are not abstract moral aspirations but a reflection of my family’s life experience. None of us experienced what the migrant crisis brought to Slovenia as something that only happens to others, but as something that had already happened to us too. After the war, my grandparents returned to Slovenia, first to Gornja Radgona and then to the Styrian capital. This gives me the moral right today to support NK Maribor, at least when they are winning or not playing against Olimpija. My mother attended the First Maribor Grammar School, where her already eventful academic path was further complicated by meeting a journalist from Ljubljana a few years her senior. That little girl with the somewhat misshapen, elongated head had long since turned into a beautiful blonde young woman. She passed her final exams after two resits and with a ring on her finger. She spent the first years of marriage with two small children in Trieste. My father was in his natural social and professional element there; my mother certainly was not. After a few years she had had it up to here with housekeeping and decided she would not spend her life cooking and cleaning. Before she had even unpacked all the suitcases after returning to Ljubljana, she enrolled at the Faculty of Arts and finished her studies on time. With two small children and great, but exclusively moral, support from my father. Ambition, independence and a willingness, if necessary, to hit the books, we brothers got above all from our mother. During our schooling she never nagged us or looked over our shoulders. If we understood that we were learning above all for ourselves, we would manage, she thought. And although her trust in our personal responsibility was put to some very hard tests, in the end she was right. At the beginning of her studies, she brought home one day a fellow student, Darja, a young woman from Ljutomer who couldn’t find a place to live in Ljubljana and so came to stay with us for a few days. She stayed a few years. I owe my knowledge of the multiplication table and regular tooth-brushing to Darja. Darja is movable cultural heritage and deserves a column of her own, but through her, and through my parents’ other friends, with whom they had spent time almost since their teens, I discovered the meaning of true friendship. The kind that lasts a lifetime. Today, after more than half a century of close friendship, they still meet regularly. Lately, often on Friday evenings, when they like to stroll through the center of Ljubljana. During her studies, my mother saved enough from the housekeeping money my father gave her to take my brother Andrej and me, our cousin Romana and our friend Igor, together with Darja, to Denmark for a month. At the age of eight, what impressed me most were the Tivoli amusement park, the nudists at the swimming pool next to the Parken stadium, and the raid on the cold buffet that Darja, with the help of us children, carried out at a reception to which we had been rashly invited. On that first big journey, my mother passed on to us her passion for discovering the world. She traveled with my father, from Brazil to Greenland, and after his death also with friends or alone. For her 75th birthday we gave her a plane ticket to Gambia. “If you’re good,” my elder brother promised her on behalf of all of us, “you’ll get a return ticket.” A very unusual sense of humor is another thing we have to thank our parents for. When I reminded my brother of their wedding anniversary a few days ago, he replied that he had already congratulated Mum but couldn’t get Dad on the phone. My mother is an educationalist and psychologist by training. She spent most of her career at the Ministry of Justice, where she was responsible for the education of prisoners. Here another of her qualities came to the fore, namely that she sees something good in almost every person. Almost. This quality of hers has lately been increasingly put to the test. My mother never passed her driving test, and I have never seen her on a bicycle either. Which is funny, since she is so fond of cyclists.

In Slovenia, we like congress tourism. In principle, at least. This year marks two hundred years since a whole bunch of European despots, absolutists, ministers, diplomats, and their servants gathered in Ljubljana under the brand of the Holy Alliance. Today, reminders of this grand event remain in the names of Congress Square, Two Emperors Street, and The Russian Tsar Inn. For our distinguished guests, we paved streets and squares, renovated facades, and upgraded the sewage and lighting systems. During their months-long stay, the crowned heads of Europe managed to suppress several uprisings and revolutions. The Holy Alliance’s main goal was to crush nationalist-revolutionary movements, which—according to kings, emperors, and czars—threatened Europe’s political order. They met in Ljubljana to agree on more effective ways of preventing unrest, which in various parts of Europe was stirred up primarily by intellectuals and urbanites inspired by the French Revolution and the Enlightenment, demanding democracy, human rights, and personal freedom. But charmed by the pomp and profits left behind by Europe’s despots and their court entourages, Slovenians clearly didn’t hold a grudge against the reactionary goals of the Holy Alliance. The Philharmonic Society ensured their cultural comfort, and hospitality and various trades flourished. More than 160 years later, once again it was people inspired by the legacy of the French Revolution and the Enlightenment—those demanding democracy, human rights, and personal liberty—who stirred unrest in Slovenia. In the 1980s, it was mainly civil society that paved the way for democratic reforms and an independent Slovenian state: peace activists, environmentalists, feminists, and also the LGBTIQ+ community, which initially organized through the Magnus Association for the Socialization of Homosexuality, and later also Lilith, both operating within Ljubljana’s students cultural center ŠKUC. To be fair, the Slovenian authorities at the time weren’t particularly repressive toward these movements—but that doesn’t mean they weren’t concerned. A 1986 report by the State Security Service concluded that the emergence of new social movements “requires timely and ideologically comprehensive and multi-faceted responses to ideological deviations within these movements, which are incompatible with the idea of self-managed and delegate-based political organization of citizens—especially regarding ideas such as the establishment of mechanisms for democratic opposition.” One such “ideological deviation” that provoked a timely and multi-faceted response was the Congress of European Homosexuals, scheduled in Ljubljana by the Magnus Association for Youth Day in 1987. The authorities’ main concern wasn’t so much the event itself, but rather the fear of backlash from other parts of Yugoslavia, where political elites were far more aligned with the reactionary mindset of the Holy Alliance. Roman Kuhar’s 2002 research on Media Representations of Homosexuality—an analysis of Slovenian print media from 1970 to 2000—offers insight into the aggression and hatred that flared up as Slovenia’s public space became more open. For instance, the Sarajevo magazine As suggested that “all properly oriented Yugoslavs” should wear a badge reading “Fags, no thanks.” Alarmed by the intensity of these reactions, Slovenian authorities tried to reduce political demands for freedom and human dignity into a matter of sex—framing homosexuality as promiscuity and a public health threat. In March 1987, the Council for Social and Health Policy at the presidency of the RK SZDL recommended that the Republic Committee for Health and Social Welfare and relevant authorities ban the congress to “protect the population from an AIDS epidemic.” History, it seems, has a cruel way of repeating itself. The repressive stance on homosexuality in the authoritarian atmosphere of the former regime was neither exceptional nor surprising. Homophobia is part of the standard repertoire of all authoritarian ideologies and regimes. Although Lenin decriminalized homosexuality after the October Revolution, Stalin reversed that in 1934, adding Article 121 to the Soviet criminal code, which punished male homosexual acts with five years of forced labour. Between 500 and 1,000 men were convicted under this law every year. At the same time, Soviet propaganda began portraying homosexuality as a fascist trait, and Article 121 was used to persecute political dissidents as well. The tragic absurdity of this Soviet equation of homosexuality with fascism lies in the fact that around the same time, Hitler also dramatically increased penalties under Article 175 of the German Penal Code, which had banned homosexuality since 1872. Nearly 100,000 men were arrested under this law over a few decades—not only in Germany, but also in annexed parts of the Third Reich. About 50,000 were convicted, and between 5,000 and 15,000 were sent to concentration camps. Exact numbers are unclear, partly because many survivors never spoke about why they had been imprisoned—and for good reason. Many were forced to complete their sentences even after liberation or were re-convicted under the same Article 175, which remained in the German legal code until 1994. Nazi persecution victims waited until 2002 for official amnesty, and Angela Merkel later issued a formal apology on behalf of the German government. Tito’s Yugoslavia was part of the Allied forces that defeated Nazism and broke ties with Stalin in 1948, but when it came to homosexuality, it chose continuity over progress. Historian Franko Dota, who earned his PhD with a dissertation on the public and political history of male homosexuality in socialist Croatia, wrote that in socialist Yugoslavia, homosexuality was seen as something "bourgeois and deviant"—a trait of decadent intellectuals, priests, and non-working classes, deemed a threat to healthy working youth. The criminal code punished “unnatural acts between men” with up to two years in prison. Partial decriminalization came only in 1977, and only in some parts of Yugoslavia—including Slovenia. But social stigma and repression against the LGBTIQ+ community continued throughout the country—and seem to have outlived the country itself. The LGBTIQ+ community was an essential part of the social movements that in the 1980s opened, expanded, and defended spaces of freedom in Slovenia. These movements helped pave the way for independence. On the 30th anniversary of the Slovenian state, during this time of medal ceremonies and credit-taking, we should remember and recognize all who contributed to its birth. Sadly, reality is quite different. Not all legitimate expectations have been fulfilled—some have even regressed. Instead of understanding, equality, and solidarity, we face growing intolerance toward LGBTIQ+ people and other marginalized groups. We face orchestrated and politically manipulated hate. In the name of a newly concocted conservatism, new “Holy Alliances” are forming, complete with wannabe despots and their entourages, who repackage old prejudices and repressive policies into new containers—exactly the kind of repression authoritarian regimes throughout history have practiced. Politicians retweet, recycle, and import foreign “successes” in the discrimination and repression of LGBTIQ+ individuals and other minorities. In the name of patriotism for our shared country, they spread hatred toward those who helped build it and fight for the democratic freedoms we (still) enjoy. Enough is enough. The fight for LGBTIQ+ rights cannot and must not be theirs alone. Freedom and solidarity cannot be sliced like sausage—reserved only for some. If a society lacks freedom, solidarity, and respect for everyone’s human dignity, then eventually there will be no freedom for anyone.

In the second instalment of the film trilogy Back to the Future, Biff Tannen steals a time machine and travels to the past in order to create a new present. The story begins in the year 1984, when the main character, Marty McFly, is whisked away by the inventor of the time machine, Doc Brown, to the year 2015. Their mission is to prevent Marty’s future son from being manipulated by Biff’s future grandson into committing a bank robbery. A lot happens, but the crucial plot twist is that the now-elderly Biff secretly borrows the time machine and travels back to 1955. There, he hands his younger self a sports almanac containing the results of every major game through the year 2000. With it, Biff becomes rich through betting. When Marty and Doc return to 1984, the present is no longer what it was. Biff has altered the past and created an alternate reality. In this new timeline, he is no longer a humiliated buffoon, but the kingpin of a casino empire and a criminal gang that terrorizes the town and its residents. Holding a personal grudge, Biff eliminates Marty’s father from history and marries his mother. Marty is packed off to a Swiss boarding school. Though fictional, Biff is a good example of the archetypal angry, frustrated man who blames everyone but himself for his miserable life. Biff sees himself as a victim, and his life's main ambition is to exact revenge on those he holds responsible for his pathetic existence—those who are more successful, more knowledgeable, or simply different. Biff’s psychology is the same that created Trump in America—and Trump-lings elsewhere who see Slovenia’s son-in-law as a role model for their own political and authoritarian aspirations. Life, at times, cruelly imitates fiction. The story of Biff should serve as a warning to those who believe people try to change the past for the sake of the past itself. That forgetting history will somehow make us better, happier, or more successful. The film also offers a critical reflection on false equivalence—this idea that both sides of Slovenia’s infamous political divide are equally obsessed with the past. That’s simply not true. It is Biff who wants to rewrite history—because that's the path to an alternate present and a different future, one in which he is no longer a self-proclaimed victim, but an omnipotent boss. In our desperate attempt to forget the past, we’re not alone. For decades, the western half of the European political space has been obsessed with moving beyond history—or more precisely, with historical amnesia. A few days ago, a French politician and former minister who spent two decades in the European Parliament told me that, before the EU's eastern enlargement, MEPs followed an unwritten rule alongside all the official treaty articles: never mention the past. Think of Basil Fawlty, nervously muttering “Don’t mention the war” when German tourists checked into his hotel. In his book The Road to Unfreedom, American historian Timothy Snyder calls this western determination to forget history the politics of inevitability. This doctrine builds on the narrative of the "end of history," insisting that the future will merely be a slightly improved version of the present—with no alternatives—since the laws of progress are fixed and beyond challenge. In Europe, the politics of inevitability says that history created nations that, having learned the value of peace through conflict, chose integration and prosperity. The fall of communism was seen as irrefutable proof of this thesis, and even a quarter-century after the fall of the Berlin Wall, Europeans kept repeating these mantras—producing a generation of millennials who have no clue about history and couldn’t care less. The belief that historical memory is unnecessary—or even harmful—is one reason why authoritarian populism has been so successful. We ourselves disabled democracy’s immune system. If you don’t want to remember history or understand it, you won’t recognize when it returns. This intentional historical amnesia created ideal conditions for the rise of an alternative to the politics of inevitability, which Snyder calls the politics of eternity. While inevitability promises a better future for all, eternity places the nation at the centre of a cyclical narrative of victimhood and injustice. Time is no longer a journey forward, but a loop constantly returning to the same threats and wrongs of the past. Politicians of eternity argue that the government cannot help society as a whole—it can only protect it from threats. Hope for a better tomorrow is replaced by fear of an inescapable fate. The dilemma with the politics of eternity is that it has so far been much less successful at providing material well-being and social progress. That’s logical—it doesn’t even try, except for a tight circle of those close to power. But eternity populism is also aware that the adrenaline rush of fearing “the other” is not a sustainable defence against public anger. Sooner or later, citizens will notice they are less free and worse off than their neighbours. The trick populism devised to excuse economic failure is to offer the fiction of spiritual superiority in place of material goods or freedoms. This is the essence of the newly manufactured Eastern European conservatism—claiming to defend the cultural and spiritual purity of the nation against the decadence of the morally bankrupt West, supposedly ruled by feminists, cultural Marxists, homosexuals, and Soros-paid agents of globalist multicultural conspiracies. We may never be the richest or the freest—but, hey, at least we’re the purest. Though politics of eternity has many shared traits, each country has its own historical ground zero—a moment from which it derives its sense of victimhood or heroism and claims an exclusive moral right to power. Sometimes it’s based on real events—but more often manipulated or distorted. In Slovenia, that ground zero is World War II. In other words—partisans and nazi collaborators. The almanac that Slovenia’s Biff seeks is a new “truth” about who was where, why, and doing what during that war. If he succeeds in rewriting history, he can reshape the present and future. He’s not interested in reconciliation or respect for victims on both sides.
