He wants to turn memory and facts into a time loop of eternal struggle against a many-headed, undying communist monster—one that once justified collaboration and now justifies dismantling the rule of law. The prerequisite for this sleight-of-hand is discrediting anti-fascism. Biff’s problem is that anti-fascism wasn’t the exclusive domain of leftist revolutionaries—it was the shared platform of all democratic progressive forces who stood against fascism and built, after WWII, the European project as the antithesis to authoritarian, nationalist, violent politics obsessed with absolute sovereignty, the same kind that pushed Europe into war 80 years ago. Because anti-fascism and the European project are inseparable, the attack on anti-fascism increasingly becomes an attack on Europe itself, on its institutions, and on its values. History isn’t just a chronology of events, and it cannot and must not be reduced to a hunt for one single historical truth. Multiperspectivity is part of modern historical understanding. Your view of a historical event doesn’t have to match mine, and that’s completely normal and legitimate. But multiperspectivity cannot stretch into the distortion of historical facts, and above all, it cannot be used to undermine the civilizational values on which modern, progressive, democratic societies rest. History is deeply important—but it can also be a cruel and merciless teacher. If we forget it, then Biff may just end up writing our future.

“And what is the German people doing? It sees nothing, hears nothing. Blindly follows its seducers into destruction. Victory at any cost—that's what they’ve written on their flag. I will fight to the end, says Hitler, but the war is already lost… Freedom of speech, freedom of religion, protection of individual citizens against the whims of criminal, violent states—these are the foundations of the new Europe.” The words above are from one of six leaflets secretly distributed in the early years of World War II by students at the University of Munich, united in the anti-Nazi group known as the White Rose. They scrawled graffiti on the Bavarian government building: “Down with Hitler” and “Hitler – Mass Murderer.” On February 18, 1943, 21-year-old biology and philosophy student Sophie Scholl, and her 24-year-old brother Hans, a medical student, brought a suitcase full of pamphlets into the university building. Most were left in hallways for students to find after lectures, but Sophie threw the last batch down into the atrium from the top floor. She was seen by the janitor, who reported her to the Gestapo. All those arrested were brought the next day before the Volksgerichtshof or "People's Court," a Nazi mockery of the rule of law that during the war sent thousands to execution or concentration camps. The trial began just three days after the arrest. Hans attempted to take full responsibility to protect his sister, but Sophie, hoping to shield others in the group, declared that she had brought and scattered the leaflets. During the trial, she repeatedly interrupted judge Roland Freisler, at one point telling him: “Soon you will be standing where I stand now. Someone had to start. What we wrote and said is what many others think—they just don’t dare to speak it out loud like we did.” Sophie and Hans Scholl, along with fellow member Christoph Probst, were convicted of treason and sentenced to death. Just hours later, at 5 p.m. on February 22, they were executed by guillotine at Stadelheim Prison in Munich. Sophie was executed first. Hans’s final words were: Long live freedom.” I didn’t learn about the heroic and tragic story of the White Rose in school. Resistance movements among Germans didn’t fit with the official WWII narrative that prevailed during my education. But my graduating class at the College of Europe in Bruges was named after Sophie and Hans Scholl. The bridge in Strasbourg connecting the Council of Europe to the European Court of Human Rights is named White Rose. The courage of those Munich students—and other acts of resistance in the Third Reich—doesn’t change the fact that most Germans, out of fear or opportunism, looked away during Nazi crimes, while many actively participated. Yet the White Rose is still an important story, especially for postwar Germany and its efforts to move beyond its dark legacy and reemerge as a democratic, civilized European state—not through silence or revisionism, but through accountability and a clear condemnation of the crimes. In 2013, on the 70th anniversary of the White Rose executions, then-German President Joachim Gauck, a former East German pastor and human rights advocate, said their courage “allowed us to believe that not all Germans of the time were mute and cowardly servants of the regime.” The fourth leaflet the group distributed seventy years earlier ended with the words: “We will not be silent. We are your bad conscience.” While resistance to Nazism in the Third Reich never reached the level of organized movements found in other European countries—like Greece, Yugoslavia, Poland, or Norway—it’s estimated that some 77,000 Germans were executed for opposing the regime, not counting tens of thousands more imprisoned in camps, many of whom didn’t survive. Some resistance came from communist groups like Rote Kapelle (Red Orchestra), but the major influence came from segments of the Catholic and Protestant churches, or individuals within them, who had opposed Nazi policies since the 1930s. That was also true for the White Rose. Though Hans and Sophie Scholl were raised in a liberal family—their parents opposed Nazism from the start—both were involved in Nazi youth organizations in their early years: Hans in the Hitler Youth, Sophie in the League of German Girls. Their views began to change when they learned about atrocities committed against Jews and Soviet POWs, and especially after encountering Catholic and Protestant clergy and theologians. In their fourth leaflet, they addressed fellow believers directly: “I ask you, those who claim to be Christians: in this struggle to preserve what is most precious to you, is there hesitation, scheming, delay in the hope that someone else will raise the sword to defend you? Has God not given you the strength and courage to fight against this force? Evil must be attacked where it is strongest—and that is in Hitler’s power.” Of course, Germany’s situation was very specific. In most other occupied countries, organized resistance came from different social and political groups, though there were also many religious individuals who opposed fascism out of ethical or spiritual conviction. These are the same convictions that some today try to abuse as justification for collaboration. The story of the White Rose and other anti-fascist resistance fighters across Europe matters because it forms part of the moral foundation of postwar European unification—a project led in large part by Christian Democrats like Konrad Adenauer, Alcide de Gasperi, and Robert Schuman. These leaders did not build their anti-fascism in spite of their Christian beliefs, but precisely because of them. It was on the basis of these principles that they laid the foundation for European integration, grounded in pluralist democracy, the rule of law, and human rights, where citizens can freely and fairly choose their leaders, and where power is constrained by law. Guided by their Christian values, they advocated for a society that defends human dignity and builds on solidarity—both among individuals and among nations. They fulfilled the White Rose’s vision of a new Europe. The European project stands as the antithesis of the continent’s bloodiest experience and as a bulwark against the return of fascism, resurgent nationalism, and hatred of others. Respect for shared European civilizational values and principles is the test by which the European project—and with it, the security and prosperity of its citizens—will survive or fall. This does not mean that Christian Democrats were the only ones involved in postwar reconstruction. For example, Belgian leader Paul-Henri Spaak was a socialist. But it is an undeniable fact that anti-fascism is the shared platform on which various democratic political forces—with all the differences of opinion that pluralistic democracy allows and requires—have built the European project over decades. Today, undermining those democratic European values and belittling anti-fascism in the name of some rebranded Eastern-style conservatism, moral prejudice, or "return" to supposed Christian European roots is a crude insult to those who, in the name of those same Christian values, laid the foundations of postwar Europe—and especially to those who, in the name of those values, sacrificed their lives in resistance to Nazism and fascism. Long live freedom!

Every serious camper, scout, hiker or treasure hunter knows that if you want to get somewhere, you first need to know where you are. Orientation is an important thing; if you don’t know where north is, you may well end up wandering in circles and running away from ticks, panthers and bears. That is why people since time immemorial have looked for various ways to work out where they are. We all know about the North Star, moss on the north side of trees, the compass, the sextant and, nowadays, of course, the GPS on our smartphones. If anyone still manages to get lost today, they are either very clumsy or doing it on purpose. Let us now imagine, for the purposes of this text, a group of people who have decided to forget the stars, moss and GPS and rely for orientation solely on the loudest and most unruly man among them. Since he is an imaginary person, let us call him, for the purposes of this text, Polde. In this group without a compass, all the points of the compass are determined by Polde. North is always where he is, and south is where he isn’t. Those who don’t like Polde run south, but since he isn’t necessarily where they think he is, they can easily get lost, trip over a root and fall flat on their faces. Then there are those who claim they want to go neither north nor south but forward, but since they have no idea where or what forward is, out of caution or opportunism they prefer to hold on to the sleeve of Polde’s jacket, buttoned with both buttons. Polde, of course, enjoys this, because he is the alpha male who decides where the sun rises and sets, where it is warm and where it is cold. The longer all his fellow travelers run back and forth looking for a way out of the confusion, the longer he remains the one who sets the rules of the game, since the rules of the game are set around him. This clumsy parable is, of course, a comment on the state of the pluralist democracy we have managed to put together in thirty years of an independent state. Without critical reflection on who is really on the left, who on the right and who in the center, we orient ourselves solely by Polde. The right is where Polde is, and the right is whatever Polde is. On the other side, everyone who doesn’t like Polde is automatically a leftist, including those who dislike him from the right. The problem of many of Polde’s competitors is that, being busy with Polde, they run out of time to conceptualize their political beliefs and pour them into a convincing political program. But that way, of course, they get nowhere. Anti-Poldism is not a political platform but a mirror image operated by someone else on your behalf. In the Slovenian political Baghdad, the caliphs want to become Iznogoud instead of Iznogoud. The cleverest idea that those who dislike Polde have come up with in the last thirty years is to find someone who will beat Polde by being even more Polde than he is. Slovenian politics is trapped in an exhausting battle between faces, repeated ad nauseam, and cannot find its way to a democracy of programs and ideas. Between Polde and those who dislike him a large empty space has opened up, which some sell as the political center. But since in Slovenia we measure political space geometrically, not by values, our center—and many who claim to belong to it—often has little in common with the political groupings and programs found in this part of the political spectrum in functioning democracies. Here, rather, we come across politicians and parties that see the center as a vacuum of values, an opportunity for political opportunism, without a program, without commitments to voters and without values. If the “center” of Slovenian politics is more colorful than the snack bar at the railway station, at its extreme edges the situation is exactly the opposite. There, again because of the doctrine of respecting absolutely all different opinions, by default there can be no one. With perhaps two exceptions. The first concerns expressions of concern about the undermining of democratic institutions in Slovenia. In a recent interview, the President of the Republic described such opinions as too radical. The second exception is tax policy. In developed democracies, this is one of the main parameters for positioning within the democratic political space, but here some people experience the mere mention of higher taxes as hate speech and national treason. Some time ago, the flower of Slovenian entrepreneurs was one of the few endangered groups in Slovenia that, fearing the verbal violence of bloodthirsty fiscal extremists who dared to propose a higher tax on capital gains, found refuge in the warm bosom of the president’s palace. Since it has become customary not to assess and classify politicians according to their political content, still less according to their attitude to constitutionally protected democratic values, many cannot resist the temptation to throw everyone into the same basket. “They’re-all-the-same-ism” is another symptom of our poor understanding of pluralist democracy. The lack of critical, value-based assessment of political discourse and actions, and attempts to seek national consensus in an ethical vacuum at the arithmetic midpoint—where there will be no more Poldes and Non-Poldes, but we will all be Half-Poldes—of course lead nowhere, least of all forward. The story of tragic Slovenian division is a myth that serves to maintain the status quo. It is fed by a whole garbage truck of indecency, manipulation and lies dumped daily into the Slovenian public space for this purpose. We Slovenians are not divided; we are idiots. We longed for democracy for so long and fought for it, and now we behave as if we don’t know what to do with it. Our problem is not that we disagree but that we don’t know how to disagree. Pluralism not only allows but needs a diversity of opinion. It also needs political culture, of which there is tragically little in Slovenia, and less and less. In my writing I avoid commenting on day-to-day politics, since I shape my publicly expressed opinions according to my attitude to shared, constitutional and European democratic values, not according to my personal views of this or that party or politician. This time I almost made an exception. I admit that Polde is not an entirely fictional character. And yet the fact that we cannot talk about the basics of how pluralist democracy works in Slovenia without dealing mainly with the role and actions of one individual is just another indicator of the state we are in. Above all, my writing is critical not only of Polde but also of those who build their political careers solely on not being him. The sad but indisputable fact is that in Slovenia we have problems with pluralist democracy not only because of a lack of experience but above all because, after thirty years, we still do not understand that its essence is not squabbling between egos but a democratic contest of programs and ideas.

Throwing around the label of fascism and comparing people to Hitler is a very serious matter. On one hand, we’re talking about a personality who is undoubtedly at the top of the global historical rankings of evil—any revival of his image or his ideas deserves full attention. On the other hand, it has become common practice that any mention of fascism or Hitler, even when not entirely far-fetched, is automatically dismissed as exaggerated or unfounded. In either case, these matters should not be taken lightly. It is just as irresponsible to recklessly wave such comparisons around in an attempt to discredit an opponent when we’ve run out of arguments, as it is naive—or blind—not to recognize in someone who walks and squawks like a fascist something more than just an innocent little duck. In a recent and widely discussed case, a journalist from Germany’s public broadcaster ARD was compared to Nazi propaganda outlets. He was accused of censorship in the style of Der Stürmer—and Pravda, for good measure. Soviet propaganda is a topic for another day—agitprop had teeth too—but let’s focus here on the legacy of Der Stürmer and its editor, Julius Streicher. The comparison raised quite a few eyebrows in Europe. But since such important matters shouldn’t be judged hastily or offhand, I suggest we take a closer look—and then everyone can decide for themselves whether that tweet truly echoed the spirit of Der Stürmer or Pravda. Let’s start with ARD, or as Germans succinctly call it, the Consortium of Public Broadcasters of the Federal Republic of Germany. ARD has nothing in common with Der Stürmerexcept that it was founded in 1950 by the Allies precisely as the antithesis to Hitler’s propaganda machine. That machine, in addition to the official Nazi Party organ Völkischer Beobachter, prominently included the "independent" Der Stürmer. This Nuremberg-based newspaper, which reached nearly half a million readers before World War II, was at one point too radical even for the Nazis, who had to temporarily restrict its sale in Berlin during the 1936 Olympics. Believe it or not, Der Stürmer even published children’s stories portraying Jews as invasive parasites and threats to the German people that needed exterminating. If that reminds you of something, it’s probably not ARD—but it is undeniably outrageous. Imagine if a Slovenian outlet today published children’s tales with similar content? Some Nazi elites disliked Der Stürmer because of its "humorous" tone, sexually explicit content, and scandalous reporting. It especially irked Hermann Göring, as the paper published an article claiming one of his daughters was conceived via artificial insemination—hardly in line with the image of a "true" Aryan male who wouldn’t need a test tube for reproduction. Göring would likely have had a few choice words for Der Stürmer's editor Julius Streicher had they walked together from their Nuremberg prison cells to the gallows—but Göring avoided that final stroll by swallowing a cyanide capsule just hours beforehand. Streicher, who didn’t take the pill, walked to the gallows shouting loyalty to the Führer, and in his final breath, uttered the cryptic phrase: "Purim fest 1946"—and departed to Valhalla. The meaning of that phrase was deciphered only a decade ago by French authors Bernard Benyamin and Yohan Perez in their book Le code d’Esther. Heil Hitler and conspiracy theories—go hand in hand for nearly a century now. Hitler was more sympathetic to Der Stürmer than some of his Nazi comrades. Its weekly dose of unhinged anti-Semitism aligned perfectly with his political paradigm. While he didn’t publicly praise the paper, it’s said he eagerly awaited each new issue to indulge in its rabid propaganda. It was especially popular among key supporters—young and less educated citizens—who found in its content a toxic mix of hatred and crude humour. Der Stürmer effectively embodied all five pillars of Hitler’s propaganda doctrine, as identified by American communication scholars Garth Jowett and Victoria O'Donnell in their 1986 book Propaganda and Persuasion. Here's the breakdown: 1. Avoid abstract ideas—appeal to emotions. What better than a cocktail of tabloid scandal, pure hatred, and sexually explicit filth? That blend—then and now—satisfies the full spectrum of emotional needs for a certain part of the population. 2. Repeat a few simple ideas constantly—use stereotypes. This strategy outlived Der Stürmer and its editor’s grim fate. Authoritarian propaganda doesn’t speak to reason, but to blind loyalty. The ritualistic incantation of simple slogans is a staple of any self-respecting cult. It induces a trance-like state in followers, allowing them to parrot their leader’s mantras as proof of absolute devotion—no thinking, no critique, no doubt. 3. Present only one side of the argument. Quality propaganda can’t afford objectivity. 4. Constantly attack your opponents. The key word is constantly. Daily, relentless bombardment of the public—now supercharged by social media—is essential to propaganda’s success. Continuous venom, insults, and accusations, with no regard for truth or fact, dulls the public’s senses and overwhelms the targets, who no longer know when or how to respond. One scandalous, slanderous dog whistle is instantly replaced by another, even more absurd and vile. 5. Pick a specific enemy to humiliate most intensely. For Der Stürmer and the Nazis, that was the Jews. Today, the targets are LGBTQ+ people, migrants, women, political opponents—and yes, Jews still get scapegoated too, often under the poorly disguised guise of attacking Soros or supposed "global financial conspiracies" threatening the purity and survival of the nation. Hitler’s bullet points were operationalized into detailed instructions by his chief propagandist Joseph Goebbels. In his diary, he offered further advice: all propaganda should come from a single centre of authority; it should amplify reactions the audience already has; it doesn’t matter whether the message is true or false—only whether it’s effective. Lies may have short legs, but if they wear jackboots, they can still kneel on the neck of truth. The lies and hatred of Der Stürmer paved the way for a crime in which millions were murdered. That was a time we thought we had left behind—and learned something from. Today, it often feels like that’s no longer the case. When history starts to repeat itself, we can’t just shrug and look away. A journalist from German public television was accused of channelling the ideological legacy of Der Stürmer. That’s a serious charge. If you truly recognize that legacy in his reporting, that’s cause for grave concern.

Educated people who often read Wikipedia know that the Great Charter of Liberties, or Magna Carta Libertatum, was created in England in 1215 to limit the power of the reigning monarch, King John (Lackland). It emerged from disputes between King John and both the Pope and the English barons over royal privileges. The Magna Carta stipulated that the king had to relinquish certain powers, adhere to specific legal procedures, and agree that his will could be constrained by law. It was the first step in a long historical process leading to the rule of law. The English, then, have had democracy in one form or another for over eight centuries. This gave rise to the witty saying that democracy is like English grass: you plant it and then wait a few hundred years for it to grow. The English are said to be excellent gardeners, but even the best sometimes find weeds sneaking into the lawn. One such weed episode occurred in the early 1990s when The Guardian revealed that Conservative members of the British Parliament had accepted bribes in exchange for posing sponsored parliamentary questions. Because no real democrat in the position of prime minister would tolerate—let alone encourage—unscrupulous politicians tossing a spanner into the democratic works (as the English might say), then–British Prime Minister John Major decided in 1994 to establish a special committee on standards in public life. After a year of meetings and deliberations, the new body, chaired by Lord Nolan, published a report outlining seven principles of public life, which unsurprisingly came to be known as the Nolan Principles. The committee's conclusions and advice were short and to the point. With a large enough font to be legible to any member of the House of Lords without glasses, they fit on a single A4 page. Read it once and Bob’s your uncle, as the English say. And yet, despite their brevity, simplicity, and clarity, some politicians seem to find even these few rules an insurmountable and uninteresting hurdle. Here’s what these pesky principles say: 1. Selflessness. Public office holders must act solely in the public interest. Good grief, the English must have bats in the belfry, as they might say. Whose interests do they think public officials could otherwise serve? In our country, such questions aren’t even asked. Everyone claims to work "for the people" and "for the future." 2. Integrity. Office holders must avoid any obligation to individuals or organizations that might unduly influence their work. They must not act or make decisions for personal financial gain or that of family or friends. They must declare and resolve any conflicts of interest. In the cash-for-questions scandal exposed by The Guardian, it was this principle that had been violated. Setting a price list for parliamentary questions and legislating for personal financial interest is a blatant and crude breach of democratic norms. Just imagine something like that happening here! That would really take the biscuit, as the English say. 3. Objectivity. Decisions must be made impartially, fairly, and on merit, using the best available evidence and without discrimination or bias. For those who find this abstract, consider the opposite: making decisions unfairly, dishonestly, without evidence, and with bias and discrimination. The latter may be easier for some to recognize. As with most rankings, the stakes rise with each step. 4. Accountability. Public officials are accountable to the public and must submit themselves to the scrutiny necessary to ensure this. In other words, if a politician messes up, makes a mistake, or breaks the law, they have no right to point fingers, scream, or intimidate the whistleblower. They must acknowledge and accept the consequences. Eat crow, as the English say. 5. Openness. Officials must act and make decisions in an open and transparent manner. They must not withhold information unless there are clear and lawful reasons for doing so. 6. Honesty. Public office holders must be truthful. Not a little, not occasionally—never lie. Not even to blow off steam, as the English might put it. Not even on Twitter. Even if you write that a retweet is not an endorsement. Never. A politician shouldn’t be bent like a barrel of fishhooks, as the English might say. Fat chance, their cynical compatriots might reply—and not without cause. 7. Leadership. Public office holders must exhibit these principles in their own behavior. They must actively promote and uphold them and be willing to challenge poor behavior wherever it occurs. This last point is especially important. In a society striving for integrity and a truly functioning democracy, it’s not enough for leaders to personally abstain from bad behavior. They must also be willing to speak out and condemn misconduct by others—especially their own political allies. This goes double for those in the highest offices, which carry prestige and demand moral authority. That’s why it matters that we elect statesmen—and not spineless squid. As the English might say. The point of this piece is not to lecture—"salt the mind," as Slovenians might ironically say—on how well the British or any other Western country practice democracy. I’ve lived abroad long enough to know that even a long-standing democratic tradition offers no foolproof protection against populist temptations. Since Boris Johnson moved into Downing Street, British public discourse often speaks of a “post-Nolan era.” But the fact that others can go off the rails shouldn’t be a source of comfort or an excuse for us to do the same. Especially since our democracy is still more fragile. After all, more than 800 years have passed since the English clipped the absolutist wings of King John (Lackland). We, on the other hand, are dealing not with weeds vying for space on centuries-old turf, but with invasive species spreading across vulnerable patches of democratic growth barely thirty years old—saplings in our own neck of the woods. As you know who might say.

When Georges Marchais, the long-time general secretary of the French Communist Party, was invited to speak on French radio three days after the fall of the Berlin Wall, he declared that the Eastern European experience with socialism had been "globally positive." Many residents of the countries who had to endure that “global positivity” firsthand would likely disagree. Georges Marchais is no longer with us, and the French communists are rapidly fading as well. The PCF has ceased to exist as a serious political force; much of its working-class support has been taken over by the far right, particularly the party formerly known as the National Front. And if today the ideological matron of Marchais’ former flock—Marine Le Pen—were invited to assess three decades of Eastern Europe’s democratic experiment, she’d likely be thrilled by the zeal with which people worn down by prior authoritarianism are now rushing toward a new one. It’s difficult to sum up in a few words all that has gone wrong over the past thirty years. I believe we were too quick to assume we had it all figured out. Democracy, it turns out, is like chicken: at its worst when half-cooked. No matter how appealing and crispy the skin looks on the outside, if the meat around the bone isn’t cooked through, things can go seriously wrong. Some say there simply hasn’t been enough time to establish a functioning democracy. For them, democracy is like an English lawn—you sow it, and then have to wait patiently for a few centuries for it to grow in strong and resilient. I’m not convinced. Perhaps time isn’t the main factor—careful gardening is. Or cooking, if you’ll forgive another metaphor. And judging by recent behavior, even eight hundred years after the Magna Carta, the English democratic chicken still bleeds when cut. Others claim voters are to blame for the bitter taste of the democratic experience, since the choice lies in their hands. That’s true—but only partly. It's the classic chicken-and-egg dilemma: was it the blind hen or the rotten egg? Democracy—pluralist democracy, not “people’s” or illiberal democracy—requires more than an election every few years. There’s no simple fix for the hardened, half-cooked version of democracy shaped by early-carelessness and inconsistency after the end of socialist one-party rule. We certainly shouldn’t look for answers in compromises between pluralist democracy and populist authoritarianism. Doing so legitimizes everything undemocratic and unacceptable about populism, and it’s doomed to fail. Populism does not—and cannot—compromise. Authoritarianism only takes a step back when it's preparing to leap forward. Pluralist democracy, as the name suggests, is based on a plurality of opinions, on rationality, and on responsibility. Rationality calls for caution, because although responsibility is a noble virtue, it is often mishandled. That’s why pluralist democracy also demands constant and effective democratic oversight. Populism, on the other hand, is based on concentration of power, on the infallibility of authority, and on obedience. For populists, power is not a temporary, law-bound, constitutional mandate—it’s a spoils system. Populists do not try to persuade; they intimidate. They don’t seek voters and supporters—they want obedient followers. They don’t build on trust but on blind loyalty. Their personality cult doesn’t tolerate criticism. They don’t accept responsibility or admit mistakes. They don’t unify, but divide, bribe, hate, and instill fear. For populism, politics is not a democratic clash of programs and ideas—it is a battle for survival, in which defeat is unacceptable. Populists don’t need facts or truth. They claim credit for others’ achievements and deny their own failures. Their political discourse is built on myths, manipulation, and lies. The end always justifies the means. Populists love to speak of unity and national interest—which, naturally, only they can define and defend. In this paradigm, any criticism or oversight of power becomes a betrayal of the nation. Efforts to unify different opinions, expectations, ideas, and approaches from the top down, in the name of unity, lead to dogmatism. Pluralist democracy does not demand artificial unity at all costs—such unity is often an illusion, since a society inevitably and legitimately contains diverse opinions and interests. Pluralism is built on democratic and cultural coexistence, dialogue, cooperation, and competition among differences. After thirty years of democratic experience, politics is in disrepute. This erosion of political credibility—as a process and as a profession—should worry us. No matter what we think of those we’ve elected, rejecting politics just because we dislike politicians is pointless. No one says they don’t care about their health because they dislike their doctor—especially one they chose themselves. Politics is a profession that should neither be the exclusive right of an intellectual elite nor void of expertise and integrity. Negative selection, personality cults, and an obsession with “new faces” are not exactly helpful—you be the judge. Populism wants to frame the clash between liberal and illiberal democracy as a left–right battle. That’s simply not true. Liberal democracy and its civilizational values, despite what some may shout, were not invented by leftists. If anyone, Christian Democrats and conservatives had the biggest hand in its rise. One would also expect liberals—at least those who understand the fundamental mission of political liberalism is not to opportunistically buddy up with anyone—to be firmly on the side of liberal democracy. Equally misleading is the projection of the left–right divide onto the media landscape. Media criticism of populism is not inherently leftist. That view reflects a deep misunderstanding of the media’s role in a democratic society. Let me offer a hypothetical example: if most media outlets in a country praise a polka-dot-orange government, that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re all orange. It may just mean the government is doing a good job. And vice versa. The idea of a “balanced” media landscape often assumes media should simply mirror political power dynamics, regardless of the government’s actions. But democratic principles don’t require “balance”—they demand independence, professionalism, and fidelity to journalistic ethics. Only then can the media fulfill its watchdog role, essential for a functioning democracy. That doesn’t mean media can’t have opinions—but they can’t twist facts to fit them. Public media are not state media or government mouthpieces. Media independence is a vital but demanding imperative—it requires not only protection from political interference but also from abuses of ownership and other pressures. Beyond legal and professional safeguards, public vigilance matters. In a society of active, critical citizens with sound media laws, selling lies is just bad business. Such active, critical citizenship doesn’t grow on its own. It has to be cultivated—and education plays a crucial role. Civic education is more than learning the national anthem or drawing the flag. It should transmit the knowledge, skills, and democratic values—above all, critical thinking—necessary for active citizenship. We need to restore respect and esteem for knowledge. Democracy needs thinking citizens, not yes-men—regardless of political stripe. Ultimately, real democracy requires political culture. This means being willing to criticize oneself and those who think like you. The habit of excusing every blunder in your own camp by pointing to a worse offense on the other side normalizes and legitimizes indecency in society and politics. People who sincerely believe in democracy must also hold themselves to higher standards of principle, consistency, responsibility, integrity, and political culture. Otherwise, we shouldn’t be surprised when voters begin to wonder whether there’s really any difference between politics that wants to be truly democratic—and the kind that’s raw to the bone.

I hope you won’t hold it against me that this time I am writing about myself and the distant days when I too was a secondary-school student. I do so not because my experiences were anything extraordinary or special, but quite the opposite: because in many ways they reflect the spirit of that time and the things that many young people experienced and did in the last years of the former regime, when the former common state and its socio-political system were still alive but already beginning to wilt and to smell, like vegetables left too long in the fridge. In my student days I did quite a few fun things. I took part, if only briefly, in both the defense club and the Marxist club. The motive was Brechtian. The club is a weapon; join it. What drew me and some friends to join the first one was the amusement we got from the new teacher of the subject Foundations of General People’s Defense and Social Self-Protection. Freshly graduated, he had come to the Šubic grammar school from the Faculty of Social Sciences and promptly founded a club as well, presumably because regular lessons were not enough for all the socio-political and defense wisdom he wanted to pass on to his eager pupils. Anyone who thinks defense lessons can’t be fun has never heard how, in the dialect of Lower Carniola, the M48 rifle is “taken apart for disassembly.” We began our extracurricular activities with a visit to the cadet school in Tacen, where our teacher had many acquaintances and friends. The next, and last, experience was shooting with an air rifle on the terrace of a building just a stone’s throw from what was then the building of the Republic Assembly, today the National Assembly. A stone’s throw away, and us with air rifles in our hands. You can probably imagine what happened. “Ping!” echoed from the windows across the street. “Ping!”—until our mentor realized what we were doing and threatened us with the arrival of the people’s militia. We left the club, and from then on he was forced to pass on his defense activities to mummy’s boys who wanted to play with guns. I also took part in the Marxist club. Again with a group of a few older students, we joined deliberately to take over the editorship of the school magazine the club published. The story lasted a year or two, caused no small amount of dust, a lot of fun and a few bans. One of them followed our editorial decision, out of solidarity with events at the other end of the then country, to rename the magazine the Bulletin of the Members of the Marx-Kosovo Club. What protected us from worse consequences was above all that most of the teaching staff showed solidarity with us, more or less openly, and most important was the support of our mentor, the legendary teacher and DJ Albert Avguštinčič. The headmistress of the time, probably at the request of those “from above,” or out of fear of them, summoned my parents to explain themselves. My father and I went, and he listened calmly to the headmistress’s sermon about how we did not show the appropriate socio-political orientation, kept criticizing everything and had ideas of our own. When she finished her address on the importance of growing up and taking responsibility, he stood up, patted me on the shoulder, replied kindly, “Thank God they are like that,” and marched out of the office. And that was that. Except that a few days later I got a reprimand. Perhaps out of revenge, or perhaps because I was caught smoking in the girls’ toilets. In shoes. Encouraged by my parents’ support, I continued my social engagement and troublemaking even after the Šubic grammar school, fleeing the tsunami of “directed education” reform, was exiled for a few years to the building of the Poljane grammar school. We no longer needed the Marxist club there, as we founded a new school magazine, Orlando Furioso. It too went through quite a few dramas, including a cover showing an illustration of the school building being bombed, but above all a scandal after the publication of an interview with one of the teachers, known for her firm and often rather aggressive attitude to students drinking and smoking. In retrospect, I grant the lady the nobility of her intentions, but not her methods. Since she had demanded to authorize the interview, we published an editorial comment alongside it, which I wrote myself. The publication raised a lot of dust; the comrade teacher furiously demanded a public apology and socio-political sanctions. “Matjaž Gruden and his associates should be banned from this and similar scribbling, and the matter should be dealt with as an offense through the Socialist Youth League,” she thundered. After a stormy editorial meeting, at which quite a few cigarettes were smoked and the odd beer drunk, and after consulting our mentor Borut Šuklje, who stood firmly on our side, I published a reply to the reply. “I am convinced that, as a member of the youth organization, criticizing and seeking solutions to burning problems is my right and duty, so I maintain that the demand that ‘the matter be dealt with’ as an offense through the Socialist Youth League is ridiculous and just another proof of the attempt to use the youth organization as a means to shut some people up. A solution to the problem can only be reached through open, honest dialogue, not through insinuations, abuse of one’s position and demands for public apologies. Let us fight with the power of argument, not with the argument of power, esteemed comrade.” It was 1983. One of my articles, a critique of the death sentence handed down at first instance to the serial killer Metod Trobec, was also reprinted by the student paper Tribuna. At that time it was edited by Aleš Debeljak and Marcel Štefančič, then literally a junior. I suspect Marcel was responsible for the illustration of a large red male organ that accompanied my piece. The period of working with Tribuna is certainly the one that marked my adolescence—my transition to adulthood, if you like—the most. Not only because of the not exactly Jesuit atmosphere in the editorial office and the unforgettable parties and nights out, but also because of a leap in my social engagement. We investigated misconduct at the Škofja Loka bus company and wrote about the crisis in the Middle East. “Begin begun” was the title of my interview with a representative of Palestinian students in Ljubljana. And of course they banned us again. We played cat and mouse with prosecutors and the police and arranged with the staff of the Ljudska pravica printing works for printing to start earlier—the prosecutor could not execute the seizure order until at least one physical copy had been printed. Then we loaded the few hundred secretly printed copies into a Fiat 600 and drove to Tribuna’s premises in the Kazina building, divided them up and went out to sell them on the streets of Ljubljana. People, of course, knew that Tribuna had been seized again, which had an extremely favorable effect on sales. I will never forget standing in front of the bookshop in the Konzorcij building, people scrambling for every copy, while behind the pillars two secret policemen in raincoats hid, watching me grimly. The most surprising thing about it all was that that was where it ended. There were no robo-cops taking our names, no fines, no court summonses. In the early 1980s, in the former state, in those leaden, unfree times, the critical social engagement of secondary-school and university students in Slovenia was met with some reproach, but also with a great deal of tolerance and, above all, support. This became even more evident a few years later, when we stood together and protested on Roška Street. Most people, including those holding positions in the regime, already realized then that times would change, because authoritarianism and unfreedom are always defeated in the end. And once that happens, we all have to look in the mirror and live with ourselves. That is how it was then and that is how it is today. Whoever knows nothing but the argument of power and authority, especially towards young people, will sooner or later be staring at the ground in shame.

I am closely following the efforts of the President of the Republic of Slovenia to calm passions in Slovenian politics and in this way perhaps contribute to the better and more effective functioning of political institutions in Slovenia. This is especially important at a time when we face such a serious health, economic and social crisis. On top of all that, we really don’t need political self-harm, which could leave our 30-year experience of democracy gasping for breath long after we have defeated the virus. National unity is one of those notions that are noble in principle but elusive, which everyone talks about but almost everyone interprets in their own way. So, from the perspective of an engaged citizen, I offer the President a thought or two on the subject. In case it helps. The first question is whether there exists that point of convergence and national consensus at which the centrifugal forces of political and personal interests are converted into an unstoppable common force that could irreversibly catapult Slovenian society into an ever brighter future, for ever and ever, amen. In recognition of the tireless courage and perseverance with which it is sought, I would call this point the Borut point. I apologize to the President for the informality, but I trust he will not hold it against me, as I know how fond he is of a relaxed style in communicating with his fellow citizens. If the Borut point exists—and on that, as the Americans would say, the jury is still out—the next two questions are where to look for it and, should we happen to find it, what to do there. Locating the zero coordinate of national consensus in political space in Slovenia most often relies on geometry. For many, point B is the midpoint between all the views, policies and ideologies advocated in Slovenia by at least one individual with a Twitter account. The appeal of equidistance from everything, expressed in the popular slogan “all different opinions must be respected,” lies in its simplicity. For people in public office who don’t care even about their own moral authority, it is comfortable, because it requires taking a position on nothing. The problem is that democracies are sometimes confronted with threats that cannot be overcome by comfort alone. The question arises of the content on which we are supposed to be united at all. Without any selection based on values, we find ourselves in a situation in which national consensus is built on the lowest common denominator. We must be united because we are Slovenians. The vacuum of values is, of course, only apparent. The void is always exploited and filled by the most aggressive and ruthless ideology. This is not the first instance of seeking national monolithic unity solely on the basis of ethnic belonging and territory, and history teaches us that excursions into this model of society have often ended tragically. In a geometric understanding of politics, the center is defined by the extremes, so in it Pope Francis is an extreme leftist and the Neue Zürcher Zeitung a Swiss communist pamphlet. We get a different picture if we define our position in politics by content. In that case, the extremes are defined by their attitude to democratic values, not the other way round. I would suggest that the President look for point B on the same foundations on which we built our own state 30 years ago. There is no need to invent anything; it is all written down, from the principles of the rule of law and the welfare state to the separation of powers, judicial independence, media freedom, and the protection of human rights and civil liberties, to which we devoted an entire chapter. The Slovenian Constitution is neither left, nor right, nor center. It sets the framework for a functioning pluralist democracy, in which all political and ideological platforms that accept the constitutional and civilizational foundations on the basis of and in the name of which we became independent can be represented and advocated with complete legitimacy and on an equal footing. Those whose politics and discourse place them outside this constitutional framework, or who even undermine it, cannot demand that “their opinions be given equal consideration too” and moan that “unbalanced” media criticize them and most of the public dislikes them. If the President pulled off the big one and managed to unite the political forces in Slovenia in clear support for constitutional principles, and then also committed himself firmly to using his moral authority to help ensure that everyone, regardless of their different views, actually kept their commitments, he would truly deserve a place in history. That is the unity that Slovenian democracy and its citizens need. It is not only about greater politeness in mutual relations. Political culture and political language in Slovenia really have gone to the dogs, but we won’t solve the problems we face simply by having those who undermine democracy smile while doing so instead of growling. Nor is it about unifying views so that everyone thinks more alike. A real democracy needs people who think not only differently but also diversely. Of course we have common goals, starting with defeating the pandemic, developing the economy, and the security and prosperity of citizens. There is no need to convene round tables for unity on these priorities. But this unity works only at a very high level of abstraction, because these are notions that each part of the political spectrum understands and pursues in its own way. And there is nothing wrong with that. That is the diversity of opinion we are otherwise so fond of talking about. Without pluralism there is no democracy. Each political platform offers its own path to a better future for its voters. If it wins a mandate in an election, it also gets the opportunity to prove the success of its program in practice. And to take responsibility if it fails. The danger arises when some politicians start invoking “broader social and national interests” and thereby try to place themselves above their political competitors and obtain a mandate to break democratic norms and depart from constitutional principles. What Slovenia needs, including in the fight against the virus, is not a unity empty of values but a consensus on the basic democratic rules. We need integrity, transparency, competence and democratic oversight. We need politics that is accountable and answers for what it does. In today’s conditions and given the sorry state of political culture in Slovenia, the road to agreement on these goals will be neither comfortable nor simple. Point B will require a lot of courage, determination and commitment to democratic principles. Not only in words but also in practice. It won’t happen without ruffling feathers. The word will have to become flesh. Perhaps the President will find motivation in the fact that—at least judging by the latest surveys—Slovenian public opinion is nevertheless changing and beginning to lean towards politics that builds on moral authority, is faithful to its declared principles and, when necessary, is also prepared to say: this is not right.

In November 2018, I was invited to a panel discussion titled What Do We Need for a True Democracy?, jointly organized in Brussels by the International Bar Association and the European People’s Party group in the European Parliament. The keynote speaker, first among equals, was European Commission Vice President Frans Timmermans. Alongside him, there were around ten more or less significant speakers, with me at the tail end. And since, of course, no one kept to their allotted time, I was called to speak at that awkward moment when half the audience was already scrolling through their phones, the first few were leaving the room, and Timmermans’s staff were frantically tapping their watches to remind him it was time to go. Just as the moderator was about to wrap things up, he noticed me sitting at the end of the table and said, “Ah, we still have Mr. Gruden from Strasbourg—would you like to say something, but please, if possible, briefly—a minute or two.” I had no choice but to set aside my carefully prepared notes and respond with just a few sentences: “For true democracy, we need institutions that citizens trust, a society that lives up to its democratic values, and a critical understanding of history.” Because of the circumstances, the statement was quite condensed, but I believe it still holds true. A genuine democracy needs three branches of power that consistently adhere to the principles of integrity, competence, transparency, and accountability. It needs effective democratic oversight that highlights and penalizes failures—whether accidental or intentional. Unlike functioning democracies, populist and authoritarian regimes do not seek trust; they are based on obedience. They achieve this through ideological polarization, intimidation, and the stigmatization of political opponents. With utter disregard for democratic norms, they seek full control over all levers of power—including oversight mechanisms like the judiciary, the media, and civil society. When they cannot take control, they discredit and obstruct. Whoever criticizes the authorities is labelled as a traitor of the people, an enemy, and a foreign agent. Democracy is not value neutral. For it to function, it needs a politics that does not just speak of democratic values but lives them. Without human rights, political freedoms, democratic rule of law, and humanistic values like social justice, dignity, solidarity, and empathy, democracy cannot survive. A democratic society must be open and forward-looking. That doesn’t mean there’s no place for conservatism—just like there’s room for other left- or right-leaning democratic options—but it cannot be closed, unjust, or regressive. Democratic values cannot be imposed—neither from the outside nor from the top down. If we want democracy to function, citizens must understand, accept, embrace and support its values. The most important path to this is education. The key to active, engaged, thinking citizens lies in civic education—not in the form of an empty patriotism based on loyalty to symbols and obedience to power, but through the transmission of knowledge, behaviour, values, and especially critical thinking. That is what shields democracy from populist and nationalist lies and manipulation. Successful, creative, and free societies also require investment in a wide range of knowledge and professions. Narrowly focused education can only return us to places we've already been. Democratic values are also transmitted and protected through culture. I agree that culture should be patriotic and nation-building—but only when it is also a driver of creativity, resourcefulness, innovation, self-reflection, commentary, critique, openness, boldness, curiosity, and freedom. The Slovenian nation would never have survived, let alone become independent, nor would it have a future, if its culture had resigned itself to being merely a service department of those in power. Finally, a true democracy also needs memory and a critical understanding of history. We cannot understand the European democratic and civilizational model without recalling the experience from which it emerged. This is something we sometimes struggle with in Slovenia. We don’t learn from history—we try to “transcend” it. We believe—perhaps with the best intentions—in the unifying and healing power of intentional amnesia, but that carries the risk of amnesty for evil. Without knowing and understanding history, we cannot grasp what happens when there is no democracy, no human rights, no political freedoms, no respect for human dignity or empathy. Without historical memory and critical understanding of history, we are defenceless against nationalist myths, populist manipulation, and denial of what really happened. This is especially important for young people. Without historical context, democratic values can seem to them like annoying lectures from boring old boomers—irrelevant and disconnected from their lives. Until the moment those values disappear. And then it might already be too late. In the Netherlands, the homeland of my interlocutor Frans Timmermans—not exactly a country with shaky democratic foundations—only one third of young people said a few years ago that living in a democracy was important to them. Among older generations, especially those who experienced World War II, that number was close to 90 percent. “Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it,” said Winston Churchill. That’s why it’s important that young people read The Diary of Anne Frank. I welcome the fact that President Borut Pahor also advocated for this. Anne Frank, the Dutch teenager, is just one of six million Jewish victims of the greatest crime in world history. But she is also important because her writing reminds us that each of those victims had a name, a family, friends, loves, and plans for the future—just like all of us. Anne Frank is a name, a face, and a fate that prevents us from wrapping the horrors of the past in the abstraction and anonymity of millions and forgetting them. Just under three years ago, researchers discovered two pages in Anne’s diary that had been covered with brown paper, where she had written about love troubles, sexuality, menstruation, and even included some rather bawdy jokes. The Anne Frank Foundation chose to honour her wish for privacy—since she had covered them herself—and did not publish them, which was the right decision. But those pages are also another piece of the mosaic that helps us remember a girl painfully similar to today’s teenagers—our children. If Anne had lived today, she probably wouldn’t have written a diary—she would have posted her thoughts on social media. And sometimes deleted them. She would have written about her daily life, her loves, her worries, and her dreams. Perhaps even about her fear of the hatred returning to society. The Diary of Anne Frank is a story of what did happen and a warning of what can happen. Not just to others, but to people like us. To us. Now someone has decided that Slovenian high school students will no longer be required to read Anne Frank’s Diary. Maybe we should ask ourselves why?

Barbie, Mattel: a children’s toy, originally a blonde, white-skinned doll, of which more than a billion have been made since 1959. Barbie is today one of the world’s most successful brands and is also often used as a nickname for airheaded people who are not to be taken seriously. Barbie, Klaus, also known as the Butcher of Lyon: the wartime Gestapo chief in that French city. At his trial in 1987 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for his personal responsibility for the torture and murder of hundreds of members of the French Resistance and French Jews, among them the 44 children of the Izieu children’s home, who, together with seven of their teachers, were arrested in April 1944 on Barbie’s orders and deported to the Nazi concentration camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau, where all of them were murdered. Getting kicks from racism and antisemitism is surely one of the most disgusting forms of clickbaiting. As long as it is done by frustrated anonymous basement-dwellers online, it is nasty but less dangerous than when it becomes editorial policy. Recently, the television channel TV3 hit a new low in this respect with the program Faktor, which Ms. Norma Brščič took over as presenter this January. For Norma, of course, this is not her first rodeo, as the Americans would say. She became known to the Slovenian public for breaking taboos, including some that she had set for herself and others. Many believe her musings should simply be ignored, since by reacting we create unnecessary attention and give them a weight they don’t deserve. Perhaps, but we should not forget that Ms. Norma did not whisper her racist and antisemitic messages to her husband across the pillow; this was public speech. Whatever we think of the content it broadcasts, TV3, on which Norma “breaks taboos,” is still part of our media landscape, with a program, owners, editors, companies that advertise on it, and probably viewers too. In the fight against hate speech, silence is not part of the solution but part of the problem. On the program, Norma Brščič mused about the Jewish question, stupid and lazy Negroes, and the injustices suffered by people who believe the Earth is flat. She was later surprised by the outraged reaction of part of the public, since in her view the theme of the program was merely the defense of freedom of speech. “I did not say, nor do I think, that any violence should be done to Black people, for example. I just listed a few facts.” Facts, let us recall, that in the Slovenian public sphere there is no room for free thinking about stinking negroid faggots and the role of the Jews in world institutions, in politics, in the pornography industry, in the film industry and in the media. Incidentally, Joseph Goebbels mused about the “Jewish question” in a very similar way before Norma, complaining as early as 1933 that Jews had taken over the leading positions in the German media, literature, theater, film, the medical and legal professions and the stock exchange. “They control parliament and the political parties,” he lamented at a press conference in the Hotel Carlton in Geneva, while at the same time, like Norma, firmly denying any suggestion that violence of any kind would be used in solving the “Jewish question,” and promising that “this excessive Jewish influence will be dealt with in a just and humane manner.” Because of her squeaky voice, blonde hair, doll-like looks and indignation at a society unjust to racists, antisemites and people who believe the Earth is flat, many do not take Norma seriously. Perhaps, because she is a woman, they judge her mainly by her looks. That is sexist and a risky underestimation. Even if someone reminds you of Barbie, don’t forget Klaus. TV3’s editors scheduled the talk show about breaking taboos on the “Jewish question” just a few days before the anniversary of the day, 76 years ago, when soldiers of the Soviet Red Army liberated the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp, one of the largest killing sites of the Second World War, where, besides the children of Izieu, almost a sixth of the six million Jewish victims of the Holocaust were murdered, along with thousands of other victims of Nazi violence, including Slovenians. Holocaust Remembrance Day was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2005. Like every anniversary, it has its significance but also its weaknesses. The anniversary is important because remembrance is a moral imperative. It is a debt we owe to the victims, to their relatives and to the people who survived but were forever marked by an experience of indescribable suffering and evil. On the other hand, like every anniversary, Holocaust Remembrance Day also carries the risk that the memory of the victims becomes ritualized and loses its meaning. A short ceremony, a statement on the official website, a tweet or two, and that banal, hollowed-out and endlessly repeated “never again.” A ceremony as an opportunity for indulgences, for everything that responsible politics should be doing, but doesn’t, in the time before the ceremonies and after them. Until the next ceremony, the next wreath, the next photo opportunity and another “never again.” That is not enough. Remembering the victims of the Holocaust is not only an act of reverence towards millions of people killed by their fellow human beings; it should also be the foundation of a common and determined fight against the ideas, words and deeds that led to the crime and are returning today, helped by the indecision, opportunism and cowardice that prevent us from firmly standing up to them. The fight against the rehabilitation and return of evil cannot begin and end on the same day of the year, with a funeral wreath and a few phrases for the occasion. Instead of “never again,” I would suggest that politicians use the words of Primo Levi, the Italian writer of Jewish origin who survived the hell of the concentration camp: “It happened, therefore it can happen again.” On this year’s remembrance day, President Pahor also published his message. “All of us—especially those of us with a public voice—must refrain from any word and any action that anyone might understand as offensive, as hateful or even as incitement to violence,” he said, pointing to our shared moral and human duty to strive to preserve tolerance, coexistence and free-mindedness, where everyone can express their views in a way that preserves the dignity of their fellow human beings. I welcome the fact that this statement contains an echo of the realization that, today too, there are words and actions reminiscent of those that, eight or more decades ago, paved the way to crime. But given how much intolerance, hatred, relativizing of evil, stigmatizing and dehumanizing of certain groups there is in today’s world—and in today’s Slovenia—the president could and should have been clearer and more determined in his words. We are confronted with ideas and words that are understood as “offensive, as hateful or even as incitement to violence” not only by “some”; everyone should understand and condemn them as such. You may feel that I repeat myself in my writing, pointing out the same problems again and again. I promise to do the same in future. As long as it is necessary. Every time the “Jewish question” is discussed in the name of free-mindedness, every time people are compared to parasites that must be exterminated, every time a doctor publicly calls for the ethnic purity of Europe, every time a politician spreads racist messages, every time the Holocaust is denied or relativized, every time, every single time this happens, it is spitting on the memory of the victims and paving the way for a repetition of hell. It is not a defense of free-mindedness but an attack on freedom. And as long as we as a society cannot, dare not or will not respond to it, we are all jointly responsible for this spitting and paving. What is threatened in today’s Slovenia is not so much “free-mindedness,” which in the president’s statement was tacked onto tolerance and coexistence, but the civilizational foundations of post-war Europe, threatened by those who understand “free-mindedness” as a license for hatred, and abetted by those who lack the principle and courage to condemn this hatred—which is evidently becoming our new normal—clearly and firmly, every time, without dithering and shuffling.

On the early morning of May 25, 1944, Operation Rösselsprung began—known in our parts as the raid on Drvar. Around 12,000 members of the 500th SS Parachute Battalion, wearing camouflage uniforms and Nazi insignia, attacked the small town of Drvar in an attempt to capture and kill Tito and thus change the course of the war in Yugoslavia. The German forces were aided by an unknown number of local collaborators. Although they initially surprised the Partisan units and briefly controlled the area, the raid ultimately failed. Tito, Jovanka, and their dog Tiger were exfiltrated from a cave on the outskirts of Drvar where they had been hiding. The disappointed and enraged attackers had to content themselves with taking out their frustration on Tito's white marshal's uniform, which they found at a tailor’s shop while sweeping the town. Those who survived the war later tried to justify their actions by claiming they were guided by patriotism and merely following orders. In the early afternoon of January 6, 2021, a crowd of around 12,000 supporters of President Trump, dressed in camouflage, animal skins, horns, and bulletproof vests, attacked the U.S. Capitol building in an attempt to prevent Vice President Mike Pence from certifying Joe Biden’s victory—and thereby change the outcome of the U.S. presidential election. There is suspicion the attackers had help from the inside—some Capitol police officers and possibly even members of Congress. Though the mob initially overwhelmed security and stormed the building, the Capitol assault ultimately failed. Vice President Pence, who was evacuated with his family during the attack, returned to the chamber a few hours later and completed the certification of the results. The angry and frustrated rioters had to settle for stealing podiums and laptops, smashing furniture, and beating police officers—two of whom died. Many of those arrested have tried to justify their actions by claiming they were motivated by patriotism and were merely following the president’s instructions. The parallels between these two historical events are too striking to ignore for someone who finds meaning even in trivial details. What’s most amusing in this comparison is that, in the Assault on the Capitol, the role of Josip Broz Tito was played by Mike Pence. Mikey managed to walk from zero to hero in just a few hours. With a crisply tailored conservative suit, perfectly coiffed hair, a firm, vacant stare, and a statesmanlike clenching of his jaw—this is not a posture you acquire overnight. It takes years of practice in front of a mirror. After the attack, Mike Pence oozed determination and principle. He looked like someone who could erupt at any moment, slam his fist on the table, and shout: "Crucifix, so what!" Many praised Pence’s composure. Our Amy Klobuchar even greeted him with a fist bump after the results were certified. That Pence agreed to physical contact with a woman he isn't married to was another sign of his sudden and total transformation. In the days leading up to January 6, TV host and comedian Jimmy Kimmel joked that Pence hadn’t been under so much stress since the last time he saw a woman in short sleeves. Yet, for all this, I doubt that Pence’s new image as a politician with courage and integrity will withstand the judgment of history. Until very recently—and for at least the past four years—Mike Pence was anything but that. Ironically, his moral turning point came only after Trump, during a phone call the morning of the attack, reportedly called him a “pussy” (pardon the vulgarity, but it’s a quote) for not having the guts to break the Constitution on his behalf. Mike Pence became principled because he had no other choice. To survive. After years of sycophantic servitude—justifying, enabling, and legitimizing all manner of outrages—his boss backed him into a corner, wiped himself with him like a rag, and threw him into a rabid mob. Pence’s ethical awakening cannot erase the stain of many years in which, while proclaiming his Christian values, he served as a fig leaf for a man who couldn’t even read the Ten Commandments, let alone understand them—because they don't mention his name or talk about him. Mike Pence isn’t just a vice president; he’s also a sub-politician—someone who doesn’t meet the minimum standard of integrity required for the office he holds. He is someone who was willing to abandon his values and reputation to enable someone else's abuse of power—power used in ways that trample and humiliate those very values. Pence repeated Trump’s lies about a stolen election, which ultimately led to violence. He supported and excused Trump when he was separating children from their mothers and locking them in cages. He stood silently when Trump responded to the racist murder in Charlottesville by saying "there were good people on both sides." Pence didn’t say a word when Trump ordered the violent dispersal of peaceful anti-racist demonstrators so he could pose in front of a church with a Bible held upside down. Pence, the conservative overflowing with Christian values, stayed quiet as a mouse when Trump bragged about grabbing women by the same body part he eventually used to describe Pence himself. He stayed silent and assisted when Trump suggested injecting disinfectant to fight COVID, and later, when Trump simply gave up on the pandemic, which went on to kill 400,000 Americans. Pence found his spine only when Trump demanded he throw himself under a train, and then, upon refusal, unleashed a mob that hunted him through the Capitol, some of them intending to hang him. As we express collective outrage at the outgoing president’s behavior, we must not forget the responsibility of those who helped bring him to power and keep him there. There would be no Donald Trump—and no copycats—without Mike Pence and his ilk. The resurgence of authoritarian, nationalist populism, which can lead to scenes like those we saw at the Capitol, would not be possible without collaborators—whether motivated by opportunism, intellectual deficiency, or sheer corruption—who enable, support, and excuse authoritarian populists. Most of these enablers believe they’re in control, insisting that it’s possible to feed the wolf and keep your principles intact. But the idea that you can escape a falling elevator by jumping up at the last moment is one believed only by very small children and shameless politicians. Mike Pence is actually lucky that his master literally forced him into integrity at the end. Compared to other sub-politicians, he at least has a slim chance of being remembered as something more than a bootlicker and a coward. Which is more than can be said for those still riding the elevator all the way down in their raid to the moral bottom.
Luck, Wisdom and Health to Us All

Humans are stubborn and resilient creatures, so even in times of hard trials like the ones we are going through, we try by every means to fool ourselves into feeling better than we realistically should or deserve to. In December, I read lists in several places of positive things that supposedly happened in the year just ended. You know: we learned to bake sourdough bread, we spent a lot of time with our loved ones, Jan Plestenjak has a new song, Rok Snežič isn’t allowed into Bosnia, and so on. These attempts to find rose-tinted glasses through which our reality wouldn’t look so oppressively gray remind me of the legendary joke about the reporter who, as she left the theater where an assassin had just murdered her husband, asked Abraham Lincoln’s wife, “Other than that, Mrs. Lincoln, how did you enjoy the play?” And yet, if we set aside for a moment the pandemic that has thrown the world off its hinges, a few things did happen last year that give us hope that the future may be a shade less gray than the present. Besides the fact that we got a dog in the family, I would mention at least two more: first, the outcome of the American election, and then, of course, the record-fast development of a vaccine against Covid-19. What the November election and the race for a vaccine have in common is Trump’s claim that he won both. Fortunately, that isn’t true. The thought of Trump in a white coat with a syringe full of bleach would probably drive even Dr. Fafangel into the arms of the anti-vaxxers. What Biden’s victory and the vaccine’s victory also have in common is that they are not bona fide positive events but rather opportunities to stop negative trends before everything goes completely down the drain. Biden and the vaccine are also linked by the fact that, for many who like neither Trump nor the coronavirus, the cure is worse than the disease. You know: Biden is a reactionary old fart, Hillary’s pal, and the vaccine contains chips that Bill Gates put there. No point wasting words on such nonsense. Of course Biden is far from perfect—but, as with the vaccine, where, as with most other medical substances and procedures, we cannot completely rule out side effects, the risk of his presidency pales beside the threat that the alternative inevitably brings. At the same time, of course, neither Biden nor the vaccine guarantees a final solution to all our problems. On a submarine whose engines have failed, we have stopped sinking to the bottom; now we have to figure out how to get back to the surface before we run out of oxygen. Most of us spent the first days of last November tensely following the vote count in the American election. The importance of Joe Biden’s convincing victory should by no means be underestimated. This time the American electoral contest was not between two competing political options but between two completely different political and social concepts. One of them, for all its weaknesses and inconsistencies, is based on the principles of liberal democracy, that is, the democratic rule of law, political pluralism, judicial independence, free media, human rights and civil liberties; the other is not. In today’s United States, as in other countries where nationalist populism is growing or even in power, the division is not between left and right. It is a contest in which on one side are pluralist democratic options—left, right and center—and on the other an authoritarian paradigm of power that tries to camouflage as a culture war its intention to subordinate the whole of society and its subsystems to its interests. In Trump’s understanding of democracy, only his victory and dominance are allowed, regardless of the election result. But this story is far from over. Trump lost, but he is not lost. There is more rationality in the furious foot-stamping and throwing of toys against the wall than appears at first sight. Donald Trump is taking a run-up for the second half. The frantic repetition of absurd claims about a stolen election is meant to radicalize his supporters and to bring the Republican Party completely to heel, leaving room only for blind obedience to the great leader. If the institutions of American democracy withstood the onslaught of rampant populism this time, Trump and the little Trumps are determined to leave nothing to chance in four years’ time. Or to election results. Of course, it is not only about the United States; what happens in America influences the political situation in other parts of the world in many ways. Reactions to the American election in Slovenia are a projection of domestic ambitions regarding the direction of development of our political system. That is also why reactions here at home were so colorful and boisterous. From the statement by the gentleman from New Slovenia that they were disappointed because the candidate closer to their values had lost—by which of the Ten Commandments the orange pussy-grabber is closer to the Christian Democrats than Biden, who is first at Mass every Sunday, is a question to which it would be fun to hear the answer—to the foot-stamping refusal to recognize the results and the international squabbling on the part of the prime minister, who inconceivably and irreparably drew us onto the world diplomatic map. And soon after the results of the American election were known, the world also got a vaccine against the disease that has had us literally by the throat for a year. We got the vaccine very quickly, faster than expected and, it seems, for many even too fast. Just as in the first phase of the pandemic we were all epidemiologists, today we are evidently all immunologists and pharmaceutical experts. Why should I get vaccinated if I’m healthy?
