Mate, you can’t make a vaccine in a year, don’t give me that. The pharmaceutical industry cooked up the coronavirus so it can make money. Some are afraid, some refuse to be vaccinated out of selfishness, others would probably swear by cold-water cures and healthy eating even in the event of a nuclear attack, and there are many who don’t want to be vaccinated because they don’t trust science. Their self-confidence comes from the feeling that they are not alone. The internet connects them with like-minded people and gives them access to more comfortable facts and an alternative reality tailored to their fears, traumas and needs. How can it be fake news if everything is written just the way I feel and believe? A revolt that sees knowledge as a conspiracy theory is worrying. Of course the pharmaceutical industry must be under public scrutiny, but that does not mean they are in breach until every member of the tavern council and every sage on Facebook has given their approval. Imagine a world in which the speed of progress was adjusted to the cognitive abilities of the slowest common denominator. Resistance to and suspicion of vaccines reflect a broader revolt against rationality, science and expertise that began long before the pandemic—and that in the past was most ardently and opportunistically fueled and exploited precisely by populism. On the other hand, it is true that for many, reservations about vaccines express distrust of authorities that disappointed and angered them in their handling of the pandemic so far and are now trying to convince them to get vaccinated. If I can’t trust them on the purchase of protective equipment and the closing of kiosks, why should I make an exception for the vaccine? Besides the availability of sufficient quantities of vaccine and the efficient organization of vaccination, it will therefore be crucial in the period ahead for politics to regain people’s trust. Through integrity, responsibility, effectiveness and a different kind of communication. Populism and Covid-19 have different causes. The first was largely made possible by the inconsistency, indecency and mistakes of a politics that otherwise never stopped talking about liberal democratic values; the second was caused by the whims of Mother Nature, whose work was made much easier by the fact that we have long been treating her like a pig treats a bagpipe. Without a radical change in our relationship with the environment, Covid-19 will be merely the trailer for the horror films still awaiting us. Global warming, new pandemics, droughts, floods, famine, conflicts and uncontrolled migration caused by natural disasters… The worst thing that can happen to us in facing such challenges is politics that tweets during a global health crisis, plays golf, denies climate change, always shifts blame and responsibility onto others, lines its own pockets and subordinates democratic institutions and social subsystems. In the fight against global threats, things look bad for humanity if we are led by ostrich-like nationalism and a selfishness that believes every problem can be solved simply by pushing your fellow human being into the muck. Fortunately, in democracies, at least for now, voters still decide. So let us use our heads. As Abraham Lincoln said, if you turn your backside to the fire, you’ll sit on your blisters. Biden and the vaccine give us another chance to get our act together. I hope we manage it.

Not long ago, the very right wing weekly Demokracija published an article in which the author compared people of other races to vermin and weeds that need to be eradicated. If I draw a historical parallel—which is surely appropriate in this case—I would remind readers that Julius Streicher, editor-in-chief of the Nazi rag Der Stürmer, ended up before the Nuremberg Tribunal for similar writings. Whether Streicher also tried to convince the judges that it was just satire, I do not know. Whether the article in Demokracija meets the threshold for criminal prosecution for hate speech will be determined by prosecutors. In a democratic society, that threshold must remain high. But regardless of their decision, it is clear we are witnessing a new phase in the banalization of evil. Comparing people to parasites and weeds represents a strategic, long-term approach to hatred. It dehumanizes potential victims in order to gradually erode society's inhibitions against intolerance or even violence toward them. The Holocaust, too, began with training people like hunting dogs—so they would slowly become accustomed to blood. By the time the crematorium ovens were lit, most “ordinary people” were already prepared to look away, if not outright participate. If what appeared in Demokracija was satire, as some now claim, I suggest we start spelling that word differently. In light of the seriousness of what happened, I was genuinely pleased and relieved that the ruling party—which also co-owns the publishing house behind Demokracija—distanced itself from the article. This is, to be sure, the bare minimum of political responsibility and decency when it comes to defending the most fundamental constitutional and civilizational values. The statement by the SDS party condemning the article offered a rare opportunity for political and public unity in Slovenia—an opportunity that, unfortunately, ultimately did not materialize. The spoiler was ironically the biggest advocate of such unity, the President of the Republic Borut Pahor, who, faced with this latest racist outburst (as so many times before), remained deafeningly silent. But prez is just being prez. On the other hand, the SDS’s move was certainly valuable, but for that value to be effective, it requires consistency. And that's where things get complicated. First, there must be consistency regarding the media. In its response, the party emphasized that although it co-owns the publisher of Demokracija, it “does not influence their editorial policy.” If they maintain such a hands-off stance toward media they co-own, it’s even more important that they refrain from interference and pressure on media—especially public ones—that neither the party nor the government has the right to claim as their ownership. Ironically, it is often those who shout the loudest about the authoritarianism of the past who have the hardest time understanding that, in a democracy, the government is not the owner of the state, nor of its subsystems or public institutions. It is merely a manager, one whose role is limited by laws and the constitution, and contingent on a democratic mandate. This misunderstanding was painfully illustrated by a recent remark that STA (Slovenian Press Agency) and rapper Zlatko “must follow the rules” so long as they “live under our roof.” That remark reflects the ignorant arrogance of accidental power, catapulted from anonymity into parliament by our obsession with “new faces” and a shallow talent pool. More consistency would also be welcome regarding behaviour within the ruling party’s own ranks—particularly among supporters and members who too often slip in their respect for basic constitutional values. To put it bluntly: if the SDS sincerely wants to distance itself from and condemn discrimination based on religion, race, gender, and sexual orientation, then they could, for instance, give a little slap on the wrist to the government’s National Security Twitter warrior for his vulgar finger gestures. Apparently, as the Americans would say, he missed the memo about the party’s distancing from racial intolerance. The party should also more forcefully rebuke supporters who stir up hatred toward people from other parts of the former Yugoslavia, deny them civil rights, and tell them to “go home.” A political party that genuinely upholds non-discrimination and human dignity should support actors in civil society who work toward the realization and protection of these values—particularly NGOs—instead of stigmatizing them and making their work harder. If the SDS and its leadership are truly serious about rejecting discrimination and racism—and I sincerely hope they are—then their communication must reflect that consistently and unequivocally. Twitter is not and cannot be an excuse for immature or irresponsible messaging. A party that wants to distance itself from social pathologies we had hoped were defeated in Europe should also be concerned about the demonization of George Soros, which has become so normalized that we barely even notice it anymore. This is a deeply worrying sign of how discourses rooted in antisemitic tropes and conspiracies about international Jewish financiers have been mainstreamed. One of the central antisemitic narratives in history is the claim that Jews form a global cabal that uses “dirty money” to secretly manipulate the world against good, honest non-Jews. In these messages, Jews are often not mentioned by name, but through code words and symbols. How far this trivialization of antisemitism has gone was evident in an interview with Laura Towler, a British antisemite and white supremacist, published this September—where else but in Demokracija. In the interview, which was later also posted on the SDS’s official website, the deputy director of the organization Patriotic Alternative laments that “Jews dominate important positions in government and media, through which they promote open borders.” This is the dilemma that inconsistent principles create. A party that distances itself from one Demokracija article should also distance itself from another Demokracija article, as opposed to publishing it on its own website. Incidentally, the SDS party president also recently took a jab at Soros, tweeting that the Jewish-American financier should “stay out of the EU and Europe,” because his “dirty money for so-called NGOs is a major source of conflict on the continent.” I would never claim that the party president is an antisemite or a white supremacist. But I would advise him to be more cautious and moderate in his public communication. Carelessly repeating problematic imported narratives about “Soros's global conspiracies” or “cultural Marxism” (the concept that inspired Anders Breivik’s killing spree on Utøya) risks giving the wrong impression—even unintentionally—especially to someone less informed. That is surely not a message someone who genuinely wants to distance themselves from racism and other such social pathologies would want to send. In conclusion—despite some open questions and ongoing expectations—I want to commend the fact that, following the article in Demokracija, the SDS party did indeed condemn racial intolerance and all other forms of discrimination. That gives hope that, despite all our differences and disagreements—normal in a democracy—we might one day reach consensus in Slovenia on the core values that a modern, open, secure, and successful society both demands and requires. That is why the SDS’s condemnation of racism is important and positive. As the wise Chinese philosopher Lao Tzu said, “The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.” Given where we are today, I hope that every one of those miles will eventually be walked.

The recent ups and downs caused at home and abroad by the Slovenian prime minister’s comments on the US election results reminded me of an episode from a good year and a half ago that showed, in an amusing way, how human under the skin even the people who hold the reins of international relations are. In July 2019, I took part in an international conference on media freedom in London, organized by the British government together with Canada, which wanted to give the impression that it could play a visible international role on its own, without the European Union. The conference included a formal dinner hosted by the then British foreign secretary, Jeremy Hunt, for his colleagues at Lancaster House near Buckingham Palace, and the guest of honor was the well-known lawyer and human rights campaigner Amal Clooney. As the highest-ranking representative of the Council of Europe at the conference, I too was invited to the dinner. After the meal, during which the participants chewed over and digested all the global challenges, the ministers got up, smoothed their trouser legs, tugged their cufflinks out of their sleeves and tightened the knots of their ties, and then lined up like schoolboys for selfies with the patient Amal. The last thing I heard as I left the hall was a shout addressed to me in one of the languages of our former country: “Come on, brother, hold my bag so I can get a picture with the woman.” What does this have to do with the prime minister’s tweets, you ask? Nothing other than that statesmen are also people of flesh and blood. Just as they cannot resist the charm of the beautiful (and above all smart and capable) Amal, they very probably don’t like it when someone insults and attacks them without cause. In Slovenia, at the time of the notorious tweets, many came to the prime minister’s defense or at least tried to downplay the effect of what he had done, saying it was a personal opinion that no one would associate with Slovenia. Of course, just as Trump’s tweets didn’t damage the international reputation of the United States. In short, between the lines one could sense the hope that the damage would not be too great because others would be smarter and more mature than us. Perhaps, but here I would remind you of the anecdote above. International movers and shakers can also be vain, and if they are vain, they can also hold grudges. The notion of international relations governed by an invisible algorithm of responsibility, interests, judgment and rules, dressed in a pinstriped suit, does not, of course, stand up to serious criticism, still less in a world shaped by the prime minister’s favorite. Paradoxically, what protects our chief tweeter to some extent from the consequences of his own rowdiness is precisely that Biden is not Trump. During my almost thirty-year career in international relations, I have taken part in many meetings with statesmen from Europe and the world. I met Barack Obama before he became president, and Bill Clinton after he had finished his term in the White House. I was twice in meetings with Putin, whom it would, of course, be hard to meet at a time when he was not president. Among the personalities who have stayed in my memory are Shimon Peres, Benjamin Netanyahu, Mahmoud Abbas, King Hussein of Jordan, David Cameron, John McCain, the Pope, Ibrahim Rugova, Franjo Tuđman, Vojislav Koštunica, Eduard Shevardnadze, Viktor Yushchenko, his namesake Yanukovych and Yulia Tymoshenko, several different sets of politicians from various parts of our former common state, including a few clients of The Hague, and I could go on. Observing these people in person, away from the TV cameras, sometimes gives you insight not only into their political views but also into their personal qualities. None of them, with the possible exception of Francis, suffers from a lack of vanity or too small an ego. Some of them, not all, are interesting and witty; many are also hot-tempered and caustic. This applies even to the politest among them. Read how Barack Obama described Nicolas Sarkozy in his recently published memoir, A Promised Land. Small in stature and big on emotional outbursts and overblown rhetoric. And all over the map. As if that were a bad thing. Being on the map. We can take comfort in the fact that Slovenia is not France, so I too think the tweets will not significantly affect our relations with the United States. Not so much because I believe Biden is prepared to forgive us, but more because I doubt he will spend much time on us. It is quite possible that he will think of Slovenia even less often than Melania Trump. So there won’t be a crisis center for relations with Slovenia in the West Wing of the White House any time soon, but if and when a file related to our country lands on the desk in the Oval Office, we can expect a note at the bottom of the last page: “Mr. President, in case it helps, here are screenshots of tweets from the time of your election.” But while we can hope that, because of our smallness, we will somehow get away with it in relations with the Americans, that does not mean the tweets will have no consequences at all for our foreign-policy reputation, influence and position. Especially among our European partners. Anyone who claims otherwise evidently doesn’t know much about international relations. Make no mistake, it is not only this government that has problems with foreign policy. In the past, the post of foreign minister was often merely a sinecure with a driver and bodyguards, mainly intended for dealing with domestic politics. As I wrote some time ago, Slovenia is not as small as we can make it ourselves, small and insignificant. Until recently, in international politics we mostly preferred to be quiet and without ideas. Instead of having clear positions on important issues, we preferred to shuffle our feet and wait to see which way the wind would blow. It must be admitted that today things are different. We are not quiet; we have ideas and clear positions. Unfortunately, not always the smartest ones. We have marched smartly and without complexes onto the international map. Unfortunately, not always in the right direction. The world has noticed us, true, but that does not mean it respects us. Small states cannot build their international position on political, economic or military power. They do not get international influence automatically; they first have to earn it by the sweat of a smart foreign policy. For Slovenia, alliances are of key importance. This is especially true of the European Union, whose presidency we will hold in seven months’ time. But membership of the EU alone does not bring either influence or power. That is the bitter lesson of all our failures so far on the European stage, from Piran to Teran wine. Influence and power, and with them the ability to protect one’s own interests, are built within the European Union too, gradually, step by step, strategically and years in advance. International trust and reputation have to be earned, maintained and consolidated. How consolidated we are today, judge for yourselves. Or read what others write and say about us. It is hard to be a foreign-policy heavyweight and international influencer, or at least someone taken somewhat seriously in the world, if the response to every statement or initiative begins with the question: “Isn’t that the one who insulted Biden and congratulated Trump?” Gaining international standing takes time. It can be lost overnight, and that cannot remain without consequences. For You, for Me, for Slovenia. For tomorrow. Let us hope not forever.

It’s been over three-quarters of a century since a senior government official responsible for national security in Europe publicly spread racist messages. That fact alone should give us pause. Reductio ad Hitlerum is a term coined in 1953 by Leo Strauss, a German-born Jewish-American political philosopher, to describe attempts to discredit an opponent's viewpoint by comparing it to Hitler or Nazism. In the early 1990s, American lawyer and author Mike Godwin adapted Strauss's idea to the digital era, famously stating that the longer any online discussion continues, the higher the likelihood someone will invoke a comparison to Adolf Hitler. Both Strauss and Godwin were right. Who among us hasn’t encountered people trying to compensate for a lack of arguments or facts with far-fetched analogies? But that doesn’t mean that every analogy to Nazism or fascism is baseless, as alt-right activists and apologists often claim. These individuals routinely misuse Strauss’s and Godwin’s insights to cover for all manner of indecency and filth. We can’t know what Leo Strauss would think of today’s resurgence of ideologies we believed were forever defeated in Europe—he died in 1973—but we do know he didn’t underestimate racism: he had to flee it once in his lifetime. We also know what Mike Godwin thinks of the current revival. In August 2017, two days after a white supremacist’s deadly attack during a demonstration in Charlottesville, Virginia, he stated: “By all means, compare these shitheads to Nazis. Again and again.” A different perspective came the next day from Donald Trump, who set a new low by saying there were “very fine people on both sides,” trying to legitimize indecency, intolerance, and hatred through a morally false equivalency. These thoughts came to mind recently when I saw a post on social media presenting photos of four white women as an example of “the only kind of diversity Europe needs.” This racist outburst so delighted the current State Secretary for National Security that he decided to share it with his followers. His vulgar response to the reaction from a female party leader shows this wasn’t a slip—it was a deliberate and calculated provocation of racial intolerance. Let’s set aside the question of where these self-appointed racial certifiers would place themselves in their taxonomy of acceptable European physiognomy. What’s most shocking about this tweet isn’t even its content, since such incidents have become disturbingly frequent and are increasingly normalized. What’s most concerning about this latest milestone in our collective descent into a new normal is once again the silence. The fact that there was no response from those who should have spoken out about a racist outburst involving a senior government official in a highly sensitive position is deeply troubling. Coincidentally, this racist tweet came at a time when national television aired an interview with the President of the Republic. I don’t know whether the president was aware of how his national security official was communicating at the time of the recording. But the tweet certainly throws an uncomfortable light on the president’s familiar refrains about how Slovenians are too divided, how we must respect all opinions, and how we must overcome differences. I don’t question the President’s noble motives for promoting national unity. However, the truth is that Slovenians are even more divided now than when he began his efforts in his first term. Perhaps despite his efforts. Or, at least in part, because of them. His doctrine of respecting all opinions—no matter how extreme—gives cover and a veneer of legitimacy to views that are fundamentally unacceptable to the vast majority of Slovenians. There are some differences that, in a democratic society, must not be bridged. We often fail in Slovenia to distinguish between tribal polarization and democratic political conflict. Political scientist Jan-Werner Müller from Princeton University recently wrote in The Guardian that polarization is a project of far-right populism, which reduces all political issues to questions of cultural affiliation and identity. According to Müller, bridging differences is not an end in itself. Rather than clinging to naïve expectations that politics can function as a neutral effort toward shared goals ("not left or right, but forward"—a quip I’ll claim), we must learn to distinguish between democratic and anti-democratic forms of political conflict. If we ignore this boundary—or refuse to see it—we fall prey to the sleight-of-hand of far-right populism, which wants to convince us that the political landscape is divided between left-liberal democracy and a supposedly balanced anti-liberal "conservatism." The absurd but logically consistent outcome of such thinking is that human rights, political freedoms, and the rule of law become leftist conspiracies, while racial intolerance becomes legitimate, presented as a counterbalance to tolerant leftists. If we seek national unity based on the lowest common ethical denominator, we may end up in a situation where that level falls below the standards enshrined in our constitution and democratic values. That leads to a perverse situation where defending fundamental constitutional and democratic principles—such as condemning racism—somehow becomes not in the national interest. Racial intolerance by a high-ranking government official should be the last straw. The President of the Republic regularly ranks highest in public popularity polls. People are tired of political squabbling and name-calling, and in their disillusionment, they gravitate toward someone who abstains from both. But the fact that the president enjoys such support is also because he takes no stand on anything. I respect his decision not to engage in party squabbles, but he should realize that a moral vacuum does not equal political neutrality. I believe the president does not wish his political legacy to be reduced to an Instagram feed. His popularity is capital that can be used to unite the country around—not at the expense of—European democratic and civilizational values. It’s encouraging that in recent times, even if still very cautiously, he’s begun to do just that. Slovenia will be a modern and successful democracy when its leaders build support not by distancing themselves from moral authority, but by embracing and embodying it.

The claim that the people can never be in opposition is the most concise and precise definition of illiberal populism I know. The key word, of course, is people—in Latin, populus—from which this political technique of seizing and maintaining power also takes its name. A populist is not someone striving to be popular among the people, but rather a politician who unilaterally claims the exclusive right to represent the people. Based on this self-proclaimed exclusivity in recognizing, articulating, and defending national interests, the populist appropriates sole authority over the fate of the state and its citizens. In the name of this right, the populist undermines democratic checks and balances and the rule of law, interferes with the judiciary, denies the legitimacy of political competitors, attacks critical media, and stifles civil society. Of course, by their own account, none of this is done for personal gain, but in the interest of the people. The populist has their own interpretation of national literature—they alone will pass judgment on the people, as Slovenian author Ivan Cankar might be paraphrased. In addition to subordinating democratic institutions, an illiberal populist must also secure adequate public support. Unlike dictatorships, which dispense with elections entirely, or authoritarian regimes where results are known in advance, illiberal democracies still technically conduct elections, giving voters the theoretical right to express their will. For any politician, elections are stressful; for the populist, they are an existential battle. A democratic politician—regardless of ideology—can lose, go into opposition, and prepare for the next contest. A populist cannot afford to lose, because they claim to be the people, and the people cannot be in opposition. Further complicating matters are the integrity issues often woven into the fabric of populist rule. Losing power can open the door to legal scrutiny. Populists also struggle because they typically fail to solve real social challenges. Like in any field, politics without accountability and fair competition will not produce miracles. Moreover, the belief that they alone possess the right to manage the state does not, diplomatically put, foster effective defense against conflicts of interest. In normal circumstances, one would expect voters not to reward such politicians. Populists try to solve this by blaming others, but every election carries risk. The more cunning illiberal populists—especially in countries with weaker democratic traditions and immune systems—find ways to ensure that the people never vote against themselves. They achieve this not only by undermining democratic institutions, but through polarization, incitement, intimidation, manipulation, and lies. In populism, politics is not a competition of ideas—it’s just a fight, in which any criticism of the leader is branded as national betrayal. Since most of their ideas cannot withstand rational scrutiny, populists reject reason and facts, and conspiracy theories become gospel. Populism is not about supporting ideas—it’s about following a leader. It is fueled by emotion, not reason. Some hope that populism will eventually burn itself out, that people will realize they’re being led off a cliff. But that’s as naïve as thinking that sobriety will spontaneously win out in the middle of a drunken party. By the time reality sets in—head in the toilet, raging hangover, blurry memories, and searing shame—it’s often too late. Until it hits bottom, populism often wins elections, even outperforming more reasonable political rivals. Trouble begins when it loses, as it did recently in the United States. Since the people cannot lose—despite receiving fewer votes—even mathematics must be branded an enemy of the people. This is the heart of the Doctrine of Stolen Elections, which recognizes only one kind of vote as legitimate: their own. This view is not just undemocratic—it’s illogical. But populism routinely refuses to bow to decency and reason. Any five-year-old understands why Trump was ahead at first and Biden later overtook him. But for those consumed by emotion and blind faith, facts only get in the way. If the populist wins, it’s a celebration of democracy. If they lose, then the election is—by default—stolen, because, as we’ve established, the people cannot be in opposition. Demands for evidence of fraud don’t matter; the only proof needed is that their opponent won. When the president of the Slovenian Democratic Party tweeted an enthusiastic congratulation to the big orange leader across the ocean immediately after polls closed, it sparked mockery at home and abroad. There’s nothing inherently wrong with hoping for a like-minded leader to win in a country as important as the U.S., but it is remarkable when a seasoned politician congratulates someone before the results are in. Now, many chuckle smugly at what they see as a premature emotional outburst. Perhaps rightly so. The tweet frenzy created a monumental reputational self-injury, which—given the tweeter’s position—does not harm only the author. But on the other hand, Trump’s loss is not entirely bad news for his ideological followers. The Doctrine of Stolen Elections is not useful as a theoretical concept—it requires practical implementation, and that can only happen after a loss. The outcry, lawsuits, lies, and agitation in the U.S. likely won’t change the result. But the episode shows that if Americans can do it, so can others. Trump’s tantrums are a test run and possible beginning of the normalization of the Doctrine of Stolen Elections. More capable populists—especially in countries with weaker democratic institutions—can implement this tactic more effectively than the orange loser ever could. For those who don’t want people’s democracy, but democracy for the people, the message from the recent U.S. election is simple: Use your vote. Every time. All of you.
Death in front of the School

On the afternoon of Friday, September 16, a 47-year-old teacher, Samuel Paty, was gruesomely murdered near the secondary school in a Paris suburb where he taught history and geography. He was beheaded with a kitchen knife by Abdullakh Anzorov, an 18-year-old Chechen born in Russia who had lived in France since the age of six. According to the killer’s posts on social media, the motive for the murder was the teacher’s lesson on freedom of speech, during which he had shown students caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad. France is in shock. Although this was far from an isolated incident in a country that has suffered numerous terrorist attacks in recent years—resulting in more than 200 deaths—the public has perhaps never been more deeply shaken than by this murder of a teacher. France is horrified not only by the brutality of the crime and the loss of life but also because this was an attack on an institution. The Éducation nationale, which raises generations of youth in the values of the Republic, is one of the most important pillars of French statehood. Immediately after the attack, many voices demanded stronger, swifter, and more effective measures against the growing threat of Islamist extremism in France. And in my opinion, they are absolutely right. There is little need to prove that the spread of militant Islamist ideology represents a grave threat in France. We only need to recall the attacks on the offices of the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo, the massacre at the Bataclan concert hall in Paris, the truck attack on the promenade in Nice, and the shootings at a Jewish grocery store in Paris and a Jewish elementary school in Toulouse. Even Strasbourg, where I live, was struck less than two years ago when a gunman killed five people at the city’s Christmas market. The fight against terrorism must include repressive measures, intelligence and police work, criminal prosecution, and, when necessary, the use of force. But in doing so, there is no need or justification for stepping outside the legal and human rights frameworks set by national and international standards. The European Convention on Human Rights allows for robust and effective responses to terrorism. When political freedoms, human rights, or democratic standards are portrayed as obstacles to effectively addressing terrorist, criminal, health, or other threats, it is often an attempt to cover up incompetence or questionable political maneuvering—or both. Some voices in the French public, while equally horrified by the bloody crime, argue that repression alone won’t defeat the threat of Islamist extremism. And they too are absolutely right. Extremism cannot be overcome without addressing why ideological violence appeals to some young people in the French suburbs. What draws them into a vortex of blindness, indoctrination, and hatred? If we don’t understand the why, we won’t know how to respond. In public debate, these two approaches are often seen as oppositional—competing or even conflicting strategies. Some refuse to consider why someone would choose violence; others believe the problem can be solved without increased security and repression. In reality, both approaches are necessary. A purely repressive strategy is doomed to fail. But it is equally naive—and dangerous—to think terrorism can be overcome solely by empathizing with human suffering. When Abdullakh Anzorov grabbed that kitchen knife on Friday, no kind word or offer to listen to his grievances could have stopped him. The French government is now rightly channeling all its efforts into investigating and preventing similar acts. This includes targeting individuals showing signs of radicalization or spreading radical ideologies and inciting violence—especially on social media, but also in certain prayer rooms and mosques. These actions enjoy broad public support, but some ask why they weren’t taken earlier. After the Charlie Hebdo attacks and the Bataclan massacre, there were already many criticisms of how security services handled known suspects who had long been on the radar of intelligence agencies. Now, in the wake of Paty’s murder, political leaders face intense public pressure, and every day brings forceful speeches and announcements: closures of prayer rooms, disbanding of associations and sports clubs, and more. The risk is that, in the rush to make up for past failures and avoid further criticism, the net may be cast too wide, impacting people who have nothing to do with extremism. This reinforces a sense among some communities that the state is stigmatizing and blaming them for crimes of which they, too, are victims. Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin recently criticized the sale of "communitarian" food products—meaning halal and kosher—in French supermarkets. “Communitarianism” in France refers to prioritizing group identity over national unity. His statement sparked public backlash and ridicule: one Green Party MP with Italian roots tweeted a photo of shelves full of Barilla pasta, joking that he too couldn’t resist communitarian cuisine. On the international front, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan chimed in by questioning the mental health of his French counterpart—a remark that certainly does not contribute to a calm and reasoned debate. The fact remains: Islamist extremism threatens all French citizens, including Muslims. Muslim communities are natural and essential allies in the fight against extremism. Yet many feel that, in the state’s response to terrorism, shortcuts and generalizations are being made. After the recent knife attack near the former offices of Charlie Hebdo, media outlets initially reported two suspects, largely because among the bloodied victims who had chased the attacker was a man who looked North African. A poll published last year revealed that 42% of Muslims living in France had experienced discrimination—most commonly in encounters with police or while seeking jobs or housing. Many people of former colonial descent live in so-called sensitive urban zones, identified in bureaucratic language by a 1996 law as “densely populated areas with degraded housing and high imbalance between population and employment opportunities.” Of course, none of this justifies hatred and violence. But it is a fact that a portion of the young generation in France is turning against the country. A few among them choose the most perverse, violent, and bloody—and above all false—interpretation of Islam, one that has nothing to do with the Qur’an. The internal conflict between a religion of hatred and the teachings of the Prophet hardly troubles them, because the decision to embrace extremism is, in most cases, not religiously motivated. The psychological blueprint of recruitment is similar to that used by street gangs in the U.S. To the extremist, it feels like rebellion against a society that shows them no respect, no opportunity, no acceptance. The suburbs of France are reservoirs of frustration and rage, which make the work of Islamist preachers all the easier. In Strasbourg just weeks ago, a girl was beaten for wearing a skirt deemed “too short.” This is a rising tide of hatred and violence that must be stopped—with all the power and tools available to the state to protect its citizens. But the methods used must be grounded in the very values that Samuel Paty taught in his classroom—and for which he gave his life. Liberty, equality, fraternity: the Enlightenment ideals inscribed in the French constitution since 1848. These are the very values that Islamist extremists fight against. And in the long term, upholding these values for all citizens, not just some, will prove more effective than repression. These are the values that can unite the nation against hatred and help defeat those who feed on it.

In the early years of my childhood, we lived in the Italian city of Trieste because of my father’s job. My father, an extravagantly sociable man, found many friends in the Slovene minority community in and around Trieste—but two of them stood out, as they couldn’t have been more different. Drago was from the countryside, Mitja from the city. One a bricklayer, the other a lawyer. Mitja drove luxury cars and wore a gold watch. Drago had a battered Fiat pickup and hands like shovels—wrists that wouldn’t accommodate a Rolex even if he could afford or wanted one. Drago voted for the Italian Communist Party (PCI). Mitja came from a traditional, conservative, affluent Catholic background, which also shaped his worldview. Drago had fought with the partisans during the war; Mitja had, or so I heard—since he rarely spoke of it—briefly joined the Chetniks, the royalist forces, at the beginning of the war. Despite their many differences, they shared certain traits that kept them meeting up, having a drink or two, debating, teasing each other—and often arguing. Drago and Mitja were both proud Slovenians who had endured and survived the tragic and brutal experience of Italian fascism. This also drove them to take up arms at the outbreak of the war, believing they were fighting for their people. Two choices, two directions taken by two young men, shaped by their upbringing, values, worldview, and social environment. After the war, they agreed politically on almost nothing, but they never argued about who had won the war or who had been on the right side. What united them was their rejection of hatred and evil. What united them was anti-fascism. Mitja had not joined the royal army to serve the Italian or German occupiers, but because he believed that with the army loyal to the king in exile in London, he could fight against them. His anti-fascism had begun before the war, and the confusing, painful wartime experience only tested and ultimately deepened it. Their acquaintance and friendship were, of course, possible because they lived in the West. For people like Mitja, there was neither understanding nor space on the Yugoslav side of the border. Many with similar experiences did not survive the end of the war and never returned home. Drago was more conciliatory toward the neighbouring country and its regime, overlooking the fact that in Yugoslavia, there was no luxury of supporting the communist party as merely one of several options in a pluralistic election. On that side of the border, there was no choice. People supported the communist regime mostly because they were forced to, or because they benefited from it. The romantic revolutionaries in Western Europe didn’t see—or didn’t want to see—how grey, suffocating, and unromantic life really was behind the ideological wall. Drago and Mitja were, each in their own way, living reminders of a time and people now gone. Drago may have been the last—and perhaps only—person I met who truly believed in communism. And even with him, I’m not entirely sure it was ideological. More than anything, Drago was an anti-fascist. In Italian politics, he simply chose the side he felt was most resolute and effective in standing up to fascism. Today, communists in Italy, at least as a political force, no longer exist. In Slovenia, there never really were many to begin with. The idealists were soon disappointed; what remained were party bureaucrats, opportunists, and those who had no other options. Communism in Slovenia today exists mostly in the rhetoric of political converts who publicly denounce their own past to distract from what they once did—and what they do now. Mitja’s views were at the opposite end of the political spectrum. He was conservative—even fiscally conservative, as Americans would say—religious, traditional in his views on social issues. He was, in a word, a right-winger. Yet I’m convinced he would never have allied himself with the people who today wear right-wing feathers with pride. He belonged to a generation of European conservatives shaped by the likes of De Gasperi, Adenauer, Schuman, even Churchill—Christian democrats and conservatives who, in response to the devastation wrought by Nazism and fascism, built the European institutional, economic, and political model. That societal system was based on pluralistic democracy, an executive branch under democratic control and limits, political freedoms, the rule of law, human rights, social and international solidarity, and humanism. If that description seems too long-winded, we can just call it liberal democracy. And this is not just one of many political ideologies or an alternative to social democracy or Christian or conservative democracy, as some now claim. Liberal democracy is not the same as liberalism. It is a political system, a societal model, a civilizational arc that includes all democratic political streams—that is, those that, regardless of ideological colour, accept and uphold fundamental democratic values. The philosophical foundations of liberal democracy—chief among them, the protection of individual rights from arbitrary state power—were laid during the Enlightenment. The fact that today some present liberal democracy as just one option among many, and even seek to dismantle it in the name of conservative, traditional, or even Christian values, is a huge fraud and a slap in the face to the conservatives and Christian democrats who were the architects of Europe’s post-war liberal democratic system. That same system underpins the European Convention on Human Rights—written by British lawyers—as well as the Slovenian constitution. Anyone who has a problem with liberal democracy has a problem with our constitutional order. The alternative to liberal democracy is elections without freedom. Regardless of the ideology in whose name democratic controls, the rule of law, individual rights, and minority protections are dismantled—the outcome is always the same. What’s being sold today as the “right” in much of the world is first and foremost an embarrassment for true conservatives. The founding fathers of post-war Europe would be appalled at how their conservative, Christian-democratic, right-wing legacy has been hijacked by those who are tearing down Europe’s civilizational model in the name of values diametrically opposed to those it was built on. What would my father’s two friends think of the world today? I don’t know—but I can imagine. Drago never hid his political beliefs; they were never in question. Yet in today’s sleight-of-hand reversal of positions, newly minted right-wingers—those knights of cognitive dissonance—would likely label even his old companion Mitja an extreme leftist. Simply because he was an anti-fascist and a humanist. They’d probably call them stronzi. And have another glass of Drago’s orange tinted homegrown wine.

"Dare to know. Have the courage to use your own understanding." Immanuel Kant The Middle Ages lasted, roughly speaking, about a thousand years—from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 to the fall of Constantinople in 1453. When darkness falls properly, the night can be very long. It's no surprise that humanity needed some time to get back on its feet. First came the Renaissance, and with it da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael, Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio. Without art and artists, we might have waited much longer for a rebirth after five centuries of darkness. The next great civilizational milestone came at the end of the 18th century, when Isaac Newton, with Principia Mathematica, and John Locke, with An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, laid the scientific and philosophical foundations of the Enlightenment. Its essence is best captured in the quote above from Kant—originally from Horace: "Dare to know." The Enlightenment marked humanity's leap from a mass that merely believes into a civilization that dares and wants to understand. Where we are today, as a society, 230 years later, is aptly illustrated by a recent statement from Donald Trump, who said during a discussion on coronavirus that the solution lay in "herd mentality." He likely meant herd immunity, but this Freudian slip says a lot about his views on social order. A herd believes but does not think. A herd doesn't know, dares not, and doesn’t want to know. A herd follows and doesn't question. In this time of very serious global challenges—from climate change to the COVID-19 pandemic—we’re witnessing increasingly widespread attacks on knowledge, expertise, science, and facts. This phenomenon is often attributed to the rise of fake news, driven by the internet and social media. That’s true—to a point. Conspiracy theories have long fuelled and fertilized a variety of reactionary ideas and ideologies, long before the internet. But it’s certainly true that the internet has created the perfect ecosystem for producing and distributing them. Still, the dynamics of the marketplace of lies are shaped not just by supply—but also by demand. The rejection of knowledge is not merely a result of ignorance or lack of access to facts. People often choose to believe lies. Many want to believe that the Earth is flat, that the virus is a conspiracy orchestrated by Big Pharma and the deep state, secretly run by Soros’s agents and cultural Marxists. Kant and Horace get reinterpreted—courage alone is enough to "know"; facts, knowledge, and reason are just obstacles. The appeal of lies is that they speak to frustrations and fears that truth does not resolve—or even deepens. The motivation for turning away from reason is psychological, born of anger, disappointment, feelings of humiliation, or fear. Rebellion against reason is often framed as rebellion against the elites. It's a hit of adrenaline—momentarily empowering, even if self-destructive. During the Brexit debate, when a respected British economist spoke about the GDP losses Brexit would bring, angry shouts rang out from the audience, suggesting where he could shove his "hoity-toity, expert GDP." Far from being blameless, elites do bear responsibility—but bidding farewell to reason isn’t the best way to fix injustices. The Brexit knot—and similar dilemmas—won’t be untangled without rational and comprehensive approaches to the social, economic, and other conditions that gave people the "courage" to forget reason and jump, often with legitimate grievances, headfirst into an empty pool. "Hatred is always strongest and most violent where there is the least culture." Johann Wolfgang von Goethe If knowledge is in trouble, culture is doing even worse. Today, many people understand culture in ways far removed from Goethe’s idea. We are nowhere close from the ideas of Michelangelo, da Vinci, and Petrarch. Far from the kind of culture the 1954 European Cultural Convention envisioned—as a tool for unity, mutual understanding, and shared values. Today, for many, culture means something else entirely. In the discourse of nationalist populism, culture is not Goethe’s shield against hatred, but quite the opposite: a bundle of prejudice, intolerance, and myths—something for the half-literate defenders of the nation to wear as a uniform and wield as a weapon against those who are different. A “culture” defended with hate and hostility. A culture without art or artists. Culture as a tool for cultural warfare. Culture for a cultural revolution. “We find ourselves in a dark place, and a little more knowledge might light our way." Yoda About a year ago, Gerfried Stocker, longtime director of Ars Electronica in Linz, Austria, gave the opening address at a conference of European education ministers in Paris. The theme was education for the digital society. Many of the ministers were surprised not just by his wrinkled shirt and ponytail. In Stocker’s view, preparing for a high-tech future rests on four pillars: 1. Understanding the digital world’s basic structures—essential for making sense of technology. 2. Social skills, emotional intelligence, and humanistic values—so we can contribute meaningfully to society. 3. Knowledge and critical thinking—as shields against manipulation. 4. Creativity—nurtured especially through art, which fuels imagination, innovation, economic success, competitiveness, and social progress. At first glance, it’s clear we’re not preparing for the future very well. We all depend on black-box technologies we don’t understand. Instead of people controlling technology, technology is increasingly used to control people. An ethic of moral relativism—and the doctrine that all opinions are equally valid, regardless of substance—has led the public to equate basic democratic and civilizational values with their opposites. As a society, we are rejecting openness and solidarity, and building our future on intolerance and selfishness. Critical thinking, which should act as an immune system against lies and manipulation, has been replaced by herd mentality. Knowledge annoys us. We prefer conspiracy theories over reason. Art—an expression and engine of creativity, inventiveness, self-reflection, critique, courage, exploration, and freedom—has become an inconvenience. To many who claim to worry about Europe’s civilization and national culture being under threat, culture is a waste of money. Artists, they argue, should go compete on the market for attention and survival, alongside soap operas and pop celebrities. According to the Slovenian Wikipedia—so you don’t say I’m making this up—Enlightenment thinkers advocated freedom of expression, religious criticism, a progressive society, and emphasized reason, science, and the value of human life. More than two centuries later, it seems we’ve grown tired of the light. The values on which modern civilization was built are increasingly annoying us. We are swapping Yoda with his dark nemesis. Welcome to the new era of endarkment. And don’t forget: once the darkness falls completely, the night can last a very long time.
I Won’t Give It Up, I Won’t Give It Up

My heart is like a stone, as the old song goes. In the first weeks of the pandemic, I wrote that we faced a test of our collective and individual responsibility, judgment and solidarity. Today I am increasingly worried that I was right. If, in the first weeks of uncertainty and worry caused by a then unknown virus, there was still hope that people would trust science, expertise, facts and reason, today they share the wisdom and advice of Dr. Werner, head physician, and of Der Bergdoktor Potrč on social networks. The phenomenon of celebrity medicine is, of course, not present only in Slovenia. The Bollywood star Akshay Kumar, for example, swears by drinking cow urine against the coronavirus and a whole host of other health problems. You can’t sink any lower, my dears, at least as far as judgment in a serious health crisis is concerned. And please don’t talk to me about the importance of different opinions. It doesn’t move me, it doesn’t move me. Without knowledge of and respect for facts, the freedom of different opinions is a farce. That is not me saying it, but Hannah Arendt. Nodding along to the musings of amateur epidemiologists is part of the revolt against knowledge and science, which of course began long before this pandemic broke out. Unreason as a revolt against “elites” and conspiracy theories are the thread that connects the “truth” about face masks, vaccines, the deep state and the flatness of our planet. This by no means implies, of course, that experts are infallible or that the public has no right to a critical attitude towards scientists and experts. Not all the responsibility can be laid on the shoulders of the Werners, Kumars and Potrčs. They are merely victims of their own self-confidence and pride, and of our stupidity. It is, however, good to distinguish between assessing scientific claims and achievements, which is probably still best left to peer review by other scientists, and assessing responsibility, consistency, integrity and communication, on which the lay public of course has every right to take a position and to judge critically. Off the top of my head, I would divide the experts’ missteps during the pandemic into three groups. In the first are the glory-seekers and opportunists. There are many doctors in the world, and in large numbers there are always a few who do not do their profession much credit. Small minds who, in the shock and fear of a new virus, sensed an opportunity for self-promotion. In the first weeks of the crisis, a white coat, a stethoscope around the neck and the most extravagant statement possible, ranging from “it’s nothing” to “we’re all going to die,” were enough for a flash of local or even global attention. They were irresponsibly helped not only by social networks, which long ago turned into a distribution system for the informational equivalent of cow urine, but also by traditional media, which in their cutthroat battle for clicks are often prepared to publish anything and anyone. If it weren’t for Covid-19, I would never have known how many “renowned experts from renowned universities” exist in this world. In the second group are the know-it-alls. I don’t in principle attribute bad intentions to them, but that does not mean that excessive and unfounded self-confidence cannot do more harm than good. Remember the inflation of overnight graphs and projections, which devalued trust in the expert methods we so badly need to overcome this health threat. On masks, too, we heard all sorts of things from experts, from the claim that no one except health workers needs them to the claim that we mustn’t go even to the mailbox without one. Such changes in expert opinions and instructions, which in the uncertainty of facing the unknown are easy and possible to understand and accept, turn, when combined with excessive self-confidence that the public may experience as arrogant, into a gift to distributors of conspiracy theories and other fighters against reason. People are not sheep, at least not all of them, and frankness, including about doubts, risks and possible mistakes, can do much more for public trust than insisting on infallibility and false self-confidence. In the third group are the pliable. Experts who are prepared to subordinate their expertise to the political interests of the authorities, out of their own ambition or lack of backbone. Perhaps the most opportunities for his medical advisers and the relevant agencies to violate the Hippocratic oath are offered by President Trump. It is quite distressing to watch their wriggling, their silence, or even their loud and formal support for his desperate search for a cure for his political problems, from drinking disinfectant to other magic medicines and therapies. Unfortunately, one Dr. Fauci does not make a spring. The greatest danger is, of course, still ahead of us. If political pressure prevails over expertise and responsibility in the vaccine approval process, things look very bad for us. Not only does it increase the risk of ineffective or even dangerous vaccines; very probably, many who otherwise do not believe stories about international conspiracies of pharmaceutical companies will hesitate to be vaccinated with politically approved substances. He who laughs last may be an anti-vaxxer. After the experts, second in this random order is the responsibility of the authorities. First, there is the temptation to use the health crisis for political purposes. How this can be done in complicity with experts I have already described. Another vivid example is the plan to attribute the colossal damage that the ideological project of breaking away from Brussels will inflict on the British economy and society to the colossal damage caused by Covid-19. That neither the economy nor society will be able to withstand the double blow evidently does not interest those responsible. As long as they are not to blame. Indecent attempts to use the pandemic to settle scores with the previous government were also present in Slovenia and are now coming back at those in power like a boomerang. The equivalent of the inappropriateness of such behavior is the revolt against any measures to contain the epidemic simply because we don’t like those in power, as certain village eccentrics clamor on the internet. The way the authorities communicate with the public is also very important. Condescension, arrogance, intimidation and underestimation often do not make the best impression on people. How we are doing in this respect in Slovenia, judge for yourselves. The most crucial thing for success in the fight against the virus is public trust. And there is no faster and more devastating way to lose trust than attempts to use the crisis to undermine democracy and line one’s own pockets. Finally, my friends, let us hold up a mirror to ourselves. In facing a crisis, it is easiest to point the finger at others, but the time we are living through is also, and above all, a test of our individual responsibility, rationality and solidarity. The revolt against masks and swearing by all kinds of conspiracy theories is not only a defeat for reason but also a defeat for solidarity. I am neither a doctor nor an epidemiologist, so I offer no medical assessments or claims. I experience this epidemic as a human being, as a citizen. I live in a country that a few days ago passed the threshold of ten thousand new cases a day. I wear a mask even when I go to the bins. If it can help ensure that we don’t shut down public life again, and above all if it helps protect the health of the most vulnerable, the people in care homes, I am prepared to wear it at night too. Dr. Ihan has explained why the mask is important. It is not an intrusion on our personal freedom but, at this moment, the most important and effective way of defending that freedom and public health. Covid-19 is not ordinary flu. I don’t say this as an expert but as a human being. I have colleagues who fell ill and barely survived. I have colleagues who lost parents and other relatives. I also have friends who lost their jobs and incomes because of the epidemic. All these people need not only our responsibility but also our reason, and above all our solidarity. We will sooner or later defeat the virus, but if in this fight we lose fundamental civilizational values, all we will have left is cow urine. As Dr. Werner would say, bye-byeee.

When U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo visited Slovenia less than three weeks ago, a stir erupted in parts of the public over reports that a workers’ paradise themed fresco by painter Slavko Pengov from 1947 had been covered up during the official reception at Vila Bled. To add flavor to the story, it emerged that the fresco’s author was the grandfather of Slovenia’s current foreign minister, Anže Logar. “The host, groveling before Trump’s envoy, denied not only his homeland but even his family,” roared some media outlets and social media users. The outrage was so intense it persisted even after it was clarified that the fresco is often covered anyway, as it tends to offend the refined tastes of those hosting weddings there—and, moreover, the reception was held on the terrace, not in the hall adorned by Anže’s grandfather. The incident is a perfect illustration of how disregarding facts that don’t align with one’s beliefs is not confined to just one part of an increasingly divided and agitated Slovenian public. You might say: “Sure, but what about them? They’re far more aggressive, offensive, misleading, and dishonest.” Maybe so—but that doesn’t absolve anyone from responsibility for their own words and actions. You can’t fight misinformation with slightly less misinformation. You can’t combat insults and lies by measuring yourself against the professional ethics of populist “media” or the tweets of basement-dwelling bots. Whataboutism—the tactic of pointing fingers at the other side—is a well-proven and highly effective weapon of populism. You know the drill: “They’re harassing a poor woman over a few hundred euros, but what about Ljubljana Mayor Janković and his millions?” Whataboutism serves populism whether it is wielded by populists or used against them. In the first case, it’s a distraction from wrongdoing; in the second, it legitimizes such behavior. The curtain controversy at Vila Bled is a good example of how zeal and neglecting facts can backfire—shooting oneself in the foot. There were plenty of legitimate concerns that afternoon at Vila Bled that warranted public scrutiny and criticism. Instead, most attention was drawn to a non-existent scandal. I see defending the dignity of public debate and political culture in much the same way I see patriotism: true patriotism is measured by critical engagement with one’s own country, not by fervent derision of others. This is not to say we shouldn’t respond to wrongdoing, mistakes, insults, authoritarianism, delusions, deception, and lies. But the effectiveness of that response depends on a principled stance that refuses the Machiavellian notion of fighting fire with fire. That’s the message of Michelle Obama’s famous line: “When they go low, we go high.” It’s not about turning the other cheek, or believing that being a moral nation-parent means loving all children equally—including those making neighborhood pets disappear. It’s simply the fact that in standing up to attacks on human dignity, reason, integrity, and tolerance, we must not abandon those same values ourselves. Whataboutism is seductive because it often builds on genuine, justified outrage—and on a very human tendency to judge others more harshly than ourselves. It easily leads us into situations where we, too, become hypocritical and inconsistent. Pointing out that “they” behave the same way provide a dubious comfort. They, by default, don’t seem to have a problem with that. In that light, I’ve spent weeks wondering why some critics of the Prime Minister Janša feel the need to so fiercely defend the legitimacy of the slogan “Death to Janšism.” This is not a legal matter—the suggestion that such a phrase deserves criminal prosecution is politically contrived. But when it comes to defending dignity, reason, and political culture, our standards cannot be measured solely by criminal thresholds. Having the right to say something does not mean you are right in saying it. "Death" is a word that causes visceral discomfort. I don’t know what its proponents are trying to express that “Down with Janšism” wouldn’t convey—but it’s very clear who benefits most from the provocation. I feel a similar unease watching mutual accusations over noncompliance with public health measures and social distancing at mass gatherings. One side blames the cyclists; the cyclists blame the kneeling, maskless pilgrims at the church of St.Mary in Brezje. And round we go. It’s idiotic, unconvincing, and dangerous. In this case, a mask isn’t just a safety imperative—it’s a matter of credibility. Put it up or shut up, as an American paraphrase might go. And then there’s the pinnacle of inappropriateness: insults and disqualifications based on personal traits. Again, while such behavior may be more common on one side of Slovenia’s tribal polarization, that doesn’t excuse those who claim to uphold human dignity from being held accountable themselves. Personal insults are not only ethically wrong; they often deflect attention from the real issues. I, for one, am sick of the snickering over photos of the current State Secretary for National Security. Of all the criticisms that can be made about his work, his appearance is the least relevant. Likewise, I don’t understand why so many people fixate on the body weight of Slovenia’s chief libertarian figure rather than the flaws in his laissez-faire ideology, which demands absolute freedom—but only for himself and like-minded individuals. And finally: When a young party activist publicly calls for Breivik to come to Slovenia, is the most important thing really how he looks? Do you need to be manly, attractive, and a “ladies’ man” to be allowed—legitimately, as a youth member of the ruling party—to idolize someone who murdered 77 people in the name of fighting “cultural Marxism”? Is that a provocative question? No—just a logical consequence of criticizing fascism based on appearances. While most of these outbursts come from anonymous commentators, public figures aren’t blameless. The remark that the current Minister of Agriculture would “fly out like a whore from a dance” received a muted reaction—even among those usually highly sensitive to misogyny. Perhaps because it came from “one of ours”? Similarly, a former prime minister—who now rightly condemns vile attacks against his party and the opposition—would have been even more convincing had he shown some of that outrage earlier, when his own state secretary was peddling dehumanizing slurs about migrants. Whataboutism is dangerous for democracy because it turns politics into a race to the bottom. Inconsistency in upholding one’s own principles leads to polarization that’s not ideological or substantive, but tribal. In this emperor’s-new-clothes version of politics, where values are absent, all that’s left is personal interest. Tribalism—"us vs. them"—forces people to align blindly and uncritically with one camp or another, or to reject all sides in disillusionment. "Everyone-is-the-same-ism" is the logical result of whataboutism. And while it may be emotionally understandable, especially amid today’s political farce, it’s ultimately an evasion and a defeat, not a solution. In a society where all politicians are seen as the same, democracy simply does not work. And that’s the end goal and triumph of those who know how—and are willing—to be the most corrupt, ruthless, and deliberate in their sameness.

Summer holidays offer a chance for deeper and more analytical reflections on the world around us. For the past few days, I’ve been turning over in my head the question of why so many politicians seem obsessed with balls. Recently, in the window of a gallery in Lyon, France, I saw a poster of former French President Jacques Chirac with a cigarette in his mouth and one of his famous quotes: "These days we transplant kidneys, hands, and hearts—everything except balls, because we lack donors." Chirac certainly had balls—or at least the literal kind—which he happily deployed in a string of extramarital affairs that his wife Bernadette bore with silent suffering. Not that her stoicism excuses his infidelity. Madame Chirac simply assumed the traditional role of many French first ladies who, in the name of the Republic and national interest, discreetly ignored their husbands’ indiscretions. These affairs were, at least until Macron, so common they might as well have been added to the official motto of the French Republic. Liberty, equality, fraternity—and have you seen the President’s mistress? Presidents like Mitterrand and Hollande had lovers. With Sarkozy, it remains unclear whether the fidelity issues were his, hers, or mutual. The love lives of Élysée Palace residents were long kept out of the public eye by both the press—which largely ignored these open secrets—and the public, which, until recently, was surprisingly tolerant of their leaders’ bedroom adventures. Not anymore. The French have stopped pretending. The dam broke when Chirac’s former driver told reporters the president was known among staff as “Monsieur Three Minutes, including the shower.” Photos of Hollande zipping through Paris at night on a scooter wearing a motorcycle helmet later made headlines even in serious media. Knowledge of how to sneak over the Élysée fence, so to speak, was passed down from generation to generation. When Hollande started seeing one of his penultimate girlfriends, Valérie Trierweiler, he reportedly sought logistical advice from one of Chirac’s old flames. When it comes to sex, it seems even the greatest political divides can be bridged. Not left, not right—just back and forth. These days, the French president can no longer count on the public’s silence when it comes to extracurricular activities—although, to be fair, Macron doesn’t appear to need such discretion. Jacques Chirac was undeniably a president of the old school—but not someone I’d cite as a role model when it comes to marital fidelity or his treatment of women. This isn’t about moralizing the Chirac-Bernadette dynamic; it’s more about the fact that, despite all his Gallic charm, Chirac often courted women from a position of power—and that, to put it mildly, is neither nice nor right. Chirac liked to project political “balls” as well. Sometimes it was charming, other times less so—depending on the context and one’s political leanings. Of political opponents he didn’t respect, he liked to say: “If one of my balls is touched, the other doesn’t even twitch.” Yes, once again—we’re talking about balls. His macho politics also came through in his belief that leaders are there to lead and that power isn’t something to be shared. Many of his political heirs, in France and beyond, still try to emulate this attitude—though without the French charm. Chirac also showed political backbone in more admirable ways—for instance, during the Iraq War, when he was one of the few Western leaders to resist American pressure for military intervention against Saddam Hussein. In Slovenian ears—and not only ours—his contemptuous remark about the Vilnius letter still resonates: “They missed a good opportunity to shut up.” Chirac passed away last year, so unfortunately, we can’t count on him to repeat the favor. Balls, as we know, were also a recurring theme for former U.S. President Bill Clinton. A quote attributed to him has stuck in my mind: “It takes balls, not public opinion,” supposedly meaning that politics sometimes demands the courage to make unpopular decisions. Whether he actually said it or not, we know Clinton had his own issues with his literal testicles—thanks to a scandal inscribed not just in the annals of history, but on the blue dress of a former White House intern. The current resident of the White House, despite his small hands, is also eager to prove he’s got, you know, big ones. His idea of courtship was summed up by the infamous quote: “Grab them by the pussy. They let you do it.” Classy! Never mind that these encounters were often transactional—and that his crotch-grabbing ways have cost him dearly, financially and otherwise. Lies may have short fingers, but a fat wallet can make up for it. Given all this, one might reasonably suggest that politics would be vastly improved with fewer balls. Especially the literal kind. Now, I’m not a fan of stereotyping and I don’t believe women are inherently better politicians just because they’re women. But the fact remains that women are severely underrepresented in politics. That means we’re systematically drawing our political leadership from only half of the potential talent pool. Increasing the number of women in leadership isn’t just a matter of gender equality—it’s a prerequisite for better politics. Simple math. And no, you won’t convince me otherwise by pointing out the occasional female politician who’s incompetent or unfit. One confused swallow does not make a spring. We could also use fewer metaphorical balls in politics. Decisions like Chirac’s stand on the Iraq War didn’t require macho posturing, just determination, dignity, expertise, and principles—qualities that are desperately needed in politics today. Instead, we’re flooded with loudmouths, trolls, and politicians whose masculinity is defined by insults, vulgarity, aggression, and utter contempt for civilized, democratic norms. Whether that proves they have balls, I leave to your judgment. Personally, I’d describe them using an adjacent body part.

On May 11, 2011, 47 senior representatives of the Council of Europe’s member states gathered in the magnificent Beylerbeyi Palace on the shores of the Bosphorus, which today is part of the Kempinski hotel chain. The Slovenian delegation was led by the then foreign minister, Samuel Žbogar. At a ceremony, 13 states signed a new convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. This international legal instrument, today better known as the Istanbul Convention, was the result of many years of effort by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, civil society and professional organizations, and some governments, which demanded a common and effective international response to violence against women, a problem that was, and still is, widespread in every country and every social class. Slovenia did not sign the convention in Istanbul but a few months later, and it is among the 34 member states that have so far also ratified it. Such a high number of accessions to a convention in such a short time is rare in the practice of international organizations. A little under a decade ago, there was consensus on the need for an effective common response to violence against women and domestic violence; no one politicized these topics or called them into question. Today, unfortunately, it is different. The Beylerbeyi Palace, where the senior diplomats signed the Istanbul Convention, was built in 1865 to designs by the Armenian architect Sarkis Balyan for Sultan Abdulaziz, the first supreme ruler of the Ottoman Empire to visit the West. Among other things, Abdulaziz modernized the state’s administration, introduced public schooling on the French model, founded the university in Istanbul and was responsible for the first civil code in the Ottoman Empire. He was a lover of literature and a composer of classical music. The signing of the first international convention against violence against women in the palace of a reformist sultan was full of symbolism. But Abdulaziz was better at classical music than at economics. He piled up debts for the empire, so in June 1876 he was deposed by his own ministers. A few days later he asked for scissors to trim his beard, but evidently had other plans for them, as he was soon found dead in a pool of blood. Supposedly it was suicide, although rumors still circulate that the sultan was murdered. I admit that at the time, leafing through the hotel brochure, I did not think of an analogy between the tragic fate of the reformist sultan and the somewhat less tragic, but still unpleasant, fate of some signatories of the Istanbul Convention, who are today being dragged through the mud in their countries as enemies of traditional values. Progressive social policies and deeds are often poorly understood and even more poorly rewarded. To understand how, in a few years, we went from progressive consensus to populist revolt on combating violence against women, three questions need to be answered. Why the convention? What solutions does it bring to victims of violence against women and domestic violence? And what is it that so irritates the defenders of “traditional values” in some countries that they start shouting and stamping their feet at every mention of the Istanbul Convention? First, some statistics. According to the World Health Organization, by now almost as notorious, more than a third of women worldwide are exposed to physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. In most cases it is violence by an intimate partner, who, among other things, commits almost 40 percent of all murders of female victims. The fact that these are global statistics is no consolation to victims of violence in Europe. A 2014 survey by the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights reveals a tragic picture for many European women. Eight percent of them had been victims of violence in the twelve months before the survey, and the statistics on the frequency of violence against women after the age of 15 are identical to the WHO data. More than one in three women in Europe is exposed to physical or sexual violence in her lifetime. This violence has very broad and destructive consequences, first of course for the direct victims, but also for children, families and society as a whole. The second important fact highlighted by both institutions is that this violence is structural in nature, since it stems from the general, often subordinate position of women and gender-based discrimination in all areas of social life. The data on the prevalence of violence against women are estimates based on surveys and interviews with victims, not official numbers of cases reported to the authorities. Many victims of violence do not decide to report it—out of fear of the consequences for themselves and their families, because of various pressures, or simply because they do not trust the police and prosecutors. In defense of its announcement that it is withdrawing from the Istanbul Convention, the Polish government recently claimed that the number of reports of violence in Poland is extremely low.
