Of course I want to believe that Poland is an exception in which the number of reported attacks is not just the tip of the iceberg of violence, but one cannot rule out that the low number of reports is itself an indication that Poland needs the Istanbul Convention very much indeed. So what do the Council of Europe and the Istanbul Convention bring to solving these tragic problems? Certainly the most important fact is that it is an international legal standard that commits signatories not to treat violence against women and domestic violence as a private matter, and the fight against it not merely as a matter of their goodwill and current interests and priorities. By acceding to the convention, the proper and effective prevention of violence, assistance to victims and prosecution of perpetrators become the subject of legal obligations. In a little under a decade, the convention has brought a series of positive changes in many signatory states, from new legislation and more appropriate forms of help for victims of violence to training programs for police officers, social workers, health and other staff. One of the more important goals is changing the definition of sexual harassment and rape, which must be based on the absence of consent, not merely on evidence of the use of force, and therefore cannot be relativized or excused by “patterns that somehow cause certain things.” Although the Istanbul Convention does not refer only to violence against women, since men are also among the victims of domestic violence, it is based on the fact that in the vast majority of cases the victims are women. Not by chance, but because they are women. Since violence against women is largely structural in nature, the problem cannot be solved without confronting the wider issues of gender inequality. This inequality, of course, is not a consequence of biological differences between the sexes but above all of social constructs, prejudices, traditions and stereotypes that put women in a subordinate position. Article 3 therefore provides that, in the convention, the term “gender” means the socially constructed roles, behaviors, activities and attributes that a given society considers appropriate for women and men. And the first paragraph of Article 12 obliges the parties to take “the necessary measures to promote changes in the social and cultural patterns of behavior of women and men with a view to eradicating prejudices, customs, traditions and all other practices which are based on the idea of the inferiority of women or on stereotyped roles for women and men.” And this is what has most enraged the supporters of “traditional values,” among which they evidently also count the inferiority of women. The arguments behind the attacks on the Istanbul Convention are a confused and illogical jumble of misinterpretations and brazen untruths, which, however, in today’s times, when lies have ever longer legs, are often effective. With the claim that the convention erases the biological differences between the sexes and thus opens the way for the promotion of homosexuality, right-wing populism tries to kill two birds with one stone: to smear both the commitment to women’s equality and the efforts for the rights of the LGBT population. The latter is, of course, an obligation stemming from the European Convention on Human Rights, but it should be stressed that, as regards the rights of sexual minorities, the Istanbul Convention introduces no new standards or obligations. What irritates the champions of “traditional values” most, however, is the term “gender,” which in their view denies the biological differences between the sexes. That is, of course, not true. All the convention says is that violence against women does not stem from biological differences between the sexes but from social constructs that often push women into a subordinate position. Just as violence against people suffering from albinism in some parts of Africa cannot be explained by their lack of pigment, but solely by the “prejudices, customs, traditions and all other practices” based on the belief that body parts of murdered albinos have miraculous healing powers, so violence against women cannot be explained by the fact that men have willies and women don’t. On that May day nine years ago, the first to proudly sign the Istanbul Convention was the then Turkish foreign minister, Ahmet Davutoğlu. Today, members of the ruling party, like their soulmates in several European countries, including Slovenia, are demanding ever more loudly a withdrawal from the convention. At the end of July, the body of 27-year-old student Pınar Gültekin was found in a forest near the Aegean coast. She was murdered by a jealous ex-partner. Last year, 474 women were murdered in Turkey, most in circumstances similar to Pınar’s. This year, because of the hardship and tension caused by lockdown, the figure will probably be even higher. In Turkey, this form of taking a human life is often called an honor killing.

In my life, I’ve only sworn a few oaths. The first time was almost in a kindergarten in Rojan, a district of Trieste, where I was cared for by the nuns who ran the first Slovenian kindergarten in the Italian borderlands. We didn’t really swear oaths there, but we did pray. There wasn’t much play. The sisters had a habit of pressing subtle messages through clenched lips, instructing us how to spend our Sunday mornings with our families so we wouldn’t fare poorly in this life—or the next. Subtlety was never my strength, so when I got home, I translated their veiled suggestions into terrified wailing that we’d all end up in hell for not going to church. In response, my father started waking me up on Sundays and taking me to church, waiting in the bar across the street while I attended mass. From a young age, my family raised me to respect difference. Upon returning to Ljubljana, I swore another oath—this time as a Pioneer (the youth organization in socialist Yugoslavia). I even became the president of our school's Pioneer organization, which remains the only political office I’ve ever held. It impressed my parents about as much as my Sunday churchgoing. The next oath was required of me when I joined the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA). I’ll admit—I cheated. It was a few weeks after I arrived at the barracks on the outskirts of Zagreb. Along with a few hundred freshly shaven recruits, I stood in formation before the Yugoslav flag, mouthing the words of the official pledge. Except, instead of the formal text, I was silently reciting the lyrics to Lennon’s Imagine in my head. I didn’t know the whole song—my memory for lyrics was never great—so I kept repeating the lines I did know like a mantra. I made an exception only for the final line, where I shouted, “not wishing to give my life in doing so.” A small but deliberate change from the official wording, which in Serbo-Croatian required only the switch of a single vowel. Lost in the roar of the enthusiastic soldiery, my minor act of resistance brought me comfort and peace, a feeling that I had outwitted the forced ideological indoctrination of the Yugoslav “people’s” army. Leaving for military service in 1984—during the Los Angeles Olympics—was deeply traumatic for me. Overnight, I was uprooted from the relatively liberal environment that had already begun to emerge in Slovenia, or at least hinted at its arrival, and plunged into an authoritarian, uniformed ideological operetta that I experienced as a violent intrusion into my personal freedom, beliefs, and individuality. My aversion to military matters ran deep—no doubt worsened by the ideological indoctrination we received in high school by an eager young teacher of the Fundamentals of General People’s Defence and Social Self-Protection, our future and recurring Prime Minister Janez Jansa. JNA built its moral authority on the legacy of the National Liberation Struggle (NOB) against the occupiers. That, in itself, wasn’t the problem. From a young age, I was—and still am—a convinced anti-fascist. But even as a naive teenager, I could see that the primary function of the ritualized, mythologized WWII narrative was to morally justify the authoritarian one-party regime. I didn’t cheat on the oath because I disagreed with the legacy of the national liberation struggle, but because I intuitively rejected the ideological instrumentalization of anti-fascism for goals and ideas that I personally felt were fundamentally at odds with that legacy. For the same reasons, I feel no nostalgia for the former country, Yugoslavia. Not because of nationalism, but because it didn’t align with the values of a free, democratic society in which I wished to live. The fact that it was more liberal than other Eastern Bloc countries was cold comfort. Just as “almost pregnant” doesn’t lead to childbirth, “almost democratic” doesn’t lead to freedom. The next oath I took, I signed—with pride. It was at the beginning of my tenure at the Council of Europe, where I pledged to act solely in the interest of the organization and not to accept any instructions from any government, authority, organization, or person outside the Council. We employees are bound to uphold and defend the principles and values enshrined in the Statute and the European Convention on Human Rights. I have never experienced these obligations as a restriction, but as a privilege. I am faithful to them not only during work hours, but as a private individual and citizen as well. That is also the basis of my writing—in my personal name, but in defence of those very values. If, in the early years, the emphasis on loyalty to the Council of Europe rather than to individual governments, organizations, or persons seemed merely formal, it has become increasingly relevant lately. The more some societies drift away from the civilizational principles they accepted when signing the European Convention on Human Rights, the more likely it is that a commitment to these values—whether in professional work or personal expression—will be met with hostility from one side or another. Interestingly, and not coincidentally, the first signs of such conflict arose around attitudes toward the LGBT population. Homophobia—like other social pathologies—is latent in many European societies and erupts whenever political opportunism legitimizes it. While in the early post–Berlin Wall years, warnings about the violation of sexual minority rights were often dismissed as misunderstandings or a matter of time, in recent years, especially in Eastern Europe, the tide has turned. Equality and the protection of human dignity for some citizens have become politically targeted and legally curtailed—openly and deliberately—in the name of “traditional values.” Through misleading interpretations of concepts like family, security, and national culture, populism seeks to fabricate a conflict between “traditional” and “Western” values. The latter group conveniently comes to include principles such as judicial and media independence, the functioning of NGOs—in other words, the checks and balances essential to democratic governance. It all gets wrapped up in the dogma of total national sovereignty, which rejects external or international standards of behaviour and demands full autonomy in defending the “purity” of the nation from the “decadent” influence of the West. The ideal of a “healthy nation” is served to citizens as consolation in exchange for freedoms and prosperity—both of which, for all its flaws, the West provides far better than the so-called traditional East. We may never be the most successful or truly free, but at least, they say, we can be the most intolerant. An important part of this populist political and social paradigm is the ritualization and mythologization of history—a constant return to events and periods whose selective interpretations help populism portray itself as a victim and delegitimize any political opposition or democratic oversight. This is eerily similar to how the Yugoslav army and regime used history to justify authoritarianism—right down to the indoctrination of youth through military-themed high school courses. But our reaction to such manipulation also invites comparison. Opposition and critique of the manipulative use of history in no way exclude condemnation and empathy regarding the crimes committed on our soil after WWII. On the contrary: it is out of respect for the victims of extrajudicial killings of the captured Nazi collaborators, that we must morally reject the political instrumentalization of their—and our—shared tragedy. This, of course, requires clarity in condemning what happened. Respect for all victims does not equate fascism with resistance to it. Postwar atrocities do not diminish the civilizational importance of anti-fascism—but nor can they be justified by it. Relativizing extrajudicial killings, regardless of context, plays right into the hands of those trying to turn our future into the second act of our past.

Let me say at the outset that I am very fond of folk songs. And of Oto Pestner. They are an important part of Slovenian culture. Not the only one, but still. But as the president says, tastes differ; you can never please everyone. Except when it comes to ideological tastes, where trying to please everyone can be a political program. Perhaps state ceremonies could be approached in a similar way. Reconciled and balanced. The Smrtnik Brothers and Zlatko. The president speaks for half the speech and is silent for the other half. Pirkovič scripts the first part of the ceremony, Živadinov the second. At the end, both step onto the stage and hold hands, like Kohl and Mitterrand at Verdun. Fade out on Pahor’s Mount Rushmore presidential expression, and off to bed. Or we can keep it simple. If you ask me, I would limit Statehood Day ceremonies to the anthem Zdravljica, an honor guard, the president’s speech, a cannon salute from the castle so that even household pets know we are celebrating, and a children’s choir with a medley of folk songs. All of it, if possible, with a visual design by someone who has had more than two art-club sessions in the fourth grade of primary school. There is really no point in tearing your hair out over taste. But at this year’s ceremony I noticed a few other things. First, a completely hollowed-out, generic concept of homeland and patriotism, based on ritual incantations of blind love and loyalty, which with minor adjustments could also be used for Paraguay. I am proud to be Slovenian because I am Slovenian. We are sturdy (whatever that means), hard-working and honest. We have beautiful nature, rivers, mountains, hills and valleys. I doubt the Paraguayans consider themselves feeble, lazy and dishonest. They have nature and mountains too. Their own, not just the neighbors’ ones that were used for our central ceremony. Today the Italian Dolomites, yesterday Rovinj. Are we really so insecure and envious in our admiration of what is ours that we can’t even put together a state ceremony without stealing a postcard or two from our neighbors? We will never be the biggest, we will never be the strongest, we don’t even need to be the best at all costs, but it would be nice if we could be at least a little bit ourselves. In the concept of patriotism that the designers of this year’s ceremony swear by, the homeland is a fate into which you happen to be born. A fate you can neither choose, nor change, nor help shape. You can only follow it blindly. In this concept of patriotism, you don’t love your homeland because you love it but because you must love it. In this concept of patriotism, you must not be critical of your homeland, even if you love it. In this concept of patriotism, patriotism is not love of the homeland but obedience to the authorities. Nothing reflects this concept of homeland better than the stock photos taken from the internet that were used at the ceremony to illustrate its citizens. The citizens whose state we were celebrating. A generic, photocopied mob, people without identity, people who don’t exist. All virtual, all without rights. Real citizens were not at the ceremony. For security reasons they had to stay behind the fence. Imagine if, for prophylactic reasons, selected representatives of the people on Congress Square had been replaced by inflatable dolls from Sežana. The president’s opening speech was immediately followed by a Darth Vader-like rumbling about those who supposedly “did not want, were not allowed, did not wish and did not believe,” which promptly gave his call for dialogue, tolerance and cooperation the middle finger. There was repeated mention of a “healthy” homeland, which of course implies the existence of another one that is sick and unhealthy. When, after the ceremony, I mentioned the comparison with Paraguay on Twitter, I was showered with accusations of being a traitor to my own culture who should rather pick up a pickaxe and shovel, since I have never done anything socially useful in my life. Nothing is more entertaining than being accused of left-wing treason by functionally illiterate characters who consider themselves right-wingers while idiotically imitating the ideological patterns and discourse of China’s Cultural Revolution, the Khmer Rouge and Stalin’s purges. Patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel, Samuel Johnson wrote back in the eighteenth century. It was not a criticism of love of one’s country but a condemnation of false patriots who sell their own interests, shady dealings and dirty tricks wrapped in the national colors. So when the homeland calls you, it is wise to check whether it is really her on the line or just someone trying to abuse your love for her. True patriotism is based on love of one’s country, but it also includes a critical attitude towards it, not because we don’t love it but because we do. True patriotism is shown above all by our attitude to moral and ethical values. We show true patriotism through our attitude to pluralist democracy, human rights, the democratic rule of law, solidarity, humanism and social justice. Blind obedience, without critical judgment, principle and courage, can lead us into the same kind of predicament in which German and Italian “patriots” found themselves in the 1930s. Torn between their conscience and taking part in the crimes the authorities demanded of them in the name of the homeland. In history, the greatest patriots have very often been precisely those who had enough courage to say a firm no to “the call of the homeland.” So much has happened in Slovenia in recent days that you may be wondering why I am still going on about the ceremony. Perhaps because I do not accept that some people claim the exclusive right to decide what the homeland is and who is a patriot. Not only patriotism but also other values, such as family, security and culture, are being twisted and abused as weapons in a culture war in which, from the extreme fringe, the progressive, democratic and humanist European values that we wrote into the Constitution twenty-nine years ago, at the founding of the state celebrated on Congress Square, are smeared and discredited. I do not accept that, in the name of patriotism, anti-fascism—the foundation of free and democratic post-war Europe—is demonized. I love Slovenia too much to just watch this in silence. Every time I come home, I can hardly wait for that tiny, faded Slovenian flag in the middle of the Karawanks tunnel to appear. Love of my homeland gives me strength and self-confidence that do not need intolerance and hatred and reject them. I love family so much that I wish it to everyone who wants one. I love Slovenian culture, not only because it is ours but because it is culture, the kind that connects us, can also anger, irritate and provoke us, but above all lets us breathe, makes us creative, bold, innovative, different, interesting and successful, and allows us to be open to others and to trust ourselves. I love the Slovenian language, not only because of Trubar, Cankar and Prešeren, but also because it is a miracle that we have preserved it, and because it is the language in which, after thirty years of living abroad, I still think, feel, love and get angry. I love Slovenia, not because it has the most beautiful lakes, rivers and sea, but because on their banks I fell in love for the first time and celebrated the births of my children. I love Slovenian forests, because bears live in them, because I picked mushrooms in them with my grandfather, and because in these forests fought patriots who answered the call of their conscience and rose up against evil. I love Republic Square, not because it is more beautiful than St Mark’s Square or the Champs-Élysées, but because on it we celebrated the birth of our shared and free state. No one can take that away from me, and no one can claim that I am not a patriot. Because I love Slovenia, I do not accept that people for whom the homeland is merely blood and soil present themselves as patriots. Those in yellow that is turning brown.

In my years of service I have had quite a few unusual adventures, most of them towards the end of the 1990s, in that turbulent period when many parts of Europe, some gradually, others more abruptly, dramatically and sometimes violently, were moving after long decades of authoritarian uniformity of thought towards a different, more open, free and democratic society. Much like today, only in the opposite direction. There were many moments I regret not documenting in more detail, relying on my then still youthful memory. Now and then I was thoroughly scared. For example, in January 2000, over Chechnya, in a helicopter that the Russians repaired with a hammer just before take-off and that the Chechens then chose for target practice. With me were a German parliamentarian, who responded to the hammer and the shots with prayer, and a seasoned Reuters journalist, who pulled a bottle of vodka from his bag. As always, I sided with the fourth estate. Or the tragic news that the Italian aircraft that ferried aid workers around the Balkans for the United Nations had crashed at Pristina airport only a few months after I had flown back from Bosnia on it. Or a visit to a polling station somewhere near Pale, during one of the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where I chatted with a Danish television crew about the hospitality of the local population. When we later drove off one after another towards Sarajevo, a few kilometers further down we passed an off-road vehicle with four armed men. They let our car pass, but welcomed the Danes with an honorary salvo from automatic weapons. One of the Danes ended up in hospital with a bullet in his shoulder. Or the time when my then boss, the President of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, Lord Russell-Johnston, and I, with a grossly overpaid Belgrade taxi driver, made our way past columns of heavily armed Serbian special forces to meet Ibrahim Rugova secretly at his unofficial presidential residence on a hill above Pristina. To this day I keep the crystal Rugova gave me then as a symbol of Kosovo’s natural wealth. But of all these escapades, my heart sank lowest at a meeting with the government of national unity of South Ossetia. It was during one of my many visits to Georgia, which always enchanted me with its natural beauty and the warmth of its people. Almost always. It was sometime around 2000; at the presidential palace, Russell and I met the old fox, Gorbachev’s foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze, who was swept away a few years later by the Rose Revolution. We also met the architect of the future revolution, Mikheil Saakashvili, who was then, if I remember correctly, minister of justice. My memory fails me particularly regarding his post at the time, as Mikheil has held a whole series of positions in his career so far, from trainee at the European Court of Human Rights to President of Georgia and governor of one of Ukraine’s regions. Even then he came across as a bright but self-absorbed and inflated man who approached politics much as my son plays computer games. Boldly and without brakes; when you crash, you reset and try again. Lots of ideas and little responsibility. At the winter ski resort of Gudauri, popular with the local political and business elite, diplomats and representatives of international organizations, I spent the night bowling with the speaker of parliament, Zurab Zhvania, and his team. At breakfast I met Saakashvili and his family. Not long afterwards, Zurab died in suspicious and still unexplained circumstances in a friend’s apartment in Tbilisi. Misha became President of Georgia. During that visit, Russell and I managed to drive to South Ossetia, a separatist region then going through a brief and unstable period of relative peace before renewed bloody fighting in 2004 and 2008. We went to the capital of South Ossetia accompanied by the head of the OSCE mission in Tbilisi, a French diplomat who made no secret of being fed up with the country and the people around him, including us. The “border crossing” was reminiscent of scenes from the Balkan wars: a no man’s land where a bunch of suspicious bearded men in uniform were busy with contraband. A landscape of canisters of smuggled fuel, cartons of cigarettes, Kalashnikovs and rosaries. The South Ossetian metropolis of Tskhinvali looked like a medium-sized village of dusty streets and single-story houses, out of which rose a single, rather battered high-rise housing all the organs of the South Ossetian authorities and the local university. In front of the tower block, two bored soldiers in mismatched uniforms loitered on cracked brick tiles and escorted us into the unlit building and an elevator that did not inspire much confidence. During the long, creaking ride, I began to regret having suggested this trip to Russell. On the top floor we arrived in a large, dimly lit chamber where the highest representatives of the local authorities sat at a long table. They looked like the drama club of the Styrian Guard performing the Last Supper. “President of the Republic, Speaker of Parliament, Foreign Minister,” the scowling, pot-bellied bearded men introduced themselves one after another, all in military uniform. They were about as friendly as our escort, except that his pressed French arrogance was replaced by a staring Soviet gruffness. After the introductory and rather one-sided protocol courtesies, Russell asked them about their political program and plans. “There are no political differences between us. We work for the nation. For the people. For development,” our hosts assured us one after another, now and then underlining their unity and patriotic fervor with a heavy bang of the fist on the table. This made no particular impression on Russell, and he did what he often did in the company of people who bored him or got on his nerves. He bowed his head, fell asleep and snored loudly. Beware of politicians who are full of talk about national interests, he always told me. The South Ossetian political leadership took the behavior of their guest from Britain as an insult, which one can’t entirely blame them for. The temperature in the already cold room dropped a few more degrees. Confused and alarmed, I turned for help to the Frenchman, who nonchalantly turned his attention to the cleanliness of his fingernails. The next half hour passed more slowly than any other in my life. I tried desperately to keep the conversation going with frantic questions and diplomatic platitudes, which provoked increasingly obvious irritation and contempt in my interlocutors. The interpreter’s translations got shorter and shorter; the sweat on his face reflected the effort of removing from their answers content he considered unsuitable for guests from Europe. The last few minutes dragged on in complete silence like chicken guts. The soldiers who had met us were no longer bored; they looked as if they were waiting for orders on what to do with this gang of international provocateurs and mercenaries. Just as I was convinced I would spend at least a few hours, if not days, in a prison cell somewhere deep in the bowels of the presidential tower, the tension was broken by the President of the Republic, who suddenly leapt up and shouted “Zakuska!” Russell instantly broke off his rest and winked at me conspiratorially. To my pleading that we return to Tbilisi at once, he merely waved his hand, saying that would be impolite. When he was in the right mood, he could be more arrogant than any Frenchman. We spent the next hour in that form of socializing that in diplomatic language is called a “frank and open discussion,” which can include anything from mutual strangling to joint drinking. The tables groaned under the weight of caviar, champagne and greasy mutton paid for by the sweat of the South Ossetian people, while I, in a corner, in the company of the still shaken interpreter, chased away post-traumatic stress syndrome with vodka. Ever since that day, whenever anyone mentions a government of national unity, a shiver runs down my spine and I get a headache.

“Unity, happiness, reconciliation, may they return to us.” The longing for unity is part of the Slovenian national genome. At least in poetry and in theory. In practice, it often seems we can’t manage to read Prešeren’s verse to the end. We Slovenians are obsessed with overcoming divisions and differences. We don’t want to be divided into left and right, into Partisans and Home Guards, into ours and yours. We swear by development governments and project governments, non-party politics, transcending “ideological” topics and the like. So that we won’t be divided, so that we will be as united as possible. Because there are so few of us. Only a million of us still live, as the song goes. If someone made a music video about the Slovenian understanding of pluralist democracy, a folk-pop tune would be a better soundtrack than Katie Melua. I think the problem of Slovenians is not so much that we are too divided as that we don’t know how to be divided in a civilized way and still live together, cooperate, respect one another, talk to one another, agree or disagree, and above all have the right for some to think one way and others another. Without differences there is no pluralism. Without pluralism there is no democracy. It is true, though, that the public’s disappointment with politics is understandable. After thirty years, it sometimes seems that instead of a functioning democracy we have a ritualized inter-tribal conflict, in which insults are legitimate political discourse and principles, election programs and commitments merely an unnecessary obstacle to political opportunism. But we won’t get rid of tribalism by merging two tribes into one. A civilized democratic society rests on responsibility, political culture and shared values, within which we can be as different and divided as we like. These shared values do not need to be invented. Thirty years ago, we wrote them into the Constitution. Part of the standard repertoire of Slovenian political folklore is also the demand to end the division into ours and yours. I agree. Partly. The concept of ours and yours implies one person’s ownership of another. A society in which we have handed over the right to think and decide for ourselves to someone else. To whoever we belong to. But in overcoming the differences between ours and yours, we should be careful, since otherwise we may end up, as once before, all being theirs again, only this time “they” may be someone else. What if, for a change, we tried something different: a society in which everyone can first of all be their own? We are trying very hard to stop dividing ourselves into Partisans and Home Guards. Here too I could agree, on condition that we clarify what we are actually talking about. About ending the quarrel over the outcome of the war and paying respect to all the victims, or about claims that it was only the first half and demands for a rematch? In the second case, it is by no means only a historical question but a question of our attitude to the present. Relativizing historical facts calls into question the European civilizational model that arose as a response to the bloody experience of Nazism, and with it the principles on which this model rests: pluralist democracy, the separation of powers, judicial independence, human rights, political freedoms, media freedom, freedom of association. But a critical understanding of history cannot be a one-way process. These days, as at the end of every May, pictures of Tito are circulating again on social networks. I understand those who are bothered by this. Yugoslavia was no liberal paradise. The post-war extrajudicial killings deserve unconditional condemnation, not denial or justification, since that only makes the job easier for those who, for current political aims, try to legitimize collaboration with Nazism by putting everything on the same level. Nor can we, or should we, forget the violence and injustice that followed. “Using methods in which ancient slavery and modern Nazism, seasoned with Balkan primitivism, were fatally intertwined, they systematically killed the body and soul of Nace and thousands of others from the same quota of indispensable enemies of the state ordered from the top, so that before the unraveling, only a tearless statistic remained,” my father wrote in the afterword to my uncle’s memoir of his horrifying experience of the prisons of Povšetova, Bileća and Grgur. Through their heroism and patriotism, the Partisans made an important contribution to the victory over Nazism and to creating the conditions for a different, freer, more humane and more just Europe, but Tito’s post-war regime was simply not part of that Europe. Among other things, because it did not allow debate on ideological topics. Slovenians evidently still don’t want to be divided into “left and right.” I would be more cautious about such wishes. We have already had an authoritarianism in which we could only be “left”; there is a risk of steering into a second half in which there will be room only for the “right.” Democracy by definition cannot be uniformity of thought, still less thoughtlessness, but a plurality of minds: a contest, but also a dialogue between different ideas, worldviews, proposals and programs. Although the division into left, right and center parties may seem somewhat outdated, it is still important because it requires, at least in mature democracies, that the content, program and activity of political options rest on a predetermined, transparent and binding system of values. This makes post-election opportunism in their own interest harder for politicians and gives voters a democratic choice and somewhat more guarantee that they will not be cheated. Democracy needs politics that does not build its authority on an arbitrary interpretation of national interests but on a mandate it receives from voters and for which it is accountable to them. The obsession with overcoming differences, the pursuit of a unity without values in which there is no division into left, right and those in between, the fiction of a technocratic, non-political and non-ideological politics that claims to act in everyone’s interest and therefore needs no democratic oversight, is a mimicry of democracy that leads to uniformity of thought. A state in which there are no ideological divisions and differences, and in which everyone is united and of the same opinion on how to manage social processes and solve social problems, can be achieved and maintained only through repression. None of this, of course, means that I advocate a society in which we cannot talk and work together. On the contrary. Unity, too, is a key value if it means consensus on basic civilizational democratic principles; the problem arises when the argument of unity and balance is abused as an excuse for ignoring, or even legitimizing, the undermining of these principles and values. There are ideological topics that cannot be avoided; one has to take a position on them. What pluralist democracy needs is not parrot-like repetition of platitudes about overcoming differences, but overcoming sectarianism, inconsistency, clientelism, cynical opportunism, threats, pressure and crudeness. We need more political culture, more integrity, more responsibility and, above all, more unity and determination in respecting and defending the democratic values in whose name we Slovenian citizens—left, right and center—won our state thirty years ago. More unity, in which, as then, power and with it honor will once again be ours.

It’s been a quarter of a century since that morning when I sat, palms sweating, in front of a panel in the building of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. It was the final test that might—or might not—pave the way for a job at the Council of Europe. I no longer remember what they asked me, except for the last question: “Do you believe that Slovenia’s independence was fully legal and legitimate, considering that the right to self-determination is quite limited under international law and has mostly applied in the context of decolonization?” Five or six pairs of eyes fixed on me with unreadable expressions, offering no clue as to what kind of answer they expected. I knew this was a make-or-break moment. If they were expecting a negative response, I would disappoint them—and frankly, let them stew, I thought. So, with more confidence in my voice than I felt inside, I replied: “Besides the fact that the right to self-determination was included in the constitution of the former federation, Slovenia’s independence was the result of an extraordinarily high level of consensus and a democratically expressed will of the Slovenian people. Above all, it was the only way to protect the democratic gains and aspirations of the Slovenian nation, which were gravely endangered by Milošević’s nationalist and authoritarian regime.” From the panel’s reaction, it was clear that I had the job in the bag. In that distant year of 1995, a Slovenian passport was still somewhat of an exotic curiosity at many borders, but for people in an organization tasked with protecting and promoting pluralistic democracy based on human rights and the rule of law, Slovenia was a success story. The contrast with other parts of the former Yugoslavia—where authoritarian converts were manipulating the masses with nationalism, chauvinism, and hate speech, seizing state institutions, persecuting political opposition, independent media, and civil society, and looting public funds—was simply too great. In their eyes, any nation’s decision to escape such a fate and commit to progressive, democratic values was legal, legitimate, and worthy of full support. My early years on the job were, in many ways, exciting. There was adrenaline in the hallways of the Palais de l’Europe, the Council of Europe’s headquarters. We were making history. Changing the world. The decades-long ideological division of Europe was over, replaced by a pan-European consensus on building a society grounded in liberal democratic values. On the other hand, I often noticed that when I told people what I did—democracy and human rights—I was met with confusion or indifference. “Democracy and human rights? Yawn. Why bother? We’re all for that already, aren’t we?” A lot has changed in 25 years. Today, the topics of democracy and human rights no longer leave anyone indifferent—and we are most certainly not all for them anymore. Part of the reason why, I think, is captured in one of the few wise remarks ever made by former U.S. Vice President Dan Quayle. “We are on an irreversible path to more freedom and democracy—but that can, of course, change,” he said after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Whether Quayle had more insight than Francis Fukuyama or simply stumbled into a moment of unexpected clarity—a lucidum intervallum, as it’s called in Roman law and psychiatry—we’ll never know. But history certainly didn’t end in 1989 or 1995. Much has changed since then—mostly for the worse. There’s a long story behind how and why, and everyone tells it in their own way. One reason, I believe, is that we had too much faith in the supposed irreversibility of the path toward democracy. In our enthusiasm, we got careless. We believed things would keep improving on their own, following some internal and unstoppable logic. We thought it would be enough to help new democracies build institutions, adopt decent constitutions and legislation, hold regular elections—and then the rest would follow naturally, on rails, toward an ever-freer, safer, and better future. But anything on rails can derail. We learned that functioning democracy requires more than institutions. It needs politicians with integrity, committed to democratic values, and effective oversight of the executive—not just formal checks. And crucially, democracy needs citizens who understand, embrace, and support its values—who are willing and able to engage and influence society. Most countries have failed that test in recent decades. Just days ago, I took part in a videoconference with a young Danish political activist from a traditional political party. He insisted that democracy and political pluralism no longer work—and that people living under authoritarian regimes often fare better than us. In the last 25 years, we’ve bred a new generation of Europeans—many of whom don’t care about democratic values, largely because they don’t know what happens when democracy is gone. When there are no more political freedoms, no more accountability, no more human rights, compassion, or solidarity. We’ve forgotten about social rights and social security, which are not some leftist conspiracy. The indivisibility of political and social rights is enshrined in both the European Social Charter (1961, revised in 1996) and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966). Social security was a fundamental part of Europe’s postwar civilizational model—at least until it was undermined by political inconsistency, shortsightedness, and opportunism. The embrace of economic neoliberalism gained new traction when Margaret Thatcher discovered Hayek and his prophetically titled book, The Road to Serfdom. The final, painful blow to social security and justice came with the last (so far) financial crisis—and, more importantly, the way most governments, including in Europe, chose to address it. This created a massive pool of angry, humiliated, and disillusioned people—eager for someone to appear and show the ruling political and economic elites the middle finger. Populism surged back—left-wing to some extent, but especially right-wing, as an authoritarian parody of democracy offering the worst possible solutions to real problems. Where populism is now in power, it’s growing bolder in dismantling democratic institutions and safeguards, political competition, independent media, judiciaries, and civil society. Yet many populist politicians in Europe still crave external legitimacy. They want to be seen as part of the traditional right and force themselves—like Cinderella’s stepsisters—into the worn but still respectable shoes of European conservatism. Ironically, they define their “right-wing” identity mainly by rejecting the values that post-WWII Christian democrats and center-right parties once championed: human rights, judicial independence, press freedom. In this rhetorical sleight of hand, anyone defending human rights, judicial independence, or media freedom is suddenly labeled a far-left radical. Ridiculous—but often effective in a climate of populist-fueled irrationality. It should be embarrassing, above all, for those conservatives who know full well that Adenauer, Schuman, and de Gasperi were not communist agents. But it’s dangerous for everyone. The path to greater democracy and freedom has clearly not been irreversible. So perhaps the current slide into darker times in European history isn’t irreversible either. But some reversals are more stubborn than others. It’s far easier to lose freedom and democracy than to win them back. Unless we come to our senses soon, we may find that this most recent and longest period of peace and stability in European history will end up being nothing more than a fleeting exception. A lucidum intervallum.

There are people who see opportunity in every crisis. No, I’m not talking about middlemen dealing in protective equipment—I don’t make a habit of commenting on the daily circus of politics, no matter how extravagant. I mean those incurable optimists who see a ray of light in every disaster, every failure, and every unpleasant event. These are the kinds of people who always interpret the headlight of an oncoming locomotive as the light at the end of the tunnel. Most of the time, they mean no harm—they’re just irritating. When COVID-19 broke out, some of them began predicting that the virus would restore respect for science, rationality, and expertise, and would generally wash away charlatans and peddlers of nonsense and lies in all areas—from anti-vaxxers to climate change deniers and, of course, populists. The light at the end of the tunnel. Populists are a curious case. Like everyone else, the crisis caught them with their pants down, though unlike most, they will never admit it. But they adapted quickly and saw opportunity in the crisis. I’m not talking about unshakable optimism here, but about the intention to press harder on the accelerator of a locomotive that’s already derailing. The pandemic significantly impacted all four pillars of the populist paradigm: fear, enemies, scapegoats, and anti-reason. When it comes to fear, the virus plays right into populists’ hands. We are all afraid—regardless of our cultural worldview or political beliefs. It’s no surprise that some people, trembling in fear of this nasty threat, fell for the false choice between health and safety on one side, and freedom and democracy on the other. I’m not referring to temporary emergency measures, which almost every country has introduced to limit or suspend certain rights. Such measures are anticipated in most constitutions and align with international standards, including the European Convention on Human Rights—so long as they’re justified, proportionate, and time-limited. What’s concerning is the possibility that, under the guise of fighting the virus, there are attempts to permanently dismantle democratic rights and safeguards—from parliamentary oversight to media freedom and civil society. The justified anxiety of citizens has also been exploited by politicians and experts who—perhaps even with good intentions—have called not just for caution and responsibility, but for panic. Yet by definition, panic is a state in which fear overwhelms reason. And rationality subordinate to fear is not only the worst response to a public health crisis—it’s also the best gift to those trying to convince people that they must sacrifice the immune system of democracy for the sake of their health. Of course, populism cannot exist without enemies. Rage is a powerful tool for deception and manipulation. In order for people to accept things that objectively harm them, they must hate someone more than they love themselves. But here, the pandemic didn’t entirely cooperate with the populist playbook. You can fear a virus, but it’s hard to hate it. That juicy, blind, boiling hatred—the fuel that drives the derailed populist train—needs a more tangible target. Preferably someone with a name and a face you can insult, kick, or bash over the head (if only metaphorically). Still, populists adapted quickly. If you can’t hate the virus, then you project your aggression onto someone you can hate. The attacks on critical voices and political opponents, and the renewed obsession with migrants, serve to stoke and sustain the prejudices populism needs to function. From the populist point of view, it doesn’t really matter who we hate—what matters is that we hate blindly and thoroughly. Populism also needs scapegoats in order to survive. This is only logical. The populist political paradigm doesn’t allow for accountability for its own actions, sins, or mistakes. To be fair, dodging responsibility is popular across the political spectrum. Some of our local politicians have a favorite trick—dismissing any criticism as “politically motivated.” Well, of course it is! Have you ever filed a complaint at a mechanic, only to be told your complaint is "automotive motivated"? Still, while most politicians shy away from accountability, populists have taken the scapegoat method to an art form. It’s not just a way to cover their own tracks—it’s a deliberate, integral part of their political model. Finger-pointing serves two goals: the first is discrediting political opponents and critical voices. In the U.S., as we know, everything is blamed on Barack Obama, the Democrats, and the “lying media.” During the COVID-19 crisis, also on China. And of course, on international organizations and the entire concept of a rule-based global order. In Europe, a favorite target is the European Union. The second goal is to create an excuse for not solving problems. When it comes to crisis management, populists often lack the ability—and more importantly, the will. Human suffering, injustice, and hardship, if they can be blamed on someone else, are not seen as problems but as political opportunities. Finally, we come to the last link in the chain by which populists shackle the state and people to their own interests: the decisive popular rejection of rationality, facts, science, and knowledge. The longer populism stays in power, the more it depends on the blind obedience of its supporters. Reason and logic get in the way of such submission. At the beginning of the COVID-19 outbreak, it seemed survival instincts might rekindle some respect for expertise. But that didn’t last long. Experts themselves partly contributed to the backlash, with their cacophony of graphs, models, and predictions of every possible and impossible outcome. If not for COVID-19, I wouldn’t have known how many “renowned scientists from prestigious universities” there are in the world. Despite legitimate criticisms, a reasonable person would still rather trust an expert than a quack—especially when it comes to their health. Or... maybe not. Sometimes it seems that expertise is increasingly seen as an obstacle in managing the health crisis. I’ve noticed subtle shifts in language. It worries me when less is said about responsibility, rationality, and expertise, and more about “common sense” and “farmer’s wisdom.” Let me say immediately: I have great respect for farmers. When it comes to farming, I trust them completely. If I decide to plant corn or raise sheep, I won’t ask my urologist for advice. And vice versa. What really makes my hair stand on end is the invocation of “common sense.” That phrase implies there’s another kind of sense—a “sick” one, a kind of rationality based on facts, science, and expertise—which in the populist worldview is somehow harmful to the nation. The similarity to the concept of “degenerate art” is, of course, not accidental. The idea of using “farmer’s wisdom” to solve a health crisis reached absurdity last Tuesday, when none other than Donald Trump suggested during a press conference that injecting bleach into the body might help fight COVID-19. “If it cleans park benches, why not lungs?” His health advisor barely managed to control her facial expressions and body language. Yet the next day she tried to defend him, saying he was just “thinking out loud,” as he often does. Her attempt was even more pitiful than his dangerous and idiotic comment—which he later claimed was “sarcasm.” What threatens our health, our freedom, and our democracy is not just those who act out of ignorance or ideology—but also those who, out of opportunism, enable them. Some stains cannot be washed out—even with bleach. And no, I don’t mean that as sarcasm.

When my editor suggested a few days ago that for my next column I write some impressions of how we are getting through the coronavirus in France, I hesitated. First, because describing my own adventures, at a time when the whole world is going through similar experiences, often in much harder, more dramatic and more dangerous circumstances, seemed too arrogant. We read a lot about the difficult conditions health workers face in some parts of the world, especially in Italy, and rightly so. Besides them, these days every shop assistant, every postal worker, police officer, refuse collector, driver, every employee in a care home—all those who allow most of us to shut ourselves in our homes in relative comfort and wait for this nightmare to end—has more material for a column than I do. The second reason for hesitating to write about the coronavirus is that, unlike many I read on social networks, I don’t consider myself an expert in epidemiology. So don’t expect graphs or forecasts of any kind from me. What is more, last weekend I decided to take a break from constantly following the situation around the world. After two days off the networks, I found that the effects of my absence on the development of the epidemic worldwide were barely noticeable, while for my mental well-being they were very beneficial. I recommend the experience to many who haven’t been able to peel their fingers off Twitter for weeks. The last reason was simply that, like many others, I realized very quickly that working and schooling from home are no holiday. Tasks that in normal circumstances we would do quickly and without much difficulty take much more time and effort. There simply isn’t time or energy left for extracurricular activities such as writing columns for Večer. But I am stubborn by nature. In the three years since I was invited to write for Večer, I have not missed a single deadline. There is no way I will make an exception for the first time because of one nasty virus. According to the latest figures, France is the European country with the fourth-highest number of cases, after Italy, Spain and Germany. It has far more deaths than its eastern neighbor. I live in the Grand Est region, which, because of one of the early clusters in the city of Mulhouse, some 120 kilometers south of Strasbourg, is one of the hardest hit in the country. Patients from hospitals in Strasbourg and elsewhere in Alsace are being transported by train and military aircraft to other, so far less affected parts of France, and also to hospitals in neighboring Germany. Such selfless gestures of solidarity between countries and people will never be forgotten, nor, unfortunately, will the all too frequent cases of selfishness, intolerance and nationalism around the world, which in the fight against a global threat are not only immeasurably stupid but also ineffective and dangerous. Strict restrictions on movement were introduced in France just under two weeks ago, after crowded parks on a sunny Sunday showed that one could not rely solely on people’s reason, responsibility and solidarity. Much has changed since then. This was helped by the soaring number of cases in the country and elsewhere in the world, and also by the fact that no one may go out without a written certificate stating they are going to work, to buy essentials or to the doctor. One hour of exercise is also allowed, no more than one kilometer from home. Those more at home in mathematics than I am quickly worked out that this allows them to run a 3.14-kilometer circuit. The certificate is, as the French say, “sur l’honneur,” on one’s honor. The form is available on the Interior Ministry’s website; you print it, fill it in and sign it yourself, or, if you don’t have a printer, like me, you simply copy it out on a piece of paper. The fine for walking around without a certificate is 200 euros. Honor or no honor, by last Thursday 3.7 million checks had been carried out and 235,000 fines issued. For repeat offenders, the penalty can quickly rise to 3,750 euros and six months in prison. Today, on those rare occasions when I do leave home, the picture is therefore quite different. There are relatively few people on the streets, and in front of shops and pharmacies, as in Slovenia and elsewhere in the world, people wait calmly at the prescribed distance. Although we are in a region whose case numbers are approaching Italian levels, there is no excessive tension or panic among people. But they are, of course, worried. And beneath a thin facade of apparent “normality” lies the horrifying reality of nearby hospitals. The harrowing stories of Italian doctors forced by circumstances to triage who gets a chance to survive and who dies are already built into the system here. Only those under 80 go on ventilators. In Mulhouse, the line between hope of survival and probable death is five years lower still. Patients from care homes are in principle not admitted to hospital. Those who die there are not counted in the official statistics. If this continues, Alsace will be left without grandparents. What I write is not a moral judgment, at least not of the doctors, whom the lack of equipment puts in an impossible position, but merely a statement of, and lament for, a horrifying helplessness and a civilizational defeat. Just as I am writing, I learn that British Prime Minister Boris Johnson has also tested positive for Covid-19. The fact that there are more and more famous faces among the sick, from Prince Charles to Tom Hanks, has led some to claim that the virus is a social leveler, threatening everyone regardless of wealth, social status, skin color and so on. Yes, of course, just like rain and cold. In winter, Tom Hanks feels the cold just like the homeless. The truth is exactly the opposite. Covid-19 discriminates and deepens social and other differences. First in access to health care; here the United States above all is a time bomb that will stop ticking any moment now. Not to mention poorer countries in less developed parts of the world, where health infrastructure barely exists. The coronavirus discriminates between young and old. Intergenerational relations have been through a series of tests recently, from local ones such as Brexit to global ones such as climate change, over which many young people accuse older people of leaving them in the lurch. With the coronavirus, the reproaches could be similar, only in the opposite direction. There are also differences in the effects of the measures to contain the crisis, which do not affect everyone equally. In the first days in France, even homeless people were fined for unauthorized movement in public spaces. After a storm of reactions this stopped, but I doubt that everyone has been provided with suitable shelter. At the Council of Europe, we are preparing a series of recommendations on the effects of isolation on some of the most vulnerable groups: women who are victims of domestic violence, and children. Very exposed are people, especially older people, who live alone, and those with other illnesses who no longer have access to treatment. Care homes, not only in France, are becoming tragic epicenters of the epidemic. The Council of Europe’s Commissioner for Human Rights and its Committee for the Prevention of Torture have issued warnings and guidance on the treatment of refugees and prisoners. A second social tsunami threatens when countries begin to face the economic and financial consequences of the epidemic. According to many economists, this will be even deeper than the one of 2009. The only hope is that we have learned something from the last crisis, and above all from the mistakes we made in handling it. If we haven’t, not even a vaccine will help us survive as a civilized, humane and free society. When our family has finished all the work and school tasks, we try to spend as much time together as possible and as little as possible in front of screens. The biggest hit of recent days is an old Indian board game with dice, drawn by hand, in which ladders help you take a shortcut on your way to the finish, but if you land on a snake, you slide back down the board. We play for hours on end, and it occurred to me how the game is a metaphor for the times we are living through. Often, just when you start to hope that things are beginning to turn for the better, you land on a nasty python and slide back into despair. On the other hand, at the moments when things are at their worst, you may unexpectedly land on a ladder that carries you forward towards victory. From my own experience I can say that it sometimes takes an annoyingly long time, but in the end it does come to an end. Someone wins, others lose. I hope that, at least as far as the latter is concerned, things will be different after the coronavirus.

Last Sunday, despite strict preventive measures against the pandemic, local elections were held in France. I won’t debate whether it was appropriate to organize elections in such a situation, but I decided to vote. I took my pencil, a pack of disinfectant wipes, got on my bike, and made sure to maintain a safe distance from other voters and the election commission. As far as my personal safety was concerned, I don’t think I risked more than I would by visiting a pharmacy. I hope, however, that I contributed to the defense of democracy—which is always one of the first casualties in times of crisis. Recent public opinion polls revealed that a third of voters had decided not to go to the polls due to the virus. Before the government ordered all restaurants and bars to close on Saturday night, this was undoubtedly the topic of much café debate. Meanwhile, other surveys showed that fear of infection had done little to improve the hygiene habits of the French. Take handwashing after using the toilet, for example: before the crisis, 29% skipped it; now it’s 28%. That’s percent—not individuals. The similarity in numbers is striking. I can’t prove correlation, but I suspect one exists. Panic and shouting are rarely allies of responsibility and reason—and in this case, not even of basic hygiene. The speed at which normal life is being turned on its head is astounding. In recent days, as Lenin might say, decades have been happening. I canceled a business trip to Zagreb last Friday—just hours before the Council of Europe suspended all travel and meetings for its employees. A multilateral organization that can’t hold international meetings is in an awkward position. The first days of the workweek were spent managing the most urgent fallout and minimizing the impact on future operations. In my directorate, we quickly began preparing for a collective shift to remote work. While teleworking has long existed in our institution—as in many others—it’s typically been used for brief, individual tasks like drafting reports, project proposals, or speeches. It’s obviously not a model that functions when 170 people from my directorate are working from home and still expected to keep the organization operational. Not everyone can sit at home writing reports from meetings that no longer happen. Within two days, my colleagues and I compiled a list of tasks that could still be performed under the new circumstances and formed small working teams of four to five people for each. Each team leader was left to determine how best to coordinate communication and collaboration based on the nature of the work and the team’s technical setup. We established protocols to ensure security and continuity of administrative and financial operations. A networked system of collaboration was developed among teams. We created simple reporting forms that group leaders would send along a designated communication chain up to me—like a digital courier service. Many of these solutions were later replicated in other parts of the organization. Only a few days later did I realize the source of my inspiration. Our emergency planning mirrored the knowledge drilled into me nearly 40 years ago by my high school teacher of “General People’s Defense and Social Self-Protection,” none other than Janez Janša. I say this with absolute sincerity and not a hint of irony: I’m very grateful to him. Since Friday, the Council of Europe’s Directorate for Democratic Participation has been organized like a territorial defense unit. One of the most encouraging experiences during this time has been people’s responses—despite their anxiety, they’ve acted with responsibility, efficiency, creativity, and humor. The latter is especially vital in situations like this, which is why I can’t understand the public outcry in Slovenia against anyone who dares crack a joke. Humor is the immune system of sanity and mental health. Remember the wartime jokes about proverbial Bosnians Mujo, Haso, and Fata? They were invented by Bosnians to keep from going mad. To help maintain perspective, I rely on my friend Goran, who spent the entire war in Sarajevo under siege. “Over a thousand days with mortar shelling,” he says. “We survived largely because we didn’t have Twitter.” Goran doesn’t tweet. You won’t find him on Facebook or Instagram. His social network consists of family and friends. He takes the coronavirus very seriously—because of the tragic war experience in which his family lost a close relative to a shell explosion outside the Bosnian presidency building. “If you want to stay alive, you have to be careful,” he told me. “But if you want to stay human, you have to overcome fear.” These words might be the best guide for the times we’re living through. Let’s stop behaving as if the first excludes the second. Or vice versa. The coronavirus is a test of our individual and collective responsibility, solidarity, and character. On an individual level, we’re learning a lot about ourselves and those around us. We’re being tested on our human qualities. Are we capable of empathy? Are we willing to give up some comfort and routine to protect others? To help those most at risk? This is what guided my communication with colleagues. Even though I (still) can’t force anyone to work from home, I made it clear that I expect everyone to do so—except in exceptional cases tied to workflow, not personal preferences. This is a matter of social responsibility. The battle against the coronavirus is like the epic Yugoslav WWII film the Battle of Sutjeska—a battle to save the wounded. Though in the sequel, the hero is not Richard Burton but Elizabeth Taylor, barricaded on Sveti Stefan. The health crisis will eventually end—but the economic and social consequences will be deep and lasting. The way we respond to them will critically shape the world we live in afterward. We have an opportunity to make it a better one than before. Are we mature and rational enough to recognize the importance of solidarity and cooperation in addressing global, regional, and local challenges? Will we understand just how small, fragile, and interdependent this world really is? Will we see how dangerous it is, in the face of a global threat, to rely on populism and mock science and experts? Will we appreciate the importance of international solidarity, multilateral cooperation, and global governance—which has lately become a favorite target of nationalists, whose power depends on convincing you that every threat comes from outside? There are no guarantees that we’ll get the right answers to these questions after the crisis. Threats like this breed fear, and fear drives irrationality, panic, division, and hatred. And yet—I haven’t lost hope. What other choice do we have? Without cynicism, I say this: Too many of us will survive for us to ignore the fact that the coronavirus threatens not only our health but the very kind of society in which we can live with dignity—not merely survive. If at all.

There’s no single answer to the question of why so many people, after enduring decades of authoritarianism and ideological conformity, so quickly became disillusioned with the democracy they once longed for. Eastern Europe’s disappointment with pluralist democracy is certainly part of a broader story—the global resurgence of populism driven by unbridled neoliberal globalization, which gave us Brexit, Trump, and others like them. But Eastern Europe has its own story, with its own reasons for the renewed flirtation with authoritarianism and strong leaders—reasons that are related, but not identical, to those that put a Slovenian son-in-law in the White House or convinced the British to free themselves from the Brussels yoke of European integration, solidarity, and cooperation. While globalization without social safeguards led to stagnating or declining living standards for the middle and lower-middle classes in most developed Western economies, people in the East—at least on average—do have more than they did before political transitions. That’s a broad generalization, of course. It doesn’t take into account the loss of even minimal social security or the stark income disparities, which can’t always be convincingly explained by differences in talent, work ethic, or intelligence. Still, the differences are clear. On average, we earn more and have more. This was especially evident in Poland, which almost completely avoided the effects of the global financial crisis and maintained steady economic growth, yet it still didn’t escape the temptation of illiberal populism. Bulgarian political scientist Ivan Krastev recently explained this paradox with Nutella. He argued that the growing rejection of pluralist democracy can, at least partly, be explained by psychology. Political change in Eastern Europe came after years of yearning to live like those on the other side of the ideological divide. The reason for the quick reversal after the fall of the Iron Curtain, he suggests, is that the desire to imitate someone else is inherently negative—it puts the imitator in a second-class position, breeds frustration, and undermines self-respect. The outrage in Poland over Nutella allegedly being of lower quality than in Italy or France illustrates this sensitivity and the feeling that, despite all the political changes built on liberal democratic values—or, as authoritarian populists subtly suggest, because of them—Eastern Europeans are still second-rate Europeans. Add to that the fact that most people, despite a higher standard of living, still don’t live as well as they hoped or expected. This brings us to another oft-cited reason: relative deprivation—the frustration of people whose lives have improved, but not nearly as much as those whose success doesn't seem deserved by merit or effort. Eastern populists have found their path to power eased by the fact that those who preached democratic values during the political transition often failed to practice them. Instead of functioning democracies, many Eastern European countries ended up with half-baked systems lacking proper safeguards and checks. The rapid accession to the EU was interpreted as a stamp of democratic excellence, which in turn stalled reforms at a critical moment—when democratic immune systems were still under construction. This idea of incomplete democracies is confirmed by the latest Global State of Democracy report from the international organization IDEA, which concludes that while there are more democracies in the world than ever before, their quality is deteriorating. The problem is that sloppy democracy is dysfunctional—it enables abuse and undermines public trust in institutions. This became especially clear during the financial crisis, which further weakened trust in both political and financial establishments, opening the door to populist, authoritarian, and nationalist alternatives. People, justifiably angry at elites who offered them a corrupted version of democracy riddled with self-interest, turned their frustration not just on the “democrats” but on democracy itself. Disillusionment with democracy always takes on local flavors. In Slovenia, it often surfaces as resistance to so-called ideological polarization and an embrace of “project-based” politics in the national interest. But this term, ideological polarization, is slippery. It's never quite clear what we’re talking about. If it means polarization between democracy (based on human rights, political freedoms, and pluralism) on one side, and illiberal nationalism on the other, then overcoming it would run counter to the principles of the organization I work for. If it refers to ending the division between partisans and collaborators (a reference to WWII history in Slovenia), we have to ask whether that’s about respectfully bringing closure to our painful past—or a veiled attempt at historical revisionism aimed at reshaping the future. If it means abandoning divisions between left, center, and right, then we are rejecting the essence of democratic political pluralism, which is built on the democratic contest of diverse ideas, programs, and opinions. We’ve already lived through ideological conformity in the past. Slovenia is now getting a new government. I don’t deny the legitimacy or democratic nature of some political parties forming a new coalition based on the mandates they received in the last elections. Whether some of them have disappointed their voter base is fair game for commentary, criticism, and even protest—but it doesn’t strip them of the right to make decisions. That said, we shouldn’t pretend those decisions are apolitical or ideologically neutral. In a democracy, coalitions are always built on political interests. No single party represents the entire population or all interest groups. As long as there is transparency, accountability, legal and political oversight—including by the media and civil society—and, crucially, regular elections where voters can render judgment, this is not undemocratic. Quite the opposite. We should be more concerned when particular interests are cloaked in nationalistic rhetoric. Our problem isn’t political division—it’s a lack of political culture. In a democracy, “not left, not right, not center, but forward” means consistent respect for democratic principles, the rule of law, human rights, freedom of expression, media independence, judicial autonomy, and the rejection of authoritarian nationalism. The Slovenian constitution also states that we are a social state. These are binding commitments. Any attempt to justify deviations from these constitutional and European principles in the name of progress or unity is unacceptable. Pluralist democracy requires a left, center, and right. That doesn’t rule out cooperation—but every combination remains a political one. How the baggage of each side is handled depends on whether it stays in the trunk or becomes shared political responsibility. Look at our neighbors. Austria’s new black-green coalition (conservatives and Greens) is not just a “project”—it’s political and ideological. The People’s Party accepted political responsibility for the green part of the platform, and vice versa. What comes of it will be judged at the next election. In a democracy, we can’t expect only ideologically similar parties to rule. But we have the right to demand that whoever governs—regardless of political color—respects democratic rules.

When MP Primož Siter from the Slovenian Left party recently appeared at the National Assembly’s podium wearing a t-shirt of the American punk band Bad Religion—featuring a crossed-out Christian cross—a segment of Slovenian politics, the public, and the media (in the broadest sense) erupted in outrage. They called for his criminal prosecution under Article 297 of the Penal Code, which addresses public incitement to hatred, violence, or intolerance. Just over a week before Siter’s appearance, a teenage girl named Mila from the southern French town of Vienne also voiced her opinion on religion on social media—and she certainly didn’t mince words. “I hate religion,” she said. “The Quran is full of hate, Islam is just shit.” She went even further in her outburst, apparently provoked by insults from a rejected admirer, presumed to be Muslim. Her post immediately triggered a response from the French authorities. Prosecutors launched an investigation into public incitement to hatred, and the justice minister condemned the insult to religious sentiments, calling Mila’s outburst “an attack on freedom of conscience.” Former presidential candidate and Socialist Ségolène Royal chimed in: "Je ne suis pas Mila" (“I am not Mila”). The backlash on social media was even fiercer. The 16-year-old was subjected to a barrage of insults and threats, including threats of violence. Her parents had to withdraw her from school, and she was placed under police protection. After a few days of widespread outrage, there was a sobering shift. First, the justice minister apologized for her “clumsy” remarks. Then, the magazine L’Express published a letter signed by a group of prominent intellectuals, led by philosopher and historian Élisabeth Badinter. The letter expressed outrage at the cowardice of the media and authorities, who had left a minor at the mercy of a frenzied commentariat. “We may disagree with what this young girl said,” the letter stated, “but nothing she said was illegal.” Mohammed Moussai, president of the French Council for the Muslim Faith, responded similarly, affirming that criticism of Islam must be allowed and that all discussions should be accepted while rejecting any form of violence. Finally, President Emmanuel Macron spoke out in Mila’s defense, asserting that she had the right to safety and protection. Macron emphasized the right to a critical—even mocking—attitude toward religion. In a democracy, he said, we have the right to blasphemy. This is a highly sensitive topic in France. The threat of violence in response to criticism or caricature of Islam is not theoretical. This year marks the fifth anniversary of the terrorist attack on the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo, which published cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad and lost ten of its staff, along with two police officers. The stories of Primož and Mila are instructive, as they highlight the complexity and sensitivity of freedom of speech, and the societal responses to legal expressions that are subjectively perceived as offensive. First, it must be emphasized that being offensive is not enough for prosecution. According to rulings of the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression includes speech that “offends, shocks, or disturbs.” The local French prosecutor ultimately acknowledged this by dropping the case against Mila—likely disappointing those in Slovenia who demanded prosecution for the Left’s MP. But just because freedom of speech permits insult, that doesn’t mean every insult expands the space for freedom or democracy. And just because something isn’t forbidden doesn’t mean it’s right, decent, or good. The quote often falsely attributed to Voltaire—that we must defend someone’s right to say something even if we hate what they say—does not mean we have to applaud every such statement. Au contraire, as a French philosopher might say. We can also flip the logic: just because we disagree with someone doesn’t mean we’re excused from defending their right to free speech. That’s the core of the appeals made by Badinter and Macron. We must protect those who, because of their expression, face responses that can’t be justified as others’ freedom of expression. Especially when the speaker is young and vulnerable, like Mila. Consistency is also vital in democracy. Unlike many of our compatriots who were offended by the t-shirt, Macron does not interpret the right to defamation selectively. In other words, the right to critique applies to all religions—not just some.
