Around the same time Mila posted her comments, French public radio France Inter featured comedian Frédéric Fromet, who made such off-color jokes about Jesus that Primož Siter, by comparison, looked like a squeaky-clean altar boy. There’s also the matter of what kind of societal response is appropriate to legal speech that may offend, shock, or disturb—and when that response is warranted. Here, perhaps the most important criterion is the balance of power. On this front, there is a major difference between Primož and Mila. Siter is an MP. Even though his party is in opposition, it’s hard to deny he speaks from a safe and comfortable position of relative social influence and power. The audience for his t-shirt was not the marginalized or powerless—it was his peers. His gesture was not a provocation from the weak against the strong, but more like one from equal to equal. That he broke no law is clear. That he threatened no one is also clear. Less clear is whether his action was politically wise or appropriate, or whether it genuinely contributed to greater freedom of expression or a higher level of political culture in Slovenia. Opinions on that are divided—even within his own party. And that’s fine. Protecting free speech does not mean immunity from criticism—not even from insulting counter-criticism. In Mila’s case, the power dynamics are far more complex. While her words were objectively harsher and more offensive than Primož’s t-shirt, Mila is, in significant ways, a victim. She is unquestionably more vulnerable and at risk. First, there’s the gender dynamic—her outburst followed verbal abuse from a boy who couldn’t handle rejection. Mila is also endangered as a young girl targeted by anonymous but dangerous extremists, which forced her to change schools and accept police protection. For these reasons, society’s support for Mila was necessary and justified. There’s one more power dynamic at play in Mila’s case: the one between the white French majority (to which she belongs) and the immigrant minority. The social marginalization and discrimination faced by the latter in no way justifies the harasser’s actions—much less the violent threats from extremists—but it does require a degree of solidarity and respect toward people who, even while rejecting extremism, feel hurt by attacks on their religion and identity. President Macron understood this too when he emphasized that the right to blasphemy does not include the right to incite violence or attack human dignity. The line between the two is thin. Navigating it requires great social and political wisdom, sensitivity, and above all, an unwavering commitment to democratic values. Without these values, politics is not true democracy—it’s a project doomed to social tension, conflict, and failure.

I’m writing this column on a plane en route to Kraków, where I’ve been invited by Education International, the world’s largest global organization of educators, representing more than thirty million teachers worldwide. I’ll be speaking about how to pass on the memory of the Holocaust to younger generations—or about Holocaustology, as some dissenters sarcastically call it—one day after world leaders once again laid wreaths near Auschwitz, bowed in remembrance of the victims, and repeated the words “never again.” Like most of you, I grew up in a country that no longer exists—a country Slovenia left just in time, before what was left of it exploded in a bloody outburst of blind nationalism and interethnic hatred. In the years since Srebrenica, the ceremonial repetition of “never again” rings even more hollow and unconvincing. Like many of you, I went to school at a time when the narrative of World War II events was heavily influenced by the ruling ideology. That ideological indoctrination irritated me, as it did many others, but it never clouded my understanding of who was the victim and who the perpetrator, or my moral stance toward the crimes committed just twenty-some years before I was born—whether in the name of race, nation, or the treacherous opportunism of Nazi collaborators. Part of that understanding came from personal family experience: my grandparents were deported from Nazi-annexed Styria to Bosnia. My grandmother, still bleeding from childbirth, lay on the floor of a cattle wagon with her newborn daughter, whom she had been forced to leave behind with neighbours—because the baby had just been born and her name had not yet made it onto the deportation list. These were bureaucrats of fanatical precision. They were tidy, organized, and ruthlessly efficient. They built excellent highways—the best in the world, in fact. No one built highways like they did. My grandmother and grandfather never saw their baby girl again. There is nothing unusual about this story. Millions were murdered. Many others, like my aunt, died as collateral victims of Nazi crimes. But this family history helped me retain empathy—and avoid the comforting lie that such horrors happened only to other people, and only could happen to other people. I remember, as a teenager in the formative years when a sense of self and worldview begin to solidify, seeing a photograph many of you likely know. It was taken in 1942 near the Ukrainian city of Ivanhorod, during the Holocaust by bullets, when SS Einsatzgruppen and their local collaborators murdered nearly 1.5 million Jews in the occupied Soviet territories. In the photo, a desperate mother clutches her child, shielding them from the terror around them—from the inevitability of death. A man in uniform—killer, not soldier—stands with his rifle angled at 90 degrees, legs slightly spread for better aim as he prepares to kill a woman and her child. The mother cannot save her child. She dies before the bullet even strikes. The man radiates protocol, training, discipline. The Holocaust was not carried out by a random gang of homicidal maniacs. It was a crime ordered by politicians, prepared by bureaucrats, and carried out by men in uniform—enabled by ordinary people. People without empathy, or without the courage to resist the evil surrounding them. Auschwitz didn’t fall from the sky, as Holocaust survivor Marian Turski reminded world leaders at the Monday ceremony. The Holocaust didn’t begin when the Einsatzgruppen began raiding Jewish communities in Ukraine. This darkest stain on humanity’s collective memory—one that some in Slovenia now dismiss or question with no consequence—didn’t begin with the first trains to Auschwitz, or when Zyklon B was piped into fake showers, or when the crematoriums were fired up. The Holocaust, in which six million people were murdered, began long before that—the moment politicians discovered the political utility of peddling hatred. When the legal and bureaucratic dehumanization of future victims began. When ordinary people were trained, like hunting dogs, to become used to blood. When they lost the capacity for compassion, solidarity, and basic humanity. When indifference prevailed. When people were ready to shrug at atrocity and look the other way. Never again, you say? Because today we live in a world governed by empathy? One where antisemitism and racism have been vanquished? A world where we are not indifferent to those in distress—people dying before our eyes? Where the brave prevail—those willing to stand up to political merchants of hate? Because our politics consistently and resolutely reject intolerance and call for solidarity and humanism? Because we live in a society where there are no scapegoats for all our misfortunes? Where newspapers don’t compare people to parasites? A world where faith and culture are not worn like uniforms or wielded like clubs against those who are different? A world without paramilitary patrols lurking in the woods and on national stages? A world where blind, unbridled nationalism isn’t once again growing stronger? Tears over yesterday’s crimes are meaningless if they are accompanied by indifference to today’s racism and exclusion, Marian Turski told the politicians gathered at Auschwitz. It would be nice if they took his words to heart. Our own president was there, too. But laying a wreath once a year, lighting candles, and uttering a few hollow, worn-out phrases is not enough to protect us from plunging once again into the abyss of total inhumanity. What matters is what politicians—and all of us—do during the 364 days before and after. Every day. At every outburst of hate and intolerance. At every attack on human dignity. At every sign that, as a society, we are once again losing empathy, humanity, solidarity. At every sign that we are once again being conditioned, slowly, like hounds, to accept blood. That we might be ready, when the second act comes, to look away. Or even take part. I don’t know—and I can’t say for certain—that history will repeat itself. I damn well hope it won’t. But I am absolutely sure of one thing: There is no guarantee that it can’t. Especially if we remain this indifferent to the hatred that surrounds us. The least we can do is to add a question mark to that tired phrase “never again.” Let’s remember the words of Primo Levi, the Italian-Jewish writer who survived the horrors of Auschwitz: “It happened. Therefore, it can happen again.”

If anything good came out of the recent early-morning session to rescue our soldiers from Iraq, it is that we now know our president likes little videos. That can be very useful. In my job, for example, we have produced a whole series of short videos and other illustrated educational material that explain the basic information and knowledge in our field of work to eager young learners in an accessible way. Unfortunately, our organization’s remit explicitly excludes defense and military matters, so I can hardly offer help on how the supreme commander of the armed forces should behave in situations involving important military and foreign-policy issues. But even though I don’t know much about military matters, I would venture to say: not the way we saw in the president’s video. I am not entirely convinced that citizens’ legitimate expectations of how a supreme commander should act in such situations can be satisfied by a presidential scowl about which, with the best will in the world, you can’t tell whether it is caused by the weight of command responsibility or just one or two cabbage rolls too many. There is, however, a whole range of videos and picture books that can explain to the president—and not only to him—the basic concepts of some of the fundamental institutions on which a functioning pluralist democracy rests and depends. Freedom of expression, for example. In Slovenia we all know everything about these things, and yet, or perhaps precisely because of that, we have a whole host of problems with them. In the name of respecting different opinions, the President of the Republic of Slovenia recently listened to a ceremonial speech by a man serving a prison sentence for economic crime. If this becomes a habit, it would be worth including an honor guard of judicial police officers in state protocol. It would come in handy again as early as the commemoration at Osankarica. The belief that respecting freedom of expression requires us to respect any speech and all different opinions is, of course, wrong. You won’t find it in any handbook, any picture book, any video or any judgment of the European Court of Human Rights. On the contrary, freedom of expression as defined and protected by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights functions normally only if society is able and willing to respond clearly and firmly to abuses of this freedom to express intolerance and hatred or to undermine the democratic institutions and values that we protected in the Constitution at independence. It probably goes without saying that in this social response, the voice of people in elected political office is particularly important. For example, the voice of the President of the Republic. So when, some time ago, one of the Slovenian MPs vulgarly attacked the members of the Constitutional Court, the problem was not that there was no criminal prosecution, but that instead of a firm public reaction in defense of one of the key institutions of the rule of law, we were confronted with silence—in the name of respecting different opinions. This silence legitimizes hatred and gives it cover. Tolerance of intolerance does not defend freedom of expression and democracy; it endangers them. On the other hand, a video about freedom of expression might also be watched by those who, whenever they encounter speech that disturbs, offends or shocks, start grasping for repression, bans and prosecutors. Democracy is not a real democracy if its survival depends on censorship. In this light, it cannot and must not be a problem if the leader of the largest opposition party in the country is given the opportunity on public television to present his views, even though his public appearances, especially on social networks, are often tinged with offensive messages. The threat to democracy would arise if the opposition leader did not have this opportunity. The problem is rather that, when he appears on television, he doesn’t have to answer for such views. Because a “balance” derived from a misunderstanding of freedom of expression prevents journalists from asking uncomfortable questions. Which, in a functioning democracy, they ought to. A weak understanding of freedom of expression is also reflected in the increasingly tiresome political replaying of the film Home Alone, in which you no longer know who is Kevin, who is the burglar and who is Donald Trump. Those who lost it over a state secretary’s tweet are now making a racket in the streets and on social networks, demanding his resignation. Others mock them, saying this contradicts their usual positions on freedom of expression, which they use mainly to legitimize their own intolerant views and statements. I would suggest both sides calm down. The tweet was clumsy and inappropriate. Someone in political office should have enough judgment to avoid such a mess. And if he slips up, he must be prepared to accept the consequences, including public criticism and outrage. In a democracy, it is perfectly legitimate for people to protest against a statement they subjectively experience as shocking, offensive and disturbing. Another question is whether this anger is really entirely spontaneous and free of political motives. I also doubt that this unfortunate tweet can really be characterized as hate speech that should be followed by resignation and all the other sanctions loudly demanded by the indignant right. A thoughtless blunder is one thing; a political witch-hunt and hatred of people who celebrate Christmas is quite another. Which, let us be clear, here at home is not something only right-wingers do. I found no indication that this was anything other than stupidity and a slip-up. Unlike many other public statements that are without doubt part of deliberate and continuous intolerance and the spreading of hatred against certain groups and individuals. And about which, including those clearly tinged with racism and antisemitism, no condemnation was heard either from those now demanding Štromajer’s head or from those who, in the name of a misunderstanding of freedom of expression, are always and ever more deafeningly silent. Moreover, the state secretary repented and apologized for his statement. In the Slovenian context, this is a great rarity that should be taken into account. In this story, the prime minister should also watch a picture book or video. His statement that this state secretary should resign over his slip-up because it happened while he was already in office—unlike his own state secretary, who can stay where he is because he spread his own considerably cruder, intolerant and racist statements “only” before being appointed to his cabinet—is, to put it mildly, not serious. In the second case there was neither distancing nor an apology. What is more, in a later interview the state secretary even boasted of his statements, saying that with them he had pushed the boundaries of freedom of expression in our country. In Slovenian politics, the prime minister certainly deserves the compliment of being the sharpest tongue in the local tavern, but sometimes that is simply not enough. When it comes to intolerance and racism, for example, it is good to be clear, principled and consistent. “Those are my principles!” Groucho Marx declared in one of his films. “And if you don’t like them… well, I have others.” Good joke, you’ll say, but Groucho was a comedian.

It isn’t always easy being a father. For example, in moments when your child is in distress, when you sense that fear is about to overwhelm him and helplessness will prevail. When the football team your ten-year-old son plays for is losing nil–three at half-time to those show-offs in the dark blue shirts of Racing, Strasbourg’s top-flight club. In the imagination of every local kid, and many of their parents, this club is the first step and an obligatory stop in dreams of a successful career that will eventually take them to Barcelona, Liverpool, Bayern or PSG. Every year Racing holds a kind of audition at which hundreds of boys and girls aged eight to twelve from every club in Alsace chase desperately after the ball in indescribable chaos, trying to show off their football skills under the bored gaze of Racing’s club coaches. Whether anyone has ever actually been picked at this fair, I don’t know; perhaps it is more a PR operation than a serious attempt to find new talent. Tristan didn’t go last year or the year before, not, of course, because I as his father wasn’t convinced he was more than good enough, but mainly because he didn’t want to. Otherwise, we at home are very happy with the club he plays for, because of the coaches’ attitude to the children and the attention they pay to mutual respect, fair play, responsibility to the team and all the other values and qualities we attribute to team sports but in the real world most often forget because of uncompromising and heartless competitiveness and the chase for money. After all, even Mbappé didn’t start his career at Monaco but at AS Bondy, a club from the Paris suburbs. Uncompromising and heartless competitiveness or not, a match against those snotty, stuck-up kids in Racing’s dark blue shirts is still a special challenge. Tristan’s team had been preparing for it since the start of the season. And then came that Saturday when we drove our budding stars to the training center and talent incubator meant to have them playing in a few years’ time against the stars of Marseille, Lyon and PSG. There, of course, they have real grass, and a covered pitch when it rains, not the artificial turf on which our boys and girls from ASS scrape their knees in snow, sun and rain. The match has a special significance because the two clubs share a long history. ASS, the Association Sportive de Strasbourg, is one of the oldest football clubs in France. It was founded in 1890 as the Strassburger Fussball Club, since Alsace was then part of the German Empire. Racing was put together only a good fifteen years later. When a professional league was established in France in the 1930s, Racing joined it, while ASS, as Jacques, the club president, often and very loudly explains, chose to remain amateur. “Le foot,” says Jacques, “has never been a business for us, but a mission. If you don’t have a decent school report at the end of the year, you don’t play.” That Saturday it was raining, as befits a proper derby. On the touchline there was a crowd of supporters, mostly parents of the home team’s stars, arrogantly and rowdily predicting that the match was decided in advance. A small group of ASS parents, much more calmly and with the dignity befitting a club for which football is not a business but a mission, quietly and fearfully expected a similar result. And then came that terrible first half, in which dark blue shirts were everywhere and red-and-white ones nowhere. You could feel the nervousness and fear. The ball wouldn’t move, there was no game; Salimu, Tristan’s rival for the striker’s spot, first tormented every ball he got with forced dribbling and then lost it. Three goals, in very quick succession, like a burst of gunfire. These are the moments when you try to explain to your child that defeats are part of life, that without them we cannot, and do not know how to, truly appreciate future victories. That real strength of character shows in the moments when we must admit that this time we won’t succeed. I looked in my son’s eyes for a spark of understanding, perhaps of anger, which, once he got over his disappointment, would help him overcome despair and kindle new hope. At my words, Tristan rolled his eyes and went off to the coach instead, from whom he evidently expected more useful advice for the second half. Salimu was angrily twitching his ears, looking alternately at the ground and at his father, who stood scowling on the touchline. Salimu was born in France; his father is from Senegal. Tristan’s team is very diverse. Although all of them except Tristan are French citizens, most come from the nearby Strasbourg district of Cronenbourg, dominated by immigrants from France’s former colonies and many other parts of the world. It is not so much a demographic reflection of today’s France. Tristan’s team, with a few exceptions, reflects above all the most forgotten, most marginalized and most unheard part of French society. Salimu, Gaddiel, Aziz, Sabri, Mathis, Issham and Teva come from second- or third-generation immigrant families who are formally all French, but in the eyes of most people they are not. My friend Ridha, whose parents immigrated to France from Tunisia, graduated years ago from a prestigious business school in Strasbourg. All his classmates found jobs within a few weeks of graduating, while Ridha was still unemployed a year and a half later. Send your application as Claude Martin, I once advised him, as a joke. He didn’t find it funny. In the end he had had enough of equality, fraternity and liberty and went to Switzerland, where he immediately found a job. The French don’t count themselves by ethnicity or religion, because they are nominally and formally all equal. This has led to a hidden segregation that very much exists, even though official statistics don’t register it. These are topics people prefer not to mention. When, four years ago, the then prime minister, the Socialist Manuel Valls, spoke of fellow citizens living “in ghettos… in territorial, social and ethnic apartheid,” he was attacked from all sides, especially from the right. Eking out a living in the suburbs is not a theme of the social protests against President Macron either. The fate of Tristan’s teammates and their families is of little interest to the yellow vests, which are above all a revolt of the white lower middle class from the provinces against Paris, or to the striking railway workers, doctors, lawyers and ballet dancers of the Paris Opera fighting to preserve special statuses in jobs to which immigrants from the suburbs mostly have no access. Their fellow citizens are prepared to accept and respect them only if they bring them victory at the football World Cup. Only in those moments of euphoria and celebration on the Champs-Élysées is a certain Zinedine no longer just an Algerian from Marseille but a true Frenchman, a national hero. And in this sad truth lies the reason for Salimu’s father’s scowl. For him, his son’s sport is not just a healthy way to spend free time and hang out with friends, along with more or less serious dreams of breaking through to stardom. It is a serious, planned attempt to escape social marginality and hopelessness. After every training session, when Tristan and I head home, Salimu is still on the pitch, listening to his father’s stern analysis of missed chances and mistakes. Of course he knows that the chances of success are extremely small, but at least there are some. That Saturday, in the match against Racing, the coach’s advice worked much better than mine. The boys threw themselves onto the pitch with incredible energy and soon silenced those little show-offs in Racing shirts and their parents. They pushed the game forward, squeezed Racing in its own half and completely confused their opponents. Spoiled stars are not used to anyone resisting them. In very quick succession, like a burst of gunfire, Tristan managed to put the ball in the net three times. In the excitement at their own efficiency, attention slipped for a moment and Racing took the lead again. Right at the end of the match, Salimu got the ball. This time he didn’t get flustered, didn’t try to imitate Messi’s feints, but passed to Sabri, who had no trouble beating Racing’s helpless goalkeeper. A draw, sweeter than any victory. Uncompromising and heartless competitiveness or not, the feeling was divine. While I was jumping up and down and shouting undignifiedly, a small smile appeared on the face of Salimu’s father for the first time since I have known him. It isn’t always easy being a father, but sometimes it is really very nice.

Lenin once said there are decades when nothing happens, and days when decades happen. The one that’s about to stumble to its end in a few days fell somewhere in between. A decade full of fateful turning points that—perhaps precisely because of that—dragged on like a string of chicken guts. And in most ways, things got worse. Part of this period, I was professionally responsible for analyzing geopolitical changes in the international environment. The job wasn’t too demanding; in most cases, it was enough to predict the worst-case scenario. I’m exaggerating a bit—but not enough to feel any relief. If I had to choose one feature that most characterizes the changes of recent years, it would be the loss of a sense of security. People are no longer optimistic. The excitement and belief in a better future, so characteristic of the late 1990s and early 2000s, has been replaced by fear. In the situation we’ve found ourselves in, there are plenty of wrong responses. For example, we can pretend everything is fine. We ignore the obvious signs that things are heading in the wrong direction—because it’s easier, because it scares us less, or because it lets us continue acting selfishly while fooling ourselves that someone else will pay the price. We can also throw up our hands and say we can’t change anything. We complain without seeking solutions. Or complain that we’re complaining—still without seeking solutions. Because we don’t know where to start. Solving the existential problems of today’s world is hard, especially since reality isn’t a Hollywood production with a single villain. It’s what the Americans would call a clusterfuck. We’re not in a mess—we’re in many messes. Many of the issues that keep us up at night—climate change, growing inequality, social frustration and tension, real and imagined religious and cultural conflicts, a sense of threat, fear of migration—are not root causes, but symptoms of deeper, structural processes that have been developing for decades. Which means they won’t be solved without deep, structural, and long-term responses. The problem is, to solve today’s challenges effectively, we’d need a different world than the one we live in. Fear and powerlessness breed distrust, selfishness, and hatred. They block solidarity and shared responsibility—without which, there can be no solutions. The threats remain unresolved, generating more fear, deeper divisions, and more selfishness. And the circle closes. Still, I believe it’s not too late. We have to start somewhere. Perhaps by addressing the wreckage caused by the last financial crisis. Although it began in 2007 and peaked around 2009, its consequences—and even more so, the consequences of how it was handled—hit hardest years later. They’re still hitting us. The middle class—that broad band of society that, since WWII, formed the backbone of left-wing, centrist, and even conservative parties in Western democracies—was already eroding before the crisis. The culprit was the long-standing alliance between politics and economic neoliberalism. The financial crisis broke the dam. Stripped of social security, dignity, a sense of future, and of control over their lives, much of the middle class was driven into the arms of right-wing populism. Aristotle already explained that stable democracy cannot exist without a strong middle class. His lesson that nature abhors a vacuum helps us understand how quickly a deceived and resentful public can veer ideologically. Their anger became the fuel for manipulative politics based on fear and hatred, on division and fantasies of returning to the “good old sovereign times” that never actually existed. We need to defuse this time bomb before it unleashes its full destructive force. That won’t fix everything overnight—but it’s a precondition for turning back toward the values of solidarity, empathy, and shared responsibility. Without those, there can be no civilized social coexistence. And without that, we’ll be helpless to address every other pressing societal and global challenge. It won’t be easy. The middle class isn’t a vase you can smash against a wall and then just glue back together. Today’s middle class is fading; the emerging one is structurally different. Workers and clerks are being replaced by people in far more fluid professional situations, many of whom will work in jobs that don’t yet exist. If fluidity and flexibility are just softer terms for living on the edge of poverty, we’re in trouble. If we patch up the middle class at the expense of those at the bottom, we’re in even deeper trouble. The European democratic and economic model is utterly dependent on solidarity. Populism is what happens when European politics forgets this. Neither pluralistic democracy nor market economies can survive without the support of a broad majority. And that support will vanish if most people feel like they’re systematically left behind. Investing in social justice is investing in stability and security. Without it, we risk falling into extreme ideologies that Europe already knows too well from its past. On one side, authoritarian repression in the name of the nation; on the other, the wet dreams of Sunday revolutionaries for a replay of social utopias that only work with an iron fist. I don’t believe either of those throwbacks would last long—but before they failed, they could still cause a great deal of harm and suffering. This isn’t the naïve moralizing of a salon socialist. Neoliberalism is a factory of social tension and instability. It doesn’t just threaten pluralistic democracy—it also undermines the market economy. At least the kind roughly aligned with the European Social Charter or Article 2 of the Slovenian Constitution. From the standpoint of capital, neoliberalism is about short-term greed winning out over long-term interest. But the call for more social justice isn’t about party politics. It’s not about supporting one party or another. Supporting greater solidarity, justice, and shared responsibility doesn’t mean there’s only one right approach. On the contrary—it leaves space for a wide range of solutions, ideologies, political platforms. The added value of democracy is precisely that: a forum for competing views. Forced unity always serves uniformity. The only boundaries are the values we wrote into our constitution and invoked during our independence: the values that should prevent us from structurally pushing people into poverty—or leaving them there—and the values that allow people to live well from their work, knowledge, and talent, even to thrive. That last part is what I wish for you in the new year—and the years after that. If you can’t get rich, I hope at least you live better. Not at the expense of others, but together with them. May the new decade not just be a continuation of the one we’re leaving behind. Enough with the chicken guts.

Two elderly ladies sit in the restaurant of a mountain resort, scowling at their plates. “The food here is terrible,” says the first. “Yes,” replies the second, “and such small portions too.” With this joke, Woody Allen illustrated his view on life in Annie Hall. The older I get, the less funny it seems. I was reminded of it recently while moderating a panel organized by the European Commission on strengthening democracy in the 21st century at the World Forum for Democracy in Strasbourg. To kick off the discussion, a representative of the international organization IDEA—which focuses on democracy and elections—presented their latest report on the state of democracy in the world. “You’ll be surprised,” he said enthusiastically before starting. And we were. According to IDEA’s data-driven analysis of global freedom, democracy has never been better off. The world is becoming more democratic. The number of democratic countries is constantly rising. Everything is super-duper, declared the enthusiastic IDEAlist. And then, almost as an afterthought, he acknowledged a small problem: while democracy is spreading, its quality is deteriorating. “The portions are large,” the first lady might say. “Yes,” the second would reply gloomily, “but the food keeps getting worse.” IDEA’s findings are only seemingly surprising. They reflect a concept of democracy shaped three decades ago, when Fukuyama declared the “end of history.” After the fall of the Berlin Wall, it was widely assumed that all ideological battles were over, that liberal democracy had triumphed by a landslide, and all that remained was to set up the institutional infrastructure in places where it hadn’t existed—then we’d all live happily ever after in peace and democracy. Democracy as IKEA: a box of parts, a screwdriver, and instructions. Today it’s clear we celebrated too soon. Even if, as IDEA asserts, the number of countries that have established the bare minimum of democratic infrastructure—constitutions, laws, party pluralism, nominally independent judiciaries, free media, and so on—is increasing, the final result is a major disappointment for many. Some explain this as inexperience. Decades later, many still blame the “growing pains” of new democracies. “Look at the UK,” they say. “It took them centuries to build what they have.” Just be patient, and we’ll have democracy like the British. Sadly, it’s starting to seem like we already do. The UK is a cautionary tale: even democracies with centuries-old institutions are not immune to illiberal populism. Institutions don’t function in a vacuum; they require a supportive democratic environment—not just parliaments, laws, and courts, but politics and politicians committed to democratic values, and a critical mass of citizens who support, understand, and believe in democracy. Each in their own way, with differing views—since democracy can’t survive groupthink—but grounded in shared civilizational values. The institutional checklist IDEA uses gives an incomplete picture. If instead of ticking boxes, we ask people how they feel about the system they live in, the results are far more worrying. Most public opinion research, even in mature democracies, shows growing dissatisfaction, cynicism, and distrust toward the system—and a rising openness to authoritarian alternatives. The trends among young people are especially alarming. The 2016 study The Danger of Deconsolidation, by Yascha Mounk (Harvard) and Roberto Stefan Foa (Melbourne), found that only one-third of Dutch youth believe living in a democracy is very important. Two-thirds don’t care. Youth. In the Netherlands. Of course, democracy needs institutions. IDEA is right about that. Historical detours “in the name of the people” have brought too much suffering. Freedom can’t exist without a pluralist parliament, democratically accountable executive, independent judiciary, free speech, and civil society. But institutions are a necessary, not sufficient, condition for a functioning democracy. It also requires a democratic environment, a minimal standard of political culture and integrity among politicians, and citizens who trust institutions and see democracy as a system that reflects and respects their economic, social, and security expectations—and responds accordingly. We won’t achieve this overnight or by simply preaching that liberal democracy is great and that everyone who’s skeptical is a primitive fool manipulated by populists. We won’t save liberal democracy or its institutions without addressing the real suffering and injustice that have pushed large segments of the population into the arms of manipulative, nationalist, illiberal, intolerant, and increasingly authoritarian populism. Liberal democracy has been undermined by its own flirtation with the callous selfishness of economic neoliberalism. Democracy cannot survive if people have no hope or realistic prospects for the future—for themselves and their children. Hope for a job. Hope for housing. For a livable environment. We must invest in education, understanding, knowledge, skills, and opportunities that allow people—especially the young, but not only them—to engage with society and influence it. We need a clear and firm commitment to the values that underpin and sustain democracy. A political and civic engagement for a progressive society built on capacity, creativity, openness, and solidarity—one whose success, effectiveness, stability, and security stem from these traits. Democracy requires tolerance, humanism, and empathy. A society where compassion is reserved only for “our own” is doomed to fail. Without these core civilizational values, there is no freedom. For anyone. Not even for “us.” What remains is zero-sum social Darwinism, where you only win by beating someone else—and in the end, we all lose. Democracy demands integrity, competence, and accountability from its politics. We can’t defend the values of a democratic, progressive, civilized society with PR polish alone—we need responsibility, consistency, and the courage to stand up against ideas, discourses, and policies that seek political power by dismantling democratic and humanistic values. Without that responsibility and courage, there is no democratic culture, no democratic environment, no functioning democracy. We risk being left with hollowed-out institutions, vulnerable to those who will treat them like a pig treats a bellows—abusing them for their own gain. When we reach that point, even IDEA throws up its hands. Not only is the food worse— the portions are getting smaller, too.

The call that my father had died came on a sunny January Sunday morning almost thirteen years ago. I got in the car and drove to Slovenia. From Strasbourg to Ljubljana is just under 800 kilometers—usually spent in cheerful anticipation of holidays and seeing loved ones. This time was different. So sooner or later, everyone faces the loss of someone they love. But the fact that it's universal and inevitable doesn't make it any less painful. Grief and driving are not a good combination. That became obvious after just a few kilometers when I crossed the Rhine into Kehl, Germany. I had last seen my father there a few weeks earlier, boarding a train back to Ljubljana with my mother. The last image of him: waving from the train door, wearing his trademark wrinkled coat. Just a little wave with his fingers, like the Queen. “Goodbye,” he called. He looked tired. Goodbye. And the train left. At the intersection near the station, I almost crashed into a car in front of me. Luckily, it was Sunday, the weather was nice, and there were no trucks. If you have to drive while emotionally wrecked, those were ideal conditions. Eight hours of reflection, memories, and mourning. I don’t know exactly where in Germany the two Syrian brothers live—the ones who, in early November, received a desperate call from their twenty-year-old brother, begging them to come rescue him in Slovenia. But it’s possible they traveled the same highways I did that Sunday thirteen years ago. Except theirs was a Thursday, not a weekend. And unlike me, they were racing against time. Weekday traffic on German autobahns is a nightmare of cars and trucks. Imagine your GPS repeatedly announcing another traffic jam between you and your dying sibling. “Alternative route available?” the robotic voice asks. “Thirty kilometers longer, five minutes faster.” Five more minutes of hope in a terrifying race against time. How much strength did their brother still have, alone, exhausted, freezing in some Slovenian forest? The first major hazard on the road to Slovenia appears less than 100 kilometers in, near Pforzheim, where the six-lane autobahn abruptly narrows and plunges into the narrow Enz River valley. Pforzheim is known for having looked like today’s Syria by the end of WWII, after the Allies leveled it for its munitions factories. Near Stuttgart, about ninety minutes in, I called my boss, Terry Davis, then Secretary General of the Council of Europe, to say I’d be out of the office for a few days. As always on Sundays, he was in his office sipping espresso—banned at home by his wife because of his high blood pressure. Terry is an interesting character. Like many older British Labourites, he's a fierce Brexit supporter. That meant we traditionally clashed during his annual visits to Strasbourg. The last time we met, I told him it was easy for him to support Brexit—he wouldn’t have to live with the consequences for long. He called me a “snotty ageist.” A few days ago, as every year, I received a birthday card from him. A sweet old fart, despite some political delusions—above all, a decent human being. A bulldog-faced Englishman for whom I used to write speeches, always careful not to make them too emotional; otherwise, he’d get a lump in his throat and couldn’t go on. He didn’t spend weekends in the office just for the banned caffeine—he meticulously went through the mountains of paperwork our giant bureaucratic machine churned out each week. Once, I walked in and saw him reviewing applications for a secretarial post in our office in Graz, Austria. “Do you think the President of the European Commission sits in Berlaymont on Sundays reviewing secretary contracts?” I asked, full of smug bureaucratic arrogance. Terry, for once, didn’t snap. “I don’t know,” he said. “That’s his choice. But you can’t pretend to care about people if you forget the person. That contract might not mean much to you—but for her, it could change her life.” I still blush with shame when I think about it. Somewhere near Stuttgart Airport, I choked out the words, “My father died.” I didn’t cry. Terry did. The highway to Munich is mostly upgraded now, except for a narrow, steep stretch near Mühlhausen—built, they say, in the Third Reich. Hitler, as some like to say, got many things wrong but nailed it with highways. But when half of Europe’s cars hit that hill, not even the Führer’s infrastructure vision holds up. In a flash, you lose an hour. I hope the Syrian brothers took another route, but I have a feeling they got stuck there. It's entirely possible their brother lost the battle for his life because of the Slovenian cold, our indifference, and that damned Nazi-grade incline. At the summit, there's a sign showing the altitude and marking the European watershed divide. On one side, rivers flow to the Mediterranean; on the other, to the Baltic and North Seas. The Danube, which begins nearby, ends almost 3,000 kilometers away in the Black Sea. What the hell is a German river doing in the Black Sea? Why doesn’t it stay where it started? Rivers are tricky. Water inspires fear; it can be dangerous. We fight over it. We flee because of it. Water floods. You can drown in it. You can drown in the Kolpa River. We can direct water, but we can’t stop it. Water feeds us. Water connects us. Water gives life. Water is life. From there, the road to the Austrian Slovenian border in Karavanke Tunnel is more or less a straight line—if you make it through Munich, which lies roughly halfway between Strasbourg and Ljubljana. A lot has happened in Munich—more than just traffic jams. It’s smart to hit Austria early to avoid night speed limits. Imagine it’s a matter of life and death, and you’re not allowed to drive over 100 km/h. Luckily, I wasn’t in a hurry. My father was nearly seventy-five. He was already dead. On his way to the ceremony marking the nazi destruction of the village of Dražgoše in WWII, after feeling unwell, he bowed his head in a friend’s car and closed his eyes. That was it. Gone. That young man from Syria was twenty. The same age my eldest son is now. He died of hypothermia and exhaustion—waiting for his brothers, hoping those damn German autobahns in that promised German land weren’t as long and clogged as they were. My father had already died. That boy was still dying. I was already mourning. His brothers were still hoping. In vain. I think about what some of my fellow Slovenians write and say about people enduring inhuman trials in our rivers, on our barbed wire, in our forests. “Warning: Kolpa is polluted. One less. Bullet to the head—God will know his own.” That Thursday in the woods near Ilirska Bistrica, a human being died. In some Slovenians, something human is dying, too. During those days, the Prime Minister visited border towns and talked with locals about the troubles and challenges migrants and irregular border crossings cause. The President, meanwhile, spoke in Berlin about values, walls that no longer exist, and a Europe without borders. Neither of them mentioned the young man who died of exposure and exhaustion on one of those borders. But they could have—and should have. It’s good to care for people. But it’s not enough if, in doing so, you forget a human being.
Protecting the European Way of Life

Putting together a European Commission is no small feat. Every five years, the president-elect has to distribute portfolios determined not by the logic of the Commission’s competences but by the number of member states. In addition, the president has rather limited options in choosing team members, being more or less dependent on candidates chosen by the member states and approved by the European Parliament. It is roughly as if a national football coach had to put together a team of twenty-eight players he hadn’t chosen himself, all of whom had to be on the pitch the whole time. Preferably all in attack. Portfolios in the European Commission often give the impression of being illogical and artificially created. Most influence therefore lies in the hands of the unelected bureaucratic apparatus. From the point of view of the European Union’s democratic legitimacy this is rather questionable, but from the point of view of minimal efficiency, given the EU’s current institutional setup, it is practically inevitable. The newly appointed President of the European Commission tackled the distribution of roles with zeal and plenty of imagination. We got a proposal for dividing up the commissioners’ responsibilities that sounds like a mix of a TED Talk and Alan Ford. One of the most amusing appointments is the split between the Italian Paolo Gentiloni, responsible for “the economy,” and one of the three executive vice-presidents, Valdis Dombrovskis from Latvia, who will be in charge of “an economy that works for people.” I leave it to your imagination whom the Italian’s portfolio will work for. In this muddle, our Janez Lenarčič did quite well, with responsibility for crisis management. His portfolio is clear and concrete. Most of Europe’s population understands that crisis management is a portfolio that works for people. Some of the other newly minted commissioners may have considerably more trouble with the clarity and visibility of their mission. We Slovenians, of course, turned our noses up at the crisis management portfolio, which is not surprising. Once again we proved that no one can make us smaller and more insignificant than we can ourselves. In our eyes, a commissioner from Slovenia cannot get an important portfolio, because any portfolio a commissioner from Slovenia gets is by definition unimportant, because it was given to a commissioner from Slovenia. The most attention and criticism, however, was caused by the name of the portfolio given to the Greek Margaritis Schinas. The former chief spokesperson of the Juncker Commission is to be responsible in the new line-up for “protecting our European way of life.” What irritated some most about this poetic denomination is that the portfolio is to include migration policy. Although von der Leyen denies it, many understand the terminology as a message that the European way of life is most threatened by migrants. Whether von der Leyen’s decision was a deliberate flirtation with the populist far right or just clumsiness is not known, but the fact is that the incoming Commission president is sticking to it for now. In fact, she has little choice. The procedure for appointing the new Commission so far, both because of the choice of candidates by some member states and because of the European Parliament flexing its muscles, gives the impression that the former German defense minister does not have all the reins in her hands. In the dilemma between a concession to far-right populism and the need to maintain the new Commission president’s political authority, there is also a third way. Von der Leyen can keep the name but give the future commissioner new responsibilities. Instead of migration, which deserves a portfolio of its own, the future commissioner for protecting the European way of life could be put in charge of fighting the anti-liberal populism that threatens this way of life the most. To help shape the portfolio, I therefore offer a proposed organization chart for a new EU Directorate-General for the Fight against Populism (DG POP OUT), which would come under the remit of the future commissioner for protecting the European way of life. Directorate for History To understand the importance of protecting the European way of life, it is good to know how we Europeans arranged our lives in the past. Apart from rare and short-lived periods of peaceful coexistence, the history of the European way of life has been marked above all by the search for ways to take each other’s lives as efficiently as possible. The European project arose from the need to protect Europeans from themselves. As a rule, danger did not come to Europe from outside. The directorate’s task is to prevent historical amnesia and the political manipulation of historical facts aimed at undermining the European way of life. The directorate also includes an officer to assist heads of state, especially in Southeastern Europe, who do not understand why laying wreaths at monuments to collaborators of Nazi criminals is not cool. Could be an intern. Task Force for Critical Thinking The European way of life requires critical thinking, knowledge and the ability to make rational decisions, as opposed to populism, which is based on so-called common sense, the term we usually use for the accumulation of all the prejudices and fears people collect by the age of eighteen. Among other things, the task force provides pedagogical and therapeutic help to anti-vaxxers, to those who claim the Earth is not round, and to those who believe that reckless deregulation, privatization and aggressive tax cuts for the wealthiest end up benefiting all sections of the population and society as a whole. Inter-Service Group for Political Integrity The mandate of the inter-service group stems from the fact that populism is the opportunistic exploitation of problems, injustices and discontent that, in most cases, were not caused by the populists—for the simple reason that they were not in power—but by those who otherwise never stop talking about Europe and liberal democracy. The aim of the Inter-Service Group for Political Integrity is to help this politics, through more integrity, consistency and principle, stop sawing off the branch it is sitting on. Think Tank for a Democratic European Architecture In the name of the people, populism undermines democratic oversight of the executive and narrows the space for democratic decision-making in society. Technocracy without democratic legitimacy and oversight can have a similar effect, even when it acts with the best possible intentions. The Think Tank for a Democratic European Architecture is responsible for bureaucratic self-reflection. Directorate for Social Justice The European way of life is based on the liberal democratic values of pluralist democracy, human rights and the democratic rule of law. These values can truly come to life only in a society that is not excessively stratified. The populist attack on the European way of life was largely made possible by the neoliberal economic doctrine that has prevailed over the past thirty years in the politics of many European countries and within the EU institutions. Economic neoliberalism has economically, socially and politically marginalized a good part of the traditional electorate of Europe’s traditional social democratic, centrist and conservative parties and pushed them into the arms of populist extremes. Without social justice, there is no Europe as a political, economic, social and civilizational model. The directorate’s mandate is based on the fact that social justice is not an obstacle to economic success but, on the contrary, a necessary condition for long-term competitiveness. It is the difference between a low-wage economy and a society that is creative, innovative and able to mobilize all its resources fully. If we want to preserve our European way of life, it is not enough just to have a European Union; we need a European Union that works for people.

Patriotism without a flag is like soup without salt. Few things bring a lump to people’s throats as quickly as the sight of a sea of flag-waving patriots. Others, again, find such scenes hard to stomach, because they associate them with nationalism. It is not simple. It is true that nationalists love flags, but even the most die-hard of them would struggle to gather as many as the Danes hang out for an average children’s birthday party. On the house, the windows, the pavement, the cake, the wall, the chandelier and the neighbor’s underpants. The Danes are very proud of their flag. Supposedly God sent it to them about a thousand years ago when they were giving a beating to one of the Baltic peoples, even smaller than themselves. In those days God probably bought his flags wholesale, since he handed out very similar ones to the other Scandinavians. We Slovenians did not get our flag from God but through a public competition, but that does not mean it can’t whip us into a patriotic frenzy too. Remember the lady in Ilirska Bistrica beating the asphalt with the national banner. Our president is also a very passionate standard-bearer. When it comes to the size of the flagpole, you won’t find a hero in any stadium or sports hall with a longer one than the head of the Slovenian state. Only the Croatian president can compete with him to some extent, although she plays on other attributes and prefers to show off the state symbols in tight-fitting national team shirts with the coat of arms. Many like this; others don’t, saying, look at them, populists. I am more reserved in such judgments. I am not claiming that President Pahor is not a populist; I am only saying that he is not a populist merely because he waves a flag and cheers for every sport popular with his voters. Like-chasing and an obsession with being liked may cross the boundaries of good taste, but not necessarily democratic principles. Stadiums and sports halls are, however, a place where the popularist comes dangerously close to the populist. The message of a cheering, flag-waving politician in a national team jersey is that he is just one of us. And between “I am of the people” and “I am the people” there is only a small step, but one that can be fatal for democracy. Flag-waving is important in the context of populism also because populism casts itself as the sole defender of traditional values. People who care about democracy don’t pay enough attention to this. In the eyes of many voters in Europe, politics today is divided into two groups. In the first are those who advocate an open, progressive society, human rights, gays, lesbians, gender equality, migrants and the like. In the second is politics that claims to be on the side of security, family, national culture, identity and patriotism. When the cards are dealt like this, the game is already over and the winner known in advance. Caught in panic and helplessness, democratic politics has so far had more or less only two ideas in response to the populist challenge, each worse than the other. Part of this politics accepts and defends the division above with suicidal courage. We are progressives fighting for human rights, they say; the rest of you are undemocratic, narrow-minded yokels. This is a lovely gift to populism and a disservice to the real protection of human rights, which cannot be effective unless people understand and accept these rights as something that also protects them and what matters to them. Others, in despair at the populists’ electoral successes, resort to imitating them and compete with them in stoking hatred and fear. This is an even lovelier gift to extremists, since it legitimizes their politics, and in the end voters will always prefer the hard original to the soft version of political opportunism, which in its populist foreplay teases the basest emotions but never dares to go all the way. But there is also a third way. One that has the maturity and determination to stand up to the populists and strip them of the exclusive right to interpret traditional values. These values not only mean a great deal to many voters in European countries but are also one of the main criteria in deciding whom to vote for. People are devoted to their families, and rightly so. But why should love of family be based on prejudice and discrimination against homosexuals? Why shouldn’t love of and respect for the family be based on the right to family life of all people who love each other, and on the right of all children to a family, regardless of their parents’ sexual orientation? People want security, and they have every right to it. But why should they agree that security can only be ensured with razor wire, fences and walls? Why don’t we ensure it for people, who have every right to security, with an effective, rational, humane and firm security policy that is not based on political stoking and exploiting of prejudice and fear? People are attached to their culture and identity, and that is a good thing. But instead of the populist perversion of culture as a weapon for dividing people into ours and others, why not offer people an understanding of culture, heritage and identity that helps us get to know and respect one another? That allows us to be proud of who we are as individuals, as members of our nation and as members of the wider communities we belong to? Why not offer them a culture that helps us understand one another, not to the detriment of our identity but to its benefit? And finally, why not respect patriotism? People love their homeland and are glad to love their homeland. And that is very good and very right. But if we want to respect patriotism, we must defeat nationalism. We cannot and must not build love of our homeland on hatred of others. Patriotism demands more than flag-waving. Love of one’s homeland also needs to be defined in terms of values, by thinking about what fills us with pride in our homeland and why it is good to be Slovenian. Without this, patriotism is a devalued, generic label, without content or meaning. An empty shell that sooner or later is inhabited by nationalist hatred. True patriotism must also be able to be critical. Since we are devotees of traditional values, we can borrow a comparison from family life. Between children and parents there is, as a rule, deep and sincere love, but when a family member goes astray, true love shows itself through responsibility, help and, if necessary, firmness. What do you do if, in her old age, mother homeland wraps herself in a flag, sits down in the nearest bar and spends the whole afternoon drinking, smashing glasses, shouting and making threats? There are children who will sit down at the table, order another round of beer and join their red-faced parent in raising hell until someone punches them in the face and the police arrive, or the waitress throws them all out the door. History teaches us that such drunken brawls can also end very tragically. On the other hand, there are people with enough courage and sense to take the car keys from their drunk and rowdy homeland so that she doesn’t endanger herself and others, and drive her home to sober up and sleep it off. As far as I am concerned, there is no doubt who in this story really cares for their parents, who really cares about security and who is the true patriot.

Some people are color-blind; Brad Pitt apparently suffers from face blindness, which is why he doesn’t greet acquaintances in the street; I am blind to acronyms. It is not carelessness or snobbery but a cognitive dysfunction that prevents me from remembering any acronym longer than two letters. In my profession, this is a major handicap. A bureaucrat who struggles with acronyms is like a baker allergic to flour. I have devised a few tricks to help me avoid looking like an idiot at every single conversation or meeting, but my recognition of acronyms does not extend beyond WC. It is not hard to imagine my enthusiasm for the idea of naming one of the joint programs of the Council of Europe and the European Union DISCO. Finally, a name that won’t immediately slip my mind. DISCO stands for Democratic and Inclusive School Culture in Operation. Of course, it is bureaucratic jargon, and in the Slovenian version the acronym DDVKŠ loses all the simplicity and playfulness of the English original, but fortunately the content makes up for this shortcoming. The activities funded under the DISCO program are based on an excellent invention that we prepared at the Council of Europe with the help of experts from member states, including Slovenia. Of course, it too has an impossible name; once it is fully translated into Slovenian, it could be called the Reference Framework of Competences for Democratic Culture. Despite its terrible name, the thing is basically simple, understandable and, above all, very useful for its main purpose, namely supporting education for democracy and democracy in education. In Slovenian translation, it offers a wonderful opportunity for a people-friendly acronym: ROK (a common Slovenian first name) for democratic culture. When President Pahor once asked me to explain in 30 seconds what it was about, I told him that the Reference Framework for Democratic Culture is an attempt to pass on to pupils the knowledge, skills, abilities and capacity for critical thinking and judgment that we would like to see, and need, in politicians. ROK for democratic culture imitates another great success from the Council of Europe’s education workshop, namely the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, familiar to all of you who claim in your CVs and job applications that your knowledge of foreign languages is at least C2. Just as the language framework describes what language learners need to learn in order to communicate, ROK describes the values, attitudes, skills, knowledge and critical understanding that pupils need to acquire for active democratic citizenship. ROK includes twenty competences, each with descriptors that make it possible to transmit and assess the knowledge acquired. Among them we find the ability to argue that all public institutions must respect, protect and implement human rights; an understanding that all laws must be consistent with international human rights standards; the conviction that people holding public office must not abuse power. The descriptors also include openness to getting to know other people and their cultures, respect for people of different social and economic status, the ability to take responsibility for one’s actions, using facts as the basis for forming one’s own views, empathy, social solidarity and the ability to listen to different opinions. This random selection nicely illustrates what I wanted to convey to the President. It would be great if we could pass these competences on to pupils; even better if we managed to pass them on to politicians. But back from ROK to DISCO. In this cycle, nine international projects were supported, among them cooperation between universities in France, Great Britain, Belgium and Italy that enabled refugees with appropriate qualifications to teach again and contribute in their field of expertise to the society that took them in. A very sensitive but important program supported LGBTI pupils, their teachers and parents in Ukraine. DISCO also supported an Austrian-Greek project on building young people’s resilience against fake news, together with a handbook on digital citizenship that we will present at the World Forum for Democracy in November. For Slovenia, which unfortunately has not so far been represented in the DISCO program, the recommendations on addressing controversial issues in education, also a product of DISCO cooperation, would be very interesting too. At least one copy would be needed, for example, at the Kranj grammar school, and probably elsewhere too. During the project presentation, a figure was cited showing that in one of the participating countries, an EU member state, almost half of teachers want a strong leader, and one in six would even like to see democracy replaced by a military dictatorship. Of course, in Slovenia we are not that far yet. I have a very high opinion of Slovenian teachers, their professionalism and their commitment to democratic values, but they too are not immune to what is happening in society. Objectively, it is hard to imagine successful education for democratic culture in an environment in which that culture is weakening and disappearing. That is another reason why it matters how the introduction of citizenship education in secondary schools will be received and how successful it will be. I don’t know the details of the future curriculum, but I am confident that in many respects it will be based on the Council of Europe’s Reference Framework of Competences, not least because it was created with Slovenian expertise as well and contains experiences and approaches developed in Slovenian schools. Even the name of the subject is important, and, if I am not mistaken, it has not yet been finalized. That is good, because the name “civic education”—without an adjective that defines citizenship in terms of values—is not the happiest and can be misleading. The reason may be that in Slovenian we use the same word for holders of a passport and for active participants in social processes. The confusion was also evident in a recent report on one of the Slovenian TV channels, in which a teacher complained that civic education was needed because pupils did not know the state symbols well. It is right that they should know them, but the aim of the subject should not be just singing the national anthem and intimate knowledge of the coat of arms and the flag. After all, North Korea has an anthem, a coat of arms and a flag too. Patriotism is an indisputably positive value that should have its place in school, but for true love of one’s homeland, pupils need to be able to ground their patriotism in values and also be critical of their homeland. Without this, there is no true patriotism, only nationalism. The future subject should give priority to understanding the state through values over defining values through the state. The condition Pitt suffers from is known among experts as prosopagnosia. For a society that is blind to values and, instead of patriotism and openness, is based on selfishness, worship of strong leaders and fearful nationalism, there are also quite a few expert and less expert terms. But if we are looking for an acronym, I think the most appropriate would be the only one my memory has no trouble with. That is where the last one out can flush and turn off the light.

From the center of Oslo to Lake Tyrifjorden, it’s just over half an hour by car. By the lake, there’s a gravel parking lot and a small dock. If you don’t know it’s there, it’s easy to miss. A few hundred meters from the shore lies a small island. Next to the dock stands a sign explaining that on July 22, 2011, a right-wing extremist attacked a summer camp for the Norwegian Social Democratic youth on this island and killed 69 people. Utøya. The sign explains that Utøya is today a place for political engagement, dialogue, and learning about democracy. The island is a classroom built on the belief that knowledge is stronger than hatred of foreigners, hate speech, and conspiracy theories. There is no regular ferry service. You can only go to Utøya by prior arrangement. The reasons are security-related and also to ensure the island does not become just another tourist destination. The memorial erected on the island by the victims' families is private. A public memorial center is located in Oslo. Ana, the director of a partner institution of the Council of Europe who runs youth workshops on Utøya in cooperation with Norway’s Ministry of Education, and I had, of course, scheduled our visit. After a few minutes of waiting, we were picked up by a tiny ferry — the same kind used on that fateful July 22 eight years earlier, when the killer Breivik arrived on the island in a police uniform, pretending to check the security situation after a bombing that same morning in Oslo, which had already claimed eight lives. The first impression of Utøya is that it’s like a postcard-perfect image of Scandinavian idyll. Above the dock sits a white wooden villa — the former holiday home of pre-war industrialist and politician Jens Kristian Bratlie, who in the 1930s became a supporter of Vidkun Quisling and his Nazi-inspired Nasjonal Samling party. Bratlie’s far-right politics did not prevent him from selling the estate to a youth organization representing his ideological opponents. The second impression is how small the island is. You can walk across it in five minutes, around it in fifteen. It's no larger than Congress Square in Ljubljana. On July 22, 2011, over five hundred young people were camping there, many of them just teenagers — fifteen, sixteen years old. From the moment the shooting began to the arrival of the first police officers, an hour and a half passed. Ninety minutes for Breivik to carry out his infernal plan, foretold and explained in detail in his 1,500-page “manifesto.” They say words don’t kill. Perhaps. But this 1,500-page document of hatred was written precisely to announce and justify his crime. The mass murder of teenagers — whose deaths, in the killer’s own non-lethal words, were necessary to save Western civilization. Just above the dock is a soccer field. The summer tournament held there is a yearly highlight. Above the field, next to a small building where Leon Trotsky once briefly stayed before his fatal trip to Mexico, stands a red barn that now displays photos of the people, times, and events that have marked the island through the decades. In one, I spot my former boss, the now-retired Secretary General of the Council of Europe, Thorbjørn Jagland, cleaning latrines in extravagantly tight shorts. In another, an equally youthful Jens Stoltenberg poses next to a stolen signpost for the regional NATO headquarters. Under Stoltenberg’s leadership, the young Labour activists were highly critical of Norway’s NATO membership. I wonder, chuckling, what Jens is up to these days as I leave the barn. At the island’s highest point stands a modern glass building surrounded by wooden pilings. Hegnhuset — the House that Protects. 495 wooden poles for the 495 survivors. They stand to preserve the memory of the dead. Inside this structure — whose roof rests on 69 pillars — is one of the few buildings not demolished after the attack: the old dining hall, where thirteen of Breivik’s victims died. Everything remains. Bullet holes. Open windows through which some escaped to safety. Pale spots on the walls where the blood of those less lucky was scrubbed away with chemicals. A bullet-riddled piano once used to celebrate birthdays during the summer camps. Flowers and messages left on the birthdays of children who, during the attack, tried in vain to hide behind that very piano. The cheerfulness from the barn vanishes, replaced by unspeakable horror. Those who visit the island often have a name for the emotional whiplash. In and out. Constantly. Idyllic nature and bloodstains. Light and darkness. Laughter and pain. Love and death. In and out. This emotional vortex was intentionally woven into the island’s rebirth. People come here to remember the victims and talk about what happened — but also to laugh, to be together, to play soccer, and to love. The wish of the victims’ families was not to let Breivik destroy Utøya and everything the island had meant to their children. At the entrance to the dining hall is a wall with a timeline of that fateful day and transcripts of text messages: “Mom, Dad, I don’t think we’ll ever see each other again. I love you...” “Mom, I’m scared I’m going to die...” “Mom, whatever happens, I want you to know I love you...” “Call me so I can come to you...” “Please, call me so I can come to you...” “Call me... Call me...” Do words kill? I don’t know — some say they don’t. But when hatred kills children, their words can break your heart. Next to the old dining hall, a workshop on hate speech is underway, using a methodology developed by the Council of Europe. Two dozen fourteen-year-olds from all over Norway, with their teachers, are discussing what hate speech is — and what it isn’t. Where does comparing people to rats lead us? How should society respond to public expressions of intolerance and hatred? Why can’t bans be the only answer? Can we be tolerant of intolerance? What can each individual do? Responses among peers. Responses within families. Society’s responsibility. With a maturity many politicians would envy, these young people search for answers. Breivik represents right-wing extremism, which today is the fastest-growing terrorist threat in many Western countries — but the students also discuss other forms of extremism, from white supremacism to its mirror images. Back at school, they will continue these discussions with their classmates. On the island’s western side, I walk along the “Lovers’ Path” toward the memorial. The shoreline here rises steeply above the lake; below are rocks, and the opposite shore is much farther than on the eastern side, where the killer came from. For decades a favorite spot for first loves and teenage kisses, Lovers’ Path saw the bloodiest toll. Those caught there during the rampage had nowhere to run. Love and death. In and out. The memorial was built by the victims’ families. A simple steel ring suspended in the branches of three trees. Sunlight shines now through one name etched in metal, then another. Flowers transplanted from all corners of the island bloom on the forest floor — in July, the month of the tragedy, they attract butterflies. I slowly head back to the ferry. In my thoughts are the lines of Norwegian poet Frode Grytten, written just days after the tragedy. They are inscribed on the wall of the old dining hall — and the last line also on the ramp leading onto the ferry. It is with this thought that we come to the island, and with this thought that we leave it: “Another July 22 will come, for other beating hearts the ferry will arrive, tents will be pitched on the green grass, the kiss of morning sun will awaken the island. Hey, hey — it’s time to rise and change the world.” I don’t know whether words can kill. Some say they can’t. But I do know this: the words and actions of good people restore hope in a society where humanity is stronger than hate. It is time to change the world.

On a fine summer weekend a good thirty years ago, my friend Aljoša and I went fishing on the Krka. We didn’t catch any fish, but we didn’t try very hard either; they were just an excuse for a trip into the bosom of Lower Carniolan esotericism, steeped in morning mist and homemade wine. We spent the night at Aljoša’s aunt’s, in a caravan in the garden, because there was no room in the house. Another relative had come to visit, at the time temporarily working in Kočevje, who was, if I remember correctly, a road maintenance worker by trade. Everyone knows Kočevje is no joke. They have the fattest bears, Nataša Briški and a chainsaw-throwing contest. The gentleman in question was proud of all this and much more, and began every sentence with “Back home in Kočevje…” The uncle has long since left us, and a few days ago we also said goodbye to Aljoša; I dedicate this piece to him. But since those days, the phrase “back home in Kočevje” has become a family saying. My brothers use it as a red card every time I, in the old guest-worker habit, start comparing people and customs abroad with those at home. Since I am going to commit exactly this sin in today’s piece, I apologize in advance to them and to you. Please be understanding. For those of us temporarily working abroad, convincing ourselves of the advantages of our new surroundings is a defense mechanism against homesickness. I often feel it myself, although I must admit that since I can follow Slovenian TV news from abroad, I somehow find the pain easier to bear. And it was in these news programs over the summer that I came across reports that led me to compare Slovenia and France. First, those about the village patrols in Bela Krajina and the patriots who, in flip-flops and camouflage uniforms, armed only with beer bellies and broken English, keep watch over our security and territorial integrity. Some of them reportedly walk up to fifty kilometers a day, hunting for unwanted foreigners. “Daun, daun, dis iz kantri Slovenija, daun!” A few dozen kilometers in flip-flops is no small thing, although, by their own admission, the patrolling is not terribly effective. “We shout, but they just don’t obey, they don’t lie down at all, they just keep walking.” France also has people who selflessly take on the burden of protecting the state’s borders. A few days ago, the French state thanked them by sentencing three of them to six months in prison and a fine, while their far-right association Génération Identitaire, which also has supporters and sponsors here, had to pay as much as seventy-five thousand euros. Meanwhile in Slovenia, the harshest sanction our wannabe border guards currently face is the possibility, admittedly slight, that sympathetic media reports about them won’t make the very top of the front page or the prime-time TV slot. To be fair, it should be added that the identitarians in France were convicted for “activities carried out in circumstances liable to create the impression that they were exercising a public function.” That is certainly not something we can accuse our budding heroes, patrolling in flip-flops accompanied by underage children, of. But it is not only identitarians who patrol France’s borders. In recent years, the French authorities have repeatedly arrested and even convicted Cédric Herrou, a chicken farmer and olive grower from near Nice.
