Cédric was not prosecuted for getting in the way of far-right border vigilantes. Au contraire, as the French would say, he was convicted for helping refugees trying to get from Italy into France. It is worth noting that all the first-instance convictions were eventually overturned, and the French Constitutional Council ordered parliament to change the law and severely restrict the so-called crime of solidarity and the criminalization of humanitarian aid. This does not, of course, include organizing illegal border crossings for profit, something we also have plenty of. Human trafficking quite rightly remains a criminal offense in France too. What also prompted my comparison between the two countries was a news story from a few months ago about how the Social Democratic mayor of one of Slovenia’s border municipalities managed, by exploiting fear and intolerance of refugees, to build a patriotic bridge between himself and the far right. The mayor was mortally offended because the local brass band refused to take part in the anti-migrant rally, so the only rhythm for the marching patriots was provided by a lady who, in a fit of love for her homeland, was beating the asphalt with a Slovenian flag. France also has mayors who are very concerned with refugees and migrants. One of them is Damien Carême, who was elected mayor of Grande-Synthe, a suburban municipality of Dunkirk on the English Channel coast, in 2001. In eighteen years as mayor, he managed to introduce only locally produced organic food in school canteens, set up a number of municipal community gardens, and provide free public transport and municipal social assistance to all residents below the poverty line. When thousands of refugees, mainly from Iraqi Kurdistan, poured into Grande-Synthe in 2015 and 2016, hoping to make it to Great Britain, Mayor Carême did not stand idly by but, together with Médecins Sans Frontières and without state aid, set up a humanitarian refugee camp. Despite all my guest-worker enthusiasm, both French examples above should be taken with a dose of realism. Not all that glitters is gold in Kočevje either. Like our village patrols, Cédric Herrou is more the exception than the rule. The difference is that our exceptions and the French ones go in different directions, and we should not forget what legal and political changes the activism of a chicken farmer from Provence led to. While we put up barriers on the borders and pat uniformed village eccentrics on the back in the media, in France self-appointed defenders are sent behind bars, and the Constitutional Council and parliament remove legal obstacles to humanity and solidarity with our fellow human beings. Nor can the mayor of Grande-Synthe be presented as a typical representative of local government, although it is true that across France there were far more local initiatives to welcome refugees in solidarity than the typically Slovenian initiatives to “defend” against them. One of the cities that has shown solidarity with refugees is Strasbourg, where I live. Mayor Carême’s story is instructive above all regarding the consequences that firm, effective, caring and humane politics can have for popularity and electoral support among the population. Since May this year, Damien Carême is no longer mayor of Grande-Synthe. In the European elections, he was comfortably elected to the European Parliament. To avoid misunderstandings, plenty goes wrong in France too, and I would have no trouble finding quite a few examples where Slovenia could be a model for the French. But the treatment of foreigners, refugees and migrants, and solidarity with our fellow human beings, are not among them. Of course intolerance and racism exist in France too; the difference is that all serious politics, whether left or right, rejects them in principle. When the right-wing Republicans tried to flirt with chauvinism before the European elections, they got a bloody nose. Meanwhile here, a good part of politics still behaves as if feeding prejudice and fear were an investment in the security of the state and its borders. The progressive European values that we wrote into our Constitution are increasingly just one possible option, which, in the name of a poorly understood freedom of speech and political opportunism, we treat the same as any extremist agitation and hatred. Such equality is of course illusory; putting the decent and the indecent on the same level is always a victory for the latter. Until we understand this, we ourselves are leaving decisions about our future to paramilitary patriots in flip-flops and their sponsors. Although they seem stupid to us, they are no less dangerous for that. Dis iz kantri Slovenija. Vi ar going daun.
Luck on a String II: The World Is Cast in Gray Concrete

“Sir, sir,” the cashier at Hofer shouted after me as I walked off, lost in thought, with a bag containing milk and tomatoes. I decided to ignore her until an older man tapped me on the shoulder and pointed out the agitated shop assistant. “Your card was declined,” snapped a barely adult brat with a piercing in her left nostril, “do you have cash, perhaps?” Red-faced and sweating with humiliation, I climb the concrete footpath to the plaza and stop for a moment, not so much because of memories as to catch my breath. More than forty of the “best” years of my life, I think bitterly, and I’ve managed to get from here to here. Milk and tomatoes again, only there are no Indians to smash them in the face of. At least Rok is coming, I tell myself; it’ll be great to see him again after all these years. In front of the entrance to the apartment block stands a younger man in a cheap suit, with scuffed shoes and teeth yellowed by tobacco. “Matic Škerjanc?” he addresses me, taking my elbow not very gently. “Yes,” I reply warily. “And who are you? Why do you ask?” “We’ve got a little enforcement order for you to sign,” he explains contentedly, shoving some sort of paper in my face. The armchairs in my mother’s living room have been there as long as I can remember. When I was a child, she covered them with zebra skins in a desperate attempt to hide the patches of worn velvet and the truth about the real reasons for my father’s absence. “He’s in Libya, drilling in the Sahara,” she told me every night before bed when I asked where he was and when he would be back. Drilling he was, all right, but not in the Sahara, I think, surrendering to the bittersweet embrace of self-pity, from which Rok’s thunderous laughter wrenches me. “What did you do to him? You’re not quite right in the head.” His enthusiasm is infectious. “I smashed the lot in his face, mate, like in the old days. I even busted his eyebrow, but it’s hardly my fault they don’t sell milk in bags anymore,” I answer proudly. “And why’s he talking to me like some half-witted waiter? ‘We’ve got a little enforcement order,’” I mimic him. “Get lost, you debt-collecting cow, go back to the one who sent you and enforce your orders on her.” “Speaking of ‘her,’ as you call her…,” Rok asks, flicking a speck of dust visible only to him from his designer jeans, ironed to a sharp crease, “…how’s Milena? I didn’t even know you weren’t together anymore.” “Of course you didn’t. You don’t give a damn about me or her or any of us; you went off abroad to play the gentleman, and then you come back here now and then to crap on our heads about what half-witted yokels we all are,” I reply with a sharpness that surprises even me. Embarrassed, I try to busy myself with my bottle of Laško, but it is empty again. My outburst doesn’t throw Rok. “I gather you didn’t part by mutual agreement,” he says, his eyes flicking over the combed-over remains of my blond curls and the beer belly pushing out from under my polo shirt, freshly put on yesterday. “She left me. For one of those fucking Indians. That Southern immigrant Perot, who made his money in the voucher privatization. Now he’s supposedly into cryptocurrencies. Not very successfully, if you ask me, if they still have to live in the house I bought and I’m still paying off the mortgage. Cryptocurrencies. Crypto-faggotry, if you ask me.” Rok doesn’t answer, just raises his eyebrows slightly. My remarks about the personal circumstances and business acumen of the guy screwing my ex-wife are evidently too much for his European humanist sensibilities. Any minute now we’ll get a lecture on hate speech. I wonder who the threatened minority is here: me or the two of them? “Well,” he breaks the silence after a long pause, “so you’ve moved back in with your mum. How is she?” “She’s in a home. Dementia. Always the path of least resistance, if you ask me. And I get to deal with all this crap,” I reply, waving my hand at the worn furniture, lost hopes and wrecked expectations. “How’s work?” Rok asks, evidently keen to steer the conversation elsewhere. “Where do you work again? People say you’re a secret agent. Škerjanc, Matic Škerjanc,” he adds, laughing, but turns serious as soon as he notices my glare. “Sure, James fucking Bond. In accounts. And even that was fixed for me by Milena’s dad. Which she never forgot to mention. That I wouldn’t even earn the few euros I bring home if it weren’t for her. Secret agent 000, she called me.” I open another beer. Rok has barely touched his first. In a low voice I say: “I was just about to go to the Home.” “The home?” Rok replies in surprise. “Your mum’s? Aren’t you a bit young? You’re not even fifty-four.” “The Home, not the home. The Homeland League. You know, that new party, supposedly patriotic and all that.” Rok doesn’t answer, but his silence speaks louder than words. “Who are you to look down on me!” I explode, banging my fist on the table. “You lot in Brussels and Strasbourg don’t give a damn about us; you sit there with full bellies lecturing us. Meanwhile here, people walk all over us and treat us like dirt. Faggots and migrants and feminists; my ex was always going on about rights and values and equality too, and then she goes off and spreads her legs for someone else,” I shout, red in the face. Rok watches me calmly. “Well?” “Well what?” “Did you join the Home?” Suddenly all the anger drains out of me. “I went to sign the membership form. And ran into one of my bosses there. Can you imagine? ‘Škerjanc?’ he asked me, staring with those bulging eyes. ‘Aren’t you from my department?’ ‘Yes,’ I said, and turned and left. I admit I’m a loser, but I’m not that much of a loser. I did feel like slashing the tires on that car of his, though,” I blurt out, clenching my fists in a spasm of adrenaline born of imaginary courage. “Have you thought about getting a dog? To get out a bit, among people?” Rok asks, glancing at his watch. For a long time I don’t answer, because I don’t trust my voice. “No,” I finally manage, with a lump in my throat, “not since they took Jakob away… She did leave me a Chihuahua she got when we were still together. On purpose, I swear, just to provoke me. I took it back and left it on her doorstep. Let that crypto guy of hers look after the mangy mutt,” I fall silent, because Rok is raising his eyebrows again. “I’m thinking of buying a bike. Like every real Slovenian. A patriot, you know,” I try desperately to turn the conversation into a joke. “A bike you can ride or leave in the cellar, but a dog has to be taken out three times a day. Because a bike is a bike, but a dog is alive. Who can be bothered? You even have to pick up its crap. I’ve got enough of that in my life without a puppy,” I declare. Rok has slowly had enough of everything. He looks at his watch again, stands up and straightens the legs of his trousers. “It was really great to see you, mate. Let’s do this again soon,” he says, very unconvincingly, waves and leaves. I don’t wave back. I stay sitting in the armchair, absent-mindedly rearranging my curls, which slipped out of position in all the excitement. “It’s you old folks’ fault,” I mutter into my beard, and open another beer.

A few days ago, I posted on social media warning how uncritically we in Slovenia have adopted and started using the term “differently-minded.” On social networks and even in some media, the phrase has become a kind of universal excuse to cover all sorts of indecencies—from paramilitary training in the woods to intolerance, hatred, and racism toward certain individuals and groups. Overnight, ideas, phenomena, and discourses that once would have deserved the harshest social condemnation have become completely normal and legitimate. Racism, antisemitism, homophobia? “People just have different opinions.” To illustrate the problem, I used a provocative analogy: calling a fascistoid racist merely “differently-minded” is like saying a pedophile is just “differently-sensitive.” After the post, I received a wave of offended and outraged responses: why was I attacking and insulting the differently-minded? These reactions puzzled me. Many of those who reacted strongly are people I often disagree with—but I would never consider them fascistoid racists. If anything, I was defending the integrity and reputation of those who genuinely identify as differently-minded—at least those who don’t harbor sympathies for fascism and racism. They, of all people, should be upset that such filth is being smuggled into public acceptability under their flag. After all, am I not differently-minded myself, since I often think differently from those who got their knickers in a twist because of my post? But it turns out things aren’t that simple. My naïve understanding of the term “differently-minded” was based on the belief that it simply meant thinking differently from someone else. In a democracy, that’s not just useful—it’s vital. A society where everyone thinks the same doesn’t exist; uniformity of thought is only possible through force. In my well-meaning naïveté, I was willing to believe that those who reacted so intensely misunderstood me, but acted out of a sincere desire to defend my right to disagree with them. As noble as such an interpretation would be, I’m afraid that’s not what happened. Being “differently-minded” is apparently not just about thinking differently—it’s about thinking differently in a very specific way. In fact, it seems that “Differently-Minded” (capital D and M) is a proper noun, almost a brand. It’s less about promoting open dialogue between opposing views, and more about forming a resistance movement aimed at liberating the public sphere from the constraints of civilization’s core values—values upon which Western democracies, and Europe in particular, built their social, political, and economic systems after the trauma of World War II. European integration is based on respect for human rights. The Differently-Minded don’t particularly care for human rights—except maybe their own. Nor are they big fans of political freedoms, except for freedom of speech, which they interpret very differently from how it’s defined and protected by the European Convention on Human Rights. For them, freedom of speech is mostly a weapon—used to undermine and cancel out other Convention-protected rights and freedoms. This is explicitly forbidden by Article 17 of the Convention, but who cares about details when you’re on a mission to liberate the nation from humanism, solidarity, and the dignity of the person? In the ideological worldview of the Differently-Minded, freedom of speech becomes the right to intolerance and hate—but even this “right” is one-way only. While they loudly defend their right to express hatred, they’re quick to be offended if they feel someone is being intolerant toward them. By trivializing hatred, the Differently-Minded also endanger themselves. No matter how convinced they are of their own cultural, racial, or religious superiority, in a world based on hate, there’s always a bigger bully ready to send them to the back of the bus. In the Differently-Minded world, there’s only us and them. They try to disguise this polarization as a left–right divide, which is not only laughable but also quite awkward for the right. On the “other” side—those who think differently in a different way—you’ll find supporters of human rights, political freedoms, humanism, and solidarity of all political stripes and ideological origins. Far from a politically homogeneous group. But the Differently-Minded still label them all as far-left radicals. Like all revolutionaries, they ignore facts that don’t support their ideology. One of the more absurd (and common) claims is that defending human rights is a leftist conspiracy—a view sometimes even espoused by those who identify as Christian democrats or conservatives. This is especially ironic, since the modern concept of human rights in Europe was largely shaped by Christian Democratic politicians. Why some are so eager to disown the proud heritage of the political tradition they claim to represent is beyond me. Then again, maybe I don’t get it—because I’m not Differently-Minded. The key difference between the Differently-Minded and the merely-minded lies in their concept of freedom. The Differently-Minded argue that promoting absolute freedom of speech, including the right to spread and legitimize hate, expands the space of freedom. In their worldview, any criticism or condemnation directed at them (but not at those they despise) is an attack on liberty. In their society, freedom is measured by the unchecked dominance of the majority over minorities and individuals. In contrast, liberal democracy guarantees freedom based on human and social rights and political liberties available to all members of society—not just to ethnic, racial, or religious majorities, or those in positions of political and economic power. Of course, liberal democracy isn’t always consistent or successful in this, and that very inconsistency has helped fuel the rise of nationalist populism. The question is: how do we fix these failures? History teaches us what happens when we try to “correct” the weaknesses of a liberal democracy with authoritarianism in the name of “the people.” This fundamental difference in how freedom is understood imposes a particular responsibility on liberal democracy, especially when it comes to freedom of speech, which is essential for the functioning of democracy. Without it, there can be no social progress or effective protection against abuses of power. With the recent, long-overdue efforts to align Slovenia’s handling of hate speech with European Court of Human Rights jurisprudence, it’s important to remember that most of the indecencies now being disguised as “differently-mindedness” should be addressed not through repression, but through public debate, social argument, and political response. A healthy democracy must be able to defend itself—its survival cannot depend solely on prosecutors. In contrast, a society that tolerates or is built on intolerance, discrimination, and hatred cannot afford such open debate without countering it—because it wouldn’t survive it. In the world of the Differently-Minded, there is no room for those who think differently.
Our Sunday with the Styrian Guard

A para-true story Saturday, 2:20 p.m., a small village somewhere in Kozjansko, the snack bar by the bus stop Guardsman A (in civilian clothes): “Julčka, two Laško beers, and then leave us alone, we’ve got something to sort out.” Guardsman B (in civilian clothes): “And make them nice and cold.” Julčka (in uniform) rolls her eyes and mutters to her colleague behind the bar: “Playing soldiers again. Mine was saying something about joining too, but I gave him such a hiding he doesn’t need a camouflage uniform to be covered in spots.” Guardsman A: “We meet tomorrow at six in the morning, assembly point Hill 405.” Guardsman B: “Huh?” “Hill 405. Don’t you know where Hill 405 is?” “No idea.” “Back there, behind Kaučič’s scrubland, that path that goes up into the woods, up to the meadow with that big linden tree. Where Joža had his fiftieth birthday picnic and then threw up all over the place.” “So why don’t you just say where Joža threw up all over the place?” “Three hundred devils, because we’re an army, not some half-witted gang shuffling around in flip-flops and swilling beer.” Guardsman B (under his breath): “Well…” Guardsman B (out loud): “Is the boss coming?” “No, that lady lawyer says it’s better if he keeps a low profile. But he sent a speech for me to read; she went over it too. And apparently a reporter from Delo is coming, they’re doing a feature on us. The ones from Ljubljana fixed all that.” “The ones from Ljubljana?” “Shut up. Better you don’t know.” “Why isn’t Večer doing a feature?” “They don’t want to. Say they’re not interested.” “Traitorous lot. What a damn country, where people from Ljubljana are bigger Styrians than people from Maribor.” Sunday, 7:45 a.m., Hill 405 (where Joža threw up all over the place) Guardsman A (in uniform): “What kind of army are you, dragging yourselves in only now? We said six. Good thing the boss isn’t here.” Guardsmen (to themselves): “Six? On a Sunday? You’re completely off your head.” Guardsman A (smartly): “430th Special Battalion of the Styrian Guard, atteeeen-tion! I will read you a message from our supreme commander, who, owing to an unjust verdict by the regime’s crooked judiciary and on the advice of his lawyer, is unfortunately not with us today.” In his hands he clutches a scribbled sheet of paper on which some words have been crossed out and others written in with a red marker, in nervous, nasty handwriting. “That woman won’t let the boss so much as fart without her permission anymore,” he whispers to Guardsman B, standing beside him. “Now she decides what we say and what we do.” Guardsman B (glancing around nervously): “Women. That one’s even worse than mine.” Guardsman A (reading, even more smartly): “Greetings, Styrian Guardsmen, members of the volunteer defense group of the free people of the land of Styria. The day will soon come when we shall ride the mighty bora wind and defend our land against…” Guardsman A pauses for a moment, squints at the paper and the words written in fat red letters, “…against faggots, migrants, feminists, Soros’s hirelings, Muslims and…” Guardsman A (whispering): “That bit’s from the lawyer. She says we should keep quieter for a while about the armed uprising and an independent Styria and all that. We can lay into the faggots and the migrants and the rest, because that’s not inciting the violent overthrow of the constitutional order, it’s just thinking differently. Apparently it’s really democratic if we’re dissenters and if we give those…” (he squints at the paper again) “…a bit of an ear-pulling so they don’t threaten our Styrian culture.” Guardsman A (reading on, moderately smartly): “…and together we shall rise up as a steel Styrian fist that will crush to dust the leftist lies about climate change…” Guardsman B (surprised): “What’s this climate change now?” Guardsman A (whispering): “Supposedly from now on it’ll just be heat and rain and hail. Like now, only even more crap. Apparently Kučan and his lot are behind this too. I didn’t understand all of it, but the ones from Ljubljana told me I had to say it.” “The ones from Ljubljana?” “Shut up. Better you don’t know.” Guardsman B (to himself): “What kind of Styrian Guard are we, if the ones from Ljubljana decide everything?” Guardsman A (out loud): “Take the company out for training.” “You mean the battalion?” “Yes, the battalion. Take it out for training.” “What are we training in?” “Target shooting.” “With what, for God’s sake? Didn’t the boss say no weapons this time?” Guardsman A (conspiratorially): “I’ve got a shotgun in the boot. Just chuck out the cartridges after training so there’s no trouble. And tell that guy from Delo not to take pictures.” Guardsman B (under his breath): “Target practice with a shotgun? He’s completely mad. Even Joža can hit something with that, without training. What kind of army are we?” Sunday, 9:35 p.m., by the campfire on Hill 405 (where Joža threw up all over the place) Guardsman A (with comradely warmth): “Comrades, after a hard day’s training we can relax a little now. Only you, Joža, take it a bit slower, you know what happened last time we were here. And you’ve got the first watch.” Guardsman Joža (with difficulty): “Don’t mess with me, what watch? What am I supposed to stand guard with, my own dick? I can do that at home. What kind of army are we?” Guardsman A (reproachfully): “Take the shotgun. Just chuck the cartridges out first so there’s no trouble.” Guardsman Joža (into his beard): “Better my dick than an empty gun. I’m not chucking anything out.” Sunday, 11:40 p.m., a few hundred meters below Hill 405 (where Joža threw up all over the place) Younger voice (irritated): “Come on, Dad, can you explain why it’s not enough that we’ve been tramping through every possible backwater all week, but now we have to climb up here at night instead of sleeping down in the village and moving on tomorrow?” Older voice (soothingly paternal): “Son, somewhere around here I once gave a speech at a ceremony. I don’t remember whether it was for the Partisans or the Home Guard, it doesn’t matter, but I remember a meadow facing due east, and an enormous linden tree, the symbol of Slovenianness. I want to be up there by morning; the light will be phenomenal for selfies.” Younger voice (still irritated): “Dad, what’s actually the point of all the selfies and Instagram and stuff? Aren’t you supposed to be…?” Older voice (proudly): “I am.” Younger voice (increasingly irritated): “And?” “And what?” “What’s the point?” “There is no point. That’s the point.” Younger voice (confused): “Huh?” Older voice (statesmanlike): “Without content there are no ideas, without ideas there are no ideologies, without ideologies there are no divisions. Only without ideas and without values can the Slovenian nation be truly free and united. Why argue about what is right and what isn’t when we can simply be Slovenians?” Younger voice (appalled): “A vacuum of values as the foundation of national unity? Jeez! Have you ever heard of Aristotle?” Older voice (patronizingly): “Exactly! I knew you’d understand. What do you think, for the morning selfie, would a warm, human look and smile be better, or something more statesmanlike, serious and staring into the distance?” Younger voice (resigned, in his head): “A straitjacket. On a paddleboard. Or in Kozjansko. Whatever.” Voice from the darkness (frightened): “Halt. In the name of the Styrian Guard. Who goes there?” Older voice (even more frightened): “Crucifix, what’s this now?” Younger voice (frightened but composed): “Dad, get down, the guy’s got a gun!” Gun (very loudly): “Bang!” Guardsman Joža (in his head, perhaps also out loud): “Long live free Styria. I’m going to throw up again.” Author’s note This is, of course, a fictional story, in which any resemblance to real events or persons is purely coincidental and not entirely ill-intentioned. Moreover, fortunately, despite a full day’s training, Guardsman Joža was unable to hit his target even in fiction. Once he had recovered, the distinguished guest inspected the guard of honor, pardon, the battalion, and then, in an impromptu address, stressed the importance of patriotism and of spending free time in nature. He invited Guardsman Joža to attend one of his upcoming consultations on regional development in Slovenia.

In 1983, the hit movie Trading Places was released. In it, two wealthy brothers amuse themselves by manipulating the fates of two men, played by Eddie Murphy and Dan Aykroyd. Some may remember the film as a comedic critique of American inequality and the social irresponsibility of capital. Others will remember it because Jamie Lee Curtis bares her breasts. What stuck with me was one of the final scenes, where the villainous henchman, dressed as a gorilla, ends up locked in a cage with a romantically inclined real gorilla. The scene ends with a close-up of his wide, panicked eyes—everything else is left to the imagination. A man dressed as a gorilla is also the central figure in a psychological experiment by American researchers Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons, described in their 2010 book The Invisible Gorilla. The two won an “Ig Nobel Prize” for the most trivial scientific research that year—which, in my view, was well deserved. In the experiment, volunteers were asked to count how many times players in white shirts passed a basketball. The observers were so focused on the task that they failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. The point of the experiment was to demonstrate that people intensely focused on one thing can easily miss everything else. I haven’t read Chabris and Simons’ book, but I do know a joke where the proverbial Bosnians Mujo and Haso use experimental psychology to unhook and steal a German tourist’s trailer. Distraction and misdirection are key political skills as well. That’s understandable—everyone would rather be known for their successes than for their mistakes. But populism elevates this “experimental psychology” to a much higher level. The aim isn’t just to distract from failure but to intentionally manipulate voters, to bring them to a state where they fail to notice—or even actively support—policies that objectively harm them. You have to keep people busy so you can steal their trailer. The self-harm involved in supporting populists is twofold. First, there’s the loss of political freedom. Claims of exclusive rights to represent “the people’s will” are used to delegitimize opposition and undermine independent judiciaries, free media, and civil society. Once populists dismantle the democratic checks and balances “in the name of the people,” it becomes very difficult for that same people to democratically remove them when they’ve had enough. Second, there are economic consequences. While populist Mujo keeps the German tourist entertained, neoliberal Haso unhooks the trailer. In Europe, this threatens the collapse of the post-war social model, based on a private economy balanced by protections of the public interest and a form of capitalism that accepts it needs the rule of law, democratic governance, quality education and healthcare, and infrastructure. For this to work, capital must be willing to give up some profit. This model was perfected in Scandinavia, particularly in the welfare state pioneered by Denmark, which was long guided by Nikolaj Grundtvig’s idea of an ideal society “where few have too much and even fewer too little.” Grundtvig wasn’t a leftist or a revolutionary—he was a Protestant pastor, who died in 1872. The Western European welfare state flourished after WWII. Rooted in liberal democracy, human rights, and the rule of law, it was both a response to wartime atrocities and a bulwark against communist ideology from the East. Postwar leaders couldn’t have known the Soviet dream would end in such failure. When it did, neoliberalism saw its chance to go after the welfare state and the European model of socially responsible capitalism. The process began in the early 1980s with the neoliberal triumph of Reagan and Thatcher, both intoxicated with Hayek. Of course, the welfare state wasn’t perfect. It struggled with rigidity in adapting to modern global challenges. Some responses have been panicked: Denmark’s new Social Democratic government, for example, has taken a populist turn on migration, in an effort to preserve its welfare system. But this is unlikely to work—you can’t carve up the principles of the welfare state like salami and serve them only to “your own.” Solidarity in society is for all or will ultimately be for no one. Neoliberal capital hates the welfare state even more than it hated communism—at least communism is gone, and not coming back. It has no problem with Putin’s Russia, which inherited the Soviet legacy and aligns ideologically on key issues. Since the welfare state is inseparable from liberal democracy, neoliberalism hates that too. Its holy trinity—deregulation, minimal taxation, and aggressive privatization—is incompatible with a society based on the social responsibility of capital. Right-wing populism enables neoliberalism to attack the foundational values of both the welfare state and liberal democracy: solidarity, human rights, political freedoms, social justice, non-discrimination, tolerance, dignity, empathy, openness, and dialogue. Trump’s recent tweets targeting four U.S. congresswomen offer a perfect example of racism and intolerance weaponized for political and economic dominance. He told them to “go back to where they came from” because they supported such values—branding them “socialists,” a worse insult in parts of America than being from Murgle neighborhood in Ljubljana, where the first Slovenian president Milan Kučan resides.. The tragic fate of people lured into populist hatred is that they may become its greatest victims. Their hostility toward outsiders helps build a world in which they themselves may one day be forced to flee their homeland. When a society is stripped of empathy and solidarity, it becomes inhumane to all but a select few at the top. And most of populism’s supporters won’t be in that select few. You don’t need to be clairvoyant to see it coming—just think critically about the real substance of populist promises and their inevitable consequences. But because populism is emotionally driven, only a small portion of its supporters are capable of rational thought and behavior. In that regard, human behavior deviates from Chabris and Simons’ model. In their experiment, once observers were alerted to the gorilla, they couldn’t see anything else. In populism, it’s the opposite. Despite all the signs of looming disaster, many still keep counting the ball passes. They won’t see the neoliberal gorilla until tears are streaming down their panicked face.
A Rainbow as Red as Blood

When soldiers of the Soviet Red Army’s 322nd Division liberated Auschwitz on January 27, 1945, they found around 7,000 inmates—most of them sick, emaciated, or dying. Among them was 33-year-old Karl Gorath, a medical orderly from Bad Zwischenahn, near Bremen. Karl had spent several years in the camps after being arrested in 1937 by agents from the Reich Central Office for the Combating of Homosexuality and Abortion, which operated as part of the Gestapo’s Second Executive Department. The combination of responsibilities within this arm of Hitler’s secret police is peculiar—at least in one sense, the Gestapo was a passionate defender of the right to life. Karl was not persecuted for involvement in abortion, but because he had been denounced by a "jealous lover." He was sentenced to internment under the infamous Paragraph 175 of the German Penal Code, which criminalized homosexuality. The law had been in effect since 1871; the Nazis simply made the penalties far more severe. Nearly 100,000 men were arrested under it over a few decades, not only in Germany but also in annexed territories of the Third Reich. Around 50,000 were convicted, and between 5,000 and 15,000 ended up in concentration camps. Many prisoners from Alsace were sent to the notorious Struthof-Natzweiler camp near Strasbourg, where Slovenian writer Boris Pahor was also imprisoned. Among them was Alsatian Pierre Seel, arrested by the Nazis shortly after their occupation of the region. In his testimony, he described unimaginable cruelty by SS guards against prisoners held under Paragraph 175. They pulled out their fingernails, forced them into sexual acts with each other, and raped them with wooden sticks. Pierre’s lover, an 18-year-old named Jo, was stripped naked by the guards in front of him, a tin bucket placed on his head, and then German shepherds were sicced on him. The dogs tore the boy to pieces. Karl Gorath survived the war in Auschwitz, where he had been transferred as punishment for helping Polish inmates. His years in Nazi camps were filled with suffering and unspeakable brutality, but he was lucky enough to live. So was Kurt von Ruffin—also known as Kurtis von Reidffin—a prewar German film actor and opera singer who, before the introduction of the standardized pink triangle, wore a prison uniform marked with a large letter A. The "A" stood for Arschficker—a vile slur that survived the Nazi regime and is increasingly used again today on social media and in the public discourse of certain “dissenting” individuals and public figures. Not all were as strong, stubborn, or fortunate as Karl, Pierre, and Kurt. Of the 5,000 to 15,000 homosexuals imprisoned in the camps, around 60% died—the highest mortality rate among prisoner categories who were not targeted for total extermination, but for so-called “re-education.” The belief that homosexuality is an illness or degeneracy that can be cured or corrected also outlived the Nazi era and still has many supporters, including in Slovenia. Accurate figures on how many homosexuals were interned remain unknown, largely because many survivors chose not to reveal the reasons for their imprisonment—and for good reason. Many were re-incarcerated after the camps were liberated, under the same law. The Allies and postwar German authorities—especially in the police and judiciary, where "former" Nazis were plentiful—insisted they serve out the sentences handed down by Nazi courts. When Karl Gorath returned to court in 1947, he was met by the same judge who had sentenced him before the war. "You again!" the judge barked—and sent him back to prison. Homosexuals were also the only group of Nazi victims who received no compensation for the time and suffering they endured in the camps. In the eyes of the authorities and much of public opinion, “perverts” had gotten what they deserved. Paragraph 175 was not removed from the German penal code until 1969. About 50,000 homosexual victims of Nazi persecution had to wait until 2002 to be formally pardoned. German Chancellor Angela Merkel later issued an official apology on behalf of the government. Placing the current rise of intolerance toward LGBT+ people in the historical context of Nazi crimes is a sensitive matter—but a necessary one. Today’s hatred is not a repeat, but a continuation. This doesn’t mean calling everyone who denies equal rights to homosexuals a Nazi, or labelling those who feel uneasy around gay people as fascists. But it is absolutely right to confront those who deny others their rights out of prejudice, with the truth about the injustice and suffering caused by political exploitation of hatred toward homosexuals in modern European history. Prejudices stem from many places—family upbringing, ideological blindness, religious indoctrination, or discomfort with one’s own sexuality. They can’t be eliminated overnight. Dialogue, listening, explanation, and counselling are needed. Changing deeply entrenched prejudice requires patience and time—but not at the expense of respecting human dignity and rights. A civilized, democratic society that respects human rights and freedoms is based on protecting individuals and minorities from the will of the majority—not on facilitating or legitimizing the violence of the majority against the few. Understanding this historical context is also important because political attempts to exploit prejudice and hate toward the LGBT+ community are on the rise again. I’m not saying everyone who panders to these instincts is a Nazi, but that doesn’t mean we can ignore the fact that similar emotional triggers—deep-seated prejudice and hatred—are once again being pushed for political gain, just as they were before, with such devastating consequences. Today, in some parts of Europe, intolerance toward LGBT+ people is growing once again. Equal rights for homosexuals, along with women’s reproductive rights and migrants, have become the scapegoats in a populist triptych. Politicians exploit hatred against these groups to seize or maintain power. In this light, the first Pride parade in Maribor and the now-traditional one in Ljubljana send a powerful and meaningful message—one that all people of Maribor and Ljubljana, and all Slovenians can be proud of. In defending the rights and dignity of LGBT+ people, we also protect our own rights and our own dignity. It’s a way of honouring the historic role of the first LGBT organizations in Slovenia, which in the early 1980s expanded the space of political and personal freedom for all Slovenians, regardless of sexual orientation—and which, as a result, faced rage and humiliation from other parts of the former Yugoslavia. The organization Magnus, active within Ljubljana’s student association ŠKUC, did far more for an independent, democratic, and humane Slovenia, than many of today’s self-proclaimed patriots who call gay people slurs in the name of family values. Those who were upset or angered by the Pride parade in Maribor or Ljubljana, those who think of themselves as tolerant because they’re fine with homosexuality “as long as they do it at home,” those whose mouths are full of insults—think of Karl, Kurt, and Pierre. Before they open their mouths next time, they should think of Jo—and the German shepherds. They should remember that red in the rainbow is the colour of blood that was shed. And perhaps some of them will reflect on the fact that, despite all the pain and injustice they have endured—and still endure in some places—homosexuals do not respond with anger or vengeance, but with parades of pride, love, tolerance, and respect for all. That takes a tremendous amount of humanity, dignity, principle, and courage. The least the majority can do is follow that example—in their attitudes toward the minority. For all of us. And so that “never again” truly means never again.

One of the tasks that takes up a considerable amount of my time in public office is trying to convince politicians and bureaucrats about the importance of knowledge and education for the proper functioning of democracy. Some agree, others nod absentmindedly and pat me on the back. “Don’t call us—we’ll call you.” For the latter, I’ve changed my approach. I no longer argue why education is important for democracy, but instead explain why ignorance, stupidity, and “alternative facts” are so popular among populists and autocrats. Objectively speaking, being an autocrat is a tough and lonely profession. You have few real friends; many are just waiting for the chance to stab you in the back and take your throne. That loneliness brings very practical difficulties in running a state and maintaining power, which autocrats solve in three main ways. The first is corruption. Money can buy a lot—including people. The problem is that loyalty bought with cash spoils quickly, since there’s always someone willing to offer your supporters a better deal. And bribery is a capital-intensive hobby, not well-suited to autocrats who didn’t get into power to share hard-earned loot with others. The second method is intimidation. No decent autocrat will allow public criticism or dissenting opinions. Sloppy authoritarianism is doomed to collapse even faster. But suppression also has its drawbacks. It’s labor-intensive—if your survival depends on spies, police, and the army, you can’t afford to have too few of them. And it damages the reputation of populist strongmen who haven’t yet completely stopped caring about their international image. The third and perhaps most important tool of populism and autocracy is manipulation. Its main advantage is that it’s effective even before taking power. It requires some investment, particularly in media, but thanks to the rise of social networks, it’s become cheaper, more effective, and easier. Plus, a savvy populist will always find a comrade willing to slip them a few euros, forints, or rubles for startup costs. But the most essential lubricant of manipulation is not money—it’s stupidity and ignorance. The rise of right-wing, illiberal, autocratic populism is inseparably linked to the rejection of facts, irrationality, and the uncritical, blind parroting of all kinds of nonsense and drivel. In the brave new populist world, scientific facts are seen as tools of alien exploitative elites, which the honest people can only resist by heroically kicking into the dark. Lies are glorified as virtues, experienced by the humiliated and aggrieved as a rallying cry, and used by populist manipulators as a tool for distraction, fueling public rage, making profit, consolidating power, and discrediting opponents. Lies are plastered on buses, whipped up in stadiums and arenas, spark international tensions, destroy democratic institutions, shake the foundations of the post-war global order, justify the most inhumane policies against vulnerable groups, and ultimately undermine efforts to address global threats to humanity's survival. Which brings us to the recent presidential consultation on Slovenia’s climate strategy. Of course, it’s absolutely right to involve not only experts but also politicians, who have the scissors and cloth in hand—and the responsibility to shape our country’s future strategy, whatever it may be. But given the President’s selection of participants, it seemed as if he believed this strategy should be anchored somewhere in the arithmetic middle between those who deny scientific facts about the climate crisis and those who actually understand them. In the name of unity at all costs, we’re expected to compromise halfway between populist delusions and scientific evidence. If we’re lucky, maybe our children and grandchildren will still vacation by the sea, just a few miles inland, in Dekani or Kozina. In the short term, lies in politics are undoubtedly more effective than the truth. Politics grounded in the gray reality of facts is far less attractive to voters than a thrill ride through the dreamland of populist promises. This is especially true when it comes to climate change. Here, lies and manipulation are weapons used to defend neoliberal capitalism’s total freedom, which, unsurprisingly, doesn’t give a damn about the climate and is unwilling to sacrifice even a fraction of today’s profits for a safer—or even remotely livable—future for coming generations. The alliance between right-wing populism and neoliberalism benefits both. Populism, by obstructing climate action, simply returns the favor to unregulated capital, which has tarnished the image of liberal democracy, impoverished vast swaths of the population, and paved the way for populism to rise to power. In such a scenario, responsible politicians can’t act like my grandmother when we grandchildren fought among ourselves. It’s one thing to bridge differences in implementing constitutional values and the vital interests of citizens—which surely include the survival of the human species—but it’s another thing entirely to compromise those values and interests in the name of overcoming differences. Compromise is not always a sign of moderation, strength, or wisdom. In the conflict between tolerance and intolerance, liberal and illiberal democracy, truth and falsehood, the “middle ground” is a victory for hatred, unfreedom, and lies. I support the President’s enthusiasm for listening to diverse views—in fact, I was invited to one of the consultations myself. But I would suggest he move away from the value-neutral search for the lowest common denominator, to achieve unity as a purpose in itself. I believe we can and must be more ambitious and consistently strive for a country whose value lies in the very values on which we built our independence. When it comes to human rights, political freedoms, democracy, dignity, a decent life, and the well-being of all citizens—let alone the long-term survival of human civilization—there is no wisdom in splitting the difference with populists.

For many years, a kind elderly couple of Italian descent lived in the house across from ours in Strasbourg. We weren’t particularly close, but we exchanged polite greetings and signed for each other’s registered letters and packages. Recently, both passed away—one shortly after the other, as often happens with longtime couples. Their children sold the house, but first organized a sale of the furniture and personal belongings. There was a lot of stuff, though little of real interest. Still, my wife and I found a beautiful Art Nouveau mirror, a pair of tasteful bedside lamps, and a charming glass trinket box with a tin lid adorned with tiny Bakelite roses. Just before leaving, I glanced inside a dining room cabinet. There, among the dishes and cutlery, I noticed a small bust of Benito Mussolini. Evidently, the Duce only made it to the table on special holidays, when the whole family gathered for Sunday lunch and grandpa, or nono, after a few glasses of wine, would reminisce about the good old days when he was young. My own nono was from Nabrežina near Trieste, and he too had dealings with Mussolini—albeit of a different nature. As a result, he was forced to flee in the mid-1920s to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. He ended up in Unec near Rakek—back then, the border was near Postojna. Many things happened to him there, but that’s material for another story. History is a fascinating subject. It can teach us a lot—lessons that remain very useful today. Our grandfathers lived in strange times, but it seems we’ve learned very little from them. And we should have. A few days ago, I attended a session of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance in Luxembourg—a governmental organization of which Slovenia is a member. As part of the session, a panel was held on the distortion of history. It was a response to the increasingly frequent and less and less veiled attempts to manipulate, obscure, and lie about historical facts concerning the Holocaust and the era that led to the greatest crime in human history. There was discussion not only of causes but also of possible responses to trends that seek to relativize or even deny the murder of over six million Jews and other victims of Nazi violence. Several interesting studies were cited, including those showing a connection between Holocaust distortion and right-wing populism, and even correlations with other types of denialism. Simply put: people who deny or relativize the Holocaust are more likely to deny climate change, oppose childhood vaccinations, and believe the Earth is flat The correlation isn’t perfect, of course. People reject historical and scientific facts for different reasons. Many anti-vaxxers in the U.S. come from Orthodox Jewish communities, while on the other hand, there are surely vaccinated people who believe the Earth is not round. Among the causes of the increasingly open and aggressive historical revisionism, participants pointed to the influence of social media and the growing societal and political tolerance of hate speech. Experts stressed that Holocaust distortion is also fuelled by attempts to excuse and glorify nationalist collaborators, and by the false equivalence of Nazi and communist crimes. No one, of course, denied the crimes committed in the name of communism, which deserve the strongest condemnation—but it was clear that such equivalencies are often efforts to divert attention or diminish responsibility for the atrocities committed by the Nazis and their accomplices. All of this has important implications for the Slovenian context. I don’t have empirical data on the rise of antisemitism in Slovenia, but based on research linking it to far-right populism, it’s safe to say we shouldn’t feel completely at ease. And then there’s the anecdotal case of the failed European Parliament candidate—someone who hasn’t (yet) broken into the first league of European nationalist "patriots." This gentleman once claimed that “the German people are victims of Jewish indoctrination and brainwashing with so-called Holocaustology.” I don’t even want to imagine what he might have tucked away between the fine china in his cabinet. Whether this was outright Holocaust denial or merely distortion is less important. I cite the statement mainly to highlight the unthinkable silence of those in positions of political and public responsibility who should have condemned such an outburst of hatred—but didn’t. This speaks to a deep misunderstanding of freedom of expression in Slovenia, a point recently raised by the Council of Europe’s Commission against Racism and Intolerance. There is a difference between protecting this vital human right and political liberty, and excusing, legitimizing, or even endorsing the spread of intolerance and hatred. Just days ago, the Secretary of State in the Prime Minister’s office tripped over this very issue. He tried to excuse some of his highly questionable past statements by invoking Slovenia’s supposedly strong protections for free speech. He even added—almost with pride—that he was never criminally prosecuted for them. Bravo, indeed. By spreading intolerance, he apparently considers himself a defender of our rights and freedoms. The political system Slovenia chose with its independence is not value-neutral. This was never about left or right—the country was founded on the principles of liberal democracy, protected by the Constitution. Let me remind you what it says in Article 1: Slovenia is a democratic, legal, and social state. We dedicated an entire chapter of the Constitution to human rights and fundamental freedoms, which are enforceable directly under the Constitution or international treaties. This constitutional framework—not some arithmetic midpoint between constitutional values and extremism, nor political opportunism—should guide elected officials in deciding when they can remain silent, and when they are obliged to speak out. In other words: when it comes to public statements and ideologies that run counter to constitutionally protected values and principles—statements or actions that deny the foundations of our state and society, such as democracy, human rights, and the rule of law—the highest state representatives have a duty to respond and condemn them. The fact that such a statement may not meet the legal threshold for prosecution—which, in my view, must remain high in a democratic society—is not and cannot be an excuse for silence. This is not about prosecutorial intervention in free speech. It’s about political reaction and societal condemnation of hatred, nationalism, racism, and antisemitism. And that applies to all constitutional principles—not just the ones named above. If nationalist populism distorts historical facts and relativizes the inviolability of our national borders, the answer cannot simply be “respect and cooperation.” Appeasement of the unacceptable—as the English call it—has never led to anything good in history. Churchill described appeasers as people who feed the crocodile, hoping it will eat them last. Sometimes you need to slam your fist on the table and say: for heaven’s sake, enough. Because once the Duce escapes from the cupboard—it’s very hard to put him back in.

When it comes to giving presents to children, I admit I often behave like that old fart who begins every sentence with “When I was your age.” It is not that I begrudge young people their joy; it is more the sadness of realizing that there is much less of that joy than back then—you know, when I was their age. We live in an age that expects instant gratification, with very short attention spans and quick boredom. We Slovenians have a similar attitude to democracy and Europe, at least judging by the recent European Parliament elections. And by a series of elections before them. As if we were already tired of everything. We treat such important historical achievements as the ability to freely choose our political representatives and membership of the European Union like someone who spends a fortune on a new car and then can’t be bothered to maintain it. Twenty-eight years after the proclamation of an independent Slovenia and fifteen years after joining the EU, Slovenian democracy is driving towards a bright future with a seized-up engine and bald tires. This statement is not related to the results of the last European elections. There is nothing wrong with them, and I will not comment on them either, as I avoid party-political positions in my writing. Nevertheless, I can’t help expressing my satisfaction that some people were not elected after all—the brown leaguers, for example, or the expert on trickery who has already left a lasting, if not the best, impression on parliamentary Europe. The turnout was dismal. Despite the few percentage points gained compared with the elections five years ago, it is extremely worrying that almost three-quarters of voters could not be bothered to walk to the polling station, or at least to a mailbox. Of course, we must ask who is to blame for such a dismally low turnout. The classic answer is the candidates, who were not convincing enough in their appearances and programs. This time, that is more an excuse than an answer. I am not trying to diminish the responsibility of politics for people’s growing distrust of politics, but I think that in these European elections Slovenian voters had a perfectly decent choice of names and candidates, among whom anyone could have found someone to put a circle around. The second common answer, specific to European elections, is that Slovenian representatives in the European Parliament have no influence. This argument cannot simply be waved away with “people have no idea,” since it is an impression created partly by the media and some more or less expert commentary. Such an attitude to the importance of the European Parliament for Slovenia is not serious. On the one hand, it is true that an individual’s influence in a body of 751 members does not come by itself, but it is far from true that someone with exceptional qualities, knowledge and political experience cannot become visible in the European Parliament and build influence and alliances that can be useful to the voters they represent and the country they come from. The fact that Slovenia is among the smaller countries and has only eight members is an objective handicap, but not an insurmountable obstacle. No one can make us as small as we know how to make ourselves small and insignificant. We Slovenians also don’t like politicians who are already in politics, but we must be aware of the consequences that an obsession with new faces could have for Slovenia’s influence in the European Parliament. Criticizing Fajon or Zver just because they have stood several times makes no sense. Influence in such a large and complex body is not built overnight; it takes several terms. This is not, of course, blanket support for those who have already been MEPs or criticism of those starting their first term. A closed political space is like an open fridge: it doesn’t take long for things to start to stink. On the other hand, it is also true that we cannot improve our influence if we send only new people every five years. At least in this respect, we can conclude that this year’s choice, as far as the mix of experience and freshness goes, is not bad. Slovenian representatives in the European Parliament are often criticized for a lack of unity. That is why in this year’s campaign the candidates swore one after another that things would be different from now on. In principle there is nothing wrong with that, at least as far as key issues are concerned: the arbitration ruling, environmental protection, the values of human rights, the rule of law and the welfare state, which we Slovenians protected in the Constitution, as well as the response to historical revisionism and the revival of ideas that in the past brought Slovenians and other Europeans so much grief. But it is one thing to talk about unity in televised debates and another to assert it on the European stage. The problem is not so much the lack of unity among MEPs in Strasbourg and Brussels as the fact that we have no consensus on these issues at home. Part of the responsibility for the low turnout must also be attributed to the media. Although in my view reporting on European affairs has improved in recent years, mainly thanks to good correspondents in Brussels, the media never manage to cover the campaign properly. Tabloid sensationalism is pushed, more concerned with how much MEPs earn than with what they do there. It is not that MEPs’ spending doesn’t deserve media attention—quite the opposite—but cheaply feeding Slovenian envy is not, and cannot be, journalism. The so-called fact-checking was also at times rather amateurish, ranging from setting juvenile traps and a subjective understanding of truth to lumping together completely insignificant slips with deliberate manipulation and lies. Finally, we must also think critically about the attitude of voters. Despite all the justified reasons for disappointment with politics, you can’t fix democracy by giving it the middle finger and going to the pub to rant about how everything is going to the dogs instead of going to vote. No voters, no elections; no elections, no democracy; no democracy, no freedom; no freedom, and we’re screwed. All of us. Society cannot change only from the top down. Each of us has the opportunity to start changing things in ourselves and around us. Mutual back-patting among the like-minded on social networks is no substitute for social engagement and civic responsibility. You can tweet until you drop, but if you don’t vote, don’t complain about the consequences. Democracy is like oxygen. It is too late if we only realize its importance when it is gone.

Many have called this year’s European Parliament elections historic. Whether they really were, history will show best, but they were certainly important. Most media and analysts had billed them as a critical test of the strength of the nationalist far right and even as an opportunity for a dramatic reshuffling of the cards between pro-European and populist forces in Europe. But if we were expecting tectonic shifts, today we may be disappointed. Rather than a turning point in history, yesterday’s elections resemble another round in a boxing match in which the populist challenger managed to land a punch or two more but in the end still got a bloody nose and lost heavily. On points, admittedly, but still. The picture of the new European Parliament is, of course, merely the aggregate reflection of twenty-eight very different national results. But here too, it is striking that there were no significant breakthroughs by the far right and populists, except perhaps in the very specific environment of Brexit-obsessed Great Britain and in the Flemish part of Belgium. In most other cases, the result more or less reflected the current balance of power at national level, as in Italy, Hungary and Poland, and in quite a few countries the populist right even won fewer votes than in national elections. This happened in Spain, and also in Germany, Estonia, Austria, Denmark, Finland and elsewhere. This is particularly interesting because in the past it was precisely European elections, in which many voters still vote with their middle finger, that allowed anti-establishment rabble-rousers to do better than in their national results. This time it was the other way round. When you are in power, or close to it, the anti-elitist card is simply not as effective as it is in the comfort of grumbling far from power. France produced an interesting result. Once again, many described the fact that the National Front, with a new name and a new frontman, beat President Macron’s list by a good percentage point as a breakthrough for the far right. Although comparisons with the results five years ago are complicated, since the political landscape in France has changed substantially, the fact remains that the National Front under its new name won less than in the previous elections, when it was already the strongest French party, and with two more seats than it will have from now on. Interestingly, Marine Le Pen did not manage to increase her result even at the expense of the Republicans, once the dominant force in French politics, whom a sharp turn to the right and flirting with populism by Sarkozy’s successor Laurent Wauquiez pushed below ten percent and into fourth place, behind the Greens. Macron did fail in his aim of beating the far right, but he kept his support close to his first-round score in the presidential election, which, after three years of not always the most skillful leadership of the country, is a relatively solid result, especially in light of the months-long yellow vest protests, which objectively benefited the far right more. So the picture across Europe is rather mixed. There is too much populism, but after the elections there is not significantly more of it than before. We need critical analysis, not hysteria. But since the momentum of cataclysmic sensationalism is hard to stop overnight, the first reactions in the media are still quite bombastic. Reading the first headlines, one would get the impression that all the seats lost by the EPP and S&D in the new EP were picked up by nationalists and populists. That is, of course, far from true. When the good results of the liberals and the Greens are added in, the change in the balance between the pro-European groups and the “others” shrinks considerably. Media reporting on populism has traditionally favored adrenaline over analysis. In this way, the strength and influence of the loudest and most aggressive are artificially inflated, which of course boosts their ratings. Such a competition in sensationalist emphasis on the negative can in the end lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy. That did not happen this time, despite some truly incredible headlines. Even the British Guardian wrote that the biggest winners of the elections were “radical alternatives such as the Greens and the far right.” Good Lord. It is true that nationalists, populists, Euroskeptics and the like will have a few more seats in the new parliament, but that is far from meaning that their influence will automatically be significantly greater. First because of the numbers, which even in the new, higher total are simply too low for anything other than ineffective obstruction, and second because they are an extremely heterogeneous group, united only by antipathy to the EU and the institutions of liberal democracy, while on other important issues they will find it hard to find a common language. Salvini may run into a series of problems in his wish for an influential populist bloc. Nationalism is not the best platform for international cooperation. There have also been changes in the balance between clearly pro-European political formations. The duopoly of the People’s Party and the Socialists lost quite a few seats, but mainly to the even more pro-European liberals and to the Greens, who, whatever the Guardian says, are not known for anti-European radicalism. Reshuffled cards among the pro-European groups are not necessarily bad news for the EU. Quite the opposite: the fact that a majority will now require a coalition of at least three pro-European parties can also have positive consequences, not least by helping to reduce the democratic deficit in the functioning of its institutions. This year’s election results did not tip the European political scales the other way. The weight is still firmly on the side of those who support European integration and its values. The nationalist, populist far right certainly got less than it wanted and less than many predicted. But that is far from meaning that pro-European politics can breathe a sigh of relief and carry on for another five years as it has until now. If it wants to reverse current trends, it has every opportunity to do so. It faces a loud and rowdy minority that depends on, and lives off, the opportunities created for it by the inconsistency and opportunism of those who otherwise never stop talking about Europe and democracy. The recipe for victory is, at least on paper, quite simple. European politics needs more backbone and consistency in respecting its own principles, more transparency, democracy and integrity in the functioning of its institutions, more social justice, more solidarity—between peoples and between people. We need politics that inspires and enthuses people, as opposed to populism, which manipulates them. But if we do not draw the right conclusions from these elections, the next round in five years may well end quite differently. On points, if not with a knockout of democratic Europe.

The reaction of part of the Slovenian public to the news that four migrants in Bela Krajina had allegedly abducted an elderly man, stuffed him into the boot of a car and driven him across half of Slovenia to the Italian border was very similar to the reaction of another part of the public to the recent fire at Notre-Dame in Paris. Suspicion, ridicule and conspiracy theories. You simply can’t cram an eighty-year-old into a car boot and drive him around Slovenia. Right, just as an eight-hundred-year-old oak beam can’t catch fire because of a short circuit. Believing only the truth that suits us emotionally, ideologically and politically is not peculiar to one (extreme) end of the political spectrum. Such a reaction to the news of the alleged abduction does nothing for efforts to bring more humanity, solidarity, respect for human rights and human dignity into how we treat migrants. Concern for security does not threaten a humane migration policy; it makes it possible. Realism and responsibility on security issues give humanism credibility, without which it is all too easy to dismiss it as a luxury whim of urban elites who don’t know and don’t care what life is like for people near the border. Security is not only a value; it is also a right, and if we treat people who are worried with indifference and condescension, we ourselves push them into the arms of those who claim that security can be achieved only at the expense of our humanity, with hatred and razor wire. This example is just one illustration of an increasingly fan-like way of reacting to social and political issues, in which we first choose a side and then select the facts that fit our ideological choice. Our world is black and white, with less and less room for principles, objectivity, facts and thinking for ourselves. We give all that up when we choose the team we support. We feverishly search the web for the most obscure sources of information that will confirm our preconceived beliefs. The internet has not lived up to expectations that it would tear down the communication barriers between people. Instead, social networks have created closed groups of like-minded parrots. Populism, whether left or right, encourages tribal allegiance and lives off it. The less people think, the less critical they are of the “truths” served to them, the easier it is to manipulate and govern them. In a black-and-white understanding of the crisis in Venezuela, for example, some people reflexively see no faults in Maduro because they don’t like Guaidó. Of course we can justifiably be critical of Guaidó’s moves, which are increasingly desperate and increasingly dangerous, but why should that make us overlook the fact that Maduro’s authoritarianism, the massive violations of human rights and political freedoms, and the incompetence and corruption of his regime are in many ways what led to the tragic crisis in that country? Some people in Slovenia have a similarly one-sided attitude to the Catalan question. On the one hand, from a human point of view, it is understandable that, given our own historical experience, we feel solidarity with the efforts of some Catalans for independence. Criticism of Madrid’s heavy-handedness on the Catalan question is also justified. On the other hand, the referendum was organized in great haste, on the basis of a law amended at the last minute to provide that independence could come about by a simple majority, with no minimum turnout threshold. The evident purpose was to neutralize the will and interests of almost half the population of Catalonia, who, according to opinion polls, did not favor independence. The Slovenian plebiscite and the Catalan referendum produced similar majorities, just over 90 percent of those voting, but in Slovenia this reflected the will of 88 percent of all eligible voters, while in Catalonia the share was half that, partly because of obstruction by the central authorities. Years ago, at the time of the Montenegrin independence referendum, the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s body for constitutional matters, recommended that for such far-reaching changes of constitutional status as a declaration of independence, the threshold should be set considerably higher. Caution is also warranted regarding superficial interpretations of the right to self-determination, a principle the United Nations formulated in the context of decolonization. But of course, when voters are split down the middle on independence, it is not only the appropriateness of hastily prepared referendums that is questionable, but also the legitimacy of blindly rejecting any change. A solution must be reached through negotiation and dialogue, not through party calculations, riding one nationalism or another, still less through repression. Catalonia is a typical case where black-and-white cheering for one side or the other can only do harm. Part of the Slovenian public also has a very partisan attitude to the French yellow vest movement, which, out of deep loathing for President Macron, they are prepared to excuse for its increasingly obvious slide into reactionary conspiracy theories, authoritarian ambitions, support for the far right and even antisemitism. Whatever we think of Macron, he is a politician who defends the democratic institutions that allow the French to get rid of him at the next election if they so wish. Recently, on social networks, I came across enthusiasm from the left at the news that Marine Le Pen’s far right had overtaken Macron’s list in opinion polls ahead of the European elections. I don’t know why Molotov and Ribbentrop came to mind. Finally, the attitude to Julian Assange is also a good example of ideological simplification and black-and-white polarization. While concern about the grounds of the American extradition request is justified, since it contains charges that could lead to the prosecution of established and legitimate forms of cooperation between journalists and their sources, this, in my view, is not enough to make Mr. Assange a tragic hero of freedom and democracy. It is particularly sad that many in his defense are prepared to ignore the rape allegations against him on the grounds that they were dismissed, which of course is not true. The proceedings were halted because, once Assange had taken refuge in the Ecuadorian embassy in London, there were no practical conditions for continuing them. Confirmation came in recent days, when Swedish prosecutors reopened the case. Also because of his chumminess with Russian hackers in the attempt to influence the outcome of the last American presidential election, it might be better in this story to focus on defending democratic institutions and principles rather than on beatifying Assange. And on women’s right to be safe from sexual violence. My message is by no means that I am trying to defend Guaidó and his playing with fire. I too have reservations about Madrid’s approach to the Catalan question. I think many criticisms of Macron’s policies are justified and legitimate, and in the end I too am worried about the consequences Assange’s extradition to the American authorities could have for media freedom. I am merely warning of the dangers of an “it doesn’t matter what he’s like, as long as he’s ours” attitude to the world. A society in which ideology is stronger than truth is not healthy and can be neither democratic nor free. Tribal fandom that is stronger than facts and principles prevents a rational and effective approach to solving complex social and international issues. Politics is like football: reality is often different from the one we would emotionally like. For all the joy I felt at Olimpija’s recent magnificent victory at Ljudski vrt, I accepted calmly and, as far as possible, with dignity the fact that Maribor deservedly became national champions. If you support Olimpija, you have to get used to complex emotions and a critical attitude towards your own team. Facts are facts, however much I love green.
The Future in the Grip of Populism

The recent anti-migrant protest in Jelšane, organized by the mayor of the small Slovenian city of Ilirska Bistrica, couldn’t have come at a more telling moment. Just weeks before the European elections, we were given a snapshot—like a petri dish—of the state of our society. It offers insight into who we are, where we are, and where we’re headed—in Jelšane, in Slovenia, and in Europe. The most striking image was undoubtedly the elderly woman captured on camera beating the pavement with a Slovenian flag, shouting, “Nobody’s gonna screw me!” She threw in some choice insults aimed at those she believed were trying to steal her country. She made no secret of what she’d like to do with—or to—them. Some saw pain and fear in her outburst; others saw blinding hatred and a loss of dignity and reason. Honestly, one does not exclude the other. I don’t know what led her to such a state—perhaps personal hardship that might warrant our compassion. Perhaps. But both pain and hatred are core ingredients of the populist political paradigm, which exploits legitimate frustrations, turning them into fear, prejudice, and rage, and channeling them toward scapegoats—whoever fits the bill. Today it’s migrants. If there aren’t enough of them, feminists, women in general, LGBTQ+ people, Jews, Muslims, or any other minority can serve just as well. It’s easier to manipulate people who are blinded by hate. The woman’s outburst in Jelšane was not just symbolic of populism—it was textbook populism in action. The frenzied flag-waving, profanity, and threats of violence illustrate the modus operandi of populist “solutions” to any issue. It’s not a reaction; it’s a political strategy. No matter the challenge—climate change, security risks, migration—populism always offers the same answer: a chance to vent bile. Real, effective answers? Populist politics isn’t interested in them. “Nobody’s gonna screw us!” is a response to every challenge we face. Most of today’s pressing problems require rationality, cooperation, and solidarity—three things you won’t find in national-populist politics. Instead of solutions, they offer anger. Populist leaders act much like that woman in Jelšane—except they’re not beating the pavement with a flag, but with the fates of their citizens. Hatred fueled adrenaline may provide a short-term rush in times of anxiety, fear, or perceived threat—real or invented—but it wears off quickly. It’s about as effective as squeezing a stress ball. Only, in populism, you’re not squeezing rubber bananas—you’re squeezing your own vulnerable organs. By the time you realize that, it might be too late. The pain becomes unbearable. The damage, irreversible. That is how populism imperils not just the present, but future generations. Beating the pavement in Jelšane may seem irrational, but irrationality in populism is intentional. A deliberate abandonment of reason, facts, and logic is a key part of the populist model. You can’t manipulate thoughtful people as easily. The same applies to lies. Absurd conspiracy theories spread like wildfire on social media, but they serve a very real purpose.
