This is the digital-age renaissance of what social Darwinist Hermann von Keyserling called the “führerprinzip.” As Hannah Arendt wrote, the leader is always right. Repeating the leader’s lies becomes a ritual of loyalty—a rejection of independent thought and a submission to the one and only truth. The bigger and more outrageous the lie, the stronger the bond between follower and leader. It’s a kind of mental training, preparing people to obey blindly. Then there’s fear. It’s often cited as the catch-all excuse for extreme views, prejudice, and even violence. “We don’t support it, but you have to understand—people are afraid.” Sure, fear is real and can be justified. But it can also be manufactured, stoked, and exploited. It must not become the universal alibi for cruelty and inhumanity. Take the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a completely fabricated pamphlet produced in Tsarist Russia and widely distributed by antisemites from Henry Ford to the Nazis. Its aim was to instill fear of Jews, alleged to be plotting global domination. That fear was artificially created—but deeply felt. And it unleashed a landslide that convinced ordinary people to accept—or even participate in—the murder of six million. That same fear is being stoked again today through new conspiracy theories, resurgent antisemitism, and mainstreamed hate. National-populism hinges on a black-and-white view of the world: the pure people versus corrupt elites and parasites. But this simplistic binary isn’t limited to the far right. Elements of the left also push a broad-brush anti-elite narrative that fuels the same mechanisms of resentment and conspiracy—and even feeds antisemitism. Fighting social injustice is one thing. A cultural revolution is another. The line between the two is often blurred. Populism is trying hard to pass itself off as classical conservatism—a renaissance of the true people's right. In this framework, those who defend liberal democracy, anti-fascism, human rights, dignity, solidarity—the values on which European integration was built—are labeled radical leftists, commies, or Stalinists. That’s absurd. These are civilizational values, and it was conservatives and Christian democrats who built the European project on them. This should concern anyone claiming to be the political heir of Adenauer, Schuman, De Gasperi, and other EU founders. If nationalism, chauvinism, anti-anti-fascism, and authoritarianism now define the right, that’s a serious problem—especially for conservatives. Sure, cozying up to national-populists might win them a few more seats. But it risks erasing their political legacy entirely. In 1946, in his “Let Europe Arise” speech in Zurich, Winston Churchill said the League of Nations didn’t fail because of its principles—but because the founding states abandoned them. There’s a lesson there—if we’re willing to learn it. This year’s European elections are hugely important—and highly unpredictable. It’s not about which party wins: left, center, or right. It’s about how much support and legitimization will go to those who offer nationalism over cooperation, authoritarianism over liberal democracy, and flag-beating over real solutions. At the end of May, we have the democratic power to choose Europe’s future—and our own. The outcome may well determine whether we’ll still be allowed to choose in the future at all.
In the Trenches of Western Civilization

Easter Monday, en route from Ljubljana to Strasbourg. On the radio, I hear that the death toll from Sunday’s bomb attacks in Sri Lanka has climbed to nearly 300. Most of the victims were locals, but there were also dozens of foreigners. The targets of the Islamist extremists—most likely responsible for the terrorist attacks—were Catholic churches, where Easter Mass was being celebrated, and luxury hotels packed with tourists. An attack on Western civilization? Perhaps. But certainly an attack on Sri Lanka, and a crime against humanity. I’m not among those who seek reasons—or worse, justifications—for Islamist terrorism in the sins and injustices inflicted on Muslims around the world by a cruel, hypocritical, and greedy West. Those injustices undeniably exist. But nothing, absolutely nothing, can justify or excuse the murder of innocent people. Terrorism in any form, regardless of the ideological cloak it wears, is evil and must be stopped and punished—with force, not diplomacy. At the same time, it is equally depraved when politicians attempt to extract political capital from such attacks—often before the dead have even been removed or the wounded treated. Already, we hear voices blaming all Muslims for the atrocities committed by a fanatical group of deranged extremists. This is highly effective—and extremely dangerous—misdirection. The Sri Lankan jihadists represent Islam no more than Hitler, Ratko Mladić, or the Christchurch mosque shooter represent Christianity. But that won’t stop the Sunday Crusaders and “guardians of Western civilization” from competing in generalizations, blanket accusations, insults, lies, and spreading social-media-fueled “truths” that “the mainstream media won’t show you.” What follows is a cultural war—deepening divisions based on religion, race, origin, and nationality—all in the pursuit of political power. The biggest beneficiaries of extremist crimes on one side are always their mirror images on the other. The ideological spectrum is circular—extremists of all kinds end up rubbing shoulders with those they supposedly hate the most. I’m also wary of the civilizational rhetoric that always resurfaces after tragedies like the one in Sri Lanka. After 9/11, much attention was paid to Samuel Huntington’s “Clash of Civilizations” thesis, published years earlier as a rebuttal to Francis Fukuyama’s idea that liberal democracy marked the “end of history.” Huntington replied: “Hardly. What’s coming is a clash of civilizations and an assault by Islamist extremists on Western civilization.” I believe both Huntington and Fukuyama missed the mark. Liberal democracy is, at best, limping along today—far from having delivered a final knockout to authoritarian and illiberal alternatives. Huntington’s error was even more basic: Islamist radicalism is a threat—but it is not a civilization. We can, of course, debate semantics—what counts as a civilization, and what doesn’t. When Gandhi was asked what he thought of Western civilization, he famously said: “It would be a good idea.” Given how the British Empire “civilized” the Indian subcontinent for nearly a century, who can blame him? I personally see civilization and culture differently—not as an identity or a political flag, but as the best and most valuable contributions a particular community makes to the shared heritage of humanity. Viewed this way, it’s clear: civilizations do not clash with each other. If they did, they wouldn’t be civilizations. Civilization is a shelf, where we place the greatest human achievements for all to admire—the things we are justly proud of. Europeans have a lot to place on that shelf: from Ancient Greece, the Enlightenment, and parts of the French Revolution, to the abolition of slavery, gender equality, and the liberal democracy that was built after WWII as a response to our darkest chapter—based on human rights, humanism, solidarity, and the rule of law. An integral part of European civilization is Christianity, which, through its values and contributions to culture, is part of our cultural DNA. But today’s “defenders of Western civilization” care little for culture or values. They wear Christianity like a military uniform—a tool to divide “us” from “them” in a culture war against others. In doing so, they resemble their ideological opposites—because again, the ideological spectrum is circular. Such a weaponized understanding of religion, race, culture, and identity has no place on the civilization shelf—even if it is part of our history. For the darker parts of our past, Europe has plenty of material—but that belongs in a different cabinet: pathologies preserved in formaldehyde, reminders of historical memory, so we don’t forget or repeat old mistakes. Years ago, I had lunch with Dr. Ismail Serageldin, then director of the Bibliotheca Alexandrina—a jewel of world civilization built in the time of Ptolemy II. At a time of rising tensions and misunderstandings across the Mediterranean, we didn’t discuss what divides us—but what has connected us for centuries. Dr. Serageldin believes this is where we can build an antidote to today’s conflicts, much as European integration overcame historical divisions. Forget Arab numerals and Scheherazade—he told me, for example, about the Charter of Medina, in which the Prophet Muhammad, in the 7th century, granted religious freedom and minority protections, and gave women significant social rights, including property ownership. A thousand years later, women in Europe were still their husbands’ property—and if they were unlucky enough to be accused of witchcraft, their best chance of escaping execution by fire was to drown. It’s true: in much of the modern Muslim world, women still lack rights worthy of admiration. But if anything, that only proves that misreading the Prophet’s message is not limited to Islamophobes. What’s more, opposition to gender equality unites conservatives on both sides. With not enough refugees left to sustain widespread fear and paranoia—the lifeblood of populist regimes—women’s rights have become the new target of Europe’s anti-liberal tribunes. Civilizations may not clash—but they can be threatened. Islamist terrorism is a threat, and must not be taken lightly. But like other global challenges, it demands solidarity and cooperation among peoples and nations—not division. European civilization is also under threat from those so obsessed with power that they’re willing to say and do anything—including claim that electrical faults can’t start fires. Such stupidity is not only an insult to fire safety and common sense, but to Europe’s Enlightenment heritage, which—before the resurgence of populism—valued science, logic, and facts. Today, for many, the only truth is whatever fuels their prejudice and hate. A week ago, as I watched Notre-Dame’s wooden roof engulfed in flames, I felt a deep sadness—for this jewel of European civilization, part of our global cultural heritage. But when I read the reactions of some of the people we’ve entrusted with running our countries, I felt chilled. We are in trouble—because civilization can’t be proven by 800-year-old stones and beams, no matter how beautifully arranged. In the end, the true proof of civilization is our civil behavior, here and now. And on that front, my friends, we are increasingly coming up short.

In the first year of the last century, a terrible tornado swept through the American state of Kansas and carried 12-year-old Dorothy Gale into the Land of Oz. Wanting to go home, she set off for the Emerald City to see the great wizard. On the way, she was joined by a scarecrow without a brain, a tin woodsman without a heart, and a lion without courage. It turned out the Wizard of Oz was just a fraud, who—like many politicians after him—rose to power using little more than a megaphone and a hot air balloon. The help he offered Dorothy and her companions was equally hollow: the scarecrow got a head filled with pins and bran, the tin man got a sack of sawdust instead of a heart, and the lion received a secret potion for courage. What exactly was in that drink we’ll never know—but Slovenians know well what kind of drink gives you guts. When the film version of The Wizard of Oz was made in 1939, starring Judy Garland, the filmmakers apparently thought that bran-for-brains, sawdust-for-a-heart, and headaches-for-courage didn’t make for a convincing transformation. So in the movie, the scarecrow got a diploma, the tin man a clock, and the lion a medal. But in Kansas, people still value tradition and culture over rationality and the political correctness of Hollywood elites. A few years ago, a dentist in the small Kansas town of Iola gave a 13-year-old girl polystyrene fillings. Whether this decision came from graduating at the University of Oz Medical School or from having actual bran between his ears is unclear, but the media reported that the girl’s parents couldn’t afford to finish the dental procedure, and her health insurance barely covered the styrofoam. The fillings, of course, failed—and the girl lost her jaw. Stories about people in the U.S. unable to afford even the most basic healthcare are sadly common—but Kansas stands out. The reason? The so-called Kansas Experiment of 2012, launched by Governor Sam Brownback, a man who apparently thinks with bran and feels with sawdust. His tax reform—unironically dubbed the “March to Zero”—slashed taxes for the wealthiest, drastically cut or eliminated profit taxes for most businesses and freelancers, reduced social benefits, made healthcare less accessible for the poorest (hence the styrofoam fillings), shut down dozens of schools, closed four public agencies, and laid off 2,000 public employees. Governor Brownback promised this would be an adrenaline shot for the economy, bringing in investments and boosting employment. This is, of course, the trickle-down economy in action—the belief that tax cuts for the rich will eventually benefit everyone. Brownback implemented the reform with ruthless ideological purity, making no compromises. Neoliberalism has been fashionable ever since Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s discovered Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom and fell in love with the idea that taxes and government interference lead to the loss of freedom. But few before Brownback tried to implement this doctrine in such an infantile, simplistic, and brutal way. The global neoliberal cheer squad watched Kansas’s experiment with giddy excitement, clapping their little fingers like Teletubbies watching a pancake machine. But in the end, it collapsed. Within a few years, Brownback had turned a budget surplus into a billion-dollar deficit. The promised investment boom and job growth never materialized. Economic growth lagged far behind other U.S. states—except a few that tried their own Kansas-style race to the bottom. To patch the hole, Brownback and friends raided infrastructure funds, stopped repairing highways, and raised sales tax, which hit low-income people the hardest. In the end, the poorest paid more taxes than before the reform. Neoliberalism, it turns out, is stronger than gravity: money never trickles down—it only flows upward. Years of neoliberal abuse drove Kansas voters into such a fury with the ruling elites that, in the 2016 presidential election, they gave a convincing victory to Donald Trump. If that doesn’t make sense to you, then you don’t understand populism—where it comes from and how it works. Neoliberalism and populism exist in a symbiotic relationship: the former creates the conditions for the latter, which in return undermines the democratic institutions that could threaten neoliberal power. The common enemy of both is liberal democracy—the opposite of populist, illiberal democracy. Liberal democracy is built on human and social rights, political freedoms, the rule of law, solidarity, and respect for human dignity. But such a democracy needs social justice to function. People who have everything and people who have nothing cannot coexist peacefully in the same democratic system. Yet social justice is anathema to neoliberalism, which is based on the absolute freedom of capital. And so the vicious cycle is complete. One might assume that the dismal failure of the Kansas experiment would at least slow down the triumphant march of the neoliberal-populist axis. But anyone who thinks that way doesn’t understand populism, which doesn’t run on reason but on negative emotion and manipulation—on channeled frustration, turning the ignored and the humiliated, the styrofoam-filled and disenfranchised, into prisoners of their own prejudices, hatred, and fear. Without this manipulated projection of blame, there would be no Trump, no Brexit, no Salvini, no Orbán, and no local mini-Orbáns. And here’s where the Teletubby comparison ends. When Tinky Winky and friends break the pancake machine, they just shrug, wave goodbye, and retreated into their holes. Neoliberals don’t do that. When Trump wanted to thank Kansas voters for their loyalty, he passed a federal tax reform that looked suspiciously like the Kansas disaster. Because no good deed goes unrewarded, Sam Brownback was appointed U.S. Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom. And the main architect of the failed reform, Stephen Moore—a man said to enjoy playing dress-up as an economist and babbling nonsense on TV—was just nominated to the Federal Reserve Board of Governors. “Stephen will do a damn good job,” Trump declared as he jetted off to his Florida golf court. When neoliberals drive off a cliff, they don’t retreat into holes. They send in golf balls.

In October 1945, 86 Jewish victims were buried at the municipal cemetery in the Robertsau district of Strasbourg. They had been discovered after the city’s liberation from German occupation in the premises of the anatomical institute at the medical faculty of the University of Strasbourg. The victims had been brought from Auschwitz in the summer of 1943 at the initiative of the Nazi professor Dr August Hirt. They were murdered in a gas chamber built specifically for this purpose at the Struthof-Natzweiler camp and their bodies were then transported to Strasbourg. Dr Hirt had "ordered" the bodies because he wanted to create a collection of skeletons to "prove" the racial inferiority of Jews. At the anatomical institute, the corpses were placed in vats filled with formaldehyde—until Dr Hirt simply forgot about them, at least until Allied forces approached Strasbourg in the fall of 1944. At that point, the remains of 57 men and 29 women were mutilated to hinder identification. Dr Hirt ended his project by extracting the victims’ gold teeth and pocketing them. Wikipedia describes Hirt as a "physician, torturer, and university professor." He spent most of his life near the Black Forest, where he put a bullet in his head in June 1945. But the story doesn’t end there. Four years ago, a book titled Hippocrates in Hell claimed that containers holding the remains of the murdered Jews still exist at the institute. The book caused a scandal, and the University of Strasbourg responded by establishing an international commission of inquiry—which has not yet completed its work. The possibility that generations of Strasbourg medical students trained in rooms where dusty shelves still hide traces of horrific crimes against Jews preserved in formaldehyde is an allegory for European antisemitism. For a long time, hatred was hidden in the darkest corners of our consciousness. Now, it is reemerging, boldly and brazenly. A 2018 report from the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights states that 86% of Jews in Europe feel threatened. And this is not just about subjective feelings or oversensitivity. In just the past few weeks, Strasbourg and its surroundings saw antisemitic graffiti appear at the school attended by my older children, the destruction of a memorial to the synagogue burned down during the war, and the desecration of nearly a hundred graves in the Jewish cemetery in the nearby village of Quatzenheim. There are several reasons for this renewed surge in antisemitism. First, ignorance of history. In France, 20% of young people between 18 and 34 have never heard of the Holocaust. In some places—including Slovenia—this ignorance is actively encouraged. The constant droning that we must leave history behind is irresponsible, even if not intended to relativize its lessons. Short-sightedness and political opportunism are no excuse for downplaying how forgetting yesterday’s crimes feeds today’s hatred. Second, the internet. American historian Timothy Snyder said during a recent lecture at the Council of Europe that we are all dumber today than we were ten years ago—because of the internet. The only reason we don’t notice it, he said, is because we’re all dumber together. As an example, he cited the resurgence of conspiracy theories about a global Jewish plot. Third, the normalization of hate. A CNN-commissioned study found that 20% of Europeans believe antisemitism is a justified response to Jewish behaviour. Politics is partly to blame—even here in Slovenia. The silence or even tacit justification of hatred in the name of free speech by high-ranking officials, even in cases involving Holocaust denial or claims that this greatest crime in human history—the murder of six million people—was a Jewish conspiracy, is a textbook example of extreme political irresponsibility. Latent antisemitism—which never truly disappeared, only sat quietly like those jars of formaldehyde at the Strasbourg anatomy institute—is once again gaining momentum. Parts of European politics and media are now openly playing the antisemitic card. Not long ago, the supposedly independent Hungarian magazine Figyelő ran a photoshopped cover of András Heisler, president of Hungary’s Jewish community federation, with banknotes raining down on him. At this year’s carnival in Aalst, Belgium, a float featured Jewish caricatures that would not have been out of place in Der Stürmer. The far-right Polish weekly Tylko Polska ("Only Poland") recently published a front-page guide on how to recognize a Jew—by names, anthropological features, facial expressions, appearance, personality traits, behavior, and methods of deceiving the public. Although the victims of the recent New Zealand attack were Muslims, it is part of the same story. The Christchurch killer and Robert Bowers, who murdered eleven people at a synagogue in Pittsburgh months earlier, are inhuman twins. Whether the target is Jews, Muslims, or others, these terrorist attacks are thematic variations of the same hatred and blindness. Fourth, antisemitism among some immigrants from majority-Muslim countries—both those who have lived in Europe for generations and those who arrived more recently. The quenelle salute—a kind of inverted Nazi salute made popular by controversial comedian Dieudonné—is popular among youth in French suburbs and on social media. This must not be ignored. Turning a blind eye to the presence of extreme views among a minority within this population only aids those who seek to generalize and stigmatize the overwhelming majority that rejects hatred and violence. This type of antisemitism is not rooted in traditional European prejudices but is largely fueled by Middle Eastern conflicts. And this leads us to the fifth and final chapter of Europe’s antisemitic revival: antisemitism on parts of the European left. Linking criticism of Israel to antisemitism is a delicate matter. Israeli policy often tries to use this linkage to discredit entirely legitimate criticism of its frequently unacceptable actions. On the other hand, it is also true that part of the left tries to mask its latent antisemitism as criticism of Israel. Drawing the line between the two is too complex for this column, but I believe that a clear and unconditional condemnation of all forms of antisemitism only strengthens the credibility of justified criticism of Israeli policies. That this is a problem for parts of the European left is evident in the ongoing struggle of the British Labour Party to root out deeply entrenched antisemitism in its ranks. Conspiracy theories about Jewish global cabals, hook-nosed bankers with fat cigars—these are becoming more common among France’s gilets jaunes ("yellow vests"), whose colour is, with rising antisemitism, starting to take on a brown hue. A quarter of Europeans believe Jews have too much influence in business and finance. The stigmatization and attacks on entire groups or social classes—which originally emerged from legitimate outrage over systemic social injustice—end up discrediting and weakening those movements. Instead of criticizing the system, we increasingly hear insults aimed at people. Mindless sloganeering against “the elites” is becoming indistinguishable from far-right rants about Soros—a universal weapon to discredit anyone populists see as an obstacle to power. The circle is complete. Parts of the radical left and the far right now jointly promote conspiracies, stereotypes, caricatures, patterns, and discourses of traditional European antisemitism. Across Europe, in plain view, a competition in prejudice against fellow humans is playing out. Welcome to the reality show: Hatred, the Home Edition. On all our screens. And in front of them.

These days, mentioning liberal democracy feels like letting out a fart during a philharmonic concert—met with disgust and scorn from all sides. From the right, I get called a far-left radical; from the left, a centrist, neoliberal elitist. I have no problem with people disagreeing with me or criticizing me—what bothers me is that too often, the arguments arise because we’re not even talking about the same thing. So here’s a quick overview of how I understand liberalism, neoliberalism, and liberal democracy. Yes, all three terms share the same root, but that doesn’t mean they should be thrown into the same pot. I don’t expect to convince everyone, but I hope we can at least agree on what it is we disagree about. Let’s start with political liberalism. It’s one of the traditional political orientations, flanked on the left by social democracy and other left-wing parties, and on the right by Christian democrats, people’s parties, and their kin. Liberals champion individual rights and political freedoms, which in principle includes human rights and minority rights. Where each liberal party falls on the political spectrum depends on its stance toward economic issues, tax policy, and public spending. There are big differences among them—from social liberals to apologists for the harshest forms of neoliberalism. In America, the terminology is flipped. Liberal is a slur hurled by the political right—especially the far right—at politicians like Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Alt-right columnist Kurt Schlichter recently wrote that “America can only stay united if liberals accept values like freedom, tolerance, and the Constitution—and abandon their obsession with socialism, cultural fascism, and being jerks.” Americans also differentiate between social and fiscal liberalism. A social liberal supports human rights, political freedoms, and minority rights. A fiscal liberal advocates higher taxes, more public spending, and greater social justice. Those who in Europe would be called fiscal liberals are referred to across the Atlantic as fiscal conservatives. Next, there’s neoliberalism—and yes, Americans also call it that. That it cannot be simplistically equated with liberalism is evidenced by the fact that Bernie Sanders has never been accused of being a neoliberal. Neoliberalism is an economic doctrine and social model built on extreme fiscal conservatism—i.e., as low taxes and public spending as possible. Alongside that comes aggressive deregulation, as any state intervention—even in the name of legitimate goals like environmental protection—is seen as illegitimate interference with the freedom of capital. The neoliberal trinity is rounded out by the push for widespread privatization of public services and the fetishization of the market as the only effective mechanism for managing society and meeting social needs. Then there’s liberal democracy—a concept that many people now angrily conflate with the previous two. My former high school defense and civil protection teacher Janez Janša, in a recent piece titled “Slovenians and Europe,” complained about those who elevate liberal democracy above all else, claiming it’s just one form of democracy among many. Technically, he’s right. Just like it’s true that oxygen is merely one of many gases. There’s also laughing gas, which causes euphoria, then drowsiness, and in high doses, respiratory problems and brain damage. We also have carbon dioxide, which is currently doing a fine job preventing black panthers from returning to Slovenia’s forests. And then there’s hydrogen cyanide, better known as Zyklon B, introduced to the world by a democratically elected politician known for his hostility toward liberal democracy and its values. So yes—many gases. Many democracies. But not all are equal. Democracy by itself guarantees only the chance to cast a vote at regular intervals. If there’s only one option to vote for, that’s people’s democracy. North Korea celebrated such a democracy just last Sunday: only one name on the ballot, near 100% turnout, and near 100% victory. For democracy to be minimally pluralistic, voters must be offered multiple real choices. Iran, for instance, offers such a setup—you never know whether the hardliners or the moderates will win. It may be pluralistic, but it’s not liberal. Then there’s illiberal democracy, where multiple parties exist on paper, but the ruling group so thoroughly controls and abuses the levers of power that competitors stand no chance. Nicolás Maduro’s Venezuela illustrates this well. It’s also an increasingly popular model among some of our neighbors. And then there’s this damn liberal democracy, which—on top of free elections—provides effective protection for human rights, minority rights, political freedoms, and maintains checks on executive power through separation of powers, independent courts, free media, and civil society. The confusion, however, lies not just in the terms themselves, but even more in how they relate to one another—a minefield of oversimplifications, manipulations, and misunderstandings. Let’s break it down: Many people believe that only liberals defend liberal democracy. Not true. In fact, today there are quite a few so-called liberal parties in Europe that clearly don’t care for liberal democracy—and actively undermine it. Liberal democracy is a political and social model developed after WWII, as a response to fascism and Nazism, primarily by Christian democrats in France, Germany, and Italy. It was further shaped by parties across the political spectrum—left, right, and center. They differed greatly, but all (at least on paper) shared a commitment to the institutions of liberal democracy. Outside of this spectrum lie the populist far-right and far-left movements and politicians who, in the name of “the people” or “the working class,” put themselves above democratic institutions, seeking to delegitimize political opponents and seize and hold onto power unchecked. More complex is the relationship between liberal democracy and neoliberalism. Many neoliberal politicians wrap themselves in liberal-democratic values, leading some to assume the two are inseparable. That’s false. I’m convinced that the relationship between liberal democracy and neoliberalism is not a partnership—but a conflict. It was neoliberalism that created the conditions for populism’s rise, which now threatens liberal democracy. The current crisis of liberal democracy stems from the social injustice baked into neoliberalism’s DNA. Because capital failed to “trickle down” and develop a social conscience, large swaths of the population—especially in Western democracies—have been pushed to the economic, social, and political margins. The resulting frustration and rage have been skillfully exploited by populists to undermine democratic institutions and discredit political competition. Understanding this conflict is essential if we’re to avoid two major fallacies: That tearing down liberal democracy’s institutions, as some of the increasingly “brown” Yellow Vests in France attempt, is a path to social justice. That liberal democracy can be saved without serious social reform, as much of European politics seems to believe. Without defeating neoliberalism, we won’t defeat populism. And vice versa. But this isn’t a task for just one part of the political spectrum. The responsibility lies with everyone—left, center, and right. I find a bit of hope in that earlier-mentioned piece on Slovenians and Europe. The author laments that liberal democracy is now defended not only by liberals and socialists but that “even some Christian-democratic thinkers and politicians have taken the bait.” You have no idea how much I hope he’s right on that point.

Any experienced official will tell you that in bureaucracies the biggest crises like to happen on Friday afternoons, when people are already starting to dream about the weekend. Bernhard Lösener, head of the racial legislation department at the Third Reich’s Ministry of the Interior, must surely have cursed this bureaucratic curse when, on September 13, 1935, the Führer himself called and ordered him to draft, within 24 hours, the text of the laws for the protection of German blood and honor. Hitler had decided to present the new legislation that very Sunday at the Nazi rally in Nuremberg, so Bernhard had to say goodbye to his plans to spend the weekend carousing and smashing the windows of Jewish shops with his colleagues from the ministry. Instead, he had to roll up his sleeves and draft the acts that legalized racial discrimination and stripped millions of Jews of their citizenship and human dignity. For these rules, later known as the Nuremberg Laws, to be implemented effectively, it was of course also necessary to define whom they applied to. So we got full-blooded Jews and, alongside them, Mischlinge of the first and second degree, that is, the Jewish children, or the children of Jewish children, of mixed marriages, with half or a quarter Jewish blood. The leading “experts” on racial discrimination in the Third Reich were in fact quite critical of the hastily written laws. Some found them insufficiently scientific and too lenient, especially regarding the Mischlinge. These were supposedly even more dangerous than full-blooded Jews, because they could carry out their Jewish schemes with a dose of Aryan efficiency. Hitler himself was satisfied with the laws, since, as later events confirmed, they fully achieved their purpose, namely to create enemies of the nation. Hitler himself once admitted that if the Jews did not exist, they would have to be invented. Nothing unites like a shared hatred. The pieces in the series of articles that the weekly Demokracija and Nova24TV recently began publishing about the “children of the UDBA” also seem to have been written in rather a hurry. “Children of the UDBA” (udbovska deca) is a term introduced into the Slovenian media space by the pen of a former respected judge of the European Court of Human Rights, freed from the ethical and moral shackles of a well-paid office. The gentleman, as only he can, has also given the whole matter a scientific basis. If I understand correctly, these are people in important positions who should not be there because they are related to personalities whom the gentleman and the two outlets, rather sweepingly and superficially, link to the UDBA, the Yugoslav secret police, and to all manner of immoral dealings from recent Slovenian history. Translated into the language of the Nuremberg legislation, the “children of the UDBA” are half- and quarter-UDBA Mischlinge. The point of what I am writing is not, of course, a comparison between the notorious secret police of the former regime and the Jews who were the victims of the greatest crime in human history. The Holocaust was an inconceivable crime, yet today it is being relativized and belittled, including in the name of and with the help of ideas promoted by some of the hunters of the children of the UDBA. I have a very low opinion of the UDBA, rivaled only by the contempt I feel for those who distort historical facts and spread ideas and a politics of lies, hatred and fear. What incontestably justifies the comparison with the 1930s is the attempt first to incriminate a group of people wholesale and accuse them of the worst crimes, and then, on the basis of blood ties, to disqualify their children or grandchildren as well. If the evidence of alleged misdeeds by the “UDBA men” is already on rather shaky ground, for the “children of the UDBA” there is none at all. Impure blood is enough for disqualification, together with the fact that these are people who, in one way or another, stand in the way of the populist attack on the civilizational foundations of Slovenian democracy and independence. According to the two outlets, the “children of the UDBA” are people who have “stolen the state” from Slovenians. This is what they say: “The Slovenian deep state is rooted very deeply in all spheres of society, politics and the economy, even almost 30 years after independence, when the communist regime was supposed to have been ended.” The aforementioned expert on moral questions is also worried. This is how he complained: “The political protest is directed against the UDBA men themselves, but it is forgotten that countless of their children and even grandchildren are on the scene. I have been watching the rise of UDBA children and grandchildren for at least twenty years, not only in the people’s republic but even in international organizations. There are at least two in Strasbourg; how many there are elsewhere, I don’t know.” Let us look at what Dr. Joseph Goebbels, the newly minted Reichsminister für Volksaufklärung und Propaganda—minister of public enlightenment and propaganda—said on the subject of the “hijacked state,” this time hijacked by the Jews, in the great salon of the Hotel Carlton in Geneva in September 1933, two years before the Nuremberg legislation was adopted. “The Jews have occupied the leading positions in the German media, literature, theater, film, in the medical and legal professions and on the stock exchange. They control parliament and the political parties,” he complained. In his conclusion, he did try to allay fears about where complaints about the “hijacked state” might lead. “The concentration camps are intended only for the re-education of antisocial leaders into useful citizens,” Dr. Goebbels asserted, assuring his audience “that this excessive Jewish influence will be dealt with in a just and humane manner.” Such assurances, which, as history showed, Dr. Goebbels evidently gave with his fingers crossed behind his back, are nowhere to be found in the articles about the children of the UDBA, but, as I mentioned, this is a series, so perhaps more reassuring tones can be expected in one of the next episodes. The list of “UDBA men” who supposedly spawned the “red aristocracy” includes personalities who played various roles in the past. Just as I reject sweeping accusations, I will not defend them sweepingly either. People who think and respect facts can form their own opinion about each of them. What cannot be ignored, however, is the attempt to accuse and disqualify their children and grandchildren on the basis of blood ties. Here the analogy with Nazi racial legislation is certainly appropriate. I want to believe that such writing is merely the result of moral and intellectual handicaps, since as a humanist I don’t want automatically to think the worst of people, but the whole story still comes across as sinister and frightening. It is also striking that the list of alleged “UDBA men” does not include quite a few public figures who, by any objective yardstick and on the basis of their own deeds and ideas before the Slovenian Spring, would surely deserve a place on the incriminating list. Perhaps their turn will come, or perhaps they have been left off because they are connected to the “UDBA” only through their own past deeds and former convictions, not through blood ties. Illogical? Not credible? Stupid? Perhaps, but certainly effective in achieving its purpose. You know: if enemies don’t exist, they have to be invented. Nothing unites like a shared hatred.

A few years ago, I attended, on official duty, an international conference organized by the United Nations in the city of João Pessoa in the far east of Brazil. By Brazilian standards, the city is fairly small, with barely more than a million inhabitants; it has miles of sandy beaches, restaurants, hotels and an impressive number of murders per capita. The conference center was half an hour’s drive away along a mixture of potholed dirt roads and short stretches of four-lane highway, with junctions that evidently led nowhere. None of it made a great impression, either in terms of urban planning or the sensible use of public money. When I asked the locals why the conference center had been built in such a remote place, the answer was that the governor was a good friend of the president. It is an anecdotal illustration of the corruption and clientelism that caused two left-wing predecessors of Brazil’s new president, Jair Bolsonaro, to end their terms rather miserably. First Dilma Rousseff was removed from office over a corruption scandal, and then her predecessor, Lula, was sentenced to prison for similar dealings. Both certainly contributed to the fact that Brazil, tired of corruption, finally opted for an adventure with the unbalanced far-right Bolsonaro. The first lesson of the Brazilian story is that the rise of right-wing populism is not always caused solely by economic neoliberalism; in some cases it is also due to the corruption, incompetence, lust for power and greed of those who otherwise never stop talking about social justice. The Brazilian experience also helps us understand the crisis in Venezuela in a more nuanced way. Listening to the American president talk about humanitarian motives for helping the Venezuelan people while his subordinates announce economic sanctions and even the use of military force, we are quite justifiably seized by holy anger. The American administration in general, and the current one in particular, has many reasons to be much humbler and more restrained. Not only threats of military force but also sanctions, whose aim is apparently to deepen the suffering of an already desperate population and drive them to rise up against Maduro, are not only immoral but dangerous. Historical experience shows that such an approach is often an excellent gift to sanctioned regimes, as it offers them a handy excuse to use an even harder hand in the fight to stay in power. On the other hand, justified anger at American policy, which objectively increases the danger of even greater violence, in no way excuses ideologically driven short-sightedness and the glorification of the “democratically elected” compañero Maduro. In reaction to the crisis, virtual equivalents of the Spanish International Brigades are forming on social networks, people are searching for a “no pasarán” emoji, while the internet commentariat solemnly swears it is ready to fight for Comrade Nicolás, keyboard in hand. Which is not serious. The sanctions are unjust and dangerous, but it was above all Maduro and Chávez who put the gun of economic collapse to Venezuela’s temple. In normal circumstances, the country with the largest proven oil reserves in the world could respond to threats of sanctions with a raised middle finger dipped in black gold. The problem is that both Hugo and Nicolás treated the oil industry as a private fund for maintaining their own regime. They bought loyalty with top positions, which logically led to the industry’s collapse and the destruction of its infrastructure. The state oil company is run by a National Guard general with no experience whatsoever in the field. Crude oil is mostly exported and processed in refineries in the United States. Chávez’s revolution and the broad popular support he enjoyed in the first years of his rule did not, of course, come out of nowhere. They were the result of injustices and hardships caused by previous governments with strong backing from American and other oil multinationals. A revolt against the economic colonization of the country and for greater social justice would certainly have been legitimate if it had brought the population greater prosperity, social influence and democracy. But Chávez and Maduro did anything but that. The UN Refugee Agency reports that by last November at least three million citizens had left Venezuela, and almost as many again are planning to leave. The reason for the biggest refugee crisis in the recent history of the South American continent is the growing shortage of basic foodstuffs and medical supplies. In a country literally sitting on oil, people queue for petrol and suffer from hunger. “Collapse in Venezuela,” wrote the weekly Mladina as early as July 2016. A year later, our media were writing about descendants of Slovenian emigrants dying for lack of medicines. It is also worth thinking more critically about claims of Maduro’s democratic legitimacy. In Venezuela today, there is no longer any official institution capable of overseeing the executive. Maduro and Chávez packed the courts with judges who no longer even pretend to be independent. The authorities’ repression of critical voices is reflected in the often violent suppression of protests, the jailing of political opponents and the prosecution of civilians before military courts. Human rights violations go unpunished, and the authorities persecute both human rights defenders and independent media. This assessment is not the inflammatory propaganda of enemies of the Venezuelan people but a quote from Human Rights Watch’s 2019 report. Despite having subjugated almost every lever of power, Maduro lost the last parliamentary elections in 2015 by a wide margin. But since the people cannot be in opposition, as Viktor Orbán once colorfully put it, Maduro used the courts under his control to strip the democratically elected parliament of its powers and set up a parallel constituent assembly packed with regime loyalists. In these conditions, Maduro was elected last May in elections that, according to most observers, did not meet minimum democratic standards. What is most striking in the tragedy of Venezuela and its citizens is not so much the differences between Trump and Maduro as what they and their cronies have in common and what unites them. Populists, of whatever color, need each other and complement each other. They provide each other with an alibi for legitimacy and ease each other’s path to power, while in between, both forget the people who are increasingly struggling. The “it doesn’t matter what he’s like, as long as he’s ours” attitude—part of the left ignoring or even justifying Maduro’s corruption and his violations of human rights and political freedoms—is a big gift to the populist right. Positions on the Venezuelan crisis are really not so much about divisions between left and right as about polarization over certain fundamental civilizational and democratic values. On one side are those, whatever their color, who believe that in the name of the people, or of profits camouflaged as the people, any means may be used to seize and keep power. On the other side is politics, whether left, right or center, that does not reduce democracy to elections—which, after all, they know how to organize in Hungary or Iran too—but also guarantees an independent judiciary, free media, effective protection of human rights and political freedoms, an influential civil society and the democratic rule of law with an effective defense against corruption and other abuses of power. And, of course, social solidarity and social justice, without which there is no functioning liberal democracy. Only such a democracy can bring Venezuela and its citizens lasting stability, prosperity and freedom, but neither Maduro nor Trump can, is able to, or wants to make that possible for them.

There are things that only occur to you when someone writes them on a big red bus, or repeats them to you as many times as Dr. Joseph G. prescribed, or when you read them on the Nova24TV website. That media outlet recently devoted a long article to me, in which I was described as an extreme leftist because of my criticism of hate speech and my defense of human rights. They hit the nail on the head with the claim that in my privileged youth, made possible by my “privileged communist” father, I acted in a youth propaganda film, Sreča na vrvici (Luck on a String). This statement, especially its last part, stirred up quite a lot of dust on social networks. I was more cautious in my reaction, above all because you can think what you like about Nova24TV, but you cannot deny their expertise and experience in the field of propaganda. So I decided to watch the film again, frame by frame. And damn it, they were right. You may remember that seemingly innocent scene on the Cobblers’ Bridge where I return to Milena, dressed in pink frills, the balloon I rescued from a wicked black-clad villain by jumping into the Ljubljanica. Hello? A rubber balloon? Forty years of New Year’s Eve reruns, and before Nova24TV no one noticed that this was not kitschy teenage romance but an attack on the reproductive duties of Slovenian girls and women. In the light of this realization, the limping bandit with a wooden leg who, fleeing a rampaging invasive Newfoundland dog, overturns a stall of non-native watermelons was no villain at all but a Slovenian patriot. A guardsman of the homeland, so to speak. The accusations about my late father being an agent of the former regime were quickly upgraded by a disciplined phalanx of internet trolls into charges of having been in the UDBA, the Yugoslav secret police. Unfortunately, Nova24TV offers no evidence for its claims other than a photograph showing my father, dressed up in tails, together with then Slovenian President Kučan and the Queen of Denmark. The problem is that in the picture my father is bowing not to Kučan but to the Queen. If this is proof of my father’s collaboration with secret services, one would first think of the notorious Danish secret police, famous for interrogating suspects by making them walk on Lego bricks. With their shoes on, of course; they are not monsters. It is quite possible he was recruited when he studied in Denmark in the 1950s, a country that stayed in his heart for the rest of his life. He began and ended his television career with a documentary about that country, which he saw as the ideal of a democratic, open and caring society. After retiring, he founded the Slovenian-Danish Friendship Society, and Queen Margrethe II thanked him for all this with the Order of the Dannebrog. In his admiration of Denmark and the Danes, which in my opinion was sometimes rather uncritical, my father came closest to being a “regime journalist,” as a former respected judge of the European Court of Human Rights called him, in a statement that says a great deal about the judge and very little about my father. Whichever way you look at it, in the end the only reason my father is being called a regime agent and secret policeman seems to be my defense of liberal democracy based on human rights and political freedoms. The fact that these are not values traditionally associated with the former regime, still less with the UDBA, nicely illustrates how illogical, and indeed how stupid, such accusations are. At first sight, such insinuations may come across as rather comic, but the cognitive weakness of the arguments cannot hide the fact that beneath the avalanche of idiotic insults lies a clearly worked-out strategy. The media lynching carried out by Nova24TV and its like has a purpose and a goal. Those who defend human rights are today declared “children of the UDBA,” critics of hate speech are traitors to freedom and the homeland, humanism and solidarity with our fellow human beings are branded extreme leftism, Pope Francis threatens Christianity, and Soros has become a Jew you can hate out loud. In the Newspeak of populist Slovenia, the civilizational values of post-war democratic Europe are stigmatized as a conspiracy of left-wing totalitarianism. Before our very eyes, on a pitch we won at independence in defense against authoritarian nationalism and in the name of human rights and political freedoms, someone is moving the goalposts and changing the rules of the game. Gradually, but ever faster, the civilizational foundations of the Slovenian state, which we wrote into the Constitution a good quarter of a century ago, are being undermined. Unfortunately, we cannot count much on the head referee either, who lacks the authority and courage to blow the whistle even when the offside is obvious. I thought for a long time about whether to write this column, as it is very personal and may rub some people the wrong way for that reason, but in the end I decided not to leave the primitive abuse of my late father unanswered. If you must hang Jakob the dog from a verbal willow, you will not get my father. My last memory of him is from the railway station in Kehl, on the border near Strasbourg, around Christmas a good twelve years ago, as he and my mother boarded the train for Ljubljana. Only a few weeks later he died during the annual commemorative march to Dražgoše. Even this was used as crowning proof of his regime corruption. In today’s Slovenia, for some people it is enough to label you an anti-fascist to carry out your media execution. My father was a man I kept discovering all my life. At fifteen I learned that in his youth he had played basketball for Enotnost, as Olimpija was once called. A few years later he surprised me by being able to play the piano. Just a few days ago, a former colleague of his mentioned to me that while serving in the Yugoslav People’s Army he testified before a military court in defense of a fellow soldier accused of espionage, a well-known Slovenian intellectual who was eventually acquitted. In those days, my dear Nova24TV, doing something like that took not only moral principles but also balls. After retiring, for eleven years in a row he took a group of fifty final-year students from all Slovenian grammar schools to Denmark. For free. He raised money from sponsors for these trips, and only after his death did we discover that the sponsorship money was often not enough and he had covered the difference from the family’s savings. If someone proves to me that he really was in the UDBA, then I hope he was in charge of finances. My father was not without faults, but he had qualities that are the complete antithesis of everything the UDBA and Nova24TV have in common. He was someone people respected and loved, and above all someone who loved people. He and my mother passed this on to their children. And on this point Nova24TV is absolutely right. Thanks to parents like these, we Gruden brothers really did have a privileged youth.

On the first day of summer in 1791, the postmaster of Sainte-Menehould in northeastern France was gazing idly out the window at the dusty road leading toward Verdun, when a lavish carriage and a smaller wagon briefly stopped in front of the post station. On the latter sat three footmen dressed in yellow vests (no joke). An hour later, a breathless National Guardsman arrived at the post and inquired whether anyone had seen the fugitive King Louis XVI, who had fled Paris the previous night with his family. Our postmaster, Jean-Baptiste Drouet, was a revolutionary, a republican, and a patriot. So he promptly reported the king to the Parisian authorities. Then, he mounted his own horse and tracked down the royal family in nearby Varennes-en-Argonne, personally detaining them until the revolutionary forces arrived to make the arrest. Drouet was handsomely rewarded—he received 30,000 livres and, a little over a year later, was elected to the Convention, the assembly of the First French Republic, where he joined the radical Montagnards alongside Robespierre, Danton, and Marat. He was one of the most vocal advocates for the death penalty for Louis XVI, who met his end on the guillotine on 21 January 1793. Two hundred and twenty-seven years later, another Drouet, this time Eric, a 33-year-old truck driver and fan of pimped-up engine cylinders from Melun, launched himself into public view. In mid-November, outraged by a seven-cent per liter gas price hike, he put on a yellow vest and headed to Paris with fellow protestors. Thus was born the Yellow Vest movement, and Eric Drouet became one of its most visible figures. When, in a fit of revolutionary fervor, he called for the occupation of the Élysée Palace, he earned not just a criminal complaint but also a glowing tribute on New Year’s Eve from Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party and bronze medalist in the 2017 presidential election. The crafty veteran—once a Socialist Party apparatchik and ardent Europeanist, now a bitterly euroskeptic revolutionary—saw in the truck driver echoes of his namesake Jean-Baptiste, famed for his enthusiasm for the purifying force of revolutionary violence. Mélenchon admired Eric’s courage to defy the cruelty and injustice of the legal order and to do whatever it took to end Macron’s presidential monarchy. Mélenchon himself has never hidden his revolutionary disdain for legal constraints—especially those rules regulating how his party may (and may not) use EU funds. Likewise, Marine Le Pen has repeatedly rebelled against the hegemony of Europe’s elites. The Yellow Vests are a chaotic movement of people united by their shared frustration with a political system they believe has pushed them to the economic, social, and political margins. What leaves a bitter taste is the opportunism of Mélenchon and his pathetic attempts to garner attention among protestors—nearly half of whom, according to recent surveys, now vote for the far right. Glorifying revolutionary violence and calling for the total destruction of institutions will hardly shift this dynamic in Mélenchon’s favor. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen can afford to stay on the sidelines, knowing full well that the fruits of the revolt will fall into her lap. Compared to the increasingly frothy far-left, she appears like a calm and reasonable alternative to a beleaguered President Macron. Mélenchon’s rhetoric—evoking a second storming of the Bastille—reveals a recurring pattern within parts of Europe’s left: faced with a choice between serving their voter base and expanding their support, or clinging to rigid dogmas and personal ambitions, they too often choose the latter. This consistently benefits right-wing populists. A similar, if slightly less hysterical, scenario is unfolding in Britain’s Labour Party. Despite the fact that most Labour voters oppose Brexit, party leader Jeremy Corbyn continues to behave as though the only thing wrong with Brexit is that the Tories initiated it instead of him. His rigid left-wing euroskepticism—which still sees the EU as a conspiracy against the British working class—ignores the views of Labour’s pro-European majority, especially the youth who helped elevate Corbyn to the leadership. Worse, Corbyn’s behavior directly helps the already discredited Conservatives, who—faced with a more competent opposition—might have long since collapsed, taking their Brexit delusions with them. The pattern is evident elsewhere too. In Italy, the Five Star Movement, born as an ideologically vague, anti-elite, euroskeptic movement for direct democracy, has now become the sidekick to Salvini’s far-right populism. Beppe Grillo and his gang will be discarded the moment Salvini no longer needs them—and judging by current polling, that moment is fast approaching. As we head toward the European elections, the political arena is locked in a fake conflict between populist extremes. From both ends, they are doing everything they can to undermine the liberal democratic institutions established after World War II to preserve stability and peace. In between them stumble the “traditional” parties—headless chickens who, through their past actions, triggered today’s economic, social, and political crises. Now, they respond to voter defection with opportunism devoid of values, principles, courage, or ideas. They have surrendered, without a fight, the leadership role in defining and defending the issues people care about most: security, family, patriotism, identity, culture—even social justice. If we don’t see a serious awakening soon, the result will be the dominance of nationalist, reactionary authoritarianism over democracy. We can only guess at the consequences of liberal democracy’s decline in Europe—but let us not forget that throughout European history, periods of peace and stability have only ever been brief flashes of light in long stretches of darkness. Some, of course, will manage to adapt. Even our postman Jean-Baptiste Drouet did. After Napoleon’s 1799 coup, he moderated his republican zeal, became sub-prefect in his hometown of Sainte-Menehould, and was awarded the Legion of Honour by the new autocrat. Revolutions end—power stands.

Mist was thickening over the Bosphorus, and one of the most beautiful and cosmopolitan cities in the world was slowly disappearing into the February fog. “It has never been as hopeless as it is today,” said Hakan. “You never know when they will come and take you away.” There was no anger or fear in his voice, only sadness and disappointment. One of my first trips in the year that has just ended was to Istanbul, for the graduation ceremony of the Council of Europe’s Turkish School of Political Studies. The school is a partnership between a Turkish university, civil society and the Council of Europe, devoted to non-formal education in the knowledge and skills we need in a democracy. Hakan, the school’s director, and I handed out the diplomas in the rectorate of Boğaziçi University, in a wonderful setting reminiscent of American universities, which is not surprising, since it was founded by Americans after the Crimean War. A century and a half later, Boğaziçi is no longer a private university, but it remains true to its founders’ commitment to accept students of all faiths and nationalities and not to interfere in politics. Years ago, when the Council of Europe founded the school together with the university and the Anadolu Kültür association, the condition of staying out of party politics was no obstacle at all. At that time, liberal democracy—that is, democracy based on human rights and the democratic rule of law—was still, at least on the surface, a project of national consensus, in Turkey as elsewhere in Europe. Hakan, the school’s director, is an intellectual, a humanist and a cosmopolitan who loves his Turkey boundlessly. Hakan is my friend. The first school in the Council of Europe’s network of schools of political studies, which today has twenty-one members, was founded a quarter of a century ago in Moscow, in the kitchen of human rights activist Lena Nemirovskaya and her husband, the philosopher Yuri Senokosov. It grew out of the realization that a society only recently freed from an authoritarian ideological straitjacket needs politicians, journalists, civil servants, civil society activists and others who know and understand what democracy is and how it works. Over the Moscow School’s many years, countless people attended its courses in democratic political culture. Many of them are in influential positions today but are reluctant to talk about their ties to the school, because a few years ago it was put on the list of foreign agents, that is, organizations that receive money from abroad for their work. That most of this money came from the budget of an international organization of which Russia is also a member did not soften the Kremlin; Lena’s cookery school of democracy simply got on the Russian authorities’ nerves too much. It is not that Lena and Yuri changed their recipes; it is just that their surroundings changed their taste for liberal democracy and lost their appetite. Today the school still operates, but it organizes its seminars elsewhere in Europe, from universities in Spain to Oxford and trade union centers in Sweden. When I can, I go and visit them. Despite its foreign-agent status, which is not currently the most recommended reference on a CV in Russia, hundreds of people attend the seminars, from all corners of the Russian Federation, not just urban and liberal Moscow. What also draws me to Lena and her travelling band of hunters of lost illusions are the long hours of conversation after the official program, in hotel rooms, in cigarette smoke and with vodka as the only interpreter to and from Russian. In these conversations there is neither hatred nor conspiracy, only sadness at lost hopes for a better and more beautiful future. Ilgar Mammadov, director of the Council of Europe school in Baku, looks to the future with a little more hope. Ilgar was released a few months ago from prison, where he spent more than five years, even though the European Court of Human Rights ruled just months after his conviction that it had been a political trial. When we talk on the phone, he sounds incredibly relaxed for someone who says he doesn’t know whether he will be locked up again tomorrow. Ilgar is no exception in the brave new Europe. Before my lecture at Boğaziçi University, I met the wife of Osman Kavala, chairman of the board of Anadolu Kültür, co-founder of the Council of Europe’s Turkish school. Osman, a wealthy Paris-born businessman and philanthropist, was arrested in October 2017. To this day, the prosecution has not filed an indictment. After more than a year, Osman still does not know what he is accused of. “It is a message to liberal Turkey,” one of the people I spoke to in Istanbul told me. “If we can lock up Osman Kavala for no reason, the authorities are saying, then we can lock up any of you.” Being liberal means something different in today’s Turkey than in Europe and Slovenia. It is not about party affiliation but about the civilizational outlook of people who believe in an open and progressive society based on humanism, social justice, human rights and real, liberal democracy. In Europe, this is slowly becoming a term of abuse, both for increasingly self-confident right-wing populists and for armchair revolutionaries who hate Hillary and Macron even more than Trump or Orbán. In Turkey, Russia and many other places, people can less afford to gloat over the troubles of liberal democracy. It is not that they are great fans of those who talked endlessly about liberal values while, through their inconsistency and lack of integrity, creating the conditions that paved the populists’ way to power. It is that for them the end of democracy, the end of human rights, the end of the democratic rule of law is not a theoretical concept you can simply dismiss while bashing Hillary, but a reality in which you never know when they will come for you and take you away. In conversations with friends from Istanbul, Moscow and Baku, I sense a bitterness born of the conviction that the European democracies left them in the lurch. That the hopes and expectations born of the fall of the Berlin Wall ultimately mattered less than the West’s geostrategic and economic interests. But I sense no envy in our conversations. If anything, in relation to us they feel like canaries in a coal mine. Europe today is less and less a model and more and more a cause for cynical pity. This year we face European elections. Although everyone is asking what the balance of votes between democrats and populists will be, the real question is how low those who until yesterday lectured about democracy and human rights will sink this time, now that, in panic at the populists, they are capable of nothing but aping their discourse. Populism is winning in Europe’s elections regardless of the final result. In the coming European elections, we will be defended against it by political forces that do not understand, cannot shoulder or do not want their historical responsibility. By politics that, through its lack of principle and competence, first created fertile ground for populism to flourish and now competes with it in the political manipulation of hatred and fear. By politics that normalized intolerance with its attitude to refugees and is now confronted with the fact that hatred cannot be channeled and controlled. Old demons are awakening in Europe. Nationalism, which reminds us that Europeans have always been most threatened by other Europeans. Antisemitism, which is rising steeply, even though some try to disguise it by shouting “damn Soros” instead of “damn Jews.” Fascism, which behaves as if it had never heard of Slavko Bobovnik. No wonder we are no longer a model for anyone. Hakan was arrested on Friday, November 16. He was released after a few days but is still subject to criminal proceedings. Among other things, he is accused of having lobbied against the import of tear gas into Turkey. I wish Hakan the very best of luck in the coming year, but we will all need it.
The Learning Years of Inventor Macron

The Yellow Vest protests are a nightmare for lovers of simple, black-and-white truths. On one side, we have President Emmanuel Macron—a man you simply have to admire. A year and a half ago, as a young newcomer, he came out of nowhere to convincingly defeat Marine Le Pen, the leader of the right-wing populist National Front, in the second round of the presidential election. Macron invented a new political paradigm that transcended traditional divisions in France’s fossilized political landscape. He offered hope for the first credible response to populism—one that did not rely on flirting with or half-heartedly mimicking populist rhetoric. Macron attacked populism head-on, offering as an alternative a progressive political program grounded in the traditional liberal-democratic values of European integration. Alongside Angela Merkel, he became the only credible European and global leader to firmly oppose Trump’s dismantling of the international multilateral order and the undermining of the Paris climate agreement. On that same side, though, we also find a Macron who gets on your nerves. From the night of his victory—marked by a meticulously choreographed solo march through the shadowy courtyard of the Louvre—he struck many as self-absorbed and arrogant, often brusque toward those he felt didn’t show him enough respect. This is the Macron who placed a bust of Charles de Gaulle on his desk—one he likely strokes in moments of trembling admiration for his own brilliance. And then there's the Macron who has bitterly disappointed us by failing—at least so far—to live up to the hope that he would shield us from populism. This Macron failed to understand that millions across Europe and the world didn’t fall for the deceptive charm of populist charlatans simply because they hadn’t heard of Emmanuel Macron. He failed—and may still fail—to grasp that many people are driven into the arms of right- and left-wing demagogues by accumulated frustration with political, economic, and financial elites who have long ignored, marginalized, and pushed them to or beyond the edge of a dignified life. This Macron assumed he could implement many otherwise justified and beneficial reforms—as well as an ambitious energy transition program, without which we won’t save the planet—by a method that seemed to place the greatest burden yet again on the shoulders of the weakest. The fuel price hike meant to fund the shift to greener energy was the final straw. “It’s easy to preach ecology if you’re a wealthy Parisian riding your €2,000 electric scooter down the Champs-Élysées,” said rural protesters. “But what about us, the people in the countryside, who can’t take our kids to school or get to the doctor without a car? What about the farmer whose rising fuel costs devour his meager earnings? What about small business owners and tradespeople who gain nothing from the tax breaks awarded to the wealthiest?” On the other side are the Yellow Vests—whom we must stand with. Their demands for greater social justice are justified and legitimate. They represent the voices of those who have borne the heaviest burdens of years of austerity, and who are now being told, amid economic recovery, that their turn still hasn’t come. Macron’s brave new world promised better times—but only someday, maybe tomorrow or the day after. The Yellow Vests’ revolt isn’t just an uprising of the most destitute. It’s a protest by a broader swath of the population who feel their standard of living has stagnated and that their voices go unheard. For many, it reflects a syndrome of relative deprivation—the accumulated anger of the middle class after years of tightening belts. At one point, nearly 80% of French citizens supported the protests. But among the Yellow Vests are also those who must be condemned—those who used the mass protests to loot and burn across Paris and other cities, leaving destruction and millions of euros in damages that, of course, will be covered by taxpayers. Among them are also many who spread nonsense and lies amplified by the internet, leaving any reasonable person shaking their head. A few days ago, I listened to a conversation between two self-proclaimed leaders of the movement who told their followers they must accelerate protests because Macron was about to sign the Marrakech agreement in order to bring 480 million migrants into Europe. They also claimed he planned to give up France’s seat on the UN Security Council so that UN peacekeepers could be deployed to France to crush the protests by force. Minutes after gunfire erupted in Strasbourg last week—killing five people—messages circulated on social media claiming the terrorist attack had been staged by the government to halt the protests. Among the Yellow Vests are also many who wear blue—Marine Le Pen’s National Rally color—and red, the color of far-left France Insoumise and its populist-nationalist leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Both Le Pen and Mélenchon are working hard to redirect popular anger toward their political mills. The protests caught Macron off guard, and he responded too late—with concessions such as raising the minimum wage—but these won’t satisfy everyone. To survive politically and for his anti-populist platform to succeed, he’ll need to do much more. Macron must understand that without social justice—which is not a matter of left, center, or right, but a condition for the normal functioning of liberal democracy—none of his noble and ambitious ideas will take root or endure. He needs effective solutions for the accumulated rage of the middle class, which has been created by years of unchecked globalization without social safeguards, austerity policies, and the handling of financial crises on the backs of taxpayers. A society that fails to prevent excessive inequalities, hardships, and injustices—a society where the government shows no solidarity or empathy toward its own citizens, and where many voters feel unrespected and unheard—is a pressure cooker where everyone soon starts hating everyone else—especially those who are different. For people living in France, the Yellow Vest protests are not always pleasant—but perhaps they were necessary. I hope Macron has learned something from this experience and that it’s not too late. Annoying traits aside, I still hope he succeeds—not out of any special loyalty to “Inventor Macron,” but from the hope that a democratic, rational, and progressive alternative still exists to the increasingly self-confident and aggressive populism. Populism looks at the Yellow Vests with lust and the worst of intentions—and that should worry us. If we mix yellow, bleu marine (as the French call the deep blue of Marine Le Pen), and Mélenchon’s populist red, we could end up with brown—a color that has never brought Europe anything good.
Shall We Go Our Own Way?

Few words carry as much autoerotic charge as sovereignty. We love to hear it, and we love even more to say it. It gives us a pleasant jolt in the gut—like speeding over a speed bump. It gives us confidence and a sense of power. Perhaps because the word comes from the term for a ruler, a sovereign, who in the dark Middle Ages could do whatever he pleased—including, allegedly, testing local virgins on their wedding night. By the way, ius primae noctis, or the “right of the thighs,” as the ever-elegant French referred to it in matters of the bedroom, is likely more myth than historical fact. Medieval lovers of sovereignty usually avoided brides from the lower classes—out of both aesthetic and health concerns, since life didn’t treat the poor kindly even back then. The German legal historian Karl Schmidt convincingly debunked the recreational aspects of medieval executive power in his 1881 study “Jus primae noctis. Eine geschichtliche Untersuchung.” A few decades later, another Karl—Carl Schmitt, a fellow German—also took up the question of sovereignty. His theories on the ruler’s unlimited power earned him the reputation as Hitler’s court jurist and philosopher. Schmitt defined sovereignty as the right to declare a “state of exception,” which, in the defense of a nation’s vital interests, frees executive power from all legal obligations and constraints. In other words, the sovereign ruler may, in the name of the people, rise above the law and do as he pleases. History shows that Hitler interpreted Schmitt’s Ausnahmezustand rather broadly—and didn’t limit it to the right to mess around with his subjects. Schmitt’s and Hitler’s idea of sovereignty had its legal reckoning at the Nuremberg Trials, where in response to Nazi atrocities, a new legal concept was introduced into international law: crimes against humanity. This significantly curtailed the sovereign right of states to treat people under their jurisdiction as they pleased. Limited state sovereignty, the obligation to respect human rights and freedoms, and multilateral international cooperation became the foundations of the post-war world order. European countries took this a step further. Both the European Convention on Human Rights and the European Union are based on transferring part of national sovereign powers to supranational institutions. In light of historical experience, this limitation—or pooling—of national sovereignty was seen as a civilizational step forward and an investment in a safer shared future. That is also why the European Union was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize a few years ago. Lately, obsession with national sovereignty is back in fashion. Part of the blame lies with the fading of historical memory, and part with politics' shallow commitment to its own democratic and humanist principles. This is cleverly exploited by those who, in the name of “vital national interests,” place themselves above laws and above the people. While many sovereignty enthusiasts in our country look for inspiration among our neighbors or our American son-in-law Donald Trump, I think their aspirations are more closely aligned with North Korea—a country that is arguably the most uncompromisingly sovereign state in the world. Kim Jong-un handles international relations with his middle finger. There are no migrants in North Korea; its border fences are designed only to stop people from fleeing the country. North Koreans, though often with empty stomachs, can sleep soundly knowing that their culture and identity are in no danger. And if someone bangs on their door at night, it’s certainly not a Syrian refugee—it’s the secret police. Closer to Slovenia is the United Kingdom, which, though clearly not North Korea, illustrates well—through Brexit—the economic, political, and social consequences of fetishizing national sovereignty and politically exploiting migration challenges.
