Populism interprets sovereignty as the right to arbitrariness and selfishness—at the expense of others, and ultimately to one’s own detriment. This understanding of sovereignty undermines efforts to combat global warming, rejects rational approaches to migration, and destabilizes global peace and security. We get a different picture if we view sovereignty as a measure of a state’s real capacity to influence its own fate. Every country has not only the right but the duty to its citizens to ensure safety and public order and to find effective answers to economic, social, and security challenges—including, of course, managing migration. The problem arises when politics pretends—or outright lies—that these goals can be better achieved through barroom swaggering at home rather than through international cooperation. Populist dismantling of the international institutions and mechanisms established after the world’s disastrous experience with Schmitt-style sovereignty is particularly dangerous for small countries like Slovenia. It prevents them from using international cooperation and law to increase their actual sovereignty and effectively protect their interests—and from offering their citizens long-term security, freedom, and economic development. The future is being endangered by politicians who talk the loudest about security and patriotism. The great nationalists of small nations forget about the selfishness and brutality of a unilateral world. In the jungle, where rules are set by the biggest and strongest orangutan, there are no consensual international relations. For small countries, there is neither candlelight nor romance—only the sovereign right of the big and powerful to take whatever they believe belongs to them. In other words, without international law, institutions, and cooperation, our sovereignty and safety could end up depending on overpriced armored vehicles, poorly equipped troops, and some used warship bartered via a clearing debt. I respect the army—especially when commanded by a woman—but let’s first try intelligent policy and proactive diplomacy. Whenever nationalists start rattling the sabers of sovereignty, I instinctively clench my thighs and try to remember how many days’ worth of food we have stored in the basement.

For the past few days I have been haunted by nightmares. The stomp of boots in the middle of the night, banging on the door, men in the uniforms of the Slovenian Guard. “Gruden? We have a search warrant for your apartment.” Scared to the bone, I try to keep calm. The guardsmen ransack the apartment with practiced routine; evidently it is not the first time. “Aha,” one of them shouts. He shoves a yellowed piece of paper in front of my eyes and spells out gleefully: “Matjaž Gruden, student at the Faculty of Law of the University of Ljubljana, is hereby awarded a prize for his thesis entitled The European Union as a Party to the European Convention on Human Rights.” “Not the European Union, the European Communities,” I object feebly, “I graduated before the Maastricht Treaty.” His look tells me that facts these days count for nothing, not even in dreams. Undeterred, he reads on, then his eyes bulge and he roars: “The prize is awarded by the Slovenian United Nations Association.” Red with rage, he cocks his pistol and holds it to my temple. “The United Nations, you treacherous dog…” The belief that the United Nations is an enemy of the people is not new. For many years it has been part of rural folklore in the remote hills of the American Northwest, where armed village eccentrics with a distinctly unpatriotic attitude to paying taxes dig bunkers and swap recipes for squirrel stew while waiting for an attack by black-clad commandos of a conspiratorial organization headquartered on the East River. From a safe distance, stories about guys living underground and eating rodents because they fear the United Nations will steal their freedom, take away their sovereignty and change their way of life always seemed funny and thrillingly romantic to me. Now there is no safe distance anymore. More and more countries, using rhetoric rarely heard since Germany and Japan left the League of Nations, are raising their voices against the hegemony of international cooperation over the sovereign right of nations to harm themselves and others. In Slovenia, too, the fighters against the United Nations are not hiding in bunkers but pontificating on the evening news. Among people who respect facts and value reason, there would be no need to waste words on the nonsense that self-appointed defenders of Western civilization spout about the Marrakesh agreement, the UN Global Compact for Migration. But we live in times when lies have their not-so-short legs propped up on the desk of the Oval Office. It doesn’t help that every Grimm fairy tale contains more verifiable facts than the agitation against an initiative for the international community to respond rationally and effectively to the challenges of migration. Populism has recognized in migration an opportunity to undermine international stability and the institutions that democratic societies established in response to their last historical experience of unbridled sovereignty and rampant nationalism. Critics accuse the Marrakesh agreement of everything possible and impossible, without a shred of shame at the idiocy of the lies they spread. But the main thorn in the populist heel is the fact that the agreement does not condemn migration as such; it seeks, on the basis of agreed standards and cooperation between states, to regulate migration flows so as to protect both the economic, social and security interests of the participating states and respect for international humanitarian law, human dignity and basic human rights. For politics that builds its power on fear and hatred of migration as the source of all evil, this is of course unacceptable. As a substitute for a global solution to a global problem, they offer the illusion that migration flows must and can be stopped with nationalist rhetoric, ostrich-like unilateralism and walls on the borders. Such undermining of multilateral efforts to find a common response to migration challenges in fact increases the risk that the response will remain chaotic, hysterical and ineffective, with all the security, humanitarian, political and economic consequences we will all eventually suffer. The campaign against the Marrakesh agreement is a symptom of the bottom we are racing towards. Cooperation, rationality and humanity have become obstacles to achieving political goals. But not to lay all the blame on the populists: an even greater responsibility lies with those politicians who are full of talk about democracy and humanism at the declaratory level but, in concrete situations, lack the resolve to stand up for their own values. This is not just an ethical lapse; it is sawing off the branch they are sitting on. Instead of opposing demagogic manipulation and lies without hesitation, they legitimize them and give them weight with statements about “changed circumstances.” A rational and effective migration policy requires moral integrity, authority and the courage to stand up to populists. It also requires a positive and proactive policy, not limp excuses that the agreement is “acceptable” because it is not legally binding. When politics and society no longer have a critical mass of individuals and institutions firmly and convincingly defending rational and humane approaches to migration, people will of course come to believe that the best leader is the one who is most hostile and unyielding towards migrants. Once that happens, wishy-washy, a-bit-here-a-bit-there politics is doomed. I fully understand that people who have been convinced that refugees pose a mortal threat to the survival of the Slovenian nation—or, as the foreign minister would put it, “to the preservation of our way of life”—prefer to vote for uncompromising nationalists rather than their half-hearted sotto voce imitators. And with their ethical limpness, the latter are putting at stake not only their own political credibility and fate but also our future. For small countries like Slovenia, international institutions, law and cooperation are especially important, and crucial from a security point of view as well. Populist fairy tales have no happy ending. If you don’t fancy life in a bunker, the stomp of military boots in the middle of the night and squirrel stew, stick to the Brothers Grimm.

Before Robert Bowers stormed into the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh with an automatic rifle and murdered eleven people, he posted his intentions on the social media platform Gab, which is popular among American white supremacists, anti-Semites, and Islamophobes. Gab’s founder, Andrew Torba, often appears in public wearing a green baseball cap that reads “Make Speech Free Again.” Freedom of speech is a very important matter for peddlers of intolerance. Far-right warriors and their enablers interpret it as a right to hate. Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects the right to freedom of expression. It is one of the fundamental safeguards of individual liberty and a check on those in power. Without free and independent media, without public criticism, dialogue, and the clash of differing opinions, there is neither freedom nor democracy. Freedom of expression includes not only the content we agree with—no matter how convinced we are of our own righteousness—but also that which offends, shocks, or disturbs. This is confirmed by the case law of the European Court of Human Rights. But this does not mean that Torba and his ilk are right. Condemning hatred and intolerance does not violate freedom of speech—it protects it. The Court does not forbid offensive, disturbing, or provocative speech because it believes such speech should be respected or heeded, but because it considers that a democratic society responds better and more effectively through social and political reactions rather than legal sanctions. However, many people—including in Slovenia—under the pretense of defending free speech, are unwilling or unable to mount such a response. This emboldens those who take their manipulation of free speech even further: in the alt-right’s newspeak, any criticism of intolerance or incitement to hatred is itself labeled as “hate speech.” This turning of fundamental human rights and democratic safeguards on their head would be laughable—if it didn’t have such dangerous consequences for democracy, social stability, and public safety. How we got here is a long and complicated story, but one of the pivotal moments was the "gift" handed to populist bigots by Islamist extremists in their attack on the French satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo. In terrorist attacks, killing is not the goal but a means to an end. This is not in any way a justification for terrorist crimes—on the contrary—but we must understand that fanatics are not necessarily fools. While many of the actual attackers may not be intellectual giants, the same cannot be said for the planners and masterminds behind such acts. Terrorism kills with clear objectives and intentions. On 7 January 2015, when brothers Saïd and Chérif Kouachi entered the Paris offices of Charlie Hebdo armed with a Zastava M70 rifle and several handguns, and murdered twelve people—mostly staff of the magazine—their goal was not to silence one of France and Europe’s most renowned, bold, and provocative satirical voices (they certainly failed at that), but to trigger a long-term social reaction, as planned by their Al-Qaeda handlers. In that, they were very successful. The intended outcome of the attack was to deepen social tensions and legitimize intolerance toward Islam and Muslims in the eyes of many. The attack on Charlie Hebdo helps us understand how the hateful hijacking of freedom of speech in the name of the “right to hate” was born. The prelude to the Charlie Hebdo attack came in September 2005, when the Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten published caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad to, as the editors explained, “contribute to the public debate on criticism of Islam and self-censorship.” Merely depicting the Prophet is blasphemous to Muslims, and the content of some cartoons—openly and at times quite rudely mocking the Prophet and his followers—sparked angry protests from Muslims in Europe and around the world. Personally, I wasn’t convinced by the premise Jyllands-Posten used to justify publishing the cartoons. Publishing content that a part of the population experiences as deeply offensive, without clear social commentary or critical context, seems questionable to me. I don’t see the social benefit of insulting people just to prove that we can insult them. In some parts of the world, adultery is punished by stoning and death; in the Western world, it is—thankfully—completely legal. But that doesn’t mean we should start organizing swinger parties in defense of freedom. “Hey Peter, your wife isn’t home, come on over, let’s defend our culture, faith, and civilization.” In any case, the bigots quickly created a context for the cartoons with violent protests and death threats. In solidarity with their Danish colleagues, many media outlets began reprinting the cartoons—Charlie Hebdo among them, adding their trademark dose of boldness, rudeness, and dark humor. They regularly mocked other religions too. In the deepening polarization, Al-Qaeda saw an opportunity. They knew that stoking tension and hatred would eventually lead Europeans to cut off the very branch they were sitting on. The planners of the attack fully understood the impact it would have. After the massacre, criticism and condemnation of intolerance became politically risky. Few dared to highlight the difference between hatred and satire. Islamist terrorists had handed Islamophobes a gift they haven’t stopped celebrating. For many, freedom of speech became the right to hate. “Speech,” as Andrew Torba’s cap declares, “is great again.” The exploitation of the Charlie Hebdo tragedy in the name of intolerance is disgraceful. Charlie Hebdo has always been unapologetic and uncompromising in its satire. Toward everyone. It mocks power, stupidity, corruption, and fanaticism—of all stripes. It often crosses the line, but never in the name of hatred. So, if you want to be Charlie, it’s not enough to just defend freedom of speech—you also have to publicly and clearly condemn intolerance and hate. Every time. Specifically. Firmly. Vague clichés and rhetorical fluff are not enough. If you want to be Charlie, you cannot remain silent. If you truly care about freedom of speech and democracy, you cannot remain silent. The political beneficiaries of the Charlie Hebdo tragedy are the defenders of illiberal, authoritarian populism—those who tolerate no criticism, especially not satire. If anyone fits the populist label for free and independent media as “enemies of the people,” it is Charlie Hebdo. In the alt-right vision of the world, freedom of speech is meant only for expressing hatred of others—not for criticizing those in power. In that, they are closely aligned with those whose hate and terrorism help pave their path to power. The partnership between extremists on both sides may not be coordinated, but it’s effective. This is not a conspiracy theory—it’s simply that both sides, if not fully aligned, at least share overlapping or complementary goals and visions for how society and the world should be organized and run.

Mrs. Müller brought little Hans to the doctor, visibly worried. "Doctor, my boy has never caused me so much concern. He’s tired and irritable all day long, even though he has an enormous appetite. Just yesterday at lunch, he ate more than my husband and I together. But he still looks so pale—look at his face, so drawn, and his tired eyes. Something must be wrong." The doctor examined little Hans and then reassured the mother that the boy would be fine. However, he warned her that any further delay in treatment could have very serious consequences for the boy’s health. Hans had a tapeworm. "What is a tapeworm?" asked Hans's mother, frightened. "A tapeworm is a worm that can grow several meters long. Tapeworms live in the human intestines and—dear Mrs. Müller—your Hans has just such a worm in his body," explained the doctor patiently. After a long explanation of the many horrifying things a tapeworm can do to the human body, Hans and his mother went home. There, he obediently took his medicine, which swiftly killed the foreign parasite in his intestines, and brought a smile back to his parents’ faces. But the story doesn’t end there. To make sure that no thick-skulled reader would miss the message, the author added a moral to this educational tale. He wrote: "Tapeworms don’t exist only in the animal world, but also in human form. These are the Jews! … Tapeworms are dangerous because they rob the body of the nutrients it needs to live… Jews behave the same way within the nations they infest… Tapeworms and Jews are the worst kind of parasites. If we want to get rid of them, if we want to become healthy and strong again, there is only one remedy—their extermination." This little story was published in 1940 in a children's book written by Ernst Hiemer, the second-in-command at the publishing house and namesake of the newspaper Der Stürmer, whose editor-in-chief was Julius Streicher. The publisher was based in Nuremberg, which was quite convenient for Streicher—at least logistically—since he didn’t have to move even when, a few years later, he was tried and convicted of crimes against humanity. The book compares Jews to a range of invasive or unpleasant foreign and domestic species—drones, hyenas, locusts, bedbugs, vipers, even bacteria—but the tapeworm stands out with certain features that might still appeal to modern-day fans of comparing humans to repugnant animal species. Tapeworms, or cestodes in Latin, are worms. They have suckers and hooks on their heads, clearly symbolizing foreignness, invasiveness, and parasitism. They also produce offspring in staggering numbers, laying millions of eggs. And the crowning insult: tapeworms don’t reproduce as male and female—they are hermaphrodites, a slap in the face to all those who hold sacred the traditional family. And while we’re talking about analogies, there are people who feel that certain recent events are just begging to be compared to Mr. Hiemer, editor Streicher, and Der Stürmer. Others argue that historical comparisons like these are unhelpful, because they give extremist and racist provocateurs exactly what they want: attention. This line of reasoning assumes that if we simply ignore today’s Hiemers and Streichers long enough, they’ll eventually give up and go away. Maybe—but by that same logic, one would have to believe that Hitler rose to power simply because people were too squeamish about his pre-genocidal ranting and hatred. There are other opinions, though. Irish literary and theatre critic and columnist Fintan O’Toole wrote a few months ago that to understand what’s happening in today’s world, we need to consider two things. First: we are living in a time of testing. Second: what is being tested is fascism. O’Toole says it’s a word we should use carefully, but without hesitation, when it so clearly appears on the horizon. "In a functioning democracy, fascism doesn’t appear out of nowhere. It’s not easy to get people to abandon their ideas of freedom and civility. Testing is necessary, and when successful, it serves a dual purpose: it helps prepare people to accept things they initially resisted; and it allows us to improve and fine-tune our approach," O’Toole wrote. "You have to erode the boundaries of morality, get people to accept acts of extreme cruelty. Like dogs, people must be accustomed to the sight of blood. They must acquire a taste for savagery. Fascism does this by instilling fear of despised minorities. That enables the dehumanization of those groups. Once that is achieved, you can build further—from smashed windows to extermination." Maybe Fintan O’Toole was describing the situation in his own uncivilized and wild Ireland, and we can comfort ourselves by thinking that such a thing couldn’t happen here. And yet, while some are busy rewriting Kekec’s adventures—now featuring a bearded Muslim harassing the innocent Mojca and Pehta hiding an explosive belt under her burka—we should not forget how, during Hans’s struggle with the evil tapeworm, Hans’s father and his uniformed comrades were defending their country against multiculturalism.

President of the Republic Borut Pahor gave a solid speech at the recent session of the UN General Assembly in New York. He expressed clear support for a multilateral world order as the only way to ensure lasting peace and security in the world. He also stressed the importance of respecting human rights, without which, in his view, there can be neither peace nor development. We heard the message of a responsible statesman defending, from the rostrum, principles threatened by nationalist populism, or the “ideology of patriotism,” as Pahor’s counterpart Donald Trump put it in his speech the following day. In Slovenia, some noticed above all what was left out of the President’s speech, namely the arbitration agreement. They wondered why the President had not used the opportunity to complain to the world about the injustice being done to us. Pahor had an answer to this question too, and it deserves praise. He avoided mentioning the arbitration agreement, he said, because everyone interested in it already knows about it, and at the same time he does not want Slovenia to become a “one-issue” country. Slovenia has had problems with “one-issue” politics and with a diplomacy that cannot tear itself away from navel-gazing since the first years after independence. I remember the early nineties, when, as a young diplomat in the team of the first Slovenian ambassador in Brussels, Dr Boris Cizelj, I helped pave Slovenia’s first steps towards Europe. One after another, senior representatives of the young Slovenian state came to the Belgian capital, and every single one of them opened every conversation with European officials with the same sentence: “Slovenia is a young Central European and Mediterranean country that has nothing to do with the war in the Balkans.” From a purely human point of view, the message was understandable. The war had grazed Slovenia only a few years earlier. But from the foreign-policy point of view of presenting Slovenia as a reliable member of the international community, it was a shot in the foot. European Commissioner Hans van den Broek constantly, and not at all discreetly, rolled his eyes at the Slovenian lamenting. His reaction was understandable too. While blue helmets from Ghana, Nepal and Finland were risking their lives in our immediate neighborhood, he had to listen to how Slovenia had, and wanted to have, nothing whatsoever to do with a war raging just a few kilometers from its borders. After one of these meetings, I suggested a different approach to the envoys from Ljubljana: “Listen, Hans, we are part of this story; we know the people, the mentality and the language. Bringing Slovenia closer to Europe rewards the option that chose democracy, human rights and the rule of law at independence; a European Slovenia can be part of the solution for the Balkans.” My naive initiative was, to put it mildly, not well received, and the Europeans went on rolling their eyes for some time. This example illustrates a problem that dogs Slovenian diplomacy to this day. We have a foreign policy that is directed inwards. The message of a non-Balkan Slovenia was never meant for van den Broek, only for the domestic public. Of course, foreign policy is part of domestic political reality and must not ignore public opinion, but at the same time it must be able, in the long term, to build the international position and influence with which a state can defend its strategic interests. We have always been worse at the second part of the equation. Small states are always weaker and more vulnerable in international relations, which makes the Slovenian President’s emphasis on multilateralism all the more appropriate, since it alone offers a framework for asserting and protecting the interests of states like Slovenia. But even in a multilateral world, influence and the protection of interests do not come by themselves; they require investment that is long-term, strategic and intelligent. That has never interested us much. In international politics we usually prefer to be quiet and without ideas; the exceptions are more the result of the efforts and talent of individuals than the fruit of strategic planning. Instead of being active, we prefer to be servile. Instead of having clear positions on important issues that would bring us visibility and standing, we shuffle our feet and wait to see which way the wind blows. When you try to please too many people, in the end no one respects you. And as everywhere, in foreign policy half the battle is showing up. We are not good at that either. As was recently reported, Slovenia is at the very bottom when it comes to ministers’ attendance at meetings in Brussels. Slovenia is not as small as we make it ourselves, small and insignificant. You simply cannot successfully defend your interests with a foreign policy that does not reach beyond the state border. It is too late to wake up only when an arbitration agreement happens to you. And it doesn’t help at all if we then use every opportunity to whine and moan about the injustice being done to us. We can expect as much understanding, sympathy and support as a man at a party who tells everyone that his wife cheated on him with the neighbor. This does not mean that we must not or cannot work to have the arbitration agreement implemented, but it would be useful to approach this and other foreign-policy challenges more intelligently, more professionally and with a longer-term view than we do today. It would be wise for Slovenia to entrust the handling of the arbitration procedures to someone with international legal and foreign-policy experience, knowledge and standing, not to someone saddled with a record of racist boorishness. For small states without any particular economic, political or military power, reputation is a very important and sometimes decisive asset in international relations. That is another reason why President Pahor’s speech in New York was certainly more useful to Slovenia, including for the future of the arbitration agreement, than if he had used the General Assembly rostrum to lament our fate and the injustice done to us. In his speech, he presented himself as a responsible, principled statesman concerned about the future of the world. That is how standing and influence are gained internationally. Imagine how much more could be achieved if the President maintained his statesmanlike posture and principles a little longer than the queue in which Eastern Europeans waited for a chance to take a selfie with Donald and Melania Trump.

Kandel is a small German town near the French border, some 70 kilometers from Strasbourg. My family and I like to go there on day trips, as the town of nine thousand inhabitants offers plenty of opportunities for recreation. On Sundays, a local accordion orchestra plays by the town pond, and the kiosk serves spritzers made with the local Pinot Gris and warm pretzels. In this idyllic little town in the Palatinate, on December 27 last year, fifteen-year-old Mia Valentin was murdered outside the local drugstore. The perpetrator was her ex-boyfriend, Abdul D., a refugee from Afghanistan who had come to Germany two years earlier. In August this year, he was sentenced in Karlsruhe to eight years in prison. The horrific murder understandably caused great outrage in Germany, but many of the reactions were very quickly removed from social networks. Germany’s new law, known as NetzDG, requires internet platforms to remove hate speech themselves. As Harvard professor Yascha Mounk, author of The People vs. Democracy, mentioned during a recent lecture in Strasbourg, the posts removed from Facebook included several statements that the murdered girl’s mother had addressed to German Chancellor Angela Merkel. Faced with extremely high potential fines of up to 50 million euros, Facebook simply did not want to take the risk of analyzing in detail whether this really was hate speech, nor did it take into account the context that these were the words of a grieving mother who had lost her child in horrific circumstances. The far right’s propaganda army, of course, did not let such a gift slip through its fingers. On March 11, 2004, 193 people died in a bomb attack on Madrid’s Atocha station. The Islamist terrorist organization Al-Qaeda claimed responsibility. It was not Spain’s first experience of terrorism. Over the past 50 years, attacks by the Basque terrorist organization ETA killed hundreds of people. In this context, it is understandable that Article 578 of the Spanish Criminal Code prohibits “glorifying terrorism” and “humiliating the victims of terrorism.” The problem is that in recent years the number of convictions has soared; in the last two years alone there have been more than seventy. Among them are quite a few artists and creators. Last week, a court in Ghent rejected a request to extradite Valtònyc, a 24-year-old rapper from Majorca who fled to Belgium in May after Spain’s High Court upheld a sentence of three and a half years in prison for lyrics that, in the judges’ opinion, glorified terrorism. A few days ago, a French court ordered a psychiatric assessment of Marine Le Pen. The leader of France’s far-right party is on trial for spreading images of the horrific crimes of the Islamic State. If the court finds her guilty, she faces up to three years in prison. On hearing this news, many in Slovenia grumbled about why we can’t have trials like this too. But it is worth pointing out that this is not Le Pen’s first such experience. Years ago, she was convicted over statements about the “Islamic occupation of France,” only to be acquitted on appeal. Her supporters enthusiastically celebrated the victory of a martyr fighting for truth in the name of the nation against censorship by corrupt elites. These three cases differ from one another, but each in its own way illustrates the risk that ill-considered and overly deep intrusions into freedom of expression bring to the fight against hate speech. This does not mean, of course, that we must not or cannot limit that freedom, but we must be careful not to do more harm than good. That is why the European Court sets the threshold for legal prohibition, and especially for criminal prosecution, very high, and also defines as lawful speech that shocks, disturbs or offends. In Slovenia, we undoubtedly have an extremely serious problem with the spread of hate speech and intolerance, but in my view it cannot be solved by prosecutors alone. Although there have recently been quite a few cases involving direct threats of violence, where questions about the prosecution’s decisions are certainly justified, for a significant part of the speech we might consider hateful we cannot categorically claim in advance that it reaches the high threshold set by the Strasbourg court for the most serious restrictions on freedom of expression. This does not mean, of course, that such speech does not need and demand firm condemnation. On the contrary, the Strasbourg court not only permits such political and social reactions but expects them in a democratic society. That is a message for those who justify their silence by respect for democratic values. What is most lacking in the response to the growing spread of hatred in Slovenia is above all a firm and clear social reaction from politicians, as well as from other personalities and institutions that enjoy respect or influence in society. We need a democracy whose survival does not depend on prosecutors alone but which can also defend itself. In a civilized, modern democratic society, the hatred, racism and vulgar lies spread in our public space by certain public figures and media should mean a one-way, non-refundable ticket out of public life and influence. Here, it is often exactly the opposite. The biggest problem with the tweets of the Ljubljana lawyer is not that the police did not handcuff her after she posted them and take her away to prison, but that her party, a member of the European People’s Party, put her up as a candidate for parliament without hesitation and without consequences, despite her regular outbursts of vulgar hatred. The biggest concern about Demokracija’s recent front pages is not that the police did not raid the newsroom and confiscate every copy from the newsstands, but that the President of the Republic believes, or wants to believe, that he must not respond to cases of obvious hate speech, racism and intolerance in the media. The most worrying thing about the clearly hateful and racist statements by our security expert is not that his intolerance was not censored, but that, despite it, the gentleman became a state secretary. Our weakness in responding to the growing spread of hatred is not only that we prosecute too little, but that we are too quiet and not ashamed enough. Silence gives hatred cover and legitimizes it. If we want to defeat hate speech, which is not only an ethical imperative but also a security one, we need politics that clearly and firmly defends constitutionally protected democratic values. Politics that stands up for those who are hated, instead of keeping silent about, excusing, nominating or even employing those who hate.

My boss and friend, Lord Russell-Johnston, a Scottish Liberal Democrat, humanist, and bon vivant, often said that the two biggest lies in the English language are: “Of course I’ll still love you in the morning” and “I’m from the government and I’m here to help.” Russell died in July 2008. Had he lived a few months longer, he would have found that joke even funnier—or perhaps sadder. Even before the September 2008 bankruptcy of the investment bank Lehman Brothers triggered the deepest and longest recession since the 1930s, millions of people in developed Western economies have already understood that, despite all the claims by Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, money doesn’t trickle down from those who have plenty to those who have the least. The collapse of Lehman Brothers and the taxpayer-funded rescue of financial institutions showed instead that, in moments of crisis, money can very much trickle upward. The state and its institutions, which should have prevented the greedy orgy of Lehman Brothers and their friends with toxic subprime securities, failed to do their job. Deregulation—which tied the hands of supervisory mechanisms—also played a role. After all, the market, including the financial market, supposedly regulates itself best. But when the crisis hit, the "elites" quickly found a way to use state intervention to shift the burden onto those who were not responsible for the crisis and who gained nothing from the financial manipulations that caused it. This statement is, of course, somewhat simplified, but it contains enough truth to explain the devastating impact this had on public trust and support for politics, the government, and its institutions. The distrust and rejection of these institutions, and the anger felt by the humiliated and insulted toward political and financial elites, didn’t start with the fall of Lehman Brothers, but that event certainly broke the dam. It created fertile ground for cynical hucksterism and manipulation of people’s emotions—people justifiably outraged by the injustices and the economic, social, and political marginalization that had begun long before that fateful September in 2008. In 1944, British philosopher and Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek published The Road to Serfdom in London. In it, Hayek argued that government interference in the economy leads to the loss of freedom, repression of individuals, and political tyranny. The book was quite successful from the start and has sold more than two million copies to date. At least two copies were surely bought by the previously mentioned U.S. President Ronald Reagan and his British counterpart Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who, in the 1980s, shaped domestic and international economic policy strongly inspired by Hayek. Out of fear—real or feigned—of the threat of tyranny that supposedly lurked in any state intervention in the economy, they laid the foundations for a neoliberal policy framework built on aggressive privatization, shrinking of the public sector, and deregulation of rules that restricted the free operation of economic actors—including rules that protected the public interest. The centerpiece of it all was tax policy, marked by dramatic reductions in taxes on the wealthiest, under the pretext that this would ultimately bring prosperity to the entire society. You know—the trickle-down theory. We know what happened. The blind and frantic fetishization of the market as the only effective and legitimate regulator of economic and social relations led to stagnation in living standards for large segments of the population in many developed Western economies. The expectation that capital—once freed from the shackles of state intervention and regulation—would develop a social conscience and act responsibly toward the public interest... well, let’s say that didn’t quite pan out. The shrinking of the public sector hurt those who couldn’t afford paid alternatives to services they had previously received for free or at a lower cost. The middle class—the largest and most reliable voting bloc for social democratic, centrist, and center-right parties that built post-war welfare state models across Western Europe—dwindled and lost its influence. A significant portion of the working class was pushed—if not into poverty—then at least to the brink of human dignity. The traditional electorate of the left thus became easy prey for right-wing chauvinist extremism of the Salvini and Le Pen variety. The great paradox of the entire story is that the fertile ground for a populist attack on democratic institutions—based on liberal democratic values such as human rights, political freedoms, and the democratic rule of law—was created by the ideas of a man who sought to protect freedom from tyranny. And once again, the money trickled in the opposite direction. Populists are also aided by many—on both the left and right—who equate economic neoliberalism with liberal democracy. This demagogic lumping together makes it easier for populists to deceive the victims of economic neoliberalism, who then believe that their problems stem from democratic institutions, the media, civil society, and human rights. And, of course, migrants. As an alternative, populists offer economic neoliberalism without freedom and without rights. In the end, the biggest victims will be those who support the populists most fervently today. The truth is that a social state that creates the conditions for a competitive and efficient economy, while maintaining an effective public sector through sound tax policy and regulation and preventing excessive social inequalities, is in no way incompatible with the principles and values of liberal democracy. On the contrary, it is a necessary condition for the normal functioning of such a democracy. This is not about being left or right, but about an economic, political, and social model that, with different emphases, was used by post-war European governments across the democratic political spectrum to build society. Excessive social inequality is not only a barrier to the normal functioning of liberal democracy but also an obstacle to sustainable economic growth, as even the OECD acknowledged in 2014. Based on this wealth of empirical evidence, one might assume that the doctrine of trickle-down economics has been discredited by time. Fake news! Donald Trump may not have read Hayek’s book, but he probably believes he wrote it. He is encouraged by the current strong performance of the American economy—for which he naturally takes full credit. When that ends, he’ll blame someone else. Boris Johnson is also excited, seeing in the hardest possible form of Brexit a chance for a new Great Britain, where bold tax cuts will create “a happy and dynamic economy that promotes entrepreneurship and rewards the truly hardworking and innovative, where people can hope to bring home higher wages.” The operative word here is, of course, hope. Boris is clearly counting on the fact that the British haven’t yet realized that nothing will trickle down to them. Of those two million copies of Hayek’s book, a few have clearly been sold in Slovenia as well—at least judging by some of the positions taken in the recent heated debate on tax policy. That those annoyed by the democratic institutions of liberal democracy and the social state are enamored with Hayek’s ideas is no surprise. But perhaps others might take a moment to reflect on how, why, and where the world has drifted over the past thirty years. If not, we might very well wake up one morning with a splitting headache and a moral hangover—in bed with someone who doesn’t love us.
Is There a Pilot on the Plane?

In mid-August this year, 68-year-old Robert Chain of Encino, California, repeatedly called the newsroom of the Boston Globe and threatened to kill journalists because they were “enemies of the people.” On August 24, Matija Stepišnik, editor-in-chief of Večer, posted an ironic comment on his Facebook profile about entrepreneur Ivo Boscarol’s announcement that he intended to move abroad because of the proposed changes to tax legislation. After a “journalistic piece” in which Nova24TV described Stepišnik as a “hooligan commissar,” the comments included a post by user Boris Ivicak (quoted here unedited): “A bullet in the head for such scum, he is not worthy to walk on slovenian soil.” On August 25, in the eastern German city of Chemnitz, a fight broke out in which 35-year-old Daniel H. was stabbed to death. Police arrested a 23-year-old Syrian and a 22-year-old Iraqi as suspects. In the days that followed, Chemnitz saw mass far-right demonstrations organized by the Alternative for Germany together with other far-right groups. The riots turned violent, and several foreigners were injured after demonstrators hunted them through the streets. On August 27, the editor-in-chief of Večer reported the death threat to the Maribor police. On August 28, Italian Interior Minister Salvini and Hungarian Prime Minister Orbán named French President Macron as their main political opponent. Macron agreed with them and said he would not back down in defending Europe against nationalism and hate speech. On August 30, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation arrested Robert Chain on suspicion of sending “threatening communications,” an offense punishable by up to five years in prison. On the same day, the weekly Demokracija published on its front page a photograph of a white female body with black hands reaching for it, under the headline “Migrants bring rape culture to Slovenia.” The cover provoked a wave of protest and condemnation. While many recognized it as hate speech, the Office of the President of the Republic of Slovenia said that “the President always refrains from commenting on the media so that he cannot be accused of interfering with freedom of speech and of the press.” The statement also stressed “the President’s well-known positions on the need for mutual respect,” though unfortunately without explaining who, in this particular case, was supposed to respect whom. Demokracija demonstrated its respect for the culture of intolerance again in its very next issue, with a blatantly homophobic cover. In the first days of September, the proposed tax changes, which had been added to the coalition agreement at the initiative of the Left party and had so angered entrepreneur Boscarol and some of his colleagues, became the subject of heated debate in the media and on social networks. It culminated in an open letter from the Slovenian Entrepreneurs’ Club, whose leadership complained bitterly about “the inflammatory tone, the spreading of untruths, indecent political culture, populism, bias and, above all, inadmissible hate speech against entrepreneurs…” After the letter was published, Borut Pahor promptly invited representatives of the club to a meeting at the presidential palace. On Monday, September 3, German Chancellor Angela Merkel strongly condemned the far-right riots in Chemnitz. The same day, more than fifty thousand people gathered for a concert against racism under the slogan “We are more.” The concert, publicly supported by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, began with a minute’s silence in memory of the murdered Daniel H. In the first week of September, videos appeared online of masked men in uniform, with beer bellies, axes and semi-automatic weapons, who had allegedly been parading and training in the forests of Styria. When it turned out that this paramilitary formation was led by Andrej Šiško, failed candidate for President of the Republic of Slovenia and self-proclaimed commander of the armed forces of the land of Styria, politicians stirred too and even condemned and deplored the whole affair. On September 6, the Slovenian police detained Šiško on suspicion of inciting the violent overthrow of the constitutional order. Some columns write themselves, but still, from my side, a thought or two. First, about taxes. Debates, including heated ones, about tax policy, the interests of business, the needs of the public sector and the welfare state are not unique to us. Entrepreneurs, of course, have every right to defend their interests, but the same right must be granted to those who defend the interests of the public sector and the welfare state, even if we don’t always agree with their rhetoric or all their arguments. And let us not forget that we enshrined the welfare state as a value in Article 2 of the Constitution. Tax policy and redistribution are ideological topics par excellence, at the center of political battles in every election in every democracy. But here we don’t like ideological topics and divisions. Instead of seeking the balance that best reflects the public interest (which of course includes ensuring the conditions for a competitive economy), we “transcend” ideological divisions by turning one of the options, which defends a logical but partial interest, into a state religion and a test of patriotism. Criticism from entrepreneurs is thus by definition the voice of reason, while criticism of their criticism is hate speech, whose victims are promptly invited into the warm bosom of presidential attention and protection. But evidently there is not room in that bosom for everyone. For victims of hate speech, that is. When it comes to racism, intolerance and homophobia, the President’s attention, judging by his office’s statement, turns elsewhere, out of fear of being accused of interfering with freedom of speech and of the press. Let me reassure the President at once: such worries are completely unnecessary. Condemning unacceptable, offensive, racist, homophobic, antisemitic and similar statements, even when published in the media, can in no way be understood as interfering with freedom of speech or of the press. What is more, since such statements attack and undermine constitutionally protected values, condemning them is something one could even expect from the President of the Republic, as part of his job, if you like. If he needs inspiration, he can hop on the Franco-German train. But far be it from me to discourage the President from caring about media freedom. If that care is sincere, then in today’s Slovenia he unfortunately has no shortage of opportunities to prove it. But again, silence will not do; it will take moral authority, an ethical stance and clear positions. For example, when an editor is threatened with “a bullet in the head,” or when a party leader calls women journalists prostitutes, or perhaps when a writer and columnist receives a threatening letter and white powder in an envelope. For example. I don’t yet know how the police will act on the report of the death threat against Večer’s editor-in-chief, but in the case of the Styrian militia they have, at least so far, done their job professionally. That, however, in no way diminishes the responsibility of politicians. It is not enough just to wring one’s hands and sigh, “Oh dear, oh dear, how terrible, who would have thought such a thing could happen.” We cannot and must not pretend that there is no causal link whatsoever between tolerating hate speech, racism and nationalist populism on the one hand and armed masked men tramping through Slovenian forests on the other.

I don’t know if I’m the only one, but the gatherings and pontifications of the Assembly for the Republic often remind me of those two grumpy old men on the balcony of the Muppet Show—with the difference, of course, that the Assembly for the Republic has a bigger balcony and less sense of humor. That was also my first impression of their recent press conference. “I see mobilization, a revival of revolutionary socialist traditions, hatred of capitalism and hatred of the Church,” complained the first man. “The new government will operate under the baton of the Yugo-nostalgic left,” snapped the second angrily, adding that everyone “who does not accept the post-communist interpretation of recent history” is regarded as an internal enemy. “There are demands for censorship of those who question the mythology about the time of the Second World War and after,” fumed the third. “These are open or covert attempts to deny the Slovenian holocaust,” concluded the last man grimly, not forgetting to add that “in some democratic countries, Holocaust denial is even a criminal offense.” Colorful, certainly, though, as I said, not very funny. Not much of a Muppet Show, really. The sleight-of-hand manipulation of facts and history is more reminiscent of the men on the street who move a ball between three cups at lightning speed and invite passers-by to guess where it is hidden. They are helped by a seemingly unconnected accomplice, a neat and polished gentleman in a suit and tie, who, with feigned impartiality, assures the audience of the honesty and credibility of the whole business and invites them to reconcile. Pardon, to bet. But joking aside, the question is what the participants actually wanted to achieve with the press conference. The purpose was certainly not to inform the Slovenian public that crimes against unarmed people took place in the post-war period. That is a generally accepted truth that no one denies. Nor was the aim a political condemnation. The post-war events have been condemned from all sides, except perhaps by a few ideological hotheads who would really do better to keep quiet. Such condemnation is also the only acceptable and decent response. Any attempt to justify the post-war killings is grist to the mill of those who want to use these tragic events to turn history on its head. Nor is it about a desire to remember the victims with respect. No one disputes that either. Least of all, despite all the efforts of the neat and polished gentleman, is it about a sincere desire for reconciliation. That reconciliation actually happened twenty-eight years ago, thanks to the president and the archbishop of the time. If you like, it was also cemented in marble, thanks to the current head of state. But this reconciliation does not interest the members of the Assembly for the Republic, and it interests their choirmaster even less. Even the moral equidistance between anti-fascism and collaboration that the reconciliation process, in its marble version, implies does not satisfy their ambitions to reinterpret history. So what is it about? First, an attempt to discredit political competitors and deny them legitimacy, based on far-fetched accusations and imaginary links between their political opponents and all sorts of things, including the post-war events. You can think what you like about Marjan Šarec, Alenka Bratušek, Miro Cerar, Dejan Židan, Karl Erjavec and Luka Mesec, but claims that these people are in any way connected to, or bear responsibility for, the post-war killings are really too idiotic to deserve a serious answer. But we live in strange times, and idiotic lies have ever longer legs. As the participants stressed in their introduction, without a trace of irony, “the political environment is turning into fertile ground for the flourishing of ideological intolerance.” The second aim of invoking the post-war events, and in my view the main one, is an attempt to recast the losers of history as winners. That is the light in which their indifference to the reconciliation process should be understood. They are not interested in indulgences and the relativization of responsibility; they expect and demand a moral victory over anti-fascism. In the discourse and logic of the Assembly for the Republic and its sympathizers, the post-war killings—which here, as in some other countries, unfortunately prevailed over court trials as the only proper way of sanctioning collaboration with the Nazis and crimes against one’s own people—become a moment of absolution from responsibility for taking part in a criminal enterprise that caused the deaths of twenty million people in Europe. Among them were six million Jews who died as victims of the Holocaust. The statement by the president of the Assembly for the Republic calling the post-war events—that is, the killing of people who supported or collaborated with the executioners of the concentration camps—a “Slovenian holocaust” is, to put it mildly, indecent and offensive to the victims of Nazi crimes. That in this context he also mentions that Holocaust denial is a criminal offense in some countries is cynicism without equal. I do not recall the president speaking out on this subject when, some time ago, a prominent member of the assembly he chairs publicly belittled and denied the Holocaust. The manipulation of historical facts is above all a springboard for an attempt to gain political dominance in the present and to reshape the future in the spirit of ideas that have already caused Europe so much grief once. Under the increasingly thin cover of anti-communist clamor and the fight against phantom enemies and totalitarian regimes that no longer exist, the real ambitions of revising historical truths are becoming ever clearer. They are about undermining the civilizational achievements of European society, based on liberal democracy, humanism, solidarity, human rights, social justice, the democratic rule of law and, above all, anti-fascism. In other words, the society that democratic Europe established after the Second World War precisely so that the ideas and forces defeated in that war would never again come to power. Never again.

When I was a child, we lived in Trieste. My parents enrolled me in a Slovenian Catholic kindergarten, where we were looked after by nuns. It left no major consequences, except that every day after coming home I shouted at my father and mother that we would end up in hell because we didn’t go to Mass. I think that is when I acquired the penchant for preaching that is still with me today. But what stuck in my memory most is that we three-year-olds spent most of the day sitting at our desks with our arms behind the backs of our chairs. “If you don’t sit up straight,” the sisters told us, “your back will hurt when you’re old.” I remembered those words recently when photographs were published from the NATO meeting in Brussels showing the President of the European Commission staggering. Back pain is a nasty thing. From someone who was elected to his current post as the Spitzenkandidat of the Christian Democratic European People’s Party, I would have expected a much longer Catholic upbringing in his youth than mine. But perhaps he skipped class when they covered upright posture. But let me be clear straight away: I do not agree with the wave of reproach and indignation that poured down on Juncker the moment the footage of his wobbly walk across the ceremonial stage was published. There are two possibilities, and in both cases the staggering Luxembourger deserves more sympathy than outrage. Perhaps it is true, as his spokespeople said, that he was struck by sciatica. Back pain is a serious matter and nothing to make fun of. If, however, his paso doble was the result of drinking before such an important meeting in full view of the world, that too is an illness that calls for treatment, not a reason for ridicule. The President of the European Commission responded to reports of his alleged drunkenness by saying that he demanded respect. Here, despite all my sympathy, I have certain reservations. Respect is not something you get on demand; respect has to be earned. The best way to achieve it is an upright posture, which, incidentally, also helps against back pain. And it is precisely with an upright posture that many European politicians today have quite a few problems. At a time when we advocates of liberal democracy compete in outrage at those who treat its values like a pig treats a bagpipe, we should not forget the responsibility of those who declaratively support the same values but whose conduct, inconsistency, duplicity, political calculation, unprincipled struggle for power, lack of integrity or simple incompetence have created the opportunity for a nationalist and populist comeback on the political scene in Europe and the world. The European People’s Party, to which the President of the European Commission also belongs, is an illustrative example of this trend in its attitude to populism within its own ranks. Anxious to get the best possible result in the coming European elections, and with it the largest possible slice of the power and financial pie, they are prepared to forget the values on which their predecessors built the European institutional, legal, social and economic model after the Second World War, as a defense against nationalism, populism and the politics of hatred and division. They are therefore prepared to keep everyone in their ranks, including those whose discourse and policies undermine the values of the very Europe that our worthy politicians are otherwise always talking about. This lack of consistency in defending their own values is skillfully exploited by politicians who build their political power on division and hatred in a growing number of European countries. The normalization and legitimization of the unacceptable for the sake of short-term political gain is becoming a general trend with extremely dangerous long-term consequences. One of the latest examples here at home was the frightening absence of an appropriate political response to open flirting with neo-Nazism—not by anonymous internet trolls, but by an official candidate of one of the political parties in the recent parliamentary elections. It is truly incredible that those from whom one would expect immediate condemnation and distancing are still full of talk about building the state. Given that we built our state on the support and participation of most Slovenians in the Allied struggle against fascism, and at the time of independence on values diametrically opposed to those the would-be MP sympathizes with, such appeals to state-building are, to put it mildly, not credible. If anything, they show the desperately low level of political culture, responsibility and decency in Slovenian politics. One or two unacceptable tweets can be seen as an isolated incident; the absence of an appropriate political response legitimizes that incident and turns it into the mainstream. We live in the age of salonfähig populism, for which the Trumps, the Orbáns and our domestic imitators are not the only ones to blame; it is also, and above all, the fault of those who invited populists and nationalists into the living room and made every effort to make them feel at home. The way out of this mess cannot come from feigned ignorance and further relativization of the basic civilizational values on which Europe built its post-war stability and peace, but only from a strong ethical backbone and a responsible, determined and consistent insistence on those values, even at the expense of partial and short-term political interests. So my advice to European and Slovenian politicians who, at least declaratively, defend democratic values, is above all to stand up straight. It is not only the best way to defend a Europe based on democracy, human rights and the democratic rule of law, but the only one. Besides, it also helps against sciatica. If they don’t look after their spine, all they will have left is a back aching from shame and despair.

A few years ago, the city authorities renovated the outdoor swimming pool near our home in Strasbourg. The investment was considerable, and the result looks dazzling at first sight, not least because of the stainless-steel walls of the pool, which, although outdoors, is open every day of the year. So when global warming bared its teeth again this April and temperatures rose to almost thirty degrees, my family and I went for a swim. We were not the only ones. A long queue stretched in front of the pool, and inside the crowd was even more indescribable. But while the people waiting, despite the crush, were in a typical holiday mood, inside the complex, fenced in by panels and patrolled by a crowd of uniformed staff armed with whistles, the tension was palpable. The trouble started soon after we arrived. Having lived in France for more than twenty years, I was sure we had come properly prepared. Tristan and I had swapped our usual swimming trunks for tighter “Speedo” models, since I know from experience that they won’t let you into the water in looser swim shorts, which are far more suitable for middle-aged men. For reasons of hygiene, apparently. I wasn’t worried about Maša and Tara. As long as they don’t jump into the water in a burkini, I thought, they’ll be left in peace. First they came for me. I heard a piercing whistle, and then a patrol of two lifeguards approached and demanded that I take off the T-shirt that, because of my sensitive skin and on medical advice, I always wear when swimming. My medical reasons met with no understanding whatsoever from the Alsatian Bademeister, who lectured me on the safety and hygiene risks that my individual concern for my own health posed to the common interest and well-being of all bathers. If, despite everything, I wished to insist on exercising my rights and freedoms, they went on, I would have to obtain a medical certificate on a special form and send it to the city services, which, after careful examination of my application, might allow me to dip myself, in a T-shirt protecting me against skin cancer, into the pool under their jurisdiction. “You’re lucky it’s only April,” one of them joked good-naturedly, “you might get the permit before the end of the swimming season.” “But you’ll need a new one next year,” added his less jocular colleague. So I crouched at the edge of the pool with my back unprotected, shielding my eyes with my hand to keep an eye, among the mass of bathers, on my children, who were desperately trying to have fun in the overcrowded pool. Sunglasses, you see, are not allowed. At that moment someone tapped me on the shoulder. “Sir,” said an attendant dressed in white, “there are a lot of families here.” Since it was obvious I wasn’t following, she explained that my trunks were too small and that I was showing the people at the pool more of my backside than the statutes and rules of the Strasbourg city administration allow. “It doesn’t bother me,” she said, trying coquettishly to soften this new attack on my individual rights—an attack caused by first forcing me into trunks I had last worn a decade ago, and then making me take off the T-shirt that would otherwise have covered the sinful display of my curves—“but it’s about the children.” She waited patiently while I pulled my trunks up as far as they would go, then marched on, unaware that the maneuver had caused an even greater assault on family values on the front of my body. I slowly began to regret the decision to make a Sunday outing of it. To lift the family’s morale, I went looking for a snack bar. In vain. The worthy renovators of the pool had, intentionally or not, overlooked the fact that swimming makes you thirsty and hungry. You cannot buy so much as a bottle of water at the pool. When I pointed this out to the staff, they told me that food and drink could be bought outside. “But once you go out, you can’t come back in,” they explained. People in this fortress of chlorinated authoritarianism are condemned to deprivation; the only solution is exile with no possibility of return. The regime slowly began to achieve its aims. I started to accept further episodes of law enforcement with a certain resignation, with the bitter realization that my freedom had been sacrificed in the name of safety, order and family values. When Tara came running out of the pool in tears, having been chased out because her hair wasn’t tied up, I just stroked her head somewhat absently. When I was told, while photographing my own children, that taking pictures was not allowed, I just smiled and put my phone away. I lay helplessly on my towel and stared at the European Parliament building, separated from the pool only by a road and a fence. During sessions, the pool is apparently very popular with MEPs and Eurocrats, who swim to ease their back pain. Suddenly a siren sounded over the loudspeakers, and then a voice warned us, in three languages, that the evacuation of the pool would begin in half an hour. Given the circumstances, the choice of words seemed particularly apt. We quickly gathered our things and went home, crestfallen. I wanted to spare the children the experience of the evacuation as well. I don’t know why I imagined they would carry it out with German shepherds. After all, the English used to call this breed Alsatians. Welcome to the age of illiberal recreation.

The space-time continuum is a concept developed by Dr Albert Einstein in his special theory of relativity at Princeton University—and in its more practical applications, by Dr Emmett Brown in the film Back to the Future. It’s a four-dimensional space made up of three spatial and one temporal dimension, through which you can travel in a modified, nuclear-powered sports car. But time travel isn’t without danger: meddling in the past can lead the present down an undesirable path. Technically, this is known as a disruption of the space-time continuum, or the causality problem. The classic example is the grandfather paradox: what happens if you go back in time and kill your grandfather before he fathers your father? In Back to the Future, the space-time continuum is disrupted the moment the protagonist’s own mother falls in love with him, thereby threatening the likelihood that she’ll later conceive him with his father. Physics and the past are both complicated matters—and we Slovenes have trouble with the latter. The more we try to leave it behind, the more it comes back to kick us in the ass. Perhaps it would be wiser to stop turning our backs on it and instead look it straight in the eye. This is especially true of the period that causes us the most difficulty—what we usually call our “recent history.” As if that weren’t enough, we’ve lately been having increasing trouble even with some later events, which by logic could be called our “semi-recent history.” Until recently, it was generally accepted that Slovenia became independent so that we could build a free, open, solidaristic, democratic society based on respect for human rights, political liberties, and the democratic rule of law. So firmly were we committed to liberal democracy that we wrote all of this into the constitution—along with a host of other important things, from declaring Slovenia a social state, to the right to freely decide on childbirth, and the validity of ratified international treaties—not to mention the separation of church and state. We spoke more about citizens than we did about the nation. Until recently. Today, many are acting as if in June 1991, the space-time continuum was broken and history twisted in an unwanted direction. Of course, I’m not saying anyone regrets independence itself. I believe we all support an independent state—many out of sincere patriotism, others perhaps because they believe that a smaller political format makes it easier for mediocre politicians to gain power. We Slovenes have no issue with independence—we do, however, have trouble with the reasons we so passionately repeated, to ourselves and others, as justification for independence 27 years ago. And in dismantling those reasons, we are becoming increasingly effective. We’re reconfiguring the past quite successfully—even without a nuclear-powered sports car. In Back to the Future, the main character nervously checks a family photo after every failed attempt to deflect his infatuated mother, watching whether his image fades or strengthens. Here, we have no need for anxiety: we are efficiently erasing all traces of our semi-recent liberal democratic aspirations from the photograph of our political present. In their place, a society is emerging that very much resembles the one we supposedly wanted to leave behind. Let me illustrate. Let’s recall the kind of society we once lived in: The state from which we became independent was based on very strong leaders—or rather, one leader. In politics, there were no relative winners. All victories were absolute and irreversible. We had tightly secured borders. Guards, German shepherds, outposts, and no-man’s-land patrols protected us from the dangers of crossings in both directions. There were no immigration pressures. Foreigners only came here on vacation; it never occurred to them to move here and threaten our culture with their customs, languages, and habits. If anything, it was our gastarbeiters (migrant workers) who threatened theirs. The political process ran smoothly and efficiently. There were no problems with fragmented parties or coalition building. All governments were, by definition, focused on development and reform-oriented. All reforms were, by definition, successful. We were completely safe from the threat of ideological polarization. We turned unity into a state religion. We even named a highway after it. We called journalists “socio-political workers.” They were expected to have no opinions of their own. Human rights and political freedoms were seen as a conspiracy by Western liberal elites—at the expense of the ordinary, honest folk, or as we liked to say back then, the working people and citizens. Yet despite all the similarities, there is one key difference between the society of that time and our society today. In the final years before independence, we lived in a liberal non-democracy; today, we are striding ever more boldly into an illiberal democracy. The difference isn’t so much in substance as in direction. In the previous system, liberalism was undermining non-democracy. Today, anti-liberalism is undermining freedom. In the name of the people, we march forward—into the past.
And It Was Such a Beautiful Day

“These trousers are mine, from Dachau,” Jean Villeret told me as we slowly climbed the steep path of the memorial center at the Struthof-Natzwiller concentration camp. “The jacket belonged to a friend who has already passed away.” “The one I wore here had the letters NN on the back—Nacht und Nebel. Night and Fog—this is how political detainees and resistance fighters were marked in concentration camps, those condemned to die without any form of legal process. People taken by night and fog. “How did you manage to survive?” I asked him. “I was twenty-two,” Jean replied, “young, stubborn, and strong as a horse.” But many others weren’t so lucky. Out of 52,000 internees—including young Slovenian author from Trieste Boris Pahor—22,000 died in Struthof, many as victims of “medical” experiments. They were tortured, killed, and cremated in an incinerator hidden a little further down in the Alsatian forests above the Bruche River valley. “And it was such a beautiful day when they brought me here,” Jean added. “You look at these hills, this beauty, just yesterday you were chasing girls and partying with friends—you don’t believe something horrible can happen to you. But it can. Oh, it really can.” Nacht und Nebel is a logical extension of the concept of sovereignty as defined by Nazi legal scholar and philosopher Carl Schmitt. Sovereign is he who has the power, in defence of the vital interests of the nation, to place himself above all legal and ethical rules and laws. Today, many are once again enamoured with strong leaders, a unified nation, and national sovereignty. Personally, this fills me with unease and concern. I met Jean on Sunday, June 24, at the annual commemorative ceremony organized by the European Center of Deported Resistance Fighters in cooperation with the French state. Alongside the French Secretary of State for Defence, I was invited to speak at the ceremony on behalf of the Council of Europe. When the Ministry of Defence gets involved, things become serious. There was an honour guard, official protocol, dozens of flag bearers, a diplomatic corps, and the German military wind band played La Marseillaise. This is how the Germans and the French transcend past divisions—through a shared expression of respect for the victims of Nazism. In my speech, I quoted Boris Pahor and his Necropolis, in which he described his Struthof experience, and emphasized how vital historical memory is for understanding today’s world, and shared the story of my aunt Marija. It was another beautiful June day in 1941 when the Germans came for my grandparents at their home near Sveta Ana in the Slovenske gorice hills. Marija, barely two weeks old, was too young to be listed in the deportation papers by the otherwise exceptionally efficient occupation bureaucracy. Packed into cattle cars for deportation to Bosnia, my grandmother was bleeding from childbirth, forced to leave her newborn with neighbours. Yes, they separated children from parents back then. That’s what the authorities said—order must be maintained. My grandparents never saw Marija again; she died a few months later in the arms of a woman who was not her mother. Marija’s story is a symbolic bridge between yesterday and today. The point is not to label those who separate parents and children today as Nazis—such rhetoric is excessive and unhelpful—but rather to remind us that the peak of inhumanity and evil the world experienced less than eighty years ago didn’t begin in the crematoria of Struthof or other death camps. It began the moment people, for various reasons, started accepting—or even supporting—the political manipulation of hatred and fear. It began when humanity started to erode. When people, gradually and almost imperceptibly at first, then more and more rapidly, began to lose their humanity. After the ceremony, I returned to Strasbourg. Thanks to the recent loosening of digital content restrictions, I can now watch Slovenian TV at home. Sometimes, I’m not particularly grateful to the European Union for this. In the news, the anchor-woman, with thinly veiled schadenfreude, reported on the disputes at the EU member state meeting on the migration crisis. “Will Slovenia join the countries ready to take decisive action,” she asked, “or those still advocating open borders?” I heard that migrants are dying—but mainly because of traffickers, possibly in collusion with humanitarian organizations rescuing men, women, and children from drowning in the Mediterranean. No mention was made of figures showing that irregular arrivals have halved since last year and dropped by 80 percent since 2016—perhaps because that wouldn’t serve those who politically exploit public misery, fear, and hatred. The crisis most acutely felt in Italy and Greece was not caused so much by migrants as by the indifference, selfishness, shortsightedness, and political opportunism of other EU member states—especially those “ready to act decisively.” Salvini didn’t come to power because of migrants but because Europe abandoned Italy and Greece. We are not facing a migration crisis—we are facing a crisis of our institutions, our humanity, and our values. Meanwhile, in the U.S., Melania swapped Zara for Gucci, and her husband tweeted that, to protect America, migrants must be deported without any legal proceedings. In the name of the nation’s vital interests, the rule of law must be abolished. Sovereignty. In the news, I heard that Slovenians have evolved from a people into a nation. Though I’m not entirely sure what that’s supposed to mean, the words made me uneasy. I’m worried about placing the nation above the state and its citizens, just as I’m worried about that understanding of national unity and national interests that prevents us from responding to hatred—and in whose name we gradually become less and less human. This is not a discourse that helps us overcome past divisions; it is a discourse that can return us to the very reasons those divisions arose. Summer is here again, and beautiful days lie ahead. A time for romance, holidays, and joyful gatherings with friends. But sometimes, even on beautiful days, terrible things can happen. The fog descends, and night falls.

On October 30, 1922, at five to eleven in the morning, a sleeper train from Milan arrived punctually at the main Roman train station, Roma Termini. From the train clambered down a stocky little man dressed in black, with a pronounced lower jaw. Since one cannot enter history looking disheveled, he first stopped at the Hotel Savoie, then—with a cluster of personal bodyguards and a black top hat on his head—made his way to the Quirinal Palace, where King Vittorio Emanuele III nervously awaited to grant him the mandate to form a new Italian government. Despite concerns about the chaos the Blackshirts were causing across Italy, Vittorio Emanuele chose Mussolini because he saw in him a rising political star and a strong personality who could overcome the shortcomings of a divided and ineffective Italian liberal democracy of the time. Just over a decade later, German President Paul von Hindenburg was also disappointed in the shortcomings of democracy—and not entirely without reason. The Weimar Republic, introduced in 1919 by a coalition of Catholic parties, liberals, and social democrats, had by then been paralyzed by internal conflicts. After several failed attempts with democratically inclined but weak chancellors, von Hindenburg—under pressure—granted the mandate to a strong personality meant to bridge the weakness and inefficiency of German liberal democracy at that time. Before you angrily begin to complain on social media, let me reassure you that I am not comparing the above-mentioned historical “strong personalities” with anyone in Slovenia. Such comparisons are inaccurate and inappropriate. I also believe that those in our country who flirt with the idea of strong individuals do not desire authoritarianism or dictatorship. But on the other hand, it is quite likely that neither did Vittorio Emanuele nor von Hindenburg.
