What concerns me is the collective obsession with driving history, ideology, and substance out of Slovenian politics—and thus, out of democracy itself. This is what is paving the way for authoritarianism at the expense of plurality and freedom. History is clearly seen as an irritating element in Slovenian politics. Overcoming past divisions seems to be a universally accepted virtue, but in practice, it prevents us from realizing that these divisions are still very much alive—and today, more than seventy years later, they are resurfacing and can fatally shape our present and future. “Never again” has become a ceremonial ritual that begins and ends with laying wreaths at memorials. It is absent where it is truly needed—in the social, political, and legal response to the revival of discourses, ideas, and actions that led to the horrors of recent European history. In addition to the specific Slovenian trauma of the Partisan-Nazi collaborator divide, the negative attitude toward history also stems from a broader phenomenon that American historian Timothy Snyder calls the politics of inevitability. This belief holds that there are no more ideas, no alternatives, and that the future can only be a repetition or improvement of the present. The problem is that faith in the irreversibility of history weakens our immune system and dramatically increases the risk that we will repeat old mistakes. Since in the politics of inevitability there are no longer ideas, ideology too becomes a nuisance. Overcoming ideological differences is another mantra we endlessly repeat in the Slovenian public sphere from all sides. In this view of democracy, a party with a clear program and firm commitments to voters is seen as disruptive—or even, as one political commentator recently put it, radical. A clear and ideologically defined program—be it left-wing, right-wing, liberal, social-democratic, or conservative—is, in this interpretation of democracy, inappropriate because it complicates political bargaining in the name of the so-called national interest. At first glance, this may seem perfectly logical and even appealing, but the devil lies in how we understand what this common, state, and national interest is supposed to represent. While such an interest does exist, it only does so at a very general level. All citizens want a successful, safe, and socially just state, with quality education, healthcare, a pension system, and so on. The problem is that individuals, interest groups, and social subsystems see and interpret each of these goals differently. Moreover, there are many paths to these goals, and each path is ideologically tinted. In a democracy, choosing between alternatives that offer different options for social development—within constitutional principles—is not an anomaly; it is democracy’s fundamental characteristic. Parties go to elections with programs that specify, with concrete measures and figures, how to achieve a certain goal. If—with like-minded parties—they convince a majority of voters under our electoral system, they get the chance to govern. At the end of their term, they are held accountable for their success or failure in new elections. In our country, democracy seems to be understood differently—as a reality show of old and new faces, empty programs, and vague platitudes that turn politics into opportunistic manoeuvring dictated by the current whims of public opinion. Left, center, or right—with rare exceptions—are not labels of ideological profiles of parties in Slovenia, but mere reflections of their current emotional stance toward a single individual. Any substantive discussion about coalition-building quickly degenerates into haggling over positions. Since this leads nowhere, it's no surprise that, on the one hand, people are increasingly staying away from the polls, while on the other hand, disappointment with such politics creates a desire for strong leaders who will impose order in the name of the national interest. But the fact remains that this interest is always partial—no matter how much it is disguised in national colours, grand coalitions, and development-focussed governments that, if I understand correctly, unlike “non-developmental focussed” ones, are committed to development. Due to weak political culture and institutions, lack of experience, and half-digested historical frustrations, Slovenia is again trying to invent a different political model. One that is not based on democratic conflict between different ideas and programs, but on the forced promotion of fictional unity, manipulation of the national interest, and politicians who understand this interest better than the people—as the Guardian wrote in the autumn of 1922. Rejecting ideological diversity and substantive political choice as something supposedly not in the national interest undermines democracy and objectively leads us back to where we have already been: to a system with one truth, one ideology, and one leader. If we want to avoid this, then we should fix the shortcomings of democracy by strengthening its institutions—not by pledging allegiance to strongmen.

Much has already been written about the reasons why individuals become radicalized to the point of violence and suicide terrorist attacks. There are no simple, clear-cut explanations, but among the motives one often finds the terrorists’ belief that a suicide attack on people of other faiths and views, and on random passers-by, will earn them a reward in the afterlife. Many terrorists believe that their explosive belt will blow them all the way to the gates of the Islamist paradise, where seventy-seven virgins will reassemble them and service their jihadist pride for all eternity. It is much the same with the followers of the politics of fear and hatred. They believe that the fight against the nation’s enemies—from migrants and refugees, via faggots, to people from the former Yugoslav republics, degenerate artists, NGOs, liberal democrats of all stripes, emancipated women, Muslims, Soros and other Jews, all the way to multi-culti activists and random passers-by—will, after the final victory, bring a morally unpolluted and ideologically monolithic prosperity in which the Slovenian nation will blissfully bloom like a water lily on Lake Balaton. Virgins play no role in this sub-Alpine idyll. Women exist only as breeding support for patriotic machismo. Both, of course, are badly mistaken, but since one should not equate and generalize sweepingly in such sensitive matters, it must be acknowledged that there are also important differences between them. The first difference is that Islamist fanatics expect to be rewarded for their earthly crimes and atrocities only in the afterlife. The vanguard of the culture war, by contrast, believe that an ethnically and ideologically pure paradise is possible within a few days or weeks. On Earth, not just in heaven. A second important difference is linked to the first. Islamist fanatics have fewer empirical proofs at their disposal that could help them understand that they are shooting in the dark. Complaints from self-detonated yet ultimately unsatisfied terrorists are relatively rare. Just as it is hard to prove the existence of heavenly virgins generous to jihadists, it is hard to prove the opposite. In the end, you either believe it or you don’t. It is different with the legionnaires of the Kulturkampf. They have a whole range of instructive historical examples at their disposal that can vividly illustrate, even to the slower learners, where politics based on vampirized nationalism, the cult of personality, exclusion, closure, fear and hatred ultimately leads. Every time in history, these stories have ended tragically, and not only for those who were hated but, without exception, in the end also for those who did the hating. Let me be specific. Four million Germans died in uniform in the Second World War. But it was not only soldiers who died. In July 1945, damaged sewers and contaminated water caused a dysentery epidemic in Berlin that killed two-thirds of all newborn babies. Seventy-five percent of residential buildings were destroyed or uninhabitable. More than fifty thousand abandoned or lost children and orphans wandered the streets. In the first days of May, Russian soldiers raped almost a hundred thousand women in Berlin alone. Immediately after the end of the Second World War, more than twenty million people in Germany were homeless. There was a shortage not only of homes but also of food. In June 1945, in the American occupation zone, the daily ration for an adult did not reach nine hundred calories, too little for normal survival. Into all this misery poured millions of ethnic Germans expelled from the eastern parts of the ultimately not-so-eternal Third Reich. This was surely not the fate the Germans expected when, in the 1930s, they raised their right arms enthusiastically and en masse. Post-war German suffering is described by the late British historian Tony Judt in his book Postwar: A History of Europe Since 1945. Deprivation, hunger and death, of course, did not afflict only Germany and the Germans; the war left even worse consequences elsewhere in Europe, especially in its eastern part. What is worth reflecting on in this story today is the fact that the Germans themselves ultimately paid a very high price for the sins of leaders they had, until recently, ardently and blindly supported. The hatred, inhumanity and crimes committed in their name by the German state came back to the German people like a boomerang, cruelly and without mercy. Only the solidarity and help of their former enemies gave them back human dignity and the chance of a better future. Those who find the comparison with Nazism historically too remote can think about what Slobodan Milošević and his Greater Serbian politics brought the Serbs. From surfing the waves of the “yogurt revolution” adrenaline to today’s marking time in a traumatized country that an entire generation of young people has left. They know that there is neither bread, nor future, nor freedom in nativism, nationalism and hatred. It is human nature that we find it hard to learn from other people’s mistakes. Some of you probably believe you will succeed because you know how to hate better, more cleverly and more effectively than many before you. Believe me, the moment will come when you will regret it. Perhaps not for the people you are deliberately causing hardship and injustice, but in the end you will surely regret and lament your own fate. Hatred is like an explosive belt. Once it is detonated, we all inevitably end up as victims, you included. On Earth already, and perhaps in heaven too.

I am a great patriot. I love Slovenia. I often pester friends and acquaintances abroad with enthusiastic descriptions of the beauty of my homeland, from its nature to its food and people. I love my language and Slovenian culture. I cheer passionately for Slovenian athletes. I am also a family man. My four children matter enormously to me. So does my wife. Family values are among the most precious things to me. I value security. I respect and share people’s expectation that the state will properly ensure public order and protection against terrorism and crime—preventively if possible, and with repressive measures if necessary. I believe that a state, however small, needs not only an appropriately trained, equipped and paid police force but also an army. I believe Slovenia must take on its share of responsibility for ensuring stability and peace, not just within its own borders but in the world. During the refugee crisis two years ago, I was worried. I am convinced that uncontrolled crossing of state borders is unacceptable and requires an appropriate and effective response from all competent institutions and authorities. I believe that people cannot be fed on slogans and demagoguery, only on a successful economy. I support measures that encourage creativity, dynamism, development and growth. I believe we must not spend more than we earn. In other words, some of you will say, I am a typical narrow-minded right-wing Slovenian redneck. On the other hand, it is also true that I am often very critical of Slovenia, and especially of Slovenian politics. I am a convinced, if critical, European. I believe in good-neighborly relations. I am worried by the renewed rise of nationalism and the fetishization of national sovereignty. I am open to others and to difference. Multiculturalism is not a swear word for me but a value. I support the rights of same-sex couples. I believe that as a society we are obliged to ensure respect for human dignity and the full enjoyment of rights for all citizens, without discrimination of any kind. I am an ardent advocate of human rights, political freedoms, humanism, openness and solidarity in society. I believe there is no democracy without effective protection of the individual against the arbitrary (mis)use of power by the authorities. I reject the arbitrary, two-faced and economically motivated use of force in international affairs. I am worried by the selective respect for international law. I do not believe in razor wire. I maintain that Slovenia is obliged to help refugees who come to our country, in line with the principles and values protected by the Slovenian Constitution and on the basis of our international legal obligations. I am convinced that this is to the benefit of Slovenia and its citizens. I believe that without social justice there is neither democracy nor freedom. In other words, some of you will say, I am a typical left-wing multi-culti activist. Both descriptions of my values above are authentic and sincere. You may agree or disagree with my views of the world, and there is absolutely nothing wrong with that. One of the attractions of democracy is that it allows us, and even expects us, to do so. But I insist that the first and second views are entirely compatible, that I have not (yet) lost my mind, and that I am not making fun of you either. The labels “Slovenian redneck” and “multi-culti activist” largely reflect an artificially created, but very real, polarization in our society. Out of naivety, opportunism or cynicism, we have walked into the populist trap of black-and-white binary thinking and started believing in a world in which one can live and survive only at the expense and to the detriment of some of the most basic principles and values. In this world, patriotism excludes openness to neighbors and to the world. A true patriot is someone who dislikes other nations. In this world, your culture threatens mine. In this world, love of family is expressed by discriminating against gays and lesbians. In this world, security can be achieved only by restricting human rights and political freedoms and by ignoring international obligations and international law. In this world, a refugee or economic migrant is always a threat, so the issue can be resolved only at the expense of our solidarity and humanity, rationality, economic logic and demographic needs. In this world, you have to be for Trump if you are against Assad. And vice versa. In this world, you can spend only as much as you earn. In it, social justice and social security threaten economic success. The benefit populists gain from false dilemmas is obvious. They create an artificial conflict between the institutions of liberal democracy and values that matter greatly to a large part of the population. Once we manage to convince people that they must choose between their own security and helping refugees, between family values and the rights of the LGBT community, between public order and human rights and freedoms, between love of their homeland and openness to others and to difference, between their own social security and solidarity, the answer is known in advance. To hell with liberal democracy, human rights and humanism; I will look after myself and my own first. The people who think this way are not to blame; the politics that created, enabled and exploits an artificially polarized, black-and-white vision of society and the world is. The solution is not to label people who love their homeland, security and family as narrow-minded yokels, but to stop leaving the interpretation of these values exclusively to populists and their opportunistic imitators. To defeat the populist polarization that threatens democracy and freedom, we need a reconciliation between values. Not so that we all think the same, but so that we realize we can be content, safe and happy, and still be free, and still be human. This reconciliation does not need marble monuments, only politics with ethical principles and moral authority.

Although on May 9, 1865, US President Andrew Johnson declared the victory of the Union forces over the Confederacy, the end of the American Civil War and the abolition of slavery in the United States, Americans went on playing partisans and home guards for quite a few years. Johnson’s predecessor, the Republican Abraham Lincoln, had championed Reconstruction, a process that was meant both to help the impoverished South back on its feet and to give freed slaves, in addition to physical freedom, a modest dose of equality. To Johnson, a Democrat who inherited the White House as vice president after Lincoln’s assassination, even that seemed too much. His intention to put Black Americans in what, in his Democratic opinion, was their rightful place came to nothing after the 1866 elections, when the Radical Republicans won a majority in Congress. They promptly adopted the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, purged Confederate grandees from positions of power and guaranteed Black Americans all political freedoms, including the right to vote and to stand for election. This, of course, did not please the Southern Democrats, the representatives of white plantation owners, who had not only lost their free labor but were also forced to watch their former slaves strutting about under their noses—sometimes in uniform and carrying weapons—and even daring to elect their own representatives to positions of power, from local mayoralties to the US Congress. Those were funny, upside-down times. Republicans championed progressive ideas, Democrats wanted to turn the wheel of history back to the good old slave-owning days, and Black Americans believed the future would bring them freedom, equality and social justice. The American partisans and home guards—pardon, Republicans and Democrats—pardon, opponents and defenders of slavery—were, as one would say in today’s terminology, polarized over these questions for more than a decade. The ones who came off worst in these exchanges of views were above all the newly freed Black people, who in the first years after the war were slaughtered across the American South like rabbits. On Easter Sunday 1873, in the town of Colfax, Louisiana, white plantation owners murdered more than one hundred and fifty Black members of the state militia. It was not a battle but an execution, since most of the victims were killed in captivity after they had already surrendered their weapons. Things were slowly getting out of hand, so Republicans and Democrats agreed on a reconciliation based on the arithmetic mean between their differing views of their recent history. In other words, they met halfway and agreed that from then on Black Americans would be equal, but segregated. This principle, later confirmed by the US Supreme Court in Plessy v. Ferguson, underpinned a system that enabled and maintained racial segregation and the political and economic dominance of white Americans over Americans of other colors. All this lasted almost a century, until the mid-1960s, when the Democrats, now in reversed roles, decided it was time to put the historic reconciliation with the Republicans aside. At President J. F. Kennedy’s initiative, civil rights legislation was adopted that, at least formally, abolished racial discrimination in voting, employment and education. JFK did not live to see the law take effect: the year before, he met the same fate as Abraham Lincoln. The story above is not just an interesting historical detail; it also gives us a code for understanding the present. It can help us answer, for example, the question of why the red baseball cap of the forty-fifth US president reads “Make America Great Again,” why the slogan is so popular with white supremacists and the alt-right, and when exactly, in their view, America was last great. You guessed it: back when everyone still knew and respected who could sit in power, who at the trough and who at the back of the bus. Trump’s cap is an excellent example of what Timothy Snyder, in his new book The Road to Unfreedom, calls the politics of eternity. Instead of a future, this politics offers a cyclical repetition of history in which the nation, or part of it, is always the victim. Time is no longer a line leading us into the future but a circle that keeps bringing us back to mythologized “injustices” of the past. Donald’s cap does not promise Americans that America will ever be great again; above all, it reminds them that for the (light-skinned) part of Americans, that greatness is gone. This politics offers neither progress nor hope, only defense against enemies lurking on all sides. We, too, have politicians who swear by eternity. Like the Confederate grandees and cotton plantation owners of old, and their modern alt-patriotic soulmates today, our politicians of eternity are trying to change the outcome of a war they lost. They do this not because they want to leave the past behind in a spirit of reconciliation, but solely to change the present by reinterpreting history, and, in the spirit of ideas that were defeated once already, to seize power and rearrange it to their liking. If they want to wear baseball caps decorated with slogans while doing so, I offer them a translation adapted to our circumstances: Make this country great again for me.

In February 1921, Vienna saw the premiere of Dracula’s Death, a horror film shot in Hungary. Although the film, directed by Károly Lajthay, was quite popular across Central Europe, every copy has since been lost, leaving only a few yellowed promotional photographs. A year after its premiere, this first screen adaptation of Stoker’s Dracula was completely overshadowed by the success of the German film Nosferatu, a shameless but brilliant plagiarism of Stoker’s story, with the remarkable Max Schreck as Count Orlok. To avoid paying royalties, the Germans simply changed the name of the villain from the original and the Hungarian version. Almost a century later, plagiarized Hungarian productions designed to spread fear are coming our way again. A good example is a poster that the Slovenian National Party (SNS) published on its website. Although the post is apparently not new, in the run-up to the elections the poster has once again attracted attention. The black-and-white image shows the silhouette of a clawed phantom, with the words “No migrants” in bold letters across it. If I wanted to be undeservedly generous to the SNS, I would say it is merely stating the obvious: the figure in the picture is not a migrant, it is Count Orlok. Opinions on his manners may differ, but he was a native Transylvanian. Unfortunately, it is more likely that this is not a mischievous prank but a serious political message. The SNS is telling us that if they win, they will defend the Slovenian nation against migrants. Because migrants are repulsive, have claws and drink our blood. Migrants—the term the SNS, along with most of Slovenian politics and media, uses for all people on the run, regardless of what they are fleeing—are therefore vampires. They are not like the good-natured barber who cuts Ljubljana residents’ hair for free in the Rog squat, nor like five-year-old Alan Kurdi, who drowned and whose body the sea washed up on the Turkish coast near Bodrum in September 2015. For the SNS, migrants are not people but monsters. Although the SNS claims it is a provocation, it is much more than that. It is hatred. It is evil. A symphony of horror, as the subtitle of the Nosferatu film that so inspired the SNS propagandists put it. Dehumanizing people is not a provocation. In history, it has often been the prelude to crime. Among the examples we have recently adopted from Hungary is the relentless witch-hunt against George Soros, the American billionaire of Hungarian-Jewish origin who, alongside migrants, was the main target of our neighbors’ recent election campaign. The story of the wicked rich Jew was evidently effective, so it quickly found imitators here too. One Slovenian media outlet recently published an article about the “frightening links” between Soros and some Slovenian members of the European Parliament. Among Soros’s cardinal sins, besides the “systematic suppression of the right” and the “deliberate destabilization of Europe,” this outlet also lists efforts “to prevent violence against migrants” on the US–Mexico border. Whether Slovenian MEPs work with Soros, I do not know, but I confess that I have worked with him myself in the past. Years ago, we met in his office in a Park Avenue skyscraper in New York, with a wonderful view of Central Park. We discussed cooperation on Roma integration, which has long been one of the priorities of Soros’s Open Society Foundations. One of the results is the European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture, based in Berlin, which started work a little less than a year ago with the support of Open Society, the Council of Europe and the German government. I do not remember anyone mentioning the suppression of the right or the destabilization of Europe during our conversation in New York—unless, of course, these terms also cover efforts to achieve the social and cultural emancipation and integration of Roma into European society. Nor was there any talk of preventing violence against migrants, although, to be fair, it is not entirely impossible that Soros does in fact disapprove of violence against people, even if they are migrants. At the end, the article reveals that Soros does not act alone: he is part of a conspiracy that also involves Ronald Lauder, the owner, if I understand correctly, of POP TV and Kanal A, as well as a “political activist” and “president of the World Jewish Congress.” So once again we are dealing with an international conspiracy of rich Jews plotting against honest ordinary people. If this reminds you of something, you are absolutely right. For populists, Soros offers a propaganda hat-trick. First, he is a tool for discrediting civil society, an important democratic safeguard and a thorn in populists’ increasingly jackbooted heels. Second, he makes it possible to surf on the waves of latent antisemitism, which, despite Europe’s horrific historical experience, has evidently not yet had its last word. Finally, Soros has been saddled with an entirely fabricated accusation of deliberately Islamizing Europe. This last one is particularly stupid, but no less effective or dangerous for that. The increasingly aggressive discourse, based on stoking hatred and fear, on lies and on poorly disguised antisemitism, should worry everyone, but especially the parties on the right of the political spectrum. The trap that populism sets for them is to present the institutions and values on which post-war (above all Christian) democracy built European stability and peace as a political conspiracy of the left against the right. If the heirs of Schuman, De Gasperi and Adenauer accept that their political project be equated with an increasingly ruthless populist attack on the democratic institutions of the European political and social model, with nationalism, chauvinism and scaremongering about Jewish conspiracies, then of course there is no helping them. What is incomprehensible is why so many of them accept the destruction of their own reputation, historical achievements and political future, or even take part in it, without clearly distancing themselves from it and condemning it. In one of my earlier columns, I wrote that the words of the Slovenian national anthem read as if they had been written by some Soros scholarship holder. I am beginning to wonder whether I made a mistake. In our country, those who consider themselves patriots are people who claim to love the state but evidently do not understand, or do not want to understand, the message of its symbols, nor the values on which Slovenia built and won its independence. Once they have finished with Soros, they may well turn on Prešeren.

Le 2 novembre 1995, j'étais assis dans un bureau au 6ème étage du Palais de l'Europe. C'était mon premier jour au Conseil de l'Europe et je fixais le clavier devant moi. Chaque touche était marquée d'une tache brune. J'étais perdue dans mes pensées, nerveusement excitée, essayant de comprendre ce qu'il fallait faire, par où commencer et ce que l'on attendait de moi. Et si j'étais à la hauteur des attentes. Et pourquoi le clavier était sale. Et surtout, comment diable en étais-je arrivé là ? Il ne m'a pas fallu longtemps pour résoudre le mystère du clavier. Il s'est avéré que le précédent occupant du bureau, Hans, était un jardinier passionné - une passion qui m'était aussi étrangère que la plupart des autres choses au cours de ces premiers jours de novembre à Strasbourg. Quant à savoir comment je suis arrivé là, je n'en suis toujours pas sûr. Mais si je devais retenir une date qui a compté dans ce voyage, le 4 mai 1980 figurerait certainement sur la courte liste. Ce jour-là, à 15h05, le président de la République socialiste fédérative de Yougoslavie, Josip Broz Tito, est mort sur son lit d'hôpital à Ljubljana, à deux pas de la maison de mon enfance. Le nombre de personnes endeuillées était beaucoup plus important qu'on ne veut bien l'admettre aujourd'hui, et tout le monde était inquiet. Il n'y avait aucun signe de l'implosion et du bain de sang qui ont suivi une décennie plus tard, mais le pays avait déjà commencé à changer, à pâlir et à se rider, comme un légume laissé trop longtemps dans un réfrigérateur Cette année-là, les Jeux olympiques d'été se tiennent à Moscou, et le Pacte de Varsovie remporte bien plus de médailles que l'OTAN, notamment parce que l'Occident est resté à l'écart pour protester contre l'invasion de l'Afghanistan par l'Union soviétique. « Mad Max et American Gigolo venaient de sortir au cinéma, même en Yougoslavie, et Ashes to Ashes de David Bowie nous a sauvé la vie, nous qui ne pouvions pas supporter Abba. J'avais quinze ans, j'étais amoureux et je n'étais donc que modérément conscient ou affecté par les événements qui se déroulaient. Enfin, à part Mad Max et Bowie. Et le procès du premier véritable tueur en série de Slovénie. Metod Trobec était un ancien cheminot, alcoolique et criminel professionnel, arrêté deux ans plus tôt après qu'un touriste allemand, que Trobec a tenté de voler, a noté le numéro d'immatriculation de sa voiture. Lorsque la milice populaire - comme on appelait la police à l'époque - est arrivée dans sa ferme isolée près de Ljubljana, elle a découvert les cadavres de cinq femmes. Elles ont toutes été étranglées par Trobec et brûlées dans le four à pain. Il a par la suite admis avoir commis un sixième meurtre. Lors du procès, Trobec a été condamné à mort. Si la sentence avait été exécutée, il aurait été la première personne exécutée en Slovénie après 1957. Mais ce qui s'est passé, c'est une très forte réaction de l'opinion publique. Il ne s'agissait pas de sympathie pour Trobec, qui était un être humain exceptionnellement antipathique, mais d'une protestation contre la peine de mort en tant que telle. Je me souviens des discussions interminables avec mes amis, des questions que nous posions aux enseignants pour leur demander pourquoi l'État devrait avoir le droit de mettre fin à une vie humaine. Nous avons tous grandi avec des histoires et des images de résistants exécutés par des pelotons d'exécution nazis. Certes, Trobec n'était pas un résistant ; c'était un être humain méprisable. Mais il s'agissait tout de même d'un être humain, et je me sentais mal. J'ai écrit un article pour le journal de l'école qui remettait en question le fait que quelqu'un soit considéré comme suffisamment fou pour recevoir des électrochocs, mais suffisamment sain d'esprit pour être exécuté. Mes parents ont été convoqués chez le directeur, car même dans la Yougoslavie relativement libérale, il y avait une réticence persistante à accepter la critique des autorités, en particulier de la part des adolescents. Plus tard, mon article a été reproduit dans le journal étudiant national et la Cour suprême a remplacé la peine de mort par une peine d'emprisonnement maximale de 20 ans. Ceci étant dit, même si je le souhaite, je ne peux apporter aucune preuve convaincante que ces deux événements sont liés. En 1989, le Parlement slovène a aboli la peine de mort - qui est néanmoins restée théoriquement applicable en vertu du code pénal fédéral yougoslave jusqu'à l'indépendance, deux ans plus tard, lorsque l'abolition a été inscrite dans la nouvelle Constitution. L'article 17 de cette dernière stipule que « la peine capitale n'existe pas en Slovénie ». À ce moment-là, en raison de cette disposition et d'autres engagements en faveur des droits de l'homme et des libertés fondamentales, je me suis sentie très fière d'être slovène. Pour moi, l'indépendance était avant tout un jalon civilisationnel. Mais je m'avance un peu. Bien d'autres choses se sont produites avant ce mois de juin 1991. Les Jeux olympiques d'hiver de Sarajevo en 1984, par exemple. Ce moment où le monde entier est tombé amoureux de la belle ville sur la rivière Miljacka et de ses merveilleux habitants. Nous espérions tous que les souvenirs tragiques et amers de l'intrusion antérieure de Sarajevo dans l'histoire mondiale seraient à jamais remplacés par des images d'un Sarajevo plus heureux, de l'amitié, de l'hospitalité et de l'esprit bosniaques. Nous étions loin de nous en douter. En 1984, Ronald Reagan a été réélu haut la main, Youri Andropov est mort et « Wham » a dominé les charts britanniques avec « Freedom ». C'est aussi l'année où la campagne pour les libertés civiques et les droits de l'homme a commencé sérieusement dans mon pays. La Yougoslavie n'était pas le pire des régimes totalitaires. À certains égards, elle ressemblait à une prison en Norvège ou en Suède. Des paysages magnifiques, sans serrures ni tours de garde, des gens souriants qui allaient et venaient presque à leur guise. Mais même la prison la plus libérale reste une prison. Et face à tout ce qui pouvait sérieusement remettre en cause sa mainmise sur le pouvoir, le régime a réagi d'une manière typiquement non scandinave. Il s'est déchaîné comme un serpent, sans pitié ni remords. En 1984, ce défi est venu de Slovénie. Il est venu du mouvement pacifiste qui a défié l'influence et le pouvoir omniprésents de l'Armée populaire yougoslave, des mouvements de jeunesse qui ont ouvertement remis en question l'idéologie de leurs mentors et de la communauté LGBT. Pour les homosexuels, la vie dans une société communiste était dure. Ils étaient considérés comme déviants et la plupart d'entre eux avaient pris soin de ne pas révéler - et encore moins de vivre - leur identité en public. Je n'ai donc pas connu beaucoup d'homosexuels, mais j'en ai connu beaucoup qui les détestaient. Les homophobes d'aujourd'hui ont appris à haïr depuis hier. Ils ont peut-être changé de couleur et d'idéologie, mais pas l'intensité et la méchanceté de leur bigoterie. Et puis, un jour, les homosexuels slovènes ont décidé de ne plus se cacher. Ils ont défendu leur liberté et leur dignité, et la mienne. J'ai admiré leur courage et j'ai espéré leur succès. En 1984, le centre culturel pour étudiants ŠKUC a fondé MAGNUS en tant qu'organisation culturelle pour la socialisation de l'homosexualité. Il s'agissait d'une étape clé dans le début d'un profond changement social et politique. Les premières réactions ont été négatives, mais relativement discrètes. Jusqu'à ce que les nationalistes naissants d'autres régions du pays se déchaînent. Leur réaction contre « les pédés de Ljubljana » débordait de haine au vitriol. Aujourd'hui encore, je pense que la plupart des habitants des autres régions de la Yougoslavie, quel que soit le malaise qu'ils aient pu ressentir à l'égard des homosexuels, ne partageaient pas cette haine. Mais ils sont restés passifs et ont gardé le silence. Et c'est la leçon que j'ai tirée de la diatribe homophobe qui est restée sans réponse - on ne peut pas plaider l'ignorance quand on est confronté à la haine. Si vous ne vous élevez pas contre elle, vous serez complice de son éventuel triomphe. Aujourd'hui, les attitudes homophobes n'arrivent plus en Slovénie de l'étranger, mais elles sont bien ancrées dans le pays, et cette injustice est honteuse. Tant que la discrimination, le manque de respect et l'inégalité persisteront, mon pays aura une dette morale envers nombre de nos concitoyens qui ont tant fait pour son indépendance et sa liberté. Nous leur devons non seulement le respect, mais aussi la gratitude. Mais une fois de plus, j'ai laissé mon doigt trop longtemps sur l'avance rapide. Retour à l'été de ma dix-neuvième année. Le moment est venu de servir dans l'armée populaire yougoslave. Nous étions en 1984, et je me suis retrouvé dans un reality show de George Orwell. En juillet, je buvais de la bière dans les repaires d'étudiants du Quartier Latin à Paris, échouant lamentablement à draguer les demoiselles, à compter mes centimes, à sauter des repas et à me sentir comme la personne la plus riche et la plus chanceuse du monde. En août, je creusais un trou pour installer un camion-citerne et je mettais en place des douches de campagne. Bienvenue dans la guerre anti biologique, chimique et nucléaire, à la mode de l’armée yougoslave. Si vous êtes touché par une bombe sale, vous prenez une longue douche chaude. Et vous utilisez un shampoing antinucléaire pour éviter que vos pellicules ne scintillent dans l'obscurité longtemps après qu'on vous a réduit en miettes et que vous n'existez plus. Ce qui m'a le plus choqué, ce n'était pas l'absurdité de la situation. Il y a, après tout, un parfum d'innocence romantique dans l'idée que l'on peut se protéger d'une bombe atomique en prenant une douche. Ce qui m'a vraiment frappé, c'est l'implacable croisade idéologique qui propageait et manipulait les préjugés et la paranoïa. C'était intelligent, calculé et efficace. Chaque soir, nous regardions d'abord les informations, puis nous écoutions les mêmes informations qui nous étaient expliquées. Le message était toujours le même : nous contre eux. Le peuple contre les traîtres internes. Le peuple contre les ennemis extérieurs. Ne pensez pas, haïssez. Obéissez ou trahissez. Dans cette salle de télévision bondée, sentant les jeunes hommes qui ont construit de nombreuses douches mais qui ont rarement eu l'occasion de les utiliser, j'ai découvert le pouvoir du populisme. Cela m'a dégoûté et effrayé. C'est encore le cas aujourd'hui. J'ai survécu à l'armée sans trop de dommages durables pour ma santé mentale. J'ai passé les années suivantes à me concentrer principalement sur mes études (et quelques autres choses qu'il n'est peut-être pas nécessaire de mentionner ici, ni ailleurs d'ailleurs) à Ljubljana et à l'étranger. En juin 1991, je suis sorti de mes études supérieures en Belgique, prêt à affronter le monde. Cette année-là, le groupe culte de Belgrade Ekaterina Velika a sorti son album « Dum Dum » (Bang Bang) avec de sombres prémonitions d'horreurs sur le point d'être déclenchées. Le 24 juin 1991, le championnat d'Europe de basket-ball a débuté en Italie. Deux jours plus tard, la Slovénie et la Croatie déclarent leur indépendance. Le 29 juin, Dino Radja marque vingt-trois points lors du dernier match contre l'Italie, apportant à l'équipe yougoslave de basket-ball son cinquième et définitivement dernier titre européen. Il s'agit probablement de la seule compétition sportive de l'histoire remportée par une équipe d'un pays qui, à toutes fins utiles, n'existe plus. Et vous savez quoi, nous avons toujours soutenu cette équipe. Mais c'est une autre histoire. En juin 1991, la désintégration de la Yougoslavie est passée à la vitesse supérieure. Le vendredi, il y avait une fête. Le samedi, nous nous sommes réveillés en guerre. À l'âge de vingt-six ans, j'ai vu mon pays s'effondrer et se désintégrer dans la violence. Même sans connaître les horreurs bien pires qui allaient encore frapper d'autres régions de mon ancien pays, et aujourd’hui, d’autres pays en Europe et dans le monde, j'étais inquiet. Le nationalisme est une bête séduisante et méchante qui se nourrit de sa propre adrénaline et apporte douleur et destruction à ceux qui sont haïs et à ceux qui haïssent. Un jour après cette légendaire finale de basket-ball au Palazzeto dello sport de Rome, par un bel après-midi de début d'été, je me trouvais à un poste-frontière près de Trieste. Du côté italien, des baigneurs bronzaient en sirotant leur apéritif, tandis qu'à quelques mètres de là, des policiers slovènes et des conscrits désorientés de l'armée qui n'était plus du tout yougoslave et qui n'était plus l'armée du peuple, étaient engagés dans une grotesque confrontation armée. Deux pensées me sont venues à l'esprit à ce moment-là avec une clarté alarmante : la première était que la frontière entre la paix et le chaos total est extrêmement mince et fragile. La seconde était que la guerre n'arrive pas toujours qu'aux autres. J'ai pensé que je ferais quelque chose à ce sujet. Je ne pensais pas pouvoir changer le monde à moi tout seul, mais je pouvais peut-être au moins essayer de faire ma part pour l'empêcher de devenir complètement fou. C'est ce qui m'a amené au bureau du Palais. Presque trente ans plus tard, j'ai repris le jardinage. Mais je me suis acheté un clavier noir. Dans l'ensemble, ce voyage a été fantastique (jusqu'à présent) et je me sens privilégié d'être à bord. Quand j'étais jeune, j'ai vécu dans un pays où la liberté était rationnée et j'ai appris à ne pas la considérer comme acquise. J'ai grandi dans un pays où tout le monde croyait que la paix durerait toujours. Cela n'a pas été le cas. J'ai vu à quelle vitesse la peur et l'ignorance peuvent se transformer en haine, et à quel point elles constituent un terrain fertile pour ceux qui souhaitent régner en colportant des préjugés et en semant la division. C'est pourquoi je crois au Conseil de l'Europe, à la Convention européenne des droits de l'homme, au type de société que ces deux institutions ont contribué à construire et qu'elles aident à protéger. Il ne s'agit pas d'un passe-temps noble et idéaliste. C'est notre ligne de défense centrale contre la folie et la destruction nationalistes. Je parle en connaissance de cause. Cette expérience traumatique et douloureuse m'a aidé et m'a motivé dans mon travail. Ces derniers temps, elle me rend également inquiet. Je regarde autour de moi, et le monde semble devenir toute pâle et toute ridée.
Les six cercles de l'enfer de Nace

Pančevo, Novi Sad, Grgur, Ugljan, Bileća, Povšetova - six cercles d'enfer pour le journaliste, alors âgée de vingt-deux ans, jeune communiste, qui croyait au paradis d'une société plus juste. Quelques jours avant qu’il devrait enlever sa veste militaire et remplacer son fusil par le plume, pour contribuer à la création d’un système dans lequel la vie sera meilleure pour tout le monde, les bourreaux remplie d’un patriotisme bestial, agissant au service de planificateurs de ce meilleur avenir, lui ont éteint la lumière du soleil et l’ont laissé dans une nuit de près de mille jours. Avec des méthodes dans lesquelles l'esclavage ancien et le nazisme moderne, assaisonnés de primitivisme balkanique, étaient fatalement liés, Nace et des milliers d'autres ont fait partie du même quota des ennemis de l'État, fixée d'en haut. Leurs corps et leurs âmes ont été systématiquement tués, de sorte qu’avant leur destin final, il ne restait qu’une statistique sans larmes. Et lorsque les derniers atomes d'espoir se sont éteints pour le numéro 3017, au-delà des ténèbres sans fin, seul un rayon a brillé, qui a lentement, trop lentement pour la personne affectée, rendu à la fois l'espoir, l'âme et le corps, et a finalement allumé la lumière du matin de la naissance d'une nouvelle vie. Pendant quatre décennies, Nace n’a jamais parlé de son enfer, ni en public, ni en privé Pas seulement parce qu'il n’avait pas le droit de le faire. Même s'il le pouvait, il ne le ferait pas. Il a essayé de se convaincre qu'il ne s'agissait que d'un détour marginal dans la réalisation d'un grand projet, et parce qu'il espérait qu'en oubliant son Moyen Age, il vivrait plus facilement le Nouveau. Même ses amis ne l'ont jamais interrogé, même s'il n'a pas pu nous cacher que la formation cancéreuse de la mémoire, poussée dans le subconscient, lui fait mal et qu'un jour il devra recourir à une auto-intervention chirurgicale. Et en effet, avec ce livre qui est devant vous, ce qui s'est produit - au grand soulagement de mon ami Nace, et de nous tous qui l'avons et allons le lire, ce sera comme une heure d'histoire terrible qui ne devrait jamais être répété à nouveau. Pourtant ça se répète ! La terrible guerre en Bosnie n’est qu’une autre version de ce mal que Nace a vécu ! Cet œuvre littéraire et un dernier reportage autobiographique, exprimée en monologues poignants et en évasions oniriques vers le monde qui lui a été si violement arraché. Igor Gruden, journaliste
Young People, Democracy and Climate Action

A very warm welcome to all of you at the Council of Europe Youth Center here in Strasbourg. I’d also like to extend a heartfelt greeting to those who are very much at home here but still deserve a special welcome: Nina Grmusa, Chair of the Advisory Council on Youth, George Orlando, Chair of the Joint Council on Youth, our colleagues from the EU Council of Youth Partnership, and the dedicated team from the European Youth Center and the youth sector in Strasbourg. I hope I haven’t missed anyone—if I have, please accept my apologies. It’s truly fascinating when you reflect on the major global issues we face today. These challenges need not be global in scope, but they are undeniably large, critical, and often threatening. And, time and time again, young people are at the heart of it all. It’s as if you are always directly involved, no matter the issue at hand. Whether it’s unemployment, economic crises, mental health struggles, or climate change, young people bear the brunt of it all. Unemployment rates rise, and who fills the unemployment offices? Young people. Mental health crises grow, and who suffers disproportionately? Young people. The climate crisis, which is shaping our future, is one that will have far-reaching consequences for today’s youth, who will live with its impacts long after many of us in this room have passed on. I apologize for the bluntness, but I think it’s appropriate given the urgency of the situation—things are escalating. The "shit is really starting to hit the fan," so to speak. And alongside this environmental crisis, we are witnessing democratic backsliding, which is also intensifying day by day. It’s a worrying trend, affecting not only democratic institutions but also the ability for civil society—especially youth organizations—to voice concerns and bring forward solutions. These two crises, the climate crisis and democratic backsliding, are deeply interconnected. The consequences of the climate crisis, which we feel more acutely each day, often lead to heightened anxiety and fear. This fear, in turn, can transform into negative emotions like intolerance and hatred. These emotions are being manipulated by those who seek to undermine democracy, often using these fears to advance alternative political agendas. And, in turn, these alternative political forces are blocking meaningful actions to address climate change. This is the vicious circle we find ourselves in—democratic decline and the climate crisis feeding off each other, spiraling ever faster. And, as always, it’s young people who are in the middle of this storm, facing a shrinking space to voice their concerns, protest inaction, or propose solutions. That’s exactly why you’re here today—to explore the connection between the climate crisis and democracy. This link hasn’t always been clear, especially within the Council of Europe. When it was founded 70 years ago, the organization’s mission was focused on defending democracy, human rights, and the rule of law. Although it began working on environmental issues early on, including biodiversity protection, for many years the connection between environmental crises and democracy was not widely recognized. However, things have started to shift, particularly in recent years, as the reality of these crises becomes more evident. In many ways, young people have driven this change, raising awareness and demanding action on both climate change and democratic backsliding. You, the young leaders within the Council of Europe, have been at the forefront of this movement, calling attention to these issues and pushing for solutions. Thanks to your advocacy, we’re starting to see concrete action, particularly in the last two to three years. In 2022, the Committee of Ministers recognized that humanity’s well-being is dependent on our ability to safeguard human rights and ensure a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment for future generations. All Council of Europe member states supported the UN General Assembly Resolution of 2022, which declared the human right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment. Although some countries may still struggle to fully implement this right, the resolution marks a significant step forward. The Reykjavik Declaration, issued a year and a half ago, underscored the urgent need to protect the environment and address the triple planetary crisis—pollution, climate change, and biodiversity loss—highlighting their impact on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Since then, the Joint Council on Youth has been working on a recommendation to address these issues. At its 50th meeting in Budapest last year, the Committee agreed on a draft recommendation on "Young People and Climate Action," which will be discussed this afternoon by the Committee of Ministers' Rapporteur Group on Education, Culture, Sport, Youth, and Environment. This is a pivotal moment, and I apologize that some of us will need to leave shortly to present and perhaps defend the recommendation. I promise I will return—if not today, then tomorrow—because this is an extremely important symposium. Incidentally, the same day the Joint Council on Youth made its decision was the same day the European Court of Human Rights issued a landmark ruling in the case of Vereine Klimasenior in Schweiz and Others vs. Switzerland. While this ruling, especially in Switzerland, has garnered significant attention, it marks a crucial step forward in recognizing the legal implications of climate change. The Court found violations of the right to respect for private and family life (Article 8) and the right of access to the courts (Article 6) under the European Convention on Human Rights. Climate activism today is not just about raising awareness; it is increasingly about combining social movements with targeted legal action. Young climate defenders are now looking to the law to claim their rights, whether through civil disobedience, direct action, or strategic litigation, as they hold states accountable for their failure to uphold human rights obligations related to climate justice. However, this advocacy often comes at a cost. We are seeing a rise in the criminalization and repression of young climate activists and human rights defenders, with many being arrested or prosecuted for their activism. This is yet another example of how the climate crisis and democratic backsliding are intertwined. As we look to the future, young people are calling for a shift from mere climate change mitigation to broader climate justice. They are demanding that we recognize the differentiated impact of climate change on vulnerable communities, including marginalized groups and youth in rural or remote areas. Anxiety about the future is also on the rise, particularly eco-anxiety, as young people’s mental health and well-being are increasingly affected by these crises. Understanding and addressing these concerns is vital as we move forward. This symposium was organized with the intention of contributing to our collective efforts on these pressing issues. Your discussions and recommendations will play a crucial role in shaping the future of the Council of Europe’s work on the environment, climate change, and youth. Moreover, the outcomes of your work will also inform the newly established ad-hoc multidisciplinary group on the environment, which is preparing a draft Council of Europe strategy on the environment—a significant shift in acknowledging the importance of environmental issues for democracy. With this symposium, the European Commission and the Council of Europe continue our long-standing collaboration, making an important contribution to our shared goals of youth empowerment and environmental protection. As I conclude, I want to emphasize the connection between the climate crisis and democratic backsliding. As we face growing environmental challenges, we must not ignore the anxiety, uncertainty, and fear these crises evoke. These emotions are being exploited, turning into intolerance and hatred, which threatens to destabilize our democracies. The way forward is not to deny these challenges or to say there’s nothing to worry about. We have real reasons to be concerned, but the answer is to find effective solutions to both the environmental crisis and the crisis of democracy. We must act to mitigate climate change, and, just as importantly, to protect and strengthen our democracies. That’s why you’re here today—working toward saving our democracies and our environment. It’s no small task, but it’s one we must undertake, because the alternatives are too dire to ignore. Thank you very much.
Launch of the 4th European Youth Work Convention

Thank you. Thank you very much, Miriam, dear Parliamentary Secretary, Nina Emusha, colleagues and friends. First of all, I'd like to extend really our gratitude to the Maltese authorities, Minister of Education and Youth Research and Support, for this important support in organizing not only one, but two important, very, very important events in the next months during the forthcoming presidency of Malta to the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. The first, the one we'll be talking today, the fourth convention, European Youth Work Convention, which we are organizing together with the European Union every five years. And the second one following, in October, the Conference of Specialist Ministers of Youth of all the Council of Member States, which will also take place here in Malta, and about which I've discussed with the Minister of Education this morning. To put these two events into a context, and I cannot help myself because being in a place like this, in a country like this, in a city like Malta, and in a building like this one, where history is oozing from every stone and every corner, really, the Council of Europe celebrated 75th anniversary last year. I mention it because you have to imagine the time when it was created, 1949, only four years after that devastating, horrible conflict. And it was created as a reaction, of course, to that conflict, what happened, but also to the period before, marked by social turmoil, economic difficulties, people's uncertainty and fear about future, frustration about the politics and the political parties, and especially intentional, deliberate orchestration and manipulation of hatred for political purposes, which all led to that unprecedented descent into inhumanity that has caused the Holocaust, millions of dead people, and so much devastation. So, four years after, the Council of Europe was created as a response, as a response to make sure something like this doesn't happen again. And that response was based on democracy, on human rights, on the rule of law, on the European Convention of Human Rights, which followed just a year later. And just four years later, with the European Cultural Convention, we've had the basis to create an environment in which that new Europe would be able to function. And an important part of that environment was work with young people, to create the necessary fabric, which is necessary for our democracies to be resilient, to be functional, to be resistant. That fabric that is built with the values of solidarity, cooperation, empathy, inclusion, non-discrimination. Why I'm mentioning all this is because we are living today in times which are echoing some of those experiences from the past. And I think we have to take a lesson and find a way to bring that same response even more forcefully, even more effectively today. And if you want to repair that fabric based on those values, I think working again with young people is essential. And the fourth European Youth Work Conference is an ideal place to make that executive, because it's through youth work that young people are participating, engaging, contributing, working with other young people, but contributing to the broader society, practicing those very values that I have mentioned, solidarity, inclusion, non-discrimination, openness, dialogue, in all the different spheres that the youth work represents, all its richness and diversity. So we have great expectations from this event in May. Not just because it's going to bring significant results for the specific objective of supporting, finding additional ways to support and reinforce the conditions for youth work in Europe, but even more so because of its enormous significance for the protection of our democracies in our world today, in our Europe today. Thank you very much.

Question : Vous voyez, nous avons eu une vue d'ensemble des défis auxquels l'Europe fait face. En observant les élections en Allemagne, nous avons constaté que les jeunes sont également fortement attirés par l'extrême droite. Comment peut-on lutter contre cela ? Merci beaucoup, Fernanda. Merci beaucoup pour l'invitation. Je suis un peu embarrassé d'intervenir ce soir pour plusieurs raisons. D'abord, à cause de mon français, car vous allez vite vous rendre compte que ce n'est pas ma première langue, et même pas ma deuxième. – Mais tu parles très bien français. Non, non, non, attendez un peu. Et surtout, je suis embarrassé d'intervenir à côté de deux personnes qui, à mon avis, savent beaucoup plus que moi sur le sujet de ce soir : professeur de droit, professeur d'histoire, expert des sciences politiques, expert de l'Allemagne... mon ami Ulrich, qui possède bien plus de sagesse et d'expérience que moi. En plus, il est allemand. Je vais peut-être parler un peu moins de l'Allemagne, bien que tu aies posé une question dans cette direction. D'abord, pour expliquer mon titre : directeur pour la démocratie. Je trouve ce titre un peu prétentieux, mais il mérite quelques explications. En effet, il reflète une nouvelle approche au Conseil de l'Europe concernant le travail sur les questions de démocratie. Nous avons réalisé qu'avec les institutions démocratiques, que nous avons construites et défendues - ce qui est essentiel - nous avons quelque peu négligé un point fondamental : ces institutions ne fonctionnent pas dans le vide. Elles ont besoin d'un environnement, de citoyens motivés, compétents, ayant confiance en leurs institutions et en leur capacité à s'engager dans le fonctionnement de la démocratie. Là, cela ne fonctionne pas. Cela ne marche pas depuis longtemps. Je pense qu'il est positif que nous commencions enfin à parler de résilience démocratique. C'est une bonne chose, mais un peu tard. Bien sûr, ce n'est pas trop tard, mais c'est tout de même tard. Il y a quelques années, personne n'en parlait, car nous étions tous convaincus que la démocratie était une valeur acquise, partagée par tous, et que, quoi qu'il arrive, elle resterait intacte. Aujourd'hui, nous parlons de résilience démocratique. Mais ce qui est problématique, et je vais répondre à ta question sur les jeunes, c'est qu'on est encore dans une phase où on grattouille à peine la surface. On aborde les problèmes de manière confortable, comme si c'était un malentendu, un accident technique, une phase transitoire, qu'on se réveille demain et tout sera redevenu normal. Nous ne sommes toujours pas prêts à réfléchir profondément, à reconnaître et à agir sur les causes structurelles qui nous ont menés à cette situation. On parle beaucoup des réseaux sociaux, de l'intelligence artificielle, de la désinformation. C'est nécessaire, car ce sont des outils utilisés pour fragiliser nos démocraties. Mais les causes profondes remontent à bien avant l'avènement d'Internet, aux changements économiques, politiques et sociaux des années 80-90. Nous n'avons pas encore atteint cette phase de réflexion. La désinformation, bien sûr, est un enjeu important, mais elle reste une réponse confortable : elle nous permet de dire que la menace vient de l'extérieur, que c'est un « grand méchant » venu manipuler nos citoyens et les détourner de la démocratie. C'est vrai, mais c'est aussi une vision partielle de la réalité. Il faut aussi aborder la demande de désinformation, des mensonges, et la manipulation de l'histoire, un phénomène très présent. Beaucoup de gens cherchent activement ces informations parce qu'elles confortent leurs convictions et leurs émotions. Nous devons aussi chercher des solutions à ce phénomène. Il ne suffit pas de dire qu'on va forcer les gens à aimer à nouveau la démocratie grâce à la vérification des faits. Ce n'est pas suffisant. Il faudra comprendre pourquoi tant de gens ont perdu confiance dans la démocratie et les institutions. Tu m'as posé des questions sur les jeunes. À mon avis, il y a trois grands groupes concernés, bien que ce ne soit pas exhaustif. Il y a ce qu'on appelait en Yougoslavie la classe ouvrière, qui aujourd'hui représente une part importante de ceux qui soutiennent l'extrême droite, pas seulement en Allemagne, mais aussi ailleurs. Il y a une situation spécifique à l'Europe de l'Est, mais l'Occident, avec sa longue tradition démocratique, ne l'a pas non plus protégée de cette menace. Les contextes sont différents, mais les résultats similaires. Il y a aussi les jeunes. Autrefois, les jeunes étaient traditionnellement parmi les plus progressistes, les plus ouverts. Et il en reste encore beaucoup. Il faut éviter de généraliser. Mais ce que l'on observe aujourd'hui chez les jeunes, c'est un déclin marqué du soutien au centre démocratique, et c'est, à mon avis, la tendance la plus préoccupante. On a vu ce qui s'est passé, mais je tiens à souligner qu'il ne faut pas réduire la discussion à l'extrême droite. Il faut aussi parler des extrêmes à gauche. Il existe aussi une gauche en Europe qui est socialement conservatrice, nationaliste, prorusse, eurosceptique et qui séduit une part de la population, en Allemagne comme ailleurs. Les jeunes, donc. En Allemagne, aux États-Unis, ou encore au Royaume-Uni, une étude a révélé qu'environ 52% des jeunes de la génération Z préféraient une dictature à une démocratie. Cette tendance n'est pas isolée, bien que des doutes puissent subsister sur la méthodologie de cette étude. Quoi qu'il en soit, nous sommes tous choqués, préoccupés, et nous condamnons à juste titre ce phénomène. Mais il est crucial de se poser la question : pourquoi ? Comment en sommes-nous arrivés là ? Pourquoi avons-nous perdu les jeunes pour la démocratie ? Si l'on se place du point de vue des jeunes de 17, 20 ou 25 ans, qu'ont-ils vécu ? Cette génération a grandi dans un contexte de crises successives : la crise financière, la guerre en Ukraine, la pandémie de Covid-19, les préoccupations sécuritaires, les enjeux environnementaux. Cette génération n'a connu que des incertitudes. Et l'incertitude, la peur, détruisent la confiance dans l'avenir, et sans cette confiance, la démocratie est en difficulté. Elle devient manipulable, et c'est ce que nous observons aujourd'hui. Il est donc primordial de comprendre que la réponse ne peut pas se limiter à la vérification des faits ou à la lutte contre la désinformation. Après tout ce qu'ils ont vécu, ces jeunes ont le droit de s'exprimer politiquement. Et parfois, cela se traduit par un rejet de la démocratie, une forme de révolte, de protestation. Ils se disent : « Nous avons vécu dans la démocratie toute notre vie, et voilà ce qu'elle nous a apporté ». C'est là la difficulté. Mais je ne crois pas que ces jeunes soient perdus pour la cause démocratique. Nous devons aller au-delà de la vérification des faits. Nous devons redonner espoir, confiance en l'avenir et leur montrer que la démocratie peut les entendre, les respecter, et leur offrir un avenir. C'est en redonnant ce sens qu'ils retrouveront leur place dans la démocratie. Merci beaucoup.

Last week, I attended a conference organized by the Luxembourg presidency of the Committee of Ministers, focused on youth participation in the digital era. It was a two-day event at the University of Luxembourg, primarily for academics, and I was the only non-academic among the group. There were about 20 presentations, but if you were to sum them all up, they really boiled down to two key points: First, technology—especially artificial intelligence—is crucial. Second, trust is a major issue. I think these points resonate with what we’ve been discussing here today. What struck me in the discussions around technology is that there’s broad agreement on the importance of protecting society from its negative consequences while also harnessing the positive potential of technology, especially artificial intelligence, to strengthen democracy. However, so far we have been much more successful at identifying the risks rather than exploring the good uses of technology to empower and enhance democracy. Similarly, when it comes to trust, we all acknowledge the declining confidence in democracy. We understand some of the reasons behind this erosion of trust, but we're still far from finding effective solutions to restore that confidence. This makes our discussion today on deliberative democracy all the more important. In this complex and still foggy landscape of emerging potential solutions, deliberative democracy clearly has an important place. In my view, under the right conditions, deliberative democracy can have a significant and positive impact. We've already seen this in various examples, as discussed today. It can help rebuild confidence in democracy, particularly among those participating in these processes. Under one condition. If we get it right. As much as deliberative democracy can be a force for good, it can also be damaging if citizens are asked for their opinions and then ignored. Giving people a voice and then disregarding their answers can have devastating consequences. This is not just a theoretical issue; it’s something that can happen in practice. In the Directorate for Democracy, we're deeply committed to democratic engagement and regularly participate in deliberative discussions. We challenge each other constantly. I’m sometimes accused of being skeptical, but that’s not the case. I believe in deliberative democracy, and I think it’s incredibly important. But with the current level of trust in democracy, we may not get a second chance to get it right. Therefore, before scaling deliberative democracy to a national or even European level, we need a solid foundation in how to do it right. The second point I want to address is one that Art O’Leary touched on earlier—that deliberative democracy is not a threat or an alternative to representative democracy. Deliberative democracy clearly supports representative democracy, and that’s crucial. However, we must also recognize the underlying problem: the declining confidence in democracy is largely due to frustration with representative democracy. While deliberative democracy can help restore trust, it is not a magical cure and it cannot be used as an excuse for the flaws in representative democracy. Our efforts to expand deliberate democracy must go hand in hand with tackling the inefficiencies, lack of transparency, accountability, and integrity that have contributed to the erosion of trust. If we don’t, not only will deliberative democracy fail to restore confidence, it could backfire. The third point I want to raise concerns the examples of successful deliberative democracy at local and regional levels, as discussed earlier. These examples are crucial because it's at this level that most citizens interact with and experience democracy. This is where their attitudes toward democracy are shaped, making it a critical area for trust-building. While these local and regional efforts have been successful, and organizing them is relatively easier, the real challenge lies in scaling them to the national level. Although we’ve seen some success, we’re not yet at the point where this becomes a systematic, regular practice. There's still much work to be done before we can implement deliberative democracy on a national or supranational level. So, where does the Council of Europe fit into all of this? We have clear marching orders, as laid out in the Reykjavik Declaration of the heads of state two years ago, which highlighted the need to counter democratic backsliding and emphasized democratic participation, including deliberative democracy, as a priority. The Secretary General's new Pact for Democracy also identifies declining confidence as the biggest challenge and emphasizes innovating for democracy—specifically mentioning deliberative democracy as a key avenue for this innovation. Additionally, the Pact aims to facilitate critical discussions on these issues, just as we’re doing here today, and integrate the results of these discussions into the Council of Europe's work. It’s clear where we are headed and what our priorities are. We are not starting from scratch. Several people in this room, including Claudia and Alina, have been working on these issues for a long time and have brought us to this point. I want to express my sincere gratitude to them. We have the recommendation, which is a great starting point, but there’s still work to be done, particularly considering everything we’ve discussed today. I’d also like to thank Cornelia, especially for her work in organizing this exercise. She has been a true force for deliberative democracy, and we will miss her dearly when she leaves the Council of Europe. She’s the kind of person who can move mountains, and although we’ll continue her work, her absence will be felt. In conclusion, deliberative democracy is not just a priority for the Council of Europe; it is essential for the future of democracy in Europe. We now have the structures in place, including the Special Steering Committee on Democracy, which is already working to create the necessary policy and legal frameworks to elevate deliberative democracy to the next level. Finally, when I was given the title for my intervention—"Deliberative Democracy: A Must-Have for the Council of Europe"—I loved it. But I would say it’s not just a must-have for the Council of Europe. It’s a must-have for the citizens of Europe and for the future of democracy itself. Thank you very much.

First of all, I would like to say how happy I am to be here in Lviv today. I can tell you there's a lot of jealous people back in Strasbourg, because, if you believe in young people, if you believe in Ukraine and if you believe in Europe, Lviv is the place to be tonight. And I am the one with the honor to convey to you the message of the Secretary-General of the Council of Europe, Alain Berset, and all my colleagues in the Council of Europe. And that message is, you're not alone. You will never be alone. And tomorrow the Deputy Secretary-General of the Council of Europe, Bjorn Berge, will be here to participate in the big public opening of the Lviv 2025 on Saturday. I'm happy to be here with the delegation that we brought together with the European Youth Forum, and I'd like to congratulate the European Youth Forum for selecting Lviv as a 2025 youth capital of Europe, because I think it reinforces that same message that young Ukrainians are not alone, That they will never be alone. I welcome the presence of high representatives of the European Union, Commissioner Glen Micallef, and the distinguished member of the European Parliament, Nela Riehl, because I think it is reinforcing that common message of European solidarity and support for Ukraine. I'm happy to be here with the Mayor of Lviv Andriy Sadovyi, and our long-standing partner, Minister for Youth and Sport, Matvii Bidnyi. We have been cooperating for quite some time and will be launching very soon a new phase in our cooperation projects, aimed at supporting young people of Ukraine. And finally, my message of support and congratulations goes to Lviv 2025 Organizational Committee for the fantastic work they have done to make all this possible. And of course, a message of support to the young people of Ukraine and all Ukrainians. And I'd like to honour the memory of Yarina Bazilevich, who was tragically killed, together with her mother and her sisters in September last year, and of course, also the memory of all the victims of this horrible war of aggression. When I was 25 years old, many, many years ago, I returned to my country from studies abroad. My country at the time, just for a few days more, was the former Yugoslavia. And I remember that warm, nice night in June when I went to bed after celebrating my country's independence and then woke up next morning in a war, a war waged by a military machine controlled and led by nationalist authoritarians who felt threatened by the prospects and commitment to democracy, human rights and rule of law in their neighbourhood. And I'm sure this is something that rings a bell with people in Ukraine. And I will not pretend that that experience helps me to understand what Ukrainians are going through. After all, the war I experienced only lasted for 10 days. And that pales compared to what the people in other parts of Yugoslavia had to go through after that and pales even more compared to the horrors the Ukrainians are going through now for 11 years already. But nevertheless, it does help me to understand certain things that I think are relevant here today. The first one is that cold, sudden understanding of how thin and fragile is the line between seemingly normality and total chaos. Between waking up in the morning and looking forward to the future and fearing for your life and the life of your loved ones. Between peace and war. It made me understand how peace is fragile, how it can disappear immediately, suddenly. And how peace and security is something that has to be nurtured and protected. This is something that Ukrainians have learned the hard way, but it's also something we all Europeans should be aware of. And my third point, based on that experience, is that all nightmares come to an end. And the end of the nightmare of Ukrainians is long overdue. But I hope, sincerely hope, and I believe that that day will come soon and that you will be able to enjoy peace, a just peace and a safe peace. And until then, the Council of Europe will continue to support you, including when it comes to the needs of the young people, helping you to support them through that evolving realities and traumatism of war conditions, in all aspects, through youth work and youth policies related to young veterans, IDPs, minority youth, access to housing, education, public health information and other areas. And when peace comes, hopefully soon, and that gargantuan task of reconstruction begins, we will be there to reinforce our support and help you to put young people at the center of that reconstruction process, both as beneficiaries, but also as one of its driving forces. I have a long conclusion to explain in detail what we've been doing so far and what we'll be doing in the future, but I will not do so. Let me simply assure you that we have done a lot together and we shall do even more. I will finish with a short message. Being here in Lviv today made me understand even more how important it is to continue to support and reinforce our support to Ukraine and young Ukrainians. But it also made me understand even more how important it is for Europe to have Ukraine, to have young Ukrainians on board with us, because we can benefit from their resilience, from their determination, from their courage to go on, even when it is not easy, from their creativity, sheer will and the commitment for the values of democracy, human rights and their law, which they are not only defending rhetorically, they are defending it against a ruthless aggressor for them and for all of us. So simply, thank you. You are not alone. You will never be alone.
Youth Centres and the Naked Island

Your Royal Highness Minister, dear friends. First of all, I'd like to thank our hosts for welcoming us here in this fantastic setting, this youth centre. I'd like to thank you all for being here. I'd like to thank the Luxembourg Presidency of the Committee of Ministers of the Council for a fantastic six months during which they have really focused on, you know, democracy. At least all the areas of work for which the Director for Democracy, the Council Europe, that I'm responsible for, is working on culture, education, media freedom, and of course, now, young people. I would also like to thank the teams here, the one in Luxembourg, to prepare this event, led by Georges Metz, and also, of course, our Council of Europe team, led by Gordano Berian and Marcos Andrade. Now, I'd like to start with my personal first experience with youth work and youth centres of a sort. Now, as you can see, I can no longer qualify as a young person. I haven't for a while, but I was young once, and I was young in a country that no longer exists. And we had youth centres, we had youth work of a sort, even if the whole thing was, how shall I call it, semi-spontaneous, you know, regimes like the one in Yugoslavia and similar ones was very big on young people. It was not very big on young people, always in the way that young people would want or appreciate, but it was, you know, giving a lot of attention to young people. So we had youth work, mostly it was physical work, and we even had uniforms, and volunteerism was almost compulsory. But I became quite skilled in evading this kind of volunteerism, because I was never a big fan of uniforms of any kind. But finally, it caught up with me, or I succumbed to temptation, because it was about building a youth centre on an island in the Adriatic Sea. So who could resist six, no, four weeks of sea, hard work, and sun. So I spent that summer there, and, you know, with all and everything that I said about it, it still was a great time. Because I felt that magic, even in those circumstances, I felt that magic, that spark that happens when you bring young people together from, you know, different backgrounds, different paths, different languages, different experiences, and bring them there, and something happens. That magic really happens. So, and then I said to myself, so, you know, so what? And I'm doing something that is going to serve young people for many years to come in this beautiful setting.
