So recently, I looked up what happened with that, the island of young people, the island of youth. It turns out that it's not a youth centre. It has been released to some company agency from France, Italy, Germany, I don't know, which is organising adult-themed camping tours on that island now. I don't know exactly what adult-themed camping is about. It's probably like Disney-themed camping just without Mickey Mouse. But, and I have nothing against it. I just, you know, think there is symbolism somewhere there, even if I don't dare explore it in every detail. You know, and they had another island just north of there where, you know, they could put their adults in camping. It was there, it's bare. If it wasn't for its sinister past, because there used to be a very harsh prison camp on that island in the 50s, where my uncle spent three years in his 20s, thousand days and thousand nights, as he called his book where he described his time there. But, you know, it's there, it's available, you know, and it even has the name to go with the adult-themed camping place, because it's completely deprived of any vegetation. It's called the Naked Island. But no, they had to take our youth centre away. What I'm trying to say that in today's world, you know, we have nothing against adult-themed campings, but what we really need is what our democracies need, what young people need, is more youth centres. Places where young people can come together, can learn together, can learn about each other, can learn about democracy and practice democracy. Because there has been many recent opinion polls, there have been researches, there have been election results, which have caused a lot of concern, and with reason about the tendencies in young people's preferences when it comes to voting and elections and political parties. And there is a marked tendency to veer away from democratic parties towards more extremist ideas. We have seen that now in almost every election. Now, to be fair, it's not all black and white. I've recently had an honour to, together with the Deputy Secretary General of the Council of Europe, to welcome in the youth centre in Strasbourg, the group of Serbian students who came on bicycles from Novi Sad, from Serbia, to present their requests, their demands, their expectations with regard to the situation in Serbia. And, you know, I was really humbled. I was so impressed by their determination, how articulate they were, how passionate they were, how nevertheless non-aggressive they were, but determined in their expectations that, you know, are completely aligned with what we think and want from all our countries and governments, democracy, human rights and the rule of law. But even those young people who are having doubts, you know, who are embracing alternative ideas, to put it mildly, of course, we can, you know, we can condemn, we should definitely be concerned, but we could also ask ourselves why and try to understand why they feel as they feel, why they vote as they vote. And I don't think these young people are lost for democracy forever. I think they're angry. I think they feel left behind. I think they feel ignored. I think they lost confidence. So we need to do something to restore that conference. Actually, I think we need to do a lot to restore that conference. Because regaining confidence in democracy requires regaining confidence in the future. And you will not do that with words alone. So you're gaining confidence in the future is about education. It's about employment. It's about housing. It's about health. It's about environment. It's about peace. You know, people, young people, everyone, we need, how shall I say, material evidence of democracy as a system that can deliver on people's expectations if you want to restore that confidence in democracy. And restoring confidence in democracy also requires spaces, requires infrastructures. It requires spaces where young people can feel that magic that I felt so many years ago. Because democracy cannot be learned and practiced on mobile apps alone. And this is what youth centers do. And this is what quality youth centers do very well, very well, what they do best. Because they offer safe spaces for democratic youth participation, non-formal education, skill building, engaging young people in democratic human rights, social inclusion. Quality in quality label is not just a word, as you all know. It is a result of passion and hard work and investment by people believing in young people and in democracy. By people like you, by you. Quality label requires hard work to be earned. And it requires hard work to be kept. That is what makes it so impactful, so relevant, so respected. Quality label, quality work with young people, for young people, also requires attention and recognition. And this is why your presence here, Your Royal Highness, today is so important, is so precious. Quality label in youth work also requires investment and support. And this is why the role of local and regional authorities, of governments, of local communities, associations, of European organizations is so important. Because quality label youth centers provides us a path towards more confidence in democracy, a path towards more democracy, and a path towards a better democracy, a path towards a world where there may be some adult youth, adult theme camping places, I don't know, but there will be many, many more youth centers, spaces for young people, and no naked islands at all. Thank you.
EuroDIG 2025: Humans, With and Through Technology

Good morning, everybody. A few years back, we organized a visit of the American historian, Professor Timothy Snyder. And one thing that he said at the beginning of his lecture really stayed with me. He said that today, that was a few years back, because of the internet, the entire world population was 20% more stupid than it was before. And the only reason why nobody notices that is that we are all collectively 20% more stupid than we were. Now, I hesitate a little bit to start off with this quote from Timothy Snyder, because I felt that it may come across as too cynical, perhaps exaggerated, and definitely too technology negative. But then this morning, I read an article in the Chronicle of Higher Education about the professor from the New York University, who gave his students a set of AI-proofed assignments, And the reaction was spectacular. First of all, most of them complained it was too hard work, even when he explained that these were regular standard assignments, only prepared in a way that prevented ChatGPT to read and answer them. Then they complained that the professor was interfering with their learning styles. I like this one particularly. And then one of them even demanded an extension because chat GPT was down on that day. So perhaps Professor Snyder was even too conservative. This, after all, was something he said pre-chat GPT, which I think, with the ever-growing influence of the artificial intelligence, is now making a growing number of people very non-artificially less bright. These students risk an atrophy of their cognitive faculties, due to an excessive use of ChatGPT. Degenerative AI, sort to speak. This is not a rant against technology, because that would really be stupid. But I think we have to acknowledge that we have traveled a long way from those early days of our initial excitement about technology, and our conviction that it would transform our societies for the better, on its own, by default. We now understand we were wrong, not because we believed that technology was inherently good, but because we attributed ethical qualities to machines. Technology is neither good or bad. It is ethically neutral. What makes it good or bad is what humans do with it, and especially what humans do to other humans with it. One of the biggest mistakes, I think, is to frame and understand the digital society in terms of interaction between technology and humans alone. It remains defined by interactions between humans, but with and through technology. This may sound self-evident, but it is important to say it loud and say it often. Why? Because it reminds us that we, humans, retain agency to shape our interactions and shape our societies, even and especially in digital times. So I welcome the fact that this year's Eurodig sessions have underscored that digital governance is fundamentally about people, that it is about ensuring that innovation serves the public good, that ethical principles guide our decisions, and that the most vulnerable, especially children, are protected in the digital environment. This human-centered approach must remain at the heart of all governance efforts as we shape our future where rights, safety and dignity are preserved online. The question is how? Well, let's start by how it will not work. I think we will not succeed by repeating ritualized platitudes about minimizing the risk and maximizing the benefits, regardless of the resolve and serenity and pathos we invest in our claims. On minimizing those risks, I think we are becoming slightly better about identifying risks, even if much is still unknown. But we are not very successful in identifying effective responses to this risk, and we really have to step up this effort. On maximizing benefits, it's more of a mixed picture. It is better because digital and AI systems are built in driving many processes that are making our lives better and safer. But much of that is not very visible to the public, which is increasingly skeptical and influenced by the negative, especially when it comes to human relations by impact of technology on disinformation, manipulations of elections, fraud, polarization. This is not good, because mistrust, fear and resentment of technology is not making our societies safer, they just facilitate manipulation. So I welcome the fact that this Eurodig went beyond that. It went into the concrete and practical solutions on how to mitigate the risk of AI systems for human rights, on ways to resolve tensions and disagreements between tech giants and European regulators on the scope of freedom of expression, and on how to tackle the challenges to privacy created by neurotechnology development. To succeed, we need to work together. We need to compare notes. We need to push each other and drive innovation. This is what Eurodig does, and this is why it is so important for the Council of Europe to be involved and to contribute. I welcome the focus on human-centered approach. I'd like to recall what a young Polish artist, I think now living in Ireland, has said about AI. She said that I want the technology to do my dishes and laundry so I can do my art and my writing, not the technology to do my art and my writing so I can do the dishes and the laundry. Of course, the technology is and will even more replace many of our existing tasks, and that is in principle good. But the fundamental message of this young artist stands - that technology should make our lives better. And the same goes for innovation. While we all wholeheartedly support it, we should bear in mind that the ultimate objective is not merely to improve the technology, but to improve our lives. We need to continue our conversations and cooperation to acquire and constantly update the right mix of policies and interventions. Regulations, where and when regulation is needed, but also investments in people through education, in digital skills and competencies. But not only, we must not forget that this is about human interactions. Not every threat can be attributed to technology alone, which is regularly an amplifier, very often an amplifier, but not always the cause of every pathology we are confronted with in today's world. From polarization to hate speech, a growing sense of social, economic, political and technological marginalization and neglect. As an example, it was not technology which made people believe that a used handkerchief was a bag of cocaine. The technology only made that stupidity travel faster and reach more people. So we need to find effective responses to these challenges which are tearing our democracies apart and give people skills and power to use the technology in an ethical manner and ensure that the technology is used in an ethical manner to them. So we need to invest in education for democratic culture. We need to help citizens acquire competencies to uphold democratic values in a digital context. Now, after these three days, I think we will really be satisfied with the results of what was a good and productive session. But we should not engage in circular shoulder clapping and become complacent. This was an important step, yet only a step, in what is going to be a marathon, with a never quickening pace and no set distance. We'll just have to keep on running, and running ever faster. Because future will not adjust to our learning styles. We need to adjust our learning styles to the future. Or this future will interfere with our living styles, in ways we surely wish to avoid.

Good afternoon, everyone. As the representative of the Council of Europe at this concluding ceremony, I believe I am expected to do two things. First, to express gratitude — to say thank you to many people. And I do so with great sincerity and enthusiasm. Let me begin by thanking Malta. We are truly delighted to be here for the fourth edition of this conference. Yesterday, someone mentioned that the third youth work convention took place in Bonn. But if I remember correctly, at least as far as I am concerned, it took place in my spare bedroom. So it is especially wonderful to be here — in sunny, beautiful Malta. First, a heartfelt thank you to the Maltese Presidency of the Committee of Ministers, represented here by Ambassador Camilleri Vettiger, for prioritizing and supporting young people throughout your presidency. Thank you also to the Maltese authorities and to Agenzija Żgħażagħ for all the hard work that made this conference such a success. And a very special thanks to the head of the agency — our brilliant Miriam — for her tireless efforts here in Malta and as chair of our steering committee. And especially for that outstanding keynote speech yesterday. I’d also like to thank the European Union, represented here by Commissioner Glenn Micallef, for its continued commitment to our long-standing partnership in support of youth work. My deep appreciation also goes to my colleagues in the Council of Europe Youth Team for their dedication in preparing this conference — and for the work ahead to ensure that the results of these two days are implemented and have a real impact. And finally, thank you to all of you — not only for being here and actively contributing, but for the work you’ve done before coming and the work you will continue after you return home — hopefully with fresh ideas and renewed energy. Now, the second task is a bit trickier. There’s a tradition at the end of these events where someone stands up to tell the participants what they’ve just experienced — explaining to the people who lived through the conference what the conference was about. I’m not going to do that. I'm certainly not going to tell a room full of youth workers what youth work is. You know that far better than I do. Instead, I want to say a few words about why youth work is so crucial in our efforts to defend democracy and make it more resilient. This is, after all, the overarching goal of the Council of Europe’s number one priority — the Secretary General’s initiative, the New Democratic Pact. That pact seeks to restore trust in democracy — for everyone, but especially for young people. And youth work plays an essential role in achieving that. A few days ago, I was invited to the European School in Strasbourg — where many children of Council of Europe staff, including my own, are students. The event was titled Transitions to Democracy and organized by history teachers. I was joined by colleagues from Central and Eastern Europe to share personal memories of the time when our countries transitioned from authoritarianism to democracy. Many of my colleagues spoke about their struggles and sacrifices and reminded the students that they should feel lucky and grateful to live in democracies. My message was slightly different. First, I questioned the title. Yes, we must talk about transitions when discussing democracy, because democracy is never static. But today, the conversation should not only be about transitions to democracy — increasingly, we must talk about transitions from democracy, not just in our countries of origin, but globally. Second, about being “lucky and grateful.” I told the students that although I spent my youth in a country that wasn’t free, and life was often difficult — we never doubted that the future will be better. That things will change, and that they will change for the better. And that we were a part of that change. We didn’t feel powerless. We felt powerful. That belief — that conviction — is something many young people today no longer feel. Despite living in freer, wealthier societies, they face a different kind of burden: uncertainty. They are often frustrated, even afraid of what the future may hold. And uncertainty breeds fear — and fear, as we know, can give rise to many dangerous outcomes. So I told the students: You don’t have to feel grateful. You have the right — indeed, the duty — to be critical. You have the right to be impatient. You even have the right to be angry. But you must be cautious about what you do with that anger and impatience. Do not let anyone manipulate or weaponize your frustration. Because those who seek to exploit your discontent will ultimately use it against you — against your rights and freedoms. Instead, use your energy to demand change. To be the change. To be powerful. At that point, a young woman in the audience asked a simple but profound question: How? I told her that there are many ways to effect change — through our actions, our choices, our words, and our silences. Through how we engage with others. But most importantly: through participation. Through youth work — because youth work works. It works for young people. It works for communities. It works for democracy. I have witnessed the magic that happens when young people come together around a shared goal. One recent example stands out. Together with a number of other people here today we were in Lviv for the opening ceremony of the 2025 European Youth Capital. While there, we visited what an “urban camp.” A group of young people from Kharkiv — passionate about street sports — had taken over a derelict cultural center and transformed it into something remarkable. They now provide shelter for families from frontline regions, organize activities for local youth, and host children from war-affected areas for short stays to offer them recovery, normalcy, and hope. These moments of respite are crucial for their mental health and emotional well-being. These young people in Lviv — they are powerful. They deserve our admiration. But more importantly, they deserve our support. And they deserve a just peace. An end to this nightmare. You all know — better than I do — that youth work only works if we make it work. That means investing in it. It means creating supportive infrastructure, legal and institutional frameworks, stable funding, and political recognition. With those elements in place, youth work can move mountains. It can transform anger into action, frustration into engagement, and powerlessness into empowerment. That is how we build stronger democracies — by working with young people, for young people, but ultimately for all of us. The Secretary General’s New Democratic Pact will demand time, effort, and commitment from many institutions and individuals. But one thing is clear: youth and youth work must be at the heart of it. The results of this conference will be presented at the Council of Europe’s ministerial session — right here in this building — in October. Together with the European Union, we are also exploring new ways to strengthen our partnership and further support youth work. In short: we’re in this for the long haul. Now, I mentioned earlier that I don’t have much personal experience in youth work — but actually, I do have one story from my younger years. I apologize to those of you who were recently in Luxembourg — you may have heard this already. But repetition, I’ve learned, is not only tolerated at my age — it’s almost expected. And there was an update on that story. When I was growing up in Yugoslavia, we had our version of youth work. It was semi-spontaneous and very ideology-driven — not exactly my cup of tea. But I did make one exception: I spent four weeks on a small Adriatic island helping to build a youth center. For a good cause. And, I admit, for the beach. Recently, in preparing for the Luxembourg conference, I looked up what became of that youth center — the one I helped build with my own two hands. It’s gone. It’s now an adults-only camping resort. I don’t even want to speculate what that means — though I might have a guess. Either way, it’s not a youth center. That was a little depressing. But just two days ago, I learned something new. British Channel 4 is filming a reality show on that very island. It’s now called the “Virgin Island.” The show features twelve adults confronting their intimacy issues — in full view of millions — for the chance at a financial reward and, presumably, other forms of... fulfillment. So who says romance is dead? Strangely, that brought me some comfort. At least, I told myself, it wasn’t all for nothing. We didn’t just build infrastructure — we left a vibe. I spent a lot of time thinking about how to use that personal anecdote — so rich in symbolism — to wrap up this speech. I had many ideas. Unfortunately, none of them appropriate for a public audience. So I’ll just say this: We must support youth work. Because youth work works. It works for all the most important things — and sometimes even for the most unexpected ones. It moves mountains. And yes — it has a vibe.

Villano has already extended the official thanks on behalf of the Council of Europe, so I could skip that part—but still, I want to once again thank our hosts here: Charles University, the Ministry, and the Czech authorities for welcoming us. You can never be too grateful—well, sometimes you can. Let me go straight into why we at the Council of Europe consider this partnership, including this Global Forum, so important. A few days ago, I was invited to a conference at the European School in Strasbourg called Transitions to Democracy. Many people working at the Council of Europe have children who attend this school. I was invited not as the Director for Democracy, but as a parent—alongside colleagues from Central and Eastern Europe—to share our personal testimonies about the time when our countries transitioned from non-democratic, authoritarian regimes to democracy. I was there with colleagues from Albania and Romania. I'm from Slovenia, which at the time was part of Yugoslavia. The event was organized by history teachers, and we heard many heartfelt, rich testimonies. What struck me was that all of them concluded with a similar message to the students: You are so lucky, you should be grateful to live in a democracy. And I felt uncomfortable with that message. My take was a little different. I told the students: You don’t have to be grateful. Not at all. First, we were speaking about a time of transition to democracy. That’s not how we can describe the world today. Many parts of the world are transitioning away from democracy—at different speeds—and that makes a big difference. Second, even in those difficult times—materially harder for some than others—when freedoms were limited, we had one immense privilege: we never doubted, not for a moment, that the future would be better. That things would change for the better, and that we were part of that change. That gave us a sense of power, not powerlessness. And that kind of certainty is something young people today often don’t have. Uncertainty about the future breeds insecurity, loss of confidence, and many challenges to democracy itself. So I said: Don’t be grateful. You have every right to be frustrated. You have every right to be angry. Just don’t let anyone manipulate your anger—because sooner or later, they’ll use it against you: against your rights, your freedoms, and your interests. Instead, I told them: Be critical. Be critical like hell. At that point, the history teachers and school principal started to look a bit nervous, so I had to clarify. Being critical doesn’t mean rejecting everything with cynicism or indifference. Critical thinking means challenging the information you receive—but also challenging your own convictions, opinions, and beliefs, testing them against knowledge and facts. It’s a constant process, and it makes you powerful. That group of 17- and 18-year-olds, most of whom will soon start university, will now have the opportunity to grow into true critical thinkers—understanding the importance of knowledge, contributing to it, valuing science and data. And that, to me, is the democratic mission of higher education. Because universities are not political institutions. Their mission is not to steer young people toward one ideology or another. And in my experience, they don't—except perhaps in a world where liberal democracy and basic decency are portrayed as left-wing controversies. In such a world, let’s face it—we’re all branded as raging communists. That’s one part of the mission. The second crucial role of universities is their leadership in science, research, and problem-solving. Populism—especially authoritarian populism—thrives in uncertainty. It feeds on our collective inability to find effective solutions to global challenges: environmental, demographic, technological, economic, you name it. We face a stark choice: either we develop and apply effective solutions based on knowledge and science, or we allow populism to continue exploiting fears and undermining democracy. The third element—and a challenge to both us and to universities—is the perception that critical thinking is reserved for university graduates. That we are the enlightened few, saving democracy from the so-called "ignorant masses." If you think that’s a malicious caricature, you’re right. But if you think public opinion isn’t being shaped by such caricatures, you haven’t been paying attention. And that should concern us. We live in times of declining trust—not only in universities but in knowledge, in science, in facts. We must rebuild that trust. Democracy needs electricians and plumbers, to borrow a phrase from a recent White House spokesperson. Electricians and plumbers who are critical thinkers, who value knowledge, who trust in science. Without them, everything else falls apart. This is also about access to education, about openness, about the engagement of universities in their local and broader communities. And that’s something we’ll discuss in this forum. At the Council of Europe, we’ve launched the Secretary General’s New Democratic Pact. Its overarching ambition is to find ways to strengthen and make democracies more resilient. And the path to that resilience lies in restoring confidence—confidence in democracy, in institutions, and in one another. Education—especially higher education—is central to that effort. Villano will later speak in more detail about our work. Let me close with one final thought. At the Council of Europe, we are officials of an international organization—which is a polite way of saying we’re bureaucrats. We do our work according to the professional standards of our roles, with objectivity, impartiality, sometimes even detachment. And we respect that. But this is also not a job you can do without personal conviction—without ideas, and without passion. That’s why this partnership and this forum are so important. It’s where we meet people from around the world who share our passion and belief in democracy and education. This conviction became even stronger for me recently when I met a group of Serbian students who cycled from Novi Sad to Strasbourg to speak to European institutions. A few days later, I met with a group of professors from Serbia. I rarely encounter such articulate, committed, intelligent young people—calm but determined. What struck me was how much the students spoke of their concern for their professors, and how much the professors worried about their students. They both asked: Are we doing something to help? To protect universities, to protect academic freedom and student rights? And I said: Yes, and we will do even more. Because democracy cannot be defended or rebuilt from the outside alone. But when we work with those who are committed to that goal, we in the Council of Europe—together with this partnership—can do truly important things. And I promise: we will. I fully intend to keep that promise. Thank you very much

Thank you very much. Let me start by thanking the Maltese Presidency for this event, before I forget. I may do it again at the end, but they deserve all our gratitude, for this event and for everything they are doing during their Presidency on democracy, especially in the context of the New Democratic Pact for Europe. On your question, I think the Deputy Secretary General has already answered with great clarity, so I won't repeat what he said. Instead, I would like to make the link with what the Council of Europe is doing about it, and to explain the logic and the philosophy behind the Council of Europe's multi-layered approach. Because if we want to be effective in countering disinformation, it's not about doing this, or doing that, or doing something else. We need to do everything, together. I thought I would go with Jamie Oliver. It's not the perfect analogy, but there are lessons to be learned, so bear with me. You probably remember this — maybe you don't. He had a programme, Jamie's School Dinners, in the UK, and then Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution in the US. Horrified by what pupils were being fed in schools, he wanted to change that. And he did two things. First, he stopped the bad stuff from coming into the cafeteria: the processed food, the trans fats, the hamburgers. And second, he replaced it with healthy food — with carrots and fruit and the like. So far, the analogy works perfectly. Because if you are concerned about the health of our democracy, this is what you need to do. You need to stop the junk — disinformation — from coming in, and you need to replace it with quality information. On the first, the Council of Europe has proposed the first-ever convention on disinformation and foreign interference. Jamie Oliver had it easier: there is no European convention on hamburgers and hot dogs. There is a lot on freedom of expression. But if anyone is able to pull off that delicate balance — countering disinformation without damaging or undermining freedom and democracy — I think it is the Council of Europe. The second part is trickier. How do you replace the junk with quality information? Our information systems, the traditional media models, are under serious threat, first of all for economic reasons. There will be more discussion on that later, so I will not go into it now. But I think what is important is to recognise that quality information is a public good — and then to act accordingly: invest in it and protect it. If we manage to do that, we will get to where Jamie Oliver got. And he failed. It was good television, but there is still junk in the school cafeterias, both in the US and in the UK. Because what we are witnessing is not only the crisis of an economic model. It is a crisis of confidence. And that crisis of confidence did not come about spontaneously, or by coincidence, or organically. It was prompted, it was planned, and it was executed. Maria Ressa, the Filipino journalist who won the Nobel Peace Prize a few years ago, said that when there is no agreement on facts in a society, you no longer have democracy. And I think the enemies of democracy know that. The way to destroy a modern democracy is to destroy our confidence in facts. That is where the next pillar comes in: fact-checking and media literacy. All of these pillars are essential, and these two absolutely so. But again, they will not do the job on their own. What do I mean by that? Imagine you are in a discussion on social media — and I strongly suggest you don't get into one — about some hot topic, with a group of very engaged people. And at the end you tell them: listen, guys, the problem is that you are media illiterate and you got your facts wrong. It's not going to work. We will not be able to fact-check people back into democracy. Because this is a crisis of confidence, as I said, and of mistrust, nourished and driven by fear, uncertainty and frustration. We need to look at the reasons why, find answers to them, and then find ways to influence and shape those attitudes. And this is where culture comes in. It is absolutely essential. We are talking about narratives, about transmitting values. Let me give you one example — and then I will finish, I promise. In 2011 there was a film in Serbia, supported by Eurimages, called Parada — The Parade — about the organisation of a Pride parade. That film, on its own, did more to defeat homophobia in that country and in the region than any political action or conference we could have organised. So don't underestimate culture. It is essential. Secondly, youth. Young people are very often the first targets and victims of disinformation. But if we support them and invest in them, they can be the most effective first responders. And finally, education. Education, education, education. We are talking about critical thinking, about competences, skills and values that we can transmit through education. And we are talking about history teaching, because history is weaponised through disinformation every day. So, to finish, what I am trying to say is this. All the things I have mentioned, from the proposed convention to culture, are essential in their own right. But none of them will work on its own. That is the multi-layered approach, and this is where I think the Council of Europe can make a difference, because it brings all these different areas of work together. They are also reflected in the RESIST project, and I would like to thank the EEA and Norway Grants for supporting it, because it gives us the opportunity to put these policy orientations into practice in a very concrete way. Thank you very much.

First of all, thank you so much for being here, sincerely. It is important. I'm going to do my best to meet the high expectations about explaining the new Democratic Pact. I prepared for this, I promise. I really did. I'm saying this just in case it doesn't immediately, or maybe not at all, become evident later on—but I did. I know many of you, but not all, and vice versa. So, first, let me introduce myself. My name is Matjaž Gruden. I'm Director for Democracy at the Council of Europe, which means I'm responsible for the areas of youth, education, media, civil society, and culture and heritage. But I'm also here as the person the Secretary General asked to coordinate the preparation of the new Democratic Pact for Europe, which I guess is a dubious honor—at least we’ll know who’s going to be blamed internally if things go sideways in the end. But they won’t. And if it goes well, there’ll be somebody who gets to take the credit. But before I start about the New Democratic Pact, just a few words to explain the context, part of where I see the Democratic Pact coming from—where I think it’s most important, particularly regarding young people and their contribution to it. Let me start with a story. This happened to me in June. Sorry if anyone’s already heard it—it was one of the more interesting things that’s happened to me in the last couple months, so I might have mentioned it before. I was invited to a European school in Strasbourg as a parent, not as the Director for Democracy. The history and political science teachers invited several parents from the Council of Europe—there were people from Slovenia, Albania, Ukraine, Romania—to talk to students about our experiences with transitions to democracy. We were there as parents from countries that had undergone that transition, telling our stories. It was a great event. It was Friday afternoon in June—I could tell the students’ attention wasn’t at its peak initially, but honestly, they were brave and stuck with us through the session. There were a lot of moving and very relevant, heartfelt testimonies from my colleagues, recalling times of enormous political and social changes, about 30 years ago or so. What struck me is that, nearly every time, the conclusion was the same: it was hard, but now democracy is here, freedom is here, and you should be grateful that you live in freedom and democracy. I felt, well, uncomfortable with that conclusion. All our experiences were different—it wasn’t the same growing up in Slovenia (then Yugoslavia) or Albania—and sure, specifically for that group of young people in Strasbourg, the material standard of life has improved a lot. But the idea that young people should be grateful for what they have bothered me. So I couldn’t help myself—when it was my turn, I said, “Don’t be grateful. Be angry, be demanding, be critical—but don’t be grateful.” And I could see the principal and teachers in the corner starting to sweat profusely. So I had to qualify a bit. I said, you have to be all three—not just angry, not just demanding, but also critical. And critical doesn’t mean just flipping off everything you don’t like—being critical means thinking critically. Look for facts, listen to other people, be critical of yourself, test your opinions, and then be angry and demanding. So I think I got away with the principal there. The reason I said this is, for the first 25 years of my life, I didn’t live in a democracy. Yugoslavia may not have been the worst of them, but it certainly wasn’t a liberal democracy. I can tell you that. Materially, we had less and so on. But there was a huge advantage: when I was the age of those students, I had no doubt the future was going to be better, and that I was going to be a part of that change. That’s the difference: that confidence in the future, that sense of empowerment, that certainty that things would get better, maybe not for everyone and not in every aspect, but collectively. That sense is no longer there. That’s dangerous. It’s dangerous for democracy because if people lose confidence in their future, and that loss is replaced by uncertainty or fear, it creates a space for things like manipulation and what is now called democratic backsliding. It applies to young people, but not only young people. The Secretary General, Alain Berset, in a recent interview for Newsweek described the last 20 or 25 years as a “perfect storm.” And it’s true. If you were born around 2000, you’ve had it all: the financial crisis, the first Ukrainian war, COVID, the migration crisis, another economic crisis, the second Ukrainian war—you name it. Every time, it seems that whatever bad stuff fate throws at us, young people get the double serving. This has clearly affected young people’s perceptions, attitudes, and motivation to sustain, engage, and participate in democracy. And that’s really the essence of the new Democratic Pact. It’s about finding ways to restore confidence in democracy today. Not renegotiating what democracy is, not horse-trading over which values matter more, which group perhaps deserves less attention or protection, whose rights we can set aside, but finding new, effective ways to make democracy resilient against all the challenges we’re facing. The overall concept is “democratic security”—security through democracy, based on the understanding that security isn’t only about hard security, though hard security concerns do exist, but sometimes it’s even more important to achieve security through a properly functioning democratic system. Society must invest in a culture where people support, engage, and participate in democracy, because otherwise, democracy erodes—not from tanks and artillery but from someone pressing on its neuralgic points, exploiting fragility and polarization. It can collapse from within. That’s the idea: we need both forms of security. The Pact has several phases. We’re in the earliest one now, which started when the Secretary General presented it to ministers in May. There were a couple of events already, but the youth event and ministerial session are really among the first major milestones. The first stage is called consultation—or conversation. It’s about bringing people together, even those not normally heard, listening to them, being critical, identifying problems: why have people lost confidence, why are they disengaging from democracy, and what are we doing, are there things that should be done differently. The next stages will be shaped by this conversation. Your contributions will be taken into account for the next steps. At a certain point, all these contributions, ideas, and proposals will be collected, analyzed, and synthesized—the most important or innovative ones will be transformed into concrete policy proposals for Council of Europe member states. That’s when the real work begins. The exercise isn’t just about making fancy declarations, but about changing the situation—democratic backsliding isn’t just a technical issue, it’s political, ideological, economic, so it requires a political response. The Pact is also there to create momentum and coalitions for democracy, and what happens this week is part of building those coalitions. I’ll wrap up, because I want to hear your questions. But I also want to say how the youth sector in the Council of Europe and advisory council have played a vital role in the Democratic Pact—long before the Pact was formalized. The youth perspective is already emerging as one of its most important outcomes—it started in Reykjavik in 2023, and even before. There’s been 50 years of co-management—hugely important—but the youth perspective takes it even further. For example, the “no hate speech” campaign started by young people, demanding something be done at a time when nobody else was talking about polarization. Now everyone talks about it. The fact Reykjavik happened in 2023, with two main priorities—to support Ukraine and respond to democratic backsliding—was also thanks to young people's contributions. The 50 recommendations of the Democracy Here – Democracy Now, not only helped to pave the way to the Summit, they also represent a highly relevant contribution to the Pact. In closing—I can’t give you a complete, clear picture of what the Pact will look like in the end, because that’s the point. If we already knew, we wouldn’t need all these phases. The final shape of the Pact relies also on your inputs. This meeting and this conference are really important milestones. In conclusion and in short, let me return to the notion of ungratefulness. The idea behind this youth event is to extract from this congregation of ungrateful brats the reason why you are so ungrateful, and then, together, find reasons to make you happier. If we figure that out and make it happen, together, the chances are we’ll get a happier and a more democratic world for everyone. Thank you.
Closing Conference of the European Year of Digital Citizenship Education

Dear Minister, dear participants, There is only one thing better than a very, very well prepared and interesting conference, and that is a very, very well prepared and interesting conference in Ljubljana. Believe me, I am very objective about that. I am from Ljubljana myself. Welcome to this closing conference of the 2025 European Year of Digital Citizenship, so kindly hosted by Slovenia. I would like to thank the Slovenian team of the Recovery and Resilience Plan project »Strengthening Digital Citizenship in Slovenian Educational Institutions«, supported by the Slovenian Ministry of Education, for their hard work in preparing this conference and for their contribution to the European Year of Digital Citizenship Education. In 1966, the German philosopher, cultural and music critic Theodor Adorno had a radio program. I guess it was a podcast before podcasts. And in that famous radio program, he said that the premier demand upon all education is that Auschwitz should not happen again. I believe in 1966 that was understandable; it was only 20 years after the 27th of January 1945, when the Allied forces liberated Auschwitz. So the first question would really be whether Adorno today would have said the same thing. Would he not? Would we, if he did, call him a drama queen and say he exaggerates? I’m not so sure. The second question is whether, if he reflected upon the role of education today, the unprecedented technical development—digital, and especially artificial intelligence—would have an impact on his views. We can be certain that in 1966, digital technology was not high on his mind. In fact, it was just a year after IBM produced its System 360—a revolution at the time, but the size of a concert piano. I Googled it: it was in order of millions slower than my iPhone 15. Imagine watching a TikTok video on that or trying to download an app. That difference in magnitude is not just symbolic; it really reflects the difference between 1966 and today. In the world we live in, good things can happen faster and go further—but bad things, too. Not because technology itself is good or bad. Technology is value-neutral, but people often are not. Even with all our technological development and the unthinkable progress of AI, we are still talking about human-to-human interaction through and with technology. That’s why fostering human agency is so important. That’s why education is crucial, including—and especially so—that Auschwitz does not happen again. Now, if I can go back to the origins of this European Year of Digital Citizenship that brought us to this conference: The Council of Europe started to work on these matters a few years earlier, but it was in November 2019—just before the COVID pandemic—when the French presidency of the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers organized a conference of Ministers of Education in Paris. At that conference, we were asked to provide the keynote speaker. I think at the time we got as subversive as bureaucrats ever do: we invited the director and president of the Linz Ars Electronica Festival, Gerfried Stocker. Gerfried of course came to the ministerial conference in his crumpled t-shirt and ponytail, and his speech mesmerized the ministers. If I may sum up what he said: for successful digital citizenship education, you need four ingredients. First, you have to teach learners to understand the infrastructure of digital technology and especially AI—not just how to use it, but to understand it; to know what’s in the box. This is necessary to benefit fully from its potential and to protect yourself so it can’t be misused against you. Understanding its human and environmental costs as well—use it responsibly. I often think that one short sentence or question— “Grok, is this true?” which peppers through everyone’s Twitter feed—probably has a higher carbon imprint than all airline companies together. Don’t believe me? If you’re checking this with Grok now, you are complicit in this environmental recklessness. Second, and this leads us to competencies for democratic culture: values, attitudes, knowledge, critical understanding, and skills—notably, critical thinking. These are not alternatives to EdTech, nor competitors; they go hand in hand. The AI transformation of our society makes both the competencies for democratic culture more important and more challenging. Third, classical knowledge: literature, languages, geography, history—critically important. And, as much as it pains me remembering my own school days, I guess kids should still learn math and physics. There’s no critical thinking without knowledge. Investing in knowledge is essential if you want to counter the distortion that has framed “critical thinking” as a rejection of knowledge, facts and rationality. Fourth, art. Art is essential because it fosters creativity and innovation, provides an important means of reflection, learning, and transmitting values, and reinforces our human and social confidence and intelligence. Most of Gerfried’s advice—or as much as ministers could digest—found its way into the 2019 Committee of Ministers Recommendation on Digital Citizenship Education (2019/10). This recommendation built on Council of Europe work since 2016 and led to the 2025 European Year of Digital Citizenship and this final conference in Ljubljana. The last years brought significant progress, but there are also gaps. We see national implementation of digital citizenship education is still too low, with the exception of Slovenia and its projects strengthening digital citizenship in educational institutions. There is also a lack of standards, leading to overlapping mandates and a lack of policy cohesion. Hence the road map for digital citizenship education for 2027–2031. I look forward to the rich discussion here with so many stakeholders; I think this provides the perfect launch of the digital citizenship road map, which will build on successful national practices, bring together all concerned, put students and teachers at the heart of the process, be flexible—not prescriptive—and above all, concrete. Theoretical ideas discussed at the European level won’t by themselves change the situation; what happens in the classroom really matters. The objective is clear: to empower learners to act as engaged, responsible, and ethical digital citizens. At the Council of Europe, digital citizenship education is part of the Directorate for Democracy and supports the new Democratic Pact for Europe, aiming to respond to democratic backsliding seen in recent years. The new Pact has three pillars: learning and practicing democracy; protecting democracy; and innovating for democracy. Education for digital citizenship, this conference, and the future road map will contribute to all three. In May 2027, we expect the New Democratic Pact for Europe to be presented to the Council of Europe Ministers and we are determined that bold and ambitious commitment to education, including and especially education for digital citizenship, will figure as one od its most significant outcomes. The future is already here: fast, unpredictable, sometimes a bit frightening. Digital citizenship education is a critical tool to foster human agency—to manage and master change and make the best of it for everyone. At the end, the premier demand on every education has not changed that much since 1966; perhaps it has even become more urgent. Digital citizenship education is a way to make our world a safer, more just, and kinder place. Perhaps not at the order of millions of times better—but if we make it just a little bit nicer, it will already be huge. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Ida, and good morning, everybody. Welcome to the Council of Europe Youth Center in Budapest, the wildest place in town, where all sorts of cool and important things are unleashed on a regular basis. Thank you again, Ida, not only for the introduction, but first and foremost for what you and your colleagues have been doing over the last year. It is a major task to put together such a big event, and I would particularly like to thank you for coordinating this effort. This is also, at least for the time being, the last event that Ida will be doing as part of the Council of Europe team, so let this not be a goodbye, but rather a “thank you so far.” I would also like to thank all our partners in this important, regular event, the Forum. We are very pleased to be with you. This event has real merit and produces results, and in the times we live in, it would be an understatement to say that we need results on human rights education and human rights in general. In my brief intervention, I will zoom out and speak about democracy as well. I do this not only because I am the Director for Democracy and almost contractually obliged to mention it every time I speak in public, but also because we have to put this event and the importance of human rights education into context. You cannot organize education on safe navigation on the third deck of an ocean liner without having somebody on the bridge looking out for the icebergs, and we all agree that today’s icebergs are many, big, and scary. Democracy is inseparable from human rights. We are not talking about two different things. You cannot have the kind of democracy that the Council of Europe was set up to defend and sustain without an effective system for the protection of human rights, and you cannot have such a system without proper human rights education in all its different forms. Equally, you cannot expect an effective system for human rights protection outside democracy. This is also linked to my responsibilities for the new Democratic Pact for Europe, a major initiative the Council of Europe launched this year as a follow-up to the Summit of Heads of State and Government to organize an effective response to democratic backsliding. This event is an important contribution to that effort. When talking about democracy, it is striking how quickly the tone changed. A few years ago, nobody really talked about democracy being in crisis. There was a widespread belief that democracy and human rights formed a natural, inevitable, irreversible path that everyone would eventually follow. Then, suddenly, we moved from denial to acceptance, skipping some of the normal steps in between, and now we almost behave as if we are already grieving for democracy. That is dangerous. One reason for the misconception that democracy is inevitable and invincible is related to the notion that democracy has been with us for a very long time, over two thousand years, since ancient Greece. Right, democracy did exist there, and that system lasted for about 200 years before Antipater of Macedonia put an end to the civilizational erosion unleashed by Athenian democracy upon its citizens and the world. After that came a very long period of darkness, without democracy until the mid to late 19th century, when the first modern forms began to emerge. After the First World War, constitutional republics erupted across Europe when the empires fell apart. A little more than 100 years ago, people were convinced, as many of us were not long ago, that this was the irreversible, natural path for Europe and beyond. But a few years later, those democracies had largely disappeared, and we know what followed. After the Second World War, and again after 1989, democracy re-emerged, accompanied by the belief that it would simply continue, regardless of what we did or failed to do to protect and invest in it. That belief is a serious mistake, and we are now seeing its consequences. If we add up the years of modern democratic existence, they do not even amount to a full century. There are turtles in Madagascar that live longer than that. Clearly, something has to be done. The European Union is acting with its Democracy Shield, and in the Council of Europe we have launched the process for the new Democratic Pact for Europe. This Pact responds to three key needs. First, it counters the feeling that the battle has already been lost. That sense of helplessness—that things have gone too far, that opponents of democracy are too strong, that we have lost our agency—is dangerous. The new Democratic Pact for Europe sends a political message: it is not too late. It brings together all those who still believe in this model of democracy and aims to restore the self-confidence and resolve needed to stand up to the threats and challenges undermining it. We must acknowledge the magnitude of the problem and end denial, but at the same time affirm that we are able to defend democracy because it is too important and the alternatives are too frightening. Second, the Pact addresses the question of what we mean when we say “democracy.” Democracy is a broad, popular term, interpreted in many ways across different contexts. The Council of Europe was set up to defend a specific model: liberal democracy. The term may no longer be fashionable, but it refers to a system based not only on regular, free and fair elections, but also on an effective constitutional and legal framework for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Attacks on this model often begin with attacks on human rights and the protection of certain groups and individuals, attempting to unravel the entire system for everyone. One of the early outcomes of the Pact process is the work on parameters for the Reykjavik Principles for Democracy, recently adopted by the Steering Committee on Democracy. These parameters provide detailed normative guidance on what it means to be a democracy today. Based on the eleven Reykjavik principles, they set out in detail what a government should and should not do to be considered a functioning democracy. Third, the Pact distinguishes between democracy itself and the administration of democracy. When people say they are frustrated with democracy, they are usually not rejecting democratic values as such. They are frustrated with how democracy is administered, with the gap between what politicians say and what they do. If nothing is done, this frustration can eventually lead people to reject democratic values and embrace alternative ideologies and narratives. At the same time, this frustration also shows the path forward: improving how democracy is administered, restoring trust, strengthening governance, and finding new, creative, and innovative ways to sustain democracy and enforce democratic values in a rapidly changing environment. The new Democratic Pact for Europe works across three pillars. The first is learning and participating in democracy. The second is protecting democracy. The third is innovating for democracy. This Forum contributes in a very important way to at least two, if not all three, of these pillars. Let me say a few words about the role of young people. The Council of Europe’s decision to step up its action is, to a large extent, thanks to young people. They were the first to insist that something needed to be done, at a time when much of the political decision-making in Europe and beyond was still in denial. They did this through many initiatives, including the “Democracy Here, Democracy Now” campaign, which significantly contributed to the Summit and its results. This led to the youth perspective adopted by ministers responsible for youth in the Council of Europe member states in October in Malta, where most delegations already included youth representatives in their ministerial teams, putting the youth perspective into practice. In human rights and human rights education, the role of young people will be essential to success. Our priority now is to apply the youth perspective across all areas of public policymaking. This may sound technical or even boring, but it is, in fact, a game-changing, revolutionary concept. The aim is not simply to be nice to young people or to stop them from complaining, but to invest in our collective capacity to find effective solutions to the problems we face. We will not be able to find those solutions without the specific experience, perspective, creativity, energy, disruptiveness, and impatience that young people bring. If we do this—starting here and now, on the crucial subject of education for human rights—we will already be taking a big step forward. It is encouraging that this Forum is not only taking stock but also looking ahead, which is exactly what is needed. In short, if we want democracy to survive and grow old—older than turtles, to begin with—we need young people. Perhaps we should aim for the Greenland sharks, which can live for 500 years. Thank you very much.

You already introduced me with my function, and I think I probably have one of the most pretentious titles in the European institutional architecture: Director for Democracy. It started off as something even worse — they originally wanted to call it "Directorate of Democracy." I objected to that quite strongly. There are already enough people in the world trying to direct democracy, and what we are trying to do at the Council of Europe is really the opposite of that. The title is relatively recent. It came out of the Summit of Heads of State and Government of the Council of Europe, which took place in Reykjavik in 2023, with the objective of identifying, articulating and agreeing on ways in which member states could respond effectively to what has been described as democratic backsliding — not an easy task, because democratic backsliding is not happening in outer space. It is happening within the European space, within the Council of Europe space. So it is a complex and challenging task to identify and agree on measures in those circumstances. Nevertheless, some important decisions have been taken — the Reykjavik Principles for Democracy among them — and one of the outcomes was also a reorganisation of the Council of Europe. Reorganisation always sounds very exciting. I believe it was Petronius, in the Satyricon, who wrote that if you want to create the resemblance of progress, you restructure. Bureaucracies have been doing that successfully for over two thousand years, and we did it too. But this one mattered, because it created the directorate that reflects a broadened paradigm on how we see democracy and how we sustain, support and reinforce it, and make it more resilient. It is not a new paradigm — it is a broadened one. We have long worked on the institutional side of democracy, because any functioning democracy requires institutions: legislation, parliament, judiciary. All of that remains important. What had been neglected, and what is now reflected in the directorate I lead, is the substantive part of democracy — the democratic environment that those institutions need in order to function, because they do not exist in a vacuum. I don't think that reorganisation simply created the resemblance of progress. At the very least, it laid the conditions for real progress, by bringing together the different ways in which member states, at all levels, invest in and nurture that democratic space. The directorate now brings together education, including civic education, youth, culture and heritage, media freedom and civil society. That does not cover every relevant area, but it brings together a good number of the important ones. Thank you very much for inviting me to be a keynote speaker. I always find this rather intimidating, because in my experience I usually end up speaking on a subject that most people in the room know far more about than I do — which is very likely the case today, since I'd wager that nearly everyone here knows more about national libraries than I do. There is an expression, in the part of Europe I come from, for "semi-expertise": a semi-expert is someone who overhears a conversation on public transport in the morning and is able to give a conference on the subject that same evening. It's a phenomenon known the world over — it's just that in that particular region, we've turned it into an art form. That's often how I feel in situations like this one. I hope I won't disappoint you. I will, of course, speak on the suggested subject, but I want to approach it from two angles. The first is the perspective of a citizen. I mentioned that I met the director of the National Library in Ljubljana just before this event. I spent a great deal of time in the National Library of Slovenia when I was a student, many years ago now. I'm sure you are all very proud of your own national libraries, and rightly so — they are iconic buildings. I won't claim to be entirely objective, but I think the National Library of Ljubljana really stands out, with the possible exception of this one, and certainly the one in Sarajevo. The Ljubljana library was completed just before the Second World War by the famous Slovenian architect Jože Plečnik — one of his most celebrated buildings. He designed much of the city centre, and had time left over for work in Prague, including Prague Castle, and buildings in Vienna. It's a truly remarkable place. Its iconic status is also evident in the fact that Slovenia has been trying to build a second national library building since 1987 — and still hasn't seriously started. There are all sorts of official reasons given, but I think the truth is simpler: the original is just too intimidating. It would be like trying to build a second Eiffel Tower in Paris — unimaginable. I spent a great deal of time in that building because a fellow law student and friend of mine, Max, worked there. I went almost every day — sometimes to study, but mostly just to spend time with Max, a person of enormous intellect and spirit, even though he managed to study law even longer than Nelson Mandela did, and with far less excuse. He knew everybody. He knew everything — about culture, about sport, about football especially. He was a walking encyclopedia, a piece of living cultural heritage, made all the more tangible by how tangible a presence he was himself. He seemed the perfect person to be stationed at the gate of that house of knowledge which every national library represents. What struck me then, and has stayed with me since, is that even going there day after day, it was still deeply impressive simply to walk in and be there. Of course architecture plays a part, but what really matters is what emanates from the role, the mission, the importance a national library holds in a nation's culture and life. I think that for a secular state, building a national library may be the closest thing to building a temple. That's genuinely the feeling it gives. From the very beginning, national libraries have been of extreme importance and relevance to citizens, even those who don't visit every day. Now let me turn to the perspective of the Director for Democracy, and offer a brief historical view of the role of culture, knowledge and cultural heritage for the Council of Europe. Let's go back to the period immediately after the Second World War, when the Council of Europe was created, in 1949. Looking back today, it can feel almost inevitable, logical, spontaneous, that a few years after that terrible trauma of global conflict we began that remarkable journey of European integration. When I speak of Europe, I mean both the Council that came first and the European Communities — now the European Union — because they were born of the same historical experience, the same vision of how to answer that bitter and bloody history. But none of it was natural or inevitable. From the perspective of the time, it would have sounded like science fiction to imagine that in a Europe still in ruins, still bearing the wounds of war, traumatised, grieving, suspicious of one another, one could say: let's build something that brings all these nations to work together toward European unity and cooperation. Science fiction. And the founders of the European project were not blind to the difficulty. What's striking is that they knew that simply setting up institutions was bound to fail — that they had to create an environment in which those institutions could actually take root, be understood, be embraced by European citizens. That's why it's so telling that the European Convention on Human Rights was adopted in 1950, a year after the Council of Europe was founded — and the very next convention, before any other, was the European Cultural Convention of 1954. We now have over two hundred conventions, but the fact that culture came second, right after human rights and before anything else, was no accident. It was a deliberate political act to build the environment the European project needed in order to have any chance of success. The European Cultural Convention covers education, culture, cultural heritage, languages, the teaching of history — and from that alone, you can see how fundamental the role of national libraries is in supporting, sustaining and enriching that space. It worked, at the time. Yet we seem to have forgotten this just when the European project, in its broadest sense, faces serious threats from multiple directions. We are slow to recognise how important it would be to reinforce exactly these contributions — the ones that can help repair and restore the fabric of unity and commitment to democratic values on which Europe was built. It remains an uphill struggle to explain to political decision-makers why culture matters for democracy, why cultural heritage matters, why libraries matter. But I think it's something we need to keep doing together — perhaps one of the priorities of our future cooperation. The second reason this matters, from the perspective of the Director for Democracy — and I promise to keep this brief, though I'm not sure I'll manage — is how democratic backsliding, through authoritarian populism, so often manifests as an assault on culture itself. It works by reframing notions of culture, heritage, identity and tradition — the very notions at the heart of the European Cultural Convention — instrumentalising and even weaponising them to undermine the democratic values underpinning the European project. That demands a response. We need to reclaim the space to define what culture means in a democratic society, what tradition means, what identity means. Here again, national libraries have an extremely important role to play. History itself is being weaponised. The distortion of history is a weapon in today's world, tied to a broader rejection of science, facts and reason that gained real momentum during the pandemic. We need to respond to this collectively, and we won't be able to do so without libraries — national libraries above all — playing an important part in that effort. National libraries are a country's preeminent repository of information. Your institutions have collected countless rare and significant works from the past, forming an important part of what we now consider cultural heritage. But your duty to collect and preserve the nation's literature, within and beyond its borders, may constitute an equally important part of the cultural heritage of the future. Your role as custodians of cultural memory, now and going forward, should not be underestimated. As you know, the core mandate of the Council of Europe is to promote, defend and protect human rights and democracy through international conventions and other legal instruments, and to enable Europe's citizens to participate effectively in today's complex and diverse democratic societies — encouraging active, responsible citizenship by giving people a genuine sense of ownership over decision-making and institutions. In that context, libraries not only continue to play a crucial democratic role in the twenty-first century, but have both the opportunity and, I would say, the responsibility to take on new roles — creating spaces for democratic participation and adapting to the technological, societal, economic and political challenges we all face. If anyone thinks the role of libraries is diminishing in this highly technological world, I would argue the opposite is true. It needs reflection and adaptation, but the mission of libraries — national libraries in particular — should only grow, and should be recognised as such. Libraries must continue to be, and to expand as, places of equal access to information and knowledge; places that integrate different communities; places of socialisation and social cohesion, learning and education; places that enable democratic participation and support democratic values. Let's not forget that totalitarian and autocratic regimes routinely restrict access to information, including through restricted access to libraries. Many of you will be aware of the legislative changes in a former Council of Europe member state, Russia, where arbitrary decisions have banned and narrowed access to information in libraries, shrinking the budgets of public and scientific libraries by some 15 percent — and, in some municipal libraries, by as much as 70 percent. And it isn't only censorship and restricted access. National libraries and cultural heritage more broadly are, in conflict, very often the first targets of aggression. One example is one that image just behind me: the National Library of Sarajevo was not destroyed by accident during the war — it was targeted, deliberately, to erase the cultural presence of the people, of every nationality and ethnic group, living in that city. We are seeing the same today in Russia's aggression against Ukraine, where important cultural sites are not damaged incidentally but targeted as part of a deliberate campaign, with the same objective as the destruction of the Sarajevo library. Only last night, important European cultural heritage in Kyiv was targeted again, with fires reported at a cathedral and monastery there. These are not theoretical threats. They are very real, and they underline how important it is to reinforce our support, our resources and our attention to everything that sustains culture and heritage, at every level and in every setting. Our work on libraries — including with your association, EBLIDA, notably on the Recommendation on library legislation and policy in Europe — goes back more than a quarter of a century, to the first guidelines on the responsibilities of the state, local authorities and professionals, prepared and adopted by the Council of Europe's Intergovernmental Committee on Culture. These have recently been updated, in cooperation with EBLIDA, into a new non-binding legal instrument adopted by the Committee of Ministers. It is soft law — non-binding — but I believe it provides a very important basis for member states as they shape their national policies in this area. I had the honour, two years ago, of presenting this recommendation in this very building. It has five main sections, all relevant to national libraries given the role and leadership you represent in this ecosystem in your respective countries: freedom of expression, free access to information and democratic participation; the place of libraries within the European agenda on sustainable development; global and local threats to library operations; digital transformation and the expansion of AI-based library networks; and, finally, copyright and the protection of library heritage. We hope this recommendation will serve as useful guidance for the steps and policies that today's situation requires. Two aspects strike me as particularly important from the perspective of the Director for Democracy — and then I really will conclude. First, that libraries should ensure access to information and act as inclusive institutions. Second, that libraries should act as spaces that promote democratic participation. Access to information is indispensable for a functioning democracy. We rightly speak often about freedom of expression, grounded in Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. But Article 10 protects not only the freedom to express and impart information, but equally — and importantly — the freedom to receive information, to have access to it. If you are skilled at restricting or manipulating access to information, you can leave people entirely free to express themselves however they like, and still achieve your objectives — less visibly, perhaps, but no less effectively or damagingly for democracy. This is why access to information, and the role of national libraries in securing it, cannot be underestimated. Second, libraries as spaces for democratic participation. One factor — certainly not the origin of all our problems, but one that is clearly not helping — is the loss of spaces and opportunities for people to actually meet, speak and engage with one another. Without that, it's hard to imagine a functioning democracy. We can do a great deal on our phones, but we cannot run a democracy by replacing all human interaction and engagement with digital means. Libraries are among the precious, and increasingly rare, spaces that can offer that opportunity — and can help counter these trends and support democracy. All of this feeds into a major Council of Europe initiative — we are good at launching major initiatives, and I'm confident this one will deliver results — called the New Democratic Pact for Europe. In essence, it says: we are in a difficult situation, and we need to critically assess what we have been doing, identify what we should have been doing but weren't, and decide what we should do going forward — by engaging the broadest possible range of interlocutors, going beyond the usual circle where everyone already knows what everyone else will say. That critical dialogue is ongoing, which is one reason I'm glad to attend meetings like this one, and I will stop shortly so that I can hear your questions, reactions and criticisms, all of which I will bring back to Strasbourg and feed into the Pact. We are organising the Pact around six workstreams, and I think national libraries have something to contribute to every one of them: countering disinformation; social issues; non-discrimination and equal access to democratic participation; functioning democratic institutions; and new technologies — not only how to defend ourselves against the risks of artificial intelligence, but also how to use new technologies and AI to protect and strengthen democracy. The process will conclude in about a year. What is already becoming clear is that we have managed to carry that broader understanding of what democracy requires into this work, and that everything about it is deeply transversal. In short: protecting democracy, saving democracy, halting democratic backsliding, means that a great many people need to do a great many things better than they have so far — and do them together. That, in essence, is the philosophy of the New Democratic Pact for Europe. Let me close by returning to my friend Max, from the National Library of Ljubljana. When he passed away, far too young and far too early, more than a hundred people contributed to a book in his memory — artists, politicians, people from civil society, friends, and librarians who each wrote him a message. That book now sits in the National Library of Ljubljana. I think he'd deserve a memorial plaque too — I see the Director of the Slovenian National Library is in the room, so we can talk about that later. The book is titled "Max, the Midfielder of the City." For those unfamiliar with football, the midfielder is a vital position: the player who connects everyone else, organises the game, links defence and attack, and keeps the whole thing moving forward. It's an unusual analogy, I know, but I think national libraries play a similar role in a democratic society. So that's what I'll leave you with: be a bit like Max. Be a midfielder. Connect. Make things move forward. Thank you.

I'd like to start by congratulating and thanking the young artist for beautiful music. One of the things we believe in, in our work on democracy, is that there's no democracy without culture. It's good to be here among people who have the same attitude and understanding of the role culture and art have to play in a democratic society.
